D is incorrect because ultrasound cannot reliably measure the compartment pressures required to diagnose compartment syndrome. E is incorrect because although urinalysis might be relevant for evaluating potential systemic complications, it does not address the urgent need to diagnose compartment syndrome.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department complaining of ocular discomfort and decreased vision after sustaining facial injury from a bottle strike 2 hours earlier. On examination under low light conditions, both pupils constrict when light is shined on either the right or left eye separately. When the light is shifted from the right eye to the left eye, both pupils seem to dilate. What is the most likely pathological condition in this patient?
A) Central retinal artery occlusion
B) Oculomotor (III) nerve injury
C) Preexisting cataract
D) Symmetrical acute glaucoma
E) Vitreous hemorrhage
questions.answer:
A)

This patient exhibits a Marcus Gunn pupil, representing a relative afferent pupillary defect caused by optic nerve damage (between retina and optic chiasm) or substantial retinal disease. This abnormality is identified through the swinging-flashlight examination, where pupils seem to dilate (actually constrict less effectively) when light shifts from the unaffected eye to the damaged eye. The injured eye retains some light perception and can still produce pupillary constriction, but this response is reduced. A) Central retinal artery occlusion is correct as it produces severe retinal ischemia resulting in a relative afferent pupillary defect. B) Oculomotor nerve injury is wrong because it impacts efferent pupillary control rather than afferent pathways and would not create a Marcus Gunn pupil. C) Preexisting cataract is wrong since cataracts don't cause afferent pupillary defects as they merely obstruct light transmission without harming neural circuits. D) Symmetrical acute glaucoma is wrong because bilateral symmetric pathology wouldn't generate a relative difference between the eyes. E) Vitreous hemorrhage is wrong as it simply blocks light passage without damaging the neural pathways controlling pupillary responses.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple wide and thin scars from previous surgical excision of cutaneous lesions. His mother reports a history of late walking, joint hypermobility, and easy bruising. Given these clinical manifestations, what is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Vascular fragility disorder
B) Loose skin syndrome
C) Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
D) Marfan syndrome
E) Brittle bone disease
questions.answer:
C)

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is the correct answer as it uniquely encompasses all the presented clinical manifestations. EDS comprises a collection of hereditary connective tissue abnormalities featuring joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue weakness. The classic form of EDS stems from autosomal dominant defects in COL5A1 or COL5A2 genes that impair type V collagen production, resulting in hyperextensible skin, distinctive broad atrophic "tissue paper" scars, widespread joint hypermobility, and tendency to bruise easily. A) Vascular fragility disorder is wrong because it usually lacks delayed motor development or the specific scarring pattern described. B) Loose skin syndrome is wrong as it doesn't involve easy bruising or the particular scar characteristics mentioned. D) Marfan syndrome is wrong since it doesn't produce atrophic scarring or the described skin features. E) Brittle bone disease is wrong because it mainly impacts bone development and typically doesn't cause the characteristic atrophic scarring observed in this case.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old male presents to the clinic after sustaining a "jamming" type injury to his right middle finger (dominant hand) while playing football. On examination, when the patient attempts active extension, there is a 40-degree extension lag at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with concurrent hyperextension observed at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. What is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Central slip rupture
B) Flexor digitorum profundus tendon avulsion
C) Volar plate injury of the PIP joint
D) Sagittal band tear
E) Swan neck deformity
questions.answer:
A)
Central slip rupture is the correct diagnosis based on the clinical presentation showing a positive Elson test pattern. In this condition, when the PIP joint is held in maximum flexion, the intact central slip normally shifts distally, creating laxity in the terminal extensor tendon. However, with central slip injury, this laxity is compensated by the lateral bands, which redirect extensor forces to the DIP joint, allowing active DIP extension even when the PIP is maximally flexed. B) is incorrect because flexor digitorum profundus tendon avulsion would result in loss of DIP flexion rather than the described PIP extension deficit with DIP hyperextension. C) is incorrect because volar plate injury typically presents with PIP hyperextension contracture and associated pain/instability, not the specific combination of PIP extension lag and DIP hyperextension seen here. D) is incorrect because sagittal band tear primarily affects metacarpophalangeal joint function and extensor tendon centralization, not the PIP-DIP joint interaction pattern described. E) is incorrect because swan neck deformity stems from terminal extensor tendon rupture, which would cause complete loss of DIP extension capability irrespective of PIP joint positioning.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman seeks body contouring evaluation after losing 150 pounds (68 kg) through laparoscopic gastric banding surgery. Her past medical history includes deep vein thrombosis 7 years prior during progestin-based contraceptive use. Family history shows two first-degree relatives with pulmonary emboli. Lab work confirms factor V Leiden thrombophilia. What is the most likely pathophysiologic mechanism of this condition?
A) Elevated coagulation factor V concentrations
B) Enhanced resistance to activated protein C
C) Ongoing antibodies against coagulation factor V
D) Deficient protein C levels
E) Deficient protein S levels
questions.answer:
B)

Enhanced resistance to activated protein C is correct because factor V Leiden constitutes the most prevalent inherited thrombophilia and genetic predisposition to venous thromboembolism. Under normal circumstances, activated protein C collaborates with protein S to suppress coagulation by cleaving and inactivating factors V and VIIIa at designated sites. The factor V Leiden mutation alters the primary cleavage site, rendering factor Va roughly 10-fold more resistant to deactivation by activated protein C. A) is incorrect because factor V Leiden involves structural modification of factor V and resistance to breakdown rather than elevated production quantities. C) is incorrect because factor V Leiden represents a hereditary mutation rather than an autoimmune process involving antibody development. D) is incorrect because protein C deficiency constitutes a distinct coagulation abnormality characterized by diminished protein C concentrations, not the factor V Leiden variant. E) is incorrect because protein S deficiency represents an alternative hereditary coagulation disorder involving decreased protein S concentrations, not factor V resistance to activated protein C.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old man is assessed after sustaining a cut that runs from the tragus to the antitragus of his ear. A ring block around the ear using 1% lidocaine is performed prior to surgical closure. While suturing the conchal skin near the external auditory canal, the patient feels pain. Which nerve is most likely insufficiently blocked?
A) Auricular branch of the vagus (X) nerve
B) Branch of the glossopharyngeal (IX) nerve
C) Great auricular (C2, C3) nerve
D) Lesser occipital (C2, C3) nerve
E) Trigeminal (V2) nerve
questions.answer:
A)

The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve) is correct as it provides sensory innervation to the external auditory canal and conchal bowl, regions that cannot be effectively numbed with a conventional circumferential ear block and require direct local infiltration for complete anesthesia. B) Branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve is incorrect as it mainly supplies the middle ear cavity and tympanic membrane, not the external conchal skin causing the patient's discomfort. C) Great auricular nerve is incorrect since it supplies sensation to the ear lobule and most of the outer ear surface, which would be successfully anesthetized by the ring block procedure. D) Lesser occipital nerve is incorrect because it innervates the upper portion of the external ear and would be properly blocked by the circumferential technique. E) Trigeminal (V2) nerve is incorrect as the maxillary branch of the trigeminal nerve does not supply sensory innervation to ear structures.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the office for consultation regarding her nasal tip contour. She is interested in rhinoplasty to improve her facial harmony. Physical examination shows asymmetric nasal tip projection with a pinched nasal configuration. Which cartilage graft would be most suitable to correct this structural defect?
A) Columellar strut graft
B) Lateral crural strengthening graft
C) Septal extension graft
D) Spreader graft
E) Subdomal graft
questions.answer:
E)
The subdomal graft is the best option for treating a pinched nasal tip deformity and uneven dome projection. This rod-shaped graft is placed below both domes, allowing precise control of horizontal and vertical dome positioning while correcting the reduced interdomal width typical of constricted tip abnormalities. A) Columellar strut grafts are incorrect as they mainly treat inadequate projection rather than tip narrowing. B) Lateral crural strengthening grafts are wrong because they address alar rim irregularities from lateral crus weakness, not pinched tip configurations. C) Septal extension grafts are unsuitable since they manage overall tip projection, contour, and rotation rather than specifically treating dome constriction. D) Spreader grafts are incorrect as they expand the internal nasal valve and mid-nasal vault but do not address tip narrowing.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman in good health seeks consultation for bilateral breast lift surgery. Her last mammography performed 2 years ago revealed normal findings. Physical examination reveals a palpable lesion in the upper outer region of the right breast that the patient was unaware of. What is the most appropriate first step in management?
A) Core biopsy procedure
B) Diagnostic mammography combined with ultrasonography
C) Fine needle aspiration
D) Breast lift surgery with surgical biopsy
E) Routine screening mammography
questions.answer:
B)
Diagnostic mammography combined with ultrasonography represents the optimal initial evaluation for a newly identified palpable breast lesion in women older than 30 years. This imaging combination offers thorough assessment to define the characteristics of the lesion and examine both breasts for additional abnormalities, while ultrasound aids in differentiating between solid and fluid-filled masses and can facilitate future tissue sampling if needed. A) Core biopsy procedure is inappropriate without first obtaining imaging to characterize the lesion. C) Fine needle aspiration is incorrect because tissue acquisition should occur after proper imaging assessment. D) Breast lift surgery with surgical biopsy is unsuitable since performing surgery that alters breast anatomy could interfere with cancer treatment if malignancy is discovered. E) Routine screening mammography is wrong because this patient has a specific abnormal physical finding that necessitates diagnostic rather than screening evaluation.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old woman with a strong family history of breast cancer receives genetic testing results showing she carries a pathogenic BRCA1 mutation. How does her lifetime risk of developing breast cancer compare to women who do not have this genetic variant?
A) Twice as high
B) Six times as high
C) Ten times as high
D) Fifteen times as high
E) Twenty times as high
questions.answer:
B)

Women carrying BRCA1 mutations face approximately six times higher lifetime breast cancer risk than the general population. The general population has roughly 13.2% lifetime risk, while BRCA1 mutation carriers have 36-85% lifetime risk, representing a 3-7 fold elevation, with six times falling within this established range. A) Twice as high significantly underestimates the risk increase documented for BRCA1 mutations. C) Ten times as high overestimates beyond what research has established. D) Fifteen times as high substantially exceeds the proven risk elevation for BRCA1 carriers. E) Twenty times as high dramatically overestimates the actual risk increase linked to this genetic alteration.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old African American woman comes to the clinic with a large recurrent keloid on her left earlobe. The treatment plan involves surgical re-excision with subsequent postoperative radiotherapy. What is the most likely long-term complication of this therapeutic approach?
A) Pigmentary changes
B) Skin peeling
C) Pruritus
D) Malignancy
E) Dilated blood vessels
questions.answer:
A)

Pigmentary changes (either lightening or darkening of the skin) represent the most common long-term complication after radiation treatment for keloids, affecting roughly 62% of patients. This side effect is especially significant in African American patients where changes in skin color are more apparent and problematic. B) Skin peeling is incorrect because it is an acute radiation reaction rather than a long-term effect, seen in about 24% of cases during the treatment period. C) Pruritus is wrong since itching associated with keloids usually decreases rather than increases following effective therapy. D) Malignancy is incorrect as radiation-induced cancers after keloid treatment represent exceptionally rare complications. E) Dilated blood vessels is less probable as the primary long-term issue, developing in only 27% of patients versus the higher rate of pigmentation alterations.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old healthy woman underwent liposuction of her abdomen, flanks, and thighs 72 hours ago and now presents with breathing difficulties, altered mental status, and pinpoint hemorrhagic skin lesions. Her vital signs reveal temperature 38.2°C (100.8°F), blood pressure 110/80 mmHg, pulse 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 89%. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
A) Allergic drug reaction
B) Fat embolism syndrome
C) Local anesthetic toxicity
D) Systemic infection
E) Low platelet count
questions.answer:
B)

Fat embolism syndrome is the most probable diagnosis, characterized by the typical triad of breathing problems, altered consciousness, and petechial skin lesions developing 1-3 days following liposuction procedures. This uncommon but potentially life-threatening complication demands prompt identification and treatment. A) Allergic drug reaction is incorrect because although it may produce petechiae, it rarely causes the combined presentation of severe respiratory and neurological manifestations. C) Local anesthetic toxicity is wrong since it can lead to neurological and respiratory effects but seldom presents with petechial rash. D) Systemic infection is improbable considering the patient's hemodynamically stable condition and only modest temperature elevation, making fat embolism more likely. E) Low platelet count is incorrect because although it can result in petechiae, it doesn't commonly present alongside respiratory compromise and cognitive impairment.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with a benign 4-cm tumor located in the superficial lobe of the parotid gland. The surgeon performs excision of the lesion through a 12-cm preauricular approach. Which Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code best represents this surgical procedure?

Code Description
21013     Excision of subfascial soft-tissue tumor of the face under 5 cm
42420 Excision of parotid tumor or total parotidectomy with facial nerve identification and preservation
64716 Neuroplasty and/or transposition of cranial nerve
14041 Adjacent tissue transfer or rearrangement for facial defect 10.1 to 30.0 sq cm
12054 Intermediate repair of facial wound 7.6 to 12.5 cm

A) 21013 only
B) 21013 and 64716
C) 21013, 64716, and 12054
D) 42420 only
E) 42420 and 64716
questions.answer:
D)

Code 42420 is the appropriate selection because it represents a complete parotid tumor excision with facial nerve identification and preservation, including wound closure as an integrated procedure. A is incorrect because 21013 does not apply when a specific parotid gland procedure code is available. B is wrong because 64716 represents separate neuroplasty work that is already incorporated into parotid surgery protocols. C is incorrect because both 64716 and 12054 represent bundled components that cannot be separately reported with parotid procedures. E is wrong because 64716 is an integral component of parotid surgery and routine closure is included in the primary procedure code.

questions.question:
What constitutes the most essential therapeutic strategy for patients with xeroderma pigmentosum?
A) Cryosurgical treatment
B) Topical fluorouracil therapy
C) Oral isotretinoin administration
D) Strict avoidance of ultraviolet radiation
E) Surgical skin reconstruction
questions.answer:
D)

Strict avoidance of ultraviolet radiation is the most vital management approach because xeroderma pigmentosum is characterized by impaired DNA repair pathways that cannot properly correct UV-induced genetic damage, resulting in extreme photosensitivity and premature malignant transformation. A is incorrect because cryosurgical treatment only addresses existing lesions without preventing ongoing UV damage or treating the underlying defect. B is incorrect because topical fluorouracil therapy targets current actinic keratoses but fails to prevent the fundamental photodamage that drives disease progression. C is incorrect because oral isotretinoin may help reduce precancerous lesion development but carries substantial adverse effects and does not tackle the primary issue of extreme UV vulnerability. E is incorrect because surgical skin reconstruction addresses established tissue damage but serves as a corrective rather than preventive therapeutic measure.

questions.question:
Which complication occurs most commonly following circumareolar mastopexy?
A) Square-shaped breast contour
B) Greater nipple to inframammary crease distance
C) Decreased nipple sensitivity
D) Nipple tissue death
E) Areolar expansion
questions.answer:
E)

Areolar expansion represents the most frequent complication because the circumareolar approach creates tension along the areolar perimeter, leading to gradual stretching despite reinforcement suturing methods. A is incorrect because square-shaped breast contour typically results from Wise pattern mastopexy procedures, not circumareolar methods. B is incorrect because greater nipple to inframammary crease distance develops with vertical mastopexies when tissue pillars are excessive, not with circumareolar approaches. C is incorrect because decreased nipple sensitivity rarely occurs in circumareolar mastopexy since breast tissue removal is not performed. D is incorrect because nipple tissue death more frequently accompanies combined breast augmentation-mastopexy operations rather than standalone circumareolar mastopexy.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old healthy man arrives 2 hours after sustaining a complete traumatic amputation of his left thumb from a machete wound. Clinical examination shows a fully detached segment with both phalanges intact, while the remaining hand displays an exposed metacarpal bone. No other injuries are identified. Which treatment option is most appropriate?
A) Groin flap coverage
B) Reverse radial forearm flap coverage
C) Volar advancement flap coverage
D) Microvascular replantation
E) Revision amputation
questions.answer:
D)
Microvascular replantation represents the best treatment option since thumb amputations at any level are ideal candidates for replantation given the thumb's essential function in hand mechanics, and this patient has no medical contraindications to the surgery. A is wrong because groin flap coverage necessitates extended immobilization with the hand attached to the groin, leads to finger stiffness, requires multiple surgical stages, and fails to maintain thumb length. B is incorrect because reverse radial forearm flap compromises a major hand vessel, does not preserve thumb length, and should be reserved for cases where replantation has failed. C is wrong because volar advancement flaps are only appropriate for defects beyond the interphalangeal joint and cannot adequately cover defects at the metacarpophalangeal level. E is incorrect because revision amputation would cause significant functional disability and should only be considered if replantation is unsuccessful.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old Hispanic woman comes for evaluation of a biopsy-proven basal cell carcinoma on her right cheek. She says that the lesion has been present for 8 months and has grown rapidly during the past 3 months. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?


A ) Cryotherapy
B ) Electrodesiccation and curettage
C ) Mohs micrographic surgery
D ) Radiation therapy
E ) Wide local excision
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The patient described has a basal cell carcinoma (BCC), which is the most common type of cancer worldwide affecting approximately 1 million people per year. These types of cancers were once more common in people over 40 years of age, but they now are often diagnosed in younger people (85% of lifetime sun exposure occurs before age 18).


BCC starts in the epidermis and grows slowly and painlessly. It most often appears on areas of skin that are regularly exposed to sunlight or other ultraviolet radiation, such as the face, scalp, ears, chest, back, and legs.


These tumors can have several different forms. The most common appearance of BCC is that of a small dome-shaped bump that has a pearly white color. Telangiectasias may be seen on the surface. BCC can also appear as a pimple-like growth that heals, only to come back again and again. A common sign of BCC is a sore that bleeds and heals up, only to recur again; oozing or crusting spots within the sore are also common.


While there are many ways to treat BCC, Mohs micrographic surgery is the most appropriate option in the scenario described, as the lesion demonstrated has indistinct borders, is located in both a high-risk and cosmetically sensitive area, and is growing rapidly. Wide local excision would be indicated for BCC with discrete, distinct borders. Radiation therapy is not a primary option for BCC. Cryotherapy and electrodesiccation and curettage have lower cure rates and higher recurrence rates compared with Mohs micrographic surgery.


Generally accepted indications for Mohs micrographic surgery include the following:


1. Recurrent or incompletely excised BCC or squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
2. Primary BCC or SCC with indistinct borders
3. Lesions located in high-risk areas (ie, eyelids, nose, ear, nasolabial folds, upper lip, vermillion border, columella, periorbital, temples, preauricular and postauricular areas, scalp)
4. Cosmetically and functionally important areas, including genital, anal, perianal, hand, foot, and nail units
5. Tumors with aggressive clinical behavior (ie, rapidly growing, greater than 2 cm in diameter)
6. Tumors with an aggressive histologic subtype (ie, morpheaform BCC) and/or those with perivascular invasion
7. SCCs ranging from undifferentiated to poorly differentiated, and SCCs that are adenoid (acantholytic), adenosquamous, desmoplastic, infiltrative, perineural, periadnexal, or perivascular
8. Tumors arising in sites of previous radiation therapy
9. Tumors arising in immunosuppressed patients
10. Basal cell nevus syndrome patients
Mohs micrographic surgery has the highest 5-year cure rates for primary and recurrent BCC.


Five-year recurrence rates for primary BCC:


1. Mohs micrographic surgery ‚Ç¨‚Äu1%
2. Surgical excision ‚Ç¨‚Äu10.1%
3. Curettage and desiccation ‚Ç¨‚Äu7.7%
4. Radiation therapy ‚Ç¨‚Äu8.7%
5. Cryotherapy ‚Ç¨‚Äu7.5%
Five-year recurrence rates for recurrent BCC:


1. Mohs micrographic surgery ‚Ç¨‚Äu5.6%
2. Surgical excision ‚Ç¨‚Äu17.4%
3. Curettage and desiccation ‚Ç¨‚Äu40%
4. Radiation therapy ‚Ç¨‚Äu9.8%
5. Cryotherapy ‚Ç¨‚Äu13% (< a 5-year period)
References
1. Habif TP. Clinical Dermatology: A Color Guide to Diagnosis and Therapy. 4th ed. St. Louis: Mosby; 2003:724-735.
2. Bennett RG. Current concepts in Mohs micrographic surgery. Dermatol Clin. 1991 Oct;9(4):777-788.
3. Ponten F, Lundeberg J. Principles of tumor biology and pathogenesis of BCCs and SCCs. In: Bolognia JL, Jorizzo JL, Rapini RP, eds. Dermatology. Vol 2. London: Mosby; 2003:1663-1676.
4. Preston DS, Stern RS. Nonmelanoma cancers of the skin. N Engl J Med. 1992 Dec 3;327(23):1649-1662.
5. Ratner D, Skouge JW. Surgical management of local disease: basal cell carcinoma. In: Miller SJ, Maloney ME, eds. Cutaneous Oncology: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management. Oxford, England: Wiley-Blackwell; 1998:664-671.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of hemifacial microsomia. Physical examination reveals underdeveloped maxilla, asymmetric orbits, and complete absence of the mandibular condyle. Which accompanying clinical finding would be most indicative of Goldenhar syndrome?
A) Epibulbar dermoids
B) Cranial nerve VII dysfunction
C) Port-wine birthmark on the midface
D) Multiple lower lip pits
E) Colobomas of the upper eyelid
questions.answer:
A)

Epibulbar dermoids represent the characteristic feature that distinguishes Goldenhar syndrome from simple hemifacial microsomia, making this the most specific additional sign. B is wrong because cranial nerve VII palsy can occur in both Goldenhar syndrome and isolated hemifacial microsomia, lacking diagnostic specificity. C is incorrect as port-wine stains in the trigeminal nerve distribution are associated with Sturge-Weber syndrome, not Goldenhar syndrome. D is wrong because multiple pits on the lower lip are a hallmark of Van der Woude syndrome, which typically presents with orofacial clefting. E is incorrect since upper eyelid colobomas can be present in various forms of hemifacial microsomia and are not pathognomonic for Goldenhar syndrome.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man comes to the office for evaluation of a 2-cm growth over the lower half of his nose that has been growing slowly during the past 15 years. A photograph is shown. Medical history includes acne rosacea. Physical examination shows a broad, exophytic mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?


A) Application of 5-fluorouracil
B) Direct excision and coverage with a forehead flap
C) Direct excision and coverage with a skin graft
D) Direct excision and healing by secondary intention
E) Observation only
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.





Rhinophyma occurs on the far end of progressive acne rosacea involving the sebaceous glandular overgrowth of the skin. It most commonly occurs on the nose but phymas can occur elsewhere on the face.


In early stages, rhinophyma can be treated with isoretinoin and antibiotics; however, in advanced states it needs to be resected. Ablation modalities include dermabrasion, carbon dioxide laser excision, scalpel excision, or a combination of techniques. Since the procedure resects the skin to mid-dermis, skin grafting or other coverage is unnecessary and can lead to unsatisfactory aesthetic results. The best option is excision with secondary epithelialization.


References
Ferneini EM, Banki M, Paletta F, Ferneini CM. Surgical Management of Rhinophyma: A case report and review of literature. Conn Med. 2014 Mar;78(3):159-60.
Madan V, Ferguson JE, August PJ. Carbon dioxide laser treatment of rhinophyma: A review of 124 patients. Br J Derm. 2009 161: 814-818.
Bogetti P, Boltri M, Spagnoli G, Dolcet M. Surgical treatment of rhinophyma: a comparison of technques. Aesthetic Plast Surg. 2002 Jan-Feb;26(1):57-60.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child has Blauth/Manske Grade IIIa thumb hypoplasia characterized by first web space constriction, underdeveloped thenar musculature, metacarpophalangeal joint instability, and stable carpometacarpal joint. Clinical assessment reveals impaired grip function when handling toys and eating utensils, with no improvement after 6 months of occupational therapy. What surgical intervention would best enhance this patient's grip capability?
A) Abductor digiti minimi transfer
B) Free great toe transfer
C) Fusion of the thumb interphalangeal joint
D) Pollicization of the index finger
E) Thumb CMC ligament reconstruction with tendon interposition arthroplasty
questions.answer:
A)
The abductor digiti minimi (ADM or Huber) transfer is the most appropriate surgical treatment for Blauth/Manske Grade IIIa thumb hypoplasia. This classification indicates the presence of a stable CMC joint with metacarpal hypoplasia, making reconstruction feasible and preferable to ablation. The ADM transfer effectively addresses the thenar muscle deficiency and provides improved thumb opposition and pronation, which are essential for functional grasp. B) is incorrect because free great toe transfer is not indicated when the CMC joint is stable and reconstruction is possible; additionally, great toe harvest would cause significant donor site morbidity affecting gait and balance. C) is incorrect because interphalangeal joint fusion alone does not address the primary issues of thenar muscle weakness and MCP joint instability that are causing the functional deficits. D) is incorrect because pollicization is reserved for more severe grades (IIIb-V) where the CMC joint is unstable or absent, not for Grade IIIa where reconstruction is preferred. E) is incorrect because CMC ligament reconstruction is not needed when the CMC joint is already stable, and this approach fails to address the thenar muscle deficiency that is the primary cause of functional impairment.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents for routine follow-up 9 years following bilateral breast augmentation performed by a different surgeon to address breast hypoplasia. The procedure involved placement of 450-mL smooth, round silicone gel implants in the subglandular plane. She recently discovered she carries the BRCA2 mutation and had breast MRI performed for high-risk screening. The MRI demonstrated a "linguine sign" in the right breast. Which of the following physical examination findings would be most expected with the condition indicated by the "linguine sign"?
A) Greater rippling visible in the right breast compared to the left
B) No notable difference between the right and left breasts
C) The right breast appears considerably larger than the left
D) The right breast appears considerably smaller than the left
questions.answer:
B)
The right breast would not show notable differences from the left breast. The linguine sign represents multiple low-signal curved lines seen on MRI that correspond to the folded implant shell, indicating intracapsular silicone implant rupture. Physical examination lacks sufficient sensitivity and specificity to reliably detect all intracapsular ruptures, making ultrasound and/or MRI necessary for diagnosis. A) is incorrect because increased rippling is not typically associated with intracapsular rupture. C) is incorrect because significant breast enlargement would suggest late seroma formation and warrant evaluation for breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma. D) is incorrect because marked breast size reduction would indicate saline implant rupture or deflation.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female patient is preparing for transcutaneous lower eyelid surgery. Fat repositioning and lateral canthal support procedures are intended. During dissection, the inferior oblique muscle is at highest risk for damage when working between which anatomical structures?
A) Central and lateral fat pads
B) Lateral fat pad and orbicularis retaining ligament
C) Medial canthal tendon and medial fat pad
D) Medial and central fat pads
E) Orbicularis retaining ligament and arcus marginalis
questions.answer:
D)
The inferior oblique muscle runs between the medial and central fat compartments, making it susceptible to injury during manipulation or removal of these fat pads. Potential injuries include transection, thermal damage, scarring, bleeding, swelling, and suture trauma during septal repair. Research indicates that sectioning less than half the muscle may not result in lasting double vision. A is incorrect because the muscle does not lie between the central and lateral compartments. B is incorrect as the orbicularis retaining ligament is superficial to the muscle location. C is incorrect because the medial canthal tendon is not adjacent to where the muscle runs. E is incorrect since both the orbicularis retaining ligament and arcus marginalis are located superficial to the inferior oblique muscle.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient presents 2 days following non-surgical cosmetic facial treatment. The treatment involved neuromodulator injections to the forehead and glabellar region, plus hyaluronic acid filler placement in the tear trough area, nasal region, cheeks, and lips. She complains of increasing pain, and examination reveals discoloration at the nasal tip. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this complication?
A) Antibiotic treatment
B) Aspirin administration
C) Hyaluronidase injection
D) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment
E) Warm compress therapy
questions.answer:
C)
This patient demonstrates signs of vascular compromise and tissue ischemia following hyaluronic acid filler injection, evidenced by pain and nasal tip discoloration. The immediate and most critical intervention is hyaluronidase injection, an enzyme that breaks down hyaluronic acid through hydrolysis. This should be administered promptly and generously, with dosing adjusted based on clinical response to reverse ischemic signs including pallor, livedo reticularis, erythema, and pain. Daily repetition may be necessary. The enzyme will diffuse effectively into tissues without requiring vascular cannulation. A) Antibiotic treatment is incorrect because the symptoms result from vascular occlusion rather than infection, though antibiotics might be considered as adjunctive therapy. B) Aspirin administration is incorrect as it serves only as supportive care and does not address the primary problem of hyaluronic acid-induced vascular compromise. D) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment is incorrect because while it may provide supportive benefit, it lacks strong clinical evidence and does not directly reverse the underlying cause. E) Warm compress therapy is incorrect as it represents only supportive care and fails to address the fundamental issue of hyaluronic acid causing vascular obstruction.

questions.question:
A 57-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a rectourethral fistula that occurred following radiation therapy for prostate carcinoma. A pedicled muscle-only gracilis flap reconstruction is planned. The medial femoral circumflex artery pedicle approaches the gracilis muscle from which of the following orientations?
A) Anterior
B) Inferior
C) Lateral
D) Medial
questions.answer:
C)
The medial femoral circumflex artery pedicle approaches the gracilis muscle from the lateral direction. The gracilis muscle serves as an excellent option for perineal reconstruction procedures. This muscle is the most superficial member of the adductor muscle group and can be readily identified in the middle portion of the thigh, extending from the pubic tubercle to the medial femoral condyle. The primary vascular supply originates from the profunda femoris, either as a direct branch or as a terminal branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery. The dominant pedicle penetrates the muscle from its deep surface (lateral aspect), which allows for safe dissection of the superficial muscle layers. A is incorrect because the pedicle does not enter from an anterior approach. B is incorrect because the entry point is not from an inferior direction. D is incorrect because although the muscle is located medially, the pedicle enters from the lateral side of the muscle.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old woman developed numbness in the distribution identified in the picture shown. Which of the following nerves was most likely injured?


A) Lateral antebrachial
B) Medial antebrachial
C) Medial brachial
D) Posterior antebrachial
E) Posterior brachial
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The posterior brachial nerve innervates the dorsal aspect of the upper arm. The lateral antebrachial nerve innervates the radial side of the forearm. The medial antebrachial nerve innervates the ulnar side of the forearm and medial upper arm.

The medial brachial nerve innervates the medial aspect of the upper arm between the medial antebrachial cutaneous (MABC) and intercostobrachial nerves.

The posterior antebrachial nerve innervates the lateral posterior aspect of the forearm.


ReferencesGuarantors of Brain. Aids to the Examination of the Nervous System. 4th ed. London, United Kingdom: WB Saunders; 2000.Netter FH. Atlas of Human Anatomy. 7th ed. Philadelphia, PA: Elsevier; 2019.Li H, et al. Anatomical analysis of antebrachial cutaneous nerve distribution pattern and its clinical implications for sensory reconstruction [published correction appears in PLoS One. 2019 Oct 10;14(10). PLoS One. 2019;14(9) 2019 Sep 11.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female patient with type 1 diabetes presents with a 1-cm penetrating injury to her lower extremity that occurred 48 hours prior. Clinical examination reveals surrounding tissue inflammation, pain throughout the entire calf region, and the presence of gas in the tissues. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this wound?
A) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment
B) Silver sulfadiazine topical application
C) Operative tissue removal
D) Unna boot compressive bandaging
E) Negative pressure wound therapy
questions.answer:
C)
This patient presents with an aggressive necrotizing soft tissue infection requiring immediate surgical debridement. The combination of systemic symptoms, compartment-wide tenderness, and tissue crepitus in a diabetic patient indicates necrotizing fasciitis, which demands urgent operative intervention to remove all devitalized tissue and prevent further spread along fascial planes. A) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is incorrect because it is an adjunctive treatment used after surgical debridement, not as initial management. B) Silver sulfadiazine dressing is incorrect because topical antimicrobials are inadequate for deep necrotizing infections requiring surgical intervention. D) Unna boot compression dressing is incorrect because compression therapy is contraindicated in acute infections and would worsen tissue perfusion. E) Vacuum-assisted closure therapy is incorrect because it is used after debridement for wound healing promotion, not as primary treatment for active necrotizing infection.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child in good health is planned for tissue expansion surgery to excise a large congenital pigmented nevus. Which anatomical location carries the greatest risk of complications during tissue expansion?
A) Head
B) Lower extremity
C) Neck
D) Torso
E) Upper extremity
questions.answer:
B)
The lower extremity presents the highest complication risk during tissue expansion procedures. A comprehensive 20-year meta-analysis by Huang et al. demonstrated that lower limb expansion had a pooled odds ratio of 2.80 for complications compared to other body regions (95% CI: 1.14-6.86). The lower extremities are subject to constant movement and mechanical stress from surrounding muscles, creating disruptive forces during expansion. Additionally, the curved, cylindrical anatomy of limbs makes flap design and expander placement technically challenging. A) Head is incorrect because it showed a lower odds ratio of 1.31 for complications. C) Neck is incorrect as it was grouped with head regions and showed lower complication rates than lower extremities. D) Torso is incorrect because it had the lowest complication rate with an odds ratio of 0.78, making it the safest expansion site. E) Upper extremity is incorrect as it demonstrated a lower odds ratio of 1.24 compared to the lower extremity.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male patient with a prior history of lower eyelid fat pad prolapse receives bilateral lower eyelid surgery using a transconjunctival method for fat compartment management and pinch technique for removing redundant skin. During surgery, the surgeon encounters challenges identifying the medial fat compartment on the right side despite extensive dissection. At the 3-week postoperative visit, the patient reports persistent problems with eye elevation, abduction, and external rotation. Which muscle was most likely damaged during the operation?
A) Inferior oblique
B) Inferior rectus
C) Pretarsal orbicularis oculi
D) Superior oblique
E) Superior rectus
questions.answer:
A)
The inferior oblique muscle is a slender extraocular muscle located near the front edge of the orbital floor. It originates from the maxillary bone and inserts on the posterior-inferior-lateral aspect of the eyeball, receiving innervation from the inferior division of the third cranial nerve. This muscle produces extorsion (primary function), elevation (secondary function), and abduction (tertiary function) of the eye. Anatomically, it forms the key boundary separating the medial and central fat pads of the lower lid. Proper identification and protection of this muscle is crucial during lower eyelid procedures. Given the surgical difficulty accessing the medial fat pad and the patient's specific movement deficits, injury to the inferior oblique is most probable. B) is incorrect because the inferior rectus causes depression, adduction, and extorsion - not the elevation deficit seen here. C) is incorrect because the pretarsal orbicularis oculi controls eyelid closure, not eye movements. D) is incorrect because the superior oblique produces intorsion, depression, and abduction - opposite to the patient's symptoms. E) is incorrect because the superior rectus causes elevation, adduction, and intorsion, which doesn't match the abduction and extorsion deficits observed.

questions.question:
What provides the vascular supply to the flap used for fingertip reconstruction as depicted?
A) Distally based circulation from the opposite digital artery
B) Dorsal penetrating blood vessels
C) Perineural penetrating blood vessels
D) Proximally based circulation from the same-side digital artery
questions.answer:
A)
The answer is A. A reverse homodigital island flap is demonstrated, which is a distally based flap effective for fingertip injury repair. The arterial blood supply originates from the opposite digital artery through the crossing ladder vessels of the palmar digital arch located just dorsal to the volar plate at each joint level. This procedure requires sacrificing the same-side digital artery, and careful preservation of the digital nerve is essential during skin paddle elevation. The donor area typically requires skin grafting. B is incorrect because dorsal perforating vessels do not provide the primary blood supply for this specific flap design. C is incorrect because perineural perforating vessels are not the main vascular source for this reconstruction technique. D is incorrect because the flap is distally based from the contralateral artery, not proximally based from the ipsilateral artery.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old female presents with several ulcerating, persistent wounds on her left shoulder that developed 8 years following a left modified radical mastectomy and adjuvant chest wall radiation. She has experienced chronic lymphedema for 5 years. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Brachytherapy
B) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
C) Incisional biopsy
D) Isolated limb perfusion with chemotherapy
E) Skin resection only with 5-mm margins
questions.answer:
C)
Incisional biopsy is the most appropriate next step because these clinical findings are highly suspicious for Stewart-Treves syndrome (lymphangiosarcoma), which can develop in patients with chronic lymphedema following mastectomy and radiation. Tissue diagnosis is essential before initiating any treatment, as this condition can mimic radionecrosis but requires entirely different management. A) Brachytherapy is incorrect because it would be inappropriate without first establishing a tissue diagnosis, and radiation therapy could potentially worsen lymphangiosarcoma. B) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is incorrect because it may actually accelerate tumor growth in lymphangiosarcoma and is contraindicated in this setting. D) Isolated limb perfusion with chemotherapy is incorrect because while this may be a treatment option for confirmed lymphangiosarcoma, tissue diagnosis must be obtained first. E) Skin resection with 5-mm margins is incorrect because adequate margins for lymphangiosarcoma require at least 1 cm, and surgical intervention should not proceed without histologic confirmation.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old male with a history of surgically corrected cleft lip and palate is preparing for jaw surgery to correct his malocclusion. When discussing potential complications during the preoperative consultation, which of the following complications occurs most commonly after jaw surgery?
A) Dental injury
B) Hardware failure
C) Hemorrhage
D) Surgical site infection
E) Nerve injury
questions.answer:
E)

Comprehensive studies involving large patient populations have documented the complication rates associated with jaw surgery procedures. Among all potential complications, nerve injury represents the most common adverse outcome, with reported incidence rates ranging from 12.1 to 19% of cases. Surgical site infection is incorrect because it occurs in only 2-3.4% of procedures, making it less frequent than nerve complications. Hardware failure is incorrect as it develops in up to 2.5% of cases, which is substantially lower than nerve injury frequencies. Dental injury is incorrect because it affects only 0.14-5% of patients undergoing these procedures. Hemorrhage is incorrect since clinically significant bleeding complications occur in merely 0.5-1.4% of cases. Additional possible complications may include jaw joint problems, wound healing concerns, and the requirement for additional surgical procedures.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man presents to the emergency department with malocclusion sustained during an assault. Examination shows isolated mandibular subcondylar fracture. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most likely location of the mandibular fracture?


A) Left
B) Right
C) Bilateral
D) Not possible to determine with information provided
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


Posterior mandibular fractures, such as those of the subcondylar subunit, cause foreshortening of the vertical height of the mandible and early contact of the molar teeth on the ipsilateral side of the fracture. This results in an open bite on the anterior contralateral side of the fracture as demonstrated in the picture (right open bite).

A displaced right subcondylar fracture usually presents with a left open bite.

The malocclusion pattern from bilateral subcondylar fractures is more difficult to predict. If displaced, they may present with an anterior open bite, caused by early contact of the molar teeth on both sides of the face.


ReferencesFractures of the condylar process and head. AO Surgery Reference. https://www2.aofoundation.org/wps/portal/!ut/p/a0/04_Sj9CPykssy0xPLMnMz0vMAfGjzOKN_A0M3D2DDbz9_UMMDRyDXQ3dw9wMDAx8jfULsh0VAdAsNSU!/?bone=CMF&segment=Mandible&soloState=fbox&teaserTitle=&contentUrl=srg/91/01-Diagnosis/ao_srg_diag_condyle_all.jsp. Accessed January 29, 2020.Howlader D, Ram H, Mohammad S, et al. Surgical Management of Mandibular Subcondylar Fractures Under Local Anesthesia: A Proposed Protocol. J Maxillofac Surg 2019 May;77(5):1040.e1-1040.

questions.question:
Which antiseptic agent below carries the highest risk of causing severe eye injury and must be avoided in ocular regions?
A) Chloroxylenol 3% solution
B) Chlorhexidine 4% solution
C) Povidone-iodine 5% solution
D) Unscented baby shampoo with sterile saline rinse
questions.answer:
B)

Chlorhexidine 4% solution is a known ocular toxin that can cause severe corneal damage and chemical injury, especially if it contacts the eye during surgical interventions. Antiseptics like chlorhexidine gluconate and hexachlorophene are contraindicated for use in eye and periocular regions. Note that extremely diluted chlorhexidine (0.04%) is ophthalmologically safe and used therapeutically for acanthamoeba keratitis in contact lens users. A) is wrong because chloroxylenol 3% causes only minor eye irritation and may be used carefully near ocular areas. C) is wrong since povidone-iodine 5% is available in sterile ophthalmic preparations made for eye surgeries, and 10% povidone-iodine is safe for adjacent facial skin. D) is wrong because unscented baby shampoo with sterile saline provides a safe cleaning option for patients allergic to povidone-iodine.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old boy is referred for evaluation of an abnormal frontal prominence that his parents report has become more noticeable during the past year. A photograph is shown. He is otherwise healthy and is meeting all developmental milestones. A CT scan obtained at the request of his pediatrician shows closure of the metopic suture with ectocortical thickening; no other abnormalities are noted. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?


A) Endoscopic suturectomy and postoperative helmet therapy
B) Fronto-orbital advancement
C) Spring-mediated frontal distraction
D) Total calvarial remodeling
E) Observation
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


This patient has a metopic ridge and would not be correctly classified as having the phenotype associated with pathologic metopic closure-trigonocephaly. Consequently, observation is the only correct answer. Thickening of the metopic suture is a normal variant and should not be interpreted as abnormal unless it is accompanied by frontal narrowing and retrusion of the superior-lateral orbital rims. These findings are not present in this patient.


The metopic suture closes normally within the first year of life, so the presence of a fused metopic suture on CT scan in a child this age is not necessarily abnormal. The degree of frontal narrowing required to classify a patient as having pathologic cranial shape is a matter of much debate and is not settled. Some authors point to the importance of additional clinical (hypotelorism, biparietal widening) or radiographic (endocortical thickening or omega sign on CT) findings to secure the diagnosis of metopic craniosynostosis.


The other responses are surgical interventions and should be invoked only in the context of pathologic metopic closure and resultant trigonocephaly. Endoscopic suturectomy and postoperative helmet therapy, spring-mediated frontal distraction, and fronto-orbital advancement are all viable options to correct the frontal narrowing associated with trigonocephaly. Total calvarial remodeling is rarely if ever required to correct trigonocephaly.


References
Birgfeld CB, Saltzman BS, Hing AV, et al, Making the diagnosis: metopic ridge versus metopic craniosynostosis. J Craniofac Surg. 2013 Jan;24(1):178-85.
Wood BC, Mendoza CS, Oh AK, et al. What's in a name? Accurately diagnosing metopic craniosynostosis using a computational approach. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2016 Jan;137(1):205-13.
Yee ST, Fearon JA, Gosain AK, et al. Classification and management of metopic craniosynostosis. J Craniofac Surg. 2015 Sep;26(6):1812-7.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old man develops painless swelling of his right cheek 2 months after sustaining a knife wound to the mid-cheek area during an assault. The laceration was sutured in the emergency department by a physician assistant. What is the most appropriate management at this point?
A) Drainage of fluid collection with antisialagogue therapy
B) Open surgical debridement with subsequent skin grafting
C) Surgical exploration and ductal repair
D) Total parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation
E) Ultrasound-guided aspiration only
questions.answer:
A)

Penetrating injuries along a line from the external auditory canal to the midportion of the upper lip can injure the parotid duct or glandular tissue. The parotid anatomy is classified into three zones: Zone A (gland parenchyma), Zone B (duct over the masseter), and Zone C (duct from masseter to intraoral opening near the second maxillary molar). The buccal branch of the facial nerve often runs with the duct and may cross the masseter surface after leaving the gland, with injury causing weakness of upper lip movement during facial expression. Without immediate repair, delayed complications like salivary fistulas or sialoceles can occur. Most cases respond favorably to conservative management with drainage, compression, and antisialagogue drugs. B is incorrect because open debridement with skin grafting doesn't treat the salivary pathology and is overly invasive. C is incorrect since delayed ductal reconstruction is technically difficult and rarely successful, being better suited for acute trauma. D is incorrect as total parotidectomy is reserved for conservative treatment failures. E is incorrect because aspiration alone provides insufficient drainage and fails to control the persistent salivary leakage.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man reports pain in one of his right lower posterior teeth 6 months after open reduction and internal fixation for a right mandibular angle fracture. Physical examination shows grayish discoloration of the tooth and tenderness to vertical percussion of the mandibular second molar. Panoramic X-ray shows an intact mandibular second molar with a 1.5-cm radiolucent lesion at the apex of the root. What is the most likely diagnosis based on these clinical findings?
A) Dentigerous cyst
B) Mucocele
C) Keratocystic odontogenic tumor
D) Radicular cyst
E) Simple bone cyst
questions.answer:
D)

The radicular cyst is the most common type of odontogenic cyst. The typical development involves a non-viable tooth that becomes infected, leading to necrosis of the pulpal tissue. Bacterial byproducts leak through the apex of the root, creating periapical inflammation that manifests as a radiolucent area on X-ray imaging. A) Dentigerous cyst is incorrect because it is the second most frequent odontogenic cyst that develops around the crown of an unerupted tooth (like third molars or cuspids) from the dental follicle, usually found incidentally and asymptomatic. C) Keratocystic odontogenic tumor is incorrect as it is the third most prevalent odontogenic cyst, known for rapid expansion, aggressive nature, challenging surgical removal, high recurrence potential, and connection to nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome. B) Mucocele is incorrect because it is a pseudocyst involving minor salivary glands in the lips after injury, unrelated to dental pathology. E) Simple bone cyst is incorrect as it is a self-limiting radiolucent cavity of unclear etiology that forms an empty or fluid-filled space, typically found in the mandible but not specifically associated with tooth disease.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman comes to the office with a vascular malformation involving capillaries on her right facial area. What laser technology would be the optimal therapeutic choice for this condition?
A) CO2 laser (10,200 nm wavelength)
B) Erbium:YAG laser (2940 nm wavelength)
C) Neodymium:YAG laser (1064 nm wavelength)
D) Pulsed dye laser (585 nm wavelength)
E) Q-switched ruby laser (694 nm wavelength)
questions.answer:
D)
The pulsed dye laser at 585 nm wavelength specifically targets oxyhemoglobin as its primary chromophore, making it the ideal choice for treating vascular lesions such as capillary malformations. A) is incorrect because the CO2 laser uses water as its target chromophore and is primarily utilized for ablative resurfacing procedures to address wrinkles, scarring, and pigmentary disorders rather than vascular pathology. B) is incorrect since the Er:YAG laser functions at 2940 nm, targets water molecules, and is employed for gentler skin resurfacing with reduced thermal injury compared to CO2 systems, but is not effective for vascular abnormalities. C) is incorrect because although the Nd:YAG laser operates at 1064 nm in the near-infrared range, it is mainly utilized for acne scar management alongside other lasers in the 1064-1540 nm spectrum, not for treating vascular malformations. E) is incorrect as the Q-switched ruby laser functions at 694 nm, specifically targets melanin and carbon-containing pigments, and is primarily indicated for tattoo removal procedures rather than vascular lesion therapy.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old female presents with contracture deformities affecting right wrist and digit flexion, sensory loss in the radial-volar aspect of the hand, and muscle wasting in the forearm occurring 6 months following an electrical injury to the right upper limb. A functioning free gracilis muscle transplant is being considered to restore digital flexion capability. Which nerve provides motor innervation to this muscle flap?
A) Femoral
B) Genitofemoral
C) Ilioinguinal
D) Obturator
E) Pudendal
questions.answer:
D)
The obturator nerve supplies motor innervation to the gracilis muscle, making it the correct answer. The gracilis serves as a reliable option for functional muscle transfers and has proven effective in restoring hand function in cases of severe Volkmann contracture. The obturator nerve branch to the gracilis contains 2-3 fascicular groups and measures approximately 7.7 cm from the obturator foramen to muscle insertion, allowing for fascicular separation and muscle segmentation when needed. A) Femoral nerve is incorrect as it innervates the quadriceps and other anterior thigh muscles, not the gracilis. B) Genitofemoral nerve is incorrect as it provides sensory innervation to the genitalia and upper thigh skin. C) Ilioinguinal nerve is incorrect as it supplies sensory innervation to the inguinal region and does not innervate the gracilis. E) Pudendal nerve is incorrect as it innervates the perineal muscles and external genitalia, not the gracilis muscle.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male experiences forced wrist hyperextension after falling onto his extended hand. Physical examination reveals anatomical snuffbox pain. A scaphoid bone fracture is suspected. What imaging modality should be obtained initially to evaluate this patient's potential injury?
A) Radionuclide bone scintigraphy
B) Computed tomography
C) Magnetic resonance imaging
D) Standard radiographic films
E) Ultrasound examination
questions.answer:
D)
Standard radiographic films are the appropriate initial imaging study. Plain radiographs detect approximately 70% of scaphoid fractures, making them cost-effective as the first-line imaging despite missing up to 30% of fractures. Clinical examination alone has limited predictive value (13-69%, average 21%), so radiographs provide important additional diagnostic information at low cost. If initial radiographs are negative but clinical suspicion remains high, advanced imaging may be considered. A) Radionuclide bone scintigraphy is incorrect because while highly sensitive (96-97.8%), it is more expensive and not indicated as initial imaging. B) Computed tomography is incorrect because although it has good sensitivity (85-94%) and specificity (96-99.5%), it involves radiation exposure and higher cost than plain films for initial evaluation. C) Magnetic resonance imaging is incorrect because despite excellent sensitivity (97.7%) and specificity (99.8%), it is expensive and should be reserved for cases with negative initial radiographs but persistent clinical concern. E) Ultrasound examination is incorrect because it is not a standard or reliable method for diagnosing scaphoid fractures.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female presents to the emergency room with a pruritic cutaneous eruption that began 2 weeks following trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy for a urinary tract infection. Her vital signs show: temperature 99.5°F (37.5°C), heart rate 110 bpm, respirations 28/min, and blood pressure 95/60 mmHg. Pulse oximetry reveals oxygen saturation of 96%. Clinical examination reveals a desquamating skin lesion involving 35% of her total body surface area. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Initiation of systemic steroid therapy
B) Obtaining a full-thickness dermal biopsy
C) Intravenous immunoglobulin infusion
D) Application of topical silver sulfadiazine cream
E) Immediate transfer to a specialized burn unit
questions.answer:
E)
Immediate transfer to a specialized burn unit is the most appropriate next step. This patient presents with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), a life-threatening condition with 30% mortality that requires specialized critical care and wound management available only at burn centers. The combination of medication exposure (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), timing (1-3 weeks post-exposure), extensive skin involvement (35% body surface area), and systemic symptoms indicates TEN. Transfer to a burn center is the only universally accepted priority intervention that has been shown to impact survival. A) Systemic corticosteroids are controversial and may worsen outcomes in TEN. B) While skin biopsy can confirm diagnosis, it should not delay urgent treatment and transfer. C) Intravenous immunoglobulin remains controversial with unclear benefit and potential harm. D) Topical silver sulfadiazine is contraindicated as the sulfa component may exacerbate the immune response in this sulfa-drug-induced condition.

questions.question:
What mechanism is most likely responsible for impaired wound healing in cigarette smokers?
A) DNA strand breaks and helical cross-linking
B) Enhanced cosubstrate availability for collagen synthesis enzymes
C) Decreased platelet aggregation
D) Improved oxygen delivery to tissues
E) Nicotine-mediated vasoconstriction
questions.answer:
E)
The correct answer is E. Nicotine is a potent vasoconstrictor. In cigarette smokers, nicotine-mediated vasoconstriction reduces cutaneous and subcutaneous perfusion, producing tissue hypoxia, decreased fibroblast proliferation, impaired collagen deposition, and reduced wound tensile strength. Carbon monoxide further lowers oxygen-carrying capacity by binding hemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen, and hydrogen cyanide inhibits enzymes required for oxidative metabolism; together with vasoconstriction these effects account for the increase in wound-healing complications. Smoking cessation for approximately 4 weeks before elective surgery is generally recommended to reduce wound complications. A is incorrect because DNA strand breaks and helical cross-linking describe radiation-induced injury to fibroblasts and endothelial cells, not smoking-related impairment. B is incorrect because increased availability of cosubstrates for prolyl and lysyl hydroxylase (oxygen, iron, ascorbate, alpha-ketoglutarate) would enhance collagen synthesis; smoking reduces oxygen availability for these reactions. C is incorrect because nicotine increases, rather than decreases, platelet adhesiveness and aggregation, promoting microvascular thrombosis; that prothrombotic effect can worsen ischemia but is not the mechanism named by the correct choice. D is incorrect because smoking decreases, rather than improves, oxygen delivery through carboxyhemoglobin formation and vasoconstriction.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with left facial swelling that developed 3 days following gallbladder removal surgery. Physical examination reveals redness and pus discharge from the parotid gland opening. What is the most suitable first-line treatment approach?
A) Antimicrobial treatment combined with saliva-stimulating agents
B) Needle withdrawal of fluid from the swollen area
C) Surgical opening and draining of the swollen mass
D) Mouth cultures with antibiotic irrigation of the oral cavity
E) Partial removal of the parotid gland
questions.answer:
A)
The appropriate initial approach for acute bacterial inflammation of the salivary gland involves comprehensive conservative medical treatment, including immediate fluid and electrolyte correction, maintaining oral cleanliness, addressing reduced saliva production, and providing antimicrobial medication. Enhancing saliva production through saliva-stimulating substances like citrus candies, along with warm compresses and glandular massage, helps promote secretion and natural drainage. B) is incorrect because needle aspiration is typically reserved for diagnostic purposes rather than initial treatment. C) is incorrect because surgical drainage is only considered when conservative management fails to resolve the infection. D) is incorrect because oral cultures are often contaminated by normal mouth bacteria and don't provide reliable guidance for antibiotic selection. E) is incorrect because surgical gland removal is contraindicated during active infection and represents an unnecessarily aggressive approach for initial management.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old man with Fitzpatrick type II skin is scheduled to undergo photoaging treatment with a carbon dioxide fractional laser. Which of the following measures is most likely to decrease this patient's risk of hypertrophic scarring?


A) Decreasing fluences
B) Heat stacking
C) Increasing surface area coverage
D) Treating the neck skin
E) Using multiple laser passes
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


Fractional laser resurfacing of photo-damaged or acne-scarred skin has supplanted traditional carbon dioxide ablative laser devices while diminishing the incidence of adverse effects and effecting a more rapid recovery. However, hypertrophic scarring (HTS) is a noteworthy complication that requires the utilization of preventive measures to minimize its occurrence. Conservative treatment of the neck is foremost among these measures. Use of lower fluences (energy density, defined as Joules/cm2) treating reduced surface areas, abstinence from heat stacking, and avoiding multiple passes by a carbon dioxide laser all contribute to less incidence of HTS. Patient selection, preoperative education, and preparation for treatment of this complication are appropriate adjunctive measures as well.


ReferencesAvram MM, Tope WD, Yu T, Szachowicz E, Nelson JS. Hypertrophic scarring of the neck following ablative fractional carbon dioxide laser resurfacing. Lasers Surg Med. 2009;41(3):185-8.Shah S, Alam M. Laser resurfacing pearls. Semin Plast Surg. 2012;26(3):131-136.Duplechain JK. Severe neck scarring: a consequence of fractional CO2 laser resurfacing. J Cosmet Laser Ther. 2016;18(6):352-4.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old male presents to the emergency room following an open comminuted tibial fracture of the left leg sustained in a car accident. Clinical examination reveals a laceration exceeding 10 cm in length with extensive periosteal stripping at the midshaft region. What is the correct Gustilo classification for this patient's fracture?
A) I
B) II
C) IIIA
D) IIIB
E) IIIC
questions.answer:
D)
This patient has a Gustilo type IIIB open fracture. The Gustilo classification system categorizes open fractures based on soft tissue damage severity and vascular involvement. This case demonstrates a wound larger than 10 cm with severe comminution and significant periosteal stripping, but no vascular compromise requiring repair, which defines a type IIIB injury. A is incorrect because type I fractures have clean wounds less than 1 cm with minimal bone comminution. B is incorrect because type II fractures have contaminated wounds greater than 1 cm but typically less severe than this case. C is incorrect because type IIIA fractures have wounds between 1-10 cm, whereas this patient's wound exceeds 10 cm. E is incorrect because type IIIC fractures involve major vascular injury requiring surgical repair for limb preservation, which is not present in this case.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with midline wound dehiscence with tissue necrosis 2 weeks after undergoing uneventful abdominoplasty. A photograph is shown. The patient reports that she did not stop smoking before surgery as instructed. Which of the following mechanisms has the greatest impact on delayed wound healing in this patient?


A) Decreased catecholamine production
B) Decreased leukocyte function
C) Decreased levels of hemoglobin
D) Increased fibrinogen production
E) Increased microvascular vasoconstriction
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Cigarette smoking is a leading cause of preventable death and disability in the United States. Over the past 20 years, several studies have demonstrated an increased risk of postoperative complications following plastic surgical procedures including rhytidectomy, breast reconstruction, digital replantation, muscle flaps, and body contouring procedures.


Tobacco smoke is a complex mix of particulate matter, volatile acids, and gases. There are over 4000 different compounds in cigarette smoke, many of which are toxic, mutagenic, and carcinogenic. Tobacco-induced vasoconstriction is mediated directly and indirectly by nicotine, a colorless, odorless, and poisonous alkaloid.


Elevated cellular levels of nicotine cause direct microvascular vasoconstriction. Indirect pathways of vasoconstriction include the enhancement of thromboxane A2 and stimulation of catecholamine release. Random skin flaps, such as abdominoplasty, rhytidectomy, and mastectomy flaps, are predominantly supplied by the subdermal plexus, which is very sensitive to sympathomimetic agonists such as catecholamines.


Smoking also increases carboxyhemoglobin levels, which shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin saturation curve to the left. The net result is decreased oxygen-carrying capacity by direct competitive inhibition from carbon monoxide. Other effects caused by smoking include decreased prostaglandin I2 (prostacyclin) production, increased platelet aggregation and blood viscosity, decreased collagen production, decreased red blood cell deformability, increased fibrinogen production, and decreased leukocyte function (mediated by hydrogen cyanide). The net effect is a prothrombogenic state with impaired inflammation that also contributes to slow wound healing. Although fibrinogen production is increased and leukocyte function is reduced, the primary mechanism by which wound healing is impaired is related to the nicotine-induced vasoconstriction of the subdermal plexus.


Rhytidectomy patients who smoke are 12.5 times more likely to develop skin necrosis compared with nonsmokers. One study showed a 47.9% rate of wound healing problems in abdominoplasty patients who smoked compared with 14.8% in nonsmokers. Another large study of patients undergoing free transverse rectus abdominis musculocutaneous (TRAM) breast reconstruction showed no difference in free flap survival in those patients who smoked, but the smoking population had a significantly higher rate of mastectomy skin flap loss, abdominal donor site complications, and hernias. Active smoking is not only a risk factor for wound complications, but the overall number of cigarettes smoked in a lifetime can affect the rate of wound infections. One study showed a risk for infection of 14.3% in patients who claimed to have stopped smoking 4 weeks before their abdominoplasty compared with 1.2% of nonsmokers. This study also showed higher infection rates were associated with more years of smoking, a higher number of cigarettes smoked per day, and a higher number of estimated cigarettes smoked during a lifetime. Current recommendations for smokers who desire elective cosmetic surgery are to avoid smoking and all nicotine products for 2 to 4 weeks before and after surgery.


ReferencesChang DW, Reece GP, Wang B, et al. Effects of smoking on complications in patients undergoing free TRAM flap breast reconstruction. Plast Recontr Surg. 2000;105(7):2374-2380.Dutot MC, Serror K, Ameri O, et al. Improving safety after abdominoplasty: a retrospective review of 1128 cases. Plast Recontr Surg. 2018;142(2):355-362.Hurvitz KA, Olaya WA, Nguyen A, et al. Evidence-based medicine: abdominoplasty. Plast Recontr Surg. 2014;133(5):1214-1221.Krueger JK, Rohrich RJ. Clearing the Smoke: The scientific rationale for tobacco abstention with plastic surgery. Plast Recontr Surg. 2001;108(4):1063-1077.Manassa EH, Hertl, CH, Olbrisch RR. Wound healing problems in smokers and nonsmokers after 132 abdominoplasties. Plast Recontr Surg. 2003;111(6):2082-2087.Netscher DT, Wigoda P, Thornby J, et al. The hemodynamic and hematologic effects of cigarette smoking versus a nicotine patch. Plast Recontr Surg. 1995;96(3):681-688.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents for evaluation of an abdominal wall lesion that has been enlarging over recent months. Radiologic studies and histopathologic analysis of the biopsy specimen establish a diagnosis of desmoid-type fibromatosis originating from the anterior abdominal wall musculature. Which statement below most accurately describes this condition?
A) It correlates with prior radiation therapy exposure
B) It demonstrates local invasiveness with minimal potential for distant spread
C) It typically develops from an existing untreated lipomatous lesion
D) First-line therapy consists of combined chemotherapy and radiation treatment
E) It follows an autosomal recessive hereditary transmission pattern
questions.answer:
B)
This patient presents with a desmoid tumor, an uncommon, locally invasive mesenchymal tumor typically occurring in adolescents and young adults. While these tumors do not spread to distant sites, they exhibit highly unpredictable and aggressive local behavior. Management approaches vary from active surveillance (since some lesions may spontaneously regress) to extensive surgical resection with negative margins. Historically, surgical removal has been challenging due to elevated rates of local recurrence. A is incorrect because desmoid tumors are not linked to chemical or radiation exposures. C is incorrect because these tumors do not originate from lipomas. D is incorrect because while treatment approaches for desmoids continue to evolve, chemotherapy and radiation are not the primary treatment modalities - observation is often preferred for small or stable tumors, while extensive excision is typically performed for rapidly growing lesions. E is incorrect because there is no established genetic inheritance pattern for desmoid tumors, though they are associated with sporadic mutations in β-catenin (CTNNB1) and adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) genes.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male athlete sustains a contact burn to the right foot. Serial debridement results in exposure of the medial aspect of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate option for definitive wound management?


A) Amputation of the great toe
B) Bony debridement and primary closure
C) Coverage with a fasciocutaneous free flap
D) Local tissue rearrangement
E) Negative pressure wound therapy
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The most appropriate option to obtain definitive wound coverage is a fasciocutaneous free flap harvested from outside the zone of injury. Amputation is not indicated when the majority of the great toe is viable. In addition, this would be highly morbid for this young athlete. Negative pressure wound therapy alone would promote healing by secondary intention, but with an exposed joint this would likely result in an unstable wound. Local tissue rearrangement in this area results in marked donor site morbidity. Bony debridement and primary closure may lead to a healed wound, but functional morbidity would be high in this athlete.


References
1. Koul AR, Patil RK, Philip VK. Early use of microvascular free tissue transfer in the management of electrical injuries. Burns. 2008 Aug;34(5):681-7.
2. Baumeister S, K√∂ller M, Dragu A, et al. Principles of microvascular reconstruction in burn and electrical burn injuries. Burns. 2005 Feb;31(1):92-8.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old carpenter presents to the emergency department following a 10-foot fall from scaffolding. He reports left wrist pain and loss of sensation in the thumb, index, and middle fingers of his left hand. Initial trauma evaluation reveals no additional injuries, and left wrist radiographs are obtained (displayed). What is the most appropriate management?
A) Finger trap application with traction placement
B) Closed reduction with carpal tunnel decompression
C) Open reduction with internal fixation
D) Wrist immobilization in 30 degrees of extension
E) Complete wrist arthrodesis
questions.answer:
C)
Open reduction with internal fixation is the correct treatment for this perilunate dislocation. These high-energy wrist injuries disrupt both carpal arcs and require surgical restoration of carpal alignment with ligament repair and rigid internal fixation of any associated fractures like the scaphoid to prevent poor long-term outcomes. A) is incorrect because finger trap traction alone cannot adequately reduce the dislocation or address the need for ligament repair and internal fixation. B) is incorrect because closed reduction without internal fixation has been shown to result in poor long-term outcomes, and carpal tunnel release alone doesn't address the primary injury. D) is incorrect because simple splinting in extension is appropriate for carpal tunnel syndrome but inadequate for perilunate dislocations which require surgical reduction and stabilization. E) is incorrect because total wrist fusion is reserved for salvage procedures in chronic cases with nonreconstructible damage, not as acute treatment.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old male patient presents with Stage II squamous cell carcinoma located at the tongue base. He has smoked for 30 years. What type of cervical lymph node dissection would be most suitable for this case?
A) Modified: lymph node levels I through V
B) Radical: lymph node levels I through V, cranial nerve XI, internal jugular vein, sternocleidomastoid muscle excision
C) Selective (anterior compartment): level VI
D) Selective (lateral cervical): lymph node levels II through IV
E) Selective (supraomohyoid): lymph node levels I through III
questions.answer:
E)
Selective excision of lymph nodes in levels I through III represents the optimal surgical approach for N0 and N1 malignancies of the oral cavity. The lateral cervical and anterior compartment approaches fail to address Level I nodes, which represent the primary lymphatic drainage pathway for tongue base malignancies.
