Given the large size of the wound, only the omentum from the listed options can adequately fill the defect and eliminate dead space throughout the entire wound. A) Latissimus dorsi is incorrect because it cannot adequately reach and fill such a large anterior sternal defect. C) Pectoralis major is incorrect because while useful for smaller sternal defects, it cannot adequately fill such an extensive wound, especially the lower portions. D) Pectoralis minor is incorrect because it is not utilized for sternal reconstruction and lacks sufficient tissue volume. E) Serratus is incorrect because it is primarily used for posterior chest wall reconstruction and cannot adequately address large anterior sternal wounds.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old female patient presents for evaluation of a protrusion that appeared on her nasal bridge 6 months following reconstructive surgery using an auricular cartilage onlay graft to address a trauma-related nasal defect. What is the most probable etiology of this patient's complication?
A) Bacterial contamination
B) Calcification
C) Immunologic response
D) Graft dissolution
E) Structural deformation
questions.answer:
E)
Structural deformation is a recognized limitation of ear cartilage grafts, as they have a tendency to curl and change shape over time. This deformation occurs more frequently when the perichondrial covering remains attached to the graft. Grafts consisting of pure cartilage without perichondrium demonstrate less tendency toward structural changes. The deformation process with auricular cartilage typically develops slowly over weeks to months. A) Bacterial contamination is incorrect because infection would typically present with signs of inflammation, drainage, or systemic symptoms and would occur earlier in the postoperative period. B) Calcification is incorrect as this is not a recognized complication of cartilage grafts. C) Immunologic response is incorrect because autologous cartilage grafts do not trigger rejection reactions, and any graft failure would more likely present with extrusion or drainage rather than a protruding bump. D) Graft dissolution is incorrect because resorption is uncommon with cartilage grafts and would more likely create an indentation rather than a protruding deformity.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male patient experiences burns covering 35% of his body surface area, affecting his neck, chest, armpits, and upper arms. Following skin graft procedures, he develops a restrictive scar band in the right anterior axillary region. The patient is planned for scar revision using Z-plasty technique. What lateral limb angle would theoretically provide a 75% increase in the length of the central limb?
A) 30 degree
B) 45 degree
C) 60 degree
D) 75 degree
E) 90 degree
questions.answer:
C)
The correct answer is 60 degrees because this angle provides the optimal balance for achieving a 75% theoretical gain in central limb length during Z-plasty reconstruction. The standard Z-plasty technique involves three equal-length incisions forming two identical angles, with the central incision running parallel to the scar's long axis. The triangular flaps created are then transposed, reorienting the scar perpendicular to its original direction and placing it within relaxed skin tension lines. The mathematical relationship between limb angles and length gain demonstrates that 60-degree angles yield the desired 75% increase. A) 30 degrees is incorrect because this smaller angle produces insufficient length gain for effective contracture release. B) 45 degrees is incorrect as it generates less than the required 75% length increase. D) 75 degrees is incorrect because this angle, while providing length gain, creates flaps that are more difficult to transpose and may compromise blood supply. E) 90 degrees is incorrect as this creates right angles that are impractical for transposition and may result in flap necrosis due to excessive tension.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents with bilateral subcondylar mandibular fractures that are minimally displaced, maintaining posterior vertical height, but she experiences subjective bite misalignment. What is the most suitable treatment approach for this patient?
A) Recommend a soft food diet for 6 weeks
B) Place a gunning splint for 8 weeks
C) Intermaxillary fixation (IMF) for 4 to 6 weeks
D) IMF for 1 week
E) IMF for 8 to 10 weeks
questions.answer:
C)
Intermaxillary fixation for 4 to 6 weeks is the most appropriate treatment. For minimally displaced subcondylar fractures without condylar head involvement, a longer period of IMF (4-6 weeks) allows proper healing and union of fracture segments without significantly increasing ankylosis risk, since the fracture is below the joint capsule. This duration provides adequate stabilization for bone healing while maintaining functional occlusion. A) is incorrect because diet modification alone is insufficient for fracture stabilization and healing. B) is incorrect because gunning splints are typically used for edentulous patients or specific dentoalveolar injuries, not subcondylar fractures. D) is incorrect because one week of fixation is too brief to allow adequate bone healing and union of the fracture fragments. E) is incorrect because 8-10 weeks of fixation is excessively long and may increase the risk of joint stiffness and complications without providing additional healing benefits.

questions.question:
Mobilization of the semimembranosus, semitendinosus, and biceps femoris muscles for flap reconstruction is most suitable for treating which of the following pressure ulcer locations?
A) Calcaneal
B) Ischial
C) Sacral
D) Trochanteric
questions.answer:
B)

The semimembranosus, semitendinosus, and biceps femoris muscles form a posterior thigh flap that is ideally suited for ischial pressure ulcer reconstruction. Ischial pressure ulcers develop in seated patients, predominantly paraplegics, and typically require substantial tissue volume for adequate closure. The posterior thigh muscles provide reliable vascularization, can be configured in a V-Y advancement pattern, and allow for re-advancement if recurrence occurs. These leg-based flaps are often preferred initially as they preserve more proximally based options for potential sacral or trochanteric defects. A) Calcaneal ulcers are incorrect because they are typically managed with local foot and ankle flaps rather than thigh-based reconstruction. C) Sacral defects are incorrect because they are primarily reconstructed using gluteal muscle flaps rather than posterior thigh muscles. D) Trochanteric wounds are incorrect because they are most commonly treated with tensor fascia lata flaps rather than hamstring muscle flaps.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female presents to the clinic with oral hemorrhage and a 20-year documented history of a radiographically confirmed arteriovenous malformation. Treatment with embolization followed by surgical excision is being considered. Which of the following characteristics is most likely to correlate with an elevated risk of lesion recurrence?
A) Growth of the malformation
B) Patient's age
C) Patient's sex
D) Dormancy of the malformation
E) Surface breakdown
questions.answer:
E)
Surface breakdown (ulceration) represents a higher Schobinger stage lesion, which correlates with increased recurrence risk according to Boston Children's Hospital data on arteriovenous malformations. Advanced Schobinger staging is the most significant predictor of recurrence, whether treated with embolization alone or combined embolization and resection. A) Growth of the malformation is incorrect because this describes a Schobinger Stage I lesion, which actually has the lowest recurrence risk (80% with embolization alone, 21% with combined treatment). B) Patient's age is incorrect because age did not correlate with lesion recurrence in the Boston Children's series. C) Patient's sex is incorrect because gender was not associated with recurrence risk in the study data. D) Dormancy of the malformation is incorrect because quiescent lesions typically represent lower Schobinger stages with better prognosis compared to ulcerating lesions.

questions.question:
Which cranial nerve supplies parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland?
A) V
B) VII
C) VIII
D) IX
E) X
questions.answer:
D)
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries parasympathetic fibers that innervate the parotid gland and also conveys taste sensations from the posterior third of the tongue. A is incorrect because the trigeminal nerve (CN V), specifically its maxillary division (V2), is purely sensory and provides sensation to the midface region. B is incorrect because the facial nerve (CN VII) provides parasympathetic innervation to the submandibular and sublingual glands through the chorda tympani, not the parotid gland. C is incorrect because the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII) is responsible for hearing and balance functions, not glandular innervation. E is incorrect because the vagus nerve (CN X) has an auricular branch that innervates the external auditory meatus and can trigger the Arnold reflex when stimulated, but does not supply the parotid gland.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male presents to the emergency room following head trauma from a high-velocity automobile accident. Physical examination reveals nasal discharge. The beta-2 transferrin assay of the discharge is positive. Computed tomography demonstrates a fracture of the frontal sinus. Both the anterior and posterior walls are undisplaced. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Frontal sinus cranialization
B) Repair of the dura
C) Frontal sinus obliteration
D) Open reduction and internal fixation of the anterior frontal sinus wall
E) Conservative management
questions.answer:
E)
Conservative management is most appropriate initially. A positive beta-2 transferrin test confirms cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea, and the primary goal is to allow the CSF leak to seal spontaneously. This involves bed rest with head elevation and possibly lumbar drain placement. Surgical intervention should only be considered if conservative measures fail. A) Cranialization is reserved for displaced posterior table fractures, which is not present in this case. B) Dural repair is premature since most CSF leaks resolve with conservative treatment. C) Obliteration should only be considered if conservative management fails to stop the CSF leak. D) Reduction and fixation of the anterior table is not indicated for nondisplaced fractures and should wait until CSF leak resolution.

questions.question:
A male newborn is evaluated because of the scalp anomaly shown in the photograph. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management of the affected area?



A) Application of a skin substitute
B) Local wound care with antibiotic ointment
C) Primary closure
D) Skin grafting
E) Tissue expansion
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


This child has aplasia cutis congenita, or cutis aplasia, of the scalp. First described in 1767 by Cordon, cutis aplasia is the congenital absence of all skin layers including the epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous fat. This process most commonly affects only focal areas of tissue but involvement can be extensive. The majority of cases involve the scalp, but this process can occur in any cutaneous area of the body. Cutis aplasia can occur in isolation or as part of a syndrome, the most common being Adams-Oliver syndrome. Cutis aplasia of the scalp can range from small areas of involvement that often heal in utero and appear at birth as a ‚Äucongenital scar‚Äu to massive defects that are devoid of scalp and cranium. Most small- or intermediate-sized full-thickness defects heal quickly (as in the patient described) if kept moist and the resultant scar can be excised secondarily. Bone healing is often complete in small lesions, and residual defects can be reconstructed when the child is older if needed. Large areas are more problematic and extensive scalp defects that threaten dural integrity may require early operative intervention. Cutis aplasia involving large areas of the scalp has a reported mortality ranging from 20 to 55%, typically as a result of sagittal sinus hemorrhage or associated congenital defects. In such cases, coverage of the dura can be life-saving. Described methods of soft-tissue coverage include skin graft, cultured allograft, acellular dermis, and immediate or delayed reconstruction with a flap. Tissue expansion of the scalp in a newborn presents many challenges and is not recommended.


References
1. Harvey G, Solanki NS, Anderson PJ, et al. Management of aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp. J Craniofac Surg. 2012 Nov;23(6):1662-1664.
2. Bharti G, Groves L, David LR, et al. Aplasia cutis congenital: clinical management of a rare congenital anomaly. J Craniofac Surg. 2011 Jan;22(1):159-165.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male patient arrives 8 days following open reduction and internal fixation of an unstable fracture of the distal tibia. Following surgery, the surgical incision has opened. Physical examination reveals a 5 × 2-cm open defect with marginal tissue death and visible implants. What is the most suitable next approach for soft-tissue reconstruction?
A) Wound debridement with skin substitute application
B) Implant removal, cast application, and wound management
C) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy and wound management
D) Surgical debridement and VAC placement as preparation for skin grafting
E) Surgical debridement and vascularized flap reconstruction
questions.answer:
E)
The optimal treatment to preserve the fracture repair is surgical debridement followed by vascularized flap reconstruction. Adequate fixation has been established and delayed wound breakdown has developed due to tissue ischemia or devitalization of the overlying soft tissues. This results from the initial traumatic forces and potential additional tissue damage during the surgical procedure. Without infection present, immediate soft-tissue reconstruction will establish stable vascularized coverage over the fracture and implants. Therefore, vascularized flap reconstruction is indicated. In the lower leg region, this frequently necessitates free tissue transfer, though soleus flaps or perforator propeller flaps may be utilized depending on defect location and dimensions. A) is incorrect because skin substitutes alone cannot provide adequate vascularized coverage for exposed hardware. B) is incorrect because the fracture fixation is stable and there are no signs of infection requiring hardware removal. C) is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone is insufficient for this acute situation requiring immediate vascularized coverage. D) is incorrect because VAC therapy with delayed skin grafting creates prolonged exposure time that significantly increases risks of hardware infection and osteomyelitis.

questions.question:
An 85-year-old critically ill patient needs arterial line placement for frequent blood gas analysis and continuous hemodynamic monitoring. What is the most probable complication associated with brachial artery cannulation in this patient?
A) Higher catheter occlusion rate versus radial artery access
B) Greater infection risk versus femoral artery access
C) Numbness affecting the thumb, index, and middle fingers
D) Development of claw deformity in the fourth and fifth digits
E) Temporary inability to extend the wrist and fingers
questions.answer:
C)
The most probable complication of brachial artery cannulation is numbness in the thumb, index, and middle fingers resulting from median nerve damage. The median nerve runs alongside the brachial artery throughout the upper arm until they diverge beneath the bicipital aponeurosis, making the nerve vulnerable to inadvertent injury during catheter insertion attempts in the lower arm region. A) is incorrect because larger vessels like the brachial artery actually have lower thrombosis rates compared to smaller vessels such as the radial artery. B) is incorrect because studies have not demonstrated increased infection rates with brachial versus femoral catheterization; femoral sites typically show higher infection rates than radial sites. D) is incorrect because claw deformity of the ring and little fingers indicates ulnar nerve injury, which is not a recognized complication of brachial artery catheterization. E) is incorrect because loss of wrist and finger extension suggests high radial nerve injury, which has not been reported as a complication of brachial artery access.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient with a history of three pregnancies and three deliveries has undergone breast reduction surgery. Histological analysis of the removed tissue reveals a fully excised 1-cm papilloma. What is the most suitable next management approach?
A) External beam radiation treatment
B) Mammographic imaging
C) Sentinel lymph node sampling
D) Subcutaneous breast removal
E) Tamoxifen treatment
questions.answer:
B)
The appropriate response is mammographic imaging. When papillomas are discovered during breast reduction surgery and are completely excised with benign pathology results, routine mammographic surveillance is the most suitable follow-up approach. Complete surgical excision of a benign papilloma constitutes adequate treatment, eliminating the need for additional aggressive interventions. A) External beam radiation treatment is incorrect because radiation therapy is not indicated for benign breast lesions like papillomas. C) Sentinel lymph node sampling is incorrect as this procedure is reserved for malignant conditions, not benign papillomas. D) Subcutaneous breast removal is incorrect because such extensive surgery is unnecessary when dealing with completely excised benign lesions. E) Tamoxifen treatment is incorrect since hormonal therapy is not warranted for benign papillary lesions.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old right-handed male construction worker presents to the emergency department 6 hours after sustaining a high-pressure latex paint injection injury to the palm side of his left index finger. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?
A) Hospital admission with intravenous antibiotic therapy
B) Surgical exploration and debridement
C) Application of radial gutter splinting with 3-day follow-up
D) Topical acetone application
E) Heat therapy, limb elevation, and watchful waiting
questions.answer:
B)
Immediate surgical exploration and debridement is essential for high-pressure injection injuries. Despite appearing minor externally, these injuries often cause extensive deep tissue damage. Small volumes of injected material can trigger compartment syndrome, impaired circulation, and closed-space infections leading to tissue death and potential amputation. High-pressure equipment generates forces of 2,000-12,000 psi, far exceeding the 100 psi needed to penetrate skin, driving material deep into tissues along fascial planes and neurovascular structures. Amputation rates reach 30% overall, with optimal surgical intervention within 6 hours showing 40% amputation risk versus 57% when delayed beyond 6 hours. A) is incorrect because antibiotics alone cannot address the mechanical tissue damage and foreign material requiring removal. C) is incorrect because splinting without surgical intervention ignores the urgent need for debridement and decompression. D) is incorrect because topical solvents cannot reach deeply injected material and may cause additional tissue damage. E) is incorrect because conservative management leads to amputation rates as high as 87% due to progressive tissue necrosis and infection.

questions.question:
Which artery serves as the primary vascular supply to the nipple-areolar complex?
A) Anterior lateral intercostal
B) Internal mammary
C) Lateral thoracic
D) Superior epigastric
E) Thoracoacromial
questions.answer:
B)
The internal mammary artery represents the predominant blood supply to the nipple-areolar complex (NAC). While the anterior lateral intercostal, lateral thoracic, and thoracoacromial arteries also contribute to NAC vascularization, the internal mammary artery delivers the most reliable and consistent perfusion, as demonstrated through numerous cadaveric dissections and in vivo magnetic resonance imaging investigations. A) is incorrect because the anterior lateral intercostal artery provides only supplementary circulation to the NAC. C) is incorrect because the lateral thoracic artery offers secondary vascular contribution rather than primary supply. D) is incorrect because the superior epigastric artery, which branches from the internal mammary artery, primarily perfuses the anterior abdominal wall rather than the NAC. E) is incorrect because the thoracoacromial artery contributes auxiliary blood flow but not the dominant supply to the nipple-areolar region.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old female patient presents to the clinic expressing dissatisfaction with her nasal appearance (illustrated), particularly regarding scarring from adolescent acne. She has previously undergone scar revision through punch excision with primary closure and dermabrasion performed by four separate practitioners, yet remains unsatisfied with the outcomes. She dedicates roughly 1.5 hours daily to applying facial cosmetics before venturing outside. She remains unmarried and experiences shame about public appearances, believing others constantly observe her nose. What percentage range best describes how common this condition is among plastic surgery patients?
A) Under 1%
B) 2 to 4%
C) 7 to 15%
D) 22 to 25%
questions.answer:
C)

This patient exhibits body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), which occurs in 7 to 15% of plastic surgery patients. BDD is characterized by excessive preoccupation with perceived physical defects that are minimal or nonexistent to others, leading to significant distress and functional impairment. The patient's extensive time spent on makeup application, avoidance of social situations, and persistent dissatisfaction despite multiple procedures are classic features of this condition.

A) Under 1% is incorrect because this represents the prevalence in the general population, not in plastic surgery patients where rates are significantly higher. B) 2 to 4% is incorrect as this underestimates the actual prevalence found in plastic surgery populations through research studies. D) 22 to 25% is incorrect because this overestimates the prevalence; while BDD is common in cosmetic surgery patients, it does not affect nearly a quarter of them.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old female patient diagnosed with invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast presents to discuss immediate breast reconstruction options. Physical examination reveals the malignancy is positive for estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) expression. There is no family history of breast or ovarian malignancies, and genetic analysis demonstrates no mutations. A bilateral mastectomy procedure is scheduled. What outcome is most probable for this patient after prophylactic mastectomy of the contralateral right breast?
A) Reduced total number of expected surgical procedures
B) Lower likelihood of known cancer recurrence
C) Enhanced survival rate for her current malignancy
D) Greater potential for future lactation capability
E) Higher probability of postoperative wound complications
questions.answer:
E)
Contralateral prophylactic mastectomy (CPM) results in increased risk of surgical site complications because performing surgery on both breasts essentially doubles the operative risks. Since mastectomy and reconstruction procedures on each breast are largely independent operations, the complication risks are nearly additive, approximately doubling the overall surgical risks. A is incorrect because CPM typically requires the same number or more operations due to potential complications, not fewer. B is incorrect because CPM does not reduce recurrence risk of the original cancer on the primary side. C is incorrect because CPM has not been demonstrated to improve cure rates for the known cancer being treated with therapeutic mastectomy. D is incorrect because bilateral breast removal eliminates any future ability to breastfeed.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old woman develops a superficial surgical site infection at her abdominal incision site two weeks after undergoing deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) breast reconstruction. According to CDC guidelines, a "superficial incisional surgical-site infection" is defined as occurring within what timeframe following the operative procedure?
A) Within 7 days maximum
B) Within 14 days maximum
C) Within 30 days maximum
D) Within 60 days maximum
E) Within 90 days maximum
questions.answer:
C)
Superficial incisional surgical-site infections are defined as occurring within 30 days of a surgical procedure, involving only the skin and subcutaneous tissue at the incision site, with specific clinical criteria including purulent drainage, positive cultures, deliberate opening due to symptoms, or physician diagnosis. A is incorrect because 7 days is too short a timeframe and would miss many legitimate superficial SSIs that develop later. B is incorrect because 14 days, while closer, still falls short of the established 30-day surveillance period. D is incorrect because 60 days exceeds the CDC definition for superficial infections and applies to deeper tissue infections. E is incorrect because 90 days is far beyond the timeframe for superficial SSI classification and would apply to implant-related infections.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male patient receives gracilis muscle free flap reconstruction to address exposed orthopedic implants 6 weeks following right ankle fracture repair. Subcutaneous heparin was given during the initial hospitalization for venous thromboembolism prevention. The reconstructive surgery is complicated by arterial anastomotic thrombosis requiring thrombectomy and revision anastomosis. Systemic heparin therapy is initiated due to this complication and maintained postoperatively. On postoperative day 3, his right lower limb, including the transferred flap, demonstrates edema and vascular congestion. Peripheral pulses are diminished. What is the most appropriate diagnostic test for this patient?
A) Prothrombin time (PT)
B) Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)
C) Factor V Leiden mutation analysis
D) Platelet count
E) D-dimer level
questions.answer:
D)
The most appropriate diagnostic test is platelet count to evaluate for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) with associated thrombosis. This immune-mediated adverse reaction occurs in 3-5% of heparin-treated patients, particularly those with prior heparin exposure within 3 months. Approximately 20% of HIT patients develop thrombotic complications with severe outcomes including 30% mortality and 30% limb amputation rates. HIT pathophysiology involves heparin-platelet factor 4 complex formation, triggering IgG antibody production that causes intense platelet activation, aggregation, and excessive thrombin generation. Clinical diagnosis relies on recognizing a 30% platelet count decline from baseline combined with thrombotic events in heparin-exposed patients. Immediate heparin discontinuation and alternative anticoagulation (danaparoid, lepirudin, or argatroban) are critical interventions. A is incorrect because PT measures extrinsic coagulation pathway function, not platelet-mediated thrombosis. B is incorrect because aPTT assesses intrinsic and common coagulation pathways rather than HIT-related thrombocytopenia. C is incorrect because Factor V Leiden testing evaluates inherited hypercoagulable states, not acute heparin-induced complications. E is incorrect because D-dimer indicates fibrin breakdown products from thrombosis but doesn't identify the underlying HIT mechanism.

questions.question:
A 57-year-old female presents to the emergency room following a closed crushing trauma to the back of her right hand. Radiographic imaging reveals no evidence of fractures or joint dislocations. Physical examination demonstrates edema and inability to actively straighten the middle finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint when starting from a bent position. Nevertheless, once the examiner positions the finger in a straight position, the patient can keep the finger extended and oppose applied pressure. Damage to which of the following anatomical components most likely accounts for this clinical presentation?
A) Central extensor tendon
B) Juncturae tendinum
C) Lumbrical muscle
D) Oblique retinacular ligament
E) Sagittal band
questions.answer:
E)
Damage to the sagittal band most likely explains this clinical presentation. The sagittal bands maintain the extensor tendon in proper dorsal alignment over the metacarpophalangeal joint. When ruptured through trauma or inflammatory conditions, the extensor tendon can slip laterally into the groove beside the joint, preventing active initiation of extension. However, passive positioning allows the tendon to return to its proper location, enabling maintained extension and resistance to force. A) Central extensor tendon injury would cause complete loss of both active extension and the ability to maintain extension against resistance. B) Juncturae tendinum damage would not create extension deficits if the main extensor tendon remains intact, as these connections between tendons may actually compensate for some tendon injuries. C) Lumbrical muscle injury affects MCP flexion and interphalangeal extension but would not impair MCP extension. D) Oblique retinacular ligament injury affects coordination between interphalangeal joints and has no impact on MCP joint function.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male arrives at the emergency room via ambulance following a tibial fracture from a motorcycle accident. Physical examination reveals an open, segmental fracture with a 4-cm laceration and significant avulsion flap, though soft-tissue coverage remains sufficient. Which Gustilo-Anderson classification most accurately categorizes this fracture?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type IIIA
D) Type IIIB
E) Type IIIC
questions.answer:
C)
This injury represents a Type IIIA open fracture according to the Gustilo-Anderson classification. Type IIIA fractures are characterized by high-energy trauma resulting in extensive soft-tissue damage with wounds greater than 1 cm, but with adequate soft-tissue coverage of the bone despite the presence of comminution or segmental fractures. The 4-cm wound size and segmental nature with adequate coverage fits this classification. Type I is incorrect because it involves wounds less than 1 cm with minimal soft-tissue damage. Type II is incorrect as it describes wounds 1-10 cm without extensive soft-tissue damage, but this case has significant avulsion and segmental fracturing. Type IIIB is incorrect because it would require inadequate soft-tissue coverage necessitating flap coverage. Type IIIC is incorrect as it specifically involves arterial injury requiring vascular repair, which is not mentioned in this case.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old female patient comes to the clinic with a multicolored ornamental tattoo on her lower extremity. She desires laser-based tattoo removal treatment. Physical examination reveals that more than 80% of her tattoo contains red and orange pigments. Which laser therapy would be most suitable for treating the orange and red pigmented areas?
A) 755-nm Q-switched alexandrite laser
B) 532-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG laser
C) 1064-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG laser
D) 694-nm Q-switched ruby laser
questions.answer:
B)
The 532-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG laser is the optimal choice for removing red, orange, and yellow tattoo pigments due to its specific wavelength absorption characteristics. A) is incorrect because the 755-nm alexandrite laser is primarily effective for green pigments and less optimal for red/orange colors. C) is incorrect because the 1064-nm Nd:YAG laser is best suited for black and dark blue pigments rather than red/orange. D) is incorrect because the 694-nm ruby laser is most effective for green, blue, and dark pigments, not red or orange colors.

questions.question:
In embryonic limb development, which signaling protein family primarily regulates the outgrowth of limb buds?
A) Bone morphogenetic proteins
B) Fibroblast growth factor
C) Retinoic acid
D) Sonic hedgehog (SHH)
E) Wingless-type proteins
questions.answer:
B)
Fibroblast growth factor is the correct answer. Limb bud formation initiates during the fourth gestational week through lateral plate somatic mesoderm outgrowth covered by ectoderm. The hindlimb bud develops several days after the forelimb bud, positioned across from L3-5 vertebrae. Ectodermal cells at the limb bud tip thicken, creating the apical ectodermal ridge (AER). Mesenchymal FGF10 triggers AER formation, which then secretes FGF8. This signaling cascade stimulates underlying cell mitosis, driving limb elongation. A) is incorrect because BMPs primarily control interdigital tissue apoptosis rather than initial outgrowth. C) is incorrect because retinoic acid mainly influences proximal-distal limb patterning, not primary outgrowth. D) is incorrect because sonic hedgehog from the zone of polarizing activity controls anteroposterior axis formation, not outgrowth. E) is incorrect because wingless-type proteins, particularly Wnt7a, regulate dorsal-ventral patterning of the overlying ectoderm.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old woman with no previous pregnancies presents to the clinic expressing concern about the "droopy" appearance of her breasts after losing 120 pounds (54 kg). Clinical examination reveals bilateral Grade 3 breast ptosis. Which of the following additional examination findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
A) Upper pole flattening
B) Elevated inframammary crease
C) Absence of lateral axillary tissue
D) Minimal skin redundancy
E) Medially positioned nipple-areola complexes
questions.answer:
A)
Upper pole flattening is the most characteristic finding in patients with massive weight loss-related breast deformities. Following significant weight reduction, patients typically develop severe breast ptosis with a deflated, flattened appearance of the breast tissue, particularly in the upper pole region, due to loss of glandular volume and skin elasticity changes. B) is incorrect because the inframammary fold typically becomes lower, not elevated, due to deflation of the skin envelope. C) is incorrect because patients usually have extension of breast tissue into a lateral axillary fat roll. D) is incorrect because significant skin laxity and excess skin are hallmark features of post-weight loss breast changes. E) is incorrect because the nipple-areola complex typically becomes medialized, not laterally displaced, in these patients.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old Chinese-American male who is right-handed receives a cadaveric hand transplant following traumatic amputation at the right wrist due to a machinery injury. The donor is a Hispanic male. Which of the following best characterizes the immunological nature of this transplant?
A) Allograft
B) Autograft
C) Isograft
D) Xenograft
questions.answer:
A)
The correct answer is allograft. Any tissue transfer between genetically distinct humans is classified as an allograft, formerly called a homograft. Since these transplanted tissues are immunologically foreign to the recipient, they will ultimately face rejection by the host's immune system unless immunosuppressive therapy is administered. Multiple antigens drive the rejection mechanism, with the most significant being the major histocompatibility complex (MHC) antigens, designated as HLA-1 and HLA-2, located on cell surfaces. B) Autograft is incorrect because it refers to tissue transfer within the same individual, such as moving skin from one body part to another. C) Isograft is incorrect because it involves transplantation between genetically identical individuals, typically identical twins, which is not the case here given the different ethnicities. D) Xenograft is incorrect because it describes transplantation across different species, such as using pig skin as temporary wound coverage.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old female patient had her cast removed 2 weeks ago after 5 weeks of immobilization for a minimally displaced fracture of the left distal radius. She now presents with inability to extend her thumb. Physical examination reveals she cannot perform thumb retropulsion while her palm is flat against the table. What is the most appropriate next management step?
A) Nerve conduction studies
B) Splinting
C) Direct tendon repair
D) Tendon transfer procedure
E) Radiographic imaging
questions.answer:
D)
This patient has sustained a rupture of the extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon, which occurs in approximately 5% of patients with minimally displaced distal radius fractures around 7 weeks post-injury due to attritional rupture from compromised blood supply. The appropriate treatment is tendon transfer using the extensor indicis proprius to replace the EPL function. A) is incorrect because nerve conduction studies would not address the mechanical tendon rupture. B) is incorrect because splinting cannot restore function to a completely ruptured tendon. C) is incorrect because primary repair is not feasible due to tendon fraying and retraction. E) is incorrect because radiographs would not change the management of this soft tissue injury.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old female presents for evaluation of discomfort occurring 2 weeks following subglandular breast augmentation surgery. She denies any history of fever, chills, or discharge. On physical examination, there is a painful, tender cord-like structure noted in the inframammary area of the left breast. What is the most appropriate next step in treatment?
A) Prescribe antibiotics
B) Initiate anticoagulation therapy
C) Provide anti-inflammatory medication
D) Order duplex ultrasound examination
E) Explant the breast implant
questions.answer:
C)
This patient has Mondor disease of the breast, which is a benign, self-resolving condition involving thrombophlebitis of the inframammary veins. This condition typically presents 2-3 weeks after surgery as a painful, tender cord-like structure in the superficial veins of the thoracoepigastric system. Treatment consists of conservative management with warm compresses and anti-inflammatory medications for symptomatic relief. A) is incorrect because antibiotics are not indicated as this is not an infectious process. B) is incorrect because anticoagulation therapy is not necessary for this self-limiting condition. D) is incorrect because duplex ultrasonography is not required for diagnosis or management of this clinical condition. E) is incorrect because implant removal is not warranted in the absence of infection or other complications.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old man who was in a house fire has burns on 55% of his body including the upper limbs, chest, abdomen, and left leg. He underwent escharotomies and has been resuscitated, but he requires mechanical ventilation because of an inhalation injury. He has an evolving acute kidney injury. A photograph is shown. Immediate excision is planned for management of a suspected fungal infection of the burn wounds. Which of the following is the most appropriate method for initial excision in this patient?


A) Excision down to fascia without a tourniquet
B) Excision down to viable tissue using tumescence
C) Excision down to viable tissue with a tourniquet
D) Excision down to viable tissue without a tourniquet
E) Hydrosurgical debridement without a tourniquet
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


The best method for initial excision in this critically ill patient is excision down to fascia (fascial excision). Excision down to viable tissue (tangential excision) with or without a tourniquet would result in a large amount of blood loss, which would be a significant physiologic insult for this patient; additionally, it may not eradicate the suspected fungal infection. Tangential excision using tumescence may not result in significant blood loss, but the ability to judge viable from nonviable tissue is compromised, and this approach would have a high likelihood of requiring further debridement to achieve a healthy tissue bed unless performed by extremely experienced burn surgeons. Fascial excision is also much faster than tangential excision, which is an important consideration in this critically ill patient. Hydrosurgical debridement is adequate for superficial burns but has no role in a large flame burn and would result in excessive blood loss and operative time.


References
Duteille F, Perrot P. Management of 2nd-degree facial burns using the Versajet(¬Æ) hydrosurgery system and xenograft: a prospective evaluation of 20 cases. Burns. 2012 Aug;38(5):724-9.
Mosier MJ, Gibran NS. Surgical excision of the burn wound. Clin Plast Surg. 2009 Oct;36(4):617-25.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old male with traumatic paraplegia of 5 months' duration presents with a severe grade IV pressure sore over the right ischial tuberosity. During surgical debridement and reconstruction with an inferior gluteal rotational flap, the patient develops cardiac dysrhythmias including peaked T-waves, ventricular tachycardia, and hypotension immediately after anesthetic induction. Oxygen saturation remains 100% with normal capnography. Core temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). It is determined that succinylcholine was administered for rapid sequence intubation. Which of the following electrolyte disturbances is most likely responsible for this patient's clinical presentation?
A) Elevated serum potassium
B) Elevated serum sodium
C) Decreased serum calcium
D) Decreased serum glucose
E) Decreased serum magnesium
questions.answer:
A)

The correct answer is A) Elevated serum potassium. This paraplegic patient has developed acute hyperkalemia following succinylcholine administration. In patients with spinal cord injuries, burns, crush injuries, or other conditions causing muscle denervation, succinylcholine can trigger massive potassium release due to upregulation of extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in affected muscle tissue. This leads to dangerous hyperkalemia with characteristic ECG changes including peaked T-waves and ventricular arrhythmias. Treatment involves calcium to stabilize cardiac membranes, insulin with glucose to drive potassium intracellularly, and sodium bicarbonate to correct acidosis. B) Elevated serum sodium is incorrect because hypernatremia does not typically cause the specific ECG pattern of peaked T-waves and ventricular tachycardia seen with hyperkalemia. C) Decreased serum calcium is incorrect because hypocalcemia usually causes QT prolongation rather than the peaked T-waves characteristic of hyperkalemia. D) Decreased serum glucose is incorrect because hypoglycemia primarily causes altered mental status and sympathetic responses, not the specific cardiac conduction abnormalities described. E) Decreased serum magnesium is incorrect because hypomagnesemia typically causes QT prolongation and torsades de pointes rather than the peaked T-waves and ventricular tachycardia pattern of hyperkalemia.

questions.question:
A healthy 35-year-old male presents with a 15-year history of bilateral Grade III gynecomastia. He measures 5 ft 10 in (178 cm) tall and weighs 187 lb (85 kg), with a BMI of 27 kg/m2. Clinical examination reveals breast tissue enlargement with excess skin and palpable glandular and adipose components. The patient desires ultrasound-assisted lipectomy to avoid conspicuous scarring. Which of the following techniques would most effectively reduce the requirement for skin excision?
A) Disruption of the inframammary fold
B) High energy setting
C) Peripheral feathering with standard liposuction
D) Treatment of the intermediate fat layer
E) Tumescent infiltration with a 3:1 ratio
questions.answer:
A)
Disrupting the inframammary fold is crucial because it permits the skin to naturally conform and drape onto the abdominal contour, which is characteristic of the male chest anatomy. This maneuver enhances skin retraction and redraping, potentially eliminating the need for additional skin excision procedures. B) is incorrect because high energy settings (above 90%) should be avoided as they increase the risk of thermal burns and dermal damage. C) is incorrect because while peripheral feathering improves contour transitions at the breast borders, it does not specifically address skin redundancy issues. D) is incorrect because treating the intermediate fat layer alone does not provide the skin retraction benefits achieved by disrupting the inframammary fold. E) is incorrect because tumescent infiltration with a 3:1 ratio is a standard safety measure to prevent burns but does not enhance skin retraction or reduce the need for skin excision.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man is evaluated for unstable plantar scar 3 years after undergoing skin grafting for a traumatic amputation at the tarsometatarsal joints. A photograph is shown. An anterolateral thigh flap is planned for coverage of the resultant plantar defect. Which of the following coaptations is most likely to allow for sensory recovery of the flap?


A) Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve to a deep peroneal nerve branch
B) Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve to a superficial peroneal nerve branch
C) Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve to a tibial nerve branch
D) Medial femoral cutaneous nerve to a deep peroneal nerve branch
E) Medial femoral cutaneous nerve to a tibial nerve branch
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The medial femoral cutaneous nerve provides sensation to the anteromedial, not the anterolateral, thigh flap.


Achieving durable results after reconstruction of defects on the weight-bearing surface of the foot is challenging for two main reasons: flap donor sites (other than the medial plantar artery flap) do not have the specialized skin structures of the sole of the foot and are thus less durable than native foot skin; a transferred flap will always be less sensate than native, uninjured plantar foot skin. Flaps are thus more vulnerable to trauma because they cannot feel, and they are less able to tolerate trauma because they lack the native characteristics of plantar skin.


Coapting the sensory nerve of a flap to the native sensory nerve of the recipient area will allow a flap to recover some sensibility, and thus it may be more able to tolerate weight bearing. The sensory innervation to the anterolateral thigh flap is the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve. The sensory innervation to the plantar midfoot is the medial plantar nerve, a terminal branch of the tibial nerve.


The superficial peroneal nerve provides sensation to the dorsal foot.


The deep peroneal nerve provides sensation to the dorsal foot.


References
Dayan JH, Lin CH, Wei FC. The versatility of the anterolateral thigh flap in lower extremity reconstruction. Handchir Mikrochir Plast Chir. 2009;41:193-202.
Netter FH. Atlas of Human Anatomy. 6th ed. Philadelphia: Elsevier; 2014:Plate 528.
Zhang Q, Qiao Q, Gould LJ, Myers WT, Phillips LG. Study of the neural and vascular anatomy of the anterolateral thigh flap. J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg. 2010;63:365-71.

questions.question:
A 12-month-old male infant is brought to consultation by his primary care physician due to concerns about possible premature suture fusion. The child is otherwise well and meeting developmental targets normally. The family notes a prominent ridge along the center of his forehead that became apparent around 3 months of age. On examination there is a palpable, narrow midline frontal ridge, but the forehead is broad and rounded without a keel-shaped or triangular contour, the supraorbital rims and lateral orbits are well positioned, interpupillary distance is normal, and there is no biparietal widening; head circumference is at the 50th percentile. Computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction obtained by the referring physician shows a fused metopic suture with a small endocranial ridge, patency of all remaining cranial sutures, and a normal cranial vault and orbital contour. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Additional imaging with plain skull films
B) Minimally invasive strip craniectomy followed by cranial molding helmet
C) Frontal bone and orbital rim reconstruction
D) Genetic analysis for fibroblast growth factor receptor mutations (types 1, 2, and 3)
E) Continued monitoring without intervention
questions.answer:
E)
The appropriate management is continued observation without surgical intervention. The metopic suture differs from other skull sutures because it physiologically closes within the first year of life (typically between 3 and 9 months), unlike other cranial sutures that remain open until the third decade. Therefore, finding a fused metopic suture at 12 months is within normal limits. True pathological metopic synostosis produces trigonocephaly, characterized by a triangular, keel-shaped forehead with midline frontal prominence, narrowed frontal and lateral orbital regions, biparietal widening, and hypotelorism. This patient exhibits only an isolated metopic ridge with normal cranial and orbital morphology, which represents a normal anatomical variation rather than pathological synostosis. The cranial and facial morphology, not the fused suture itself, determines whether surgical correction is needed.

A is incorrect because the CT study already documents the suture status and vault shape; plain films add nothing to the diagnosis and only add radiation exposure. B is incorrect because this patient has normal cranial contours without trigonocephaly, so surgery is not indicated; in addition, endoscopic strip craniectomy with helmet molding is best performed in the first few months of life and is not appropriate at 12 months. C is incorrect because the normal forehead and orbital contour and absence of trigonocephaly do not warrant fronto-orbital advancement. D is incorrect because fibroblast growth factor receptor mutations are characteristically associated with syndromic coronal synostosis (Apert, Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Muenke), not with an isolated metopic ridge.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old female patient presenting with a BMI of 32 kg/m2 has severe hidradenitis suppurativa affecting the inguinal region, lower abdominal area, and proximal thigh. Which therapeutic approach is most likely to achieve optimal long-term outcomes in this case?
A) Antibiotic therapy combined with surgical excision
B) Antibiotic treatment with needle aspiration
C) Clindamycin lavage
D) Corticosteroid injection directly into lesions
E) Sclerosing agent injection
questions.answer:
A)
Antibiotic therapy combined with surgical excision provides the highest probability of long-term success for advanced hidradenitis suppurativa. This approach addresses both the infectious component with antibiotics and removes the affected apocrine gland tissue through excision, preventing recurrence. For advanced disease, radical excision of high-density apocrine gland areas yields the best long-term results. B) is incorrect because needle aspiration only provides temporary symptom relief without addressing the underlying pathology, leading to high recurrence rates. C) is incorrect because clindamycin irrigation alone is insufficient for advanced disease and does not remove the source of recurrent inflammation. D) is incorrect because corticosteroid injections may temporarily reduce inflammation but do not eliminate the diseased apocrine glands that cause recurrent episodes. E) is incorrect because sclerotherapy has no established role in hidradenitis suppurativa treatment and is not appropriate for this inflammatory condition.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents to the office with a protruding breastbone and forward projection of the rib cartilages. He experiences no heart or lung symptoms but is concerned about the cosmetic appearance of his chest wall. The plastic surgeon intends to address this abnormality by dividing the pectoralis major muscles, removing cartilage tissue, and using bioabsorbable fixation plates. What is the most suitable CPT code assignment for this surgical correction?
A) 21740 (reconstructive repair of pectus excavatum or carinatum, open)
B) 21740 (reconstructive repair of pectus excavatum or carinatum, open) and 21600 (excision of rib, partial)
C) 21742 (reconstructive repair of pectus excavatum or carinatum; minimally invasive approach, without thoracoscopy)
D) 21742 (reconstructive repair of pectus excavatum or carinatum; minimally invasive approach, without thoracoscopy) and 21600 (excision of rib, partial)
E) 21743 (reconstructive repair of pectus excavatum or carinatum; minimally invasive approach, with thoracoscopy)
questions.answer:
A)
The appropriate CPT code for pectus carinatum correction is 21740. This code encompasses the open surgical technique, cartilage removal, bone cuts, internal stabilization, and tissue closure as a comprehensive procedure. Option B is incorrect because adding 21600 would constitute improper unbundling since cartilage resection is already included in 21740. Options C and D are incorrect because 21742 describes minimally invasive techniques without thoracoscopy, which does not match the described open approach with muscle splitting. Option E is incorrect because 21743 refers to minimally invasive repair with thoracoscopy, which is not the surgical method being performed in this case.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old male child is brought for assessment of uneven facial features. His caregivers state they observed this asymmetry from birth and expected it to resolve over time, but no improvement has occurred. The child has no prior surgical or therapeutic interventions. Physical examination reveals cranial asymmetry and uneven facial features, including orbital involvement; no apparent cervical tilting is present. Head CT imaging would most likely demonstrate which of the following findings?
A) Positional plagiocephaly
B) Lambdoid suture fusion
C) Muscular torticollis
D) Unilateral coronal suture fusion
E) Zygomaticotemporal suture fusion
questions.answer:
A)
Positional plagiocephaly is the correct answer because it became the leading cause of cranial and facial asymmetry following the implementation of supine sleeping recommendations in the early 1990s. This condition results from external molding forces on the developing skull and commonly presents with the described clinical features of cranial and facial asymmetry without neck positioning abnormalities. B is incorrect because lambdoid suture fusion is much less common than positional deformities and typically presents with different clinical patterns. C is incorrect because torticollis would be expected to show obvious neck tilting on examination, which is absent in this case. D is incorrect because unicoronal suture fusion, while the most frequent type of craniosynostosis, is still much rarer than positional deformities. E is incorrect because zygomaticotemporal suture fusion is the least common form of craniosynostosis and would be extremely unlikely compared to positional causes.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old individual who experienced a shark attack to the left leg presents to the emergency room. The patient maintains stable vital signs. Clinical assessment reveals an actively bleeding wound in the middle portion of the thigh. The left foot appears pale and cold with diminished sensation. Pedal pulses cannot be detected. During operative exploration, a 6-cm defect in the superficial femoral artery is discovered. Following local tissue debridement, what represents the most suitable subsequent management approach for the arterial injury?
A) Direct end-to-end repair
B) End-to-side repair
C) Synthetic graft interposition
D) Autologous vein graft interposition
questions.answer:
D)
The appropriate choice is autologous vein graft interposition. This patient presents with an extensive arterial defect exceeding 5.5 cm in a contaminated field from a shark bite injury. Vein grafting provides the optimal solution for bridging large arterial gaps while offering superior resistance to infection compared to synthetic materials. A) Direct end-to-end repair is incorrect because the 6-cm arterial gap is too extensive for tension-free primary anastomosis. B) End-to-side repair is incorrect as it does not address the significant length of missing arterial segment requiring reconstruction. C) Synthetic graft interposition is incorrect due to the contaminated nature of the wound, which significantly increases infection risk with prosthetic materials.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old male child has a mass on the nasal bridge that has been there from birth. The lesion has gradually grown larger and the child shows widely spaced eyes. The mass feels soft, can be compressed, and light passes through it. Visible and felt pulsations are present, and the lesion becomes larger during crying episodes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Encephalocele
B) Glioma
C) Hemangioma
D) Nasal dermoid cyst
E) Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma
questions.answer:
A)
Encephaloceles represent neural tube malformations causing sac-like herniation of meninges (meningocele) or brain tissue with meninges (meningoencephalocele) at different skull locations, including frontonasal, naso-orbital, and nasoethmoidal sites or occipital regions. These lesions typically appear as soft, compressible masses that allow light transmission and may be broad-based or have a stalk. Tissue sampling risks cerebrospinal fluid leakage. B) Glioma consists of displaced neural tissue that does not allow light transmission. C) Hemangiomas are benign blood vessel tumors present at birth with rapid expansion between 1-6 months, then slow regression over 1-12 years, lacking intracranial connections or cerebral pulsations. D) Nasal dermoid cysts are benign fluid-filled lesions without pulsation or light transmission properties. E) Nasopharyngeal angiofibromas are benign but locally aggressive vascular masses occurring mainly in teenage boys, causing nasal blockage and nosebleeds.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old woman undergoes radical resection of the left breast, left hemisternectomy, four-rib resection, and visceral pleurectomy because of invasive inflammatory breast cancer extending through the thoracic wall into the mediastinum and chest. Examination of specimens obtained from intraoperative frozen section biopsies shows no residual disease. Postoperative adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation therapy to the area are planned. An intraoperative photograph of the 17 √o 17-cm defect is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate technique for soft-tissue reconstruction?


A) Left latissimus muscle flap with skin graft
B) Left rectus muscle turnover flap and skin graft
C) Omental flap and skin graft
D) Reverse abdominoplasty flap
E) Right transverse rectus abdominis musculocutaneous (TRAM) flap
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.






The most appropriate option for this patient would be a right TRAM flap. The defect encompasses a composite defect of the left side of the sternum, including the left internal mammary artery, four contiguous ribs, and the entire left breast. The question specifically asks for soft-tissue thoracic reconstruction. The analysis of the defect yields a very large soft-tissue requirement. Given this, the most logical choice of flaps to provide this amount of soft tissue on a reliable pedicle would be a right (contralateral) TRAM flap. Furthermore, this flap could also be shaped to provide a breast mound versus all the other choices.


A left latissimus muscle flap with skin graft is not the optimal choice as it would not provide sufficient soft-tissue coverage with its associated skin paddle without undue donor site morbidity in this particular patient with a large defect that spans parasternal and lateral chest wall. As a muscle-only flap with skin graft, however, it may be considered as a backup option in case of primary flap failure.


An omental flap with skin graft is an option for reconstruction of this defect; however, it would not be the most appropriate option in this case as it would necessitate an otherwise unnecessary intra-abdominal procedure and would not reshape a breast mound. It has been shown, however, to be optimal in contaminated areas due to its associated lymphatic vessels and nodes associated with its pedicle, so in different circumstances, this may be a preferred choice.


A left rectus turnover flap with skin graft would not be a good option for two reasons: the left internal mammary artery has been harvested, thereby compromising the superior epigastric vessel on which this flap would be based; and it would not cover the entirety of the defect.


A reverse abdominoplasty flap would not be able to reach the full superior extent of the defect.


References
1. Arnold PG, Pairolero PC. Chest-wall reconstruction: an account of 500 consecutive patients. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1996 Oct;98(5):804-810.
2. Riedel K, Kremer T, Hoffmann H, et al. [Plastic surgical reconstruction of extensive thoracic wall defects after oncologic resection]. Chirurg. 2008 Feb;79(2):164-174. German.
3. Losken A, Thourani VH, Carlson GW, et al. A reconstructive algorithm for plastic surgery following extensive chest wall resection. Br J Plast Surg. 2004 Jun;57(4):295-302.
4. Chang RR, Mehrara BJ, Hu QY, et al. Reconstruction of complex oncologic chest wall defects: a 10-year experience. Ann Plast Surg. 2004 May;52(5):471-479.
5. Bosc R, Lepage C, Hamou C, et al. Management of chest wall reconstruction after resection for cancer: a retrospective study of 22 consecutive patients. Ann Plast Surg. 2011 Sep;67(3):263-268.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old boy is brought to the clinic by his mother because of an abnormality of the fifth digit of his right hand. She reports that it has been present for about 3 years but has become increasingly noticeable over the past year. On examination, the small finger rests in approximately 40 degrees of flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint. He can actively flex the joint fully, but neither active nor passive extension corrects the deformity. There is no triggering, no palpable nodule, and no angular deviation in the coronal plane. The skin over the volar aspect of the joint is soft with normal flexion creases. The fifth digit of the left hand shows similar involvement, though to a lesser degree. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Camptodactyly
B) Delta phalanx
C) Kirner deformity
D) Symphalangism
E) Trigger finger
questions.answer:
A)
Camptodactyly is the correct diagnosis because it is a congenital, painless flexion contracture of the proximal interphalangeal joint of the small finger that typically becomes more pronounced over time, matching this patient's progressive inability to extend the PIP joint beyond a fixed flexed position with preserved flexion. Bilateral involvement with asymmetric severity is also characteristic. B) Delta phalanx is incorrect because it produces clinodactyly (angular deviation in the coronal plane) rather than a flexion contracture, and imaging would demonstrate a triangular or trapezoidal phalanx with a longitudinally bracketed epiphysis; this patient has no angular deviation. C) Kirner deformity is incorrect because it affects the distal phalanx of the small finger with palmar and radial curving of the fingertip, typically presenting in preadolescence, and does not involve a fixed PIP flexion contracture. D) Symphalangism is incorrect because it presents with complete joint stiffness and absent flexion creases from failure of joint segmentation, whereas this patient retains full active flexion and normal creases. E) Trigger finger is incorrect because pediatric trigger digit most commonly involves the thumb interphalangeal joint with a palpable A1 pulley nodule and catching or locking, rather than a fixed painless contracture without triggering.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male patient presents for evaluation of surgical options for panniculus morbidus (massive abdominal overhang). His medical history includes a recent severe infection of the abdominal pannus that required prolonged intensive care management. Physical examination reveals abdominal fat distribution abnormalities with associated lymphatic swelling and skin breakdown. The patient experiences severe mobility limitations and cannot maintain adequate personal cleanliness. What is the most suitable surgical approach?
A) Tummy tuck procedure
B) Suction-assisted fat removal of the overhanging tissue
C) Surgical connection of lymphatic vessels to veins
D) Removal of excess abdominal tissue with open wound management for subsequent skin transplantation
E) Excision of redundant abdominal tissue with direct wound closure
questions.answer:
E)
Panniculectomy with primary closure is the most appropriate treatment for this severe condition. This conservative approach effectively removes the problematic tissue while minimizing complications through direct wound approximation. A) Abdominoplasty is incorrect because it involves more extensive procedures like muscle tightening and umbilical repositioning that would increase morbidity unnecessarily. B) Liposuction is incorrect because it poses significant risks due to large blood vessels and potential hernias within the pannus. C) Lymphaticovenous anastomosis is incorrect because it addresses lymphedema but not the primary problem of the massive tissue overhang. D) Leaving the wound open for grafting is incorrect because it creates unnecessary complexity and risk when primary closure can be achieved safely.

questions.question:
A 6-month-old female infant presents for evaluation of cranial asymmetry described as a "flattened head." On examination, there is posterior flattening on the right side of the skull with a transcranial measurement difference of 7 mm (mild to moderate severity), along with ipsilateral mastoid prominence. The right ear and left forehead show anterior positioning. Parents note the infant has a preference for turning her head toward the right side. The child is otherwise well and meeting age-appropriate developmental markers. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
A) Physical therapy and repositioning techniques alone
B) Cranial remodeling orthosis
C) Computed tomography imaging of the head
D) Plain radiographs of the skull
E) Parental reassurance only
questions.answer:
C)
The clinical presentation suggests right unilateral lambdoid craniosynostosis (synostotic plagiocephaly), which requires CT imaging for confirmation before potential surgical intervention. The combination of ipsilateral mastoid bossing, contralateral forehead prominence, and the specific pattern of cranial asymmetry are characteristic findings that distinguish this from positional plagiocephaly. A is incorrect because conservative management alone is inappropriate without first ruling out craniosynostosis, which may require surgical correction. B is incorrect because helmet therapy should not be initiated until synostosis is excluded, as it would be ineffective for fused sutures. D is incorrect because plain films are inadequate for evaluating suture fusion and CT provides superior detail for surgical planning. E is incorrect because reassurance without proper diagnostic workup could delay necessary treatment for a condition that may require surgical intervention.

questions.question:
The vascular supply to the central abdominal region is derived mainly from which of the following arterial arcade systems?
A) Deep epigastric
B) Deep internal mammary
C) Mid epigastric
D) Superficial epigastric
E) Superficial internal mammary
questions.answer:
A)
The deep epigastric arcade serves as the principal vascular supply to the central abdominal area. This arcade is formed by the superior epigastric artery (which branches from the internal thoracic artery and travels downward within the posterior rectus sheath) and the deep inferior epigastric artery (which originates from the external iliac artery and travels upward within the posterior rectus sheath). These vessels provide branches that nourish both the rectus abdominis muscle and the overlying skin. B is incorrect because the deep internal mammary artery primarily supplies the chest wall, not the abdominal region. C is incorrect because there is no recognized "mid epigastric" arterial arcade in anatomical classification systems. D is incorrect because the superficial epigastric artery supplies the lower abdomen and originates from the femoral artery, running superficially to supply skin rather than forming the main arcade for the mid-abdomen. E is incorrect because the superficial internal mammary artery does not exist as a recognized anatomical structure.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old male presents to the clinic with nasal bridge deformity and numbness at the tip of his nose occurring 2 weeks following a baseball impact to his nose. Radiographic imaging reveals nasal bone fractures. Which nerve injury most likely accounts for the sensory loss?
A) Anterior ethmoidal
B) Infraorbital
C) Infratrochlear
D) Nasopalatine
E) Superior alveolar
questions.answer:
A)
The anterior ethmoidal nerve's external branch exits between the nasal bone and upper lateral nasal cartilage, providing sensory innervation to the nasal dorsum, lower nose skin, and nasal tip. This nerve would be directly affected by nasal bone fractures, explaining the numbness at the tip. B is incorrect because the infraorbital nerve supplies the lower lateral nasal area but not the tip. C is incorrect because the infratrochlear nerve innervates the nasal bridge and upper lateral areas, not the tip. D is incorrect because the nasopalatine nerve supplies the nasal septum and anterior hard palate, not the external nasal tip. E is incorrect because the superior alveolar nerve does not provide nasal sensation.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old female patient receives breast reconstruction using a free SIEA flap. The vascular pedicle measures 1.5 mm in diameter for both arterial and venous components. The recipient vessels chosen are the second/third intercostal perforators on the left side. The surgical team completes a hand-sutured microvascular arterial connection using 9-0 suture material and employs a 1.5-mm anastomotic coupler for the venous connection. What complication is this patient most likely to experience?
A) Arterial blockage
B) Need for interposition vein graft
C) Vascular pedicle kinking
D) Vessel spasm
E) Venous clot formation
questions.answer:
E)
This patient faces elevated risk for venous clot formation due to the use of the 1.5-mm anastomotic coupler. Research by Hansen and colleagues analyzing 5643 reconstructions demonstrated that 1.5-mm diameter couplers had a thrombosis rate of 6.9%, which is substantially higher than larger coupler sizes. When recipient veins measure less than 2.0 mm, surgeons should consider hand-sewn anastomosis or alternative recipient vessels. A) Arterial blockage is less likely since the arterial anastomosis was performed with hand-suturing rather than a coupler. B) Interposition vein grafts are not indicated in this scenario as the pedicle length appears adequate. C) Vascular pedicle kinking is not specifically associated with coupler size. D) Vasospasm can occur but is not the primary risk factor related to using small-diameter couplers.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with an exposed wound in the right inguinal region and visible distal connection of a vascular graft 3 weeks following aortofemoral bypass surgery. A sartorius muscle flap reconstruction is being considered to provide coverage for the graft. Which of the following arteries serves as the direct source of blood supply for the sartorius muscle flap?
A) Deep circumflex iliac
B) Lateral circumflex femoral
C) Medial circumflex femoral
D) Profunda femoris
E) Superficial femoral
questions.answer:
E)
The superficial femoral artery is the correct answer because the sartorius muscle demonstrates a Type IV vascular pattern with 8 to 10 vascular pedicles arising directly from the superficial femoral vessel, entering the muscle along its medial aspect. A) Deep circumflex iliac is incorrect as it does not supply the sartorius muscle. B) Lateral circumflex femoral is incorrect because it primarily supplies other thigh muscles but not the sartorius. C) Medial circumflex femoral is incorrect as it serves different muscle groups in the thigh region. D) Profunda femoris is incorrect since it does not provide direct vascular supply to the sartorius muscle.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male patient with a history of below-knee amputation presents to the clinic with persistent pain along the lateral aspect of his amputation site. He receives a diagnosis of common peroneal neuroma. The treatment plan includes targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR), which involves transferring the severed peripheral nerves to recipient motor nerves within remaining muscle tissue to restore muscle innervation. Which of the following CPT codes best describes this procedure?
A) 64708: Neuroplasty of major peripheral nerve
B) 64772: Transection of other spinal nerve
C) 64787: Burial of neuroma in muscle
D) 64859: Suture of major peripheral nerve
E) 64905: Nerve pedicle transfer; first stage
questions.answer:
E)
The appropriate response is Option E. The targeted muscle reinnervation technique involves severing a sensory or mixed motor nerve and connecting it end-to-end with a smaller motor nerve within adjacent muscle tissue. Because the surgeon is joining two distinct nerves, this procedure is classified as a nerve transfer. Option A is incorrect because neuroplasty codes are typically included within nerve transfer procedures. Option B is incorrect because while the common peroneal nerve is transected during neuroma removal, this transection component cannot be separately billed as it is incorporated into the nerve transfer procedure. Option C is incorrect because the proximal nerve stump is not being implanted into innervated muscle tissue, making the neuroma burial code inappropriate. Option D is incorrect because peripheral nerve suturing codes are designated for repairing nerve lacerations, not for connecting different nerves together.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old male patient is planned for bilateral arm lift surgery to address excess skin on the arms following significant weight reduction after bariatric surgery. Which of the following approaches is most suitable to reduce the risk of sensory nerve damage to the skin during this operation?
A) Position the lengthwise incision in front of the bicipital groove
B) Cut through the intermuscular septum during skin and fat removal
C) Lift and reposition the basilic vein prior to closing the arm lift defect
D) Preserve a minimum of 1 cm of adipose tissue above the brachial fascia in the upper arm
E) Keep dissection in a sharp plane beneath the brachial fascia
questions.answer:
D)

The correct answer is D because maintaining at least 1 cm of subcutaneous fat over the deep fascia provides a protective buffer that minimizes injury to sensory nerves, particularly the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve, which is at high risk during brachioplasty procedures. A is incorrect because the longitudinal incision should be placed slightly posterior to (not anterior to) the bicipital groove to reduce nerve injury risk. B is incorrect because dividing the intermuscular septum increases the risk of nerve damage and is contraindicated. C is incorrect because the basilic vein is not transposed during brachioplasty procedures, and this maneuver would not protect sensory nerves. E is incorrect because dissection deep to the brachial fascia significantly increases the risk of sensory nerve injury and should be avoided.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old female patient, G3P3, is scheduled for panniculectomy combined with hernia repair. The surgical plan includes retrorectus hernia repair using polypropylene mesh without components separation. What represents a primary benefit of polypropylene mesh over biologic scaffold materials?
A) Reduced requirement for components separation
B) Lower hernia recurrence rates
C) Enhanced collagen cross-linking properties
D) Superior infection resistance
questions.answer:
B)
Polypropylene mesh demonstrates superior long-term durability with lower recurrence rates compared to biologic scaffolds. Synthetic mesh maintains its structural integrity over time, while biologic scaffolds undergo degradation by collagenase enzymes, contributing to higher failure rates. A) is incorrect because the need for components separation depends on hernia characteristics, not mesh type. C) is incorrect because collagen cross-linking is a feature of biologic scaffolds, not synthetic mesh. D) is incorrect because biologic scaffolds actually provide better infection resistance due to tissue incorporation and reduced foreign body reaction.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female patient, G2P2, receives breast augmentation surgery 12 months after delivery. Three days following the procedure, she presents to the clinic with compromised healing at the surgical site. Clinical evaluation reveals thick white fluid draining from the wound margin, characteristic of milk secretion. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Prescribing bromocriptine therapy
B) Prescribing metoclopramide therapy
C) Prescribing trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy
D) Implementing negative pressure wound therapy
E) Performing wound edge debridement with moist-to-dry dressings
questions.answer:
A)
Bromocriptine is the correct treatment as it is a dopamine agonist that suppresses prolactin secretion, thereby reducing milk production and galactorrhea, which allows proper wound healing to occur. B) is incorrect because metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that actually increases prolactin levels and would worsen galactorrhea. C) is incorrect because antibiotics like trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are unnecessary since the milk discharge is sterile and not infected. D) is incorrect because negative pressure wound therapy could potentially stimulate further milk production and worsen the galactorrhea, impeding healing. E) is incorrect because debridement is not needed when the issue is ongoing milk leakage rather than necrotic tissue.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old male patient is being assessed for scaphoid fracture nonunion. A vascularized bone flap reconstruction using a medial femoral condyle flap has been selected. During the harvesting procedure, the vascular pedicle of this flap travels between which of the following anatomical structures?
A) In front of the tensor fascia lata and behind the vastus lateralis
B) In front of the vastus medialis and in front of the adductor tendon
C) In front of the vastus medialis and behind the rectus femoris
D) Behind the rectus femoris and in front of the vastus lateralis
E) Behind the vastus medialis and in front of the adductor tendon
questions.answer:
E)
The medial femoral condyle vascularized bone flap serves as an excellent reconstructive option for extremity bone defects, especially for scaphoid waist and proximal pole nonunions. The blood supply originates from the descending geniculate artery located in the distal medial thigh region.
