When musculocutaneous perforators are encountered, harvesting a cuff of vastus lateralis muscle with the perforators helps ensure optimal perfusion, since intramuscular dissection can be challenging and may compromise the perforating vessels. A is incorrect because the gracilis muscle is located in the medial thigh and is not involved in anterolateral thigh flap anatomy. B is incorrect because while the rectus femoris forms one border of the flap territory, the perforators typically pass through the vastus lateralis rather than requiring rectus femoris muscle. C is incorrect because the sartorius muscle is located more medially and superficially, and is not part of the anterolateral thigh flap's vascular anatomy. D is incorrect because the tensor fascia lata is located more laterally and proximally, outside the typical anterolateral thigh flap harvest area.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency room after sustaining facial injuries from a bicycle handlebar accident. Which mandibular fracture site is most frequently linked to the development of anterior open bite?
A) Angle
B) Body
C) Coronoid
D) Subcondylar/condylar
E) Symphysis/parasymphysis
questions.answer:
D)
Anterior open bite (apertognathia) represents a vertical gap between the upper and lower front teeth. This condition results from early contact of the back molars, which occurs most frequently after bilateral subcondylar mandible fractures. In cases of unilateral subcondylar/condylar fractures, the open bite typically develops on the contralateral side to the fracture. A) Angle fractures do not typically cause premature posterior contact leading to open bite. B) Body fractures generally do not result in the mechanical changes needed for anterior open bite development. C) Coronoid fractures rarely affect occlusion in a way that produces anterior open bite. E) Symphysis/parasymphysis fractures may affect anterior teeth alignment but do not commonly cause the posterior premature contact that leads to open bite.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old female patient presents for a follow-up visit following left breast reconstruction using an implant. She exhibits a contour depression in the upper pole and requests correction. Insurance has preapproved autologous fat transfer from her abdomen to the upper pole region; 25 mL is administered to the upper pole area. What is the most suitable Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code?
A) 15877 and 11954
B) 15877 and 19380
C) 19380
D) 20926
E) 20926 and 19380
questions.answer:
D)

The appropriate response is Option D. Fat transfer procedures, like skin grafting, encompass both donor site management and recipient site preparation. The process involves fat collection, donor site closure with dressing, fat processing, and injection into the target area. Fat transfer is coded using 20926 (tissue grafts, other [e.g., paratenon, fat, dermis]) which encompasses: harvesting fat graft material through any technique (syringe, suction-assisted lipectomy, incision), donor site closure when necessary with proper dressing, fat graft processing, injection into recipient area, recipient site dressing, and 90 days of standard postoperative care. Code 20926 is neither anatomically specific nor volume-dependent, making it applicable whether injecting 50 mL into facial areas or 500 mL for thigh contour correction. Option A is incorrect because 15877 (suction-assisted lipectomy; trunk) cannot be billed separately as harvest is included in 20926, and 11954 is for off-the-shelf injectable products. Option B is incorrect for the same reason regarding 15877, and 19380 is not the primary code for this procedure. Option C is incorrect because 19380 alone does not adequately describe the complete fat grafting procedure. Option E is incorrect because while 20926 is correct, adding 19380 would be inappropriate coding for this specific procedure.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man has decreased grip strength in the right hand 4 years after sustaining a volar forearm laceration. A photograph of the hand posture is shown. No nerve repair was performed at the time of injury. During testing with the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints blocked, the patient attempts to extend the interphalangeal (IP) joints (Bouvier maneuver) but is unable to do so. Passively, the IP joints can be extended. Tendon transfer to improve grip strength is planned. During this procedure, the tendon is best inserted distally at which of the following locations?


A ) A2 pulley 
B ) Dorsal apparatus lateral band
C ) MCP joint volar plate 
D ) Palmar fascia 
E ) Proximal phalanx
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B. The patient described has a classic case of ulnar nerve palsy. If MCP hyperextension is passively prevented by dorsal pressure, the extensor digitorum communis may be able to extend the middle and distal phalanges (Bouvier maneuver). If this cannot be done, then the tendon transfer insertion is into the dorsal apparatus. Tendon transfer insertion into the A2 pulley and proximal phalanx will result in MCP joint flexion, but will have no effect on IP joint extension. Tendon transfer insertion into the MCP joint volar plate and palmar fascia are not appropriate locations.


References
1. Omer GE Jr. The palsied hand. In Evarts CM, ed. Surgery of the Musculoskeletal System. 2nd ed. WB Saunders; 1990:849-878. 
2. Omer GE Jr. Ulnar nerve palsy. In: Green DP, Hotchkiss RN, Pederson WC, et al, eds. Green ‚Ç¨‚Ñ¢s Operative Hand Surgery. 4th ed. Philadelphia: Churchill Livingstone; 1998:1526-1541.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male arrives at the emergency room with severe left wrist pain following a motorcycle accident. Radiographic images of the left wrist are provided. Which ligament below retains its connection to the lunate bone?
A) Dorsal intercarpal
B) Lunotriquetral
C) Radioscaphocapitate
D) Scapholunate
E) Short radiolunate
questions.answer:
E)
This patient demonstrates a type IV perilunate dislocation, also known as lunate dislocation. This condition involves complete disruption of all ligamentous stabilizers surrounding the lunate bone, with the exception of the preserved short radiolunate ligament, which serves as the axis around which the lunate rotates. The short radiolunate ligament remains intact and maintains the lunate's connection to the radius, allowing it to serve as a pivot point during the injury mechanism. A) Dorsal intercarpal ligament is incorrect because it becomes disrupted during the progression of perilunate injury as described in Mayfield's classification. B) Lunotriquetral ligament is incorrect because it ruptures during stage III of the injury sequence as the dislocation progresses from radial to ulnar. C) Radioscaphocapitate ligament is incorrect because it tears early in the injury process during stage I of Mayfield's progression. D) Scapholunate ligament is incorrect because it is the first ligament to rupture in stage I of the perilunate dislocation sequence.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old male patient with end-stage heart failure and a recently implanted left ventricular assist device (LVAD) presents to the clinic with an ulcerating lesion on the mid-parietal scalp. Punch biopsy confirms cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. His medical history includes bilateral temporal and midline craniotomies for symptomatic meningioma removal. Wide local excision results in an 8-cm diameter scalp defect with exposed calvarial bone lacking periosteal coverage. What is the most suitable reconstructive approach for this defect?
A) Synthetic dermal matrix followed by skin graft
B) Free fasciocutaneous flap transfer
C) Full-thickness cutaneous autograft
D) Rotational scalp flaps with skin grafting of donor sites
E) Pericranial flap reconstruction with overlying skin graft
questions.answer:
A)
Synthetic dermal matrix (such as Integra) followed by skin grafting represents the optimal reconstructive choice for this oncologic defect. This bilaminate artificial dermis consists of a collagen scaffold topped with a silicone membrane, with single-layer variants available for layering when additional tissue thickness is needed. The collagen matrix typically becomes vascularized within 3-4 weeks, after which the silicone layer is removed and a thin split-thickness skin graft is placed. When periosteum is absent, drilling the exposed skull to bleeding bone is recommended. B) is incorrect because free tissue transfer carries uncertain risks in LVAD-dependent patients with compromised hemodynamic status. C) is incorrect because full-thickness skin grafts cannot survive when placed directly on bone without periosteal coverage. D) is incorrect because this patient's multiple previous craniotomies have created scarring that significantly increases the risk of flap necrosis due to compromised blood supply. E) is incorrect because finding an adequately sized, unscarred, well-vascularized pericranial flap would be unlikely given this patient's extensive craniotomy history.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old female patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with sudden onset inability to straighten her ring and small fingers on the left hand. Operative examination reveals attritional tendon rupture and caput ulnae syndrome. Besides tendon repair, which of the following procedures would most effectively prevent this condition from recurring?
A) Distal ulna resection
B) Proximal row carpectomy
C) Radiocarpal arthrodesis
D) Scaphoid excision and four-corner fusion
E) Trapeziectomy and ligament reconstruction
questions.answer:
A)
Distal ulna resection (Darrach procedure) is the most appropriate intervention to prevent recurrence because it addresses the underlying cause of attritional tendon rupture in caput ulnae syndrome by removing the eroded, unstable ulnar head that causes tendons to abrade against it. This procedure eliminates the mechanical irritation that leads to tendon rupture while improving forearm rotation and relieving pain associated with distal radioulnar joint arthritis. B) is incorrect because proximal row carpectomy treats midcarpal arthritis, typically in osteoarthritic conditions like SLAC wrist, not DRUJ pathology. C) is incorrect because radiocarpal arthrodesis addresses radiocarpal joint arthritis rather than the DRUJ instability causing the tendon ruptures. D) is incorrect because scaphoid excision and four-corner fusion treats scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC) wrist, which is unrelated to DRUJ problems. E) is incorrect because trapeziectomy with ligament reconstruction treats thumb carpometacarpal arthritis, not DRUJ arthritis or caput ulnae syndrome.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male patient with a transplanted organ is planned for surgical removal of a scalp squamous cell carcinoma with subsequent flap reconstruction. Which immunosuppressive medication would most likely help this patient prevent postoperative wound healing problems?
A) Antilymphocyte antibody (basiliximab)
B) Antimetabolite (azathioprine)
C) Calcineurin inhibitor (cyclosporine)
D) Glucocorticosteroid (prednisone)
questions.answer:
A)
Antilymphocyte antibody therapy is the correct choice because it is the only category of immunosuppressive agents that does not interfere with wound healing processes. This makes it the safest option for patients undergoing major reconstructive procedures like flap surgery. B) is incorrect because antimetabolites like azathioprine have been demonstrated to impair wound repair mechanisms. C) is incorrect because calcineurin inhibitors such as cyclosporine negatively affect wound healing. D) is incorrect because glucocorticosteroids like prednisone are well-known to compromise wound healing by interfering with collagen synthesis and inflammatory responses.

questions.question:
What is the most probable etiology of congenital constriction band syndrome affecting the lower limb?
A) Abnormality in the zone of polarizing activity
B) Loss of the gene controlling the apical ectodermal ridge
C) Premature rupture of the amnion
D) Contact with retinoic acid
E) Thalidomide administration during gestation
questions.answer:
C)
Premature rupture of the amnion followed by entanglement of fetal structures (primarily limbs and extremities) by amniotic strands represents the leading theory for disease development. This condition presents with a broad range of clinical abnormalities from simple circular constrictions to severe organ defects. Lower limb malformations are very frequent and include asymmetrical digital ring constrictions, distal tissue loss, prenatal amputations, acrosyndactyly, lymphedema, and clubfoot deformity. A is incorrect because the zone of polarizing activity controls anterior/posterior limb orientation and does not cause truncation defects. B is incorrect because apical ectodermal ridge gene deletion causes limb shortening rather than constriction bands, affecting proximodistal growth patterns. D is incorrect because retinoic acid exposure interferes with apical ectodermal ridge function but does not produce constriction band pathology. E is incorrect because thalidomide causes various limb defects including phocomelia and amelia through vascular interference, but does not create constriction bands.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old female patient with bilateral cleft lip and palate comes to the clinic presenting with velopharyngeal insufficiency. A secondary speech operation is being considered. Which of the following surgical interventions has the greatest risk for postoperative obstructive sleep apnea development?
A) Furlow palatoplasty conversion
B) Palatal extension using bilateral buccal flaps
C) Secondary palate reconstruction with intravelar veloplasty
D) Pharyngeal sphincter plasty
E) Velopharyngeal enhancement with autologous fat injection
questions.answer:
D)
Pharyngeal sphincter plasty carries the highest risk for developing postoperative obstructive sleep apnea among the listed procedures. Pharyngoplasty techniques like sphincter pharyngoplasty add tissue to the velopharyngeal opening and partially block airflow, making them highly effective for correcting velopharyngeal dysfunction but resulting in OSA rates of 50-69%. A) Furlow palatoplasty conversion is incorrect because palatoplasty techniques have lower OSA risks (10-54%) compared to pharyngoplasty procedures. B) Palatal extension with bilateral buccal flaps is incorrect as this palatoplasty approach has moderate OSA risk but significantly less than sphincter pharyngoplasty. C) Secondary palate reconstruction with intravelar veloplasty is incorrect because this palatoplasty technique has lower OSA incidence than pharyngoplasty methods. E) Velopharyngeal enhancement with autologous fat injection is incorrect as this augmentation procedure has the lowest OSA risk at only 11%.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old manual worker presents with severe pain in his non-dominant left hand. His history reveals a palmar laceration affecting the ring and small fingers at the proximal phalanx level one year prior. During the initial injury, he had surgical repair of the flexor digitorum profundus tendon to the small finger and direct reconstruction of the ulnar digital nerve to the ring finger. All remaining nerves were undamaged. Current examination shows pain at the nerve repair location that impairs his occupational activities. No sensation exists beyond the repair site. A positive Tinel sign is present over the ulnar aspect of the ring finger scar. What surgical approach is most suitable for this patient?
A) Neuroma excision only
B) Neuroma excision with nerve burial into bone
C) Neuroma excision with nerve reconstruction using allograft
D) External and internal neurolysis while preserving neuroma continuity
E) Targeted muscle reinnervation or nerve transfer to adjacent motor nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The patient has developed a symptomatic neuroma in continuity following digital nerve repair, with complete loss of distal sensation and significant functional impairment. Neuroma excision followed by nerve reconstruction with allograft is the most appropriate treatment because it addresses both the painful neuroma and provides the best opportunity for sensory recovery in a young laborer with an intact distal nerve target. Studies by Moran et al. and Lans et al. demonstrate superior outcomes with excision and repair/reconstruction compared to other approaches, showing lower pain scores and better functional outcomes. Option A is incorrect because simple excision alone provides inferior results compared to excision with reconstruction. Option B is incorrect because nerve implantation into bone is typically reserved for cases without viable distal targets, such as amputations. Option D is incorrect because neurolysis preserves the problematic neuroma tissue and is unlikely to restore sensation or adequately address the pain. Option E is incorrect because targeted muscle reinnervation is primarily used for amputation scenarios rather than intact digits with viable distal nerve targets.

questions.question:
What complication is most frequently linked to prosthetic breast reconstruction when combined with postoperative radiation therapy?
A) Reduced implant failure rates
B) Lower seroma occurrence
C) Enhanced patient satisfaction scores
D) Higher capsular contracture risk
questions.answer:
D)
Prosthetic breast reconstruction combined with postoperative radiation therapy significantly increases the risk of capsular contracture. Radiation therapy also elevates the likelihood of seroma formation, impaired wound healing, and infectious complications. A is incorrect because radiation does not reduce implant failure rates. B is incorrect because radiation actually increases seroma occurrence. C is incorrect because radiation therapy typically decreases patient satisfaction due to increased complications and aesthetic concerns.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old female patient requests panniculectomy for managing skin irritation after losing 100 pounds following bariatric surgery performed 18 months prior. Her weight has remained constant for 3 months, and her present BMI is 30 kg/m2. Which factor in this patient's medical history is most likely to create barriers to insurance approval?
A) Current BMI of 30 kg/m2
B) Weight stability duration of 3 months
C) Time elapsed since bariatric surgery (18 months)
D) Chief complaint of skin irritation
E) Total weight reduction of 100 pounds
questions.answer:
B)
Insurance companies typically require a longer period of weight stability before approving panniculectomy procedures, with many carriers mandating 6 months of stable weight rather than the 3 months this patient has demonstrated. A) is incorrect because a BMI of 30 kg/m2 is relatively low and would generally support insurance coverage criteria. C) is incorrect because 18 months post-bariatric surgery provides adequate time interval and supports coverage eligibility. D) is incorrect because symptomatic skin irritation (intertrigo) is a valid medical indication that insurance companies recognize for panniculectomy. E) is incorrect because significant weight loss of 100 pounds demonstrates substantial improvement and supports the medical necessity for the procedure.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old female patient is scheduled for Er:YAG laser treatment (2940 nm wavelength) to address fine lines around her mouth. This laser procedure primarily targets which substance?
A) Collagen
B) Elastin
C) Hemoglobin
D) Melanin
E) Water
questions.answer:
E)
The Er:YAG laser at 2940 nm wavelength specifically targets water as its primary chromophore. Water has peak absorption at approximately 2900 nm, making the Er:YAG laser highly effective with 12-16 times greater water absorption compared to CO2 lasers. This targeted water absorption creates controlled thermal damage that stimulates skin rejuvenation. A) Collagen is incorrect because while collagen remodeling occurs as a secondary effect of laser treatment, collagen itself is not the direct target chromophore. B) Elastin is incorrect because like collagen, elastin regeneration happens as a healing response rather than being the primary laser target. C) Hemoglobin is incorrect because targeting hemoglobin would not effectively treat perioral wrinkles and is more relevant for vascular lesions. D) Melanin is incorrect because targeting melanin could cause unwanted pigmentation changes or burns rather than wrinkle improvement.

questions.question:
A 13-year-old female presents for assessment due to a 4-month duration of intense pain at the tip of her right index finger. No traumatic injury is reported. Physical examination reveals a normal-appearing finger without observable swelling or color changes. The discomfort worsens with local pressure during writing activities and her weekly swim sessions. An MRI T2-weighted image is provided. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Digital fibroma
B) Giant cell tumor
C) Glomus tumor
D) Neuroma
E) Venous malformation
questions.answer:
C)
This represents a glomus tumor. Glomus tumors are benign hamartomatous lesions arising from glomus bodies, which are neurovascular structures involved in skin temperature regulation. These subtle tumors typically manifest with pain, localized tenderness, and cold sensitivity. Radiographic studies may demonstrate cortical bone erosion near the lesion, while ultrasonography can provide diagnostic confirmation. MRI represents the most precise imaging technique, with these tumors appearing as bright, well-defined masses on T2-weighted sequences. A) Digital fibroma is incorrect because it represents a cutaneous fibroblastic growth that would be clinically visible, rarely produces pain, and would not demonstrate enhancement on T2-weighted MRI. B) Giant cell tumor is incorrect because while it can occur in this location, it rarely causes pain or cold intolerance and would not present as the well-circumscribed enhancing lesion seen on the T2-weighted image. D) Neuroma is incorrect because although it can produce focal pain similar to this case, the enhancing focal mass on T2-weighted MRI excludes solid lesions like neuromas. E) Venous malformation is incorrect because while it would enhance on T2-weighted MRI, it typically presents with visible swelling and lacks the well-defined borders characteristic of the lesion shown.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old female patient seeks buttock enhancement surgery. Her BMI measures 19.1 kg/m2. Given insufficient donor tissue availability for autologous fat grafting, gluteal enhancement using silicone implants is recommended. What represents the most frequently encountered complication after this surgical procedure?
A) Fat embolism
B) Hematoma
C) Infection
D) Seroma
E) Wound dehiscence
questions.answer:
E)
Wound dehiscence is the most frequently reported complication following gluteal augmentation with silicone implants, occurring in approximately 9.6% of cases. This higher complication rate compared to fat grafting is attributed to the increased surgical trauma and tension on wound closure sites. Bilateral parasacral incisions have been adopted to minimize wound healing problems compared to single gluteal cleft incisions. A) Fat embolism is incorrect because this complication is specifically associated with fat transfer procedures, not silicone implant placement. B) Hematoma is incorrect as it occurs in only 0.6% of patients, making it much less common than wound dehiscence. C) Infection is incorrect since it affects only 1.9% of patients, significantly lower than the dehiscence rate. D) Seroma is incorrect because it occurs in 4.6% of cases, which is less frequent than wound breakdown complications.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old female presents to the clinic seeking aesthetic enhancement of her nasal appearance. During physical examination, facial expression (particularly smiling) results in significant lowering of the nasal tip, reduction in upper lip length, and formation of a horizontal groove across the middle portion of the philtrum. These clinical observations are most characteristic of which muscle's activity?
A) Depressor septi nasi
B) Nasalis
C) Procerus
D) Risorius
E) Zygomaticus major
questions.answer:
A)
The depressor septi nasi muscle is responsible for this dynamic nasal deformity. This paired muscle originates from the medial crural footplates and inserts into either the maxillary incisive fossa or orbicularis oris muscle fibers. When activated during facial animation, it pulls the nasal tip downward while simultaneously shortening the upper lip and creating the characteristic horizontal philtral crease. B) is incorrect because the nasalis muscle primarily compresses nasal cartilage and draws the ala toward the septum without causing upper lip shortening. C) is incorrect because the procerus muscle acts on the medial eyebrow area, creating horizontal wrinkles over the nasal bridge rather than affecting the nasal tip. D) is incorrect because the risorius muscle retracts the mouth corners in a grinning motion without influencing nasal tip position. E) is incorrect because the zygomaticus major elevates and retracts the mouth corners during laughing without affecting the nasal tip or upper lip length.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old female presents for assessment due to sudden onset of complete left facial weakness with flaccid paralysis that began when she woke up 3 hours prior. She reports an altered metallic taste sensation and increased sensitivity to sounds. Loss of innervation to which muscle below would most likely explain her sound hypersensitivity?
A) Levator palatini
B) Stapedius
C) Tensor tympani
D) Tensor veli palatini
E) Zygomaticus major
questions.answer:
B)
This patient presents with classic Bell's palsy symptoms. The stapedius muscle is innervated by the facial nerve, and its denervation results in hyperacusis (sound hypersensitivity) because the muscle normally dampens loud sounds by stiffening the ossicular chain. A) Levator palatini is incorrect because it is innervated by the vagus nerve, not the facial nerve. C) Tensor tympani is incorrect because it is innervated by the trigeminal nerve and its dysfunction would not cause the described symptoms. D) Tensor veli palatini is incorrect because it is also innervated by the trigeminal nerve and controls eustachian tube function. E) Zygomaticus major is incorrect because while it is innervated by the facial nerve, its denervation affects facial expression (smiling) rather than auditory function.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old male experiences an avulsion trauma to the front of his ankle with tendon exposure following a motorcycle accident. After wound assessment, reconstruction using a reverse sural artery flap is scheduled. While raising the flap, which of the following would most likely jeopardize flap survival?
A) Damage to the lesser saphenous vein
B) Damage to the median superficial sural artery
C) Damage to the sural nerve
D) Cutting of the gastrocnemius muscle perforators
E) Cutting of the peroneal artery perforators
questions.answer:
E)
The primary vascular supply to the reverse sural artery flap depends on perforating vessels from the peroneal artery, which mainly arise approximately 5 cm above the lateral malleolus. A) is incorrect because damage to the lesser saphenous vein would not significantly affect venous drainage due to the presence of accompanying small veins that can bypass the main vein's valves. B) is incorrect because the median superficial sural artery provides forward blood flow to the flap and is routinely divided when creating the reverse flap. C) is incorrect because the sural nerve does not supply the primary blood flow to the flap but rather can provide sensation when the flap is harvested as a neural-veno-adipofascial flap. D) is incorrect because gastrocnemius perforators contribute to forward blood supply and are typically ligated during reverse flap elevation.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old woman comes to the office for evaluation of her breasts. Photographs of the patient are shown. Which of the following statements most accurately describes the anatomy of this patient's breasts?


A) The areola is normal size although the breast is small
B) The breast tissue is uniformly distributed throughout the breast pocket
C) The inframammary fold is elevated
D) The skin envelope has greater laxity than in a normal breast
E) The underlying musculature is underdeveloped
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The tuberous breast deformity results in a protruding, oblong shape that resembles a tuberous root plant (Latin derivation tuber = to swell). The features noted in the tuberous breast deformity include a constricted breast base, decreased breast parenchyma, abnormal elevation of the inframammary fold, a decreased skin envelope, and herniation of the breast parenchyma through the central breast and into the areola. The areola is large and lacks firm underlying structure, thus allowing the breast tissue to protrude through this path of least resistance. The deformity is also often referred to as a tubular breast, constricted breast, doughnut breast, nipple breast, breast with narrow base, dome nipple, and snoopy dog breast.


The overall etiologic factors leading to the full expression of the constricted breast deformity are still largely unknown and likely involve a delicate balance of anatomic and endocrinologic forces. A constricting fibrous ring at the level of the areola periphery, representing probably a thickening of the superficial fascia coupled with the normally absent fascial layer in the NAC, has been proposed as a likely cause. The ring is composed of dense fibrous tissue made of large concentrations of collagen and elastic fibers arranged longitudinally. It is usually denser at the lower part of the breast and does not allow the developing breast parenchyma to expand during puberty. It has been suggested that a thickening of the superficial fascia combined with the absence of a superficial fascial layer under the NAC is the underlying anatomic/histopathologic cause of the deformity. The cause of the thickened fascia is unknown, although at least one study by Klinger, Caviggioli, et al. demonstrated altered collagen in both disposition and quantity. The same study excluded amyloid deposition as a component of the fibrosis.


The areola in the tuberous breast still contains the normal muscular structures that result in areolar changes with stimulation and temperature changes, although the tissue beneath the areola may be thinned.


References
1. Pacifico MD, Kang NV. The tuberous breast revisited. J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg. 2007;60(5):455-464. Epub 2007 Feb 21.
2. Costagliola M, Atiyeh B, Rampillon F. Tuberous breast: revised classification and a new hypothesis for its development. Aesthetic Plast Surg. 2013 Oct;37(5):896-903. Epub 2013 Apr 30.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a laceration to her non-dominant fifth digit that occurred 6 months ago while preparing an avocado. Following the trauma, she reports decreased grip strength. Examination reveals a healed 1-cm cicatrix on the palmar surface of the proximal phalanx. She cannot actively bend the distal interphalangeal (DIP) or proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. Two-point discrimination testing is normal on both ulnar and radial aspects of the affected digit. Tendon reconstruction is planned to restore fifth digit flexion. What is the most crucial factor to verify prior to surgical intervention?
A) Integrity of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon
B) Position of the proximal flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) remnant
C) Adequate passive joint mobility
D) Availability of palmaris longus in either upper extremity
E) Bilateral grip strength comparison
questions.answer:
C)

The most critical preoperative requirement is ensuring adequate passive flexion of the affected digit, which will enable active motion following surgery. A) is incorrect because examination already demonstrates absence of flexor digitorum superficialis function, which cannot be restored given the nature of the sharp injury. B) is incorrect because the proximal FDP stump location is not a determining factor for secondary tendon reconstruction timing, and delayed primary repair would not be considered 6 months post-injury; additionally, in Zone 2 injuries without FDP function, the stump will be retracted into the palm due to lumbrical tethering. D) is incorrect because palmaris longus is not the sole donor option for secondary flexor reconstruction - plantaris and long toe extensors are also viable alternatives. E) is incorrect because preoperative grip strengthening would not contribute to preparing the fifth digit for reconstruction.

questions.question:
An 8-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with intense, progressively worsening pain along with digital swelling and numbness occurring three days following cast application for a left forearm fracture. Following cast removal, her discomfort persists and is exacerbated by passive wrist movement. What is the most suitable next diagnostic step for evaluating this patient's condition?
A) Angiography
B) CT scan
C) Duplex ultrasound
D) Electromyography
E) Manometry
questions.answer:
E)
The most suitable next diagnostic test is manometry. This patient demonstrates clinical signs consistent with compartment syndrome developing after swelling from her fracture beneath a constricting cast. Clinical manifestations of compartment syndrome include pain during passive stretching, elevated pressure upon palpation, sensory changes, motor weakness, skin color changes, and absent pulses. Prompt identification and intervention are essential to avoid irreversible damage. Elevated pressure within muscle compartments impairs circulation and nutrient delivery. Fasciotomy is warranted when compartment pressure surpasses 30 mmHg, or when the differential between compartment pressure and diastolic blood pressure falls below 30 mmHg. Without intervention, muscle ischemic necrosis may develop, resulting in Volkmann contracture and permanent functional impairment. Muscle scarring and shortening can lead to characteristic intrinsic minus hand deformity. Compartment pressures are measured using handheld devices (Stryker pen) or needle manometry techniques (Whitesides method) with arterial monitoring equipment. Surgical fasciotomy is necessary to decompress compartments and prevent tissue death in compartment syndrome cases.

A) Angiography is incorrect because while it evaluates vascular anatomy and perfusion, the clinical presentation of pain with passive stretching is not characteristic of arterial insufficiency.

B) CT scan is incorrect because although it provides detailed anatomical imaging, it would not be appropriate in this clinical scenario and would unnecessarily delay urgent treatment.

C) Duplex ultrasound is incorrect because while it can detect deep vein thrombosis which may cause pain and swelling, the specific symptom pattern here indicates the need for immediate compartment pressure measurement and potential fasciotomy.

D) Electromyography is incorrect because although it assesses nerve function, it would not be the appropriate immediate diagnostic step in this urgent clinical situation.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old female patient with Type V Fitzpatrick skin presents for assessment of a facial nevus on the right side. Clinical examination reveals a flat, blue-gray, asymmetric hyperpigmented patch extending across the right lower eyelid area, nasolabial crease, and cheek region. Scleral pigmentation is observed on the right eye. What is the most suitable therapeutic approach for this condition?
A) Cosmetic concealer therapy
B) Liquid nitrogen treatment
C) Mechanical skin resurfacing
D) Mohs surgical technique
E) Q-switched ruby laser therapy
questions.answer:
E)
This patient presents with nevus of Ota (oculodermal melanocytosis), a dermal melanocytic hamartoma characterized by blue-gray pigmentation in the trigeminal nerve distribution. Q-switched ruby laser therapy is the gold standard treatment, utilizing specific wavelengths (694 nm) and pulse parameters that selectively target dermal melanin through photothermolysis, providing optimal results with minimal complications. A) Cosmetic concealer therapy is incorrect because it only provides temporary cosmetic coverage without addressing the underlying condition. B) Liquid nitrogen treatment is incorrect as cryotherapy is ineffective for deep dermal melanocytes and can cause scarring and atrophy. C) Mechanical skin resurfacing is incorrect because dermabrasion cannot adequately reach deep dermal melanocytes and carries significant risk of scarring. D) Mohs surgical technique is incorrect as this precise excision method is not indicated or described for treating nevus of Ota lesions.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old female patient seeks cosmetic enhancement of her upper eyelids. She uses contact lenses daily without requiring eye lubricants. Compared to the left eyelid, the right upper eyelid shows a higher lid fold and the marginal reflex distance-1 (MRD-1) measures 1.5 mm. The left eyelid MRD-1 is 3.0 mm. Levator function is 12 mm on both sides. What is the most suitable eye examination for the next step in evaluating this patient for surgical intervention?
A) Phenylephrine test
B) Schirmer test
C) Tear breakup time
D) Visual acuity test
E) Visual field test
questions.answer:
A)
The phenylephrine test is the most appropriate next step because this patient has unilateral ptosis of the right eyelid with an elevated lid crease suggesting levator aponeurosis weakness. Due to Hering's law of equal innervation, the brain compensates for ptosis by sending increased signals to both eyelids, potentially masking ptosis in the contralateral eye. The phenylephrine test helps determine if bilateral ptosis repair is needed by stimulating Müller's muscle in the more ptotic eye, which reduces compensatory signals and reveals any hidden ptosis in the opposite eyelid. B is incorrect because the Schirmer test measures tear production, which is unlikely to be abnormal in this patient who comfortably wears contact lenses without symptoms. C is incorrect because tear breakup time assesses tear film stability and dry eye symptoms, but this patient shows no signs of dry eyes given her comfortable contact lens wear. D is incorrect because visual acuity testing provides baseline information but does not assist in surgical planning for ptosis correction. E is incorrect because visual field testing is primarily used for insurance documentation rather than surgical planning in ptosis cases.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old female presents for scar revision following a facial laceration on the left cheek that was sutured in the emergency room 2 years prior. Physical examination reveals a 4 × 0.7-cm scar that appears pale, flat, and widened. The scar runs obliquely from the corner of the mouth toward the cheekbone. A W-plasty technique is being considered. What is the most probable result of performing W-plasty compared to straight-line closure in this case?
A) Reduced initial tension on the wound
B) Shorter operative duration
C) Enhanced wound contracture
D) Greater excision of normal tissue
questions.answer:
D)
The W-plasty technique requires excision of considerably more healthy tissue compared to simple linear closure, which represents its primary disadvantage. This increased tissue removal leads to greater wound tension and necessitates more extensive undermining. The W-plasty creates multiple triangular flaps in an interdigitating pattern, requiring removal of normal skin on both sides of the existing scar to accommodate the geometric design. A is incorrect because the increased tissue removal actually creates more initial wound tension, not less. B is incorrect because the complex geometric pattern of multiple triangular flaps takes significantly longer to perform than a simple linear closure. C is incorrect because the broken-line configuration of W-plasty actually decreases contracture by creating an accordion-like effect that provides flexibility to the scar.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents to the clinic with painless swelling of his right index finger that has been present for 6 months. Radiographic imaging has been obtained. The treatment plan includes lesion curettage and reconstruction using demineralized bone matrix. What is the most probable result of this intervention?
A) Metastatic spread to distant sites
B) Tumor recurrence at the original location within 2 years
C) Bone fracture through the lesion with spread to adjacent soft tissues
D) Spread to nearby lymph nodes
E) Complete healing without tumor return
questions.answer:
E)
Complete healing without tumor return is the most probable outcome for this patient. The radiographic appearance is consistent with an enchondroma, which is a benign cartilaginous tumor that develops from displaced cartilage cells within the bone marrow cavity. These tumors represent approximately 90% of all bone neoplasms in the hand and typically affect the proximal phalanx, middle phalanx, and metacarpals. Enchondromas are benign lesions that respond well to curettage, with complete removal being curative and recurrence being rare. A is incorrect because enchondromas are benign tumors that do not metastasize to distant organs. B is incorrect because properly treated enchondromas have very low recurrence rates, and recurrence might actually suggest misdiagnosis of a low-grade sarcoma. C is incorrect because while pathologic fractures can occur due to cortical weakening, enchondromas do not extend into surrounding soft tissues. D is incorrect because these benign lesions do not spread to regional lymph nodes.

questions.question:
For which of the following cosmetic surgical procedures is prophylactic antibiotic administration most indicated?
A) Tummy tuck
B) Eyelid surgery
C) Arm lift
D) Breast lift
E) Facelift
questions.answer:
D)
Mastopexy (breast lift) is the procedure that most appropriately requires prophylactic antibiotics according to ASPS consensus guidelines. The guidelines specifically recommend systemic antibiotic prophylaxis for clean breast surgery procedures to reduce surgical-site infections, as breast surgery has been shown to benefit from routine antibiotic prophylaxis unlike other clean cosmetic procedures. A) is incorrect because abdominoplasty is specifically listed as a clean procedure that does not require antibiotic prophylaxis. B) is incorrect because blepharoplasty is a clean head and neck procedure for which prophylaxis is not recommended. C) is incorrect because brachioplasty falls under clean skin procedures that do not benefit from routine antibiotic prophylaxis. E) is incorrect because rhytidectomy is a clean head and neck procedure that does not require prophylactic antibiotics.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old female patient is assessed 6 hours following bilateral breast reconstruction using deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flaps. Doppler ultrasound reveals robust arterial flow in both reconstructed breasts. The right breast demonstrates a bluish discoloration with capillary refill occurring in 1 second, while the left side shows normal capillary refill of 3 seconds. What is the most suitable immediate management?
A) Administering tissue plasminogen activator
B) Placing medicinal leeches
C) Applying topical nitroglycerin paste
D) Immediate surgical exploration
E) Continued monitoring
questions.answer:
D)
The patient exhibits clear signs of venous congestion requiring immediate surgical intervention. Venous compromise in free flap breast reconstruction occurs in 2-20% of cases and may result from venous thrombosis, poor perforator selection, or inadequate deep venous drainage. Clinical indicators include cyanotic appearance, accelerated capillary refill, increased tissue firmness, temperature differential exceeding 2 degrees, dark blood on needle stick, and absent venous Doppler signals. Emergency operative exploration is essential to evaluate the vascular pedicle for clot formation, hematoma compression, vessel kinking, or inadequate venous drainage. Flap survival correlates directly with prompt exploration, with optimal outcomes when intervention occurs within 6 hours of compromise detection. A is incorrect because tissue plasminogen activator should only be administered locally within the flap tissue for suspected diffuse clotting. B is incorrect because leeches serve as an adjunctive therapy after addressing the primary vascular problem but cannot resolve underlying thrombosis. C is incorrect because nitroglycerin ointment may help random skin flaps but has no benefit in acute microvascular occlusion. E is incorrect because observation delays necessary intervention and significantly reduces flap salvage rates.

questions.question:
For a transhumeral amputation patient, targeted muscle reinnervation may be employed to enhance myoelectric prosthetic control. Which nerve transfer procedure below would provide natural prosthetic control for grip function?
A) Median nerve to short head of biceps
B) Musculocutaneous nerve to long head of biceps
C) Radial nerve to lateral head of triceps
D) Radial nerve to long head of triceps
E) Ulnar nerve to lateral head of triceps
questions.answer:
A)
Targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR) employs nerve transfer techniques to enable natural prosthetic control in upper limb amputees. Residual functioning nerves that have lost their original muscle targets are redirected to remaining proximal muscles, creating new electrical signals detectable by myoelectric prostheses. TMR also offers the advantage of potentially preventing or managing painful neuromas. In transhumeral amputation cases, the median nerve remnant is transferred to the motor branch of the biceps short head to generate signals for prosthetic hand closure, making this the correct choice. Option B is incorrect because the musculocutaneous nerve to long head of biceps is preserved for elbow flexion control rather than hand closure. Option C is incorrect because radial nerve transfer to lateral triceps head creates hand opening signals, not closure. Option D is incorrect because radial innervation of the long triceps head maintains elbow extension control. Option E is incorrect because ulnar nerve to lateral triceps head is not a standard TMR procedure for hand closure control.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old female patient with Fitzpatrick skin type V seeks consultation for acne scar treatment. A fractional nonablative laser procedure is being considered. Which laser option would be most suitable for treating acne scarring in this patient?
A) Carbon dioxide laser (10,600 nm)
B) Erbium-doped fiber laser (1550 nm)
C) Erbium:YAG laser (2940 nm)
D) Erbium:YSGG laser (2790 nm)
questions.answer:
B)
The erbium-doped fiber laser (1550 nm) is the most appropriate choice because it is a nonablative fractional laser that works by denaturing dermal collagen to promote remodeling without causing epidermal damage, making it safer for darker skin types like Fitzpatrick Type V. A) is incorrect because the carbon dioxide laser is ablative and carries higher risk of pigmentary changes in darker skin. C) is incorrect because the Erbium:YAG laser is ablative, not nonablative. D) is incorrect because the Erbium:YSGG laser is also ablative rather than nonablative.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old male patient with Crouzon syndrome presents to the craniofacial surgery department due to obstructive sleep apnea. His apnea hypopnea index measures 40. Clinical examination reveals a reverse overjet of 12 mm, moderate eye protrusion, and evidence of elevated intracranial pressure (>25 mm Hg) documented during intracranial pressure monitoring performed last month; the intercanthal distance remains within normal limits (25 mm). Which of the following osteotomy procedures would be most suitable for treating this patient?
A) Facial bipartition
B) Le Fort I
C) Le Fort III
D) Monobloc
E) Orbital box
questions.answer:
D)
The monobloc osteotomy is the optimal treatment choice for this patient with Crouzon syndrome presenting with both obstructive sleep apnea and elevated intracranial pressure. This procedure provides frontofacial advancement without altering orbital width, effectively addressing both the airway obstruction and increased intracranial pressure. A) Facial bipartition is inappropriate since the patient has normal intercanthal distance and lacks telorbitism, making orbital repositioning unnecessary. B) Le Fort I osteotomy only addresses the maxilla and cannot treat the orbital involvement or intracranial pressure issues. C) Le Fort III osteotomy would improve the sleep apnea but provides minimal benefit for the elevated intracranial pressure. E) Orbital box osteotomy fails to address either the sleep apnea or the increased intracranial pressure concerns.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old male presents to the clinic with a growth on his nasal tip. His medical history includes a decade of coronary artery disease, previous skin malignancies, facial surgical procedures, and inadequately managed type 2 diabetes mellitus. He maintains a 30-year smoking habit of one pack per day. Current medication is aspirin 81 mg daily. Physical exam reveals a 1-cm mass with uneven margins. Biopsy analysis demonstrates morpheaform basal cell carcinoma. What is the most suitable next management approach?
A) Cryotherapy
B) External beam radiation therapy
C) Intralesional injection of 5-fluorouracil
D) Mohs micrographic surgery
E) Wide local excision
questions.answer:
D)
Morpheaform basal cell carcinoma characteristically exhibits microscopic finger-like projections that extend beyond what is clinically visible and can only be detected through histological examination. This morpheaform variant has an elevated recurrence risk with standard excision techniques. Mohs micrographic surgery employs horizontal sectioning with immediate frozen section analysis, providing superior margin assessment accuracy. This technique also helps preserve healthy tissue by minimizing resection extent. Mohs surgery is especially valuable for morpheaform basal cell carcinoma, where achieving clear surgical boundaries is essential for reducing recurrence probability. A) is incorrect because cryotherapy is reserved for cases where surgery is contraindicated, which doesn't apply here. B) is incorrect because external beam radiation is only used when surgical options are not viable. C) is incorrect because intralesional 5-fluorouracil injection is rarely performed, represents off-label usage, and has poor cure rates. E) is incorrect because wide local excision on the nasal tip would create unnecessarily large defects when smaller margins could achieve clear boundaries.

questions.question:
In transgender women seeking facial feminization, forehead reconstruction primarily targets which of the following anatomical characteristics?
A) Bone density
B) Frontal bone breadth
C) Supraorbital prominence
D) Nasal root position
E) Midline frontal suture
questions.answer:
C)
Supraorbital prominence is the primary target of forehead feminization surgery. Male foreheads typically develop pronounced frontal sinus expansion and prominent supraorbital ridges during puberty, creating a masculine appearance that requires reduction and contouring to achieve feminine facial proportions. A) is incorrect because bone density is not the main concern in feminization procedures. B) is incorrect because while frontal bone width may be addressed, it is not the key feature requiring modification. D) is incorrect because nasal root position, though it may be elevated in males, is not the primary focus of forehead feminization. E) is incorrect because the metopic ridge is a developmental feature that is not typically the main target of feminization surgery.

questions.question:
A 12-month-old male child is brought in with a 3-cm lesion on his facial cheek. Which of the following features would most strongly suggest a lymphatic malformation diagnosis in this case?
A) Hard and firm consistency on examination
B) Pattern of recurring infectious episodes
C) Audible vascular sound on auscultation
D) Calcified venous stones visible on imaging
E) Initial rapid enlargement with subsequent regression
questions.answer:
B)
Lymphatic malformations represent benign collections of malformed lymphatic channels. These lesions are known by various classification systems including microcystic and macrocystic types, with historical terminology like cystic hygroma used for head and neck locations. Cystic hygromas can potentially cause respiratory obstruction in neonates. A hallmark feature of lymphatic malformations is their tendency to vary in size and their strong association with repeated infectious complications. On physical examination, they characteristically feel soft and easily compressed rather than hard and firm. While lymphatic malformations are congenital, they may not become clinically apparent until weeks or months after birth, particularly in the extremities. Unlike hemangiomas, they do not demonstrate the typical pattern of rapid proliferative growth followed by spontaneous involution. Management options range from observation for asymptomatic cases to surgical excision, sclerotherapy for large cystic components, or laser therapy for small superficial lesions. Recent research has identified PIK3CA gene mutations affecting tyrosine kinase signaling pathways in these malformations, potentially leading to targeted therapies. A is incorrect because lymphatic malformations are typically soft and compressible, not hard and firm. C is incorrect because bruits indicate turbulent flow characteristic of arteriovenous malformations, not lymphatic lesions. D is incorrect because phleboliths are calcified deposits found in venous malformations, not lymphatic ones. E is incorrect because rapid growth followed by involution describes the natural history of hemangiomas, not lymphatic malformations.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old male presents for evaluation of a 4-month history of a 2.5-cm, compressible, well-demarcated, painful dorsal mass on the right wrist. Physical examination reveals the mass is clearly defined, non-translucent, and becomes softer when the index and middle fingers are bent. An image is captured during surgical removal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Aberrant extensor indicis proprius attachment
B) Extensor digitorum brevis manus
C) Fibrosarcoma
D) Giant cell tumor of tendon sheath
E) Multilobulated ganglion cyst
questions.answer:
B)
Extensor digitorum brevis manus (EDBM) is an uncommon anomalous hand muscle (occurring in 2-3% of people) that can manifest as a painful dorsal wrist mass located distal to the radiocarpal joint near the distal border of the extensor retinaculum. This condition often mimics dorsal wrist ganglion cysts and has been frequently misdiagnosed as such. Key distinguishing features include the mass becoming firmer with resisted extension of the index and middle fingers and softening when these digits are flexed at rest as the muscle relaxes. Treatment options range from conservative management with rest and immobilization to surgical interventions including fourth compartment release alone or combined with complete muscle excision. A) is incorrect because aberrant EIP insertion is rare and wouldn't present as the described mass that changes consistency with finger movement. C) is incorrect because fibrosarcoma typically invades skin, has irregular borders, and doesn't alter firmness with digit flexion/extension. D) is incorrect because giant cell tumors of tendon sheath rarely reach this size and appear yellow rather than red. E) is incorrect because ganglion cysts would transilluminate and don't appear solid like the mass described.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a 2-cm basal cell carcinoma on her cheek that has been present for one year. The tumor is surgically removed with a 5-mm margin, creating a 3.0 × 3.0-cm tissue defect. A rhomboid flap is used to close the wound. What is the most appropriate current procedural terminology (CPT) code for this surgical procedure?
A) 11100
B) 11643
C) 14041
D) 11643 and 13132
E) 14040 and 11643
questions.answer:
C)
The correct CPT code for this procedure is 14041, which represents adjacent tissue transfer or rearrangement for a cheek defect. The rhomboid flap constitutes an adjacent tissue transfer procedure, and when this type of reconstruction is performed, the malignant lesion excision (11643) cannot be billed separately as it would constitute unbundling according to coding guidelines. A) 11100 is incorrect because this code is for skin biopsy, which significantly under-represents the complexity of this procedure. B) 11643 alone is incorrect because it only covers the excision of the malignant lesion but does not account for the reconstructive flap procedure. D) 11643 and 13132 is incorrect because these codes would only be appropriate if the wound were closed with complex suturing techniques involving extensive undermining, not with a tissue transfer flap. E) 14040 and 11643 is incorrect because 14040 is for smaller defects and the excision code cannot be separately reported with adjacent tissue transfer codes.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman sustains a traumatic amputation of her dominant thumb at the level of the trapezium. What is the most suitable approach for restoring thumb function in this case?
A) Bone grafting combined with free forearm flap coverage
B) Transfer of the great toe
C) Groin flap procedure followed by great toe transplantation
D) Pedicled radial forearm flap incorporating vascularized bone
E) Pollicization procedure
questions.answer:
E)
Pollicization is the optimal choice because it is the only option that can recreate the basal joint functionality. The index finger's metacarpophalangeal joint becomes the new carpometacarpal joint, while the digit's intrinsic muscles are repositioned to control thumb movement. This procedure also maintains excellent sensory function when the transferred finger has intact sensation. A) is inadequate because bone grafting with flap coverage cannot restore the complex joint mechanics needed at the carpometacarpal level. B) is suboptimal as great toe transfer alone lacks sufficient soft tissue coverage and requires the metatarsal base removal, which significantly impairs walking function. C) requires multiple procedures and still involves removing the great toe metatarsal with its associated ambulatory complications. D) cannot provide the articulating joint surface and intrinsic muscle function necessary for proper thumb opposition and positioning.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old female presents with hypernasal voice quality and air leakage through the nose during speech. She had tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy performed 10 weeks prior. Palatal transillumination findings are demonstrated. What is the most suitable treatment approach to restore normal speech function in this patient?
A) Autologous fat injection to tonsillar pillars
B) Orticochea pharyngeal reconstruction
C) Palatal repair surgery
D) Tensor veli palatini tendon fixation
E) Conservative management with speech therapy
questions.answer:
C)
The transillumination image reveals the absence of a normal levator muscle sling characteristic of an occult submucous cleft palate. Velopharyngeal insufficiency following tonsillectomy is an uncommon but recognized complication, occurring in approximately 1:3000 to 1:10,000 cases. This complication typically affects patients with either hidden or obvious submucous cleft palate anatomy. The surgical principle involves either reconstructing normal anatomy through two-flap palatoplasty or reconnecting the levator muscles to create a functional sling. Palate lengthening procedures, such as Furlow repair, help seal nasal air escape and improve velopharyngeal function. A) Autologous fat injection to tonsillar pillars would not address the underlying levator muscle deficiency. B) Orticochea pharyngeal reconstruction is not the primary treatment for this specific anatomical defect. D) Tensor veli palatini tendon fixation stabilizes the tensor tympani tendon during cleft repair and maintains eustachian tube patency but does not correct velopharyngeal insufficiency. E) After 8 weeks of velopharyngeal insufficiency, speech therapy alone cannot overcome the structural absence of the levator muscle sling.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male presents to the emergency room following a motorcycle accident with trauma to his left lower extremity. Radiographic imaging reveals a Gustilo IIIB tibial-fibular fracture. Following surgical debridement, a 12 cm osseous gap remains in the tibial mid-diaphysis. What is the optimal method for reconstructing this bone defect?
A) Autologous bone transplantation
B) Allograft bone transplantation
C) Reconstruction using vascularized fibular flap
D) Bone transport technique
questions.answer:
C)
Vascularized fibular flap reconstruction represents the most dependable approach for addressing such extensive osseous defects. This technique provides living, vascularized bone that promotes reliable healing and integration. A) Autologous bone transplantation is insufficient for such large defects as it lacks vascularization and would likely fail to bridge a 12 cm gap effectively. B) Allograft bone transplantation is less reliable than vascularized options due to lack of living cells and blood supply, making integration problematic. D) Bone transport technique, while feasible, requires prolonged treatment duration with extended periods of external fixation and patient immobilization, making it less optimal than immediate vascularized reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old female patient presents with bilateral swelling of both legs that began 2 years prior. Clinical examination reveals pitting edema extending throughout both lower limbs including the feet. A positive Stemmer's sign is present. Her BMI is 27 kg/m2. She recently emigrated from India. What is the most probable etiology of her leg swelling?
A) Filariasis
B) Lipedema
C) Lymphedema praecox
D) Lymphedema tarda
E) Podoconiosis
questions.answer:
A)
Filariasis represents the leading global cause of lymphedema. This parasitic infection results from the roundworm Wuchereria bancrofti, transmitted through mosquito vectors that deposit larvae onto the skin. These larvae then migrate to lymphatic vessels, causing obstruction. The condition is prevalent in India and sub-Saharan Africa, typically affecting the lower limbs. B) is incorrect because lipedema characteristically spares the feet and ankles, creating a "cuff sign," unlike this patient's presentation. C) is incorrect because lymphedema praecox is a rare primary developmental condition (1 in 100,000) that would be less likely than the endemic filariasis in someone from India. D) is incorrect because lymphedema tarda occurs after age 35, while this patient is only 19 years old. E) is incorrect because podoconiosis requires chronic barefoot exposure to silica-rich soil and typically presents with asymmetric involvement, whereas this patient has symmetric bilateral edema.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old female presents with extensive hidradenitis suppurativa affecting the inguinal and axillary regions. Which dermal structures are present in these anatomical locations and play a key role in this pathological condition?
A) Apocrine glands
B) Eccrine glands
C) Glomus bodies
D) Hair follicles
E) Sebaceous glands
questions.answer:
A)
Apocrine glands are specifically concentrated in the axillary, inguinal, and perineal regions, where they produce a thick, milky secretion that develops an offensive odor when colonized by bacteria. Blockage of these glands results in inflammatory responses and formation of subcutaneous abscesses characterized by pain, purulent discharge, and malodorous drainage. This debilitating condition typically requires management with long-term topical and oral antimicrobial therapy, though surgical intervention including drainage procedures or tissue excision may be necessary. B is incorrect because eccrine glands are distributed across the entire body surface and produce thin, clear sweat rather than the thick secretions associated with hidradenitis suppurativa. C is incorrect because glomus bodies are specialized structures found in cold-exposed areas like fingertips and ears that regulate blood flow through arteriovenous connections, not involved in this inflammatory condition. D is incorrect because while hair follicles are present throughout the body and some theories suggest follicular occlusion may contribute to the disease process, they do not form the characteristic abscesses that define the clinical presentation. E is incorrect because sebaceous glands produce oily sebum for hair and skin lubrication and are widely distributed except on palms and soles, but are not the primary structures involved in hidradenitis suppurativa pathogenesis.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents for follow-up assessment 14 months following a closed brachial plexus trauma from a car accident. Initial management at another institution included occupational therapy and conservative treatment. He has adhered to his rehabilitation program. Clinical examination reveals 4/5 motor strength in shoulder abduction, elbow flexion, elbow extension, and finger flexion. Wrist and finger extension are absent, though passive range of motion in the wrist and fingers remains intact. What is the most suitable next intervention to restore wrist and finger extension function?
A) Distal nerve transfer
B) Intraplexus nerve grafting
C) Pedicled latissimus muscle transfer
D) Tendon transfer
E) Continued observation
questions.answer:
D)

Tendon transfer is the most appropriate treatment for this patient to restore wrist and finger extension. At 14 months post-injury, this represents a chronic condition where nerve repair strategies are no longer viable due to intraneural fibrosis, Schwann cell loss, muscle atrophy, and motor end-plate degeneration that occur after 12-18 months. The patient has suitable donor muscles (4/5 strength from median and ulnar innervated muscles) and preserved passive mobility, making tendon transfers ideal. Common transfers include palmaris longus to extensor pollicis longus, pronator teres to extensor carpi radialis brevis, and flexor carpi ulnaris to extensor digitorum communis. A) Distal nerve transfer is incorrect because it should be performed within 6 months of injury for optimal results, and this patient is well beyond that timeframe. B) Intraplexus nerve grafting is incorrect because it is indicated for early/subacute injuries and is generally unsuccessful for lower trunk injuries in adults due to the long regeneration distance and time required. C) Pedicled latissimus muscle transfer is incorrect because while it can restore elbow function, it cannot reach beyond the elbow to provide wrist and finger extension. E) Continued observation is incorrect because at 14 months post-injury, spontaneous recovery is highly unlikely and active intervention is needed to restore function.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic with a 15-year progressive history of significant one-sided facial volume reduction. The patient expresses dissatisfaction with his altered facial aesthetics but reports no recent changes. Physical examination reveals substantial volume depletion confined to soft tissue structures with no evidence of skeletal deficiency. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Synthetic bone augmentation of the maxillary region
B) Soft tissue reconstruction using autologous tissue with cross-facial nerve grafting and free gracilis muscle transfer
C) Soft tissue reconstruction using a free parascapular flap
D) Soft tissue reconstruction using a pedicled temporalis muscle transfer
E) Injectable hyaluronic acid for soft tissue enhancement
questions.answer:
C)
This patient most likely has progressive hemifacial atrophy (Parry-Romberg syndrome), which is now stable. The optimal treatment is free tissue transfer using a microvascular parascapular flap, often followed by secondary fat grafting for refinement. A is incorrect because maxillary bone augmentation is unnecessary when there is no skeletal involvement. B is incorrect because cross-facial nerve grafting with gracilis transfer is reserved for facial nerve paralysis, not volume loss. D is incorrect because a temporalis muscle flap provides inadequate bulk for the affected area and may create a donor site deformity. E is incorrect because hyaluronic acid augmentation is only FDA-approved for HIV-related facial lipoatrophy, not other causes of volume loss.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents to the emergency room following a self-inflicted laceration with a kitchen blade. Operative examination reveals transection of the median nerve at the distal forearm level. The distal nerve segment remains relatively immobile, while the proximal segment has been elevated and rotated. Primary repair is intended. Where are the motor fibers of the proximal nerve stump most likely positioned in relation to the sensory fibers?
A) Dorsal and radial
B) Dorsal and ulnar
C) Volar and radial
D) Volar and ulnar
questions.answer:
C)
The motor fibers of the median nerve at the distal forearm are positioned volar and radial to the sensory fibers. At this anatomical level, the median nerve contains approximately 20% motor fibers and 80% sensory fibers. The motor component forms the thenar branch, which supplies the abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, and flexor pollicis brevis muscles. These motor fibers exit the main nerve trunk in a volar and radial direction relative to the sensory components as they branch toward the thenar muscles. A) is incorrect because the motor fibers are not located dorsally but rather on the volar aspect of the nerve. B) is incorrect because while the motor fibers are positioned volarly, they are radial rather than ulnar to the sensory fibers. D) is incorrect because although the motor fibers are volar, they are positioned radially, not on the ulnar side of the sensory components.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old woman presents to the clinic for assessment of excess abdominal skin. Physical examination reveals weakened abdominal muscles and fat distribution abnormalities in the central abdomen and flank areas. A tummy tuck combined with liposuction of the flanks and front abdominal skin is scheduled. Following this dual procedure, which abdominal zone carries the highest risk for tissue death?
A) I
B) II
C) III
D) IV
questions.answer:
A)
When abdominoplasty is performed together with liposuction, there is an elevated risk of complications including delayed wound healing, blood clots, fat embolism, tissue death, and fat necrosis. The combination of surgical undermining during tummy tuck with liposuction can compromise blood flow to the overlying skin. The abdominal wall's vascular supply is organized into three distinct zones: zone I (central abdomen fed by deep inferior epigastric vessels), zone II (lower abdomen supplied by external iliac vessels), and zone III (lateral abdomen and flanks nourished by intercostal, subcostal, and lumbar vessels). During abdominoplasty, lifting the abdominal flap cuts off circulation from zones I and II, making the flap dependent on zone III blood vessels for survival. Zone I, the central abdomen, experiences the highest rate of skin death when liposuction is combined with abdominoplasty because it loses its primary blood supply and is furthest from the remaining zone III circulation. Zone II is incorrect because while it also loses blood supply during flap elevation, it's closer to zone III perfusion. Zone III is incorrect because it maintains its blood supply and actually becomes the primary source of circulation for the flap. Zone IV is incorrect because this zone does not exist in the established anatomical classification system.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents to the emergency room 4 hours following an open mid-shaft tibial and fibular fracture sustained in a motorbike accident. A proximally based soleus muscle flap is selected for defect coverage. Which of the following vessels most likely provides the primary vascular supply to this flap?
A) Anterior tibial
B) Inferior geniculate
C) Peroneal
D) Profunda femoris
E) Superior geniculate
questions.answer:
C)

The peroneal artery is the primary blood supply to the proximal portion of the soleus muscle flap. The soleus is a large, flat muscle located in the posterior compartment of the calf that, together with the gastrocnemius, forms the triceps surae complex. It originates from the proximal third of the fibula and the medial tibial border, inserting into the calcaneus via the Achilles tendon. The soleus receives dual blood supply: the peroneal artery supplies the proximal portion while the posterior tibial artery supplies the distal portion. When used as a proximally based pedicled flap for middle third leg defect reconstruction, the peroneal artery serves as the dominant vascular pedicle. A) The anterior tibial artery supplies the anterior compartment muscles, not the soleus. B) The inferior geniculate artery supplies structures around the knee joint, not the mid-calf soleus muscle. D) The profunda femoris artery supplies the thigh muscles and does not extend to the lower leg. E) The superior geniculate artery also supplies knee joint structures and does not reach the soleus muscle.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient with type 1 diabetes presents with pyrexia, blocked nasal passages with discharge, and left periorbital edema. Endoscopic examination of the nasal cavity reveals dark-colored secretions and tissue death of the lower turbinate and surrounding nasal mucosa. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Candidal infection
B) Epiglottic inflammation
C) Mastoid infection
D) Mucormycosis
E) Necrotizing soft tissue infection
questions.answer:
D)
Mucormycosis is the correct diagnosis because this opportunistic fungal infection characteristically affects diabetic and immunocompromised patients, presenting with the classic triad of nasal obstruction, blackish necrotic discharge, and orbital involvement. The blackish secretions and necrotic turbinate tissue are pathognomonic features of rhinocerebral mucormycosis. A) Candidal infection is incorrect because candidiasis typically presents as white plaques rather than blackish necrotic tissue and doesn't cause this pattern of invasive disease. B) Epiglottic inflammation is incorrect because epiglottitis affects the supraglottic structures causing airway obstruction, not nasal cavity necrosis or orbital swelling. C) Mastoid infection is incorrect because mastoiditis involves the mastoid air cells behind the ear with associated ear pain and tenderness, not nasal cavity involvement. E) Necrotizing soft tissue infection is incorrect because necrotizing fasciitis spreads through subcutaneous tissues and fascia rather than causing the specific nasal cavity necrosis and orbital involvement seen here.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old female presents for body contouring consultation following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass performed 6 months prior. No signs of malabsorption are present. Current BMI is 36.3 kg/m2. She has lost 75 pounds (34 kg) and continues to lose weight. The patient complains of lower back pain. What is the most appropriate management at this time?
A) Liposuction
B) Panniculectomy
C) Gastric bypass revision
D) Upper gastrointestinal study
E) Continued observation
questions.answer:
E)
Observation is correct because patients typically continue losing weight for up to 2 years following bariatric surgery, and body contouring procedures should be delayed until weight stabilization occurs (usually 12-18 months post-surgery with stable weight for 3-6 months). Since this patient is only 6 months post-surgery and actively losing weight, waiting is most appropriate. A) Liposuction is incorrect because performing elective procedures during active weight loss increases surgical risks and may require revision as further weight loss occurs. B) Panniculectomy is incorrect for the same reasons as liposuction - the patient's weight is still changing and her BMI remains elevated for elective surgery. C) Gastric bypass revision is incorrect because there are no clinical indicators of bypass failure or malabsorption requiring surgical intervention. D) Upper gastrointestinal study is incorrect because the patient shows no signs of complications or malabsorption that would warrant diagnostic imaging.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient presents for breast augmentation and lift following a 50-pound (23-kg) weight reduction. She currently wears a 38B bra size. Clinical examination reveals second-degree breast drooping with a distance of 26 cm from the sternal notch to the nipple on both sides. The surgical plan includes concurrent breast augmentation with abbreviated-T lift technique using smooth saline breast prostheses placed in a dual-plane position via an inframammary approach. Which of the following elements places this patient at greatest risk for requiring additional surgery?
A) Inframammary approach for implant placement
B) Existing breast drooping
C) Utilization of surgical drains
D) Employment of saline-filled implants
E) Application of smooth-surface implants
questions.answer:
B)
The presence of existing breast drooping (ptosis) represents the highest risk factor for reoperation in this patient. Research has consistently demonstrated that combined augmentation-mastopexy procedures are technically more challenging and associated with significantly higher revision rates compared to either procedure performed independently. Statistical analysis of primary augmentation cases has specifically identified preexisting ptosis and concurrent mastopexy as independent predictors of increased reoperation rates, with higher grades of ptosis correlating with progressively elevated revision rates. A) is incorrect because inframammary incisions actually demonstrate the lowest capsular contracture rates among all surgical approaches. C) is incorrect because drain usage is not identified as a significant risk factor for reoperation in augmentation procedures. D) is incorrect because saline implants do not inherently carry higher reoperation risks compared to other fill materials. E) is incorrect because smooth implant surfaces, while associated with higher capsular contracture rates than textured surfaces, are not the primary risk factor in this clinical scenario.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old boy is seen following a pitbull bite to his face. The periorbital findings are shown in the photograph. A stent is placed and the ends of the stent are advanced across the canaliculus. The ends of the stent will enter the nasal cavity in which of the following locations?


A) Above the superior turbinate
B) Below the superior turbinate
C) Above the middle turbinate
D) Below the middle turbinate
E) Above the inferior turbinate
F) Below the inferior turbinate
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option F.


Reconstruction of the lacrimal apparatus is a critical step in addressing this patient's periorbital wounds. Failure to properly manage this aspect of the injury will lead to epiphora and the inevitable need for a secondary procedure to manage tear drainage.
