Delayed reconstruction of this injury would likely require a conjunctivodacryocystorhinostomy, a surgically created conduit between the eyelid and the nose. The best initial management of this lacrimal apparatus disruption is as described-placement of a stent through the canaliculi, into the lacrimal duct (contained within the maxillary bone), and into the nose. The exit point of the nasolacrimal duct is via the valve of Hasner, below the inferior turbinate. It is here that the ends of the stent can be identified and retrieved, although this is often quite challenging.

The frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinus cells drain into the middle meatus, just below the middle turbinate. 


The sphenoid sinus and posterior ethmoid sinuses drain into the sphenoethmoid recess, between the nasal septum and the superior turbinate.


ReferencesNetter, F. H. Atlas of Human Anatomy. Lacrimal apparatus. Ciba-Geigy. 1989.Drake, R., Vogl, W., Mitchell. A.W.M., Tibbitts, R. and Richardson, P. Gray's Atlas of Anatomy. 3rd. Edition. Churchill Livingstone. 2021.

questions.question:
A medical facility conducts a root cause analysis following an incorrect surgical site incident. The initial step involves verifying adherence to the Universal Protocol established by the Joint Commission. Which component below is mandated by the Universal Protocol?
A) Prior insurance approval for the surgical intervention
B) Preoperative identification and marking of the operative site
C) Post-procedure surgical team debriefing session
D) Implementation and recording of a surgical safety checklist
E) Utilization of uniform preoperative ordering protocols for routine procedures
questions.answer:
B)
The Universal Protocol established by the Joint Commission in 2004 mandates preoperative marking of the surgical site as one of its three essential components, along with proper patient identification by the surgical team and a final verification "time out" before the procedure begins. A) is incorrect because insurance pre-authorization is not part of the Universal Protocol requirements. C) is incorrect because post-procedure debriefing, while beneficial practice, does not prevent wrong-site surgery and is not mandated by the Universal Protocol. D) is incorrect because surgical safety checklists are part of CMS quality reporting requirements for ambulatory surgery centers, not the Universal Protocol itself. E) is incorrect because standardized preoperative order templates are not required elements of the Universal Protocol.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old female patient is having an arm lift procedure following significant weight reduction. To prevent damage to the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve during surgery, the surgeon should identify this nerve at the elbow in which anatomical position?
A) Beneath the deep fascia accompanying the basilic vein
B) Beneath the deep fascia accompanying the cephalic vein
C) Above the deep fascia accompanying the basilic vein
D) Above the deep fascia accompanying the cephalic vein
questions.answer:
C)
The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (MABC) runs superficial to the deep fascia alongside the basilic vein, making option C correct. This sensory nerve originates from the medial cord of the brachial plexus and travels with the basilic vein medially to the biceps brachii, piercing the fascia at the basilic hiatus before reaching the elbow. Option A is incorrect because the MABC lies superficial, not deep, to the deep fascia. Option B is incorrect because the nerve travels with the basilic vein, not the cephalic vein, and is not located deep to the fascia. Option D is incorrect because while it correctly identifies the superficial position, the nerve accompanies the basilic vein rather than the cephalic vein.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man comes to the office because of difficulty grasping items with the left hand. He sustained a sharp amputation of the thumb in the distal third of the proximal phalanx 9 months ago. Palmar and radial abduction of the residual thumb is symmetric to the uninjured thumb. Photographs are shown. Which of the following procedures is most likely to improve hand function in this patient?


A) Four-flap Z-plasty of the first web space
B) Groin flap
C) Heterodigital island flap augmentation of the thumb
D) Pollicization of the index finger
E) Resection of the first dorsal interosseous muscle
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


When approaching post-traumatic thumb reconstruction, two of the most important factors in determining treatment are the residual length and relative function of the remaining thumb. In this patient with a distal amputation and good active range of motion, the simplest and most beneficial procedure would be web-space deepening via a four-flap Z-plasty. Simple Z-plasty and dorsal rotational flaps can also serve to deepen the first web, but the most commonly used technique is the four-flap Z-plasty.


Groin flap can address soft-tissue defecits that this patient does not have.


Instances involving contractures of the first web space frequently require release or resection of some of the first web musculature, including the first dorsal interosseous. In a supple thumb with good abduction, this would not be necessary.


Pollicization of the index finger or the stump of an index finger can be useful when amputation occurs in the proximal third of the thumb. In the setting of a healthy index finger, however, amputations through the metacarpal would likely be best handled via toe-to-thumb transplantation.


Heterodigital island flaps are one method of restoring glabrous, sensate skin to the palmar surface of the thumb. Such flaps were useful primarily when trying to restore sensation to a thumb reconstructed through osteoplastic techniques. This flap would not add length to the thumb or serve to deepen the web space.
References
1. Muzaffar AR, Chao JJ, Friedrich JB. Posttraumatic thumb reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2005 Oct;116(5):103e-122e.
2. Friedrich JB, Vedder NB. Thumb reconstruction. Clin Plast Surg. 2011 Oct;38(4):697-712.

questions.question:
When harvesting a plantaris tendon graft, which structure faces the highest risk of inadvertent injury?
A) Dorsalis pedis artery
B) Extensor hallucis brevis muscle
C) Medial plantar artery
D) Sural nerve
E) Tibial nerve
questions.answer:
E)
The tibial nerve is at greatest risk during plantaris tendon harvest because the dissection begins behind the medial malleolus in close proximity to this nerve. The plantaris graft is accessed through a vertical incision anterior to the medial Achilles tendon, and the tendon is traced proximally, placing the tibial nerve in the surgical field. A) The dorsalis pedis artery is incorrect because it runs over the dorsum of the foot, well away from the plantaris harvest site. B) The extensor hallucis brevis muscle is incorrect as it is located on the dorsal foot, distant from the medial ankle dissection area. C) The medial plantar artery is incorrect because it courses along the plantar surface of the foot, distal to the harvest location. D) The sural nerve is incorrect since it travels near the lateral malleolus, not the medial side where plantaris harvest occurs.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male presents with a history of left-sided facial injury and mandibular condylar fracture. He reports experiencing erythema and sweating of the left cheek and ear region when consuming specific foods. Abnormal regrowth of which nerve is most likely responsible for these symptoms?
A) Auriculotemporal
B) Facial
C) Great auricular
D) Inferior alveolar
E) Lingual
questions.answer:
A)
The auriculotemporal nerve is correct. This patient has Frey syndrome, which while typically occurring after parotid gland surgery, can also develop following mandibular condylar fractures. The condition results from injury to parasympathetic fibers of the auriculotemporal nerve, leading to inappropriate reinnervation of sweat glands and causing gustatory sweating. B) is incorrect because facial nerve damage would cause motor weakness or taste disturbances, not gustatory sweating. C) is incorrect because the great auricular nerve provides sensory innervation to the ear and angle of jaw but is not involved in autonomic sweating responses. D) is incorrect because the inferior alveolar nerve supplies sensation to lower teeth and lip, not the sweating mechanism described. E) is incorrect because the lingual nerve carries taste and sensation to the tongue but does not control facial sweating patterns.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old male presents to the clinic with neurological deficits in his left leg following a femoral-distal bypass procedure performed 5 days earlier. Clinical examination reveals loss of sensation on the sole of the foot and impaired plantarflexion strength. Which nerve is most likely damaged in this case?
A) Femoral
B) Obturator
C) Peroneal
D) Sural
E) Tibial
questions.answer:
E)
This patient exhibits classic signs of tibial nerve damage. The tibial nerve, originating from the sciatic nerve, courses through the popliteal region and innervates the posterior compartment muscles including gastrocnemius, soleus, plantaris, and popliteus. It runs alongside the posterior tibial vessels and supplies the deep posterior compartment muscles (flexor digitorum longus, tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus). Distally, it divides into medial and lateral plantar branches that provide sensory innervation to the sole of the foot. Tibial nerve injury causes plantarflexion weakness and plantar foot numbness, matching this patient's presentation. A) The femoral nerve is incorrect because it supplies the anterior thigh muscles (quadriceps, iliacus, sartorius) and its injury would cause knee extension weakness, not plantarflexion deficits or plantar numbness. B) The obturator nerve is incorrect because it innervates the medial thigh adductor muscles and provides sensation to the medial thigh, not the foot. C) The peroneal nerve is incorrect because its superficial branch controls foot eversion and provides lateral leg sensation, while its deep branch controls dorsiflexion and provides first web space sensation - neither matches this patient's symptoms. D) The sural nerve is incorrect because it is purely sensory, providing sensation to the lateral foot without any motor function, so it cannot cause plantarflexion weakness.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man comes to the emergency department after sustaining a laceration of the palm of the left hand from a knife. He reports difficulty flexing the ring finger of the left hand. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate method to clinically assess the integrity of the flexor digitorum superficialis tendon?


A) Hold the distal interphalangeal joint of the ring finger in extension and ask the patient to flex
B) Hold the index, long, and little fingers in extension and ask the patient to flex
C) Hold the long, ring, and little fingers flexed at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint and ask the patient to flex
D) Hold the MCP joints of the index, long, and little fingers in flexion and ask the patient to extend
E) Hold the ring finger extended at the MCP joint and ask the patient to flex
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


The flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon flexes the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint. The flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon can also flex the PIP joint, in addition to flexing the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint. To confirm that the FDS tendon is flexing the PIP joint, FDP motion must be excluded.


The FDP tendons to the long, ring, and little fingers share a common muscle belly. Thus, holding the long and little fingers in extension will prevent the FDP to the long, ring, and little fingers from firing. Any flexion of the PIP joint of the ring finger must then be caused by the FDS tendon.


Holding the DIP joint of the ring finger in extension will prevent DIP flexion. It will not, however, prevent the pull of the FDP tendon from being transmitted to the PIP joint.


Holding the long, ring, and little fingers flexed at the MCP joint will not exclude FDP motion.


Holding the MCP joint of the ring finger extended will not exclude FDP motion.


Asking the patient to extend will not assess the integrity of a flexor tendon such as the FDS.


References
Selier JG III. Essentials of Hand Surgery. Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2001.
Zidel P. Tendon healing and flexor tendon surgery. In: Thorne CH, Beasley RW, Aston SJ, et al, eds. Grabb and Smith's Plastic Surgery. 6th ed. Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2007.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old female presents to the clinic with a 2-year history of a mass on her right ear. Clinical examination reveals a 2.5 × 2 × 1.5-cm neurofibroma located on the concha. Complete excision of the conchal bowl skin and underlying conchal cartilage is being considered. Which of the following reconstructive flaps would be most suitable for repairing this defect?
A) Postauricular island
B) Rhomboid
C) Rim advancement
D) Rotation advancement
E) Temporalis fascia
questions.answer:
A)
The postauricular island flap is the optimal choice for reconstructing large conchal defects. When lesions involve the thin anterior conchal skin and perichondrium, adequate removal typically necessitates excision of the underlying conchal cartilage. While skin grafts can close such defects, local flaps offer superior outcomes with better color match, reduced contracture, and improved contour restoration. The postauricular "revolving door" island flap is specifically designed for extensive conchal reconstruction, with the flap's security increasing with pedicle size. This technique allows complete conchal replacement by rotating the posterior skin island through the ear into the conchal defect while primarily closing the donor site. B) Rhomboid flaps are inappropriate here due to insufficient donor tissue availability in this location and are better suited for areas with loose skin like the cheek. C) Rim advancement flaps are specifically designed for helical defects, not conchal reconstruction. D) Rotation advancement flaps are also intended for helical defects, particularly larger ones requiring postauricular skin undermining. E) Temporalis fascia flaps are used for total ear resurfacing but require additional skin coverage over the fascia, making them unnecessarily complex for this conchal defect.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old child presents with a unilateral cleft lip and palate. Tympanometry reveals bilateral non-compliance. Which muscle is most likely causing this abnormal finding?
A) Levator veli palatini
B) Palatoglossus
C) Palatopharyngeus
D) Superior constrictor
E) Tensor veli palatini
questions.answer:
E)
The tensor veli palatini is responsible for this finding. Non-compliant tympanograms suggest eustachian tube dysfunction with poor drainage. The tensor veli palatini plays a crucial role in equalizing pressure between the middle ear and nasopharynx. In cleft palate patients, this muscle has abnormal insertion into the levator palatini, leading to increased eustachian tube dysfunction. A) Levator veli palatini is incorrect because its primary role is velopharyngeal closure through velar elevation and posterior movement. B) Palatoglossus is incorrect as it functions in speech modulation by depressing the velum and elevating the tongue. C) Palatopharyngeus is incorrect because it controls the velopharyngeal sphincter by regulating velar dimensions and positioning. D) Superior constrictor is incorrect as its main function is pharyngeal closure during deglutition and speech production.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents to the clinic for assessment of drooping eyelid affecting one eye. During the physical examination, the movement range of the eyelid border is assessed from looking down to looking up while the eyebrow is held stationary against the bony ridge above the eye socket. Which of the following represents the typical range of movement for normal levator muscle function in this patient?
A) 2 to 6 mm
B) 7 to 11 mm
C) 12 to 16 mm
D) 17 to 21 mm
E) 21 to 25 mm
questions.answer:
C)
Normal levator function typically demonstrates an excursion distance of 12 to 16 mm when measured from downgaze to upgaze with the eyebrow stabilized. This measurement reflects the proper contractile ability of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. A) is incorrect because 2-6 mm indicates severely impaired levator function, often requiring surgical intervention. B) is incorrect because 7-11 mm represents moderately reduced levator function, which is below normal parameters. D) is incorrect because 17-21 mm exceeds the typical normal range and would be considered hyperfunctional. E) is incorrect because 21-25 mm represents excessive levator function that is well above normal physiological limits.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old female patient has right-sided facial paralysis from birth trauma. Dynamic facial reconstruction is being considered using a free gracilis muscle transfer. Compared to utilizing the masseteric nerve branch as the motor source, what advantage is a cross-facial nerve graft most likely to offer this patient?
A) Reduced number of surgical procedures
B) Increased smile amplitude
C) Superior axonal density
D) Enhanced longevity of results during growth
E) Improved natural, synchronized facial expression
questions.answer:
E)
A cross-facial nerve graft provides a more natural, synchronized smile compared to the masseteric nerve because it utilizes the patient's inherent neural pathways for facial expression. The contralateral facial nerve that innervates the unaffected side also controls the reconstructed side, resulting in better coordination between both sides of the face during smiling. A is incorrect because cross-facial nerve grafting actually requires an additional surgical stage to harvest and place the nerve graft, increasing the total number of procedures. B is incorrect because the masseteric nerve typically provides greater commissure movement and excursion than cross-facial grafts. C is incorrect because the masseteric nerve has a higher axon count compared to the distal portion of a cross-facial nerve graft. D is incorrect because long-term studies show that children do not typically outgrow facial reanimation procedures, and durability is similar between both approaches.

questions.question:
Based on 2017 US breast cancer mortality statistics, three states with adequate statistical power demonstrated comparable death rates between non-Hispanic African American and non-Hispanic Caucasian women. Which factor most likely contributed to the enhanced survival outcomes among non-Hispanic African American women in these states?
A) Greater wealth among non-Hispanic African American women
B) Younger age distribution of non-Hispanic African American women
C) Lower incidence of "triple-negative" aggressive breast malignancies in non-Hispanic African American women
D) Enhanced availability of screening mammography and early-stage detection for non-Hispanic African American women
questions.answer:
D)
Improved access to screening mammography and early detection services was the primary factor contributing to better mortality outcomes. The three states (Massachusetts, Connecticut, and Delaware) that achieved statistical equivalence in mortality rates had sufficient numbers of non-Hispanic African American women diagnosed with in situ breast cancer, which serves as an indicator of effective screening mammography access. This enhanced access to screening and care resulted in earlier stage diagnosis and improved survival rates. A is incorrect because the studies did not address affluence as a contributing factor. B is incorrect because age was specifically ruled out as a factor in these findings. C is incorrect because there are no data suggesting that non-Hispanic African American women in these states had fewer triple-negative breast cancers, and this factor was not implicated in the mortality improvements.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old female patient experiences diminished nipple-areolar complex sensation following breast lift surgery. Surgical damage to which nerve is most likely responsible for this loss of sensation?
A) Intercostobrachial nerve
B) Lateral cutaneous branch of the fourth intercostal nerve
C) Lateral cutaneous branch of the sixth intercostal nerve
D) Medial cutaneous branch of the fifth intercostal nerve
E) Medial cutaneous branch of the third intercostal nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The lateral cutaneous branch of the fourth intercostal nerve provides the primary sensory innervation to the nipple-areolar complex. This nerve is most frequently responsible for areolar sensation and is commonly at risk during mastopexy procedures. A) is incorrect because the intercostobrachial nerve primarily innervates the medial upper arm region, not the nipple-areola. C) is incorrect because the lateral cutaneous branch of the sixth intercostal nerve contributes to lower breast sensation but not primarily to the areola. D) is incorrect because the medial cutaneous branch of the fifth intercostal nerve provides sensation to other breast areas but not the primary areolar innervation. E) is incorrect because the medial cutaneous branch of the third intercostal nerve supplies sensation to upper breast tissue rather than the nipple-areolar complex.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female patient presents to the clinic seeking breast augmentation surgery. During her preoperative evaluation, she mentions that her mother experienced malignant hyperthermia in the past. The patient has no prior surgical history. Which anesthetic medication would be the safest choice for this procedure?
A) Desflurane
B) Halothane
C) Isoflurane
D) Propofol
E) Succinylcholine
questions.answer:
D)
Propofol is the safest anesthetic option for this patient with a family history of malignant hyperthermia. Propofol is a non-triggering agent that does not cause the hypermetabolic reaction associated with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility. It can be safely administered to patients at risk for this condition without precipitating a crisis. A) Desflurane is incorrect because it is a volatile anesthetic agent that can trigger malignant hyperthermia episodes. B) Halothane is incorrect as it is also a volatile anesthetic known to be a potent trigger for malignant hyperthermia reactions. C) Isoflurane is incorrect because it belongs to the class of volatile anesthetics that can precipitate malignant hyperthermia in susceptible individuals. E) Succinylcholine is incorrect as it is a depolarizing muscle relaxant that is a well-known trigger for malignant hyperthermia crises.

questions.question:
A 69-year-old male patient is planned for surgical removal and primary closure of a basal cell carcinoma on his chest. His medical background includes taking 81 mg aspirin daily for primary cardiovascular disease prevention. In comparison to patients who are not on aspirin prophylaxis, this patient has the highest likelihood of developing which of the following complications?
A) Hematoma formation
B) Poor aesthetic results
C) Separation of wound edges
D) Bacterial wound contamination
E) None of the listed complications
questions.answer:
E)
Systematic reviews encompassing 30 studies with over 14,000 patients undergoing minor dermatologic procedures strongly recommend continuing aspirin therapy during all minor skin surgeries, as patients taking aspirin alone show no increased risk of bleeding complications compared to those not taking anticoagulants. The overwhelming evidence supports careful surgical hemostasis rather than stopping aspirin to prevent bleeding issues in minor skin procedures. A is incorrect because aspirin monotherapy does not increase hematoma risk in minor cutaneous surgery. B is incorrect because no association exists between aspirin use and poor cosmetic outcomes. C is incorrect because aspirin does not increase wound dehiscence risk. D is incorrect because aspirin use is not linked to increased infection rates.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old female presents for assessment due to a 2-month duration of a painless 1-cm nodule on the palmar radial side of her wrist. Her parents report no traumatic incident. Physical examination reveals the nodule is mobile from the overlying skin but fixed to underlying structures. She demonstrates complete wrist mobility without evidence of carpal instability. Radiographic imaging of the wrist appears normal. MRI findings are compatible with a ganglion cyst. No carpal ligament damage is identified. What is the most suitable initial management approach?
A) Watchful waiting
B) Injection therapy
C) Manual compression rupture
D) Arthroscopic wrist examination
E) Operative removal
questions.answer:
A)
Watchful waiting is the most appropriate initial management. While there is no universal agreement on optimal treatment for pediatric ganglion cysts, most experts recommend observation and splinting for asymptomatic wrist ganglions. Literature shows that the majority of pediatric wrist ganglions will spontaneously rupture and resolve without any intervention. The diagnosis has been established through clinical evaluation and MRI, eliminating the need for biopsy. Since the lesion is asymptomatic and imaging shows no carpal ligament injury, surgical intervention is not warranted. B) Injection therapy is incorrect because sclerotherapy is not an established treatment for wrist ganglions. C) Manual compression rupture is incorrect as this represents an outdated and traumatic approach to ganglion treatment. D) Arthroscopic wrist examination is incorrect because there is no indication for surgical exploration given the absence of symptoms and ligamentous injury. E) Operative removal is incorrect because surgical excision is not indicated for asymptomatic ganglions without complications.

questions.question:
A 57-year-old woman presents to the clinic expressing concern about her eye appearance. She describes them as looking "small" and "weary." On examination, she demonstrates excess upper eyelid skin, 2 mm of lid drooping, prominent horizontal forehead creases, and fine wrinkles around the eyes. When opening her eyelids, she raises her eyebrows by 3 mm. An upper lid skin excision with formal ptosis correction is scheduled. Following this surgery, which of the following outcomes is most probable?
A) Involuntary eyelid spasms
B) Eyebrow drooping
C) Reduced visible eyelid margin
D) Loss of upper lid fullness
E) Upper eyelid elevation beyond normal
questions.answer:
B)
Following blepharoplasty and ptosis correction in a patient with compensatory eyebrow elevation, worsening of eyebrow drooping is the most likely outcome. When patients habitually elevate their eyebrows to compensate for eyelid drooping, correcting the ptosis removes the need for this compensation, allowing the eyebrows to settle into their natural, lower position. A) is incorrect because involuntary eyelid spasms are not a typical consequence of this procedure. C) is incorrect because ptosis repair typically increases rather than decreases the visible eyelid margin. D) is incorrect because loss of upper lid fullness is not a primary expected finding after ptosis repair. E) is incorrect because eyelid retraction, while possible, is less likely than the unmasking of pre-existing brow ptosis.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old female patient comes to the clinic worried about how her breasts look. Physical examination reveals breast asymmetry with severe (grade III) sagging, reduced breast base dimensions bilaterally, and enlarged nipple-areolar complexes with protrusion of breast tissue through them. Which of the following features of tuberous breast anomaly accounts for the clinical presentation observed in this patient?
A) Excessive growth of one or more breast segments
B) Excessive growth limited to the inner breast segments
C) Underdeveloped areola
D) Positioned inframammary crease below normal
E) Constricting fibrous band around the areola
questions.answer:
E)
Tuberous breast deformity results from abnormal connective tissue development during adolescence. The key feature responsible for this patient's findings is the constricting fibrous band around the areola (periareolar ring constriction), which creates the characteristic enlarged nipple-areolar complex with breast tissue herniation, contributes to the narrow breast base, and leads to asymmetry. A is incorrect because tuberous breasts involve hypoplasia (underdevelopment) rather than hyperplasia of breast quadrants. B is incorrect as the condition affects various quadrant combinations, not specifically medial hyperplasia. C is incorrect because the areola is typically enlarged, not underdeveloped, in tuberous breast deformity. D is incorrect because tuberous breasts characteristically have a high (elevated) rather than low inframammary fold position.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after his left foot was severed when his leg was run over by a train. Photographs are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management? 


A ) Construction of a foot filet free flap 
B ) Replantation and ankle fusion 
C ) Revision amputation to the level of the skin edge and primary closure 
D ) Split-thickness skin grafting 
E ) Temporary revascularization with shunts and delayed replantation
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The patient described has a limb amputation that includes a significant avulsion component, exemplified in the long tendon stumps that appear ripped off from their muscle bellies, and ankle disarticulation. Avulsion amputations of the lower extremity are not suitable for replantation because of the extended neurovascular damage that is present on both ends well beyond the level of the injury. The incidence of thrombosis at the anastomosis is high. Use of vein grafts on a free flap could be considered, but, in this case, they may have to be connected as high as knee level to ensure patency. The amputated part likely has massive microscopic endothelial damage extending to terminal vessels and could only be used as a donor site for skin grafts. Therefore, there is no role for immediate or delayed replantation.


While preservation of maximum tibial length is desirable in preparing the amputation stump, prosthetic fitting for ankle disarticulations is fraught with trouble. Some tibial shortening is required to have a comfortable, reliable prosthesis. In the scenario described, tibial shortening of 2 and 4 in would have equivalent results because there is still ample length of proximal tibia


available to provide the same functionality and equivalent energy expenditure. Therefore, use of a free flap to protect an additional 2 in of tibia adds no advantage for this patient. When the level of amputation is through the proximal tibia, some benefit could be found in that a minimum of 6 in of proximal tibia is available for prosthetic fitting. Split-skin grafts are generally unstable in weight-bearing surfaces and take longer to heal and mature, which causes delay in rehabilitation. Skin grafts will not take or perform well when applied over an articular surface.


References
1. Kasabian AK, Karp NS. Lower-extremity reconstruction. In: Thorne CH, Beasley RW, Aston SJ, et al, eds. Grabb and Smith ‚Ç¨‚Ñ¢s Plastic Surgery. 6th ed. Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2007:676-688.
2. Wyatt LE, Pribaz JJ. The mutilated lower extremity. In: McCarthy JG, Galiano RD, Boutros SG, eds. Current Therapy in Plastic Surgery. Philadelphia: WB Saunders; 2006:649-657.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old female patient seeks aesthetic nasal surgery. Physical examination reveals columellar retraction, insufficient tip projection, inadequate tip rotation, and a noticeable dorsal prominence. An open approach rhinoplasty is scheduled. Which of the following graft types is most effective at maintaining tip rotation over the long term in this case?
A) Batten
B) Columellar strut
C) Onlay
D) Septal extension
E) Spreader
questions.answer:
D)
Nasal tip modification represents a crucial component of rhinoplasty procedures. Long-term positional control is essential for sustained outcomes and depends on surgical technique, procedural methods, and healing response. Tip stability relies on the structural cartilages, connecting ligaments, and supporting grafts used during reconstruction. The columellar strut and septal extension grafts are the two primary options that provide substantial tip support. While both experience some immediate postoperative reduction in projection and rotation, they demonstrate comparable maintenance of tip projection over time. Nevertheless, the septal extension graft demonstrates superior preservation of tip rotation compared to the columellar strut graft in long-term follow-up. A batten graft is incorrect because it primarily addresses alar rim support rather than tip rotation control. B is incorrect because while columellar strut grafts provide good tip support, they are less effective than septal extension grafts at maintaining rotation over time. C is incorrect because onlay grafts are used for contour refinement rather than structural tip support and rotation control. E is incorrect because spreader grafts address middle vault width and breathing rather than tip position and rotation.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female patient has bilateral breast reduction surgery to address symptomatic breast enlargement. Her medical background includes 15 years of persistent neck and back discomfort. She requires a 36H cup size bra. Histopathological examination reveals ductal carcinoma in situ that was completely removed with 2-mm clear margins. Post-surgical MRI demonstrates no further abnormal findings. What is the most suitable subsequent management for this patient's breast malignancy?
A) Systemic chemotherapy
B) Standard lumpectomy to achieve better margins
C) Adjuvant radiotherapy
D) Sentinel node biopsy
E) No further intervention required
questions.answer:
C)
The appropriate next step is adjuvant radiation therapy. Since ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) was completely excised with adequate 2-mm margins during the reduction mammaplasty, the surgical treatment is complete. For DCIS with clear margins ≥2 mm, adjuvant radiation therapy is the standard of care to reduce local recurrence risk, unless the patient chooses completion mastectomy. A) Systemic chemotherapy is incorrect because it is reserved for invasive carcinomas with metastatic potential, not for in situ lesions. B) Formal lumpectomy is incorrect because adequate margins were already achieved with the reduction specimen. D) Sentinel lymph node dissection is incorrect because it is not indicated for non-invasive DCIS. E) No additional treatment is incorrect because adjuvant radiation is recommended for DCIS to minimize recurrence risk.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old woman comes to the office after gastric bypass surgery with a weight loss of 155 lb (70 kg). Weight is 143 lb (65 kg) and BMI is 24 kg/m2. She desires an improved appearance of the upper arms. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical correction of this deformity?


A) Liposuction alone
B) Liposuction followed by brachioplasty
C) Limited medial brachioplasty
D) Full brachioplasty
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The most appropriate management for this condition is brachioplasty. Surgical management of the upper arm, particularly after massive weight loss, is dependent upon the ratio of fat and skin laxity. There are several classifications, but all address this ratio. Those with a great deal of skin laxity and little fat are best treated by direct excision (brachioplasty). Those patients who have little skin laxity (and good skin tone) and marked fat may benefit from liposuction alone. Those patients in the middle, with skin laxity and residual upper arm fat, are likely to benefit from a combination approach, either in a single or staged fashion. In this case, the patient demonstrates considerable skin laxity and has little extra fat, so a dermatolipectomy alone will address her deformity.


A limited medial brachioplasty is useful for patients with skin laxity primarily in the proximal third of the arm and involves resection of a vertical ellipse of skin, leaving the scar in the apex of the axilla. The patient described here has skin laxity throughout the upper arm, which would not be adequately addressed with a medial brachioplasty.


Liposuction followed by brachioplasty in a staged fashion will not improve her outcome and will only serve to increase the cumulative risks of two surgeries.


Liposuction alone does not address the underlying issue of skin laxity. The patient's age and her history of obesity/massive weight loss severely decrease the ability of her skin to retract after liposuction.


References
1. Appelt EA, Janis JE, Rohrich RJ. An algorithmic approach to upper arm contouring. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2006 Jul;118(1):237-246.
2. Bossert RP, Dreifuss S, Coon D, et al. Liposuction of the arm concurrent with brachioplasty in the massive weight loss patient: is it safe? Plast Reconstr Surg. 2013 Feb;131(2):357-365.
3. Song AY, Jean RD, Hurwitz DJ, et al. A classification of contour deformities after bariatric weight loss: the Pittsburgh Rating Scale. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2005 Oct;116(5):1535-1544.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old female comes in for assessment of underdeveloped right breast tissue. Physical examination reveals a poorly developed left breast, upwardly positioned nipple-areolar complex, and depressed appearance of the chest wall. The pectoralis major muscle and sternum appear normal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Amastia
B) Amazia
C) Anterior thoracic hypoplasia
D) Athelia
E) Poland syndrome
questions.answer:
C)
Anterior thoracic hypoplasia presents with breast underdevelopment while maintaining normal sternum and pectoralis major muscle structure, which matches this patient's presentation. A) Amastia is incorrect because it involves complete absence of both breast tissue and nipple-areolar complex, not just underdevelopment. B) Amazia is incorrect because it refers to absence of mammary gland tissue with preserved nipple-areolar complex, rather than hypoplastic development. D) Athelia is incorrect because it specifically describes absence of the nipple, not breast hypoplasia with chest wall depression. E) Poland syndrome is incorrect because it characteristically involves absence or underdevelopment of the pectoralis major muscle, which is normal in this case.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman presents with a 3-cm morpheaform basal cell carcinoma (BCCA) involving the left mid cheek. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is an indication for Mohs micrographic surgery over conventional excision?


A) Anatomic location of lesion
B) Diagnosis of BCCA
C) History of previous melanoma
D) Morpheaform subtype
E) Patient age
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D. Mohs micrographic surgical technique has demonstrated cure rates of 99% for primary basal cell carcinomas (BCCA) and up to 95% for recurrent BCCAs. In this particular patient, the strongest indication for utilization of the Mohs technique is the more aggressive morpheaform subtype of BCCA. This patient underwent Mohs excision with adjacent tissue transfer reconstruction. Patient age, history of previous melanoma, and the diagnosis of BCCA (without aggressive features) are not indications for Mohs excision.
Other indications for Mohs technique include the following:Recurrent basal cell/squamous cell carcinomas;Locations prone to recurrence‚Äi‚ÄuH-zone‚Äu of the face: periorbital, periauricular, temple, upper lip, nose/nasolabial fold, and chin;Tumors involving critical structures such as the eyelid or lip;Functionally important areas such as the genitals, perianal location, hands, and feet;Tumors arising in sites of previous irradiation therapy;Large tumors (greater than 2 cm);Lesions with ill-defined tumor margins;Histologic aggressive subtype (morpheaform, basosquamous, perineural, and invasive/poorly-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma);Tumors arising in immunosuppressed patients, such as transplant recipients or patients with genetic predisposition (e.g. basal cell nevus syndrome, xeroderma pigmentosum).
ReferencesConnolly, KL, Nehal KS, Disa JJ. Evidence-based medicine: cutaneous facial malignancy: nonmelanoma skin cancer. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2017 Jan;139(1):181e-190e.Denkler K, Kivett WF. Management of nonmelanoma skin cancer. In: Mathes SJ, ed. Plastic Surgery. 2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders Elsevier; 2006:391-464.Netscher DT, Spira M. Basal cell carcinoma: an overview of tumor biology and treatment. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2004;113(5):74e-94e.

questions.question:
A CT scan is presented from a 21-year-old female patient. What is the probability of transmitting this patient's condition to her children?
A) 25%
B) 50%
C) 75%
D) 100%
E) Cannot be determined
questions.answer:
B)
The correct answer is B. This patient exhibits the typical craniofacial characteristics of Treacher Collins syndrome, including underdevelopment of the cheekbones and jaw, ear malformations, lower eyelid notching (coloboma), missing lower eyelash cilia, and displaced preauricular hair. This condition results from mutations in the TCOF1 gene and follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, meaning each offspring has a 50% chance of inheriting the condition. A) 25% is incorrect because this represents autosomal recessive inheritance probability. C) 75% is incorrect as this percentage doesn't correspond to any standard Mendelian inheritance pattern for a single gene disorder. D) 100% is incorrect because autosomal dominant conditions don't guarantee transmission to all offspring. E) Cannot be determined is incorrect because the inheritance pattern of Treacher Collins syndrome is well-established as autosomal dominant.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male patient with a smoking history and uncontrolled diabetes presents to the emergency room with a 12-hour onset of one-sided eye protrusion, visual impairment, and intense headache. Nasal endoscopy reveals dried secretions and blackened tissue on the lateral nasal wall and turbinates. Imaging demonstrates a 4-cm lesion in the maxillary sinus extending into the eye socket. Tissue biopsy reveals aseptate fungal hyphae. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Craniofacial surgical resection with tissue reconstruction
B) Urgent sinus debridement with removal of the eye and surrounding tissues
C) Intravenous antibiotic therapy
D) Oral antifungal treatment on an outpatient basis
E) Oncology consultation
questions.answer:
B)
This patient presents with rhinocerebral mucormycosis, a life-threatening fungal infection requiring immediate aggressive surgical intervention. The presence of nonseptate hyphae, orbital involvement, and tissue necrosis in a diabetic patient necessitates emergent debridement and orbital exenteration to remove all infected tissue and prevent further spread to the brain. A) is incorrect because craniofacial resection with reconstruction is not the immediate priority and would delay life-saving debridement. C) is incorrect because this is a fungal infection, not bacterial, so antibiotics would be ineffective. D) is incorrect because oral antifungals are inadequate for this severe, invasive infection that requires intravenous amphotericin B along with surgery. E) is incorrect because this is an infectious process, not malignancy, and oncology referral would inappropriately delay urgent treatment.

questions.question:
A 74-year-old male patient presents to the clinic with a painful oral lesion that has persisted for three months. On examination, there is a 3-cm ulcerated mass at the left tongue base and a 4-cm lymph node in the left neck's Zone II region. Histological analysis of the lesion reveals squamous cell carcinoma. No evidence of distant spread is found. What is the most precise TNM classification for this malignancy?
A) T1 N2a M0
B) T1 N3 M0
C) T2 N1 M0
D) T2 N2a M0
E) T3 N2a M0
questions.answer:
D)

The correct classification is T2 N2a M0. For oral cavity and oropharyngeal tumors, the TNM staging system applies specific size criteria. Since the tongue base belongs to the oropharynx, and this lesion measures 3 cm (greater than 2 cm but less than 4 cm), it qualifies as T2. The single 4-cm ipsilateral lymph node (greater than 3 cm but less than 6 cm) corresponds to N2a staging. With no distant metastases present, this is classified as M0. A) is incorrect because T1 applies only to tumors smaller than 2 cm. B) is incorrect because N3 requires nodes larger than 6 cm. C) is incorrect because N1 applies to nodes smaller than 3 cm. E) is incorrect because T3 requires tumors larger than 4 cm.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old male presents to the clinic expressing concern about the cosmetic appearance of his "oversized" chest. He had bariatric bypass surgery 2 years prior, resulting in a 110-lb (50-kg) weight reduction. His current weight is 185 lb (84 kg) and has remained constant for 6 months. On examination, the nipples show enlarged areolae positioned below the inframammary crease, redundant skin with decreased elasticity, and moderate adipose tissue accumulation. No palpable or tender masses are detected. What is the most suitable surgical intervention to address this patient's condition?
A) Phosphatidylcholine injection therapy
B) Non-invasive radiofrequency lipodestruction
C) Mammary reduction surgery
D) Mastectomy with skin preservation
E) Liposuction with ultrasonic assistance
questions.answer:
C)
This patient has pseudogynecomastia (lipomastia). Mammary reduction surgery is the most appropriate treatment as it addresses all components of the deformity: repositioning the nipple-areolar complex above the inframammary fold, reducing areolar size, excising redundant skin, and removing excess fatty tissue. This comprehensive approach provides optimal cosmetic correction. A) is incorrect because phosphatidylcholine injections lack established safety and efficacy data for this condition. B) is incorrect because radiofrequency treatments have no proven benefit for pseudogynecomastia in controlled studies. D) is incorrect because mastectomy is typically reserved for painful glandular tissue in adolescent males, not for cosmetic concerns in adults. E) is incorrect because liposuction alone cannot address the skin laxity or enlarged areolae that are key components of this patient's presentation.

questions.question:
A 14-month-old girl is evaluated for surgical management of the condition shown in the photograph. Which of the following is the most appropriate classification of this congenital difference?


A) Duplication
B) Failure of differentiation
C) Failure of formation
D) Overgrowth
E) Undergrowth
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The image shown is a patient with a typical cleft hand, or ectrodactyly. This is classified as a Swanson type I (failure of formation) congenital difference of the upper extremity. This deformity is caused by a longitudinal growth deficiency of one or more central digits. This condition may have a genetic underpinning and is most commonly inherited in autosomal dominant fashion with approximately 70% penetrance.


Ectrodactyly presents with significant heterogeneity. Many patients with cleft hand do not require any type of surgical management. The most important determinants of surgical management are establishment of an appropriate thumb to index webspace for gripping and grasping and release of syndactyly. Surgical management includes elevation of skin flaps, transposition of the index finger to the ulnar side of the cleft, and creation of a web space between the thumb and index finger.


Cleft hand is classified with the Thumb-Index Classification of Central Deficiency proposed by Manske. This generally guides the treatment approach in conjunction with management of syndactyly. A myriad of techniques have been employed based upon the severity of the webspace contraction and the presence of syndactyly adjacent to the cleft.






References
Manske PR, Halikis MN. Surgical classification of central deficiency according to the thumb web. J Hand Surg Am. 1995;20: 687‚Äi697.
Kozin SH, Zlotolow DA. Common Pediatric Congenital Conditions of the Hand. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2015 Aug;136(2):241e-257e.
Upton J, Taghinia AH. Correction of the typical cleft hand. J Hand Surg Am. 2010 Mar;35(3):480-5

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient seeks bilateral immediate breast reconstruction and requests an abdominal-based flap procedure. Given her profession as a yoga and pilates instructor, she specifically requires the reconstructive option with minimal abdominal wall complications. Which of the following autologous tissue flaps for breast reconstruction is associated with the least abdominal wall morbidity?
A) Deep inferior epigastric perforator flap
B) Free transverse rectus abdominus myocutaneous flap
C) Muscle-sparing free transverse rectus abdominus myocutaneous flap
D) Pedicled transverse rectus abdominus myocutaneous flap
E) Superficial inferior epigastric artery flap
questions.answer:
E)
The superficial inferior epigastric artery (SIEA) flap is the only abdominal-based reconstructive option that preserves the abdominal fascia completely intact, making it the choice with minimal abdominal wall complications. A) The DIEP flap requires fascial incision and muscle fiber dissection, increasing morbidity compared to SIEA. B) The free TRAM involves substantial rectus muscle harvest, leading to significant abdominal wall weakness. C) While muscle-sparing free TRAM preserves more muscle than traditional TRAM, it still requires fascial violation and some muscle manipulation. D) The pedicled TRAM necessitates the most extensive muscle harvest and creates the greatest risk for abdominal wall dysfunction and hernia formation.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old child presents to the clinic with restricted neck mobility and inability to extend his head upward, occurring 2 years following thermal injuries from a gasoline explosion that affected approximately 50% of his body surface. Bilateral skin grafting was performed on the lower arms and upper legs 2 years prior to address deep partial-thickness thermal injuries. Present examination reveals significant burn scar contracture of the cervical region and healed grafted areas on the neck and chest. Following contracture release and scar excision, a 10 × 20-cm tissue defect is created. Which of the following reconstruction techniques would provide the optimal aesthetic and functional result?
A) Anterolateral thigh perforator free flap transfer to the cervical area
B) Dermal regeneration matrix (Integra)
C) Full-thickness skin graft harvested from the groin area
D) Split-thickness skin graft harvested from the dorsal region
E) Split-thickness skin graft harvested from the posterior thigh region
questions.answer:
B)
Dermal regeneration matrix (Integra) represents the optimal choice for this reconstruction. This bioengineered dermal substitute consists of a dual-layer system with a collagen-glycosaminoglycan matrix and silicone outer layer. The integration process follows four stages: fluid absorption, cellular infiltration, blood vessel formation, and tissue maturation. After 3-4 weeks, the silicone layer is removed and a thin split-thickness graft is applied. Benefits include superior cosmetic results, reduced contracture risk, improved elasticity, thinner donor grafts with less morbidity, and proportional growth in pediatric patients. A is incorrect because the thigh donor site has already been grafted, compromising aesthetic outcomes, though scapular sites could be considered. C is incorrect because the inguinal region cannot provide sufficient tissue volume to cover the entire neck defect adequately. D is incorrect because split-thickness grafts from the back carry high contracture recurrence risk in this mobile cervical location. E is incorrect because posterior thigh split-thickness grafts also pose significant secondary contracture risk and potential recurrence of the neck restriction.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old female patient comes for evaluation 6 months following surgical removal and reconstruction of a basal cell carcinoma on her right lower eyelid using wedge resection and primary closure. She complains of excessive tearing. Physical examination reveals a mature but healed surgical scar and right lower eyelid ectropion. Movement of the lacrimal punctum in which direction would most likely explain the excessive tearing in this case?
A) Forward
B) Outward
C) Inward
D) Backward
questions.answer:
A)
Forward displacement of the punctum is the correct answer. The tear drainage apparatus consists of proximal and distal components, with the proximal portion including the punctum, canaliculus, and common canaliculus. The lower punctum is located 6.5 mm from the inner corner of the eye, measures 0.3 mm in diameter, and faces dorsally. This dorsal orientation enables efficient tear drainage. The upper punctum sits 6 mm from the medial canthus, creating slight separation between the puncta when eyelids are closed. During eye opening, the ampulla expands, and with eyelid closure, tears are propelled into the common canaliculus. Post-surgical ectropion, a frequent complication following lower eyelid procedures, displaces the punctum anteriorly, impairing its tear drainage capacity. B is incorrect because outward displacement typically doesn't cause excessive tearing. C is incorrect because inward displacement generally doesn't result in epiphora. D is incorrect because while excessive backward displacement could theoretically impair drainage, the presence of ectropion makes forward displacement the more likely mechanism.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old female patient with a previous cesarean section through a low-transverse abdominal incision is planned for unilateral deep inferior epigastric perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction. Her BMI is 28 kg/m² and the nipple-to-sternal notch measurement is 24 cm bilaterally. The patient's prior cesarean section history will most likely result in which of the following outcomes?
A) Reduced abdominal seroma formation
B) Reduced flap venous congestion
C) Enhanced flap arterial thrombosis
D) Enhanced flap fat necrosis
E) No significant impact
questions.answer:
B)
The correct answer is B. Pfannenstiel incisions used for cesarean deliveries do not contraindicate abdominal-based breast reconstruction flaps since the deep inferior epigastric vascular system remains intact. However, the superficial epigastric vessels may be transected during the cesarean procedure. This results in enhanced venous drainage with a protective benefit against fat necrosis in the reconstructed flap. The venous interruption creates a delay-like effect during recovery, promoting increased collateral formation from the superficial epigastric system and potentially establishing new connections to the deep epigastric venous network. A is incorrect because evidence shows increased abdominal seroma rates (15% vs 6%) following cesarean delivery. C is incorrect as there is no documented impact on the arterial supply to the flap. D is incorrect because the enhanced venous drainage actually provides protection against fat necrosis. E is incorrect since there are documented effects on venous circulation and abdominal healing complications.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old male patient is sent to your clinic for assessment and management of a 1.2-cm cutaneous lesion on the palmar aspect of his forearm following dermatologic consultation. The lesion has a benign appearance, and surgical removal with primary closure is completed using local anesthesia in an ambulatory setting (CPT 11402). The patient returns for follow-up visits at 1 week and 8 weeks postoperatively. Based on Medicare global surgical payment guidelines, what is the duration of the global period for this surgical procedure?
A) 0 days
B) 7 days
C) 10 days
D) 14 days
E) 30 days
questions.answer:
C)
The global surgical period for minor procedures like this skin excision (CPT 11402) is 10 days. The global surgery package encompasses all routine preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative care within this timeframe. For minor surgical procedures, Medicare establishes a 10-day global period, meaning the 8-week follow-up visit falls outside this period and can be billed separately. A) 0 days is incorrect as this applies to procedures with no global period. B) 7 days is incorrect as this is not a standard Medicare global period designation. D) 14 days is incorrect as this is not the established timeframe for minor procedures. E) 30 days is incorrect as this global period length is not used for minor skin excisions.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man with paraplegia and type 1 diabetes presents to the clinic with a stage 3 pressure ulcer over the trochanter. Following appropriate debridement, myocutaneous flap coverage is being considered. Laboratory values show albumin of 3.8 mg/dL and hemoglobin A1c of 6.3%. His current diet provides 2.5 g/kg of protein daily. Which of the following is the most significant risk factor for reconstructive failure?
A) Albumin level
B) Hemoglobin A1c level
C) Age of patient
D) Anatomical site of ulcer
E) Daily protein consumption
questions.answer:
B)
Optimal preoperative preparation is crucial for successful pressure ulcer reconstruction. This encompasses proper nutrition (albumin >3.5 g/dL, protein 1.5-3.0 g/kg/day, nonprotein calories 25-35 cal/kg/day), infection control, management of spasticity and contractures, cessation of smoking, selective urinary/fecal diversion, and comprehensive postoperative care with pressure relief. Multivariate analysis has identified key predictors of flap failure including hemoglobin A1c >6%, younger patient age, albumin <3.5 g/dL, and ischial ulcer location. For this patient, the elevated hemoglobin A1c represents the primary risk factor for reconstruction failure. A is incorrect because the albumin level of 3.8 mg/dL exceeds the threshold of 3.5 mg/dL associated with increased failure risk. C is incorrect because while younger age is a risk factor, this patient's hemoglobin A1c is the more significant concern. D is incorrect because trochanteric location is not specifically identified as a high-risk site compared to ischial location. E is incorrect because the protein intake of 2.5 g/kg/day falls within the recommended range of 1.5-3.0 g/kg/day.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old male patient comes to the clinic with a 2-cm keratoacanthoma on his left ear. His past medical history is significant for melanoma of the left cheek. What represents an indication for choosing Mohs micrographic surgery instead of standard excision for this patient?
A) Anatomical site of the tumor
B) Keratoacanthoma diagnosis
C) Prior melanoma history
D) Male gender
E) Advanced age
questions.answer:
A)
The correct answer is A because the anatomical location on the ear is a primary indication for Mohs micrographic surgery. The ear is considered a high-risk anatomical site where squamous cell carcinomas (including keratoacanthomas) have increased potential for recurrence and metastasis, making the tissue-sparing precision of Mohs technique particularly valuable. B is incorrect because keratoacanthoma diagnosis alone is not an indication for Mohs surgery - the location and risk factors determine the surgical approach. C is incorrect because a history of melanoma does not influence the choice of surgical technique for treating a separate keratoacanthoma. D is incorrect because male gender is not a factor that determines the need for Mohs surgery. E is incorrect because patient age of 70 years does not constitute an indication for Mohs micrographic surgery over conventional excision.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man with right-hand dominance presents to the clinic with Dupuytren disease affecting the metacarpophalangeal joints of his left ring and little fingers, accompanied by a 40-degree flexion contracture at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint of the little finger. The ring finger's PIP joint remains unaffected. There is no trauma history. Following palmar fasciectomies, the little finger PIP joint contracture shows no intraoperative improvement. What is the most appropriate subsequent intervention?
A) Collagenase injection
B) Collateral ligament excision
C) Percutaneous PIP joint fixation in forced extension
D) PIP joint capsulotomy
E) Checkrein ligament release of the PIP joint
questions.answer:
E)
The appropriate next step is releasing the checkrein ligaments of the PIP joint. When PIP joint contracture persists after fascial excision, the checkrein ligaments should be examined and released first. These ligamentous structures extend anterolaterally from the proximal swallowtail extensions of the volar plate to the proximal phalanx neck. A is incorrect because collagenase cannot address capsular contractures that remain after fascial release. B is incorrect because collateral ligament excision is typically performed after checkrein release if needed. C is incorrect because forced extension with percutaneous fixation is not recommended and may cause injury. D is incorrect because capsulotomy is more extensive and checkrein release should be attempted first as it is less invasive and often effective.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old male patient develops left wrist weakness and impaired finger extension 48 hours following surgical repair of a closed right humeral fracture sustained during a car accident. During the operation, the radial nerve appeared undamaged with no obvious trauma signs. Clinical examination reveals inability to extend the wrist or fingers, though elbow extension remains normal. Which histopathologic characteristic of neurapraxia (Sunderland Type 1) injury is most probable in this case?
A) Perineurial disruption
B) Endoneurial scarring
C) Enhanced axonal transport
D) Segmental demyelination
E) Wallerian degeneration
questions.answer:
D)
Neurapraxia (Sunderland type 1) represents injury limited to the myelin sheath while preserving axonal integrity. This condition typically results from compression or stretching forces and is characterized by segmental demyelination that causes conduction block. Recovery is expected within days to weeks without permanent damage since axons remain intact. A) Perineurial disruption is incorrect as it occurs in higher-grade injuries (Sunderland type 4) where the protective nerve covering is damaged. B) Endoneurial scarring is incorrect as it develops in more severe injuries (Sunderland type 3) involving damage to the inner nerve structure. C) Enhanced axonal transport is incorrect as axonal transport is not a relevant histopathological feature in nerve injury classification. E) Wallerian degeneration is incorrect as it occurs in axonotmesis (Sunderland types 2-4) where actual axonal damage has occurred, not in neurapraxia where axons are preserved.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents to the clinic with complaints of facial asymmetry when smiling. Eight weeks prior, she had surgical repair of a facial nerve injury located 2 cm lateral to the corner of her mouth. On examination, the upper lip fails to elevate during smiling on the affected side. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Cross-facial nerve grafting
B) Facial sling suspension
C) Free muscle transfer
D) Injection of botulinum toxin type A
E) Observation
questions.answer:
E)
Observation is most appropriate because the timeframe since neurorrhaphy is still within the window for potential nerve recovery. At 8 weeks post-repair, there remains a reasonable chance for the primary nerve repair to succeed, and monitoring for signs of reinnervation (such as clinical Tinel sign) would be beneficial. A) Cross-facial nerve grafting is premature at this stage as adequate time has not passed to determine neurorrhaphy failure. B) Facial sling suspension is a static procedure reserved for long-standing injuries or patients unsuitable for reanimation procedures. C) Free muscle transfer is indicated only after confirming failure of primary repair, typically after 6-12 months. D) Botulinum toxin injection would interfere with clinical assessment of nerve recovery and is contraindicated during the monitoring period.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old male presents to the emergency room 2 hours following a knife injury to his hand. Clinical examination reveals a laceration on the back of the first web space. Local anesthetic administration with wound exploration is planned. Which of the following represents the most suitable anatomical landmark for local anesthetic injection?
A) A1 pulley
B) Flexor carpi radialis
C) Medial epicondyle
D) Pisiform
E) Radial styloid
questions.answer:
E)

The radial styloid is the most appropriate landmark for local anesthetic injection in this case. The superficial radial nerve provides sensory innervation to the dorsal radial aspect of the hand, including the first web space where this patient's wound is located. The nerve branches near the radial styloid and can be effectively blocked through subcutaneous infiltration over the radial styloid proximal to the anatomical snuffbox, providing adequate anesthesia for the injured area.

A) A1 pulley is incorrect because digital blocks at this location would provide anesthesia too distal to the wound site in the first web space.

B) Flexor carpi radialis is incorrect because injection at this landmark targets the median nerve, which innervates the volar radial hand but not the dorsal first web space.

C) Medial epicondyle is incorrect because injection at this site would block the ulnar nerve at the elbow level, which does not innervate the first web space.

D) Pisiform is incorrect because this landmark is used for ulnar nerve blocks at the wrist, which innervates the ulnar aspect of the hand, not the radial first web space.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old female comes for assessment of abnormal vaginal discharge due to a rectovaginal fistula. Her history includes several deliveries with episiotomies and two unsuccessful attempts at fistula repair using local tissue, resulting in tissue deficiency in the perineal body and rectovaginal septum. Physical exam is challenging due to discomfort and reveals considerable inflammation in the vaginal and perianal regions. Her anal sphincter remains intact, and she has no other medical conditions or prior operations. What is the most suitable management approach for this patient?
A) Abdominoperineal resection (APR) with pedicled vertical rectus abdominis muscle (VRAM) flap
B) Fecal diversion using an ostomy
C) Application of acellular dermal matrix to the posterior vaginal wall
D) Insertion of a seton through the fistula
E) Transposition of a pedicled sartorius muscle flap to the defect
questions.answer:
B)
Fecal diversion using an ostomy is the most appropriate initial management. Given the extensive tissue loss, significant inflammation, and two prior failed repairs, diverting the fecal stream away from the inflamed area will allow the tissue to heal and optimize conditions for future definitive repair with a vascularized flap. A) is incorrect because abdominoperineal resection is reserved for cancer cases or severe disease with anal sphincter dysfunction, which this patient does not have. C) is incorrect because acellular dermal matrix is a non-vascularized option that is unlikely to succeed given the extensive tissue damage and inflammation. D) is incorrect because seton placement is primarily for infection control and will not achieve closure in the setting of significant tissue loss and inflammation. E) is incorrect because the sartorius muscle has segmental blood supply and is not suitable for transposition to the perineum.

questions.question:
In a 70-year-old male patient, a metastatic lesion found in the mandible would most commonly originate from which of the following primary sites?
A) Colon
B) Kidney
C) Lung
D) Testis
questions.answer:
C)
Lung cancer represents the most frequent primary source of mandibular metastases in male patients. Metastatic spread to the mandible is relatively rare and typically indicates advanced, disseminated disease. These lesions commonly present as nodular masses that may or may not ulcerate, with imaging revealing radiolucent or hypodense characteristics. The peak incidence occurs in men during their fifth to seventh decades of life, with pulmonary malignancies being the predominant source in males (while breast cancer is most common in females). The posterior mandible is the preferred site of osseous involvement. A) Colon is incorrect because colorectal cancers rarely metastasize to the mandible compared to lung primaries. B) Kidney is incorrect as renal cell carcinomas are not among the most common sources of mandibular metastases in men. D) Testis is incorrect because testicular cancers infrequently spread to mandibular bone tissue.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old female presents for evaluation of a 1-year duration of lymphatic swelling affecting her right lower limb. Her BMI is 28 kg/m2. Clinical examination reveals asymmetrical appearance of the right lower limb with enlarged circumference of both the thigh and calf when compared to the left lower limb. What represents the most suitable initial therapeutic approach?
A) Prescribing diuretic medication
B) Surgical removal of involved skin and subcutaneous tissue
C) Establishing a weight management and physical activity program
D) Sequential pneumatic compression device therapy
E) Microsurgical lymphatic-to-lymphatic vessel reconnection
questions.answer:
D)
Sequential pneumatic compression device therapy represents the most appropriate initial intervention. The foundation of lymphedema management is conservative medical treatment, which includes careful hygiene practices and routine examination. Patients should be advised to reduce weight, prevent minor injuries, avoid tight-fitting garments, and keep the affected limb elevated. Continuous daytime use of compression garments is also essential for all patients. A is incorrect because diuretic medications have no therapeutic benefit in lymphedema management. B is incorrect because surgical excision procedures are typically reserved for patients who have not responded to conservative treatments. C is incorrect because while weight loss and exercise are beneficial supportive measures, they alone are insufficient as primary initial therapy. E is incorrect because microsurgical lymphatic reconstruction procedures have demonstrated poor long-term outcomes and are not appropriate for initial management.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents to the clinic seeking non-surgical correction of nasal bridge irregularity following rhinoplasty performed one year prior. Hyaluronic acid filler (0.6 mL) is administered to the upper portion of the nasal bridge. Immediately following the injection, the patient experiences partial visual loss and ocular pain on the right side. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Administration of apraclonidine ophthalmic drops
B) Intravenous administration of tissue plasminogen activator
C) Subcutaneous nasal injection of hyaluronidase
D) Percutaneous lateral canthotomy procedure
E) Retrobulbar hyaluronidase injection
questions.answer:
E)
This patient presents with signs of intravascular hyaluronic acid injection resulting in central retinal artery obstruction. Although this complication occurs rarely, immediate intervention is critical since retinal perfusion must be restored within 60-90 minutes for potential symptom reversal. The primary treatment involves delivering hyaluronidase directly to the retinal vasculature via retrobulbar injection. Using a 25-gauge needle, access the orbit through the orbital floor between the inferior and lateral rectus muscles, advance at least 1 inch past the orbital rim, and inject 2-4 mL of undiluted hyaluronidase. The mechanism likely involves intra-arterial filler injection under pressure into the dorsal nasal artery, with retrograde flow to the ophthalmic artery and subsequent antegrade distribution to the central retinal artery when pressure is released. A is incorrect because apraclonidine treats botulinum toxin-induced ptosis, not vascular occlusion. B is incorrect because tissue plasminogen activator addresses blood clots, not hyaluronic acid emboli. C is incorrect because subcutaneous hyaluronidase treats extravascular compression rather than intravascular occlusion causing vision loss. D is incorrect because lateral canthotomy decompresses retrobulbar hemorrhage, not hyaluronic acid embolism.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old male patient is preparing for a midline abdominal incision for colorectal malignancy. His medical history reveals cutis laxa. Physical examination demonstrates inelastic skin that fails to return to its original position after being pulled. This individual has an elevated risk for which of the following postoperative complications?
A) Anastomotic breakdown
B) Keloid formation
C) Blood clot formation
D) Incisional hernia
E) Surgical site dehiscence
questions.answer:
D)
The correct answer is incisional hernia because cutis laxa patients have defective elastin fibers causing skin hypoelasticity, which significantly increases their risk of hernia development due to weakened tissue integrity. A) Anastomotic breakdown is incorrect because cutis laxa primarily affects skin elasticity rather than bowel healing. B) Keloid formation is incorrect because cutis laxa patients typically have normal scar formation and healing processes. C) Blood clot formation is incorrect because cutis laxa does not inherently increase thrombotic risk (this is associated with conditions like homocystinuria). E) Surgical site dehiscence is incorrect because while wound healing may be affected in some connective tissue disorders, cutis laxa specifically predisposes to hernia formation rather than wound separation.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents for assessment due to discomfort and edema of his left wrist occurring 6 hours following a fall where he landed on his extended left hand. Physical examination reveals point tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox region. A hidden fracture is suspected. Beyond routine radiographic views of the wrist, which of the following radiographic projections would be most suitable to establish the diagnosis?
A) Anteroposterior projection with neutral positioning and perpendicular beam angulation
B) Clenched fist projection with neutral wrist position and 30-degree proximal-to-distal beam angle
C) Lateral projection with 30-degree wrist flexion and 45-degree proximal-to-distal beam angle
D) Oblique projection with radial deviation and perpendicular beam angulation
E) Posteroanterior projection with ulnar deviation and 20-degree proximal-to-distal beam angle
questions.answer:
E)
The posteroanterior projection with ulnar deviation and 20-degree proximal-to-distal beam angulation represents the specialized scaphoid view that optimally visualizes occult scaphoid fractures by elongating and clearly displaying the bone that may not be apparent on conventional radiographic views. A is incorrect because the standard anteroposterior view with neutral alignment does not adequately elongate the scaphoid for optimal visualization. B is incorrect because the clenched fist view is primarily used for scapholunate ligament assessment, not scaphoid fracture detection. C is incorrect because this lateral flexion view does not provide the necessary scaphoid elongation and positioning required for fracture identification. D is incorrect because radial deviation actually shortens the scaphoid appearance rather than elongating it for proper evaluation.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old female patient with Möbius syndrome presents to the clinic for assessment of facial nerve dysfunction. Clinical examination reveals a mask-like facial appearance, bilateral inability to produce facial expressions, and diffuse underdevelopment of the tongue. Which of the following represents the most suitable donor nerve for restoring facial movement in this case?
A) Hypoglossal
B) Ipsilateral facial
C) Masseteric
D) Spinal accessory
E) Phrenic
questions.answer:
C)
The masseteric nerve is the optimal choice for donor nerve in this patient with Möbius syndrome requiring microneurovascular muscle transfer (typically gracilis muscle). In Möbius syndrome, both cranial nerves VI and VII are affected, making the facial muscles and nerves unavailable for reconstruction, necessitating free muscle transfer with an alternative donor nerve. The masseteric nerve provides superior motor strength and results in lower donor site morbidity compared to other options. A) Hypoglossal nerve is relatively contraindicated in Möbius syndrome patients due to existing tongue hypoplasia and the risk of further compromising tongue function. B) Ipsilateral facial nerve is not viable since the facial nerve is non-functional in Möbius syndrome. D) Spinal accessory nerve provides inferior motor strength and higher morbidity compared to the masseteric nerve. E) Phrenic nerve also offers less favorable motor strength and greater morbidity than the masseteric nerve option.

questions.question:
A patient who is immediately postoperative forehead feminization as well as transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty complains of pain in the right eye and photophobia. On examination, she has marked swelling of both upper eyelids and increased epiphora and chemosis on the right. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?


A) Administer topical anesthetic eye drops
B) Increase intravenous pain medication and serial examinations
C) Perform emergent bedside canthotomy and cantholysis
D) Perform emergent bedside canthotomy only
E) Return to the operating room for examination under anesthesia
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


The most likely diagnosis in this patient is a corneal abrasion. The cornea is highly innervated (300 to 400 times greater than skin) and any abrasion is associated with marked pain and epiphora. Topical anesthetic eye drops, such as proparacaine hydrochloride or tetracaine hydrochloride, can both treat the pain and be diagnostic. In the setting of a corneal abrasion, the patient would get relief within minutes after application and a formal ocular examination would then be possible. Treatment for a corneal abrasion would include symptom control with topical anesthetics as needed and prophylactic topical antibiotics. Eye patches should be avoided since they can decrease oxygenation of the cornea. Similarly, contact lenses should be omitted until the cornea is fully healed. The cause of corneal abrasions is any mechanical injury during induction, preparation, surgery, and emergence. Particular care should be taken by all team members during the entire surgery and up until the moment when the patient is coordinated enough to touch their face. A time that is particularly dangerous is the cleaning of the face at the end of surgery.
