Camouflaging an acute pain episode with narcotics, without establishing and treating the root cause, is not sound medical care and can lead to a missed diagnosis with associated harm.


A return to the operating room, as a first step in management, is not indicated in this clinical scenario. If possible, an ophthalmological examination is best performed with an awake patient.


Both forehead feminization and lower blepharoplasty can lead to a retrobulbar hematoma, which may present similar to a corneal abrasion. Physical examination can distinguish between the two entities since a retrobulbar hematoma would present with proptosis. However, a canthotomy involves only the release of the lateral canthus without severance of the lateral canthal tendon that is found more posterior. This incision would inadequately treat a retrobulbar hematoma.


If topical anesthetic eye drops do not have an effect, then further escalation of care is warranted. If an acute retrobulbar hematoma is suspected, a canthotomy and cantholysis can be indicated. This is a procedure that can be done at bedside should the patient be unable to immediately return to the operating room. It is important that this is done properly and that the lateral canthal tendon is entirely released so that the retrobulbar pressure is released.


ReferencesMalafa MM, Coleman JE, Bowman RW, et al. Perioperative corneal abrasion: updated guidelines for prevention and management. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2016;137(5):790e-798e.McCallum E, Keren S, Lapira M, et al. Orbital compartment syndrome: an update with review of the literature. Clin Ophthalmol. 2019;13:2189-2194.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old child with a previous omphalocele repair presents with a 5-cm ventral hernia and 3-cm widened fascial defect at the surgical site. What is the most suitable initial treatment approach for this hernia?
A) Anterior fascial release technique
B) Placement of biological mesh graft
C) Insertion of synthetic mesh material
D) Tensor fascia lata muscle flap
E) Insertion of tissue expansion device
questions.answer:
A)
Anterior fascial release technique is the most appropriate initial approach for omphalocele-related hernias measuring 5 cm or less in diameter. This standard component separation procedure from the costal margin to iliac crest effectively reduces the hernia and allows reapproximation of the rectus muscle separation in most cases. B) is incorrect because biological mesh placement is typically reserved for cases where autologous repair methods have been unsuccessful or are not feasible. C) is incorrect because synthetic mesh insertion is generally used only after primary tissue repair options have failed. D) is incorrect because tensor fascia lata flaps are reserved for larger defects that cannot be managed with component separation alone. E) is incorrect because tissue expanders are typically needed only for defects exceeding 5 cm in diameter requiring staged reconstruction.

questions.question:
What vessel travels through the pedicle of the reverse sural artery flap and provides the main venous outflow?
A) Femoral
B) Greater saphenous
C) Lesser saphenous
D) Popliteal
E) Posterior tibial
questions.answer:
C)
The lesser saphenous vein is the correct answer as it runs within the pedicle of the reverse superficial sural artery flap and provides primary venous drainage. This vein travels alongside the sural nerve and the vascular anastomosis between the peroneal and median sural arteries, forming the reliable neurovascular bundle that makes this flap successful for lower extremity reconstruction.

A) is incorrect because the femoral vein is part of the deep venous system in the upper thigh and is not involved in the reverse sural flap anatomy. B) is incorrect because the greater saphenous vein runs more proximally and medially, draining the medial aspect of the lower leg rather than being part of the sural flap pedicle. D) is incorrect because while the popliteal vein receives drainage from the lesser saphenous vein, it is not the primary drainage vessel within the flap pedicle itself. E) is incorrect because the posterior tibial vein is part of the deep venous system of the lower leg and does not participate in the superficial venous drainage of the reverse sural flap.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female presents to the clinic seeking consultation due to her unhappiness with her nasal appearance. Her medical history reveals two prior rhinoplasty procedures. During the visit, she also voices concerns about her eyelid appearance, chin contour, abdominal and flank areas, and breast dimensions. In this patient diagnosed with body dysmorphic disorder, which of the following comorbid conditions is most frequently encountered?
A) Anorexia nervosa
B) Anxiety disorders
C) Major depressive disorder
D) Hypochondriasis
E) Substance use disorders
questions.answer:
C)
Major depressive disorder represents the most prevalent psychiatric comorbidity in patients with body dysmorphic disorder, with research demonstrating that more than 75% of individuals with this condition have experienced major depression at some point in their lives, and over half currently meet diagnostic criteria for major depression. A) Anorexia nervosa is incorrect because it occurs in only 7-14% of body dysmorphic disorder patients, making it much less common than depression. B) Anxiety disorders are incorrect as they affect only about 6% of patients with body dysmorphic disorder over their lifetime. D) Hypochondriasis is incorrect because it co-occurs in merely 2% of body dysmorphic disorder cases, and differs fundamentally in focus (health concerns versus appearance concerns). E) Substance use disorders are incorrect as they affect approximately 30% of body dysmorphic disorder patients, which is substantial but still less frequent than depression.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old male patient has surgical removal of the spiral cord at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint to treat a 60-degree PIP joint contracture. After spiral cord excision, the PIP joint continues to have a 45-degree contracture. What is the most appropriate subsequent step for addressing this remaining joint contracture?
A) A1 pulley release
B) Central slip release
C) Pretendinous cord release
D) Radial slip of flexor digitorum superficialis tendon release
E) Volar plate checkrein ligament release
questions.answer:
E)
The appropriate next intervention is volar plate checkrein ligament release. When treating Dupuytren PIP joint contractures, spiral cord removal with surrounding diseased tissue typically provides at least 50% contracture improvement. When complete passive extension remains limited after fascial excision, the residual contracture usually results from shortened flexor tendon sheath and/or capsuloligamentous structures. The sequential approach involves first incising the flexor tendon sheath at the A3 pulley level, followed by checkrein ligament release if needed, then accessory collateral ligaments, and finally proper collateral ligaments until full extension is achieved. A is incorrect because A1 pulley release does not address the capsuloligamentous contracture at the PIP joint level. B is incorrect because central slip release would compromise extension function and is not indicated for contracture correction. C is incorrect because pretendinous cord release would have been addressed during the initial spiral cord excision. D is incorrect because radial slip release of the FDS tendon is not part of the standard sequential approach for residual PIP contractures.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old female patient with a previous diagnosis of mild breast sagging (grade I ptosis) presents for follow-up 6 years after receiving breast augmentation surgery with silicone gel implants placed above the chest muscle. On examination, her breasts appear aesthetically normal, though there is some increased firmness detected during palpation. What Baker classification grade most accurately characterizes these clinical findings?
A) Grade I
B) Grade II
C) Grade III
D) Grade IV
questions.answer:
B)
The appropriate answer is Grade II. The Baker classification system serves as the standard method for assessing breast implant capsular contracture severity, evaluating both physical examination findings and patient symptoms. This grading system helps determine treatment necessity, with only the more severe grades (III and IV) typically requiring surgical intervention. The Baker grades are defined as follows: Grade I represents breasts that feel soft with normal appearance and shape; Grade II indicates breasts that feel somewhat firm but maintain normal appearance; Grade III describes breasts that are firm with abnormal appearance; and Grade IV involves breasts that are firm, appear abnormal, and cause pain. In this case, the patient's breasts appear normal but have mild firmness on palpation, which corresponds to Grade II. Grade I is incorrect because the breasts are not completely soft as there is detectable firmness. Grade III is incorrect because the breasts do not have an abnormal appearance, only increased firmness. Grade IV is incorrect because there is no mention of pain or abnormal appearance, and the firmness is only mild.

questions.question:
Which cranial nerve originates from the first pharyngeal arch during embryological development?
A) Hypoglossal (XII)
B) Vagus (X)
C) Trigeminal (V)
D) Facial (VII)
E) Glossopharyngeal (IX)
questions.answer:
C)

The trigeminal nerve (cranial nerve V) originates from the first pharyngeal arch during embryonic development and is responsible for forming the malleus and incus bones. The structures associated with the first pharyngeal arch include the anterior malleal ligament and sphenomandibular ligament. The musculature derived from this arch encompasses the masticatory muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoids), tensor veli palatini, tensor tympani, mylohyoid, and anterior digastric belly. The first pharyngeal pouch contributes to the external auditory canal and middle ear cavity formation.

A is incorrect because the hypoglossal nerve does not derive from any branchial arch but rather from occipital myotomes. B is incorrect because the vagus nerve is associated with the fourth branchial arch, not the first. D is incorrect because the facial nerve develops from the second pharyngeal arch and contributes to stapes formation and facial expression muscles. E is incorrect because the glossopharyngeal nerve originates from the third pharyngeal arch and innervates the stylopharyngeus muscle.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old female patient returns for a postoperative appointment one week following a right modified radical mastectomy with breast cancer and immediate reconstruction using a transverse rectus abdominis musculocutaneous (TRAM) flap. She expresses concern about her ability to cover costs for future follow-up appointments if she must pay out-of-pocket. What is the most probable length of the global surgical period for this patient?
A) 1 Week
B) 1 Month
C) 3 Months
D) 6 Months
E) 1 Year
questions.answer:
C)
The correct answer is C) 3 Months. A global surgical period refers to a federally mandated timeframe (typically 90 days following major surgery) during which patients receive postoperative care and follow-up visits without additional charges to their insurance. This period must be completed before patients can proceed to subsequent phases of breast reconstruction. A) 1 Week is incorrect as this brief period applies only to minor procedures like skin lesion removals, not major reconstructive surgery. B) 1 Month is incorrect as it is too short for the complexity of this major surgical procedure. D) 6 Months and E) 1 Year are incorrect as they exceed the standard 90-day global period established for major surgical procedures.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female presents for evaluation of a dorsal oblique fingertip amputation of her index finger that occurred while preparing food with a sharp blade. Radiographic imaging and clinical examination reveal exposed tuft bone. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Cross-finger flap
B) Groin flap
C) Moberg flap
D) Split-thickness skin grafting
E) Volar V-Y advancement flap
questions.answer:
E)
The volar V-Y advancement flap (Atasoy flap) is the optimal choice for transverse and dorsal oblique fingertip amputations with bone exposure, providing excellent durability, padding, and preserved sensation since the neurovascular bundle remains intact. A) Cross-finger flap is incorrect because it is designed for volar defects, not dorsal oblique amputations. B) Groin flap is incorrect because while it offers good coverage and padding, it represents an unnecessarily complex distant flap when effective local options are available. C) Moberg flap is incorrect because this technique is specifically indicated for thumb tip reconstructions, not index finger injuries. D) Split-thickness skin grafting is incorrect because it provides inadequate padding over exposed bone and results in poor sensory recovery compared to flap reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old male child presents to the emergency room with a 2-day course of fatigue, elevated temperature, and a purplish-red rash affecting his arms and legs. His temperature is 103.0°F (39.4°C). Clinical examination reveals petechiae distributed across the upper and lower limbs and torso. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy is started. Six hours later, the rash progresses to hemorrhaging and blistering, and his fingers and toes show signs of tissue death. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Activated protein C
B) Surgical removal of the necrotic digits
C) Withholding vasopressor medications
D) Surgical removal of affected skin tissue
E) Clot-dissolving medications
questions.answer:
A)
Purpura fulminans represents a rapidly progressive autoimmune condition characterized by septic shock and hemorrhagic skin lesions that can lead to extensive tissue loss and is often fatal. Treatment requires immediate identification of the underlying infection (commonly Neisseria meningitidis), starting broad-spectrum antibiotics, respiratory support, and aggressive fluid replacement with vasopressor support. Patients develop widespread clotting abnormalities and benefit from activated protein C replacement therapy. B) is incorrect because amputation should be delayed until clear tissue demarcation occurs, as tissue viability is difficult to assess during acute resuscitation. C) is incorrect because vasopressor support is actually necessary for managing septic shock in these patients. D) is incorrect because debridement should be postponed until tissue boundaries are clearly defined. E) is incorrect because thrombolytic agents are contraindicated in patients with bleeding disorders.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient has a mastectomy performed. Which of the following anatomical structures represents a boundary of breast tissue and thus defines the surgical extent of mastectomy?
A) Anterior edge of the latissimus dorsi muscle
B) Lower attachment of the pectoralis major muscle
C) Lateral aspect of the pectoralis minor muscle
D) Superficial fascial layer of the serratus anterior muscle
E) Supraclavicular nodal region
questions.answer:
A)
The anterior edge of the latissimus dorsi muscle serves as one of the anatomical boundaries that define breast tissue limits and guide mastectomy extent, along with the sternum, clavicle, and inframammary fold. B is incorrect because the inferior origin of pectoralis major is not a recognized breast boundary. C is incorrect because the lateral pectoralis minor muscle does not constitute a breast tissue border. D is incorrect because the superficial fascia of serratus anterior is not an established breast boundary. E is incorrect because supraclavicular lymph nodes are part of the nodal drainage system, not anatomical breast tissue limits.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency room following a fall onto his extended left hand 6 hours prior. Three years earlier, he sustained an injury to the same hand requiring open reduction with internal fixation and distal radius bone grafting for an index finger metacarpal fracture. Current physical exam and radiographic imaging reveal an exposed fractured plate. After hardware extraction and repeated irrigation, a 1-cm osseous gap remains. Bone graft reconstruction from Gerdy's tubercle of the tibia is planned. The cortical opening should be created just proximal and medial to the origin of which muscle?
A) Extensor digitorum longus
B) Extensor hallucis longus
C) Peroneus longus
D) Popliteus
E) Tibialis anterior
questions.answer:
E)
The tibialis anterior is the correct answer. Gerdy's tubercle on the proximal lateral tibia serves as an excellent source of cancellous bone graft and would provide sufficient material for this patient's reconstruction. Since the ipsilateral distal radius was previously harvested during the initial procedure, it is unavailable. Patient characteristics such as obesity may make alternative donor sites like the iliac crest less favorable. Gerdy's tubercle is positioned between the tibial tubercle and patellar tendon insertion medially and the fibular head laterally. Bone harvesting is performed through a 3-4 cm oblique incision, with the cortical window placed just proximal and medial to where the tibialis anterior muscle originates. A) Extensor digitorum longus is incorrect because it originates more distally on the tibia, not at the level of Gerdy's tubercle. B) Extensor hallucis longus is incorrect as it also originates more distally on the tibia. C) Peroneus longus is incorrect because it originates from the fibula rather than the tibia. D) Popliteus is incorrect as it is located posterior to the knee joint, not near Gerdy's tubercle.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a cut to the extensor tendon on the back of her middle finger. Clinical examination reveals that all fingers can extend to neutral position at the metacarpophalangeal joints. Which of the following anatomical structures accounts for the extension force observed in this examination?
A) Deep transverse metacarpal ligament
B) Intact paratenon
C) Interosseous muscles
D) Juncturae tendinum
E) Lumbrical muscles
questions.answer:
D)
Juncturae tendinum are tendinous connections that link the extensor digitorum communis tendons of the middle, ring, and small fingers. When the middle finger extensor tendon is severed proximal to where the juncturae tendinum connects the middle and ring finger tendons, the ring finger's extensor digitorum communis can transmit extension force through the juncturae tendinum to the distal portion of the middle finger extensor tendon, resulting in metacarpophalangeal joint extension. A) is incorrect because the deep transverse metacarpal ligament provides stability between metacarpal heads but does not generate movement at the MCP joint. B) is incorrect because the tendon is completely severed, so the paratenon cannot be intact. C) is incorrect because interosseous muscles cause MCP joint flexion, not extension. E) is incorrect because lumbrical muscles also produce MCP joint flexion rather than extension.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old woman has a 3-cm defect after excision of a basal cell carcinoma. A nasolabial flap is elevated, rotated, and inset into the lip defect. Photographs are shown. Plans are made to divide and inset the base of the flap, which contains the pedicle, in 3 weeks. In addition to CPT code 11643 (excision of malignant lesion including margins, face, ears, eyelids, nose, lips; excised diameter 2.1 to 3.0 cm), which of the following is the most appropriate CPT code for this procedure?


A) 13152
B) 14060
C) 15576
D) 15732
E) 15740
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The correct CPT code is 15576, formation of direct or tubed pedicle, with or without transfer; eyelids, nose, ears, lips, or intraoral. CPT codes 15570 to 15650 are used to describe distant pedicled skin flaps, in contrast to adjacent tissue flaps. The nasolabial flap is a pedicled flap based on the angular branch of the facial artery. Although the nasolabial flap comes from the cheek, the correct code for this situation is based on the recipient site (lip) when the flap is attached in transfer. If this flap were elevated but delayed, then the code would be based on the donor site (15620, formation of direct or tubed pedicle, with or without transfer, forehead, cheeks, chin, mouth, neck, axillae, genitalia, hands, or feet).


Complex repairs do not involve the formation of a pedicled flap and do not create a donor site, although they do include undermining. Adjacent tissue transfer involves movement of tissue directly adjacent to the flap, such as in rotation flaps or transposition flaps. Adjacent tissue transfers are usually not staged procedures, while distant flaps (15570-15650) are often staged. The nasolabial flap is not a muscle, myocutaneous or fasciocutaneous flap. Examples of flaps included in the 15732 code include temporalis muscle flaps, temporoparietal fascia flaps, and sternocleidomastoid muscle flaps. Island pedicle flaps are cutaneous flaps transposed into a nearby but not immediately adjacent defect, with a pedicle that incorporates an anatomically named axial vessel, and are transferred through a tunnel underneath the skin and sutured into the recipient site defect. While some nasolabial flap reconstructions are performed as island pedicle flaps, this one was not. The pedicle was left intact and division was planned at a later stage. Note that codes for excision of the basal cell cancer cannot be used in conjunction with adjacent tissue transfer (14XXX) or complex repair (131XX) series of codes.


References
Janevicius R. CPT Corner: Clarifications on island pedicle flap code 15740. Plastic Surgery News. 2013 Jan-Feb:12.
Janevicius R. CPT Corner: Pedicle flap CPT codes describe distant flaps. Plastic Surgery News. 2009 Aug:12.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with squamous cell carcinoma affecting her tongue and oral floor. Physical examination reveals a 3 x 3-cm partial tissue loss involving the tongue and oral floor. The tumor will be surgically removed and the resulting defect will be reconstructed simultaneously using a submental musculocutaneous flap. When the vascular pedicle of this flap is dissected and exposed, which lymph node levels become accessible for examination and biopsy?
A) Level I
B) Levels I and II
C) Levels I, II, and III
D) Levels I, II, III, and IV
E) Levels II and III
questions.answer:
A)

The correct answer is A because the submental flap's vascular supply comes from the submental artery, a branch of the facial artery, which travels between the submandibular gland and the digastric muscle belly before diving deep between the mylohyoid and geniohyoid muscles. The surgical approach to expose this pedicle involves incisions in the mental region and a transverse incision 1-2 cm below the mandible, which directly exposes the Level I lymph node region. Level I nodes are located in the submental area bounded superiorly by the mandible and inferiorly by the hyoid bone, subdivided into Level Ia (submental nodes anterior to the digastric muscle) and Level Ib (submandibular nodes posterior to the digastric muscle). B is incorrect because Level II nodes are located around the upper internal jugular vein and are not exposed during submental flap pedicle dissection. C is incorrect because Level III nodes are positioned around the middle internal jugular vein, which is not accessed during this procedure. D is incorrect because Level IV nodes are found around the lower internal jugular vein near the clavicle, far from the submental dissection field. E is incorrect because neither Level II nor Level III nodes are exposed during submental flap harvest, as these are located along the internal jugular chain rather than in the submental region.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male patient seeks aesthetic improvement of his nasal appearance following a traumatic injury that occurred 14 months previously. Physical examination reveals depression of the nasal bones and middle vault region. The patient expresses concern about additional scarring and harvest site discomfort and specifically requests a treatment approach that minimizes donor site complications. Which of the following choices would be most suitable for this patient?
A) Bone allograft
B) Costal cartilage graft
C) Iliac crest graft
D) Split calvarial graft
E) Temporal fascia graft
questions.answer:
A)
Bone allograft represents the optimal choice as it eliminates the need for donor site harvesting and associated complications. Freeze-dried bone allografts have proven safe and effective for nasal augmentation procedures, having been extensively utilized in orthopedic trauma and oncologic reconstruction. While fresh autografts may possess superior osteoinductive properties and integrate more completely with recipient bone beds, this advantage is less critical in nasal grafting where the recipient site is soft tissue rather than bone. The extensive processing of freeze-dried allografts removes all cellular components, preventing immunologic rejection similar to acellular dermal matrices. B is incorrect because costal cartilage harvesting, while commonly used for nasal reconstruction, involves significant donor site scarring and pain. C is incorrect because iliac crest grafting causes donor site discomfort and the bone shape is suboptimal for nasal contouring. D is incorrect because split calvarial grafts also cause donor site morbidity and are primarily indicated when bicoronal access is already planned. E is incorrect because temporal fascia harvesting requires a scalp donor site, which contradicts the patient's desire to minimize donor site complications.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old healthy female comes to the clinic for breast assessment. On examination, the nipple-areola complex is positioned high with no breast tissue present on the right side, while the left breast shows normal development. She uses a B-cup bra with padding on the right side. Her mother reports that this asymmetry is causing considerable psychological distress for the patient, and they wish to explore surgical treatment options. What mammaplasty approach would be most suitable for managing this patient's right breast condition?
A) Deep inferior epigastric perforator flap
B) Latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap
C) Saline implant augmentation
D) Structural fat grafting
E) Tissue expander placement
questions.answer:
E)
This adolescent patient has congenital absence of breast tissue (amastia) on the right side with a malpositioned nipple-areola complex. Tissue expansion is the most appropriate initial approach because it creates adequate breast pocket space and allows for size adjustments as the patient continues to mature, with the left breast still developing. The tissue expander serves as a foundation for eventual definitive reconstruction with either an implant or autologous tissue once growth is complete. A) Deep inferior epigastric perforator flap is incorrect because it's too complex for an initial procedure in an adolescent and requires adequate recipient site preparation. B) Latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap is incorrect as it's unnecessarily invasive for a first-stage procedure and may not provide optimal aesthetic results without prior expansion. C) Saline implant augmentation is incorrect because immediate implant placement without tissue expansion would likely result in poor positioning and inadequate soft tissue coverage. D) Structural fat grafting is incorrect as there is insufficient recipient tissue to support grafting in cases of complete amastia.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old man presents with nail pitting, leukonychia, and crumbling of the nail plate. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?


A) Arsenic toxicity
B) Human immunodeficiency virus
C) Lichen planus
D) Psoriatic arthritis
E) Subungual melanoma
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


Psoriatic arthritis often presents with auto-fusion of the small hand joints and diffuse fusiform swelling of the digits. This psoriatic dactylitis or "sausage digit" is caused by inflammation of periosteum, tendon, and tendon insertions. Nail deformities include pitting, leukonychia, nail crumbling, and onycholysis (separation of nail plate from bed). Nail deformities affect approximately 80% of patients with psoriatic arthritis, and 50% of patients with psoriasis.


Nail lichen planus (NLP) is characterized by thinning, longitudinal ridging, and distal splitting of the nail plate. NLP is usually resistant to topical corticosteroid therapy, but successful treatment has been reported with intralesional or systemic administration of corticosteroids.


Characteristic skin lesions of arsenic poisoning include hyperkeratosis and Mees‚Äo lines. Mees‚Äo lines are prominent transverse white lines in fingernails or toe-nails due to arsenic deposition in keratin-rich tissues.


Subungual melanoma has distinct cutaneous nail manifestations such as brown or black streaks in the nail without any known injury, streaks on the nails that increase in size, or a "bruise" on the nail that will not heal or move up as the fingernail grows. One of the key indications of subungual melanoma is known as "Hutchinson's sign." This is when a person has a streak that extends from the tip of the nail down to the nail bed and into the eponychium.


Nail disorders in HIV-infected patients include clubbing, splitting of the nails, or discoloration (black or brown lines going either vertically or horizontally).


ReferencesChoo AD, Middleton G, Wilson RL. Nonrheumatoid Inflammatory Arthroses of the Hand and Wrist. J Hand Surg Am. 2015 Dec;40(12):2477-2487.Kapasi, OA, Ruby LK, Calney K. The psoriatic hand. J Hand Surg Am. 1982 Sept;7(5):492-497.Mark R. Belsky, Paul Feldon, Lewis H. Millender, et al. Hand involvement in psoriatic arthritis. J Hand Surg Am. 1982 Mar;7(2):203-207.Sobolewski P, Walecka I, Dopytalska K. Nail involvement in psoriatic arthritis. Reumatologia. 2017;55(3):131-135.Tan ES, Chong WS, Tey, HL. Nail psoriasis: a review. Am J Clin Dermatol. 2012 Dec 1;13(6):375-388.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 9-month history of nail abnormality as depicted. Physical examination reveals thin skin covering a mass in the eponychial area. The digit is painless on examination. Her main concern is the cosmetic appearance of the nail. What is the most appropriate first step in treatment?
A) Surgical removal of the mass beneath the eponychial fold
B) Magnetic resonance imaging of the digit
C) Nail bed repair using split toenail bed graft
D) Destruction of the nail germinal matrix
E) Fluconazole therapy orally for 12 weeks
questions.answer:
A)
Surgical removal of the mucous cyst (ganglion) beneath the eponychial fold that is distorting the germinal matrix is the most appropriate treatment for the nail groove depicted. Following cyst excision, the grooving should improve or completely resolve. B) is incorrect because MRI is primarily used for identifying glomus tumors and would add unnecessary cost without changing management. C) is incorrect because split sterile matrix grafting is used for nonadherent nail plates from sterile matrix loss, which is not evident here. D) is incorrect because germinal matrix ablation is reserved for cases of split or thin nails after germinal matrix trauma, not for mucous cyst-related deformities. E) is incorrect because fluconazole treats onychomycosis, which presents with nail discoloration, loss of luster, and crumbling - none of which are present in this case.

questions.question:
An 11-year-old male presents to the clinic with a 12-month history of worsening unilateral facial tissue loss on the left side. The patient exhibits the characteristic linear scar-like appearance. Physical examination reveals preserved facial bone architecture. Which imaging modality should be prioritized in the diagnostic evaluation of this condition?
A) Abdominal MRI
B) Brain MRI
C) Chest radiograph
D) Hand radiographs
questions.answer:
B)

This patient presents with progressive hemifacial atrophy consistent with Parry-Romberg syndrome (PRS), a rare condition involving progressive deterioration of facial skin, subcutaneous tissue, and sometimes underlying muscle and bone, typically affecting one side of the face. Brain MRI is the most appropriate imaging study because neurological complications are frequently associated with PRS, including seizures, migraines, Horner syndrome, and hemiplegia. Additionally, brain MRI abnormalities are commonly detected even in patients without obvious neurological symptoms, making this imaging essential for comprehensive evaluation and potential intervention planning. A) Abdominal MRI is incorrect because PRS does not typically involve intra-abdominal pathology or require abdominal imaging for diagnosis or management. C) Chest radiograph is incorrect because pulmonary or thoracic abnormalities are not characteristic features of PRS and would not contribute to the diagnostic workup. D) Hand radiographs are incorrect because skeletal abnormalities of the extremities are not commonly associated with PRS, and imaging of the hands would not provide relevant diagnostic information.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman with cancer of the right breast undergoes mastectomy and axillary node dissection, complicated by mastectomy flap necrosis requiring skin grafting. She completes adjuvant chemoradiation. One year later, she comes to the office with a fungating mass growing through the skin graft. Imaging demonstrates involvement of the fourth and fifth ribs with an anticipated skeletal defect of 4 √o 4 cm. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the skeletal reconstruction?A) High-density porous polyethyleneB) Methyl methacrylate with meshC) 2.4-mm Titanium plateD) No skeletal reconstructionE) Vascularized rib
questions.answer: The correct response is Option D.The principles of management of this recurrent right breast cancer include radical resection of all involved tissues (including ribs) and reconstruction with well vascularized flaps. In this case, a right latissimus muscle flap and skin graft was used for reconstruction. No alloplastic material was placed or skeletal thoracic cage reconstruction performed. This is common in these types of patients, because excessive fibrosis caused by the radiation to the chest wall prevents loss of respiratory efficiency through paradoxical motion which otherwise occurs in patients who have more than four ribs involved or a defect larger than 5 cm.ReferencesJanis JE, Harrison B. Wound healing: part I. Basic science. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2014 Feb;133(2):199e-207e.Samuels L, Granick MS, Ramasastry S, et al. Reconstruction of radiation-induced chest wall lesions. Ann Plast Surg. 1993 Nov;31(5):399-405.Stone HB, Coleman CN, Anscher MS, et al. Effects of radiation on normal tissue: consequences and mechanisms. Lancet Oncol. 2003 Sep;4(9):529-36.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old male presents to the emergency department following a degloving trauma to the back of his non-dominant left hand from an ATV accident. Clinical evaluation reveals destruction of soft tissues and extensor tendons affecting the index, middle, ring, and small fingers, plus a positive Allen test. Shaft fractures of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th metacarpals are also identified. After multiple wound debridements, there remains a 6 × 8 cm dorsal hand wound with exposed fracture sites. What is the optimal approach for managing this soft-tissue defect?
A) Anterolateral thigh free flap
B) Full-thickness skin grafting
C) Rectus abdominis muscle free flap
D) Reverse radial forearm flap
E) Split-thickness skin grafting
questions.answer:
A)
The anterolateral thigh free flap is the most appropriate choice for this extensive dorsal hand defect with exposed bone and fractures. This perforator flap provides excellent coverage for large defects while minimizing donor site morbidity, making it ideal for complex hand reconstruction requiring durable soft-tissue coverage. B is incorrect because full-thickness skin grafts cannot reliably survive over large areas with exposed bone and lack the durability needed for this complex defect. C is incorrect because while muscle flaps can provide coverage, the rectus abdominis creates significant donor site morbidity compared to perforator flaps for a defect of this size. D is incorrect because reverse radial forearm flaps, though useful locally, add morbidity to an already injured extremity and are less favored with current microsurgical advances. E is incorrect because split-thickness skin grafts cannot safely cover exposed bone and fractures, lacking the necessary durability for this type of complex defect.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old child presents with severely limited upper eyelid elevation on the left side (2 mm levator function) and requires surgical correction of ptosis. Which material demonstrates the most favorable long-term outcomes with minimal recurrence and complications?
A) Harvested fascia lata from patient
B) Polypropylene suture material
C) Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) fiber
D) Silicone rod implant
questions.answer:
A)
Harvested fascia lata from the patient (autologous fascia lata) provides the most favorable long-term outcomes with the lowest rates of both recurrence and complications in congenital ptosis repair. This material integrates well with surrounding tissues and maintains its structural integrity over time. B) is incorrect because polypropylene suture has high recurrence rates due to suture slippage and is typically used only as a temporary measure. C) is incorrect because while PTFE (GORE-TEX) shows low recurrence rates, it carries a higher risk of infection compared to autologous fascia lata. D) is incorrect because silicone rods, despite being easily adjustable since they don't incorporate into tissue, demonstrate higher complication rates than autologous fascia lata.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old female patient with velocardiofacial syndrome presents for assessment of nasal speech quality. Following extensive speech therapy, she had surgical correction of an isolated soft palate cleft at 9 months of age. Clinical examination reveals good palatal healing with minimal soft palate movement during speech production. Video swallow study demonstrates limited velar mobility, though lateral pharyngeal wall movement appears sufficient. For optimal speech improvement in this patient's velopharyngeal dysfunction, which of the following represents the best treatment approach?
A) Posterior pharyngeal wall fat injection
B) Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty
C) Intravelar veloplasty procedure
D) Superior-based pharyngeal flap construction
E) Sphincter pharyngoplasty technique
questions.answer:
D)
Superior-based pharyngeal flap construction is the most appropriate choice given the patient's specific anatomical findings. With minimal velar motion and adequate lateral pharyngeal wall movement, a pharyngeal flap provides the most reliable method to achieve velopharyngeal competence by creating a static bridge that the lateral walls can contact. A) Posterior pharyngeal wall fat injection is incorrect because it only reduces the anteroposterior gap but doesn't address the poor velar mobility. B) Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty is incorrect as it primarily lengthens the palate but won't compensate for the severely limited velar movement. C) Intravelar veloplasty is incorrect because while it repositions muscle fibers, it cannot overcome the fundamental lack of velar motion present in this case. E) Sphincter pharyngoplasty is incorrect because it requires good muscle tone and function to create an effective sphincter, which this patient lacks due to poor velar mobility.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male patient develops progressive confusion and altered mental status one day following abdominoplasty surgery. His medical history includes a 200-pound (91-kg) weight reduction after bariatric gastric bypass procedure 22 months previously. What is the most appropriate first intervention in his care?
A) Consultation with anesthesiology
B) Venous duplex ultrasound of lower extremities
C) Anticoagulation with heparin
D) Mental health evaluation
E) Thiamine administration
questions.answer:
E)
Patients who have undergone massive weight reduction frequently experience nutritional deficiencies, particularly thiamine deficiency, which can result in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. The treatment involves intravenous thiamine 100 mg daily, followed by 100 mg every 8 hours until symptom resolution. Thiamine administration carries minimal risk and may reverse the neurological symptoms. A) is incorrect because anesthesia consultation would not address the likely nutritional cause of altered mental status. B) is incorrect because venous thromboembolism is uncommon just one day post-surgery, and duplex ultrasound would not address the immediate neurological concerns. C) is incorrect because therapeutic anticoagulation poses significant bleeding risk in the immediate postoperative period after abdominoplasty. D) is incorrect because metabolic and surgical complications should be evaluated and treated before considering psychiatric causes for altered mental status.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old male patient requires reconstruction of a posterior trunk defect one week following excision of a 3 × 3-cm recurring sarcoma. Primary skin closure was attempted during the initial operation, but tissue death and wound dehiscence developed. Past medical history is significant for spinal radiation treatment for soft-tissue sarcoma two years prior. Clinical examination reveals a 5 × 5-cm wound in the middle back at T10 level with visible spinous processes. Which of the following represents the most suitable option for achieving complete defect coverage?
A) Latissimus dorsi flap
B) Rectus abdominis free tissue transfer
C) Split-thickness skin graft
D) Trapezius muscle flap
E) Extensive undermining with primary reclosure
questions.answer:
A)

The latissimus dorsi flap is the most appropriate choice for this reconstruction. This muscle provides adequate tissue volume and skin coverage to address the described defect. As a Mathes-Nahai Type V flap, it receives primary vascular supply from the thoracodorsal vessels and secondary blood flow from posterior intercostal and lumbar perforating vessels. The muscle's humeral insertion can be released to enhance mobility. The flap can be configured as a turnover flap based on the medial secondary pedicles or transposed using the primary vascular supply, with vein grafts available for pedicle extension if necessary. Its reliable anatomy and straightforward harvest make it ideal for posterior trunk reconstruction. B) is incorrect because suitable recipient vessels are not easily accessible in this region, making microvascular reconstruction challenging. C) is incorrect because skin grafts will not take reliably on previously irradiated tissue with exposed bone. D) is incorrect because the trapezius muscle has insufficient reach to cover defects at the T10 level. E) is incorrect because extensive undermining would further compromise the blood supply to already radiation-damaged tissue, increasing the risk of additional necrosis and breakdown.

questions.question:
An 80-year-old female patient has been diagnosed with lentigo maligna on her cheek. The patient declines surgical removal. What is the most suitable alternative treatment?
A) Cryosurgery
B) Electrodesiccation with curettage
C) Laser therapy
D) Topical 5-fluorouracil application
E) Topical imiquimod 5%
questions.answer:
E)

Topical imiquimod 5% is the most appropriate non-surgical treatment for lentigo maligna when surgery is refused. Imiquimod functions as an immune response modifier by activating toll-like receptor 7, stimulating the patient's immune system to target abnormal cells. Clinical studies demonstrate clearance rates of 50-93% with a recurrence rate of 24.5% for lentigo maligna treatment. It serves as the recommended second-line therapy when surgical excision is not feasible. A) Cryosurgery is incorrect because it lacks robust evidence supporting effectiveness in lentigo maligna treatment. B) Electrodesiccation with curettage is incorrect as there is insufficient high-quality data demonstrating efficacy for this melanoma in situ variant. C) Laser therapy is incorrect because it does not have established evidence base for successful lentigo maligna management. D) Topical 5-fluorouracil is incorrect as it lacks strong clinical evidence supporting its use specifically for lentigo maligna treatment.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old electrical worker presents for assessment of a fingertip trauma affecting the index finger. The injury is managed with healing by secondary intention, which ultimately leads to a hook-nail deformity. Which anatomical component of the nail apparatus was most likely damaged in this patient?
A) Eponychium
B) Germinal matrix
C) Lunula
D) Nail groove
E) Sterile matrix
questions.answer:
E)
The sterile matrix is the correct answer because when this structure is shortened and adheres to the volar soft tissues during healing, it creates the characteristic hook-nail deformity seen in distal fingertip injuries. A) Eponychium is incorrect because damage to this cuticle structure causes rough nail appearance and loss of luster, not hook-nail deformity. B) Germinal matrix is incorrect because this structure is responsible for nail plate formation, and its injury does not produce hook-nail deformity. C) Lunula is incorrect because this proximal nail structure lies beneath the nail plate and its damage does not cause hook-nail deformity. D) Nail groove is incorrect because this lateral nail margin is associated with ingrown nails and paronychia, not hook-nail deformity.

questions.question:
A healthy 10-month-old girl is evaluated by her parents due to concerns about her head shape. Physical examination reveals flattening of the left forehead and left posterior skull with leftward deviation of the nasal root. What is the most appropriate treatment?
A) Cranial orthotic helmet
B) Head MRI
C) Repositioning therapy
D) Surgical intervention
E) Watchful waiting
questions.answer:
D)
The clinical findings of left frontal flattening, left occipital flattening, and leftward nasal root deviation are characteristic of left coronal synostosis, which requires surgical correction as the definitive treatment. A) is incorrect because cranial orthotic helmets are used for positional plagiocephaly, not synostosis. B) is incorrect because MRI is not indicated in an otherwise healthy infant with clear clinical signs of synostosis. C) is incorrect because repositioning therapy is only effective for deformational plagiocephaly, not craniosynostosis. E) is incorrect because observation alone will not correct the underlying premature suture fusion and may lead to increased intracranial pressure and developmental issues.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old woman presents with a new-onset draining sinus of the left thoracic cage with associated indurated skin. Medical history includes bilateral breast cancer that was managed with bilateral radical mastectomy with radiation therapy 27 years ago. On CT scan, the image (shown) is consistent with osteoradionecrosis. Resection of affected skin, soft tissue, and thoracic cage produces a 35 √o 20-cm soft-tissue defect and a skeletal defect spanning five ribs. A photograph of the defect is shown. The thoracic cage is fibrotic and noncompliant because of previous radiation. Which of the following approaches is most appropriate for reconstruction?


A) Free omental flap with skin graft over titanium mesh and reconstruction plates
B) Left latissimus dorsi muscle flap with skin graft over acellular dermal matrix
C) Left rectus abdominis turnover flap with skin graft over methyl methacrylate sandwich
D) Reverse abdominoplasty advancement over ePTFE patch
E) Right pectoralis muscle turnover flap over polypropylene mesh
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


The most appropriate option for this patient is a left latissimus dorsi muscle flap with skin graft over acellular dermal matrix, given the alternatives listed. Basic principles of thoracic reconstruction include: debridement of devitalized tissue, removal of foreign bodies, establishment of healthy wound bed, restoration of stability/structure (generally reconstruction of skeleton if more than four ribs or a greater than 5-cm-diameter defect is involved), restoration of normal respiratory mechanics, protection of vital structures/organs, obliteration of dead space, provision of durable coverage, and delivery of an aesthetic result. However, if a patient has been previously irradiated, and therefore loses compliance of the thoracic cage because of radiation-induced fibrosis, skeletal reconstruction may not be mandatory if there is no paradoxical motion of the thoracic cage upon respirations and there is preservation of respiratory efficiency. Such is the case with this patient.


A left rectus turnover flap would not be a good option for two reasons: 1) as can be seen in the image, the left internal mammary artery has been harvested, thereby compromising the superior epigastric vessel on which this flap would be based, and 2) it is insufficient to provide enough soft-tissue coverage of a defect this size. Furthermore, as indicated above, methyl methacrylate would not be mandatory in this patient.


A right pectoralis turnover flap is insufficient to cover a defect this size.


A free omental flap can be used to reconstruct this defect (as can a pedicled omental flap), but again, thoracic skeletal reconstruction would not be mandatory in this previously irradiated patient; furthermore, even if it were, titanium mesh and reconstruction plates would not be utilized.


A reverse abdominoplasty flap (Ryan procedure) would not be able to cover a defect this size.


References
1. Jones G, Jurkiewicz MJ, Bostwick J, et al. Management of the infected median sternotomy wound with muscle flaps. The Emory 20-year experience. Ann Surg. 1997 Jun;225(6):766-776; discussion 776-778.
2. Hultman CS, Culbertson JH, Jones GE, et al. Thoracic reconstruction with the omentum: indications, complications, and results. Ann Plast Surg. 2001 Mar;46(3):242-249.
3. Dingman RO, Argenta LC. Reconstruction of the chest wall. Ann Thorac Surg. 1981 Aug;32(2):202-208.
4. McCormack PM. Use of prosthetic materials in chest-wall reconstruction. Assets and liabilities. Surg Clin North Am. 1989 Oct;69(5):965-976.
5. Granick MS, Larson DL, Solomon MP. Radiation-related wounds of the chest wall. Clin Plast Surg. 1993 Jul;20(3):559-571.
6. Samuels L, Granick MS, Ramasastry S, et al. Reconstruction of radiation-induced chest wall lesions. Ann Plast Surg. 1993 Nov;31(5):399-405.
7. Rocco G, Mori S, Fazioli F, et al. The use of biomaterials for chest wall reconstruction 30 year after radical surgery and radiation. Ann Thorac Surg. 2012 Oct;94(4):e109-e110.
8. Bakri K, Mardini S, Evans KK, et al. Workhorse flaps in chest wall reconstruction: the pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, and rectus abdominis flaps. Semin Plast Surg. 2011 Feb;25(1):43-54.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male patient is planned for repair of a 7-cm skeletal gap (illustrated) following removal of a distal radius neoplasm. His medical history includes elevated blood pressure and a 30-year history of smoking one pack per day. What is the optimal reconstructive approach for this defect?
A) Cadaveric bone transplant
B) Vascularized fibular transfer
C) Rigid internal fixation system
D) Regional ulnar bone rotation flap
questions.answer:
B)
Vascularized fibular transfer represents the optimal reconstructive method for this case. Complex tissue restoration following oncologic resection presents considerable challenges for reconstructive surgeons. Skeletal gaps exceeding 6 cm typically necessitate vascularized bone reconstruction for successful healing. For extensive defects, the vascularized fibula represents the gold standard choice due to its dependable vascular supply via the peroneal vessels and the ability to include a skin component when needed. Free tissue transfer can achieve successful outcomes even in patients with tobacco use history and frequently represents the best reconstructive option for smokers. A) Cadaveric bone transplant is contraindicated, particularly in tobacco users due to poor integration potential. C) Rigid internal fixation system alone cannot provide sufficient long-term structural support for defects of this magnitude. D) Regional ulnar bone rotation flap is not feasible for reconstructing defects of this size and location.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents with a mass located in the left anterior forearm. MRI imaging has been obtained. Complete oncologic excision will require removal of all muscles within the volar forearm compartment. Which of the following reconstructive approaches is most suitable for restoring finger flexion function following surgery?
A) Transfer of flexor digitorum profundus to flexor digitorum superficialis
B) Flexor-pronator muscle slide procedure
C) Free gracilis muscle transfer with median nerve branch innervation
D) Oberlin-Mackinnon nerve transfer technique
E) Pedicled latissimus dorsi muscle flap
questions.answer:
C)
A free gracilis muscle transfer represents the optimal reconstructive choice as it offers excellent strength and excursion characteristics that closely match the native finger flexor muscles being replaced. The vascular anastomosis and nerve coaptation can be performed in the proximal upper arm, well away from the tumor resection site. Although individual digit flexion will not be achieved, the patient will regain the ability to form a functional composite grip following this reconstruction.

A) is incorrect because flexor digitorum profundus to superficialis transfer is designed for managing spastic flexor contractures in patients with retained voluntary control, and requires the presence of both muscle groups that would be excised in this case. B) is incorrect because the flexor-pronator slide involves releasing and advancing muscles from the medial epicondyle to treat contractures, but these muscles will have been removed during the oncologic resection. D) is incorrect because the Oberlin-Mackinnon transfer redirects median and ulnar nerve branches to restore elbow flexion via the brachialis and biceps, not finger flexion. E) is incorrect because while the latissimus dorsi provides excellent coverage and elbow flexion strength, its reach as a pedicled flap cannot extend beyond the distal elbow to restore finger function.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male motorcyclist presents with right tibia and fibula fractures following a traffic collision. Clinical examination reveals loss of sensation over the top of the right foot and an inability to lift the foot upward. The vascular examination of the right leg is unremarkable. Which nerve is most likely damaged?
A) Calcaneal
B) Common peroneal
C) Lateral plantar
D) Lateral sural cutaneous
E) Posterior tibial
questions.answer:
B)
The common peroneal nerve originates from the posterior divisions of L4, L5, S1, and S2 nerve roots. This nerve travels between the biceps femoris and the lateral gastrocnemius head, wraps around the fibular neck between the peroneus longus and fibula, then divides into superficial and deep peroneal branches. It provides motor innervation to the peroneus longus, peroneus brevis, and biceps femoris muscles. Damage to this nerve causes foot drop and loss of sensation on the foot's dorsal aspect. A) The calcaneal nerve is a sensory branch of the sural nerve that provides feeling to the lateral heel area without any motor function. C) The lateral plantar nerve branches from the tibial nerve and supplies the quadratus plantae and abductor digiti minimi muscles, along with sensation to the fifth toe and lateral fourth toe. D) The lateral sural cutaneous nerve is a sensory branch from the common fibular nerve supplying the posterior-lateral leg skin without motor innervation. E) The posterior tibial nerve stems from L4-S3 roots as a sciatic nerve branch, innervating the gastrocnemius, popliteus, soleus, tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus, and flexor hallucis longus muscles.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old female patient treated with chemoradiation for oropharyngeal malignancy a decade ago develops intense pain following tooth removal. A subsequent computed tomography reveals a pathological fracture at the mandibular angle. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment
B) Extended intravenous antimicrobial therapy
C) Referral to oncology
D) Surgical fixation with plates and screws
E) Mandibular resection with fibular free tissue transfer
questions.answer:
E)
The optimal treatment is mandibular resection with fibular free tissue transfer. In recent decades, chemoradiation has become the preferred primary treatment for oropharyngeal cancer, leading to increased rates of mandibular osteoradionecrosis. Pathological fractures commonly occur after dental extractions, particularly third molars, resulting in angle fractures. With extensive experience using vascularized bone flaps, particularly fibular flaps, the current standard involves resecting the necrotic bone and performing immediate reconstruction. A) Hyperbaric oxygen alone is controversial for osteoradionecrosis and cannot repair a pathological fracture. B) While IV antibiotics treat osteomyelitis, osteoradionecrosis with fracture requires surgical intervention, not prolonged antibiotic therapy alone. C) Although malignancy should be considered, this clinical presentation is typical of osteoradionecrosis, limiting oncology's role. D) Internal fixation would fail because irradiated necrotic bone cannot heal properly, even when anatomically reduced.

questions.question:
What anatomical reference points should guide percutaneous neurotoxin administration for treating benign masseter muscle hypertrophy?
A) Between the earlobe-to-oral commissure line and the inferior border of the mandible
B) Between the maxillary and mandibular occlusal planes
C) Between the tragus-to-infraorbital rim line and the cervicomental line
D) Between the tragus-to-mid upper lip line and the root of the helix to subnasale line
E) Between the zygomatic arch-to-mid upper lip line and the Frankfort horizontal
questions.answer:
A)
The correct answer is A because the area below the earlobe-to-oral commissure line and above the mandibular inferior border represents a safe injection zone that avoids critical anatomical structures while targeting the primary region of masseter hypertrophy. The masseter muscle extends from the zygomatic body to the mandibular inferior border, making this lower boundary anatomically relevant. B is incorrect because the occlusal planes do not correspond to the masseter muscle boundaries or safe injection zones. C is incorrect because these landmarks relate to different facial regions and do not define the appropriate masseter injection area. D is incorrect because these reference points do not align with masseter muscle anatomy or established safe zones. E is incorrect because the Frankfort horizontal and zygomatic arch landmarks are not relevant for masseter neurotoxin injection guidance.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old child presents to the emergency department with a hard palate laceration. The physician plans to repair the wound using local anesthesia with a greater palatine nerve block. During suturing of the anterior section, the patient experiences pain. Which additional nerve block would be most suitable?
A) Anterior superior alveolar
B) Infraorbital
C) Lesser palatine
D) Middle superior alveolar
E) Sphenopalatine
questions.answer:
E)
The sphenopalatine (nasopalatine) nerve emerges from the incisive foramen and innervates the anterior hard palate. Blocking this nerve is crucial for complete anesthesia of the anterior palatal tissues during laceration repair. A) is incorrect because the anterior superior alveolar nerve innervates the maxillary front teeth and surrounding structures, not the palatal mucosa. B) is incorrect because the infraorbital nerve supplies sensation to the lateral nose, upper lip, and cheek area, not the palate. C) is incorrect because the lesser palatine nerve travels through the greater palatine foramen to innervate the soft palate and uvula, not the anterior hard palate. D) is incorrect because the middle superior alveolar nerve is part of the dental nerve plexus that supplies the maxillary teeth, not the palatal tissues.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with impaired thumb opposition after sustaining a median nerve injury at the wrist level in his dominant right hand 18 months prior. Clinical evaluation reveals intact function of the flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) and flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) in the little, ring, middle, and index digits. Wrist, finger, and thumb extension remain strong. Which tendon transfer to the abductor pollicis brevis insertion would be most suitable for addressing this functional deficit?
A) Extensor carpi radialis brevis transfer
B) Extensor indicis proprius transfer
C) Ring finger FDP transfer
D) Flexor carpi ulnaris transfer
E) Palmaris longus transfer
questions.answer:
B)
The patient exhibits a distal median nerve injury characterized primarily by opposition loss. Since FDS function is preserved in all digits and FDP function remains intact in the index and middle fingers, this indicates a low-level median nerve lesion rather than a proximal injury. A proximal median nerve injury would result in complete FDS dysfunction, loss of index and middle finger FDP function, and palmaris longus impairment.

The extensor indicis proprius (EIP) transfer is optimal because its length allows routing around the ulnar forearm aspect to reach the thumb's proximal phalanx without requiring pulley construction. This eliminates potential complications from adhesion formation around an artificial pulley, making it superior to FDS transfers that necessitate pulley creation at the pisiform level.

A) Extensor carpi radialis brevis transfer is incorrect because it is not an established opponensplasty technique and would compromise the primary wrist extensor. C) Ring finger FDP transfer is incorrect because it would eliminate distal interphalangeal joint flexion in the ring finger. D) Flexor carpi ulnaris transfer is incorrect as it is typically used to create pulleys for other transfers, not as the primary transfer itself. E) Palmaris longus transfer is incorrect because it provides insufficient opposition strength compared to EIP or FDS transfers, particularly inadequate for dominant hand reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents to the clinic with a 3-week history of asymmetric enlargement of her left breast. She received textured silicone breast implants placed in the subglandular plane 4 years prior. She denies any history of injury, fever, or rigors. A 7-day course of oral antibiotics from her primary care provider did not improve the swelling. Physical examination reveals the left breast is approximately 300-400 mL larger than the right breast. No additional abnormalities are observed. Ultrasound imaging demonstrates a seroma with no evidence of hematoma or mass lesion. What is the most probable diagnosis for this patient?
A) Anaplastic large cell lymphoma
B) Double capsule phenomenon
C) Giant fibroadenoma of the breast
D) Hematoma due to capsule tear
E) Periprosthetic abscess
questions.answer:
B)
The most likely diagnosis is double capsule phenomenon. The presentation of delayed-onset breast enlargement without infectious symptoms (no fever or cellulitis), absence of trauma history, and ultrasound findings showing seroma are characteristic of late-onset seroma associated with double capsule formation. This complication occurs in approximately 1% of breast implant cases and is more frequently observed with textured implants, especially those with aggressive surface texturing. During surgical exploration, surgeons typically find a capsular layer lining the implant pocket containing significant serosanguineous fluid, with the textured implant surrounded by a second tight capsule. This phenomenon can occur in both subglandular and submuscular implant positions. A is incorrect because anaplastic large cell lymphoma, while a consideration in late-onset seromas, is extremely rare and would require cytological confirmation. C is incorrect because a giant fibroadenoma would present with a palpable mass, breast contour changes, and would be visible on ultrasound imaging. D is incorrect because a hematoma of this magnitude would typically follow trauma, cause breast pain, and result in external bruising. E is incorrect because a periprosthetic abscess would present with systemic signs of infection including fever, chills, and breast cellulitis.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old female patient presents for delayed breast reconstruction consultation. She underwent right mastectomy for breast cancer followed by chemotherapy and radiation treatment one year prior. Her BMI is 35 kg/m2. Past medical history is significant for well-managed type 2 diabetes, prior cesarean delivery via low transverse incision, and previous open cholecystectomy via subcostal incision. She desires autologous tissue reconstruction, however the surgeon prefers not to perform microsurgical free tissue transfer. What is the most suitable reconstructive approach?
A) Bipedicled transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous (TRAM) flap
B) Contralateral pedicled TRAM flap
C) Ipsilateral pedicled TRAM flap
D) Vascular delay procedure followed by contralateral pedicled TRAM flap
E) Vascular delay procedure followed by ipsilateral pedicled TRAM flap
questions.answer:
D)
In this obese patient with right breast cancer and prior subcostal surgical incision, performing a vascular delay procedure followed by contralateral TRAM flap reconstruction represents the optimal approach. The delay technique enhances flap perfusion and reduces ischemic complications, particularly beneficial in high-risk patients such as those with obesity who require substantial tissue volumes. The subcostal incision compromises the right-sided vascular supply, making ipsilateral reconstruction inadvisable. A) Bipedicled TRAM flap is incorrect because the subcostal incision disrupts one side's blood supply, making bilateral harvest unsafe. B) Contralateral pedicled TRAM flap alone is incorrect because while feasible, it carries higher ischemic risk in this obese patient without delay optimization. C) Ipsilateral pedicled TRAM flap is incorrect because the subcostal incision has compromised the right-sided vascular pedicle. E) Delay with ipsilateral TRAM is incorrect because the subcostal incision still precludes safe right-sided flap harvest regardless of delay.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old male presents for assessment of recently developed skin nodules. His medical history is significant for mandibular cyst formation, palmar and plantar pitting, and previously treated medulloepithelioma. A tissue biopsy is being considered. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Basal cell carcinoma
B) Melanoma
C) Merkel cell carcinoma
D) Sebaceous adenocarcinoma
E) Squamous cell carcinoma
questions.answer:
A)
This patient presents with nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome (Gorlin syndrome). This autosomal dominant disorder occurs in approximately 1 in 56,000 individuals with equal gender distribution. The condition results from PTCH1 gene mutations and manifests with characteristic features including numerous basal cell carcinomas, jaw odontogenic cysts, distinctive facial features, and skeletal malformations involving spine, skull, and ribs. Medulloepithelioma occurs in 5-10% of cases. B) is incorrect because melanoma is not a typical manifestation of Gorlin syndrome. C) is incorrect because Merkel cell carcinoma is not associated with this genetic condition. D) is incorrect because sebaceous adenocarcinoma is not part of the Gorlin syndrome spectrum. E) is incorrect because squamous cell carcinoma is not characteristically seen in this syndrome.

questions.question:
A 74-year-old man in good health suffers a traumatic brain injury from an open comminuted fracture involving both the anterior and posterior walls of the frontal sinus following a car accident. Clear nasal discharge is noted when the patient sits upright. Due to initial medical instability, surgery is postponed for 5 days. Which of the following factors most significantly increases the risk of central nervous system infection?
A) Leakage of cerebrospinal fluid
B) Surgical repair delayed beyond 48 hours
C) Open nature of the fracture
D) Advanced patient age
E) Coexisting traumatic brain injury
questions.answer:
B)
Delaying surgical intervention beyond 48 hours from the time of injury significantly increases the risk of serious central nervous system infection in frontal sinus fractures. Research has demonstrated that the timing of operative intervention is a critical factor in preventing infectious complications. A) is incorrect because cerebrospinal fluid leakage alone does not increase infection risk according to established studies. C) is incorrect because the open nature of the fracture is not independently associated with increased infection rates. D) is incorrect because patient age has not been shown to correlate with higher infection risk in this context. E) is incorrect because the presence of traumatic brain injury itself does not increase the likelihood of CNS infection.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old male patient requires repair of a large ventral hernia in the central abdomen measuring 10 cm in width by 30 cm in length. The surgical plan involves performing a posterior component separation technique. Which of the following best describes the anatomical location where the fascial incision should be made for this procedure?
A) Through the lateral intercostal neurovascular structures
B) Following the mid-axillary anatomical line
C) On the medial side of the linea semilunaris
D) Running parallel to the subcostal margin
E) Creating a vertical division through the rectus muscles
questions.answer:
C)
The posterior component separation technique requires making a vertical fascial incision approximately 0.5 cm medial to the linea semilunaris, then continuing laterally in the avascular plane behind the transversalis muscle. This approach allows for extensive mobilization while preserving the lateral neurovascular bundles and maintaining rectus muscle function. Option A is incorrect because cutting through the lateral intercostal neurovascular bundles would compromise muscle innervation and function. Option B is incorrect as the mid-axillary line is too lateral and not the standard anatomical landmark for this technique. Option D is incorrect because a subcostal incision orientation does not provide the proper plane of dissection needed for posterior component separation. Option E is incorrect as dividing the rectus muscles vertically would damage the muscle integrity rather than working in the posterior fascial planes.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old mobile patient presents to the clinic with a persistent pressure sore on the lower aspect of the left buttock that formed during an extended hospital stay 12 months prior. Multiple attempts at wound packing and dressing modifications have failed to achieve healing. What is the most suitable surgical approach?
A) Ulcer bursa removal with direct closure
B) Repair using a posterior thigh fasciocutaneous rotation flap
C) Repair using a superiorly based gluteal musculocutaneous rotation flap
D) Repair using a tensor fasciae latae island rotation flap
E) Repair using a V-Y hamstring musculocutaneous advancement flap
questions.answer:
B)
The optimal treatment for a mobile patient with a chronic pressure ulcer is reconstruction using a posterior thigh fasciocutaneous rotation flap. These flaps provide reliable axial vascular supply with long-lasting coverage while minimizing functional compromise. The flap better restores normal tissue architecture over bony areas. Limitations include insufficient volume for extensive ulcers with significant depth. A) is incorrect because direct closure has high failure rates due to large tissue defects and surrounding tissue induration making tension-free closure difficult. C) is incorrect because musculocutaneous flaps, while providing excellent blood supply and tissue bulk, can cause functional deficits in ambulatory patients. D) is incorrect because the tensor fasciae latae flap's distal portion reaching the ischial area is typically too thin to provide adequate cushioning. E) is incorrect because musculocutaneous flaps may impair function in walking patients despite their good vascularity and bulk.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female presents for evaluation of unilateral facial weakness following Bell's palsy that failed to improve with oral corticosteroid therapy. Treatment options including functional restoration with gracilis muscle transplantation are being considered. Which of the following represents a benefit of this muscle transfer procedure for this patient?
A) Nerve's capacity to extend to the opposite side
B) Capability to include overlying tendinous structures
C) Multiple vectors of muscular contraction
D) Consistent blood supply anatomy
E) Dual primary nerve innervation
questions.answer:
D)
The gracilis muscle is extensively utilized for facial reanimation due to its numerous benefits. This muscle is positioned in the medial thigh, allowing for straightforward harvesting while the patient is supine and ensuring the donor site remains concealed. It possesses a single reliable vascular supply with sufficient length for transplantation. While it can produce adequate force for animation, it provides only a single vector of contraction, making it most suitable for restoring one aspect of facial expression such as smiling. A is incorrect because the single dominant nerve cannot extend to the contralateral facial region. B is incorrect because there are no overlying tendinous structures associated with this muscle. C is incorrect because the gracilis provides only unidirectional pull rather than multiple directions. E is incorrect because there is only one dominant nerve, not two.

questions.question:
During a procedure with general anesthesia, a 26-year-old male intern is told that the patient in the operating room next door has a very interesting tattoo on her lower abdomen. He takes a picture of the tattoo with his cell phone. This action is a violation of which of the following health care regulations?


A) Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act
B) Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
C) Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
D) National Health Security Strategy
E) Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) was enacted by the US Congress in 1996. Title I of HIPAA protects health insurance coverage for workers and their families when they change or lose their jobs. Title II of HIPAA, known as the Administrative Simplification (AS) provisions, requires the establishment of national standards for electronic health care transactions and national identifiers for providers, health insurance plans, and employers. The AS provisions also address the security and privacy of health data. They allow the protection of individuals‚Äo health information, while also allowing communication between parties involved with patient care. The privacy rule outlines six permitted disclosures of individual health information including the following: per request of the patient, for treatment or payment, to individuals identified by the patient, incidental disclosure, limited data set with removal of individual identifiers, and public interest such as organ donation. Identifiable health information is treated as patient property.


Portable media devices and smartphones also have the ability to store data. Digital pictures and videos taken by cell phones are commonplace, and technology exists that can directly download to the Internet. Breach in HIPAA compliance from this new technology is viewed with increasing scrutiny, especially when patient features are identifiable. In addition, personal digital assistants (PDAs), cell phones, or other devices with appropriate patient lists, properly consented pictures, or other data should be password-protected and data properly disposed, destroyed, or used. Computer hard drives must be demagnetized, overwritten, and/or physically destroyed when disposed.


The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act (EMTALA) is a US Act of Congress passed in 1986 as part of the Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (COBRA). It requires hospitals to provide care to anyone needing emergency health care treatment regardless of citizenship, legal status, or ability to pay.


The Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1985 (or COBRA) is a law passed by the US Congress that mandates an insurance program giving some employees the ability to continue health insurance coverage after leaving employment.


The National Health Security Strategy (NHSS) is a strategic plan developed by the US Department of Health and Human Services that is intended to minimize the health consequences associated with significant health incidents. The NHSS is a provision of the Pandemic and All Hazards Preparedness Act (PAHPA). The purpose of the NHSS is to ensure that the nation is prepared for health threats or incidents.


The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA) is a US federal statute signed into law in 2010. PPACA reforms certain aspects of the private health insurance industry and public health insurance programs, increases insurance coverage of pre-existing conditions, and expands access to insurance to over 30 million Americans.


References
1. Pancoast PE, Patrick TB, Mitchell JA. Physician PDA use and the HIPAA Privacy Rule. J Am Med Inform Assoc. 2003 Nov-Dec;10(6):611-612.
2. Lee BT. Computer and data disposal in plastic surgery: guidelines for health insurance portability and accountability act compliance. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2009 Jul;124(1):186e-187e.
3. Amin K, Chandrasena A. The uses of the iPhone for the plastic surgeon: friend or foe? Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012 Feb;129(2):408e-409e.
4. Florman LD. Portable Surgical Mentor: A Handbook of Protocol for Interns and Residents in Surgery. New York: Springer; 2006:148.
5. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid. www.cms.gov/EMTALA.
6. United States Department of Labor. www.dol.gov/dol/topic/health-plans/cobra.
7. Employee Retirement Income Security Act, 29 USCS ¬ß 1002 (1974).
8. Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Public law 104-191. 1996: www.hhs.gov.

questions.question:
