Although the exact rate of malignant transformation for actinic keratoses is not definitively established, current best estimates indicate approximately 10% of these lesions progress to squamous cell carcinoma or basal cell carcinoma. This significant transformation risk necessitates treatment through various therapeutic approaches. A is incorrect because 1% underestimates the actual transformation risk. C is incorrect because 25% overestimates the progression rate. D is incorrect because 50% significantly overestimates the malignant transformation risk. E is incorrect because 75% greatly overestimates the actual progression rate to malignancy.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old graduate student presents to the clinic for assessment of his right ring finger 4 weeks following an axial loading injury. The diagnosis is soft-tissue mallet finger. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
A) Joint fusion
B) Splinting
C) Percutaneous pinning in extension
D) Tendon reconstruction
E) Direct tendon repair
questions.answer:
B)
Splinting remains the preferred treatment even at 4 weeks post-injury, with the DIP joint maintained in extension for 6 weeks. Most soft-tissue mallet injuries will heal with conservative management, and any remaining extension deficit is typically cosmetic rather than functional. A) Joint fusion is incorrect because it is overly aggressive for a condition that responds well to conservative treatment and would eliminate joint motion unnecessarily. C) Percutaneous pinning in extension is incorrect as it is typically reserved for specific cases where splinting is not feasible due to occupational requirements. D) Tendon reconstruction is incorrect because it is not indicated for acute soft-tissue mallet injuries that can heal with splinting. E) Direct tendon repair is incorrect as soft-tissue mallet injuries involve tendon rupture or avulsion that heals well with immobilization rather than surgical repair.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old male presents to the clinic for treatment planning 3 weeks following diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma of the soft palate. He reports experiencing left ear pain for the past 2 months. Physical examination of the ear reveals no abnormalities. Which nerve is most likely responsible for this referred pain?
A) Auricular branch of the vagus (X)
B) Auriculotemporal
C) Great auricular
D) Superficial temporal
E) Vestibulocochlear (VIII)
questions.answer:
A)
The auricular branch of the vagus nerve (Arnold nerve) is responsible for transmitting sensory information from the ipsilateral ear concha and oropharyngeal region. Persistent ear pain without visible ear pathology should prompt clinicians to investigate for potential intraoral malignancy. B) is incorrect because the auriculotemporal nerve primarily innervates the anterior and superior portions of the external auditory canal. C) is incorrect because the great auricular nerve provides sensation to the lower portion of the external ear. D) is incorrect because the superficial temporal nerve is not a recognized anatomical structure (though the superficial temporal artery does supply the anterior external ear). E) is incorrect because the vestibulocochlear nerve is responsible for hearing and balance, not pain sensation.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old male presents for assessment 9 months following a penetrating injury to the left proximal upper extremity. He did not receive medical care when the trauma occurred. Clinical examination reveals inability to flex the left elbow when the forearm is in supination. He has loss of sensation over the lateral upper arm and forearm. Besides the ulnar nerve transfer to the biceps, which nerve transfer would be most suitable to restore this patient's motor function?
A) Median nerve to brachialis
B) Musculocutaneous nerve to brachioradialis
C) Posterior interosseous nerve to triceps
D) Radial nerve to pronator teres
E) Ulnar nerve to flexor carpi radialis
questions.answer:
A)
The patient has suffered a musculocutaneous nerve injury. The median nerve to brachialis transfer is most appropriate because it provides a viable donor fascicle that can be coapted distally to restore elbow flexion function. Given the chronic nature of the injury (9 months), distal nerve transfers are preferred as they allow donor axons to reach target muscles more quickly than proximal repairs or grafts. The median nerve fascicle transfer to the brachialis nerve branch, combined with the ulnar nerve transfer to the biceps, provides dual innervation for elbow flexion restoration. B is incorrect because the musculocutaneous nerve is the injured nerve and cannot serve as a donor. C is incorrect because the posterior interosseous nerve branches distally at the elbow and cannot reach proximally to innervate the brachialis or biceps. D is incorrect because the pronator teres does not contribute to elbow flexion and the median nerve is uninjured. E is incorrect because the flexor carpi radialis is a wrist flexor, not an elbow flexor, and the median nerve remains intact.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old male presents to the emergency room 4 hours following a human bite injury to his non-dominant hand. Physical examination reveals absence of redness, edema, purulent discharge, lymphangitis, or fever. Wound exploration demonstrates no involvement of joints or tendons. The wound has been debrided and irrigated. What is the most appropriate subsequent management step?
A) Prescribe amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily
B) Prescribe clindamycin 450 mg three times daily
C) Prescribe doxycycline 100 mg twice daily
D) Prescribe trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 1 double-strength tablet twice daily
E) Monitor without treatment
questions.answer:
A)
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the correct choice because prospective randomized trials demonstrate that prophylactic antibiotics are superior to placebo in preventing infections in human bite wounds presenting within 24 hours. Human bite wounds commonly harbor S. aureus, E. corrodens, H. influenzae, and beta-lactamase-producing anaerobic organisms. Amoxicillin-clavulanate provides comprehensive coverage against all these typical oral pathogens. B) is incorrect because clindamycin lacks activity against Eikenella species, which are common in human bite wounds. C) is incorrect because doxycycline has poor anaerobic coverage. D) is incorrect because trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is ineffective against anaerobic bacteria. E) is incorrect because observation alone fails to provide the proven benefit of prophylactic antibiotic therapy in preventing infection.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old female presents with a 7 × 7-cm venous malformation on her thigh that is progressively growing and producing discomfort. The abnormality extends through the skin, subcutaneous layers, and muscular tissue. What represents the most suitable initial treatment approach?
A) Steroid administration
B) Lesion embolization
C) Propranolol treatment
D) Surgical excision of the malformation
E) Sclerotherapy procedure
questions.answer:
E)
Sclerotherapy procedure is the most suitable initial treatment approach. For large symptomatic venous malformations, sclerotherapy serves as the primary intervention. This technique involves injecting an inflammatory agent into the lesion, resulting in endothelial injury, fibrotic changes, and reduction in malformation size. Sclerotherapy offers superior effectiveness with reduced morbidity compared to surgical removal. A) Steroid administration is incorrect because corticosteroids are used for treating problematic infantile hemangiomas but lack effectiveness against vascular malformations. B) Lesion embolization is incorrect as it represents the primary treatment for arteriovenous malformations, not venous malformations. C) Propranolol treatment is incorrect since it is utilized for managing problematic infantile hemangiomas but has no therapeutic benefit for vascular malformations. D) Surgical excision is incorrect as it constitutes second-line therapy for large problematic venous malformations, carrying substantial risks including hemorrhage, nerve damage, infection, and wound complications, plus frequent recurrence due to incomplete removal.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency room 2 hours following a facial injury from a circular saw blade. On examination, there is a deep vertical laceration extending from the lateral portion of the right lower eyelid down to the neck region. The patient cannot raise his right upper lip. What is the maximum time period following injury during which the distal portion of the nerve can still be successfully stimulated?
A) 3 Hours
B) 3 Days
C) 3 Weeks
D) 3 Months
questions.answer:
B)
Facial nerve damage should be considered with any deep cut near the parotid gland and posterior cheek area. Clinical evidence includes complete or partial facial muscle paralysis. Direct end-to-end repair provides optimal outcomes, though nerve grafting may be required for segmental defects. The distal segment of a severed facial nerve remains stimulable for roughly 72 hours post-injury. After this timeframe, neurotransmitter reserves are exhausted and motor end plate depolarization in facial muscles ceases. A is incorrect because 3 hours is too short - the nerve remains viable much longer than this brief period. C is incorrect because 3 weeks exceeds the timeframe when neurotransmitter stores are depleted. D is incorrect because 3 months is far beyond the period when distal nerve stimulation remains possible.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old male child comes to the clinic for assessment of an ear abnormality. Physical examination reveals an unusual cartilaginous ridge running from the antihelix to the helix at roughly the border between the upper and middle portions of the ear. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Constricted ear
B) Cryptotia
C) Microtia
D) Question mark ear
E) Stahl ear
questions.answer:
E)
The correct diagnosis is Stahl ear, which is characterized by an abnormal cartilaginous ridge (also known as the third crus) that extends from the antihelix to the helix at approximately the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the ear. This distinctive cartilaginous bar requires surgical excision when prominent. A) Constricted ear is incorrect because it involves a deficient helical rim circumference that creates a cupped, protruding appearance rather than an abnormal cartilage bar. B) Cryptotia is incorrect because it presents with the upper ear hidden beneath the temporal scalp, not an abnormal cartilage ridge. C) Microtia is incorrect because it involves underdeveloped or absent outer ear cartilage, not an extra cartilaginous structure. D) Question mark ear is incorrect because it features excess scapha in the upper ear with deficiency at the middle-lower junction, creating a question mark shape rather than an abnormal cartilage bar.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male patient suffered a full-thickness thermal injury to his right upper extremity from an open flame during outdoor grilling. The burn covers 5% of his total body surface area. Forty-eight hours post-injury, he undergoes surgical debridement of the dorsal wrist and forearm region. Following debridement, the paratenon layer is absent. A two-layer artificial dermis (Integra) is chosen for wound coverage. Which of the following outcomes is associated with this grafting material?
A) Reduced hospital expenses
B) Fewer hospitalizations required
C) Reduced surgical procedures needed
D) Lower risk of excessive scar formation
E) Enhanced tactile sensitivity post-reconstruction
questions.answer:
D)
Bilaminate neodermis (Integra) is associated with reduced hypertrophic scar formation in burn reconstruction, which is well-documented in the literature. A is incorrect because Integra is an expensive product that increases hospital costs. B is incorrect because the use of Integra typically requires longer hospital stays to accommodate the staged surgical approach. C is incorrect because Integra necessitates a two-stage procedure, requiring an additional surgery for skin grafting over the neodermis. E is incorrect because there is no evidence in the literature supporting improved sensation following Integra reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old female patient receives breast augmentation surgery using round, smooth silicone gel implants positioned in a dual-plane technique. Following surgery, she develops unilateral redness and increased temperature that gradually improves after 10 days of oral antibiotic therapy. She inquires about how this complication might affect her long-term surgical results. What is the most probable consequence of this patient's postoperative course?
A) Sagging of breast tissue
B) Formation of scar tissue around the implant
C) Visible implant edge deformity
D) Implant failure
E) Loss of nipple sensation
questions.answer:
B)
Bacterial biofilm formation is recognized as one of the primary risk factors for developing scar tissue formation around breast implants, which can be associated with bacterial contamination and infection. A is incorrect because a history of infection does not typically cause breast tissue sagging. C is incorrect because infection history does not lead to visible implant edge problems or inframammary fold issues. D is incorrect because previous infection does not directly cause implant structural failure. E is incorrect because infection history is unlikely to affect nipple nerve function or sensation.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male experiences multiple fractures involving the mid and upper facial regions following a car accident. The patient immediately notices loss of smell after the trauma. Damage to which of the following bones most likely accounts for this patient's anosmia?
A) Ethmoid
B) Frontal
C) Nasal
D) Sphenoid
E) Vomer
questions.answer:
A)
The ethmoid bone contains the cribriform plate, which is the horizontal segment that supports the olfactory bulb and provides passages for the olfactory nerves. The cribriform plates contain numerous small openings that allow olfactory nerve fibers to pass through and are closely associated with the meninges. Trauma to this area can result in anosmia and potentially cerebrospinal fluid leaks due to meningeal tears. B) is incorrect because while frontal bone fractures can cause anosmia, they are less directly related to olfactory nerve pathways than ethmoid injuries. C) is incorrect because nasal bone fractures primarily affect the external nasal structure rather than the olfactory apparatus. D) is incorrect because sphenoid bone injuries, while potentially affecting smell, are not as intimately connected to the olfactory pathways as the ethmoid cribriform plate. E) is incorrect because the vomer forms part of the nasal septum but does not contain olfactory nerve passages.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female patient with systemic lupus erythematosus presents for evaluation of a persistent ulcer on her right lower leg. The lesion began as a small pustular formation 3 months prior and has progressively deteriorated into an ulcerative wound. Histopathologic examination of tissue samples excluded malignancy. Bacterial cultures have remained negative for over 4 weeks. Wound debridement and skin grafting procedures were performed but resulted in graft failure and formation of similar ulcerative lesions at the graft harvest site. What is the most appropriate next management approach?
A) Bilayer artificial skin substitute
B) Fasciocutaneous tissue flap
C) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment
D) Extended antibiotic treatment
E) Systemic corticosteroid treatment
questions.answer:
E)
Systemic corticosteroid treatment is the most appropriate next management step. These ulcerative lesions most likely represent pyoderma gangrenosum (PG), an ulcerative skin condition of unclear origin commonly associated with systemic inflammatory or autoimmune diseases. The diagnosis is typically made by exclusion with high clinical suspicion for persistent ulcerative wounds despite appropriate evaluation and treatment. The development of similar lesions at the donor site indicates pathergy, a characteristic phenomenon where surgical trauma triggers worsening or new lesion formation. Prednisone is the first-line treatment for PG. A) Bilayer artificial skin substitute is incorrect because it would not address the underlying inflammatory process and could trigger further pathergy. B) Fasciocutaneous tissue flap is incorrect as surgical intervention could worsen the condition through pathergy. C) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment is incorrect because PG is not primarily a hypoxic wound condition but rather an inflammatory disorder. D) Extended antibiotic treatment is incorrect since cultures are negative and this is not an infectious process.

questions.question:
A healthy 35-year-old woman presents with a 3-cm mass in her left parotid gland. Clinical examination reveals facial muscle weakness on the affected side. Imaging demonstrates multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the cervical region. Following parotidectomy, histological analysis reveals a heterogeneous mixture of undifferentiated epithelial cells and intermediate cells with some secretory cells present, along with neural infiltration. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Hemangioma
B) Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
C) Pleomorphic adenoma
D) Squamous cell carcinoma
E) Warthin tumor
questions.answer:
B)
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the correct diagnosis based on the clinical presentation and histological findings. This malignancy represents the most frequent cancer of the parotid gland and characteristically contains both mucus-producing cells and epidermoid-type epithelial cells. The presence of facial nerve weakness indicates neural invasion, which is typical of malignant salivary gland tumors. The mixed cellular population described, including poorly differentiated epithelial cells, intermediate cells, and secretory elements, is pathognomonic for mucoepidermoid carcinoma. The enlarged cervical lymph nodes suggest regional metastasis, which is consistent with high-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma.

A) Hemangioma is incorrect because these are benign vascular tumors primarily seen in pediatric patients, composed of proliferative endothelial cells lining capillaries, not the mixed epithelial population described.

C) Pleomorphic adenoma is incorrect because this benign mixed tumor consists of epithelial and connective tissue components with stellate and spindle cells in a myxoid matrix, which differs from the described histology and would not cause facial nerve paralysis.

D) Squamous cell carcinoma is incorrect because it rarely occurs as a primary parotid tumor and histologically shows sheets of epithelial cells with keratinous pearls, not the mixed cellular pattern described.

E) Warthin tumor is incorrect because this benign lesion is characterized by papillary cysts with lymphoid tissue nodules, predominantly affects males, and would not present with neural invasion or the described cellular composition.

questions.question:
A 2-day-old female infant is being assessed in the NICU. Clinical examination reveals epicanthal folds, flattened nasal bridge, and a broad U-shaped palatal cleft. She presents with micrognathia showing 12 mm overjet, substernal and intercostal retractions with oxygen desaturation when positioned supine, and inability to feed by mouth. Eye examination demonstrates bilateral cataracts. Which metabolic disorder most likely underlies this patient's presentation?
A) Defective cellular response to fibroblast growth factor
B) Impaired collagen II synthesis
C) Abnormal control of craniofacial bone and suture development
D) Developmental disruption from multigene deletion on chromosome 22
E) Insufficient pulmonary surfactant production
questions.answer:
B)
This infant exhibits classic features of Pierre Robin sequence (PRS) with respiratory compromise secondary to micrognathia and glossoptosis. PRS may occur in isolation or as part of a broader metabolic disorder, most commonly Stickler syndrome. Stickler syndrome results from defective collagen formation, leading to multiple congenital abnormalities including flattened nasal bridge, hearing impairment, cleft palate, limb defects, micrognathia, and ocular complications such as cataracts. A is incorrect because fibroblast growth factor receptor mutations cause craniosynostosis syndromes like Apert, Crouzon, or Pfeiffer syndromes, not PRS. C is incorrect because TWIST1 gene mutations affecting suture development cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, which has different features. D is incorrect because 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (DiGeorge/Velocardiofacial syndrome) has a distinct phenotype not matching this presentation. E is incorrect because surfactant deficiency is primarily associated with prematurity and respiratory distress syndrome, not the constellation of features seen in PRS.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male patient receives a unilateral hand transplant. Tacrolimus is started for immunosuppression. During routine follow-up at 6 months after surgery, laboratory studies reveal persistently elevated creatinine levels and decreased glomerular filtration rate. What is the most appropriate management approach?
A) Stop antihypertensive medications
B) Discontinue lipid-lowering therapy
C) Begin oral steroid treatment
D) Decrease calcineurin inhibitor target levels
E) Perform biopsy of the transplanted hand tissue
questions.answer:
D)
This patient is developing calcineurin inhibitor-induced nephrotoxicity and chronic kidney disease from tacrolimus therapy. Tacrolimus nephrotoxicity is a recognized complication following transplantation that requires careful kidney function monitoring. The drug causes irreversible damage to multiple kidney structures including glomeruli, arterioles, and tubule-interstitium through various pathways. Research by Krezdorn and colleagues studying 99 facial and extremity transplant recipients identified kidney dysfunction as a significant post-transplant complication in vascularized composite allografts. Their recommendations for post-operative management include minimizing tacrolimus exposure by reducing target trough levels, along with treating hypertension, hyperglycemia, and dyslipidemia while avoiding nephrotoxic agents. Therefore, lowering tacrolimus trough levels is the appropriate intervention. A is incorrect because antihypertensive medications should be continued to protect kidney function. B is incorrect because dyslipidemia treatment should be maintained as part of nephroprotective strategies. C is incorrect because oral corticosteroids are not indicated for tacrolimus nephrotoxicity management. E is incorrect because hand biopsy would not address the kidney dysfunction caused by the immunosuppressive medication.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child experiences a fall resulting in the fracture visible on the provided radiographic image. That evening, he receives closed reduction with percutaneous pin fixation. Following surgery, the patient is unable to bend his thumb at the interphalangeal joint or flex his index finger at the distal interphalangeal joint. Sensation remains intact in his thumb and remaining digits. Which nerve was most probably damaged during the initial injury?
A) Anterior interosseous
B) Musculocutaneous
C) Posterior interosseous
D) Radial
E) Ulnar
questions.answer:
A)
The anterior interosseous nerve is correct because it specifically innervates the flexor pollicis longus (thumb IP flexion) and the flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger (index DIP flexion), which are the exact motor deficits described. This nerve runs close to the median nerve near the distal humerus and is commonly injured in pediatric supracondylar fractures due to its anatomical proximity to the fracture site. The preserved sensation indicates the main median nerve trunk is intact. B) Musculocutaneous is incorrect because it only provides motor innervation above the elbow and has no motor function in the hand or forearm flexors. C) Posterior interosseous is incorrect because it innervates wrist and finger extensors, not the flexors affected in this case. D) Radial is incorrect because it primarily controls extension movements and does not innervate the flexor pollicis longus or flexor digitorum profundus muscles. E) Ulnar is incorrect because it does not supply motor innervation to thumb IP flexion or index finger DIP flexion.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old female patient presents for assessment of lymphedema affecting her lower limbs. Physical examination reveals pitting edema that fails to resolve with leg elevation. Her skin texture remains normal without signs of fibrotic changes. According to the International Society of Lymphology classification system, which stage best characterizes this patient's lymphedema?
A) 0
B) 1
C) 2
D) 3
questions.answer:
C)

This patient presents with Stage 2 lymphedema according to the International Society of Lymphology classification. Stage 2 is characterized by pitting edema that persists despite limb elevation, with normal skin texture and absence of fibrotic changes, which matches this patient's presentation exactly. A) is incorrect because Stage 0 represents a clinically normal-appearing extremity with only subclinical lymphatic transport abnormalities detectable by specialized imaging. B) is incorrect because Stage 1 lymphedema shows fluid accumulation that improves with limb elevation, unlike this patient whose edema persists despite elevation. D) is incorrect because Stage 3 involves significant fibroadipose tissue deposition and fibrotic skin changes, which are not present in this patient who has normal skin texture.

questions.question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a fixed adduction contracture of the first web space that has not improved with splinting and hand therapy for 4 months. Medical history includes a crush injury with complex laceration to the first web and dorsal hand and index finger five months ago. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan for reconstruction of the first web space contracture in this patient?A) First dorsal metacarpal artery flapB) Flexor carpi ulnaris flapC) Posterior interosseous artery flapD) Thenar flapE) Split-thickness skin grafting
questions.answer: The correct response is Option C.Contracture of the first web space may be secondary to cutaneous scarring, skin deficiency, fibrosis of the fascia and thenar muscles, or joint contractures. Mild contractures may be isolated to the skin; however, deeper structures are most likely involved as the contracture becomes more severe. It is important to understand the mechanism of injury, length of time the contracture has been present, and any prior treatments.Reconstruction of the first web space involves complete contracture release and resurfacing with adequate vascularized tissue. The dissection should be carried out palmarly and dorsally with release of the palmar fascia and adductor aponeurosis as needed. Intrinsic muscle and joint contractures should be addressed at this time, and a trapeziectomy may be needed to restore carpometacarpal (CMC) motion.This patient has a severe contracture that likely involves multiple structures given her history of deep lacerations and bony injury. This requires resurfacing with thin, pliable vascularized tissue. In this setting, the posterior interosseous artery (PIA) flap is the best choice. This flap is outside the zone of injury and provides an adequate amount of vascularized tissue for resurfacing of the web space. The PIA runs between the extensor carpi ulnaris and extensor digit quinti and forms an anastomosis with the anterior interosseous artery 2cm proximal to the distal radioulnar joint.Skin grafting alone, either split-thickness or full-thickness, should be avoided because of the inherent tendency for secondary contracture. Skin grafts may be combined with local flaps such as a 4-flap or 5-flap z-plasty in mild to moderate contractures.Tissue flaps from the dorsum of the hand such as the first dorsal metacarpal artery fasciocutaneous flap or dorsal hand transposition flap may be good options in some patients with small- to moderate-sized skin deficits. However, this patient sustained trauma to the dorsal hand with dorsal skin lacerations. This makes a random-pattern transposition flap unreliable. The defect in question is also too large to be completely resurfaced with a first dorsal metacarpal artery (FDMA) flap. The flexor carpi ulnaris flap is useful for elbow coverage as a turn-over flap but will not reach the hand.ReferencesMoody L, Galvez M, Chang J. Reconstruction of First Web Space Contractures. J Hand Surg Am. 2015 Sept;40:1892-95.Cavadas P et al. The Simplified Posterior Interosseous Flap. J Hand Surg Am. 2016 Sep;41(9):e303-7.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old male presents to the clinic following a bicycle accident resulting in a visible anterior open bite. Radiographic studies reveal a displaced fracture of the right mandibular condyle extending into the joint space. What is the most appropriate management?
A) Placement of external fixation device
B) Postponed sagittal split osteotomy procedure
C) Intermaxillary fixation using arch bars
D) Surgical reduction with internal plate fixation
E) Conservative management with soft diet only
questions.answer:
C)
Intermaxillary fixation using arch bars is the optimal treatment for this pediatric condylar fracture with associated open bite. In children, condylar fractures can lead to growth disturbances and TMJ dysfunction, making proper reduction crucial. Arch bars with intermaxillary fixation effectively treat this injury pattern during mixed dentition while avoiding surgical risks. A) External fixation is not indicated for mandibular condylar fractures and would be inappropriate for this location. B) Delayed sagittal split osteotomy is unnecessary since the patient had normal pre-injury occlusion and this procedure is not indicated for acute fracture management. D) Open reduction with internal fixation is generally avoided in this age group due to risk of damage to developing tooth buds. E) Conservative management alone would be insufficient for a displaced condylar fracture with open bite, risking malunion and growth complications.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old male patient presents to your clinic with a rapidly enlarging mass in his left breast that developed over the past month. Core needle biopsy of the lesion reveals invasive mammary carcinoma. Genetic analysis shows a positive result for BRCA2 mutation. Besides the elevated risk for male breast malignancy, which of the following additional cancer types is most commonly linked to this patient's condition?
A) Colon
B) Lung
C) Pancreatic
D) Renal
E) Thyroid
questions.answer:
C)
Males carrying pathogenic BRCA2 mutations have significantly increased susceptibility to pancreatic carcinoma, along with breast cancer and prostate cancer. While BRCA1 mutations can also predispose to pancreatic, testicular, and early-onset prostate cancers, the association between BRCA2 mutations and pancreatic malignancy is particularly well-established. A) is incorrect because colorectal cancer is not linked to BRCA mutations. B) is incorrect because lung cancer has no established association with BRCA gene alterations. D) is incorrect because renal malignancies are not part of the BRCA-associated cancer spectrum. E) is incorrect because thyroid cancer is not associated with BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents to the emergency room following trauma from a vehicle rollover accident. Imaging reveals numerous facial bone fractures and multiple system injuries. Which of the following represents a CONTRAINDICATION for nasotracheal intubation in this trauma patient?
A) Skull base fracture
B) Bilateral condylar fractures of the mandible
C) Fracture of the cervical spine
D) Altered level of consciousness
E) Maxillary bone fracture
questions.answer:
A)
Skull base fracture is the only absolute contraindication to nasal intubation among the given choices. This is because there is a significant risk of the nasotracheal tube penetrating through the cribriform plate and entering the brain's frontal lobes. B) Bilateral mandibular condylar fractures are not a contraindication to nasotracheal intubation and may actually be an indication for this approach. C) Cervical spine fractures do not preclude nasotracheal intubation, which can be performed while maintaining cervical immobilization. D) Altered mental status is not a contraindication to nasotracheal intubation and may actually be an indication for airway management. E) Maxillary fractures alone do not contraindicate nasal intubation and may actually favor this approach to maintain occlusion.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male patient needs bone grafting to reconstruct a significant nasal defect following a cycling accident. Which of the following represents the best rib harvest location for straightforward surgical access and minimal complications?
A) First
B) Third
C) Fourth
D) Seventh
E) Eleventh
questions.answer:
D)
The seventh rib is the optimal choice because ribs five through seven are widely recognized as ideal harvest sites due to their accessibility and abundant bone material compared to higher or lower ribs. The seventh rib specifically offers the benefit of being positioned above the abdominal cavity, which decreases the likelihood of pneumothorax during the harvesting procedure. Ribs five and six are also acceptable options and may provide better cosmetic concealment within the inframammary fold in female patients. A) The first rib is incorrect because it is difficult to access surgically and provides limited bone material. B) The third rib is incorrect because it is too high, offering poor surgical exposure and insufficient bone stock. C) The fourth rib is incorrect because while accessible, it doesn't provide the optimal balance of safety and bone availability compared to the seventh rib. E) The eleventh rib is incorrect because although it offers extensive medial cartilage, it is not considered an ideal bone donor site for structural grafting.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a physical altercation. Examination reveals preauricular swelling and tenderness on the left, deviation of the chin toward the left with maximal opening, and malocclusion with a crossbite on the left side and an open bite on the right side. CT demonstrates a displaced left subcondylar mandibular fracture, with the proximal (condylar) segment displaced anteromedially out of the glenoid fossa. Which muscle is most likely responsible for the displacement of the condylar segment?
A) Genioglossus
B) Lateral pterygoid
C) Masseter
D) Medial pterygoid
E) Mylohyoid
questions.answer:
B)
This patient has a displaced left subcondylar mandibular fracture. The lateral pterygoid inserts on the pterygoid fovea of the condylar neck and the joint capsule/disc, so when the condylar neck fractures, its unopposed pull draws the proximal segment anteriorly and medially out of the glenoid fossa (the same action that translates the condyle forward over the articular eminence during jaw opening). Loss of ramus height on the fractured side produces premature posterior contact and crossbite on the ipsilateral (left) side, an open bite on the contralateral (right) side, and deviation of the chin toward the fracture side on opening — exactly the pattern described.
A) Genioglossus is incorrect because it is a tongue muscle arising from the genial tubercles and influences displacement of symphyseal/parasymphyseal and body fractures, not the condylar segment.
C) Masseter is incorrect because, with the medial pterygoid, it forms the pterygomasseteric sling that elevates and displaces angle and body fractures; it does not insert on the condylar neck.
D) Medial pterygoid is incorrect for the same reason — as the medial component of the pterygomasseteric sling it acts on the ramus/angle, not on the fractured condylar segment.
E) Mylohyoid is incorrect because this floor-of-mouth muscle produces lingual displacement of body and parasymphyseal fractures, not anteromedial condylar displacement.

questions.question:
A male neonate delivered at 36 weeks gestation by cesarean section presents with a significant anterior abdominal wall defect. Physical examination reveals exposed intestinal loops protruding through the defect positioned to one side of the umbilical cord. No additional anomalies are observed. Which of the following associated findings is most likely to be present?
A) Chromosomal abnormality
B) Amniotic bands causing limb constrictions and digit amputations
C) Increased maternal serum alpha fetoprotein levels
D) Low blood sugar, enlarged body size, and enlarged tongue
E) Protective membrane encasing the protruding bowel
questions.answer:
C)
This case describes gastroschisis, which along with omphalocele represents one of the two primary congenital abdominal wall defects. Both conditions are strongly associated with elevated maternal serum alpha fetoprotein (MSAFP) levels, typically reaching values twice those seen in open neural tube defects and comparable to levels found in anencephaly. This elevation serves as an important screening marker prompting detailed fetal ultrasound examination. A) is incorrect because gastroschisis has chromosomal abnormalities in only about 1% of cases, unlike omphalocele which has abnormal karyotypes in approximately 60% of cases. B) is incorrect because amniotic band sequence with constriction rings and limb amputations is not characteristic of gastroschisis or omphalocele. D) is incorrect because hypoglycemia, macrosomia, and macroglossia are not typical features associated with gastroschisis. E) is incorrect because gastroschisis characteristically lacks a covering membrane, whereas omphalocele has a translucent membrane composed of amnion and peritoneum covering the herniated contents.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman comes to the office for consultation regarding rhinoplasty. The only camera available for preoperative photographs is a handheld digital camera with a built-in flash to the left of the lens. To avoid shadows while taking photographs of the patient?s right-sided facial profile, which of the following is the optimal orientation of the camera?


A ) Horizontal orientation, flash from the left
B ) Horizontal orientation, flash from the right
C ) Oblique orientation, flash from above
D ) Vertical orientation, flash from above
E ) Vertical orientation, flash from below
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


Horizontal orientation of the camera with the flash coming from the right for a right-sided profile will cast the shadow behind the subject. In this case, it is necessary to invert the camera so that the flash, which is left of the lens, is now on the right, the same side as the nose.


With variations in camera position, the shadows can be markedly altered, thereby affecting the consistency of your images. Horizontal orientation with the flash from the left would cast the patient‚Äos shadow in front of her profile. Oblique camera orientation should never be used in medical photography. Photographs should be taken orthogonally, either along the longitudinal axis of the patient or at right


References
1. Hoffman WY. Photography in plastic surgery. In: Mathes SJ, Hentz VR, eds. Plastic Surgery. 2nd ed. Philadelphia: WB Saunders; 2006:151-165.
2. DiBernardo BE, Adams RL, Krause J, et al. Photographic standards in plastic surgery. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1998 Aug;102(2):559-568.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old female patient is receiving scalp and forehead tissue expansion treatment prior to removal of a large congenital nevus. What change is most likely to occur in the tissue being expanded?
A) Enhanced adipose tissue development
B) Enhanced vascular perfusion
C) Enhanced muscle development
D) Dermal layer thickening
E) Epidermal layer thinning
questions.answer:
B)
The most probable change in the expanding tissue is enhanced vascular perfusion. Expansion stimulates neovascularization and increased tissue vascularity, which enhances flap viability during rotation or transposition procedures. Tissue expansion additionally results in: 1) epidermal thickening with hyperkeratosis (temporary, resolving after expander removal); 2) dermal thinning (normalizes within approximately 2 years); 3) muscle thinning with decreased mass (function remains intact); and 4) permanent adipose tissue loss of up to 50%. A is incorrect because expansion causes permanent fat loss rather than enhancement. C is incorrect because muscle mass decreases, not increases, during expansion. D is incorrect because the dermis becomes thinner, not thicker. E is incorrect because the epidermis thickens rather than thins during expansion.

questions.question:
Which of the following complications is more frequently associated with textured silicone gel implants compared to smooth silicone gel implants?
A) Capsular contracture
B) Hematoma
C) Malposition
D) Rippling
E) Rupture
questions.answer:
D)
Textured implants are associated with a notably higher incidence of rippling compared to smooth implants, with studies showing more than a two-fold increase in occurrence. This visible rippling can be reduced through subpectoral placement and by selecting patients with adequate native breast tissue coverage. The rippling phenomenon is particularly pronounced with saline-filled devices.

A is incorrect because textured surface implants actually demonstrate superior performance in reducing capsular contracture rates compared to smooth implants, though this benefit is less significant with saline implants in subpectoral positioning. B is incorrect because hematoma formation occurs at similar rates regardless of implant surface texture. C is incorrect because malposition rates do not differ between textured and smooth implants. E is incorrect because rupture rates are comparable between textured and smooth gel implants, although textured saline implants may have higher deflation rates than smooth saline implants.

questions.question:
Which anatomical structures of the lower lateral cartilages are used to measure the nasal tip divergence angle?
A) Lateral and middle crura
B) Medial and middle crura
C) Left and right foot plates
D) Left and right lateral crura
E) Left and right middle crura
questions.answer:
E)
The nasal tip divergence angle is measured between the left and right middle crura of the lower lateral cartilages. This angle extends from the medial genu to the lateral genu when viewed from an anteroposterior perspective. The optimal divergence angle ranges from 30 to 60 degrees. A) is incorrect because the lateral and middle crura form the lateral genu, not the divergence angle. B) is incorrect because the medial and middle crura create the rotation angle as the tip curves upward from columella to tip-defining point. C) is incorrect because foot plates are not involved in measuring the divergence angle. D) is incorrect because there is no specific named angle formed by the lateral crura alone.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old female patient seeks consultation for breast reconstruction following a biopsy-confirmed left breast invasive ductal carcinoma detected through routine mammographic screening, revealing a 7-cm mass. She has been directed to medical oncology and awaits genetic testing results. Her medical history includes hypertension and scleroderma. Physical examination reveals grade I breast ptosis and she wears a 34A bra size. The patient expresses a strong desire for lumpectomy with oncoplastic reconstruction rather than complete mastectomy. Which of the following factors would most likely improve this patient's eligibility for breast-conserving treatment?
A) Active scleroderma
B) BRCA-1 genetic mutation
C) Multicentric disease
D) Neoadjuvant chemotherapy
E) Small breast size
questions.answer:
D)
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy would most likely improve this patient's eligibility for breast-conserving treatment. Preoperative systemic therapy has been demonstrated to increase breast conservation rates by potentially shrinking large tumors, making previously inoperable lesions resectable. Additional advantages include providing valuable prognostic data based on treatment response, reducing the need for extensive axillary procedures, and allowing adequate time for genetic counseling and reconstructive planning. A) Active scleroderma is incorrect because connective tissue disorders like scleroderma are relative contraindications to breast conservation due to increased radiation sensitivity and poor wound healing. B) BRCA-1 genetic mutation is incorrect as hereditary breast cancer predisposition syndromes are relative contraindications to breast conservation, with these patients often considered for prophylactic bilateral mastectomy. C) Multicentric disease is incorrect because multiple tumor foci throughout the breast typically require mastectomy rather than conservation. E) Small breast size is incorrect as it would provide inadequate remaining breast tissue after excision of a large 7-cm tumor, making conservation technically unfeasible.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male patient has a nodular basal cell carcinoma removed from his nasal tip, with immediate reconstruction using a bilobed flap technique. Both procedures are completed in an outpatient setting by the same plastic surgeon. What is the most appropriate Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) coding approach?
A) Code only the excision procedure
B) Code only the flap reconstruction
C) Code both the excision and reconstruction procedures
D) Code the excision with modifier -22 (increased procedural services)
E) Code the flap reconstruction with modifier -22 (increased procedural services)
questions.answer:
B)
When a lesion is excised and an adjacent tissue transfer or rearrangement (14XXX codes) is performed at the same anatomical location, the excision is not coded separately. The appropriate code is determined by combining the defect size with the flap donor site dimensions (primary and secondary defects combined). This coding rule is unique to adjacent tissue transfers, as other closure types allow separate coding of excisions and closures. A is incorrect because the excision cannot be coded separately when performed with an adjacent tissue transfer. C is incorrect because bundling rules prevent separate coding of both procedures when done at the same site. D is incorrect because modifier -22 is reserved for significantly more complex procedures than described, and the excision isn't coded separately anyway. E is incorrect because this standard bilobed flap reconstruction doesn't meet the criteria for increased complexity requiring modifier -22.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child with Pfeiffer syndrome presents to the clinic due to progressively worsening snoring over the last 6 months. Previous tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy procedures did not resolve the airway obstruction. Clinical examination reveals moderate eye protrusion, Class III dental malocclusion, and insufficient cheekbone prominence. Nasal endoscopy demonstrates soft palate causing pharyngeal blockage. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Le Fort I osteotomy and advancement
B) Le Fort II osteotomy and advancement
C) Le Fort III osteotomy and advancement
D) Mandibular setback with glossopexy and tongue-lip adhesion
E) Mandibular setback with vertical ramus osteotomies
questions.answer:
C)
In a child with Pfeiffer syndrome presenting with progressive nasopharyngeal airway compromise, midface advancement is necessary to prevent the need for tracheostomy. The Le Fort III osteotomy and advancement is most appropriate because it addresses the deficient malar projection and advances the entire midface to relieve airway obstruction. A) Le Fort I osteotomy is contraindicated in children before permanent tooth eruption as it risks damage to developing maxillary teeth. B) Le Fort II osteotomy would not adequately advance the underdeveloped malar bones. D) and E) Mandibular setback procedures would actually worsen the airway obstruction by further reducing the pharyngeal space.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female ICU nurse is preparing for cardiac bypass surgery. Given her extensive exposure to patients with MRSA infections, she inquires about topical decolonization protocols. What is the most suitable regimen for this patient?
A) Clindamycin
B) Linezolid
C) Mupirocin and chlorhexidine
D) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
E) Vancomycin
questions.answer:
C)
The combination of topical nasal mupirocin ointment and chlorhexidine body wash for 5 days represents the standard decolonization protocol endorsed by the Infectious Diseases Society of America. This regimen has the strongest evidence base, particularly in cardiac surgery patients, where the Society of Thoracic Surgeons recommends universal prophylaxis due to demonstrated reductions in sternal wound infection rates. Healthcare workers have approximately 5% MRSA carriage rates, with nasal colonization being a primary source, making this topical approach highly effective. A) Clindamycin is incorrect because it is a systemic antibiotic used for treating active infections, not for decolonization protocols. B) Linezolid is incorrect as it is reserved for treating serious MRSA infections and is not part of standard decolonization regimens. D) Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is incorrect because it is used for treating infections rather than preventing colonization. E) Vancomycin is incorrect as it is a systemic antibiotic reserved for serious MRSA infections, not for prophylactic decolonization.

questions.question:
In rotation-advancement repair of cleft lip, what is the primary purpose of incorporating the L flap?
A) Enhance vermilion thickness
B) Enable lateral expansion of the nasal wall
C) Extend columellar length
D) Supply mucosa for the gingivobuccal fold
E) Reestablish philtral column balance
questions.answer:
B)
The L flap serves as a medially-based mucosal flap harvested from the lateral lip segment that provides essential lining for the lateral nasal cavity, positioned between the internal mucosal surface and the external skin layer. A) is incorrect because vermilion augmentation is not the L flap's function - other techniques address vermilion bulk. C) is incorrect because columellar lengthening involves different surgical maneuvers, not the L flap. D) is incorrect because the gingivobuccal sulcus reconstruction uses other tissue sources, not the L flap. E) is incorrect because philtral column symmetry is achieved through proper muscle realignment and skin positioning, not the L flap's mucosal lining function.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man with a history of base-of-tongue cancer treated with radiation therapy and chemotherapy 3 years ago presents with right jaw pain, severe malocclusion (crossbite), and drainage from a wound in the right cheek. A photograph is shown. CT scan shows a pathologic fracture and bony destruction consistent with osteoradionecrosis of the mandible. A biopsy is negative for recurrent cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?


A) Hyperbaric oxygen
B) Open reduction and internal fixation
C) Pentoxifylline and tocopherol
D) Segmental mandibulectomy and osteocutaneous free flap reconstruction
E) Sequestrectomy and treatment with antibiotic oral rinses
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


Osteoradionecrosis (ORN) is a complication caused by high-dose radiation therapy to the head and neck, most commonly affecting the mandible. ORN may be painful and can be associated with pathologic fracture, purulent infection, osteomyelitis, and fistula formation. Marx classified ORN into three stages: Stage I, exposed alveolar bone without pathologic fracture that is responsive to hyperbaric oxygen (HBO) therapy; Stage II, disease that does not respond to HBO and requires sequestrectomy and saucerization; and Stage III, full-thickness bone damage or pathologic fracture that usually requires complete resection and reconstruction. In this case, the patient has a pathologic fracture (Stage III) as well as a fistula, and segmental mandibulectomy and osteocutaneous free flap reconstruction are indicated. There is no role for open reduction and internal fixation in most cases of ORN because healing is not likely to occur. Pentoxyifylline and tocopherol (vitamin E) are more recently described treatments that have been shown to be effective in the treatment of early stage ORN.


ReferencesBennett MH, Feldmeier J, Hampson NB, et al. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for late radiation tissue injury. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016;4(4):CD005005.Marx RE. Osteoradionecrosis: a new concept of its pathophysiology. J Oral Maxillofac Surg. 1983;41(5):283-288.Raggio BS, Winters R. Modern management of osteoradionecrosis. Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg. 2018;26(4):254-259.Rivero JA, Shamji O, Kolokythas A. Osteoradionecrosis: a review of pathophysiology, prevention and pharmacologic management using pentoxifylline, ?-tocopherol, and clodronate. Oral Surg Oral Med Oral Pathol Oral Radiol. 2017;124(5):464-471.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old female patient presents with unexpected milk production 6 days following breast augmentation surgery. Which of the following elements most likely played a role in this complication?
A) Location of the incision in the inframammary fold
B) Placement of the implant in subglandular rather than dual-plane position
C) Operative disruption of intercostal nerve pathways
D) Choice of silicone implant material over saline
questions.answer:
C)
The mechanism behind post-surgical galactorrhea remains incompletely understood, but it appears more frequently in women who have given birth and is believed to result from factors that mimic nursing stimulation or alter chest wall and nipple-areolar complex nerve supply. This includes elevated tissue pressure from implant placement and disruption of intercostal nerve pathways. A is incorrect because no correlation exists between incision location (periareolar, inframammary, transaxillary, or perithelial) and post-operative milk production. B is incorrect because implant positioning (dual-plane, subglandular, or submuscular) shows no association with galactorrhea development. D is incorrect because implant composition (saline versus silicone) demonstrates no relationship with post-operative galactorrhea occurrence.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old female patient has a facelift and neck lift procedure involving SMAS plication and liposuction. Three weeks postoperatively, she still experiences diminished cutaneous sensation in the mandibular angle region. Which nerve was most probably damaged during the operation?
A) Auriculotemporal nerve
B) Buccal nerve
C) Great auricular nerve
D) Lesser petrosal nerve
E) Marginal mandibular nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The great auricular nerve, arising from the cervical plexus, supplies sensory innervation to the ear skin and the skin beneath the ear, including the mandibular angle area, making it the most likely nerve injured in this case. A) is incorrect because the auriculotemporal nerve (a mandibular division branch of cranial nerve V) innervates the anterior-superior ear skin, external auditory canal, and TMJ, not the mandibular angle. B) is incorrect because the buccal nerve branches from the facial nerve (VII) and are purely motor, innervating the buccinator and facial expression muscles above the lip. D) is incorrect because the lesser petrosal nerve is a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX) carrying preganglionic parasympathetic fibers to the otic ganglion, not providing sensory function. E) is incorrect because the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (VII) is motor only, supplying the facial expression muscles of the lower lip and chin.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy is brought to the office with a congenital abnormality of the ear. A photograph is shown. When the ear is pulled on traction, the upper pole cartilage becomes visible under the skin. This abnormality is most likely caused by which of the following?A) Anomaly of the intrinsic postauricular musclesB) Effacement of the scaphofossaC) Formation of a third antihelical crusD) Hemifacial microsomiaE) Intrauterine pressure
questions.answer: The correct response is Option A.This patient has cryptotia of the ear. It is also known as pocket ear. The upper part of the ear is adherent and the cartilage is buried under the skin in a pocket. Other deformities may be present, such as a missing upper sulcus, underdeveloped scapha, and antihelical crura.It is caused by an anomaly of the intrinsic oblique and transverse auricular muscles.Surgical treatment requires release from the pocket and resurfacing of the post- and retroauricular defects. In some cases otoplasty may be required for normalization. A number of techniques are described.Intrauterine pressure may cause ear deformities, which may spontaneously resolve or are amenable to neonatal molding techniques. It does not cause cryptotia.Stahl ear is associated with formation of a third antihelical crus.Hemifacial microsomia is associated with microtia. Microtia is sometimes the only manifestation of hemifacial microsomia, but subtle clinical findings are often present, such as mild facial nerve weakness or soft tissue hypoplasia on the involved side.ReferencesWeerda, H. Chapter 5, Abnormalities. In: Surgery of the Auricle: Tumors Trauma Defect Abnormalities, 1st edition. TPS, 2007: 156-157.Hirose T, Tomono T, Matsuo K, et al. Cryptotia: Our classification and treatment. Br J Plast Surg. 1985 Jul;38(3):352-60.

questions.question:
A healthy 29-year-old female patient seeks enhancement of her buttock contour with increased volume and projection. Following liposuction of the abdomen, flanks, and back, autologous fat transfer to the gluteal region is planned. The harvested fat has been processed and placed into 60 mL syringes fitted with 5-mm-diameter blunt cannulas for injection. To optimize cosmetic outcomes while minimizing the risk of fat macroembolism, the injection cannula should be positioned in which tissue plane?
A) Intramuscular placement exclusively
B) Subcutaneous placement inferiorly with superficial muscular placement superiorly
C) Subcutaneous placement medially with superficial muscular placement laterally
D) Subcutaneous placement exclusively
questions.answer:
D)
Subcutaneous placement exclusively is correct because the ASERF task force guidelines emphasize that intramuscular fat injection significantly increases the risk of fatal fat macroembolism by potentially injuring gluteal vessels. Restricting fat grafting to the subcutaneous layer avoids deep vascular structures and minimizes embolic complications. A is incorrect because intramuscular injection carries the highest risk of vascular injury and fat embolism. B is incorrect because any superficial muscular placement still poses unnecessary embolic risk compared to staying entirely subcutaneous. C is incorrect because superficial muscular injection in any location increases the risk of vascular complications beyond what is acceptable for safe fat grafting.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient with scleroderma presents with a 2-year history of severe rest pain affecting both hands. She is a non-smoker. Her symptoms have not improved despite proper medical management. For treating this patient's Raynaud phenomenon, botulinum toxin type A injection would be most appropriately administered at which of the following sites?
A) Surrounding the stellate ganglion
B) Into the skin at the wrist level
C) Into the skin within the palm
D) Around blood vessels at the wrist level
E) Around blood vessels within the palm
questions.answer:
E)
Botulinum toxin injection around the digital blood vessels within the palm has demonstrated effectiveness in reducing pain from vasospastic conditions such as Raynaud phenomenon. This approach represents a relatively simple, rapid, and low-risk intervention for patients suffering from debilitating ischemic hand pain. While the precise mechanism remains under study, proposed theories include effects on blood vessels and/or nerves through inhibition of sympathetic pathways, sensory nerve fibers (c-fibers), substance P, and other signaling mechanisms. Clinical studies report 75-100% pain reduction and up to 50% healing of persistent ulcers. The technique involves bathing approximately 10 units of botulinum toxin around each digital neurovascular bundle in the palm, with temporary mild intrinsic muscle weakness being the most frequently reported adverse effect. A is incorrect because stellate ganglion procedures typically use local anesthetics rather than botulinum toxin for blockade. B is incorrect because intradermal injection at the wrist has not demonstrated the same therapeutic response as perivascular palm injection. C is incorrect because intradermal palm injection lacks the efficacy of perivascular targeting. D is incorrect because perivascular injection at the wrist level is too proximal and has not shown equivalent results to palm-level treatment.

questions.question:
What is the most suitable surgical management approach for a 4-cm circular sebaceous nevus located on the scalp of a pediatric patient?
A) Removal with skin graft placement and subsequent tissue expansion
B) Sequential removal procedures without tissue expansion
C) Ongoing observation with selective removal when indicated
D) Tissue expansion followed by removal
E) Tissue expansion, removal, and reconstruction with rotational flaps
questions.answer:
C)
The most appropriate approach is ongoing observation with selective removal when indicated. Previously, malignant transformation rates of 10-15% in sebaceous nevi led to recommendations for prophylactic removal before puberty. However, recent research demonstrates malignant transformation occurs in less than 1% of cases, supporting a more conservative management strategy involving regular monitoring and removal only when lesions become irritating, difficult to monitor, or cosmetically concerning. A) is incorrect because excision with skin grafting and tissue expansion is overly aggressive for a small lesion with low malignant potential. B) is incorrect because serial excision is typically reserved for larger lesions requiring three or fewer stages. D) is incorrect because tissue expansion alone followed by excision is unnecessarily complex for a 4-cm lesion. E) is incorrect because this combination approach with rotational flaps is excessive treatment for a small sebaceous nevus that can be managed conservatively.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old female presents with shoulder pain, weakness, and inability to elevate her shoulder girdle 2 weeks following a facelift procedure that included advancement of an extended SMAS flap and complete platysmal transection with plication. A nerve injury is suspected. During which portion of the facelift procedure was this nerve most likely damaged?
A) Securing the SMAS flap to Lore fascia
B) Lateral neck dissection
C) Flap elevation at McKinney point
D) Removal of subplatysmal fat
E) Division of the platysma muscle
questions.answer:
B)
This patient's clinical presentation indicates injury to the spinal accessory nerve (cranial nerve XI), which supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. During lateral neck dissection, the spinal accessory nerve is particularly vulnerable as it exits the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle within 2 cm above the great auricular nerve, where it becomes superficial and lies between the skin and muscle fascia before traveling obliquely to reach the trapezius muscle. A) is incorrect because Lore fascia anchoring occurs in a deeper plane where the facial nerve (not spinal accessory nerve) is at risk. C) is incorrect because McKinney point relates to the great auricular nerve crossing point, not the spinal accessory nerve location. D) is incorrect because subplatysmal fat removal occurs in a plane that doesn't typically endanger the spinal accessory nerve. E) is incorrect because the spinal accessory nerve runs posterior to the platysma muscle, so platysmal division alone would not directly injure this nerve.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child presents to the emergency room following trauma from a household violence episode. Clinical examination reveals periorbital ecchymosis of the right eye. The child experiences discomfort and nausea during upward gaze. Imaging with CT demonstrates inferior rectus muscle entrapment. After three weeks, orbital floor reconstruction is performed using an implant. Twelve months post-operatively, double vision persists. What is the most probable cause of the ongoing diplopia?
A) Proptosis
B) Implant positioning
C) Neural injury
D) Ongoing inflammation
E) Surgical delay
questions.answer:
E)
Surgical delay is the most likely cause of persistent diplopia in this pediatric orbital floor fracture case. In children, delayed surgical intervention beyond 7 days after injury is strongly associated with poor outcomes including persistent diplopia, with many experts recommending treatment within 24 hours of injury. The prolonged 3-week delay before surgical repair significantly increases the risk of permanent extraocular muscle dysfunction and diplopia. A) Proptosis is incorrect because exophthalmos typically resolves after proper orbital floor repair and would not be the primary cause of diplopia one year later. B) Implant positioning is incorrect because when surgery is performed using standard techniques, implant location is rarely the cause of persistent symptoms in pediatric cases. C) Neural injury is incorrect because direct nerve damage is uncommon in typical orbital floor fractures and would not be the most likely explanation given the surgical delay. D) Ongoing inflammation is incorrect because inflammatory changes typically resolve within weeks to months after surgery and would not persist for a full year.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old boy has an interrupted aortic arch, low-set ears, broad nasal bridge, velopharyngeal insufficiency, and hypoparathyroidism. A photograph is shown. Which of the following additional findings are most likely in this patient?


A) Facial asymmetry, microtia
B) High myopia, retinal detachment
C) Lower eyelid coloboma, downward-slanting palpebral fissures
D) Lower lip pits, salivary mucous drainage
E) T-cell immunodeficiency, chronic otitis media
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


22q11.2 Deletion syndrome (also known as DiGeorge, velocardiofacial, and conotruncal anomaly face syndromes) is often identified with help of the "CATCH 22" mnemonic, which refers to its characteristics of cleft palate, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cardiac malformations, and hypoparathyroidism. T-cell immunodeficiency and recurrent otitis media infections occur secondary to thymic hypoplasia and cleft-related ear anomalies.


Van der Woude syndrome is characterized by cleft palate and/or cleft lip, and lower lip pits/fistulae. Abnormal salivary gland morphology and hypodontia may also occur.
Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is characterized by malar and mandibular hypoplasia, down-slanting palpebral fissures, lower eyelid coloboma, and ear anomalies.


Stickler syndrome type 1 is characterized by cleft palate, facies such as mid-face hypoplasia/retrusion, myopia with increased risk for retinal detachment, sensorineural hearing loss, and joint abnormalities including hypermobility and early-onset osteoarthritis.


Hemifacial microsomia is characterized by small and/or flattened maxillary, temporal, and zygomatic bones. Facial asymmetry is further apparent upon animation when soft tissue and nerve hypoplasia occur. Oral clefts and ear anomalies are commonly involved, as well as underdevelopment of the orbits.


Van der Woude syndrome, Treacher Collins syndrome, Stickler syndrome, and hemifacial microsomia are all unrelated to hypoparathyroidism.


ReferencesBoyarchuk O, Volyanska L, Dmytrash L. Clinical variability of chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Cent Eur J Immunol. 2017;42(4):412-417.Lackey AE, Muzio MR. DiGeorge Syndrome. In: StatPearls. StatPearls Publishing; August 10, 2020.McDonald-McGinn DM, Hain HS, Emanuel BS, et al. 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Published September 23, 1999. Updated February 27, 2020. In: Adam MP, Ardinger HH, Pagon RA, et al., eds. GeneReviews¬Æ [Internet]. University of Washington, Seattle; 1993-2021.Hickey SE, Kellogg B, O'Brien M, et al. Impact of interdisciplinary team care for children with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Cleft Palate Craniofac J. 2020;57(12):1362-1369.Fleming J, Morrell N, Zavala H, et al. Submucous cleft palate repair in patients with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome. Cleft Palate Craniofac J. 2021;58(1):84-89.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female patient is preparing for bilateral deep inferior epigastric artery perforator (DIEP) flap breast reconstruction surgery. The anesthesia team plans to administer a donor site regional nerve block using liposomal bupivacaine for postoperative pain management. Which of the following anatomical locations for injection would be most effective in enhancing pain relief and reducing opioid requirements for this patient?
A) Within the fascial plane separating the external oblique and internal oblique muscles
B) Within the fascial plane separating the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles
C) Beneath the rectus abdominis muscle fascia
D) Beneath the transversus abdominis muscle fascia
E) Within the subcutaneous tissue layer
questions.answer:
B)
The correct injection site is within the fascial plane separating the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, which is where the transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is performed. This location targets the segmental nerve supply that provides sensory innervation to the abdominal wall, making it highly effective for DIEP flap donor site analgesia. The TAP block can be administered either percutaneously using ultrasound guidance or under direct surgical visualization before closing the abdominal donor site. A is incorrect because injection between the external and internal oblique muscles would not effectively target the appropriate nerve pathways for abdominal wall anesthesia. C is incorrect because placement deep to the rectus abdominis fascia would not provide optimal blockade of the lateral abdominal wall innervation. D is incorrect because injection deep to the transversus abdominis fascia would place the anesthetic too deep, potentially missing the target nerve fibers. E is incorrect because subcutaneous injection would only provide superficial anesthesia and would not block the deeper sensory nerves responsible for abdominal wall pain.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old female patient is preparing for breast reduction surgery. Her medical background includes enlarged breasts and von Willebrand disease. Prior to surgery, desmopressin (DDAVP) will be given to prevent bleeding complications. The optimal preoperative dosage should be calculated by assessing vWF:RCoF (von Willebrand factor ristocetin cofactor) activity levels along with which coagulation factor?
A) II
B) V
C) VII
D) VIII
E) X
questions.answer:
D)

In patients with von Willebrand disease undergoing surgery and receiving DDAVP for bleeding prevention, the preoperative dose should be based on measuring both vWF:RCoF and factor VIII activity levels. Von Willebrand factor normally binds and stabilizes factor VIII in circulation, so both parameters must be monitored to ensure adequate hemostatic function and determine appropriate DDAVP dosing. A is incorrect because factor II (prothrombin) is not specifically associated with von Willebrand disease pathophysiology. B is incorrect because factor V deficiency is a separate coagulation disorder unrelated to vWD. C is incorrect because factor VII is part of the extrinsic coagulation pathway and not directly affected by von Willebrand factor deficiency. E is incorrect because factor X is involved in the common coagulation pathway but is not specifically linked to von Willebrand disease management.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old woman with no other medical conditions is planned for excision of recurring squamous cell carcinoma in the right temporal region. This occurs 5 years following her initial treatment which included tumor removal, superficial parotidectomy, limited upper neck lymph node dissection, skin grafting, and postoperative radiation. The expected tissue loss will measure 6 to 8 cm and will include skin and underlying soft tissue. The superficial temporal blood vessels are not identifiable. What is the most suitable approach for reconstructing this defect?
A) Lateral arm flap
B) Parascapular flap
C) Radial forearm free flap
D) Scalp rotation flap
E) Split-thickness skin grafting
questions.answer:
C)
The radial forearm free flap represents the optimal reconstructive choice because its tissue characteristics closely match the thin skin and subcutaneous tissue of the temporal region, and its lengthy vascular pedicle can effectively reach recipient vessels located in the neck area. Given the patient's history of radiation treatment and superficial parotidectomy, the superficial temporal vessels are not viable as recipient vessels. Following upper neck dissection, suitable recipient vessels may only be available in lower regions, making a flap with an extended, dependable pedicle essential. A) is incorrect because the lateral arm flap has a shorter pedicle length that may not adequately reach neck recipient vessels, despite being a viable free flap option. B) is incorrect because the parascapular flap also has limited pedicle length and may not reach distant recipient vessels in the neck. D) is incorrect because a scalp rotation flap would likely incorporate previously irradiated tissue, introduce hair-bearing skin to a non-hair-bearing area, and necessitate skin grafting at the donor site. E) is incorrect because split-thickness skin grafting typically fails in previously irradiated tissue beds due to poor vascularization.

questions.question:
A plastic surgeon is reviewing the methodological rigor of a newly published clinical trial. The surgeon observes that the investigators failed to perform a power analysis to determine if their sample size was sufficient. Which type of statistical error is best prevented by conducting a proper power analysis?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
B)

Statistical power represents the likelihood that a study will identify a true treatment effect when one actually exists, calculated as 1-β where β is the probability of committing a type II error. Power analysis helps determine adequate sample sizes to detect clinically meaningful differences, thereby minimizing type II errors. A) Type I error is incorrect because this involves falsely rejecting a true null hypothesis (false positive), which is controlled by setting the alpha level rather than sample size. C) Type III error is incorrect because this refers to correctly rejecting the null hypothesis but for incorrect reasons, which relates to study design and interpretation rather than sample size adequacy. D) Type IV error is incorrect because this involves misinterpreting a correctly rejected hypothesis, which is an interpretive issue unrelated to statistical power or sample size considerations.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman is preparing for phalloplasty using a fibular flap as part of her gender-affirming surgery. She has undergone comprehensive assessment by all relevant specialists within a multidisciplinary gender clinic. What represents the primary benefit of utilizing a fibular flap compared to a radial forearm flap for this procedure?
A) Capability to form a sensate skin paddle
B) Elimination of need for prosthetic device for sexual function
C) Reduced risk of urethral narrowing
D) Enhanced tactile sensation recovery
E) Greater anatomical consistency and predictability
questions.answer:
B)
The primary benefit of the fibular flap compared to the radial forearm flap in phalloplasty is the elimination of need for a prosthetic device to achieve erectile and sexual function. A) is incorrect because both flaps can create innervated skin islands - the fibular flap through the superficial peroneal nerve and the forearm flap through medial and lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerves. C) is incorrect because the fibular flap actually has a higher incidence of urethral stricture since it uses a full-thickness skin graft for the neourethra rather than vascularized forearm skin. D) is incorrect because sensory recovery is actually inferior with the fibular flap compared to the forearm flap. E) is incorrect because while both have reliable anatomy, the fibular flap's septocutaneous peroneal artery branch can be variable or absent, making it less consistent than the forearm flap.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female patient presents to the clinic 2 weeks following botulinum toxin type A treatment for forehead wrinkles. While satisfied with the cosmetic outcome, she has developed drooping of one upper eyelid. Apraclonidine 0.5% eye drops are given to enhance upper eyelid elevation. Which of the following best explains the mechanism by which apraclonidine improves upper eyelid drooping in this case?
A) Alpha-2 adrenergic activation of the Müller muscle in the upper eyelid
B) Beta-2 adrenergic activation of the levator palpebrae superioris
C) Muscarinic parasympathetic blockade of the levator palpebrae superioris
D) Nicotinic parasympathetic blockade of the Müller muscle in the upper eyelid
questions.answer:
A)
Apraclonidine functions as an alpha-2 receptor agonist that enhances muscle tone in the sympathetically controlled Müller muscle within the upper eyelid. B) is incorrect because apraclonidine does not target beta-2 receptors and does not directly stimulate the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. C) is incorrect because apraclonidine does not function through muscarinic parasympathetic pathways. D) is incorrect because apraclonidine does not act via nicotinic parasympathetic mechanisms.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man with a long-term history of sun exposure is evaluated because of a 2.5-cm biopsy-proven squamous cell carcinoma of the central lower lip. Physical examination shows no enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this cancer?
A) Combined surgery and radiation
B) Curettage and electrodessication
C) Photodynamic therapy
D) Surgical excision
E) Treatment with 5-fluorouracil for 3 months
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


Oral cavity cancers are staged based on the following criteria set forth by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC):


The cancer described in the scenario is a stage T2N0M0 cancer of the lip. Surgical excision with margin control is the most appropriate and probably the most common treatment for this lesion, although Mohs micrographic surgery may also be an option for surgical removal. Reconstruction would be performed after attaining adequate surgical margins and can be performed utilizing local tissue flaps in most patients.


5-Fluorouracil cream can be used in the treatment of actinic keratosis and superficial basal cell cancers.
