A 60-year-old male patient presents to the clinic seeking aesthetic enhancement of his lower eyelid and upper cheek region. Clinical examination reveals a noticeable tear trough deformity. What is the underlying anatomical structure responsible for the tear trough?
A) Connection of the orbital septum to the arcus marginalis
B) Gap between the palpebral and orbital components of the orbicularis oculi muscle
C) Osteocutaneous ligament originating from the medial aspect of the maxilla
D) Protrusion of the orbital rim due to malar fat pad ptosis
E) Triangular junction where the orbicularis oculi, levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, and levator labii superioris muscles converge
questions.answer:
C)
The tear trough ligament represents a genuine osteocutaneous ligament situated between the palpebral and orbital segments of the orbicularis oculi muscle, extending from the medial canthus inferolaterally to approximately the mid-pupillary line where it joins the bilayered orbicularis retaining ligament. This ligament constitutes the fundamental anatomical structure underlying the tear trough deformity. A is incorrect because the orbital septum attachment to the arcus marginalis does not create the tear trough deformity. B is incorrect because while there is a cleft between muscle parts, this gap itself is not the anatomical basis of the tear trough. D is incorrect because orbital rim prominence from malar fat descent describes age-related changes but not the specific anatomical foundation of the tear trough. E is incorrect because this triangular muscle confluence describes a different anatomical region and is not responsible for tear trough formation.

questions.question:
An 8-year-old child presents to the emergency room following trauma to the right arm, located 3 cm above the elbow crease. Which of the following variables is linked to better functional recovery after peripheral nerve reconstruction?
A) Using fewer suture threads in the nerve reconstruction
B) Performing nerve repair under higher tension
C) Longer delay between nerve damage and surgical repair
D) More centrally located nerve damage
E) Lower patient age
questions.answer:
E)
Younger patient age is associated with superior functional outcomes following peripheral nerve repair. Pediatric patients demonstrate enhanced regenerative capacity and neuroplasticity compared to adults, leading to better recovery of motor and sensory function. A is incorrect because using more suture strands (not fewer) crossing the repair site improves outcomes by providing better coaptation. B is incorrect because minimal tension (not higher tension) at the repair site is associated with improved function and reduced scarring. C is incorrect because earlier surgical intervention (not delayed repair) generally produces better outcomes than repairs performed later. D is incorrect because more distal injuries (not proximal) typically have better prognoses, as proximal injuries require longer regeneration distances and affect more muscle groups.

questions.question:
When performing the Jones transfer for radial nerve palsy, transferring the flexor carpi ulnaris to the extensor digitorum communis for digits III-V, what is the most significant drawback?
A) Complex surgical dissection
B) Inadequate excursion of the donor tendon
C) Need for pulley construction due to indirect pull
D) Lack of synergistic function
E) High risk of postoperative tendon rupture
questions.answer:
B)
The inadequate excursion of the flexor carpi ulnaris (FCU) is the primary limitation when transferring it to the extensor digitorum communis (EDC). The FCU has insufficient tendon excursion to achieve full finger extension, making this transfer biomechanically suboptimal. Additionally, sacrificing the FCU eliminates an important ulnar-sided wrist stabilizer and compromises wrist flexion with ulnar deviation. A) is incorrect because the surgical dissection is not particularly complex. C) is incorrect because the line of pull is relatively direct and does not require pulley creation. D) is incorrect because FCU and EDC have reasonable synergy as both are active during grip. E) is incorrect because rupture rates are not significantly elevated with this transfer.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old female patient has right breast lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) spanning a 1-cm region with no detectable axillary lymphadenopathy. Using the TNM classification system, what is the appropriate T category for this patient?
A) Tx
B) Tis
C) T0
D) T1a
E) None; LCIS is not classified under TNM staging
questions.answer:
E)
Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) was excluded from the TNM staging system in the 8th edition and is no longer categorized under pathologic tumor in situ (pTis). LCIS is considered a benign condition that carries increased risk for future carcinoma development rather than being classified as a malignancy with metastatic potential. A) Tx is incorrect because it indicates unknown primary tumor status, which doesn't apply here. B) Tis is incorrect because LCIS was specifically removed from the in situ category in current staging guidelines. C) T0 is incorrect as it denotes no evidence of primary tumor, but LCIS is present. D) T1a is incorrect because it represents invasive carcinoma ≤0.5 cm, whereas LCIS is not invasive cancer.

questions.question:
A 76-year-old woman with a history of left modified radical mastectomy and radiation therapy comes to the office because of a chronic wound of the left axilla associated with limitation of abduction and exposed rib at the wound base. A photograph is shown. Examination of a biopsy specimen excludes malignancy. In addition to appropriate debridement, which of the following is likely to be most effective in achieving wound closure?


A) Adjacent tissue transfer
B) Left latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap
C) Negative pressure wound therapy
D) Radial forearm fasciocutaneous free flap
E) Split-thickness skin graft
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.






The best option to achieve wound closure in this patient is an ipsilateral latissimus dorsi myocutaneous flap. For chronic wounds in an irradiated field, the best option is debridement followed by transfer of healthy, nonirradiated tissue. Negative pressure wound therapy is likely to result in a recurrent chronic wound, albeit a clean one. Split-thickness skin graft would be inappropriate in an irradiated wound bed with exposed bone. Autologous fat grafting can help improve the quality of irradiated tissues in the absence of a wound, and some studies have shown promise in the treatment of superficial radiation ulcers; however, this patient has necrotic rib, and following debridement the wound will be deep and large. Although wound management and fat grafting have been shown to promote healing in isolated cases, this approach is not yet an accepted standard of care. Adjacent tissue transfer will employ irradiated tissue, and is thus prone to necrosis, wound breakdown, and recurrent chronic wound formation. A free flap could be an option, but a forearm flap would not have the volume required for the expected defect. In addition, a free flap is more morbid than a local pedicled flap in this elderly patient.
References
Hameed A, Akhtar S, Naqvi A, et al. Reconstruction of complex chest wall defects by using polypropylene mesh and a pedicled latissimus dorsi flap: a 6-year experience. J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg. 2008 Jun;61(6):628-35. Epub 2007 Jul 25.
Losken A, Thourani VH, Carlson GW, et al. A reconstructive algorithm for plastic surgery following extensive chest wall resection. Br J Plast Surg. 2004 Jun;57(4):295-302.
Makboul M, Salama Ayyad MA. Is myocutaneous flap alone sufficient for reconstruction of chest wall osteoradionecrosis? Interact Cardiovasc Thorac Surg. 2012 Sep;15(3):447-51. doi: 10.1093/icvts/ivs146. Epub 2012 May 25.
Rigotti G, Marchi A, Gali√® M, et al. Clinical treatment of radiotherapy tissue damage by lipoaspirate transplant: a healing process mediated by adipose-derived adult stem cells. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2007 Apr 15;119(5):1409-22; discussion 1423-4.

questions.question:
What classification best characterizes the temporomandibular joint?
A) Condyloid (ellipsoid)
B) Arthrodial (gliding)
C) Ginglymoarthrodial (hinge-sliding)
D) Trochoid (pivot)
E) Ephippial (saddle)
questions.answer:
C)
The temporomandibular joint is properly classified as a ginglymoarthrodial joint because it exhibits both hinge and sliding movements during mandibular opening. These dual functions occur within two distinct joint compartments, upper and lower, which are effectively divided by an articular disc. In the initial 20 mm of jaw opening, the condyle performs rotational movement within the lower compartment (between the condylar head and articular disc) in an essentially pure hinge action. Additional opening requires the condyle to translate anteriorly with the articular disc through the upper compartment (between the articular disc and joint surface). A is incorrect because condyloid joints allow movement in two planes but lack the specific hinge-sliding combination of the TMJ. B is incorrect because arthrodial joints permit only gliding movements without the rotational component. D is incorrect because trochoid joints allow only rotational movement around a single axis. E is incorrect because ephippial joints permit movement in two planes but do not have the unique dual-compartment hinge-sliding mechanism of the TMJ.

questions.question:
What percentage of all congenital upper extremity malformations is attributed to congenital constriction band syndrome?
A) 6%
B) 12%
C) 18%
D) 24%
E) 30%
questions.answer:
B)
Congenital constriction band syndrome accounts for approximately 12% of all congenital upper extremity defects. This condition, also known as amniotic band sequence, encompasses a spectrum of birth anomalies including limb amputations, digital defects, and constriction rings caused by fibrous bands. The widely accepted extrinsic theory proposes that early amniotic rupture and oligohydramnios lead to fibrous band formation that disrupts normal fetal development. Research analyzing 419 upper limb defects among over 750,000 births in Finland confirmed this 12% prevalence rate. A) is incorrect because 6% underestimates the actual prevalence of this condition. C) is incorrect because 18% overestimates the frequency compared to documented studies. D) is incorrect because 24% significantly exceeds the established prevalence rate. E) is incorrect because 30% greatly overestimates the proportion, which actually represents the percentage of affected children with additional skeletal or non-skeletal anomalies.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient presents to the lymphedema clinic for assessment of bilateral lower limb lymphedema. The swelling has persisted for a minimum of 5 years. She has morbid obesity with a BMI of 58 kg/m2, well-managed diabetes mellitus, and no prior surgical procedures or injuries to her lower limbs. She has been under the care of a lymphedema specialist for continuous conservative treatment and maintains reasonable adherence to leg wrapping and elevation protocols. Nevertheless, she reports that the progressive enlargement, weight sensation, and fatigue in her legs limits her physical activity. Physical examination reveals enlarged lower extremities and a positive Stemmer sign. Bilateral lower limb lymphoscintigraphy shows delayed tracer movement to the inguinal region with dermal backflow patterns. What is the most suitable initial surgical intervention for this patient?
A) Weight reduction surgery
B) Combination of lymph node transplantation and lymphovenous anastomoses
C) Suction-assisted lipectomy
D) Lymphovenous anastomoses
E) Vascularized lymph node transplantation
questions.answer:
A)
The most appropriate initial surgical intervention is weight reduction surgery. In super morbidly obese patients with BMI above 50-60 kg/m2, lymphedema can develop and may be reversible in approximately 50% of cases with weight reduction below BMI 50 kg/m2. Since this patient has failed conservative weight loss measures, bariatric surgery referral is the most logical first step. B) is incorrect because combined procedures are typically reserved for patients who have failed simpler interventions and would not address the underlying obesity contributing to lymphedema. C) is incorrect because liposuction alone does not address the primary issue of obesity-induced lymphedema and may worsen lymphatic function. D) is incorrect because lymphovenous bypasses alone would not address the root cause of obesity-related lymphatic dysfunction. E) is incorrect because vascularized lymph node transfer is typically considered for more advanced cases after weight optimization and simpler procedures have been attempted.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old male patient presents with mandible-invading floor-of-mouth carcinoma. The surgical plan involves segmental mandibular resection and reconstruction using an osteocutaneous free flap incorporating bone from the scapula's lateral edge. Which artery serves as the vascular supply for this flap's pedicle?
A) Circumflex scapular
B) Dorsal scapular
C) Lateral thoracic
D) Thoracoacromial
E) Transverse cervical
questions.answer:
A)
The circumflex scapular artery is correct as it branches from the subscapular artery and provides vascular supply to both the lateral and medial scapular borders, making it the primary pedicle for scapular bone flaps used in mandibular reconstruction. This vessel can support chimeric flaps including various tissues from the subscapular system such as latissimus dorsi, serratus anterior, and scapular skin components. B) is incorrect because the dorsal scapular artery mainly vascularizes the trapezius muscle and associated skin rather than the scapular bone. C) is incorrect as the lateral thoracic artery supplies the lateral pectoralis major and axillary skin, not scapular bone. D) is incorrect because the thoracoacromial artery provides blood supply to the pectoralis major muscle and overlying skin. E) is incorrect since the transverse cervical artery primarily serves the trapezius muscle and related cutaneous tissue.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy is brought to the office because of the findings shown in the photograph. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?


A) Amniotic band syndrome
B) Axillary web syndrome
C) Poland syndrome
D) Popliteal pterygium syndrome
E) Waardenburg syndrome
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The patient has Poland syndrome with an unusual axillary web. The defining clinical feature is underdevelopment or absence of the sternal head of the pectoralis major muscles (seen in the photograph), but the deformity can lead to other anomalies such as absence of the nipple, the areola, or portions of the anterior chest wall. Cardiac anomalies may also be present. The ipsilateral extremity and hand are often smaller or hypoplastic, and this finding can be subtle or pronounced. The fingers are typically shorter and smaller than the contralateral side, and there may be webbing between the fingers. In severe forms, the central fingers are mere vestiges.


The other choices do not fit with this clinical photograph. Amniotic band syndrome usually leads to amputation or severe constriction of the hand or digits; this is not seen here. Waardenburg syndrome is a genetic condition that causes hearing loss and pigmentation changes to the hair, skin, and eyes. Popliteal pterygium syndrome is a condition associated with cleft lip/palate, webs of the popliteal space, and syndactyly of the toes or fingers. The axillary web seen here is not a described feature. Axillary web syndrome, or cording, is an acquired web that usually follows axillary node dissection in the treatment of breast cancer. This does not fit the clinical scenario.


References
Gishen K, Askari M. Congenital hand anomalies: etiology, classification, and treatment. J Craniofac Surg. 2014 Jan;25(1):284-94.
Ram AN, Chung KC. Poland‚Äos syndrome: current thoughts in the setting of controversy. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2009 Mar;123(3):949-53; discussion 954-5.
Sammer DM, Chung KC. Congenital hand differences: embryology and classification. Hand Clin. 2009 May;25(2):151-6.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old female patient has undergone repair of a ventral hernia with component separation technique and mesh implantation. Two days following surgery, she suddenly becomes unconscious with an absent pulse. Immediate CPR is initiated and cardiac monitoring is established. The electrocardiogram shows pulseless electrical activity (PEA). Which medication should be given first in this clinical scenario?
A) Adenosine
B) Atropine
C) Diltiazem
D) Dopamine
E) Epinephrine
questions.answer:
E)
Epinephrine is the first-line medication for managing pulseless electrical activity (PEA) in cardiac arrest situations. Its beneficial effects include peripheral vasoconstriction through alpha-1 adrenergic stimulation and enhanced cardiac contractility via beta-1 adrenergic activation. Current Advanced Cardiac Life Support protocols recommend immediate epinephrine administration once PEA or asystole is identified on cardiac monitoring. The standard intravenous dosage is 1 mg administered every 3-5 minutes, followed by a 20 mL normal saline flush. CPR should continue uninterrupted during medication administration. Alternative routes include intraosseous or endotracheal administration when IV access is unavailable. A) Adenosine is incorrect because it is used for supraventricular tachycardia, not cardiac arrest rhythms. B) Atropine is incorrect because it is no longer recommended for PEA or asystole in current ACLS guidelines. C) Diltiazem is incorrect because calcium channel blockers are contraindicated in cardiac arrest situations. D) Dopamine is incorrect because it is not a first-line agent for cardiac arrest and is used primarily for hemodynamic support in conscious patients.

questions.question:
A healthy 35-year-old female patient is planned for elective complete abdominoplasty using conscious sedation combined with local anesthetic. Which of the following IV sedation combinations would best manage this patient's discomfort and apprehension while minimizing respiratory compromise risk?
A) Fentanyl only
B) Ketamine with fentanyl
C) Midazolam only
D) Midazolam with fentanyl
E) Midazolam with propofol
questions.answer:
D)

The optimal choice is the midazolam and fentanyl combination because midazolam provides superior anti-anxiety and memory-blocking properties while fentanyl delivers effective short-duration pain relief. Clinical research has shown this dual-agent approach outperforms single-agent midazolam in reducing patient-reported pain and anxiety levels. Although fentanyl carries respiratory depression risk, its brief half-life limits this concern, and midazolam has minimal respiratory effects in most patients. Both agents have specific reversal medications available (flumazenil for midazolam, naloxone for fentanyl). A) Fentanyl alone is incorrect because it lacks anxiolytic properties needed for conscious sedation. B) Ketamine with fentanyl is incorrect because ketamine does not provide anxiety relief and may cause dissociative effects. C) Midazolam alone is incorrect because it provides inadequate analgesia for the procedure. E) Midazolam with propofol is incorrect because this combination increases respiratory depression risk and propofol lacks a reversal agent.

questions.question:
A 4-month-old boy presents for assessment of a profound circumferential groove around his right lower leg that has been present from birth. There is significant swelling of the leg and foot below the constricting ring, which has worsened considerably in recent weeks. What is the most suitable treatment approach for this patient?
A) Lower limb amputation
B) Use of compression stockings
C) Surgical removal of the band
D) Collagenase enzyme injection
E) Leg elevation with watchful waiting
questions.answer:
C)
Surgical removal of the band is the most appropriate treatment for this patient with amniotic band syndrome causing progressive edema and potential functional compromise. Amniotic band syndrome occurs in 1:1200 to 1:15,000 live births and can cause constriction bands ranging from superficial skin indentations to deep circumferential bands leading to distal swelling, vascular compromise, or auto-amputation. The condition typically affects distal portions of extremities asymmetrically and may be associated with acrosyndactyly, clubfoot, and cleft abnormalities. Given the worsening edema in this case, prompt surgical excision is indicated to prevent further complications. While traditionally performed in two stages, single-stage resection has proven safe and effective. A) Lower limb amputation is incorrect because it would only be considered for an unsalvageable extremity, which is not the case here. B) Compression stockings are incorrect as they have no established role in treating constriction bands and would not address the underlying problem. D) Collagenase injection is incorrect because this treatment modality is not used for constriction band management. E) Leg elevation with observation is incorrect as it fails to address the root cause of the progressive edema and could lead to further deterioration.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female patient arrives with a fast-expanding, ulcerative nodular mass on her left forearm. Pathological analysis shows poorly differentiated Merkel cell carcinoma. No distant spread is detected, however the tumor measures clinically T2 (2.5 cm) with palpable lymph nodes in the axilla. What represents the most suitable initial treatment approach for this case?
A) Extensive local resection of the tumor only
B) Extensive local resection combined with sentinel lymph node sampling
C) Extensive local resection paired with complete axillary lymph node removal
D) Extensive local resection, complete axillary lymph node removal, and postoperative radiotherapy
E) Preoperative chemotherapy prior to extensive local resection
questions.answer:
D)

The correct treatment for Merkel cell carcinoma with clinically evident nodal disease involves extensive local tumor removal, therapeutic lymph node clearance (axillary in this instance due to palpable adenopathy), and postoperative radiation to both the primary tumor bed and nodal regions, given the high propensity for local and regional disease recurrence. A is incorrect because it fails to address the known nodal involvement and omits necessary radiation therapy. B is incorrect because sentinel node sampling is only appropriate when nodes are clinically negative, not when they are already palpable. C is incorrect because it excludes adjuvant radiation therapy, which is essential for optimal local and regional control in Merkel cell carcinoma. E is incorrect because chemotherapy is not the standard initial treatment for localized disease and is typically reserved for metastatic presentations.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old male presents to the emergency department requiring thumb reattachment surgery. Following successful microsurgical reconnection of the digital arteries and veins, papaverine is administered to the blood vessels. This drug functions as a vasodilator via which of the following pathways?
A) Calcium channel blockade
B) Reduction of platelet aggregation
C) Thrombin and factor Xa inactivation
D) Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition
E) Phosphodiesterase inhibition
questions.answer:
E)
Papaverine functions as a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and serves as a frequently utilized vasodilating medication in microsurgical procedures. The drug is applied topically as a solution directly onto the vessel adventitia, resulting in vasodilation. Papaverine's mechanism involves elevating cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP) concentrations, which promotes smooth muscle relaxation within blood vessels. This same mechanism has made papaverine valuable for treating cardiac and cerebrovascular vasospasm. A is incorrect because calcium channel blockade is the mechanism of nifedipine, another topical vasodilator used in microsurgery. B is incorrect because reducing platelet aggregation is an anticoagulant effect, not papaverine's vasodilatory mechanism. C is incorrect because thrombin and factor Xa inactivation describes heparin's anticoagulant mechanism through antithrombin dependence. D is incorrect because glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibition is an antiplatelet mechanism used by specific antiplatelet agents, not a vasodilatory pathway.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old female patient with cleft lip and palate history presents to the clinic due to hyponasal speech patterns, which have been validated by speech-language pathology evaluation. The child and parents indicate that her speech remains easily comprehensible to others. Past surgical interventions include primary lip repair, primary nasal reconstruction, primary palate repair, and posterior pharyngeal flap procedure. What represents the most suitable next management approach?
A) Facial CT imaging
B) Genetic consultation
C) Palatal MRI study
D) Sleep study evaluation
E) Swallowing assessment
questions.answer:
D)
Hyponasal speech occurs when insufficient airflow passes through the velopharyngeal mechanism, creating a blocked nasal quality similar to speaking while pinching the nose closed. This differs from hypernasal speech, where velopharyngeal incompetence allows excessive air escape, producing a breathy nasal tone. In this case, the hyponasal speech pattern most likely results from an overly restrictive posterior pharyngeal flap that excessively obstructs the velopharyngeal port. Treatment indications include speech difficulties that impair communication and obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). Since the patient's speech remains intelligible to others, polysomnography to assess for OSA represents the most logical next step among the given options. A) Facial CT imaging is not indicated for evaluating hyponasality and would not provide relevant information for management. B) Genetic consultation is unnecessary as this appears to be a surgical complication rather than a genetic issue. C) Palatal MRI would not be the appropriate imaging modality for assessing velopharyngeal function or obstruction. E) Swallowing assessment is not indicated as there are no reported swallowing difficulties or concerns.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of progressive numbness in her right middle finger of her dominant hand. She gave birth to a healthy infant 6 months prior. She states that the numbness wakes her up at night and improves when she shakes her hand. Physical examination reveals two-point discrimination of 5 mm across all fingers. What is the most probable abnormal electrodiagnostic result in this patient?
A) Motor action potential amplitude of 25 μV
B) Motor latency of 4 ms
C) Occasional fasciculations
D) Positive sharp waves
E) Sensory action potential latency of 4 ms
questions.answer:
E)
This patient presents with early-stage carpal tunnel syndrome. She demonstrates only sensory symptoms with numbness that improves with movement. Two-point discrimination becomes abnormal in advanced carpal tunnel syndrome when permanent nerve damage occurs. No motor symptoms are present currently.

Electrodiagnostic testing includes both sensory action potentials (nerve conduction studies) and electromyography. In early carpal tunnel syndrome without motor involvement, sensory action potential distal latency becomes prolonged (abnormal when >3.5 ms), making 4.0 ms the correct finding. A) is incorrect because motor action potential amplitude of 25 μV would be normal (abnormal is typically <5 μV in severe cases). B) is incorrect because a motor latency of 4 ms, while at the upper limit of normal, would not be expected in purely sensory carpal tunnel syndrome. C) is incorrect because occasional fasciculations are normal findings in healthy muscle. D) is incorrect because positive sharp waves indicate muscle denervation, which would not be present in early carpal tunnel syndrome without motor involvement.

questions.question:
What feature distinguishes a young face from an aged face?
A) Hollowing of the cheek area
B) Sunken upper eyelid fold
C) Oval facial shape (tapered toward bottom)
D) Extended lower eyelid-cheek boundary position
E) Wide angle beneath the chin
questions.answer:
C)
A young, attractive face displays an inverted triangular or oval configuration with the narrower portion at the bottom. As aging occurs, this triangle reverses, creating a wider lower portion characterized by a square jaw and sagging jowls in the mature face.

A is incorrect because youthful faces show fullness and convexity in the cheek region, not hollowing. B is incorrect because young faces have full upper orbital volume without deep-set grooves, unlike aged faces which develop sunken upper eyelid folds. D is incorrect because youthful faces have a higher malar-eyelid junction, while aged faces show a descended or elongated lower eyelid appearance. E is incorrect because young necks demonstrate an acute submental angle of 90 degrees or less, not an obtuse wide angle.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old male presents for evaluation of a newly discovered skin lesion on his back. Surgical excision under local anesthesia is being considered. His past medical history is significant for hypertension and coronary artery disease, with a history of percutaneous coronary intervention performed a decade ago. His current medications include aspirin 81 mg daily. What is the most appropriate perioperative management of his aspirin therapy for this procedure?
A) Continue the current dose
B) Discontinue 1 day before surgery
C) Discontinue 2 days before surgery
D) Discontinue 7 days before surgery
E) Discontinue 14 days before surgery
questions.answer:
A)
For patients with elevated cardiovascular risk, continuing aspirin therapy during dermatologic procedures represents the safest management strategy. Aspirin provides cardioprotective benefits by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase, preventing thromboxane synthesis and platelet aggregation. Discontinuing aspirin in patients with established cardiovascular disease can trigger a rebound hypercoagulable state with increased thromboxane production and reduced fibrinolysis, significantly elevating the risk of thrombotic events. Research demonstrates that aspirin withdrawal is an independent risk factor for major cardiac events and mortality. Additionally, multiple studies have shown that continuing aspirin during cutaneous surgery does not significantly increase bleeding complications. B is incorrect because even a single day of aspirin discontinuation can initiate rebound effects in high-risk patients. C is incorrect because two days of withdrawal further increases thrombotic risk without meaningful bleeding reduction benefits. D is incorrect because seven days of discontinuation substantially elevates cardiovascular event risk while providing unnecessary bleeding precautions for minor surgery. E is incorrect because fourteen days represents excessive withdrawal duration that maximizes thrombotic risk for a low-bleeding-risk procedure.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman presents with muscle atrophy and numbness affecting her fourth and fifth digits. What is the most probable location of nerve compression?
A) Anconeus epitrochlearis
B) Arcade of Frohse
C) Lacertus fibrosis
D) Ligament of Struthers
E) Pronator teres
questions.answer:
A)
The anconeus epitrochlearis is responsible for the nerve compression. This clinical presentation demonstrates both motor weakness and sensory disturbances consistent with ulnar nerve entrapment. Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow represents the second most frequent upper extremity compression syndrome after carpal tunnel syndrome in younger patients. While the ligament of Osborne is the most frequent cause, the anconeus epitrochlearis muscle represents a congenital variant that originates from the medial humeral epicondyle and attaches to the ulnar olecranon. This accessory muscle occurs in 4-34% of normal elbows and can cause ulnar nerve compression at the elbow. B is incorrect because the arcade of Frohse is associated with posterior interosseous nerve entrapment, not ulnar nerve compression. C is incorrect because lacertus fibrosis causes median nerve compression, not ulnar nerve symptoms. D is incorrect because the ligament of Struthers is associated with median nerve entrapment. E is incorrect because the pronator teres muscle is involved in median nerve compression syndromes.

questions.question:
The ear anomaly depicted in the photograph shown is most commonly found in patients with which of the following syndromes?


A) Apert
B) Klippel-Trenaunay
C) Stickler
D) Treacher Collins
E) Van der Woude
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The photograph depicts a patient with lobular type microtia and represents failure of formation of the pinna of the ear. Patients commonly have stenosis or absence of the external auditory canal, and in cases of lobular type microtia, exhibit a microtic remnant composed of malformed cartilage and fibrofatty tissue that is reminiscent of the ear lobule. This condition may be seen in isolation but is commonly seen in cases of hemifacial microsomia and Treacher Collins syndrome. Treacher Collins syndrome, or mandibulofacial dysostosis, exhibits a broad phenotypic spectrum and is commonly seen with hypoplasia or absence of the zygoma, coloboma of the lower eyelid, lateral canthal dystopia, absence of the medial lower eyelid lashes, mandibular hypoplasia with a steep occlusal plane, and abnormalities of the external ear, including microtia.


Apert syndrome results from FGFR2 mutations Ser252Trp or Pro253Arg and results in multisuture craniosynostosis, mid-face hypoplasia, complex syndactyly, cystic acne, and other less common findings. It is transmitted as an autosomal dominant condition.


Stickler syndrome is inherited in autosomal dominant and recessive patterns. It results from mutations in collagen genes COL2A1, COL11A1, and COL11A2. This may manifest with ocular abnormalities including early-onset cataracts, vitreous anomalies, retinal detachments, and severe myopia. Patients may have sensorineural hearing loss. Mandibular hypoplasia and Pierre Robin sequence is common in these patients.


Van der Woude syndrome results from a mutation of the IRF6 gene and is a common autosomal dominant condition associated with cleft lip and palate. Patients characteristically exhibit lower lip pits.


Finally, Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome is a congenital capillary-lymphatic-venous malformation of the lower extremity with associated soft tissue and bony overgrowth. This condition is caused by a somatic mutation in the PIK3CA gene and is therefore on the phenotypic spectrum with CLOVES syndrome and other PIK3CA-related overgrowth syndromes (PROS).


ReferencesBuchanan EP, Zue AS, Hollier LH. Craniofacial syndromes. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2014;134(1):128e-153e.Greene AK. Vascular malformation overgrowth syndromes. In: Greene AK. Vascular Anomalies: Classification, Diagnosis, and Management. Quality Medical Publishing; 2013:183-206.Havlik RJ. Miscellaneous craniofacial conditions: fibrous dysplasia, Moebius syndrome, Romberg syndrome, Treacher Collins syndrome, dermoid cyst, and neurofibromatosis. In: Chung K, Gosain AK, Gurtner GC, Mehrara BJ, Rubin JP, Spear SL, eds. Grabb and Smith‚Äos Plastic Surgery. 7th ed. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins; 2014:295-310.Martinez-Lopez A, Salvador-Rodriguez L, Montero-Vilchez T, et al. Vascular malformations syndromes: an update. Curr Opin Pediatr. 2019;31(6):747-753.Thorne CH. Ear reconstruction. In: Chung K, Gosain AK, Gurtner GC, Mehrara BJ, Rubin JP, Spear SL, eds. Grabb and Smith‚Äos Plastic Surgery. 7th ed. Lippincott Williams and Wilkins; 2014:283-294.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male rugby player is evaluated because of the inability to flex the ring finger at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint 2 days after injuring the finger during a match. The patient reports tenderness over the pulp and distal flexion crease. A clinical photograph and x-ray studies are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?


A ) Closed reduction and percutaneous pin fixation
B ) DIP arthrodesis
C ) Extension block splinting
D ) Open reduction and internal fixation
E ) Volar plate arthroplasty
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The clinical scenario, photograph, and x-ray studies demonstrate classic symptoms of a ?jersey finger,? or avulsion of the insertion of the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) tendon. In this instance, the rupture involves a large bone fragment to which the FDP tendon remains attached (Type III). The large size of the bone fragment lends itself to repair via open reduction and internal fixation of the fracture. Use of mini-screws or transosseous wiring will provide suitable internal fixation. Type II (retraction of the tendon to the proximal interphalangeal [PIP] joint) and Type I (retraction to the palm) injuries can be addressed through transosseous suture reattachment or suture anchor.


Inadequate closed reduction would make percutaneous pin fixation a poor choice of treatment.


Arthrodesis offers a salvage procedure for failed or unrepaired FDP avulsion injuries. In this young patient with an acute condition, arthrodesis would be too aggressive an intervention.


Extension block splinting can be useful in volar plate injuries, which are often identified by a small, palmar avulsion fragment seen on the lateral x-ray study. This fracture would not be successfully reduced by attempts at flexion or splinting.


Volar plate arthroplasty can restore a functional articular surface following intra-articular fractures of the PIP joint but are not useful in the DIP.


References
1. Teo TC, Dionyssiou D, Armenio A, et al. Anatomical repair of zone 1 flexor tendon injuries. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2009 Feb;123(2):617-622.
2. McCallister WV, Ambrose HC, Katolik LI, et al. Comparison of pullout button versus suture anchor for zone I flexor tendon repair. J Hand Surg Am. 2006 Feb;31(2):246-251.
3. Lehfeldt M, Ray E, Sherman R. MOC-PS(SM) CME article: treatment of flexor tendon laceration. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2008 Apr;121(4 Suppl):1-12.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old female presents for evaluation regarding fat removal via liposuction from her abdomen, hips, flanks, and thighs. She measures 5 ft 5 in (165 cm) tall and weighs 156 lb (71 kg). Her BMI is 26 kg/m2. Clinical examination reveals fat deposits in the abdomen, hips, flanks, and thighs. The procedure will involve removing 4 L of fat using suction-assisted lipectomy with a superwet approach. What is the most probable adverse outcome for this patient?
A) Surface contour abnormalities
B) Deep vein thrombosis
C) Skin darkening
D) Fluid collection
E) Surgical site infection
questions.answer:
A)
Surface contour abnormalities represent the most frequent adverse outcome following liposuction, occurring in approximately 20% of cases. B) is incorrect because deep vein thrombosis occurs in fewer than 1% of liposuction patients. C) is incorrect because skin darkening affects only about 4% of patients and typically results from thermal injury or compromised blood supply. D) is incorrect because fluid collections are uncommon complications, though they may be more frequent in patients with elevated BMI. E) is incorrect because surgical site infections are rare complications after liposuction procedures.

questions.question:
A 3-month-old baby with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is being assessed for an isolated soft palate cleft (Veau I). A Furlow palatoplasty is scheduled for 9 months of age. When compared to non-syndromic patients with the identical cleft pattern, this child will face an increased postoperative risk for which of the following complications?
A) Air embolism
B) Palatal fistula formation
C) Respiratory failure
D) Velopharyngeal insufficiency
E) Wound breakdown
questions.answer:
D)
Patients with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (velocardiofacial syndrome) consistently demonstrate poorer speech outcomes following cleft palate repair compared to non-syndromic cleft patients. This increased risk of persistent velopharyngeal insufficiency is primarily attributed to decreased oropharyngeal muscle tone and coordination difficulties inherent to the syndrome. A) Air embolism is incorrect because this complication is not associated with cleft palate surgery in any patient population. B) Palatal fistula formation is incorrect because syndromic patients do not have higher rates of fistula formation compared to non-syndromic patients. C) Respiratory failure is incorrect because while it can occur in patients with concurrent Robin sequence, this scenario does not mention airway compromise. E) Wound breakdown is incorrect because dehiscence rates are not elevated in 22q11.2 deletion syndrome patients compared to non-syndromic cases.

questions.question:
A multicenter research study is collecting information about a diagnostic test's capacity to identify women who develop a novel breast condition, with comparison to age-matched control subjects. Which of the following best describes the specificity of this test?
A) The proportion of disease-free individuals correctly identified as negative divided by all disease-free individuals
B) The proportion of disease-free individuals incorrectly identified as positive divided by all diseased individuals
C) The proportion of diseased individuals incorrectly identified as negative divided by all disease-free individuals
D) The proportion of diseased individuals incorrectly identified as negative divided by all diseased individuals
E) The proportion of diseased individuals correctly identified as positive divided by all diseased individuals
questions.answer:
A)
Specificity measures a test's ability to correctly identify individuals without disease as negative (true negatives). It is calculated as the number of true negatives divided by the total number of disease-free individuals (true negatives + false positives). B is incorrect because it describes false positives divided by diseased patients, which is not a standard diagnostic measure. C is incorrect because it describes false negatives divided by healthy patients, which is not meaningful. D is incorrect because it describes the false negative rate (1 - sensitivity), not specificity. E is incorrect because it describes sensitivity, which measures the test's ability to correctly identify diseased individuals as positive.

questions.question:
A newborn male requires emergency intubation in the neonatal intensive care unit due to acute respiratory failure. Physical examination reveals significant micrognathia of the mandible and cleft palate. Nasopharyngeal endoscopy demonstrates posterior tongue displacement, soft laryngeal cartilages, and laryngeal web formation. What is the most suitable management for this airway obstruction?
A) Remove endotracheal tube and place infant face-down
B) Place nasopharyngeal tube
C) Perform mandibular lengthening procedure
D) Create surgical tongue-to-lip attachment
E) Perform surgical airway opening
questions.answer:
E)
Traceostomy is the most appropriate treatment because it bypasses all levels of airway obstruction present in this complex case. While mandibular distraction and tongue-lip adhesion effectively treat glossoptosis and upper airway blockage, they cannot address the laryngeal malacia and webbing affecting the lower airway. The combination of multiple anatomical abnormalities including posterior tongue displacement, unstable laryngeal cartilages, and laryngeal webbing requires surgical bypass of the entire upper airway system. A) is incorrect because extubation with prone positioning only addresses glossoptosis but not the laryngeal abnormalities. B) is incorrect because a nasal airway cannot bypass laryngeal malacia and webbing. C) is incorrect because mandibular distraction only treats the tongue-related obstruction, not the laryngeal pathology. D) is incorrect because tongue-lip adhesion similarly only addresses glossoptosis while leaving the laryngeal issues unresolved.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female patient presents with loss of sensation in the upper portion of the left ear's helical rim 1 month following neurosurgical intervention for facial pain relief. Which nerve was most probably damaged during the procedure?
A) Auriculotemporal
B) Glossopharyngeal
C) Great auricular
D) Lesser occipital
E) Vagus
questions.answer:
A)
The auriculotemporal nerve (a branch of the trigeminal nerve V3) is most likely injured because it provides sensory innervation to the anterior ear surface, including the helix, and is commonly at risk during microvascular decompression procedures for trigeminal neuralgia. B) is incorrect because the glossopharyngeal nerve primarily innervates the external auditory canal, not the helical rim. C) is incorrect because the great auricular nerve (C2-C3) supplies the posterior auricle and inferior ear regions, not the upper helical rim. D) is incorrect because the lesser occipital nerve (C2) innervates the superior posterior ear and mastoid area, not the anterior helical structures. E) is incorrect because the vagus nerve branches supply the external auditory meatus rather than the helical rim.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old girl presents to the clinic to have the lesion in the photograph removed. She has had it since birth. She does not like its appearance and has noted it has changed in size and shape during the last two years. Histopathologic examination of the specimen is most likely to show which of the following?


A) Amelanotic melanoma
B) Basal cell carcinoma
C) Nevus sebaceous
D) Squamous cell carcinoma
E) Trichoblastoma
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The photograph shows a sebaceous nevus of Jadassohn, and on pathology, a benign organoid nevus is the most likely finding. Given the patient's age, malignant transformation is very rare (around 2.5%). Until recently, the most common transformation has been thought to be basal cell carcinoma (1.1%). However, it is now thought that many of these were trichoblastomas. A melanoma present since childhood does not fit the presentation of this patient.


ReferencesKim JH, Park HY, Ahn SK. Nevus sebaceous accompanying secondary neoplasms and unique histopathologic findings. Ann Dermatol. 2011;23(suppl 2):S231-S234.Paninson B, Trope BM, Moschini JC, et al. Basal cell carcinoma on a nevus sebaceous of Jadassohn: a case report. J Clin Aesthet Dermatol. 2019;12(3):40-43.Goel P, Wolfswinkel EM, Fahradyan A, et al. Sebaceous nevus of the scalp. J Craniofac Surg. 2020;31(1):257-260.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old female patient with systemic sclerosis presents with severe, unrelenting pain and advancing digital ulceration affecting her right index and middle fingers that has not responded to conservative treatment. Duplex ultrasound examination reveals patent vessels with no detectable arterial blockage in the involved digits. What is the most suitable surgical intervention?
A) Bypass graft with interposition
B) Intra-arterial tissue plasminogen activator
C) Digital sympathectomy
D) Surgical thrombectomy
E) Arterialization using venous conduit
questions.answer:
C)
Digital sympathectomy is the appropriate treatment when arterial patency is confirmed on imaging, as vasospasm rather than occlusion is the underlying cause of ischemia, particularly in patients with autoimmune conditions like scleroderma. This procedure involves removing the adventitial layer from the radial, ulnar, and digital arteries to reduce sympathetic innervation responsible for pathological vasoconstriction. A) Bypass grafting is indicated when there is vascular occlusion with an adequate distal target vessel, which is not present in this case. B) Intra-arterial TPA is used for acute thrombotic occlusion, but imaging shows no evidence of clot formation. D) Thrombectomy is performed to remove clots from occluded vessels, but no occlusion is demonstrated here. E) Venous arterialization is reserved for cases with arterial occlusion lacking suitable distal targets for bypass, which does not apply to this patient with patent vessels.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old male comes to the office 12 months following surgical repair of an isolated brachial artery injury. Before vascular reconstruction, the hand and forearm lacked adequate blood supply. Compartment releases were not done during the initial repair. The patient cannot actively or passively straighten his fingers when the wrist is maintained in a neutral position, though he can actively form a complete fist. Tactile sensation remains normal. Which of the following treatments would be most suitable to enhance finger extension while maintaining grip strength in this patient?
A) Flexor pronator slide
B) Free functional gracilis transfer
C) Joint release and tenolysis
D) Splinting
questions.answer:
A)
This patient has a moderate Volkmann ischemic contracture best managed with a flexor pronator slide. The ability to actively flex fingers into a fist while being unable to passively extend them with the wrist neutral indicates retained flexor function with moderate contracture severity. A flexor pronator slide releases the contracted muscle origins while preserving existing muscle function and grip strength. B is incorrect because free functional muscle transfer is reserved for severe contractures with complete loss of muscle function, which this patient does not have given his retained grip strength. C is incorrect because joint release and tenolysis alone would not address the underlying muscle contracture causing the deformity. D is incorrect because while splinting can be an adjunct treatment, it would not provide definitive correction of an established moderate contracture requiring surgical intervention.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male patient is planned for great toe-to-thumb reconstruction 7 months following traumatic loss of his dominant thumb. While performing the toe dissection, the first dorsal metatarsal artery will most commonly originate from which of the following arterial sources?
A) Deep plantar artery
B) Dorsalis pedis artery
C) Plantar arterial arch
D) Posterior tibial artery
E) Proper digital artery
questions.answer:
B)
The dorsalis pedis artery is the correct answer because in approximately two-thirds of cases, the first dorsal metatarsal artery (FDMA) originates as the distal continuation of the dorsalis pedis artery, making this the most common anatomical pattern. A) Deep plantar artery is incorrect because while the FDMA can arise from this vessel in some cases, it occurs in only about one-third of patients, making it less common than the dorsalis pedis origin. C) Plantar arterial arch is incorrect because although the FDMA may occasionally originate from the plantar arch itself, this represents a minority of cases and is part of the one-third variant pattern. D) Posterior tibial artery is incorrect because this vessel runs longitudinally on the plantar surface in a superficial plane and does not give rise to the FDMA. E) Proper digital artery is incorrect because these vessels are actually the distal branches of the FDMA rather than its source.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old female patient is planned for subtotal vaginal reconstruction utilizing a pedicled deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap following oncologic resection. What is the primary benefit of employing this flap technique compared to the pudendal thigh (Singapore) flap?
A) Superior preservation of sensation
B) Reduced vaginal bulk
C) Decreased risk of intravaginal hair development
D) Enhanced mucous production
E) Single-operation approach
questions.answer:
C)
The deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap offers the significant advantage of being non-hair-bearing tissue, eliminating the risk of intravaginal hair growth that can occur with the Singapore flap. The Singapore flap utilizes hair-bearing vulvar skin which can result in problematic endovaginal hair growth requiring preoperative depilation. A is incorrect because the DIEP flap is insensate while the Singapore flap maintains sensation through its innervation. B is incorrect because the DIEP flap is actually more bulky than the thin Singapore flap, though less bulky than musculocutaneous options. D is incorrect because neither flap type produces mucus secretions. E is incorrect because both procedures are performed as single-stage operations.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old female patient presents for assessment of progressive breast firmness on the left side, occurring 5 years following subglandular breast augmentation with smooth round silicone implants. Surgical correction of the left breast is being considered. Which of the following interventions is most likely to reduce the likelihood of symptom recurrence?
A) Changing to a different anatomical plane or creating a new pocket
B) Complete removal of the capsular tissue
C) Application of botulinum toxin type A within and surrounding the implant space
D) Incorporation of autologous fat transfer within and around the implant area
questions.answer:
A)
Changing the implant location to a different plane or pocket along with implant replacement represents the only intervention that has been consistently demonstrated to reduce capsular contracture recurrence rates. While other approaches such as textured implant surfaces and fat grafting are utilized in revision breast augmentation procedures, the evidence supporting their effectiveness in preventing recurrence remains limited. B) is incorrect because research has not established the superiority of complete capsulectomy over partial capsule removal or capsulotomy in preventing recurrence. C) is incorrect because although botulinum toxin type A has been described for capsular contracture prevention, there is no established consensus that this treatment effectively reduces recurrence rates. D) is incorrect because while fat grafting is used in revision procedures, it has not been consistently proven to decrease capsular contracture recurrence compared to pocket/plane conversion.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old female patient develops a gradually enlarging lesion on her hand. Tissue sampling via incisional biopsy reveals metastatic carcinoma. What is the most probable site of the primary malignancy in this case?
A) Breast
B) Colorectal
C) Kidney
D) Lung
E) Thyroid
questions.answer:
D)
Lung represents the most frequent primary source of hand metastases, accounting for approximately 34% of all reported cases in comprehensive reviews. This makes it the correct answer. A) Breast is incorrect because it accounts for only about 5% of hand metastases, making it much less common than lung. B) Colorectal is incorrect as it represents part of the gastrointestinal group (25% combined) but individually is less frequent than lung primaries. C) Kidney is incorrect since renal tumors comprise only about 10% of hand metastases. E) Thyroid is incorrect because thyroid malignancies represent merely 2% of metastatic hand tumors.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old male child presents to the clinic with a 9 × 8 × 6-cm lesion on the left chest wall. The parents state that this mass has been evident for 8 months and has experienced rapid enlargement over the last 3 months. MRI reveals that the lesion is calcified, has a lobulated appearance, arises from the fourth and fifth ribs, and extends into the thoracic cavity where it contacts the left ventricle. Additional smaller lesions are noted in the scapulae, clavicles, and ribs. CT imaging is provided. Histopathologic examination of the biopsy specimen from the largest lesion demonstrates osteochondroma. What is the most suitable treatment approach at this point?
A) Radiotherapy combined with adjuvant chemotherapy
B) Radical surgical removal with adjuvant chemotherapy
C) Wide local resection, reconstruction, and adjuvant radiotherapy
D) Wide local resection with reconstruction
E) Observation without intervention at this time
questions.answer:
D)
The appropriate treatment is wide local resection with reconstruction. This patient has a large osteochondroma in the setting of multiple hereditary exostoses, evidenced by the presence of multiple smaller lesions throughout the skeleton. Given the size (giant osteochondroma), location near vital structures, and symptoms, surgical excision with reconstruction of the chest wall defect is indicated. Option A is incorrect because osteochondromas are benign lesions that do not respond to radiation or chemotherapy. Option B is incorrect because radical resection is unnecessarily aggressive for a benign tumor, and chemotherapy has no role in treating osteochondromas. Option C is incorrect because radiation therapy is not indicated for benign osteochondromas and may actually increase the risk of malignant transformation. Option E is incorrect because this large, symptomatic lesion requires surgical intervention due to its size, growth pattern, and proximity to cardiac structures.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the emergency room following complete ring avulsion amputation of his right ring finger at the level of the proximal phalanx. Which of the following variables most significantly affects the viability of the replanted digit in this case?
A) Concurrent middle phalanx fracture
B) Amputation site location
C) Requirement for skin grafting
D) Quantity of dorsal veins repaired/grafted
E) History of tobacco use
questions.answer:
D)
The quantity of dorsal veins repaired or grafted is the most significant factor affecting replantation success. Multiple studies and case series consistently demonstrate that repair and/or grafting of two or more dorsal veins correlates with improved survival rates in ring avulsion replantation cases. A) is incorrect because associated fractures of the middle phalanx do not impact survival outcomes in ring avulsion injuries. B) is incorrect because the level of amputation has not been shown to affect digit survival in ring avulsion cases. C) is incorrect because the need for skin grafting does not influence replantation viability. E) is incorrect because smoking history, while generally detrimental to healing, was not found to correlate with survival in ring avulsion replantation studies.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old man is referred by an orthopedic surgeon after undergoing open reduction and internal fixation of a fracture of the ankle after falling down stairs. The repair is complicated by wound dehiscence with 2 √o 2 cm of exposed tibialis anterior tendon without paratenon. A photograph is shown. After debridement of healthy tissue, reconstruction is performed using bilaminate neodermis with placement of a standard bolster dressing. At which of the following times relative to placement of the bilaminate neodermis should split-thickness skin grafting be performed?


A) At the same time
B) 1 week after
C) 2 weeks after
D) 4 weeks after
E) 6 weeks after
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.






Integra is a bilaminate neodermal material that consists of an outer silicone sheet and an inner layer of bovine collagen and glycosaminoglycan (derived from shark cartilage), which acts as a scaffold for regeneration. Specifically, there is migration of host fibroblasts into the matrix, which subsequently proliferate and form collagen. Additionally, there is migration of endothelial cells that form a vascular network within the neodermis, which can subsequently act as a foundation to support staged split-thickness skin grafting, at which time the silicone outer layer is removed and a thin (usually 6-8/1000") split-thickness autograft is applied. The success, or "take," of the skin graft depends on whether the neodermis is vascularized sufficiently to maintain graft viability. A 2001 study by Moiemen et al. demonstrated clinically and histologically that this process takes 4 weeks on average, without the use of topical negative pressure.


A follow-up article from 2004 suggests this process can be accelerated from 4 weeks to an average of 7.25 days if topical negative pressure is used. Further follow-up studies based on the clinical appearance of the bilaminate neodermal matrix have suggested reduction in complication rates, improved patient tolerance, and enhanced and accelerated neovascularization with the use of topical negative pressure wound therapy. However, a study published in 2010 looking histologically at various time points could not demonstrate that topical negative pressure wound therapy accelerates neovascularization as verified by the presence of histologically patent vascular channels. The authors found that the median percentage of the template depth that demonstrated canalized channels was 0%, 20%, 61%, and 80% for days 7, 14, 21, and 28, respectively.


Because this question pertains to the use of bilaminate neodermal matrix with the use of a standard bolster dressing and not negative pressure wound therapy, most existing evidence indicates that the most appropriate timing is 4 weeks after placement of the bilaminate neodermis.


References
1. Moiemen NS, Staiano JJ, Ojeh NO, et al. Reconstructive surgery with a dermal regeneration template: clinical and histologic study. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2001 Jul;108(1):93-103.
2. Molnar JA, DeFranzo AJ, Hadaegh A, et al. Acceleration of Integra incorporation in complex tissue defects with subatmospheric pressure. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2004 Apr 15;113(5):1339-1346.
3. Jeschke MG, Rose C, Angele P, et al. Development of new reconstructive techniques: use of Integra in combination with fibrin glue and negative-pressure therapy for reconstruction of acute and chronic wounds. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2004 Feb;113(2):525-530.
4. Baldwin C, Potter M, Clayton E, et al. Topical negative pressure stimulates endothelial migration and proliferation: a suggested mechanism for improved integration of Integra. Ann Plast Surg. 2009 Jan;62(1):92-96.
5. Moiemen NS, Yarrow J, Kamel D, et al. Topical negative pressure therapy: does it accelerate neovascularisation within the dermal regeneration template, Integra? A prospective histological in vivo study. Burns. 2010 Sep;36(6):764-768. Epub 2010 May 21.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents to the clinic with a 1-year history of clicking sounds during jaw opening. She sustained facial trauma when her face hit the steering wheel in a car accident 1 year prior. On examination, her dental midline appears normal without any deviation. What is the most probable etiology of her symptoms?
A) Lateral pterygoid muscle injury
B) Intra-articular foreign material
C) Malhealed coronoid process fracture
D) Ununited mandibular condyle fracture
E) Displaced articular disc
questions.answer:
E)
The clicking sensation during jaw movement is most commonly attributed to displacement of the articular disc within the temporomandibular joint. Normally, this disc remains positioned between the condyle and temporal bone throughout jaw motion. When displaced, it can create audible clicking as it moves in and out of proper position. Treatment typically begins conservatively with occlusal splints, anti-inflammatory medications, and physiotherapy, with surgery reserved for cases unresponsive to non-operative management. A) Lateral pterygoid muscle injury would more likely cause muscle spasm or limited opening rather than clicking. B) Foreign material in the joint would typically cause pain and restricted motion rather than clicking sounds. C) A malhealed coronoid fracture would primarily affect jaw opening mechanics and cause deviation rather than clicking. D) Nonunion of a condylar fracture would result in malocclusion, deviation, and functional impairment rather than isolated clicking.

questions.question:
A 49-year-old female patient presents for assessment following a traumatic injury to the right lower eyelid and cheek area. Clinical examination reveals impaired ability to close the eyelid, perform voluntary squinting movements, and facial expression. Which facial nerve branch is most likely damaged?
A) Buccal
B) Cervical
C) Marginal mandibular
D) Temporal
E) Zygomatic
questions.answer:
E)

The zygomatic branch of the facial nerve is responsible for innervating the extracanthal portion of the orbicularis oculi muscle, which controls eyelid closure, voluntary squinting, and facial animation. This branch's injury would explain the patient's inability to perform these functions. The buccal branch is incorrect because it innervates the medial inner canthal orbicularis responsible for blinking and lower lid tone, not the functions described. The cervical branch is incorrect as it does not supply the orbicularis oculi muscle. The marginal mandibular branch is incorrect because it innervates muscles of the lower lip and chin, not the eyelid. The temporal branch is incorrect as it does not provide innervation to the orbicularis oculi muscle.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male exercise trainer presents with oral cavity squamous cell carcinoma requiring soft-tissue free flap reconstruction. The patient expresses significant concern about preserving complete muscular function at the donor site. Which fasciocutaneous flap would best address his concerns by providing minimal muscular donor site morbidity?
A) Anterolateral thigh flap
B) Deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap
C) Medial sural artery perforator flap
D) Parascapular flap
E) Profunda artery perforator flap
questions.answer:
D)
The parascapular flap is the optimal choice because it consistently features a septal perforator that runs between the teres major, teres minor, and triceps muscles without requiring any muscle sacrifice. This flap reliably preserves all muscular function at the donor site. A) The anterolateral thigh flap is incorrect because it has variable perforator anatomy that may include muscular perforators requiring muscle division. B) The DIEP flap is incorrect as it also has inconsistent perforator patterns that can involve muscular perforators necessitating some muscle sacrifice. C) The medial sural artery perforator flap is incorrect because its vessels penetrate through the gastrocnemius muscle, requiring muscle division. E) The profunda artery perforator flap is incorrect since its perforators traverse through the adductor magnus muscle, compromising muscular integrity.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female patient seeks consultation for cosmetic breast surgery due to breast asymmetry. Clinical examination reveals a unilaterally underdeveloped breast with a restricted, raised base and protruding nipple-areolar complex. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Amastia
B) Micromastia
C) Poland syndrome
D) Tuberous breast
E) Virginal mammary hypertrophy
questions.answer:
D)
Tuberous breast deformity is characteristically defined by breast underdevelopment with a restricted and raised base, inadequate lower pole skin, and protrusion of the nipple-areolar complex. A is incorrect because amastia presents with complete absence of the nipple. B is incorrect because micromastia involves small breast size but typically does not include areolar herniation. C is incorrect because Poland syndrome primarily involves absence of the pectoralis major muscle with variable breast abnormalities, but constricted base and herniated areola are not typical features. E is incorrect because virginal mammary hypertrophy would present with excessive breast volume and a wider base rather than constriction.

questions.question:
What is the most frequently observed characteristic in individuals with vertical maxillary excess?
A) Counterclockwise mandibular rotation
B) Increased vertical dimension in the upper facial third
C) Mentalis muscle tension
D) Open bite in the posterior region
E) Retruded middle third of the face
questions.answer:
C)
Vertical maxillary excess (VME), also known as long face syndrome, is characterized by disproportionate anterior facial height in the lower facial third. The middle third of the face appears relatively protruded. Overeruption of maxillary posterior teeth leads to clockwise mandibular rotation. Patients exhibit lip incompetence, excessive gingival display, and compensatory mentalis muscle contraction when attempting lip closure. This condition is typically associated with anterior open bite. A) is incorrect because VME causes clockwise, not counterclockwise mandibular rotation. B) is incorrect because the excess height occurs in the lower, not upper, facial third. D) is incorrect because VME is associated with anterior, not posterior, open bite. E) is incorrect because the midface appears relatively protrusive, not retrusive, in VME.

questions.question:
In a patient experiencing nasal breathing difficulties, which of the following anatomical issues is most appropriately addressed using a spreader graft?
A) Rounded nasal tip
B) Prominent nasal bridge
C) Loose external nostril tissue
D) Enlarged inferior turbinates
E) Constricted internal nasal valve
questions.answer:
E)
The spreader graft is specifically designed to address internal nasal valve stenosis by being positioned between the septum and upper lateral cartilages to widen the valve angle and improve inspiratory airflow. A) is incorrect because a rounded nasal tip is an aesthetic concern that doesn't affect airway function and requires tip refinement techniques. B) is incorrect because a prominent nasal bridge is addressed through dorsal reduction, not valve widening procedures. C) is incorrect because loose external nostril tissue causing external valve collapse requires lateral wall stabilization with alar batten grafts or similar techniques. D) is incorrect because enlarged inferior turbinates require turbinate reduction procedures such as submucous resection or radiofrequency ablation, not valve grafting.

questions.question:
A medical facility wants to create an advertising campaign promoting botulinum toxin type A for treating facial wrinkles through their plastic surgery division. Which facial region would be most suitable to feature in this marketing effort?
A) Chin area
B) Periorbital lines
C) Forehead region
D) Glabellar area
E) Jawline
questions.answer:
D)
The glabellar area is the only FDA-approved location for botulinum toxin type A treatment that can be legally advertised. A is incorrect because the chin is not an FDA-approved treatment area for this indication. B is incorrect because periorbital lines (crow's feet) represent off-label use which cannot be marketed. C is incorrect because forehead treatment is considered off-label use and cannot be advertised. E is incorrect because jawline treatment is not an FDA-approved indication and cannot be promoted in marketing materials.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with facial eruption and stinging pain occurring 1 week following CO2 laser facial resurfacing treatment. Clinical examination reveals red pustular lesions distributed along the right facial V3 nerve territory. Which therapeutic option would be most suitable?
A) Oral acyclovir
B) Oral cephalexin
C) Oral prednisone
D) Topical bacitracin
E) Topical petrolatum
questions.answer:
A)
The patient's clinical presentation indicates herpes simplex virus reactivation. Following laser resurfacing procedures, viral, bacterial, and fungal infections commonly occur during the first postoperative week when tissue re-epithelialization takes place. HSV reactivation represents the most common infectious complication after resurfacing treatments. Direct laser tissue damage appears to trigger dormant viral activation and viral shedding. Despite prophylactic antiviral therapy, herpetic flares affect approximately 2-7% of laser-treated patients. Given the high prevalence of latent HSV, all patients undergoing full-face or perioral resurfacing should receive prophylactic oral antivirals to prevent viral reactivation and potential scarring. Post-laser HSV detection can be challenging due to absent intact epithelium, presenting as small superficial erosions rather than typical grouped vesicles. HSV reactivation symptoms include tingling, burning sensations, or discharge from specific foci in treated regions. Widespread eruptions may cause disseminated infection and atrophic scarring, requiring early recognition and aggressive treatment. Oral antivirals like acyclovir are standard therapy for HSV reactivation. B is incorrect because cephalexin treats bacterial rather than viral infections. C is incorrect because corticosteroids lack antiviral properties and may worsen viral infections. D is incorrect because bacitracin provides only antibacterial coverage without antiviral activity. E is incorrect because petrolatum is merely a protective emollient without therapeutic antiviral effects.

questions.question:
What most accurately characterizes the developmental source and migratory route of neural crest cells that participate in craniofacial bone development?
A) Endodermal cells originating from the primitive gut
B) Ectodermal cells traveling from the neural tube toward the pharyngeal arches
C) Mesodermal cells moving from somitic structures to the skull vault
D) Ectodermal cells moving straight to the upper jaw
E) Lateral plate mesenchymal tissue contributing exclusively to the lower jaw
questions.answer:
B)
Neural crest cells originate from the ectoderm and travel from the neural tube to populate the pharyngeal arches, where they play a major role in forming craniofacial bones, cartilage, and connective tissues. A is incorrect because endodermal tissue does not give rise to craniofacial skeletal structures. C is incorrect because while mesoderm does contribute to certain structures like muscles and parts of the cranial base, the majority of craniofacial bones originate from neural crest rather than somitic mesoderm. D is incorrect because neural crest cells do not migrate directly to the maxilla but rather populate the pharyngeal arches first. E is incorrect because lateral plate mesenchyme does not exclusively form the mandible and is not the primary source of craniofacial bones.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient with systemic lupus erythematosus needs free flap reconstruction for her right lower leg. She has no prior history of blood clots. She is currently taking corticosteroids for her connective tissue disorder. What perioperative approach is most suitable?
A) Anticoagulation during and after surgery
B) Anticoagulation during surgery only
C) Aspirin treatment before and after surgery
D) Preoperative evaluation for clotting disorders
E) Preoperative vitamin A supplementation
questions.answer:
E)
The correct answer is E. Chronic corticosteroids impair wound healing by suppressing inflammation, fibroblast proliferation, and collagen deposition. Perioperative vitamin A supplementation antagonizes those deleterious effects on wound healing without reversing the anti-inflammatory benefit of steroids, so it is the most suitable measure in this patient who is actively taking corticosteroids. She has no history of thrombosis, so a hypercoagulability workup and empiric anticoagulation are not the priority. A is incorrect because routine perioperative anticoagulation is not indicated in the absence of a clotting history or a documented hypercoagulable state and increases bleeding risk around a free flap. B is incorrect because intraoperative anticoagulation alone is likewise not indicated without a thrombotic history. C is incorrect because aspirin has not been shown to reduce free-flap failure rates and is not the indicated intervention for steroid-related wound-healing impairment. D is incorrect because preoperative evaluation for clotting disorders is driven by a personal or compelling history of thrombosis (or known antiphospholipid syndrome); this stem specifies no prior blood clots, so a clotting workup is not the most suitable next step compared with addressing ongoing steroid use.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient receives right breast reconstruction using a deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flap. Following surgery, the flap demonstrates ischemic changes requiring surgical re-exploration. During the salvage procedure, which medication should be given to block thromboxane activity?
A) Aspirin
B) Dextran
C) Heparin
D) Hirudin
E) Streptokinase
questions.answer:
A)
Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) blocks the cyclooxygenase enzyme, which normally converts arachidonic acid into various compounds including thromboxane and prostacyclin. Thromboxane promotes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, while prostacyclin also enhances platelet aggregation. By reducing the production of these substances, aspirin functions as an anticoagulant agent. B) is incorrect because dextran works by modifying platelet electrical charge and reducing blood viscosity rather than inhibiting thromboxane synthesis. C) is incorrect because heparin enhances antithrombin III activity to inactivate thrombin and clotting factors rather than blocking thromboxane. D) is incorrect because hirudin directly inhibits thrombin without affecting thromboxane production. E) is incorrect because streptokinase activates plasminogen to plasmin for fibrin breakdown rather than inhibiting thromboxane.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old male patient has undergone repair of a ventral hernia with abdominal wall reconstruction using component separation technique. On the fifth day after surgery, he develops a cough and his temperature rises to 39.0°C (102.2°F). A chest radiograph reveals pneumonia in the right middle lobe. Antibiotic treatment is started immediately. Despite receiving appropriate fluid replacement therapy, the patient becomes hypotensive with a mean arterial pressure below 65 mmHg. Which laboratory test would be most suitable to confirm the suspected diagnosis of septic shock?
A) Albumin
B) C-reactive protein
C) Lactate
D) Plasminogen
E) White blood cell count
questions.answer:
C)
Measuring serum lactate concentration is the most suitable laboratory test to confirm septic shock in this clinical situation. According to current guidelines, septic shock is diagnosed when patients meet both of the following criteria: requirement for vasopressor support to maintain mean arterial pressure at 65 mmHg or higher, and elevated serum lactate levels exceeding 2 mmol/L (>18 mg/dL) despite adequate volume resuscitation. The lactate level reflects tissue hypoperfusion and metabolic dysfunction characteristic of septic shock. A) Albumin is incorrect because while it may be decreased in sepsis due to increased vascular permeability and reduced synthesis, it is not a diagnostic criterion for septic shock. B) C-reactive protein is incorrect because although it indicates inflammation and infection, elevated CRP levels alone do not establish the diagnosis of septic shock. D) Plasminogen is incorrect because it is involved in the coagulation cascade and fibrinolysis but is not used as a diagnostic marker for septic shock. E) White blood cell count is incorrect because while abnormal WBC counts may suggest infection, they are part of the older SIRS criteria and not specific diagnostic markers for septic shock under current Sepsis-3 definitions.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old female patient is planned for autologous fat transfer to enhance the aesthetic appearance of the upper medial breast region.
