Extensive resection of radiated tissues with reconstruction using a thoracodorsal artery perforator flap is correct because radiation creates a hypoxic, poorly vascularized environment with compromised cellular function that requires complete removal of all damaged tissue and replacement with healthy, well-perfused tissue. The thoracodorsal artery perforator flap provides robust vascularized coverage that can adequately fill the axillary defect, and the thoracodorsal vessels should remain intact since they are typically preserved during axillary dissection. A is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen alone, while beneficial for radionecrosis, cannot heal such an extensive cavitary defect as monotherapy. B is incorrect because negative pressure therapy is contraindicated due to risk of vascular exposure and sponge retention in the tunneled wound. C is incorrect because skin grafts have high failure rates on irradiated beds and may expose vital neurovascular structures after debridement. D is incorrect because limited margin excision inadequately addresses the full zone of radiation injury, and acellular dermal matrix serves only as a temporary measure rather than definitive treatment for radiation ulcers.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female presents for abdominoplasty consultation requesting the lowest possible scar placement while avoiding a vertical midline incision. Examination reveals moderate upper and lower abdominal skin laxity with rectus diastasis. Her BMI is 27 kg/m2. During the planned abdominoplasty with diastasis repair, significant tension develops during lower central flap closure. Which of the following techniques would best reduce tension on the repair?
A) Making a 3-cm horizontal umbilical opening
B) Performing upper abdominal liposuction
C) Creating relaxing incisions in the external oblique fascia
D) Incising Scarpa's fascia down to the dermal layer
E) Implementing progressive tension sutures
questions.answer:
E)
Progressive tension sutures represent the optimal technique for reducing closure tension. These sutures connect Scarpa's fascia to the abdominal wall fascia, effectively eliminating dead space, reducing flap mobility, and decreasing seroma formation. By distributing tension progressively, these sutures significantly reduce final tension on the abdominal closure line, thereby minimizing healing complications. A) is incorrect because while a 3-cm transverse umbilical opening would reduce tension, it would create an aesthetically unacceptable umbilical appearance. B) is incorrect because upper abdominal liposuction, though feasible during abdominoplasty with proper perforator preservation, does not address skin tension reduction. C) is incorrect because external oblique fascial relaxing incisions are utilized in ventral hernia repair and do not reduce skin flap tension. D) is incorrect because scoring Scarpa's fascia to the dermis would compromise the subdermal vascular network that supplies the abdominal flap.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old male patient receives an elective right hand transplant 2 years following traumatic loss due to an industrial machinery injury. Following surgery, the patient is placed on immunosuppressive therapy to reduce rejection risk. For surveillance of cellular rejection during the postoperative phase, which tissue type should be primarily observed and biopsied?
A) Vascular tissue
B) Osseous tissue
C) Muscular tissue
D) Cutaneous tissue
E) Tendinous tissue
questions.answer:
D)
Cutaneous tissue (skin) represents the most appropriate tissue for monitoring cellular rejection in composite tissue allotransplantation. Skin demonstrates the highest antigenicity and immunoreactivity among transplanted tissues in hand transplantation procedures. Clinical experience has shown that acute rejection episodes primarily affect the skin while sparing deeper structures like vessels, bone, muscle, nerves, and tendons. Additionally, skin provides the most accessible and sensitive indicator of rejection since it can be readily visualized and assessed by both patients and clinicians, making it ideal for surveillance and biopsy procedures. A) Vascular tissue is incorrect because blood vessels are relatively spared during rejection episodes and are less accessible for routine monitoring. B) Osseous tissue is incorrect because bone shows minimal immunoreactivity and rejection rarely affects bony structures in hand transplants. C) Muscular tissue is incorrect because muscle tissue demonstrates lower antigenicity compared to skin and is not easily accessible for routine surveillance. E) Tendinous tissue is incorrect because tendons have low immunogenicity and are typically unaffected during rejection episodes.

questions.question:
A 6-month-old child presents to the clinic with an abnormal positioning of the head and restricted neck movement. On examination, there is a 3-cm palpable firm nodule located on the right side of the neck superior to the clavicle. Which of the following examination findings would most likely be present with this diagnosis?
A) Bending of the head toward the left shoulder
B) Neck flexion directed toward the left shoulder
C) Restricted lateral bending toward the left shoulder
D) Restricted lateral bending toward the right shoulder
E) Head rotation directed toward the right shoulder
questions.answer:
C)
This presentation is consistent with congenital muscular torticollis, which results from contracture of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. In right-sided torticollis, the affected muscle pulls the head and neck toward the right (ipsilateral) side while rotating the head toward the left (contralateral) side. This creates compensatory restriction in lateral flexion away from the affected side, meaning limited lateral flexion toward the left shoulder. A) is incorrect because the head flexes toward the ipsilateral (right) shoulder, not the left. B) is incorrect because neck flexion occurs toward the ipsilateral (right) shoulder. D) is incorrect because lateral flexion toward the affected (right) side is typically preserved or even excessive. E) is incorrect because head rotation occurs toward the contralateral (left) shoulder, not the right.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents to the clinic with a chronic non-healing ulcer that has persisted for 6 months following open reduction and internal fixation of an open ankle fracture. Physical examination reveals palpable pedal pulses and intact protective sensation in the foot. What is the most appropriate first step in treating this patient?
A) Use of collagenase-based topical treatment
B) Percutaneous bone biopsy for culture
C) Reconstruction with free tissue transfer
D) Surgical debridement
E) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment referral
questions.answer:
D)
Surgical debridement is the most appropriate initial step because this patient has a high likelihood of fracture nonunion and osteomyelitis given the persistent wound after hardware placement. Operative debridement, ideally performed with the orthopedic surgeon, allows for assessment of bone viability, thorough debridement, and consideration of hardware removal. A) is incorrect because topical collagenase treatment would not address the deeper tissue and bone concerns that are likely present. B) is incorrect because percutaneous bone cultures alone are insufficient and would not provide the comprehensive treatment needed. C) is incorrect because free flap reconstruction is premature without first addressing the underlying infection and non-viable tissue. E) is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen therapy lacks strong evidence for this clinical scenario and would not address the primary issues of infection and non-viable tissue.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old female presents for assessment of a growth on her right front thigh. She reports the growth has existed for several years and she often cuts it during leg shaving. She denies having other comparable growths and reports no family history of similar conditions. Clinical examination reveals a solitary, hard growth. The mass retracts when compressed from the sides. No additional abnormalities are observed. What is the most suitable next management approach?
A) Freezing treatment
B) Complete surgical removal with tissue analysis
C) Specialized microscopic surgery
D) Surface tissue sampling
E) Watchful waiting
questions.answer:
B)
The growth represents a dermatofibroma, a non-cancerous nodule originating from connective tissue and skin cells. Complete surgical removal with tissue analysis is the preferred treatment method to obtain definitive tissue diagnosis and ensure total lesion removal, since the growth extends into the deeper skin layers. Although this approach may result in scarring, it provides the most thorough treatment. A) Freezing treatment is incorrect because it cannot completely eliminate the lesion since it doesn't penetrate deeply enough. C) Specialized microscopic surgery is incorrect as it's not warranted for benign growths like dermatofibromas. D) Surface tissue sampling is incorrect because it typically doesn't reach deep enough into the skin to completely remove the pathology. E) Watchful waiting is incorrect in this case since the patient experiences significant inconvenience from repeatedly injuring the lesion, which prompted her to seek medical care.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents to the clinic with persistent tearing from his left eye that began 3 months following surgical repair of a deep laceration to the left medial canthus. Clinical examination reveals epiphora of the left eye. An undetected injury to the tear drainage system is suspected. Which of the following would be the most suitable test to assess the suspected injury?
A) Computed tomography scan
B) Jones test
C) Magnetic resonance imaging
D) Nasal endoscopy
E) Schirmer test
questions.answer:
B)
The Jones test is the most appropriate diagnostic tool for evaluating the drainage function of the lacrimal system. This test consists of two phases: the primary test involves placing fluorescein dye drops into the conjunctival sac and checking for dye appearance at the nasal opening within 3 minutes using a cotton applicator. If dye is present, the drainage system functions normally. The secondary test involves saline irrigation through the punctum to differentiate between functional and complete obstructions.

A) Computed tomography scan is incorrect because standard CT cannot visualize the lacrimal drainage system effectively unless performed as CT-dacryocystography, which is a specialized second-line test.

C) Magnetic resonance imaging is incorrect because MRI can only detect nasal cavity abnormalities and lacks the resolution to evaluate detailed drainage system pathology.

D) Nasal endoscopy is incorrect because it only examines the nasal cavity for structural abnormalities at the nasolacrimal duct opening and would be considered after Jones testing shows partial obstruction.

E) Schirmer test is incorrect because it measures tear production rather than drainage function, making it unsuitable for evaluating suspected drainage system injuries following trauma.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old female child comes to the office with academic struggles, articulation problems, and nasal speech quality. She has a medical history of immune system defects and low calcium levels. Physical examination reveals no visible or hidden cleft palate abnormalities. What is the most suitable initial management approach?
A) Comprehensive speech assessment
B) Magnetic resonance imaging
C) Palatal repair surgery
D) Watchful waiting
questions.answer:
A)
A comprehensive speech assessment is the most appropriate initial step. This patient presents with clinical features suggestive of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, including immune deficiencies, hypocalcemia, and speech abnormalities with hypernasality. Even without an obvious cleft palate, velopharyngeal dysfunction can occur and requires thorough evaluation at a specialized cleft center. The speech assessment will determine the nature and severity of the dysfunction and guide further diagnostic studies such as nasometry, pressure flow studies, videofluoroscopy, or nasopharyngoscopy if needed. B is incorrect because MRI is not the primary diagnostic tool for evaluating speech disorders and velopharyngeal function in this context. C is incorrect because palatoplasty would be premature without first establishing the specific type and cause of velopharyngeal dysfunction through proper assessment. D is incorrect because the combination of speech difficulties and other systemic features warrants active evaluation rather than observation alone.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old male presents with purulent discharge from his sternotomy incision accompanied by elevated white blood cell count, high-grade fever, and positive blood cultures growing Staphylococcus aureus 2 weeks following quintuple coronary bypass surgery utilizing bilateral internal mammary arteries. Past medical history is significant for diabetes mellitus type 2, elevated blood pressure, dyslipidemia, and COPD. He has a 40-year history of smoking one pack per day. His BMI is 32 kg/m2. Along with broad-spectrum antimicrobial treatment, what represents the most suitable initial approach for managing this complication?
A) Surgical debridement combined with vacuum-assisted closure therapy
B) Surgical debridement with pectoralis major turnover flap reconstruction
C) Surgical debridement with sternal plate fixation reconstruction
D) Surgical debridement followed by primary sternal rewiring and wound lavage
questions.answer:
A)
Surgical debridement combined with vacuum-assisted closure therapy is the optimal initial management because it provides effective wound preparation while serving as a bridge to definitive closure, with studies showing reduced morbidity, lower recurrent infection rates, and decreased treatment failure compared to immediate reconstruction methods in high-risk patients. B) is incorrect because bilateral internal mammary artery harvest compromises the blood supply to the pectoralis major muscle, making a turnover flap non-viable. C) is incorrect because immediate sternal plating in an infected wound carries high risk of hardware infection and treatment failure. D) is incorrect because primary rewiring in the setting of active infection has higher failure rates and increased morbidity compared to negative pressure wound therapy.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old male comes for assessment of a claw-like deformity affecting his right fourth and fifth digits. His past medical history reveals an untreated distal ulnar nerve lesion from 3 decades prior. What is the most probable underlying mechanism causing this patient's finger deformity?
A) Imbalanced abductor digiti minimi function
B) Imbalanced intrinsic muscles supplied by median and ulnar nerves
C) Compromised thenar muscle strength
D) Compromised ulnar-innervated extrinsic flexor function
E) Compromised ulnar-innervated intrinsic muscle function
questions.answer:
E)
The underlying mechanism involves paralysis of the interosseous muscles and the third and fourth lumbrical muscles, which are innervated by the ulnar nerve. Without these intrinsic muscles functioning, the long extensor tendons cause unopposed hyperextension at the metacarpophalangeal joints, while the long flexor tendons create unopposed flexion at the interphalangeal joints, resulting in the characteristic claw hand posture. A is incorrect because isolated abductor digiti minimi dysfunction would not create the full claw deformity pattern. B is incorrect because the deformity specifically results from ulnar nerve denervation, not an imbalance between median and ulnar innervated muscles. C is incorrect because thenar muscle weakness affects thumb function and would not cause ring and small finger clawing. D is incorrect because the extrinsic flexors (flexor digitorum profundus to digits 4-5) are actually contributing to the deformity through unopposed action, not weakness.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old woman in good health previously had Roux-en-Y gastric bypass 2 years ago, resulting in a 120-lb (54-kg) weight reduction maintained for 6 months. She presents for plastic surgery consultation regarding panniculectomy. Her medical background includes well-controlled hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. Preoperative cardiac assessment reveals normal findings, and pregnancy testing on the surgical day is negative. She proceeds with panniculectomy and thigh lift procedures. Upon awakening from anesthesia, she displays lethargy and mental confusion. Electrocardiogram demonstrates sinus tachycardia, with persistent drowsiness and disorientation. Laboratory evaluation of thyroid-stimulating hormone and cardiac markers, chest radiography, and ventilation-perfusion imaging are all within normal limits. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Acute thyroiditis
B) Diabetic ketosis
C) Pulmonary embolism
D) Undiagnosed pregnancy
E) Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency
questions.answer:
E)
Thiamine deficiency represents the most probable diagnosis in this post-bariatric surgery patient presenting with neurological symptoms. Thiamine stores typically last 3-6 weeks, and deficiency commonly occurs after gastric bypass procedures due to malabsorption and reduced intake. Approximately 11% of Roux-en-Y patients demonstrate thiamine deficiency at 2 years post-surgery despite supplementation. The neurological manifestations including confusion and lethargy are characteristic of thiamine deficiency, which can progress to Wernicke-Korsakoff encephalopathy if untreated, potentially causing irreversible neurological damage. A) Acute thyroiditis is incorrect because it typically presents with anterior neck pain and swelling, which are absent in this case. B) Diabetic ketosis is incorrect because it would present with dehydration, excessive thirst, polyuria, and Kussmaul respirations, none of which are described. C) Pulmonary embolism is incorrect because the ventilation-perfusion scan was normal and respiratory distress with right heart strain would be expected. D) Undiagnosed pregnancy is incorrect because the pregnancy test was negative and early pregnancy typically causes nausea rather than confusion and lethargy.

questions.question:
A 2-week-old female newborn presents for assessment of a noticeable ear malformation. What is the most suitable initial treatment approach for managing this malformation?
A) Cartilage transplantation
B) Non-surgical shaping
C) Hyaluronidase administration
D) Surgical ear correction
E) Observation without treatment
questions.answer:
B)
Non-surgical shaping represents the preferred initial treatment for a noticeable ear malformation. Optimally, this intervention should begin within 2 weeks of birth, though benefits have been observed in infants up to 3 months old and remains worthwhile to attempt. A) is incorrect because cartilage transplantation is not indicated as first-line therapy for neonatal ear deformities. C) is incorrect because hyaluronidase administration remains experimental and is not standard early management. D) is incorrect because surgical ear correction is typically reserved for cases where non-surgical methods fail and is usually performed around 6 years of age. E) is incorrect because early intervention with molding is more effective than waiting, as the ear cartilage becomes less malleable with time.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old male with right-hand dominance arrives with a right distal radius fracture sustained from falling onto an extended hand. He describes worsening pain and tingling sensations in his right hand and digits. Capillary refill distally remains under 2 seconds, radial and ulnar pulses are easily felt, however the patient experiences intense pain during passive finger extension. Acute compartment syndrome is being considered. Which compartment would most likely demonstrate the highest measured pressures in this scenario?
A) Deep volar
B) Dorsal
C) Lateral
D) Superficial volar
questions.answer:
A)
Compartment syndrome represents a serious condition where hemorrhage and/or swelling within a fascially-bound muscle compartment creates elevated pressures that compromise circulation and can cause muscle necrosis. Complications include functional loss, Volkmann contracture, and potential amputation. The hallmark presentation includes disproportionate pain relative to examination findings, along with worsening pain during passive stretching of muscles in the involved compartment. Vascular compromise typically occurs later in the disease process. This condition frequently accompanies traumatic fractures.

Distal radius fractures represent the leading cause of forearm compartment syndrome. The forearm contains four distinct compartments: dorsal, lateral (mobile wad), superficial volar, and deep volar. Following traumatic distal radius fractures, the deep volar compartment typically develops the most elevated interstitial pressures in early acute compartment syndrome. This compartment contains the flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus muscles, which are most susceptible to damage from untreated compartment syndrome and control distal interphalangeal flexion of the fingers and thumb interphalangeal flexion respectively. B is incorrect because the dorsal compartment is less commonly affected with the highest pressures in distal radius fractures. C is incorrect because the lateral compartment typically has lower pressure elevations compared to the deep volar compartment. D is incorrect because the superficial volar compartment, while it can be involved, does not typically reach the highest pressures seen in the deep volar compartment.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old female patient with rheumatoid arthritis in her medical history presents with painless inability to extend her thumb and fingers on the left hand. During attempted wrist extension, her wrist shifts toward the radial side while extending actively. When the examiner passively flexes her wrist, her thumb and fingers are able to extend. What most likely explains this patient's functional impairment?
A) Dorsal ulnar prominence; multiple extensor tendon ruptures
B) Ligament loosening; metacarpophalangeal joint subluxations
C) Synovial proliferation at the radiocapitellar joint; posterior interosseous nerve compression
D) Scaphoid bone spur; flexor pollicis longus muscle rupture
E) Extensor hood weakening; extensor tendon dislocation
questions.answer:
C)
This patient exhibits posterior interosseous nerve (PIN) syndrome. She demonstrates absent active thumb and finger extension while preserving active wrist extension with radial deviation. Synovial proliferation from rheumatoid arthritis affecting the radiocapitellar joint or radial tunnel typically causes compression at the proximal forearm level. The PIN provides motor innervation to multiple extensors but spares the extensor carpi radialis longus (innervated by the main radial nerve), explaining preserved wrist extension with radial deviation. A is incorrect because multiple extensor tendon ruptures would not show intact extension during tenodesis testing (passive wrist flexion causing finger extension). B is incorrect because metacarpophalangeal joint subluxation would not produce intact tenodesis examination findings and would not affect the specific pattern of wrist extension with radial deviation. D is incorrect because flexor pollicis longus rupture (Mannerfelt lesion) would affect thumb flexion at the interphalangeal joint, not extension. E is incorrect because extensor hood weakening with tendon subluxation would not impact wrist extension and would show different clinical findings at the metacarpophalangeal joint level.

questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman presents to the clinic for planned debulking of a free flap on her forearm 6 months following successful sarcoma reconstruction surgery. While performing the procedure, a surgical clamp left behind from the original operation is discovered. The retained clamp caused no adverse effects on the patient's recovery or the necessity for the current surgery. What is the most appropriate action to take?
A) Only inform the patient since risk management notification is unnecessary due to absence of harm
B) No action is needed since there was no injury or departure from standard care
C) Contact the risk management department and inform the patient
D) Only notify the risk management department since patient notification is unnecessary due to absence of harm
questions.answer:
C)
The correct action is to both notify risk management and inform the patient. Retained foreign bodies after surgery represent a significant patient safety event that requires full disclosure and institutional reporting regardless of whether harm occurred. Open communication with patients about such incidents is crucial and often prevents these situations from escalating to malpractice claims. The doctrine of res ipsa loquitur applies to retained foreign bodies, making negligence legally presumed. Hospital risk management must also be notified to ensure proper documentation, investigation, and implementation of preventive measures. A) is incorrect because risk management notification is required for retained foreign bodies regardless of harm. B) is incorrect because retained foreign bodies constitute a departure from standard care and require action even without injury. D) is incorrect because patient notification is ethically and legally required when foreign objects are discovered, regardless of harm.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man with a fracture of the mandibular angle is evaluated for open reduction and internal fixation. Which of the following is the most appropriate location for placement of internal fixation when using the Champy technique in this patient?


A) External oblique ridge
B) Lingula
C) Mandibular notch
D) Mental tubercle
E) Mylohyoid line
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


This technique for internal fixation of mandibular angle fractures was first described by Michelet in 1972, and biomechanical studies by Champy et al were published in 1976. In his original paper, Champy advocated placement of an internal fixation miniplate along the external oblique line of the mandible. By contouring the plate to this line, rigid fixation is achieved in two planes, taking advantage of the force vectors along the angle of the mandible to help compress the fracture site.










Mylohyoid line is not appropriate because the mylohyoid line is located along the lingual surface of the mandibular body and is not used routinely as a location for plate fixation for mandibular fractures.


Lingula is not appropriate because the lingula is located along the lingual surface of the mandibular ramus, and is the location where the mandibular nerve (V3) enters the mandible. Plate fixation should be avoided in this area because of the difficulty of exposure and the risk for damaging the mandibular nerve.


Mental tubercle is not appropriate because the mental tubercle is not an appropriate place to apply internal fixation when utilizing the Champy technique.


Mandibular notch is not appropriate because it is located between the mandibular condyle and the coronoid process and is not an appropriate place to apply internal fixation when utilizing the Champy technique.


References
Gear AJ, Apasova E, Schmitz JP, et al. Treatment modalities for mandibular angle fractures. J Oral Maxillofac Surg. 2005 May;63(5):655-663.
Laverick S, Siddappa P, Wong H, et al. Intraoral external oblique ridge compared with transbuccal lateral cortical plate fixation for the treatment of fractures of the mandibular angle: prospective randomised trial. Br J Oral Maxillofac Surg. 2012 Jun;50(4):344-349. Epub 2012 Mar 14.
Turgut G, Kayali MU, Soydan AT, et al. Biomechanical comparison of a new technique of mandibular angle fractures: biplanar and bicortical superior proximal 3 holes and bicortical inferior plate fixation. J Craniofac Surg. 2008 Mar;19(2):428-432.

questions.question:
Which of the following is the beneficial effect of pretreatment with tretinoin prior to facial chemical peel and laser resurfacing?


A) Decreased epidermal proliferation
B) Decreased fibroblast deposition of glycosaminoglycans
C) Increased collagen IV deposition
D) Increased epidermal melanin
E) Increased transit rate of keratinocytes through the epidermis
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Tretinoin has long been established as a topical treatment that can improve photoaged skin by decreasing pigmentation and fine and coarse wrinkles. This is accomplished via activation of retinoic acid receptors and other not yet well-characterized molecular mechanisms. Epidermal hyperproliferation is induced, which results in a normalization of epidermal disarray and thickening of the epidermis. Additionally, fibroblast deposition of collagen and glycosaminoglycans is stimulated, increasing skin turgor and elasticity. The breakdown of collagen is reduced via the reduction of collagenase and promotion of collagenase inhibitors. Epidermal melanin is reduced because of the stable rate of melanin transfer from melanocytes to keratinocytes, whereas the transit rate of keratinocytes through the epidermis is increased.


References
1. Pannucci CJ, Reavey PL, Kaweski S, et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial of Skin Care Protocols for Facial Resurfacing: Lessons Learned from the Plastic Surgery Educational Foundation's Skin Products Assessment Research Study. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2011 Mar;127(3):1334-1342.
2. Matarasso SL, Grossman K. Science of skin care. Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head and Neck Surg. 2002 Aug;10(4):292-296.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old woman comes to the office for large-volume liposuction of the abdomen, back, hips, and thighs. She has no history of medical issues. Tumescent liposuction using an infiltrate that contains lidocaine is performed. Thirty minutes into the procedure, the patient is noted to have tremors and a seizure. Several minutes later, the anesthesiologist states that the patient has a ventricular arrhythmia. Administration of which of the following agents is most appropriate for this patient?


A) Dantrolene
B) Flumazenil
C) Lipid emulsion
D) Naloxone
E) Steroids
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The patient is experiencing local anesthetic systemic toxicity related to the lidocaine infiltration. Patients experience nervous system effects and can progress to cardiovascular effects. Early findings associated with lidocaine toxicity include perioral numbness, metallic taste, anxiety, muscle twitching, and seizures. Cardiovascular findings can include tachycardia and hypertension that can progress to ventricular arrhythmias and, ultimately, asystole.


Treatment of lidocaine toxicity includes advanced cardiac life support and administration of a bolus of 20% lipid emulsion.


Dantrolene is used for the treatment of malignant hypothermia. Flumazenil is used as an antidote for benzodiazepine overdose. Naloxone, an opioid antagonist, is used to treat an overdose due to opioids. Corticosteroids have been proposed along with supportive therapy for the treatment of fat embolism.
ReferencesHolt NF. Tumescent anaesthesia: its applications and well tolerated use in the out-of-operating room setting. Curr Opin Anaesthesiol. 2017;30(4):518-524.Man D, Podichetty VK. Lipid rescue in resuscitation of local anesthetic-induced cardiac arrest in aesthetic surgery. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2010;125(6):257e-9e.Sekimoto K, Tobe M, Saito S. Local anesthetic toxicity: acute and chronic management. Acute Med Surg. 2017;4(2):152-160.Stephan PJ, Dauwe P, Kenkel J. Liposuction: a comprehensive review of techniques and safety. In: Neligan PC, ed. Plastic Surgery. London: Elsevier: 2018;2:545-567.Warren K, Pak A. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity. UpToDate. https://www.uptodate.com/contents/local-anesthetic-systemic-toxicity. Updated on Jul 26, 2018. Accessed Jan 9, 2019.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old automobile mechanic comes to the office because of a 3-week history of localized pain in the fingers of the dominant right hand. He does not smoke cigarettes. He says the pain occurs intermittently and that he has no symptoms anywhere else in the body. Examination shows scattered, punctate, dark petechiae at the tips of the ring and little fingers. Rubor progressing from the distal interphalangeal joints to the tips of the ring and little fingers is noted. An additional bounding pulse is palpable in the proximal ulnar palm. Radial and ulnar pulses at the wrist are normal. Digital Allen tests show decreased flow at the ring and little fingers and the ulnar aspect of the long finger. Plain x-ray studies show no abnormalities. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?


A) Buerger disease
B) Congenital vasospastic disease
C) Distal embolization from the heart
D) Hypothenar hammer syndrome
E) Raynaud disease
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.






This is a classic presentation for the patient who develops an ulnar artery aneurysm at Guyon canal. The aneurysm typically is the source of small emboli that tend to affect vessels at the ulnar aspect of the hand and fingers. The emboli cause decreased flow, cold sensitivity, ischemic pain and rubor in the small and ring fingers most commonly. This problem occurs most often in men in their 40s, who suffer repetitive blunt trauma to the hand. Some use their hand as a hammer at work. Other forms of blunt trauma have been linked to this problem, including certain sports and weight lifting. The treatment options include oral medications for vasodilation, cessation of the offending physical activity, smoking cessation if present, sympathectomy, thrombolytics, and either exclusion of the aneurysm and ulnar artery ligation in the palm, or aneurysm excision and vascular reconstruction.


Raynaud disease is not the best answer because this presentation with embolic disease localized to the ulnar fingers and the palpable pulse/mass (aneurysm) in the hand are not consistent with Raynaud disease. Patients with Raynaud disease typically present complaining of cold sensitivity, periods of finger blanching, followed by diffuse return of flow to the fingers and pain. Raynaud disease is a diffuse sympathetic problem, not a local aneurysmal problem.


Congenital vasospastic disease is not the best answer because the patient in this vignette has no symptoms prior to 3 weeks ago. A congenital vasospastic problem would have presented before, and would be unlikely to be so localized.


Distal embolization from the heart is wrong for similar reasons: emboli from the heart would be very unlikely to present unilaterally, in two fingers, adjacent to one another. There would very likely be other symptoms and sites of embolization.


Buerger disease is not the best answer for a few reasons. The patient in this vignette is a nonsmoker. Thromboangiitis obliterans (TAO), or Buerger disease, is an inflammatory arteritis seen in smokers. It improves or stops progressing with smoking cessation. Buerger disease does not typically present with such isolated symptoms, and can involve the lower extremities as well.


References
1. Koman LA, Smith BP, Smith TL, et al. Vascular disorders. In: Wolfe SW, Hotchkiss RN, Pederson WC, et al, eds. Green‚Äos Operative Hand Surgery. 6th ed. Philadelphia: Churchill Livingstone; 2011:2197-2240.
2. Koman LA, Urbaniak JR. Ulnar artery insufficiency: a guide to treatment. J Hand Surg Am. 1981 Jan;6(1):16-24.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man has a biopsy-confirmed squamous cell carcinoma of the upper eyelid. Excision of the lesion will produce a full-thickness defect of the central upper eyelid that is 70% of its width. Reconstruction of the defect with which of the following is most appropriate?


A) Cutler-Beard flap
B) Full-thickness skin graft
C) Hughes flap
D) Primary closure
E) Tenzel flap
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


The Cutler-Beard flap is the preferred flap for full-thickness defects of the upper eyelid that are greater than 66% of total eyelid width. This technique utilizes a full-thickness eyelid flap from the lower eyelid to provide a wide flap for eye coverage. In the first stage, the flap is raised and advanced into the upper eyelid defect. The flap is then inset, covering the eye. The inferior pedicle is divided in a second stage at 4 to 6 weeks and final flap inset is performed.





The Tenzel semicircular flap is an excellent technique for anterior lamellar defects of the upper or lower lid, but requires a second flap for posterior lamella reconstruction of full-thickness defects and is not generally the preferred technique for a large defect of the upper eyelid.


The Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap is a similar procedure to the Cutler-Beard flap, but is used for lower lid defects.


Full-thickness skin grafting would not restore the posterior lamellar defect, and direct closure would not likely be able to close a 70% defect of the upper eyelid properly.


References
Espinoza GM, Prost AM. Upper Eyelid Reconstruction. Facial Plas Surg Clin North Am. 2016 May; 24(2):173-82.
McCord CD, Codner MA. Upper Eyelid Reconstruction. In: Eyelid and Periorbital Surgery. Quality Medical Publishing, St. Louis, 2008:509-41.

questions.question:
Which of the following structures arises from the lateral nasal processes during embryologic development?


A) Columella
B) Nasal ala
C) Nasal septum
D) Nasal tip
E) Premaxilla
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


The nasal structures form during the sixth week of gestation. The nasal pits form the nasal placodes. These eventually deepen as a result of the formation of the medial and lateral nasal prominences. The external nasal structures appear as the medial nasal processes (MNP) enlarge and coalesce in the midline. Failure of this normal process can result in nasal deformities such as those seen in the cleft nasal deformity. The frontonasal process (FNP) forms above the nasal placode, while the lateral nasal processes (LNP) remain outside and lateral to the nasal placode. Fusion of the medial nasal, lateral nasal, and maxillary prominences produces the continuity between the nose, upper lip, and palate.


The MNP give rise to the nasal tip, columella, philtrum, and premaxilla. The nasal septum is a downgrowth from the merged medial nasal prominences. The forehead, the bridge of the nose, and the root of the nose come from the FNP. The nasal alae are derived from the LNP.


References
Gosain AK, Moore F. Embryology of the head and neck. In: Aston SJ, Beasley RW, Thorne CH, et al, eds. Grabb and Smith‚Äos Plastic Surgery. 5th ed. Philadelphia: Lippincott-Raven; 1997:223-236.
Johnston MC, Bronsky PT, Millicovsky G. Embryogenesis of cleft lip and palate. In: McCarthy JG, ed. Plastic Surgery. Philadelphia: WB Saunders; 1990:2451-2495.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman comes to the office to discuss aesthetic improvement of the lower eyelids. Physical examination shows lower eyelid pseudoherniation of fat and fine skin wrinkles. A postseptal transconjunctival approach with skin pinch excision is considered. The most significant advantage of this approach compared with a transcutaneous skin-muscle flap is a lower risk of which of the following complications?


A) Capsulopalpebral fascia injury
B) Corneal injury
C) Hematoma
D) Infection
E) Lid malposition
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Transconjunctival blepharoplasty preserves the middle lamella, which includes the orbicularis oculi muscle. Preserving this layer significantly decreases the incidence of ectropion and lower eyelid malposition. Disadvantages of this technique include more difficulty with visualization and access. Many authors believe that a cutaneous skin muscle approach is more effective in blending the lid-cheek junction and transposing fat.


Some studies have shown minor reductions in hematoma and infection rates with the transconjunctival approach; however, the differences are small and not the most significant advantage.


The potential for corneal injury is greater with the transconjunctival approach. Most surgeons use corneal shields to prevent this complication.


The capsule palpebral fascia is routinely cut to access the fat compartments during a transconjunctival blepharoplasty.


References
1. Pacella SJ, Nahai FR, Nahai F. Transconjunctival blepharoplasty for upper and lower eyelids. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2010 Jan;125(1):384-392.
2. Drolet BC, Sullivan PK. Evidence-based medicine: Blepharoplasty. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2014 May;133(5):1195-1205.
3. Sadove RC. Transconjunctival septal suture repair for lower lid blepharoplasty. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2007 Aug;120(2):521-529.
4. Lelli GJ Jr, Lisman RD. Blepharoplasty complications. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2010 Mar;125(3):1007-1017.

questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of wound separation. History includes immediate prepectoral breast reconstruction with placement of left tissue expander, and she is currently undergoing radiation therapy. Physical examination shows an approximately 0.5-cm area of incisional dehiscence with exposure of the device. Vital signs are stable, and inflammatory markers are mildly elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?


A) Admit the patient for intravenous antibiotic therapy and monitor the wound
B) Apply occlusive dressing and discharge the patient on oral antibiotic therapy
C ) Close the wound at bedside in the emergency department and discharge the patient on oral antibiotic therapy
D) Perform expander removal in the operating room
E) Perform operative replacement of the expander
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


Studies have shown that postmastectomy radiation therapy almost doubles the risk of complications, including wound breakdown. While attempts at implant salvage are tempting, they are often ultimately unsuccessful and may potentially delay necessary radiation treatments. Therefore, in the event of implant exposure during adjuvant therapy, the device should be removed and the mastectomy pocket closed over a surgical drain. This strategy will allow for the shortest delay in further oncologic treatments and does not preclude reconstruction at a later date. Closure of the wound over an exposed device should not be attempted, as any exposed device is assumed to be colonized, if not grossly infected. Although antibiotics may temporize the infectious process, it is unlikely that successful wound healing and retention of the prosthesis will occur after suppressive antimicrobials are stopped.


ReferencesAdkinson JM, Miller NF, Eid SM, Miles MG, Murphy RX Jr. Tissue Expander Complications Predict Permanent Implant Complications and Failure of Breast Reconstruction. Ann Plast Surg. 2015;75(1):24-8.Kearney AM, Brown MS, Soltanian HT. Timing of radiation and outcomes in implant-based breast reconstruction. J Plast Reconstr Aesthet Surg. 2015;68(12):1719-26.Lam TC, Borotkanics R, Hsieh F, Salinas J, Boyages J. Immediate Two-Stage Prosthetic Breast Reconstruction Failure: Radiation Is Not the Only Culprit. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2018;141(6):1315-1324.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old girl is evaluated because of a rapidly enlarging mass in the left forearm that her parents first noticed 6 months ago. Physical examination shows a 3-cm firm mass in the volar aspect of the left forearm. Passive extension of the fingers and wrist elicits pain. MRI shows a mass within the deep forearm compartment suggestive of a vascular lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in treatment?


A ) Application of a compression garment
B ) En bloc surgical resection
C ) Oral administration of prednisone
D ) Percutaneous sclerotherapy
E ) Pulsed-dye laser therapy
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


This rapidly growing vascular lesion, not present at birth, most likely represents an intramuscular hemangioma. These vascular anomalies can pose diagnostic challenges because of their depth and lack of cutaneous changes characteristic of the more common infantile hemangioma. The treatment algorithm, however, parallels that of other hemangiomas. In this case, the first line of therapy would be medical treatment with either propranolol or corticosteroids.


Compression garments may be useful in managing arteriovenous or lymphatic malformations of the extremities. In this patient, with pain caused by increased intracompartmental volume, compression may exacerbate the symptoms.


En bloc surgical resection is reserved for lesions that fail to respond to medical management or that compromise function. In the case of upper extremity lesions, this would be indicated most commonly for refractory pain or nerve compression.


Percutaneous sclerotherapy can successfully treat low-flow arteriovenous malformations and lymphatic malformations. It would not be a first-line intervention for hemangioma.


Cutaneous arteriovenous malformations may be treated with pulsed-dye laser or other light-based therapies. Deep, intramuscular lesions without a cutaneous component will not be reached by these interventions.


References
1. Buckmiller LM, Munson PD, Dyamenahalli U, et al. Propranolol for infantile hemangiomas: early experience at a tertiary vascular anomalies center. Laryngoscope. 2010 Apr;120(4):676-681.
2. Muramatsu K, Ihara K, Tani Y, et al. Intramuscular hemangioma of the upper extremity in infants and children. J Pediatr Orthop. 2008 Apr-May;28(3):387-390.
3. Jacobs BJ, Anzarut A, Guerra S, et al. Vascular anomalies of the upper extremity. J Hand Surg Am. 2010 Oct;35(10):1703-1709.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old man presents for reconstruction of a soft tissue deficit of the antecubital fossa with a reverse lateral arm pedicled flap. Which of the following arteries is the blood supply for this flap?


A) Anterior interosseous
B) Persistent median
C) Posterior interosseous
D) Radial recurrent
E) Ulnar
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


Although the lateral arm flap has predominantly been used in free tissue transfer for distant defects based on the posterior radial collateral artery, transfer as a pedicled reverse-flow flap based on the radial recurrent artery has been both anatomically and clinically proven. Occasionally, it is performed with a delay procedure at an intermediate stage.


The anterior and posterior interosseous arteries can provide circulation to perforator flaps. The ulnar artery has been occasionally used for an ulnar artery based fasciocutaneous flap. The persistent median artery passes through the carpal tunnel and runs with the median nerve.


ReferencesMorrison CS, Sullivan SR, Bhatt RA, Chang JT, Taylor HO. The pedicled reverse-flow lateral arm flap for coverage of complex traumatic elbow injuries. Ann Plast Surg. 2013 Jul;71(1):37-39.Hamdi M, Coessens BC. Distally planned lateral arm flap. Microsurgery. 1996;17(7):375-379.Heidekrueger PI, Mueller C, Thiha A, Ehrl D, Weinschenk F, Herter F, Ninkovic M, Prantl L. The lateral arm flap for reconstruction of tissue defects due to olecranon bursitis. J Plast Surg. 2018 Sep 4:1-5.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman has a draining sinus tract at the lower chest 2 weeks after undergoing a cardiac bypass procedure. After extensive debridement, there is a large central defect requiring an omental flap for obliteration of the dead space. Which of the following arteries supplies the omental flap?


A) Gastroduodenal
B) Gastroepiploic
C) Left gastric
D) Superior epigastric
E) Superior mesenteric
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


The blood supply to the omental flap is through the right and left gastroepiploic arteries.


Understanding the anatomy and blood supply to the omentum is crucial for success in omental flap transfer. The greater omentum is harvested from the transverse colon, as the short gastric vessels are ligated and the gastroepiploic vessels preserved. The omentum can be transposed to the chest through either an opening in the diaphragm or a fascial defect in the abdominal wall.


The left gastric vessels arise from the celiac vessels and supply the lesser curvature of the stomach. The gastroduodenal artery arises from the celiac trunk and provides blood supply to the pylorus and proximal duodenum. One of the terminal branches of the gastroduodenal artery is the right gastroepiploic artery. The superior epigastric artery supplies the rectus abdominis muscle and is not intraperitoneal. The superior mesenteric artery arises from the aorta below the celiac trunk and supplies the lower duodenum through the transverse colon; it does not carry the blood supply necessary for design of an omental flap.


References
1. Hultman CS, Carlson GW, Losken A, et al. Utility of the omentum in the reconstruction of complex extraperitoneal wounds and defects: donor-site complications in 135 patients from 1975 to 2000. Ann Surg. 2002 Jun;235(6):782-795.
2. Ghazi BH, Carlson GW, Losken A. Use of the greater omentum for reconstruction of infected sternotomy wounds: a prognostic indicator. Ann Plast Surg. 2008 Feb;60(2):169-173.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old primigravid woman is referred to the office because ultrasonography showed polyhydramnios at 22 weeks' gestation. Additionally, the fetus was observed to have macrosomia, omphalocele, macroglossia, and microtia. There is no evidence of nephromegaly or hepatomegaly. A groove between the lobule and antitragus is noted. Chromosomal analysis indicates rearrangements on chromosome 11p15. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?


A) Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
B) Binder syndrome
C) Diabetic fetopathy
D) Down syndrome
E) van der Woude syndrome
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


This is a rare overgrowth disorder involving genetic defect of chromosome 11, commonly characterized by the presence of macrosomia, omphalocele, and macroglossia. These symptoms typically present after 22 weeks' gestation. Additionally, infants with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome often display auricular abnormalities, including characteristic ear folds.


While a common symptom of diabetic fetopathy is macrosomia, a diagnosis of diabetic fetopathy would be incorrect. Common symptoms of diabetic fetopathy include congenital anomalies of the internal organs, such as nephromegaly or hepatomegaly; no such symptoms are detected in this fetus.


The absence of cleft lip and/or cleft palate nephromegaly also precludes the diagnosis of van der Woude syndrome. Additionally, the genetic abnormality responsible for van der Woude syndrome involves chromosome 1, not chromosome 11. Likewise, trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) is not the correct diagnosis, as the chromosomal abnormality responsible for this disease involves chromosome 21, not chromosome 11.


Finally, Binder syndrome is a congenital facial malformation most commonly characterized by a flat nose and retrusion of the midface, neither of which are observed in this fetus. Therefore, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is the correct answer.


References
1. Cohen MM Jr. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome: historical, clinicopathological, and etiopathogenic perspectives. Pediatr Dev Pathol. 2005 May-Jun;8(3):287-304. Epub 2005 Jul 14.
2. Demars J, Gicquel C. Epigenetic and genetic disturbance of the imprinted 11p15 region in Beckwith-Wiedemann and Silver Russell syndromes. Clin Genet. 2012 Apr;81(4):350-361. Epub 2012 Jan 16.
3. Weksberg R, Shuman C, Smith AC. Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Am J Med Genet C Semin Med Genet. 2005 Aug 15;137C(1):12-23.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man comes to the office because of a palpable mass of the right dorsoradial distal forearm. The patient reports that the mass has been growing slowly over the past 2 years. On examination, the mass is nontender. Excisional biopsy shows the mass is well encapsulated and separates easily from within the fibers of the dorsoradial sensory nerve, as the nerve emerges from beneath the brachioradialis tendon. Which of the following cells is the most likely origin of this mass?


A) Adipose
B) Giant
C) Glial
D) Spindle
E) Tendon
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The mass is most consistent with a neurilemmoma or Schwann cell tumor. These are benign, encapsulated tumors of the nerve sheath. Their cells of origin are glial, likely Schwann cells. These masses usually arise from the side of or from within the nerve. Symptoms can be vague and manifest as a dull ache or as symptoms consistent with nerve compression.


A lipoma derives from adipose cells, but these generally do not originate from the substance of the nerve. Tumors consisting of tenocytes are essentially unheard of, but giant cell tumors originate from the tendon sheath and are usually intimately involved with the tendon sheath and thus unlikely to be found within the fibers of a nerve.


Pathology of spindle cells which form muscle, are usually seen in the setting of sarcoma or carcinoma. In general, they are usually found in a subcutaneous, peritendinous, and intramuscular plane. They are taken with margins and are unlikely to shell cleanly out of their soft tissue of origin.


References
Kang HJ, Shin SJ, Kang ES. Schwannomas of the upper extremity. J Hand Surg Br. 2000;25:604-7.
Knight DM, Birch R, Pringle J. Benign solitary schwannomas: a review of 234 cases. J Bone Joint Surg Br. 2007 Mar;89(3):382-7.
Ozdemir, O., et al. Schwannomas of the hand and wrist: long-term results and review of the literature. J Orthop Surg (Hong Kong). 2005 Dec;13(3):267-72.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male construction worker is evaluated for weakness of grip and pinch with inability to touch index finger to thumb. The patient is referred from a neurologist with a diagnosis of anterior interosseous nerve syndrome. Which of the following muscles is most likely to be spared?


A) Flexor digitorum profundus to index
B) Flexor digitorum profundus to middle
C) Flexor pollicis longus
D) Pronator quadratus
E) Pronator teres
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


The pronator teres is innervated by the median nerve prior to its take off of the anterior interosseous nerve (AIN), which is why it cannot be affected by AIN syndrome. Pronation generated by the pronator teres or the pronator quadratus would be indistinguishable clinically. The AIN is a terminal branch off the median nerve that innervates the FDP to the index and middle fingers, FPL and pronator quadratus. The AIN arises from the median nerve approximately 4 to 6 cm distal to the medial epicondyle. It travels between the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) initially, and then between the FPL and FDP. Then it lies on the volar surface of the interosseous membrane and travels with the anterior interosseous artery, terminating in the pronator quadratus and then the wrist joint capsule and the intercarpal, radiocarpal, and radioulnar joints. The nerve originates from C5-T12, becoming the medial and lateral cords of the brachial plexus and then becoming the median nerve.


References
Maldonado AA, Amrami KK, Mauermann ML, Spinner RJ. Reinterpretation of Electrodiagnostic Studies and Magnetic Resonance Imaging Scans in Patients with Nontraumatic ‚ÄuIsolated‚Äu Anterior Interosseous Nerve Palsy. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2016 Nov;138(5):1033-1039.
Chi Y, Harness NG. Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome. J Hand Surg Am. 2010;35:2078‚Äi2080.
Rodner, Tinsley, O'Malley. Pronator syndrome and anterior interosseous nerve syndrome. J Am Acad Orthop Surg. 2013;21:268-75.
Aljawder A, Alkalifa M. Anterior interosseous nerve syndrome and intraoperative findings: a case report. Int J Surg Case Rep. 2016; 21:44‚Äi47.

questions.question:
A 57-year-old right-handed woman with rheumatoid arthritis complains of severe 10/10 right thumb pain that prevents her from painting, which is her main hobby. Radiographic imaging reveals rheumatoid changes across multiple joints, with the right thumb carpometacarpal (CMC) joint showing Eaton stage 3-4 pathology. Physical examination demonstrates prominence of the right thumb metacarpal base with a positive grind test. Which of the following represents the most suitable treatment approach to enable this patient to return to her usual activities?
A) CMC joint arthrodesis of the thumb
B) Thumb CMC joint pyrocarbon implant arthroplasty
C) Rheumatology consultation for infliximab therapy
D) Conservative treatment with splinting, rest, and ibuprofen 800 mg three times daily
E) Trapeziectomy combined with ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition
questions.answer:
E)
The patient has advanced thumb carpometacarpal joint arthritis that significantly impairs her daily activities. Trapeziectomy with ligament reconstruction and tendon interposition is optimal for this patient because she has severe CMC disease and requires functional restoration with preserved mobility rather than maximum strength, making this procedure ideal for her fine motor painting activities. A) Arthrodesis would eliminate pain but severely limit thumb mobility, compromising her ability to hold a paintbrush and perform delicate movements. B) Pyrocarbon implants are designed for osteoarthritis patients and lack the soft-tissue stability needed for rheumatoid arthritis. C) Infliximab carries significant systemic risks including infections and malignancy that are not justified for predominantly single-joint disease. D) Conservative management may provide temporary relief but will not achieve the functional improvement necessary for her to resume painting activities.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old man undergoes wide local excision of a squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip. Margins are free of involvement. A photograph of the resulting defect is shown. Reconstruction using which of the following flaps is most appropriate in this patient?


A) Estlander
B) Facial artery myomucosal
C) Karapandzic
D) Melolabial
E) Submental artery island
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


Karapandzic flaps are appropriate for reconstruction of defects involving one to two thirds of the lower lip, such as the one in this patient. The Karapandzic technique involves performing circumoral incisions and mobilizing the orbicularis oris muscle, while preserving its innervations and vascular supply. The main advantage of this technique is that a continuous sphincter of functional orbicularis muscle is created, helping to restore oral competence.


The Estlander flap is a full-thickness, cross-lip transposition flap designed to reconstruct lateral defects of the lower lip (one to two thirds) requiring recreation of the oral commissure.


Mesolabial flaps can be used to reconstruct large full-thickness lower lip defects. However, they require grafting of the deep surface of the flap, have a less reliable random blood supply, and do not provide a functional muscular oral sphincter.


The submental artery island flap is based on the submental branch of the facial artery. A paddle of skin, subcutaneous tissue, and fascia harvested from the submental area can be used for coverage of lower face and preauricular defects, as well as inferior and lateral neck wounds. Its use for reconstruction of partial lower lip full-thickness defects has not been established.


Facial artery myomucosal flaps consist of oral mucosa, submucosa, a small amount of buccinator muscle, and a more deeply lying facial artery and venous plexus. They are ideal for reconstructing the inner, most lip mucosa because they consist of similar tissue, with the same color, texture, and moisture. They can also be used for reconstruction of the dry vermilion, although some drying-out and scabbing of the mucosa will occur. They are not indicated for large, full-thickness lower lip defects.


References
1. Langstein HN, Robb GL. Lip and perioral reconstruction. Clin Plast Surg. 2005 Jul;32(3):431-445.
2. Baumann D, Robb G. Lip reconstruction. Semin Plast Surg. 2008 Nov;22(4):269-280.
3. Pribaz JJ, Meara JG, Wright S, et al. Lip and vermilion reconstruction with the facial artery musculomucosal flap. Plast Reconstr Surg 2000 Mar;105(3):864-872.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman is scheduled for bilateral mastectomies with immediate tissue expander reconstruction due to breast cancer. To minimize postoperative pain and narcotic requirements, preoperative ultrasound-guided pectoral nerve (PECS) 1 and 2 blocks using liposomal bupivacaine are planned. Following administration of the PECS 1 block, where should the local anesthetic be infiltrated when performing the PECS 2 block?
A) Between breast tissue and pectoralis major muscle
B) Between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor muscles
C) Between pectoralis minor and serratus anterior muscles
D) Between serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi muscles
questions.answer:
C)
The PECS 2 block requires infiltration of local anesthetic between the pectoralis minor and serratus anterior muscles to effectively block the intercostal and intercostobrachial nerves, providing comprehensive anesthesia for mastectomy procedures. A) Injection between breast parenchyma and pectoralis major is not part of the standard PECS block technique and would not target the appropriate nerve pathways. B) The space between pectoralis major and minor is where the PECS 1 block is performed, not the PECS 2 block. D) Injection between serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi describes the serratus plane block, which targets different nerves (long thoracic and thoracodorsal) and is a separate regional anesthesia technique.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old man arrives at the emergency department following a knife attack during an altercation. The patient is alert and comfortable. Physical examination reveals a 2-cm stab wound above the midclavicular line. He demonstrates weakened wrist flexion, impaired flexion of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers at both metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and compromised palmar abduction against resistance. Finger, thumb, and wrist extension remain normal, as do elbow flexion and extension. Which anatomical structure has most likely been injured by the sharp trauma?
A) Lateral cord
B) Medial cord
C) Median nerve
D) Middle trunk
E) Ulnar nerve
questions.answer:
B)
The patient exhibits combined median and ulnar nerve dysfunction while preserving radial nerve function. The medial cord provides fibers to both the median and ulnar nerves, as well as the medial pectoral nerve and medial brachial/antebrachial cutaneous nerves, making it the structure that when injured would produce this specific pattern of deficits. A) The lateral cord contributes to the median nerve but not the ulnar nerve, and since elbow flexion is intact, the musculocutaneous nerve (also from lateral cord) is functioning. C) Isolated median nerve injury would not explain the ulnar nerve deficits observed. D) The middle trunk contributes to radial and median nerves but not ulnar, and radial function is preserved. E) At the midclavicular level, the ulnar nerve has not yet formed as a discrete structure.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old laborer presents to the emergency department following avulsion injuries to the dorsal aspect of his right dominant hand's index, middle, and ring fingers after being caught in machinery. Each wound measures approximately 3 × 1 cm. Physical examination reveals exposed extensor tendons extending from the proximal interphalangeal joints to the dorsal web spaces. Artificial dermis has been applied. What is the most suitable reconstructive approach?
A) Full-thickness skin graft
B) Radial artery free flap
C) Reverse radial forearm flap
D) Split-thickness skin graft
E) No additional treatment
questions.answer:
D)
Split-thickness skin grafting is most appropriate because the artificial dermis provides the necessary dermal layer for tendon gliding while the split-thickness graft serves as the epithelial component. This combination prevents tendon adherence and scarring while minimizing donor site morbidity and allowing for a more aesthetic result with controlled contracture. A) Full-thickness grafts are unnecessary since the artificial dermis already provides the dermal elements, and the additional bulk is not needed. B) A radial artery free flap would be excessive for this defect size and would create unnecessary donor site morbidity. C) A reverse radial forearm flap lacks sufficient length to reach the fingertips and represents overtreatment. E) Allowing natural healing would result in tendon adherence, poor aesthetics, potential dysesthesia, and prolonged healing time.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with a soft-tissue injury to his left knee sustained during a football game fall. Which cell type will most likely be the first to arrive at the injury site?
A) Fibroblast
B) Lymphocyte
C) Macrophage
D) Neutrophil
E) Platelet
questions.answer:
E)
Platelets are the first cells to appear at a wound site as part of primary hemostasis, where they aggregate and degranulate to form clots and release growth factors that initiate the wound healing cascade. The cellular sequence in wound healing follows: platelets, neutrophils, macrophages, lymphocytes, then fibroblasts. A) Fibroblasts arrive later (3-5 days) during the proliferative phase to synthesize collagen. B) Lymphocytes appear during the later inflammatory phase after neutrophils and macrophages. C) Macrophages arrive 2-3 days post-injury, differentiating from monocytes to orchestrate the repair process. D) Neutrophils are the first inflammatory cells to arrive but come after initial platelet aggregation to sterilize the wound.

questions.question:
A 9-year-old female child is presented for assessment by her parent due to a 12-month period of cephalgia and early sexual development. Clinical examination reveals café-au-lait patches on her torso and a skeletal protrusion in her right posterior-lateral cranial region. A computed tomography image of the skull is provided. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Klippel-Feil syndrome
B) McCune-Albright syndrome
C) Paget disease
D) Proteus syndrome
E) Renal osteodystrophy
questions.answer:
B)
The correct diagnosis is McCune-Albright syndrome. The CT demonstrates fibrous dysplasia, which combined with early puberty and café-au-lait spots constitutes the classic triad of McCune-Albright syndrome. This condition typically involves multiple bones (polyostotic fibrous dysplasia), particularly affecting the cranium, long bones, and ribs. The precocious puberty results from autonomous gonadal function independent of gonadotropin stimulation, occurring more frequently in females. A) Klippel-Feil syndrome is incorrect because it involves cervical vertebral fusion with neck abnormalities, not fibrous dysplasia. C) Paget disease is incorrect as it typically presents in adults (third-fourth decade) with elevated alkaline phosphatase and different bone changes. D) Proteus syndrome is incorrect because it causes asymmetric overgrowth and different skin manifestations, not the classic triad described. E) Renal osteodystrophy is incorrect as it results from chronic kidney disease causing bone mineralization defects, not fibrous dysplasia with endocrine abnormalities.

questions.question:
Based on the code of ethics of the American Society of Plastic Surgeons, which of the following actions, if committed by a member, can be cause for disciplinary action?


A) The board-eligible surgeon chooses to advertise in an airline magazine
B) The member chooses to place patient testimonials on his or her Web site
C) The member participates in a charity raffle, fund-raising event, contest, or other promotion in which the prize is nonsurgical facial rejuvenation
D) The member uses his or her own before-and-after photos on the Web site
E) The out-of-network member charges wholly disproportionate fees for emergency care
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Disciplinary actions can be taken for charging exorbitant fees, particularly of a non-contractual nature (e.g., emergency care). Fees are exorbitant when they are wholly disproportionate to the services rendered. The reasonableness of fees depends upon the novelty and difficulty of the procedures involved, the skill required to provide proper care, the time and labor required, the fee charged for similar services by similarly situated peers, and whether or not the patient had agreed in advance to the fee. Except in instances of emergencies or urgent and life-threatening disease or injury, nothing in this principle shall be construed to prohibit a member from requiring prepayment of professional fees for all elective surgical operations.


Sanctions can be taken if the member participates in a charity raffle, fund-raising event, contest, or other promotion in which the prize is any procedure defined as a medical service that requires an incision. Examples of services that require an incision include, but are not limited to, rhytidectomy, augmentation mammaplasty, blepharoplasty, and liposuction. Examples of medical services that would not be considered procedures include, but are not limited to, injections (botulinum toxin, hyaluronic acid), microdermabrasion, and other skin surface treatments. Nonsurgical means do not fall under this category.


Sanctions can be taken if the Web site contains a testimonial pertaining to the quality and efficacy of medical care if the experience of the endorser does not represent the typical experience of other patients or if, because of the infrequency and/or complexity of such care, results in other cases cannot be predicted with any degree of accuracy. Also, sanctions may be taken if it contains a testimonial or endorsement pertaining to the quality of the member‚Äos medical care or the member‚Äos qualifications if the endorser has been compensated by the member or a third party retained by the member for making such testimonial or endorsement. Honest, well-represented, unbiased, uncoerced testimonials are allowed.


Disciplinary actions can be taken if the Web site contains photographs, images, or facsimiles of persons who falsely or deceptively portray a physical or medical condition, injury, or disease, including obesity, or recovery of relief therefrom; or if it contains photographs, images, or facsimiles of persons who have received the services advertised, but who have experienced results that are not typical of the results obtained by the average patient, without clearly and noticeably disclosing that fact; also, if it contains photographs, images, or facsimiles of persons before and after receiving services, which use different light, poses, or photographic techniques to misrepresent the results achieved by the individual.


References
1. American Society of Plastic Surgeons. Code of Ethics of the American Society of Plastic Surgeons. Available at: http://www.plasticsurgery.org/Documents/ByLaws/Code_of_Ethics_March12.pdf. Updated March 16, 2012.
2. Haeck PC. The role of ethics in plastic surgery. In: Neligan PC, Gurtner GC, eds. Plastic Surgery. Vol 1. Philadelphia: Elsevier-Saunders; 2013:55-63.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old girl has an unstable carpometacarpal (CMC) joint at the base of the thumb of the left hand. A photograph and x-ray study of the hand are shown. According to Blauth and Manske, which of the following is the most appropriate classification of this hypoplastic thumb? 


A ) II
B ) IIIA
C ) IIIB
D ) IV
E ) V
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


The Blauth classification of the hypoplastic thumb, as modified by Manske, is a true working classification that can be used for planning treatment (see table). Type IIIB has an unstable CMC joint and is the "cutoff point" for performing index finger pollicization and ablation of the hypoplastic thumb, versus attempting reconstruction of the original thumb.






References
1. Upton J. Hypoplastic or absent thumb. In Mathes SJ, Hentz VR, eds. Plastic Surgery. 2nd ed. Vol 8. Philadelphia: WB Saunders; 2005:332-338.
2. Manske PR, McCarroll HR Jr. Reconstruction of the congenitally deficient thumb. Hand Clin. 1992 Feb;8(1):177-196.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old right-handed female presents to the emergency room 18 hours following a feline bite injury to the back of her hand near the fifth knuckle joint. What pathogen is most likely to be isolated from this infected wound?
A) Eikenella corrodens
B) Group A Streptococcus
C) Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus
D) Pasteurella multocida
E) Pseudomonas aeruginosa
questions.answer:
D)
Pasteurella multocida is the most likely organism to be cultured from this cat bite infection. This gram-negative coccobacillus is the predominant pathogen in dog and cat bite wounds, causing local inflammatory signs including redness, warmth, pain, and possible purulent drainage. Without prompt treatment, it can lead to deep tissue infection or bone involvement. Treatment typically includes penicillin and surgical debridement when indicated. A) Eikenella corrodens is incorrect because it is primarily associated with human bite infections, not animal bites. B) Group A Streptococcus is incorrect as it commonly causes throat infections rather than being specifically associated with animal bite wounds. C) MRSA is incorrect because while increasingly common in community infections, it is not the typical pathogen in cat bite wounds. E) Pseudomonas aeruginosa is incorrect as it is more commonly a hospital-acquired pathogen with high antibiotic resistance, not typical of animal bite infections.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old patient returns for follow-up evaluation 9 days following surgical removal of a pigmented mole from the left leg. Over recent days, the surgical site has developed progressive redness and itching despite regular application of topical antibiotic medication. Previous use of the same medication produced no adverse effects. Physical examination reveals sharply defined redness and flaking skin around the surgical incision. This clinical presentation represents which type of hypersensitivity reaction?
A) Type I
B) Type II
C) Type III
D) Type IV
questions.answer:
D)
This represents a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction, specifically allergic contact dermatitis to the antibiotic ointment. This T-cell mediated immune response occurs when a foreign substance binds to skin proteins, creating an antigen complex that sensitizes the immune system. Upon re-exposure, sensitized T-cells trigger an inflammatory response causing the characteristic skin changes. The delayed onset and previous tolerance followed by reaction upon re-exposure are classic features of Type IV hypersensitivity. A) Type I is incorrect because these are immediate IgE-mediated reactions (like anaphylaxis) that occur within minutes of exposure, not days later with skin changes. B) Type II is incorrect as these are cytotoxic antibody-mediated reactions affecting blood cells or tissues, such as hemolytic reactions, not skin inflammation. C) Type III is incorrect because these involve immune complex formation with IgG/IgM antibodies causing conditions like serum sickness or lupus, not localized contact dermatitis.

questions.question:
Inadvertent intravascular injection of hyaluronic acid dermal filler in which anatomical location poses the highest risk for vision loss through retrograde blockage of the central retinal artery?
A) Cheek
B) Geniomandibular groove
C) Lateral lip commissure
D) Nasal dorsum
E) Nasolabial fold
questions.answer:
D)
The nasal dorsum presents the highest risk for blindness due to its vascular anatomy. The dorsal nasal artery is a terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery, which originates from the internal carotid system. Accidental high-pressure injection into this vessel can force filler material retrograde into the ophthalmic artery, and when pressure normalizes, the filler flows forward to occlude the central retinal artery, causing sudden blindness. A) The cheek is incorrect because the malar region has relatively few deep vessels and is considered a safer injection zone with lower vascular complication risk. B) The geniomandibular groove is incorrect as intravascular injection here typically causes lip and chin vascular compromise rather than retinal artery occlusion. C) The lateral lip commissure is incorrect because vascular complications in this area usually affect lip and lower facial circulation, not the ophthalmic arterial system. E) The nasolabial fold is incorrect because while angular artery injection can cause blindness, it more commonly results in nasal tip skin necrosis and mottling rather than direct retinal artery occlusion.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male patient has a biopsy performed on a pigmented skin lesion located on his neck. Histopathological analysis reveals superficial spreading melanoma without ulceration, measuring 1.2 mm in depth, with fewer than 1 mitosis per square millimeter. Beyond wide local excision, what additional treatment is most appropriate?
A) Interferon therapy
B) Radiation therapy
C) Regional lymphadenectomy
D) Sentinel lymph node biopsy
E) Observation
questions.answer:
D)
Sentinel lymph node biopsy is the most appropriate additional treatment according to current NCCN guidelines. Melanomas exceeding 1.0 mm Breslow thickness require wide local excision plus sentinel lymph node evaluation to assess regional nodal status and guide further treatment decisions. The sentinel node represents the first lymph node in the drainage pathway and is identified using radioisotope tracking and blue dye visualization techniques. A) Interferon therapy is incorrect as it is not routinely recommended as primary adjuvant treatment for intermediate-thickness melanomas without positive nodal involvement. B) Radiation therapy is incorrect because it is not standard treatment for primary melanoma management, though it may have specific indications in certain advanced cases. C) Regional lymphadenectomy is incorrect as complete lymph node dissection is no longer performed electively due to significant morbidity and lack of proven survival benefit compared to sentinel node biopsy. E) Observation alone is incorrect because melanomas greater than 1 mm thickness require nodal staging through sentinel lymph node biopsy to determine prognosis and treatment planning.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old woman presents to the clinic for assessment of nasal trauma from a canine bite. Clinical examination reveals a 3-cm tissue loss encompassing the majority of the nasal tip and lateral wall. Beyond removing the remaining nasal tip tissue, which of the following reconstructive approaches is most likely to yield the best cosmetic result for this patient?
A) Bilobed flap
B) Dorsal nasal (Rieger) flap
C) Forehead flap
D) Full-thickness skin graft
E) Nasolabial flap
questions.answer:
C)
The forehead flap is the optimal reconstructive method for complete nasal tip defects. The nose consists of nine aesthetic subunits, and when more than half of a subunit is involved, the entire subunit should be reconstructed for optimal results. A forehead flap provides appropriate tissue thickness and contour for nasal tip reconstruction. A) Bilobed flaps are suitable for smaller tip defects but cannot reconstruct an entire nasal tip.
