A) Botulinum toxin type A injections in the "crow's feet" area
B) Fat injection limited to the lower eyelid
C) Orbital malar ligament release and fat repositioning
D) Skin resection and lateral canthopexy
E) Skin resurfacing using a phenol-croton oil peel
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C. The primary factor contributing to the patient's concern is the relationship of the orbital malar ligament, orbital septum and retroseptal orbital fat. Release of the orbital malar ligament and fat repositioning offers the best option for improvement. The retroseptal fat compartments appear to be full so that fat injection alone would risk creating unwanted prominent fullness in the area. Skin resection should be conservative after fat repositioning to avoid lower lid malposition. Phenol-croton oil peeling is an effective treatment for aging changes but would not correct the anatomical relationships that underlie this patient‚Äos chief concern. Botulinum toxin type A injections would not adequately address this patient's concerns.


References
Hashem AM, Couto RA, Waltzman JT, et al. Evidence-Based Medicine: A Graded Approach to Lower Lid Blepharoplasty. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2017 Jan;139(1):139e-150e.
Drolet BC, Sullivan PK. Evidence-based medicine: Blepharoplasty. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2014 May;133(5):1195-205.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female patient sustains burns covering 85% of her body surface area and undergoes sequential debridement procedures, but has insufficient donor sites for conventional skin grafting. Cultured epidermal autografts (CEAs) are being considered for wound coverage. What represents the main benefit of CEAs compared to traditional split-thickness skin grafts?
A) Short 1-week cultivation time
B) Significant expansion of donor cell population
C) Minimal manufacturing expenses
D) Durable and stable wound coverage
E) Exclusive use of patient's own materials in culture process
questions.answer:
B)
The primary advantage of cultured epidermal autografts is the dramatic expansion capability of donor keratinocytes, achieving up to 10,000-fold multiplication from a small skin biopsy within approximately 3 weeks. This allows coverage of extensive wounds when donor sites are severely limited. A) The cultivation period is actually 3 weeks, not 1 week, which is a disadvantage rather than an advantage. C) CEAs are extremely expensive, costing up to $75,000 per 1% body surface area coverage. D) CEAs provide unstable coverage due to lack of dermal component and extreme fragility to shear forces. E) The culture process requires xenogeneic materials including murine fibroblasts and fetal calf serum, not exclusively autologous materials.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old male child presents with a 10-day history of an inflamed midline cervical mass that his parents initially observed 1 year earlier. Physical examination reveals a 35-mm lesion located just below the hyoid bone. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Branchial cleft remnant
B) Lingual thyroid gland
C) Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
D) Reactive lymph node
E) Thyroglossal duct cyst
questions.answer:
E)
This presentation is characteristic of an infected thyroglossal duct cyst, which occurs along the embryonic thyroglossal duct pathway from the tongue base to the normal thyroid position. These cysts most commonly develop just below the hyoid bone in the anterior midline neck and are typically asymptomatic unless infected. A) Branchial cleft remnants occur laterally along the sternocleidomastoid muscle border, not in the midline. B) Lingual thyroid represents ectopic thyroid tissue within the tongue itself, not a cystic lesion below the hyoid. C) Mucoepidermoid carcinoma typically arises within salivary glands, particularly the parotid, not as a midline neck mass. D) Reactive lymph nodes are usually found laterally in submandibular or jugulodigastric regions, not in the anterior midline.

questions.question:
In female patients experiencing prosthetic breast reconstruction with complications from expander/implant infection, which gram-negative organism is most frequently identified in culture specimens?
A) Escherichia coli
B) Klebsiella
C) Proteus
D) Pseudomonas
E) Serratia
questions.answer:
D)
Pseudomonas is the most frequently isolated gram-negative bacteria in expander/implant infections during breast reconstruction. While gram-positive organisms (particularly Staphylococcus species) are the predominant causative agents overall, among gram-negative bacteria specifically, Pseudomonas accounts for 10.7-14% of infections. A is incorrect because E. coli is less commonly isolated in implant-related infections. B is incorrect because Klebsiella occurs less frequently than Pseudomonas in this setting. C is incorrect because Proteus is not the most common gram-negative organism in breast implant infections. E is incorrect because Serratia is encountered less often than Pseudomonas in these infections.

questions.question:
During immediate breast reconstruction procedures, reconstructing the lateral inframammary fold is crucial. This importance stems from the fact that oncologic breast tissue removal extends to which anatomical boundary?
A) Anterior edge of the latissimus dorsi muscle
B) Anterior edge of the serratus muscle
C) Lateral edge of the pectoralis major muscle
D) Lateral edge of the pectoralis minor muscle
E) Posterior edge of the serratus muscle
questions.answer:
A)
The anterior edge of the latissimus dorsi muscle serves as the lateral boundary for mastectomy dissection in both modified radical and simple mastectomies. This anatomical landmark defines the extent of tissue removal, making reconstruction of the lateral inframammary fold essential for proper breast shaping. B is incorrect because the anterior serratus edge is not the standard lateral dissection boundary. C is incorrect because the pectoralis major lateral edge does not define the lateral mastectomy margin. D is incorrect because the pectoralis minor is not involved in defining lateral mastectomy boundaries. E is incorrect because the posterior serratus edge is not the relevant anatomical landmark for mastectomy dissection.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old female patient seeks treatment for Angle class II malocclusion with 8 mm overjet and retrognathia/retrogenia. Mandibular advancement combined with genioplasty is scheduled. What is the most probable result of this surgical intervention?
A) Decreased presence of the nasolabial folds
B) Decreased prominence of the labiomental crease
C) Increased area of the glossopharyngeal opening
D) Increased area of the velopharyngeal opening
E) Increased cervicomental angle
questions.answer:
C)
Mandibular advancement surgery increases the glossopharyngeal opening area as the tongue moves forward with the mandible, which can improve airway function and potentially help with sleep apnea symptoms. This enlargement of the posterior airway space is a predictable outcome of bilateral sagittal split osteotomy. A is incorrect because nasolabial folds are not significantly affected by mandibular advancement procedures. B is incorrect because the labiomental crease actually becomes deeper, not less prominent, after this surgery. D is incorrect because the velopharyngeal opening is not altered by mandibular advancement surgery. E is incorrect because the cervicomental angle becomes more acute (smaller), not increased, following mandibular advancement.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male college student experiences a volar oblique fingertip amputation during food preparation. Clinical assessment reveals hyponychium involvement with an intact nail. The defect measures 1 × 1.5 cm without bone exposure. What treatment approach best promotes secondary intention healing?
A) Apply negative pressure wound therapy
B) Apply povidone iodine to the wound daily and cover with dry gauze
C) Cover wound with semiocclusive dressing and change weekly
D) Leave wound open to air
E) Soak wound in hydrogen peroxide daily and cover with moist gauze
questions.answer:
C)
Semiocclusive dressings are optimal for small fingertip amputations (<1.5 cm²) with minimal bone exposure, maintaining appropriate moisture levels while allowing gas exchange. These transparent, semi-permeable dressings promote faster healing when changed every 5-7 days, minimizing wound manipulation. A is incorrect because negative pressure therapy is unnecessary and cost-prohibitive for such small wounds. B is incorrect because povidone iodine causes tissue drying and delays healing when used long-term. D is incorrect because air exposure leads to tissue desiccation and impaired healing. E is incorrect because hydrogen peroxide is cytotoxic to healing tissues and interferes with normal wound repair processes.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old man is referred for evaluation directly after undergoing excision of recurrent squamous cell carcinoma and Mohs micrographic surgery. A photograph is shown. Pathology shows some extension onto the parotid capsule. Clinical examination shows two enlarged postauricular lymph nodes. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of this patient?


A) Cervical facial flap plus radiation
B) Direct closure alone
C) Superficial parotidectomy and direct closure
D) Superficial parotidectomy, neck dissection, and coverage with a cheek rotation flap
E) Superficial parotidectomy, neck dissection, and direct closure
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


Direct closure is being used more commonly in large Mohs facial defects, especially in the elderly, as it minimizes the disruption of skin tension lines. The contraindication in this case to closure alone is the nodal involvement and the extension into the parotid capsule. Given the parotid capsule extension, adequate margins at a minimum will require a superficial parotidectomy. Radiation alone plus flap closure would have a higher recurrence rate because residual disease is left in the capsule. The nodal enlargement requires further evaluation and given the options the best combination is superficial parotidectomy, neck dissection, and a local rotation flap.


References
Ibrahim AM, Rabie An, Borud L, et al. Common patterns of reconstruction for Mohs defects in the head and neck. J Craniofac Surg. 2014 Jan; 25(1):87-92.
Rapstine ED, Knaus WJ, Thornton JF. Simplifying cheek reconstruction: a review of over 400 cases. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012 Jun; 129(6): 1291-9.
Soliman S, Hatef DA, Hollier LH, et ak. The rationale for direct linear closure of facial Mohs‚Äo defects. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2011 Jan; 127(1):142-9.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old female patient arrives at the emergency department following facial trauma from a vehicular accident. Examination reveals a 4-cm upper eyelid laceration on the left side. The levator palpebrae superioris is severed just above the tarsus, revealing underlying anatomy. Which intact structure is now visible?
A) Lacrimal sac
B) Müller muscle
C) Orbital septum
D) Preaponeurotic fat
E) Retro-orbicularis oculi fat
questions.answer:
B)
Müller muscle lies directly posterior to the levator palpebrae superioris and inserts on the tarsus, making it the structure exposed when the levator is transected just superior to the tarsal plate. This smooth muscle contributes to upper eyelid elevation and is innervated by sympathetic fibers. A is incorrect because the lacrimal sac is located medially in the lacrimal fossa, not directly beneath the levator. C is incorrect because the orbital septum lies anterior to the levator at this level, not posterior. D is incorrect because preaponeurotic fat is located posterior to the orbital septum, not directly beneath the levator at the tarsal level. E is incorrect because retro-orbicularis oculi fat lies anterior to the orbital septum, not in the deep layer exposed by levator transection.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male patient receives open reduction with internal fixation for a Gustilo Type IIIB tibial-fibular fracture. Free flap reconstruction is planned to address the associated soft-tissue defect. What is the optimal timing following trauma for performing this reconstructive procedure?
A) 3 Days
B) 10 Days
C) 21 Days
D) 60 Days
E) 90 Days
questions.answer:
A)
Godina established guidelines in 1986 for the timing of microsurgical reconstruction of lower extremity trauma, recommending free flap coverage for Gustilo Type IIIB/C fractures within 72 hours of injury. His research demonstrated that the delayed period (72 hours to 90 days) carried the highest risk of infection and flap failure. B is incorrect because 10 days falls within the high-risk delayed period identified by Godina. C is incorrect because 21 days is well into the delayed reconstruction window associated with increased complications. D is incorrect because 60 days represents the peak of the delayed period with maximum risk of flap loss and infection. E is incorrect because 90 days marks the end of the high-risk delayed period, though some authors report acceptable outcomes at this timeframe with more extensive surgical dissection.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old patient presents with a congenital sinus tract opening located at the anterior margin of the lower third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. During surgical removal of this fistulous tract, which nerve is at greatest risk of injury?
A) Accessory (XI)
B) Facial (VII)
C) Hypoglossal (XII)
D) Lingual
E) Vagus (X)
questions.answer:
C)
This patient has a second branchial cleft fistula, which typically courses along the carotid sheath upward, crosses over the hypoglossal nerve, and passes between the internal and external carotid arteries to reach the tonsillar fossa, placing the hypoglossal nerve at highest risk during excision. A is incorrect because the spinal accessory nerve is located in the posterior triangle of the neck, away from the surgical field. B is incorrect because the facial nerve is associated with first branchial arch anomalies, not second branchial cleft fistulas. D is incorrect because the lingual nerve is positioned at a higher anatomical level and remains safe during this procedure. E is incorrect because the vagus nerve lies within the carotid sheath but is positioned lateral to the fistulous tract at the carotid bifurcation, making it less vulnerable than the hypoglossal nerve.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old collegiate baseball athlete injured his left hand while batting 6 weeks prior. He experienced immediate palmar pain, grip weakness, and developed tingling in his ring and small fingers within hours that has persisted despite rest. Standard hand radiographs appear normal. CT imaging of this patient's hand would most likely reveal a fracture of which carpal bone?
A) Capitate
B) Hamate
C) Lunate
D) Pisiform
E) Scaphoid
questions.answer:
B)
This athlete has sustained a hook of hamate fracture, commonly missed on standard radiographs but frequently occurring in baseball players due to bat impact or ball catching mechanisms. The persistent ulnar nerve symptoms (tingling in ring and small fingers) are characteristic of this injury due to the proximity of the ulnar nerve to the hamate hook. A is incorrect because capitate fractures would not produce the specific ulnar nerve distribution symptoms described. C is incorrect because lunate fractures typically present with different symptom patterns and are not commonly associated with baseball batting injuries. D is incorrect because pisiform fractures would not cause the persistent ulnar nerve irritation seen in this case. E is incorrect because scaphoid fractures, while common in athletes, would not produce the characteristic ulnar-sided symptoms and nerve irritation described.

questions.question:
In affirmed male patients assigned female at birth who achieve post-pubertal male phenotype through testosterone therapy, which virilizing effect can be reversed if hormone treatment is stopped?
A) Cessation of menses
B) Clitoromegaly
C) Lowered pitch of voice
D) Male-pattern baldness
questions.answer:
A)
Menstruation can resume if testosterone therapy is discontinued after achieving post-pubertal male phenotype, as the cessation of menses is hormonally dependent and reversible. B is incorrect because clitoral enlargement that occurs with testosterone therapy is a permanent structural change that will not reverse if hormones are stopped. C is incorrect because voice deepening represents permanent changes to the vocal cords and laryngeal structures that cannot be reversed. D is incorrect because male-pattern hair loss that has occurred during testosterone therapy represents permanent follicular changes that will not reverse with hormone discontinuation.

questions.question:
A patient with an unresectable proximal forearm sarcoma will undergo elective transhumeral amputation. What are the primary benefits of performing targeted muscle reinnervation during the amputation procedure?
A) Decreased pain in residual limb and improved control of myoelectric prosthesis
B) Greater length of residual limb and improved soft-tissue coverage over bone
C) Improved sensation in residual limb and greater range of motion in native elbow
D) Improved shape of residual limb and greater range of motion in native shoulder
E) Increased muscle bulk of residual limb and improved control of myoelectric prosthesis
questions.answer:
A)
Targeted muscle reinnervation provides functional destinations for severed nerves, resulting in reduced residual limb and phantom pain while enhancing myoelectric prosthetic control through improved signal quality from reinnervated muscles. These benefits are maximized when TMR is performed at the time of amputation. B is incorrect because TMR does not increase limb length or provide additional soft-tissue coverage. C is incorrect because TMR does not significantly improve sensation in the residual limb or affect native elbow range of motion. D is incorrect because TMR does not substantially alter residual limb shape or native shoulder range of motion. E is incorrect because TMR does not increase muscle bulk in the residual limb, though it does improve prosthetic control.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old female presents with a 2-month history of increasing swelling in her left upper limb. On examination, there is edema from the hand extending up the arm. The left upper extremity has a greater diameter than the right. Ultrasound reveals no venous blockage, and CT imaging shows no tumor or mass lesion. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
A) Prescribing diuretic medication
B) Limb elevation and compression therapy
C) Surgical liposuction
D) Microlymphatic surgical anastomosis
E) Insertion of a buried dermal flap
questions.answer:
B)
Limb elevation and compression therapy is the most appropriate initial management step. Lymphedema results from impaired lymphatic drainage causing fluid and protein accumulation in tissues. Conservative treatment with elevation and compression garments, often combined with manual lymphatic drainage, is the first-line approach for newly diagnosed lymphedema cases. A) is incorrect because diuretics are ineffective for lymphedema treatment. C) is incorrect because liposuction is reserved for cases that have failed conservative management and has high recurrence rates. D) is incorrect because microlymphatic procedures are complex surgical options with uncertain long-term patency, reserved for refractory cases. E) is incorrect because buried dermal flaps are surgical interventions typically used after conservative therapy has failed.

questions.question:
For reconstruction of a traumatic soft-tissue defect on the hand, a lateral arm fasciocutaneous flap is selected for free tissue transfer. The vascular supply for this flap runs between which anatomical structures?
A) Brachioradialis and brachialis muscles
B) Lateral triceps head and biceps muscle
C) Lateral triceps head and brachialis muscle
D) Lateral triceps head and extensor carpi radialis longus
E) Lateral triceps head and humeral bone
questions.answer:
C)
The vascular pedicle runs between the lateral triceps head and brachialis muscle. The lateral arm flap is supplied by the posterior radial collateral artery, which emerges from the intermuscular septum between the brachialis muscle anteriorly and the lateral head of the triceps posteriorly. A) is incorrect because the pedicle does not course between the brachioradialis and brachialis. B) is incorrect because the biceps is not involved in this anatomical relationship. D) is incorrect because the extensor carpi radialis longus is not part of the relevant anatomy for this pedicle. E) is incorrect because the pedicle does not run directly between the triceps and humerus bone.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old female with progressive facial atrophy presents with a moderate soft-tissue volume loss on the left facial side. She is planned for a single fat grafting procedure for correction. What is the most probable outcome of this treatment?
A) Seroma at the donor site
B) Injury to the facial nerve
C) Fat embolization
D) Hypertrophic scar formation
E) Insufficient volume correction
questions.answer:
E)
Insufficient volume correction is the most probable outcome. In progressive facial atrophy (Romberg disease), fat grafting typically requires multiple sessions to achieve adequate volume restoration, and a single procedure often provides inadequate correction. A) is incorrect because donor site seromas are more common with free tissue transfer procedures than fat grafting. B) is incorrect because facial nerve injury is rare with fat grafting and more associated with major reconstructive procedures. C) is incorrect because fat embolism during facial fat transfer is extremely rare. D) is incorrect because hypertrophic scarring is uncommon with fat grafting due to the minimal incisions required.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old female with a history of cleft palate repair is being assessed for potential velopharyngeal insufficiency. Besides speech assessment by qualified speech-language pathologists, which diagnostic method is most appropriate?
A) Dynamic MRI imaging
B) Computed tomography
C) Assessment under general anesthesia
D) Lateral skull radiograph
E) Flexible nasopharyngoscopy
questions.answer:
E)
Flexible nasopharyngoscopy is the most appropriate diagnostic method. It provides direct visualization of velopharyngeal function during speech production and allows assessment of closure patterns essential for surgical planning. Most cleft centers have adopted nasopharyngoscopy as the primary diagnostic tool due to its ability to avoid radiation exposure while providing excellent dynamic evaluation. A) is incorrect because while MRI is emerging as a diagnostic tool, it is not yet the first-choice method for VPI evaluation. B) is incorrect because CT scanning does not provide dynamic assessment of velopharyngeal function. C) is incorrect because examination under anesthesia is unnecessary when nasopharyngoscopy can be performed comfortably in the office. D) is incorrect because lateral cephalograms provide only static images without dynamic functional assessment.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with fever and neck pain 2.5 weeks following posterior cervical spinal fusion surgery. Physical examination reveals peri-incisional swelling and redness. CT imaging demonstrates a deep posterior fluid collection. The orthopedic team plans surgical debridement and irrigation, consulting plastic surgery for dead space obliteration. A Mathes and Nahai type II muscle flap is planned for reconstruction. Which artery is most likely to be utilized in this reconstruction?
A) Circumflex scapular artery
B) Occipital artery
C) Thoracoacromial artery
D) Thoracodorsal artery
E) Transverse cervical artery
questions.answer:
E)
The transverse cervical artery is most likely to be utilized as it is the dominant pedicle for the trapezius muscle flap (type II), which is ideal for high cervical defect coverage. The trapezius flap's main vascular pedicle enters the muscle approximately 8 cm from midline at the C7 level, making it particularly suitable for posterior cervical reconstruction. A) is incorrect because the circumflex scapular artery supplies fasciocutaneous flaps (scapular/parascapular), not muscle flaps. B) is incorrect because the occipital artery supplies the sternocleidomastoid flap, which is unsuitable for posterior cervical defects. C) is incorrect because the thoracoacromial artery supplies the pectoralis major muscle (type V), which is not appropriate for this location. D) is incorrect because the thoracodorsal artery supplies the latissimus dorsi muscle (type V), which would not be the first choice for this cervical defect.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents with concerns about his nasal tip drooping downward. Physical examination reveals a dorsal bump, inadequate tip support, ptotic nasal tip, prominent columellar display, and elongated caudal septum. Which of the following surgical approaches would be most effective for addressing this patient's nasal abnormality?
A) Caudal septal tongue-in-groove technique
B) Columellar strut graft
C) Lateral crura spanning sutures
D) Medial foot plate excision
E) Transdomal suture
questions.answer:
A)
To address this patient's abnormality, achieving control over tip support, projection, and rotation is crucial. The septal tongue-in-groove technique provides superior and more predictable tip control. This approach resembles a tongue-in-groove septal extension graft; however, since this patient possesses sufficient caudal septal length, the medial crura can be lifted and rotated onto the existing caudal septum. When septal length is excessive (which occurs rarely), the caudal septum can be trimmed. The compromise with this technique is increased tip rigidity. B is incorrect because a columellar strut is less dependable and unneeded given adequate septal length. D is incorrect because medial foot plate excision (which removes prominent foot plates) will not address a drooping tip. E is incorrect because transdomal sutures (which narrow the nasal tip) and C is incorrect because lateral crura spanning sutures (which straighten curved lower lateral cartilages) will not remedy this deformity.

questions.question:
When performing a free gracilis muscle flap for facial reanimation, the direction of commissure movement should replicate the action of which of the following facial muscles?
A) Buccinator
B) Levator labii superioris
C) Risorius
D) Temporalis
E) Zygomaticus major
questions.answer:
E)
Free gracilis muscle transplantation is a frequently used technique to create a smile in patients with complete facial nerve paralysis. It possesses several characteristics that make it optimal for this application: it is slender, demonstrates excellent contractility, creates no functional loss after harvest, and possesses a relatively lengthy motor nerve. The muscle placement, including proper tensioning and alignment, is crucial for success. The muscle is secured proximally to the zygomatic body or temporalis fascia and distally to the orbicularis oris muscle near the modiolus just lateral to the oral commissure. While some variation in flap positioning is possible, the intended pull direction most accurately mimics the normal action of the zygomaticus major muscle. A is incorrect because the buccinator muscle is not involved in smiling. D is incorrect because the temporalis muscle is not involved in smiling. B is incorrect because the levator labii superioris originates from the anterior zygoma and inserts near the orbicularis oris in the upper lip, with its vertical orientation making it a strong vertical elevator of the upper lip. C is incorrect because the risorius does not elevate the oral commissure but instead pulls the mouth corner in an almost horizontal direction.

questions.question:
In rheumatoid arthritis patients, what is the initial triggering event that leads to boutonniere deformity development?
A) Central slip attenuation
B) Intrinsic tightness
C) Lateral band volar subluxation
D) Oblique retinacular ligament contracture
E) Proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint synovitis
questions.answer:
E)
Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune condition marked by joint inflammation and deterioration. Synovial proliferation represents the characteristic feature of rheumatoid arthritis and typically appears early in the disease course. There is progression to synovial pannus development, periarticular bone demineralization, cartilage destruction, and subchondral bone erosions. This process occurs through synovial infiltration of activated T lymphocytes, which promote persistent synovial inflammation. The boutonniere deformity occurs very frequently in rheumatoid arthritis patients, characterized by PIP joint flexion with DIP joint hyperextension. The initiating event of boutonniere deformity in rheumatoid arthritis is synovitis and synovial pannus development within the PIP joint, causing joint capsule distension and resulting central slip attenuation. Central slip insufficiency leads to PIP joint extension loss and subsequent volar displacement of the lateral bands, which further worsens the deformity by creating a flexion force across the PIP joint. Extension forces are redirected to the DIP joint. A is incorrect because central slip attenuation is a consequence, not the initial cause. C is incorrect because lateral band volar subluxation occurs secondary to the synovitis. D is incorrect because oblique retinacular ligament contracture is associated with fixed deformity but is not the initiating event. B is incorrect because intrinsic tightness would prevent PIP joint flexion when the MP is extended.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male presents for evaluation of facial trauma from a bicycle fall 5 days prior. He reports midface pain and resolved swelling. Facial physical examination reveals no trauma signs. Intraoral examination demonstrates traumatic loss of tooth #8. He has no cervical spine tenderness or pain with active range of motion. What is the most appropriate next management step?
A) Obtain cervical spine MRI
B) Obtain maxillofacial CT scan to evaluate for facial fracture
C) Recommend elevation of the head of the bed and ice pack to the face
D) Recommend soft diet and referral to a dentist
E) No further management is necessary
questions.answer:
B)
This patient most likely has a facial fracture, making a maxillofacial CT scan the most appropriate next management step. A retrospective study of facial trauma patients who underwent maxillofacial CT scanning for facial fracture evaluation identified five independent criteria highly predictive of facial fracture. Any of these five physical examination criteria—the Wisconsin criteria—predicted facial fracture: bony step-off or instability, periorbital swelling or contusion, Glasgow Coma Scale score below 14, malocclusion, or tooth absence (sensitivity, 98.2%). Since this patient has a missing tooth, he requires evaluation with a maxillofacial CT scan. While soft diet and eventual dental referral as well as head elevation with cool compress are reasonable recommendations, establishing a diagnosis is the first critical step. A is incorrect because the patient lacks cervical spine tenderness, providing no indication for cervical spine imaging. C is incorrect because while supportive care is reasonable, diagnosis must come first. D is incorrect because while dental referral is appropriate, fracture evaluation takes priority. E is incorrect because the missing tooth indicates high fracture probability requiring imaging evaluation.

questions.question:
For surgical procedures not involving the airway, which oxygen delivery method is most likely to increase operating room fire risk?
A) Endobronchial tube
B) Endotracheal tube
C) Laryngeal mask
D) Nasal cannula
E) Tracheostomy tube with cuff
questions.answer:
D)
For non-airway surgical procedures, open oxygen sources like masks or nasal cannulae most likely increase operating room fire risk, as they may permit trapping or accumulation of an oxidizer-enriched environment (oxygen with or without nitrous oxide). Operating room fire incidence in the United States is estimated at approximately 600 cases annually. Fire requires three components: fuel, an oxidizer, and an ignition source. Common operating room fuels include alcohol-based prep solutions, drapes and bandages, gowns and personal protective equipment, petroleum jelly, etc. Ignition sources include electrocautery, lasers, fiberoptic light sources, and defibrillators. The two primary operating room oxidizing agents are oxygen and nitrous oxide. Most operating room fire risk assessment protocols consider the presence of an open oxygen source, surgical site or incision above the xiphoid, and available ignition source (electrocautery, laser, fiberoptic light source, etc). For non-airway surgical procedures, closed-system oxygen sources using endotracheal/endobronchial tubes, cuffed tracheostomy tubes, or laryngeal masks present lower fire risk compared to open oxygen sources. A is incorrect because endobronchial tubes are closed-system oxygen delivery with lower fire risk. B is incorrect because endotracheal tubes are closed-system oxygen delivery with lower fire risk. C is incorrect because laryngeal masks are closed-system oxygen delivery with lower fire risk. E is incorrect because cuffed tracheostomy tubes are closed-system oxygen delivery with lower fire risk.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old child with a medical history of bilateral cleft lip and palate has undergone several surgical interventions including lip and nasal reconstruction, palatal repair, and closure of an oronasal communication. Over the last 6 months, his parents report nocturnal snoring, intermittent breathing cessation episodes, and excessive daytime sleepiness. Clinical examination reveals mixed dentition with marked midface retrusion and Angle class III bite relationship with 12 mm negative overjet. Sleep study results show an obstructive apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) of 12.5 events per hour. The child is otherwise in good health. What is the optimal treatment approach for this patient?
A) Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
B) Le Fort I advancement with bilateral sagittal split mandibular setback
C) Le Fort I osteotomy with bilateral internal maxillary distraction devices
D) Le Fort III osteotomy with external halo distraction apparatus
E) Surgical tracheostomy
questions.answer:
A)
CPAP therapy is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient. The child has undergone multiple palatal surgeries resulting in severe midface retrusion, which has led to obstructive sleep apnea as confirmed by polysomnography. CPAP provides effective non-invasive treatment for his sleep-disordered breathing. B) is incorrect because Le Fort I advancement would risk damage to unerupted permanent teeth in this patient with mixed dentition. C) is incorrect for the same reason - any Le Fort I level surgery poses significant risk to developing tooth roots. D) is incorrect because Le Fort III osteotomy would unnecessarily advance the infraorbital rims, which are typically unaffected in cleft patients, and is overly aggressive for this clinical scenario. E) is incorrect because tracheostomy, while effective at bypassing the obstruction, carries substantial risks including 1% annual mortality and significant care burden, making it inappropriate when less invasive options are available.

questions.question:
A 51-year-old male construction worker needs partial tongue removal for recurring oral squamous cell carcinoma. He maintains an active lifestyle, running five miles three times weekly. He completed radiation treatment two years ago. Which microsurgical free flap transfer would be most suitable for reconstruction?
A) Deltopectoral flap
B) Rectus abdominis flap
C) Sural artery perforator flap
D) Vastus lateralis flap
questions.answer:
C)
The sural artery perforator flap is the optimal choice for this patient's partial glossectomy reconstruction. This flap provides thin, pliable tissue ideal for tongue reconstruction while minimizing donor site morbidity, which is crucial for a manual laborer. The sural artery perforator flap typically uses perforators from the medial sural artery and results in minimal functional impairment. A) is incorrect because the deltopectoral flap is rarely used as a free flap and arises from the first intercostal perforator, making it unsuitable for this application. B) is incorrect because the rectus abdominis flap is excessively bulky for partial tongue reconstruction and would create poor functional outcomes. D) is incorrect because sacrificing the vastus lateralis muscle would significantly impair this patient's running ability and overall leg function, which is unacceptable given his active lifestyle and occupation.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old manual worker presents to the clinic with a 2-cm mass located on the back of both hands. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals an aberrant muscle structure. What is the most probable anatomical finding?
A) Extensor digitorum brevis
B) Extensor digitorum longus
C) Extensor digitorum brevis manus
D) Extensor indicis proprius
E) Extensor medii proprius
questions.answer:
C)
The extensor digitorum brevis manus is the most likely structure causing bilateral dorsal hand masses in this patient. This anomalous muscle occurs in 2-3% of the population and characteristically presents as tender dorsal wrist masses. It typically originates from the proximal dorsal radiocarpal ligament and inserts into the index finger extensor mechanism, appearing distinctively on MRI. A) is incorrect because extensor digitorum brevis is a normal muscle found in the foot, not the hand. B) is incorrect because extensor digitorum longus is a normal forearm muscle that wouldn't present as a discrete dorsal hand mass. D) is incorrect because extensor indicis proprius is a normal muscle of the posterior forearm compartment and wouldn't appear as an anomalous mass. E) is incorrect because extensor medii proprius, while a possible anatomical variant, is much less common than extensor digitorum brevis manus and doesn't typically present as bilateral masses.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old boy is brought to the office because of recurrent swelling, discoloration, and occasional discomfort of the right forearm. Discoloration and swelling have been present since birth, but these features have become more pronounced with growth and are exacerbated by limb dependency. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment in this patient?


A) Interferon alpha therapy
B) Propranolol therapy
C) Reassurance that the condition will resolve with time
D) Sclerotherapy
E) Systemic corticosteroid therapy
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The lesion shown is a venous malformation. Unlike infantile hemangioma, these lesions are present at birth and grow proportionately with the child, and therefore, cannot be expected to resolve over time. Venous malformations can become more symptomatic with growth and swelling or symptoms are exacerbated by dependency. In addition, rapid swelling and pain can result from phlebothrombosis (clotting) in the anomalous venous channels. The most effective treatment for symptomatic lesions is sclerotherapy. Operative excision is generally reserved for focal lesions or those with significant functional effects; because the lesions involve critical tissues and are poorly circumscribed, operative excision is rarely curative. The other options presented have been used to treat infantile hemangioma, but have not demonstrated effectiveness for venous, arteriovenous, or lymphatic malformations.


References
1. Greene AK, Alomari AI. Management of venous malformations. Clin Plast Surg. 2011 Jan;38(1):83-93.
2. Greene AK. Vascular anomalies: current overview of the field. Clin Plast Surg. 2011 Jan;38(1):1-5.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old patient suffers a hemorrhagic cerebrovascular accident necessitating decompressive craniotomy. The original bone flap is deemed unsuitable for replacement, and a custom-made polyetheretherketone implant is being considered. What is the most frequent complication associated with this reconstructive material?
A) Cerebrospinal fluid leak
B) Contour deformity
C) Wound dehiscence
D) Hematoma formation
E) Infection
questions.answer:
E)
Infection is the most common complication when using polyetheretherketone (PEEK) for cranial reconstruction. Despite PEEK being a reliable alloplastic material with the advantage of custom fabrication, infection remains the primary concern due to potential microbial seeding through wound dehiscence, hematogenous spread, or indolent colonization of the surgical site. A) is incorrect because cerebrospinal fluid leak, while possible, occurs less frequently than infectious complications with PEEK implants. B) is incorrect because contour deformity is uncommon with custom-made PEEK implants that are specifically designed to match the patient's anatomy. C) is incorrect because wound dehiscence, while a potential complication, is less frequent than infection and may actually be a contributing factor to infection rather than the primary complication. D) is incorrect because hematoma formation is not the most common complication specifically associated with PEEK material use.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old adolescent with asthma arrives at the emergency department 3 hours following accidental injection of his index finger on the non-dominant hand with his epinephrine auto-injector device. Physical examination reveals the finger is cold, blanched, and tender. Which medication functions as a competitive antagonist to counteract the sympathomimetic actions of epinephrine?
A) Lidocaine
B) Bupivacaine
C) Nitroglycerin paste
D) Phentolamine
E) Prostacyclin
questions.answer:
D)
Phentolamine is the correct medication that competitively antagonizes the sympathomimetic effects of epinephrine. When administered subcutaneously, phentolamine directly reverses epinephrine-induced vasoconstriction by blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors, making it the drug of choice when tissue viability is threatened or significant pain occurs after epinephrine injection. A) is incorrect because lidocaine causes vasodilation through sodium channel blockade, not by competitive antagonism of epinephrine's sympathomimetic effects. B) is incorrect because bupivacaine is an amide local anesthetic that blocks sodium channels and does not antagonize epinephrine. C) is incorrect because nitroglycerin paste works through nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation, which is a different mechanism than competitive antagonism of epinephrine. E) is incorrect because prostacyclin causes vasodilation through prostaglandin pathways, not through competitive antagonism of adrenergic receptors.

questions.question:
Which pharyngeal arch gives rise to the facial expression muscles, the digastric muscle's posterior belly, and the stapedius muscle?
A) First
B) Second
C) Third
D) Fourth
E) Sixth
questions.answer:
B)

The second pharyngeal arch is the correct source of these structures. The pharyngeal (branchial) arches are embryological formations containing all three germ layers plus neural crest cells, which develop into the bony, cartilaginous, vascular, muscular, and neural components of the head and neck region. The facial expression muscles, digastric muscle's posterior belly, and stapedius muscle all originate from the second pharyngeal arch and receive innervation from the facial nerve (cranial nerve VII), which also develops from this same arch. A is incorrect because the first arch gives rise to muscles of mastication. C is incorrect because the third arch primarily contributes to the stylopharyngeus muscle. D is incorrect because the fourth arch forms muscles of the soft palate and pharynx. E is incorrect because the sixth arch contributes to intrinsic laryngeal muscles.

questions.question:
An 11-month-old boy presents with painless, progressive enlargement of the right maxilla. Following incisional biopsy at another institution, pathology confirms sinonasal myxoma. Post-surgical MRI demonstrates remaining tumor with associated inflammatory changes. What is the optimal treatment approach?
A) Chemotherapy and radiation therapy
B) Chemotherapy alone
C) Tumor curettage and debulking
D) Complete surgical excision with negative margins
E) Watchful waiting
questions.answer:
D)

Complete surgical excision with negative margins is the appropriate treatment for sinonasal myxoma. These are benign, slow-growing neoplasms that commonly affect the maxilla or mandible in infants, presenting as painless, progressive facial enlargement. Complete removal with clear margins is essential because these tumors may not be well-demarcated, requiring resection of normal surrounding tissue to prevent incomplete removal and continued growth. A is incorrect because myxomas are benign tumors that do not respond to chemotherapy or radiation. B is incorrect for the same reason - chemotherapy is ineffective against benign myxomas. C is incorrect because simple curettage and debulking would likely leave residual tumor leading to recurrence. E is incorrect because observation would allow continued tumor growth and potential complications.

questions.question:
A plastic surgery resident discovers that a 55-year-old diabetic and hypertensive patient scheduled for immediate breast reconstruction in 4 days lacks a preoperative anesthesia consultation and required testing. After notifying attendings and arranging the evaluation, she establishes a protocol ensuring all patients 50 years and older with comorbidities receive preoperative anesthesia assessments. This demonstrates which core competency?
A) Communication and interpersonal abilities
B) Clinical knowledge
C) Patient management and technical skills
D) Professional behavior
E) Healthcare systems improvement
questions.answer:
E)

This scenario exemplifies healthcare systems improvement (systems-based practice). According to ACGME guidelines, this competency involves coordinating patient care within healthcare systems, identifying system failures, and implementing solutions to enhance care delivery. The resident demonstrated these abilities by recognizing a system gap, coordinating appropriate care, and creating a preventive protocol for similar situations. A is incorrect because while communication occurred, the primary focus was system improvement rather than interpersonal skills. B is incorrect because this wasn't primarily about applying medical knowledge. C is incorrect because this involved system processes rather than direct patient care or procedures. D is incorrect because although professional, the main demonstration was system-level problem-solving rather than individual professional behavior.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old male seeks consultation for puffy, swollen eyelids and ocular dryness. Examination reveals bilateral mild proptosis and conjunctival injection. Visual acuity and fields are normal. Extraocular movement assessment demonstrates eyelid lag. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Allergic conjunctivitis
B) Myasthenia gravis
C) Optic neuritis
D) Sjögren syndrome
E) Thyroid ophthalmopathy
questions.answer:
E)

Thyroid ophthalmopathy (thyroid eye disease) is the most likely diagnosis. This condition represents the leading cause of proptosis and diplopia in adults, predominantly affecting women. The constellation of puffy eyelids, conjunctival injection, eyelid lag, and proptosis are characteristic features of thyroid ophthalmopathy. A is incorrect because allergic conjunctivitis would not cause proptosis or eyelid lag. B is incorrect because myasthenia gravis typically presents with ptosis that worsens throughout the day, not eyelid lag or proptosis. C is incorrect because optic neuritis usually involves visual impairment, which this patient lacks. D is incorrect because while Sjögren syndrome can cause conjunctival injection, it would not produce proptosis or eyelid lag.

questions.question:
A healthy 38-year-old woman undergoes bilateral prophylactic mastectomy with immediate DIEP flap reconstruction. Intraoperatively, the left flap shows congestion despite patent, non-kinked anastomoses between the deep inferior epigastric vessels and internal mammary vessels. What is the best management strategy?
A) Connect the superficial inferior epigastric vein to an internal mammary vessel perforator
B) Switch to prosthetic reconstruction on the left
C) Administer tissue plasminogen activator to the deep inferior epigastric artery
D) Begin leech therapy
E) Revise the deep inferior epigastric vein anastomosis to the retrograde internal mammary vessel
questions.answer:
A)

Connecting the superficial inferior epigastric vein to an internal mammary vessel perforator is the appropriate salvage technique. Lower abdominal tissue drainage occurs primarily through superficial veins, with approximately 10% of patients having superficial venous system dominance. When deep venous drainage alone is insufficient despite patent anastomoses, augmenting drainage through the superficial system is necessary for flap salvage. This requires anastomosing the superficial inferior epigastric vein to available chest wall vessels. B is incorrect because flap salvage should be attempted before abandoning the reconstruction. C is incorrect because tPA treats thrombosis, but the vessels are patent without evidence of clotting. D is incorrect because leech therapy is adjunctive treatment after addressing surgical causes of congestion. E is incorrect because the deep system is already functioning, and revision wouldn't address the underlying venous drainage insufficiency.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female patient has a right dacryocystorhinostomy with an incision made at the medial canthus on the right side. Following surgery, she experiences difficulty with right upper eyelid closure. Which of the following most likely accounts for the impaired eyelid function?
A) Damage to the buccal branches of the facial nerve innervating the lateral canthal orbicularis oculi
B) Damage to the buccal branches of the facial nerve innervating the medial canthal orbicularis oculi
C) Damage to the temporal branches of the facial nerve supplying the orbicularis oculi
D) Damage to the zygomatic branches of the facial nerve innervating the lateral canthal orbicularis oculi
E) Damage to the zygomatic branches of the facial nerve innervating the medial canthal orbicularis oculi
questions.answer:
B)
The buccal branches of the facial nerve supply the medial canthal orbicularis oculi and are essential for blinking, eyelid closure, lower lid positioning, and lacrimal pump function. Injury to these branches during medial canthal surgery can significantly impair these functions. A is incorrect because the buccal branches do not innervate the lateral canthal region. C is incorrect because temporal branches provide minimal innervation to the orbicularis oculi. D is incorrect because zygomatic branches supply the lateral canthal area, not the medial surgical site. E is incorrect because zygomatic branches do not innervate the medial canthal orbicularis oculi.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male patient is assessed following a left zygomaticomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture. During surgical exploration via upper buccal sulcus, left eyebrow, and left transconjunctival approaches, the fracture extends through the infraorbital foramen, with significant depression and displacement of the left orbital floor fracture. Open reduction and internal fixation of both the orbital floor and ZMC fractures is completed. Which CPT code is most appropriate for this case?
A) 21360
B) 21365
C) 21390
D) 21360 and 21390
E) 21365 and 21390
questions.answer:
E)
21365 is the correct code for complex ZMC fracture repair requiring multiple approaches when the fracture involves the infraorbital foramen. 21390 should be billed separately for the orbital floor reconstruction as it represents a distinct procedure not bundled with ZMC repair. A is incorrect because 21360 is for simple ZMC repairs, not complex cases crossing the infraorbital foramen. B is incorrect because it omits the separate orbital floor repair code. C is incorrect because 21390 cannot be billed alone without the primary ZMC repair code. D is incorrect because 21360 is inappropriate for this complex fracture pattern.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male patient presents after failed conservative management of an exposed Achilles tendon wound. Examination reveals the tendon is becoming desiccated. A flap reconstruction is performed as demonstrated. Which artery provides the primary blood supply to this flap?
A) Anterior tibial
B) Geniculate
C) Peroneal
D) Popliteal
E) Superficial femoral
questions.answer:
C)
The reverse sural fasciocutaneous flap receives its blood supply from perforating vessels originating from the peroneal artery through a network of small vessels. This flap follows the course of the sural nerve from the lateral malleolus to the mid-gastrocnemius region. A is incorrect because the anterior tibial artery does not supply this flap. B is incorrect because geniculate arteries are located around the knee and do not contribute to this flap's blood supply. D is incorrect because the popliteal artery does not directly supply the reverse sural flap. E is incorrect because the superficial femoral artery is too proximal to provide blood supply to this lower leg flap.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old female patient develops an extravasation injury during a CT scan. A power injector delivered 100 mL of nonionic contrast through an IV cannula on the hand dorsum 60 minutes prior. Examination shows hand swelling with mild redness and moderate tenderness. The skin remains intact without blistering. Capillary refill is normal with no neurological impairment. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Corticosteroid administration
B) Immediate bedside exploration of the IV site
C) Extremity elevation
D) Surgical exploration with dorsal fasciotomy and carpal tunnel decompression
E) Surgical exploration with dorsal fasciotomy alone
questions.answer:
C)
For mild extravasation symptoms including pain, swelling, and erythema, extremity elevation combined with cold compresses typically leads to complete resolution. This conservative approach is the appropriate first-line treatment for mild cases without neurovascular compromise. A is incorrect because corticosteroids have no established role in extravasation injury management. B is incorrect because bedside exploration is not indicated for mild symptoms. D is incorrect because surgical intervention with extensive decompression is reserved for severe cases with neurovascular compromise. E is incorrect because any surgical exploration would be premature given the mild presentation.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman with a personal history of bilateral cleft lip and palate (gravida 1, para 2) seeks counseling about clefting risk in future pregnancies. One of her twin children has unilateral cleft lip and palate, while the other has lower lip pits but no clefting. No other family history of clefting exists in her family or her partner's family. What is the approximate likelihood that her next child will have cleft lip and/or palate?
A) 2.5%
B) 4%
C) 10%
D) 17%
E) 50%
questions.answer:
E)
This patient has Van der Woude syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition with incomplete penetrance that commonly presents with cleft lip/palate and lower lip pits. Since this follows autosomal dominant inheritance, each pregnancy has a 50% chance of being affected. A is incorrect because 2.5% represents the risk for isolated cleft lip with one affected sibling. B is incorrect because 4% represents the risk for unilateral cleft lip and palate with one affected sibling in non-syndromic cases. C is incorrect because 10% represents the risk with two affected siblings in non-syndromic clefting. D is incorrect because 17% represents the risk when both parent and sibling are affected in non-syndromic cases.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man presents with bilateral breast enlargement that has been stable for 3 years. Endocrine workup is normal and he takes no medications. Examination shows a firm, discrete disc of subareolar tissue measuring approximately 6 cm bilaterally, with only mild surrounding fatty fullness, normal-sized areolae, and good skin elasticity with no ptosis. Which of the following is the most important component of surgical management?
A) Reduction of nipple-areolar complex diameter
B) Excision of redundant chest skin
C) Liposuction of the lateral chest wall
D) Subtotal excision of the subareolar glandular disc
E) Ultrasound-assisted liposuction of the entire breast
questions.answer:
D)

When the dominant abnormality is firm fibroglandular tissue rather than fat, direct excision of the subareolar glandular disc — leaving only a thin (approximately 5–10 mm) layer of tissue beneath the areola — is the key maneuver. This addresses the tissue that liposuction cannot aspirate, lowers the risk of persistent or recurrent fullness, and preserves enough tissue to prevent a saucerized or adherent nipple deformity. Access is typically through an inferior periareolar incision, often combined with liposuction to feather the periphery.

A) is incorrect: this patient has normal areolar diameter, and areolar size commonly contracts once the underlying bulk is removed, so routine reduction is unnecessary.

B) is incorrect: skin excision is reserved for poor skin quality or true excess, as in massive weight loss or high-grade gynecomastia with ptosis; this patient has good elasticity and skin will retract.

C) is incorrect: lateral chest wall liposuction refines contour transitions but does not remove the fibrous glandular disc, which is the primary pathology here.

E) is incorrect: ultrasound-assisted liposuction improves aspiration of fibrous tissue and can reduce the amount of open resection required, but it cannot reliably clear a dense 6 cm glandular disc and is an adjunct rather than a substitute for excision.

questions.question:
A healthy 38-year-old man presents to the emergency room after accidentally striking his non-dominant left index fingertip with a hammer. He has a 20-pack-year smoking history. Examination reveals a subungual hematoma from nail bed injury, along with fingertip swelling and bruising. No vital structures are exposed. A digital nerve block is performed using 1% lidocaine with 1:200,000 epinephrine. Two hours post-injection, the finger appears pale and cold. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Give low-dose aspirin
B) Apply warm compresses to the finger
C) Raise the hand above heart level
D) Inject phentolamine locally
E) Apply topical papaverine to the finger
questions.answer:
D)

Local phentolamine injection is the correct treatment for epinephrine-induced digital vasoconstriction. As an alpha-receptor antagonist, phentolamine directly reverses epinephrine's vasoconstrictive effects and can salvage the digit. A) is incorrect because aspirin won't counteract vasoconstriction and is mainly used for vascular patency in replantation cases. B) is incorrect because warm compresses treat cold-induced vascular compromise but cannot reverse pharmacologic vasoconstriction from epinephrine. C) is incorrect because hand elevation will not address epinephrine-induced vasospasm. E) is incorrect because topical papaverine cannot effectively reverse epinephrine-induced vasospasm when vessels aren't directly accessible, and direct injection of a reversal agent is more appropriate.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman presents with impaired grip strength in her dominant right hand following a stab injury to her left forearm 6 months prior. Examination reveals a positive Tinel sign over the ulnar mid-forearm with a healed scar. Surgery identifies a neuroma-in-continuity, which is excised, leaving a 3-cm nerve defect. What is the optimal management approach?
A) Use a synthetic nerve tube to bridge the defect
B) Mobilize nerve ends proximally and distally for direct repair
C) Perform tendon transfers to improve grip function
D) Reconstruct using lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve graft
E) Perform sural nerve cable grafting
questions.answer:
E)

Sural nerve cable grafting is the optimal choice for bridging this 3-cm motor nerve defect. The sural nerve, derived from the tibial nerve's medial cutaneous branch, provides excellent graft material for such reconstructions. A) is incorrect because synthetic conduits are ineffective for gaps exceeding 2 cm and perform poorly in motor nerve repairs. B) is incorrect because tension-free repair is essential, and bridging a 3-cm gap would create excessive tension requiring nerve grafting instead. C) is incorrect because tendon transfers are premature at this stage when nerve reconstruction remains viable. D) is incorrect because the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve (musculocutaneous nerve continuation) is inadequate for the defect size and cable graft requirements.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy receives a free fibular flap for reconstruction after an 8-cm chondrosarcoma resection from his right humerus. What is the principal mechanism underlying bone healing in this case?
A) Endochondral ossification
B) Osteoconduction
C) Osteogenesis
D) Osteoinduction
questions.answer:
C)

Osteogenesis represents the primary healing mechanism in vascularized bone grafts, where osteoblasts form new bone at the host-graft junction. The maintained vascular supply keeps osteocytes viable, reducing remodeling and preserving bone strength and mass. A) is incorrect because endochondral ossification describes the conversion of cartilaginous callus to bone during fracture healing, not the mechanism in vascularized grafts. B) is incorrect because osteoconduction (creeping substitution) involves materials serving as scaffolds for bone growth, which applies to cortical grafts and bone matrix rather than vascularized grafts. D) is incorrect because osteoinduction involves direct stem cell stimulation by bone morphogenetic proteins to create osteoprogenitor cells, which is the primary mechanism for BMP and cancellous grafts, not vascularized bone.

questions.question:
A 52-year-old man requires reconstruction of a nasal defect after right nasal resection for advanced squamous cell carcinoma. Examination shows a full-thickness defect of the right lateral nasal wall, with preserved nasal ala and tip subunits. What vessel supplies the most suitable lining flap?
A) Anterior ethmoid artery
B) Facial artery
C) Inferior labial artery
D) Radial artery
E) Supratrochlear artery
questions.answer:
A)

The anterior ethmoid artery supplies the contralateral mucoperichondrial flap, which is ideal for lining this lateral nasal wall defect. This intranasal flap allows simultaneous cartilage graft placement and septal cartilage harvest for structural support. B) is incorrect because the facial artery supplies the nasolabial flap, typically reserved for smaller defects, particularly alar reconstruction. C) is incorrect because the inferior labial artery supplies lip tissue and isn't useful for nasal reconstruction. D) is incorrect because the radial artery supplies the radial forearm flap, usually reserved for total or subtotal nasal reconstruction rather than this specific defect. E) is incorrect because the supratrochlear artery supplies the forehead flap used for external skin coverage, not internal lining.

questions.question:
During bilateral component separation for abdominal wall reconstruction, which anatomical location typically allows for the greatest degree of tissue advancement?
A) Arcuate line
B) Ligament of Treitz
C) Suprapubic region
D) Umbilical area
E) Xiphoid process
questions.answer:
D)
The umbilical area provides the maximum advancement during component separation procedures. This technique involves releasing the external oblique fascia lateral to the rectus muscles, creating innervated musculofascial flaps that can be mobilized medially. At the umbilical level (waist area), approximately 10 cm of advancement per rectus muscle can be achieved, which is significantly greater than the 4 cm possible at other levels. A is incorrect because the arcuate line is in the suprapubic region where only 4 cm advancement is possible. B is incorrect because the ligament of Treitz is located in the epigastric area, also limited to 4 cm advancement. C is incorrect because the suprapubic area only allows 4 cm of advancement per side. E is incorrect because the xiphoid process is in the epigastric region with the same 4 cm limitation.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old girl is brought to the office because of the lower eyelid colobomas and malar deficiency shown in the photograph. Which of the following syndromes is most likely?


A) Apert
B) Crouzon
C) Goldenhar
D) Pfeiffer
E) Treacher Collins
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Bilateral lower eyelid colobomas are commonly found in patients with Treacher Collins syndrome (TCS). TCS is also known as mandibulofacial dysostosis, first and second branchial arch syndrome, and Franceschetti-Zwahlen-Klein syndrome. Edward Treacher Collins described the syndrome in 1900. It is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance and has an incidence of 1 in 7,000 live births. It has significant dysmorphology, which includes lower eyelid colobomas, clefted and hypoplastic zygomas, clefted lateral orbit, hypoplastic mandible, lateral canthal vertical dystopia, antimongolian palpebral fissure, ear deformities, long anterior sideburns, anterior open bite, cleft palate, and macrostomia.


Crouzon, Apert, and Pfeiffer syndromes involve craniosynostosis, typically bicoronal. These patients also have underdevelopment of the mid face also. They do not have any eyelid abnormalities. Apert patients also may have a cleft palate and syndactyly of the hands and feet.


Goldenhar syndrome involves epibulbar dermoids of one or both eyes and underdevelopment of one or both sides of the face. It is also known as hemifacial and bifacial microsomia. The soft tissue as well as the bone is hypoplastic.


References
1. Hunt JA, Hobar PC. Common craniofacial anomalies: the facial dysostoses. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2002 Dec;110(7):1714-1725.
2. Marszalek B, W√≥jcicki P, Kobus K, et al. Clinical features, treatment and genetic background of Treacher Collins syndrome. J Appl Genet. 2002;43(2):223-233.
3. Passos-Bueno MR, Ornelas CC, Fanganiello RD. Syndromes of the first and second pharyngeal arches: A review. Am J Med Genet A. 2009 Aug;149A(8):1853-1859.
4. Vander Kolk CA, Menezes J. Craniofacial syndromes. In: Mathes SJ, Hentz VR, eds. Plastic Surgery. 2nd ed. Philadelphia: WB Saunders; 2006:91-134.

questions.question:
What orbital abnormality is characteristically seen in patients diagnosed with Apert syndrome?
A) Enophthalmos
B) Esotropia
C) Exophthalmos
D) Exorbitism
E) Exotropia
questions.answer:
D)
Exorbitism is the characteristic orbital finding in Apert syndrome, describing globe protrusion caused by reduced bony orbital volume secondary to craniosynostosis. This differs from exophthalmos, which results from increased orbital soft tissue content rather than decreased bony space. A is incorrect because enophthalmos involves globe recession into the orbit due to increased bony volume or malposition, opposite to what occurs in Apert syndrome. B is incorrect because esotropia is inward eye deviation (strabismus), not related to globe position relative to the orbit. C is incorrect because exophthalmos describes globe protrusion from increased orbital contents, not decreased orbital volume as seen in craniosynostosis. E is incorrect because exotropia is outward eye deviation (strabismus), unrelated to orbital volume changes.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old ambulatory male develops an 8 × 4 × 4-cm stage III pressure ulcer with indurated bursa over the right ischium following 3 weeks of ICU care after head trauma. The wound persists despite 6 weeks of conservative management. Following nutritional optimization and bursal excision, what surgical approach is most suitable for reconstruction?
A) Gracilis musculocutaneous rotation flap
B) Negative pressure wound therapy followed by primary closure
C) Posterior thigh fasciocutaneous rotation flap
D) Superiorly based gluteal musculocutaneous rotation flap
E) Tensor fasciae latae island rotation flap
questions.answer:
C)
A posterior thigh fasciocutaneous rotation flap is optimal for ambulatory patients with chronic ischial pressure ulcers because it preserves muscle function while providing reliable axial blood supply and durable coverage. This approach maintains normal anatomical relationships over bony prominences without causing functional deficits. A is incorrect because musculocutaneous flaps, while offering excellent vascularity, may cause functional impairment in ambulatory patients. B is incorrect because primary closure has high recurrence rates due to large dead spaces and tissue induration making tension-free closure difficult. D is incorrect because gluteal musculocutaneous flaps can compromise function in ambulatory patients despite their good blood supply. E is incorrect because the distal portion of tensor fasciae latae flaps reaching the ischial region is typically too thin to provide adequate padding for effective reconstruction.

questions.question:
What feature most reliably differentiates keloid scars from hypertrophic scars?
A) Collagen fibers oriented parallel to the wound direction
B) Growth beyond the original wound boundaries
C) Favorable response to surgical excision alone
D) Elevated fibroblast density
E) Predominant occurrence on flexor surfaces and mobile areas
questions.answer:
B)
Keloid scars are distinguished by their ability to grow beyond the original wound boundaries, while hypertrophic scars remain confined within the initial injury margins. This characteristic expansion is the key differentiating feature between these two types of pathological scarring. A is incorrect because keloids actually contain wavier, more disorganized collagen fibers compared to the more parallel arrangement seen in hypertrophic scars. C is incorrect because keloids have high recurrence rates following surgical excision alone, making this treatment approach generally ineffective. D is incorrect because both keloid and hypertrophic scars exhibit increased fibroblast density, making this feature non-discriminatory. E is incorrect because hypertrophic scars typically occur on flexor surfaces and joints, while keloids more commonly develop on the sternum and earlobes.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old right-handed carpenter presents with progressive dominant hand discomfort, including work-related cramping, cold sensitivity, ulnar finger tingling, and difficulty gripping heavy objects. He is a non-smoker. Examination reveals diminished sensation, pallor, and prolonged capillary refill in the ring and little fingers. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Hypothenar hammer syndrome
B) Raynaud disease
C) Thoracic outlet syndrome
D) Thromboangiitis obliterans
E) Ulnar tunnel syndrome
questions.answer:
A)
This presentation is classic for hypothenar hammer syndrome, involving trauma-induced ulnar artery thrombosis from repetitive palm trauma. The condition predominantly affects males (9:1 ratio) aged 40-60 in occupations involving repetitive hand trauma, presenting with unilateral ulnar-sided symptoms including hypothenar pain, cold sensitivity, and ulnar finger ischemia. B is incorrect because Raynaud disease is an idiopathic vasospastic disorder more common in young females, typically bilateral, affecting all fingers with characteristic white-blue-red color changes. C is incorrect because thoracic outlet syndrome involves subclavian vessel and brachial plexus compression with more diffuse symptoms and rarely specific ulnar hand vascular compromise. D is incorrect because thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger disease) is a smoking-related vasculitis that is typically bilateral, not localized to the ulnar hand, and progresses to severe ischemia with ulceration. E is incorrect because ulnar tunnel syndrome involves nerve compression rather than vascular compromise and wouldn't present with the ischemic findings described.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male presents for a follow-up visit 2 weeks following open reduction and internal fixation of a right zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture. The surgery was completed using intraoral and subtarsal eyelid approaches. Physical examination reveals ectropion of the right lower eyelid. Ophthalmologic evaluation demonstrates normal vision with an intact cornea. What is the most appropriate management for this ectropion?
A) Tarsoconjunctival flap coverage
B) Lateral canthal reconstruction
C) Middle lamella allograft placement
D) External lamella skin grafting
E) Conservative management with massage
questions.answer:
E)
Conservative management with massage is most appropriate. Eyelid complications occur in 10-20% of patients following orbital fracture repair, primarily due to edema and swelling during the initial surgery. Most cases of ectropion and scleral show resolve spontaneously within several weeks. Conservative treatment including massage, tarsorrhaphy, and topical steroids is recommended initially. A is incorrect because tarsoconjunctival flaps are used for more complex reconstructions when conservative measures fail. B is incorrect because lateral canthal procedures are reserved for cases with permanent deformity after conservative treatment. C is incorrect because allograft placement is used for structural defects rather than temporary post-surgical ectropion. D is incorrect because skin grafting is indicated for cases with actual tissue loss or permanent contracture.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female with a history of scalp squamous cell carcinoma previously treated with excision, skin grafting, and complete scalp irradiation presents with osteoradionecrosis of the cranial vertex. Following complete debridement of necrotic tissue, what is the most appropriate soft-tissue reconstruction method?
A) Free latissimus dorsi musculocutaneous flap coverage
B) Pedicled trapezius musculocutaneous flap coverage
C) Local scalp rotation flap coverage
D) Negative pressure wound therapy
E) Split-thickness skin grafting
questions.answer:
A)
A free latissimus dorsi musculocutaneous flap is the optimal choice for this radiated, full-thickness cranial vertex defect. This provides well-vascularized tissue with reliable blood supply to the previously irradiated field. B is incorrect because pedicled trapezius flaps cannot reach the vertex without excessive tension and are better for occipital defects. C is incorrect because scalp rotation flaps are compromised in radiated fields and are limited to smaller defects in non-radiated scalp. D is incorrect because negative pressure therapy alone cannot provide definitive soft-tissue coverage over an implant in a radiated field. E is incorrect because skin grafts require a well-vascularized bed and are not suitable over implants in radiated tissue.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old female with a history of left mastectomy for breast cancer 10 years prior undergoes biopsy of a suspicious right breast lesion identified on recent mammography. Pathological examination of the biopsy confirms right breast carcinoma. This malignancy most likely arose from which of the following anatomical structures?
A) Fat tissue
B) Nipple-areolar skin
C) Mammary duct
D) Lymphatic tissue
E) Pectoralis major muscle
questions.answer:
C)
Mammary ducts are the most likely origin for this breast carcinoma. Breast cancers are typically adenocarcinomas arising from glandular structures including ducts and lobules. Women with prior breast cancer have increased risk for contralateral metachronous lesions. A is incorrect because sarcomas arising from adipose tissue are rare in the breast. B is incorrect because while Paget disease can involve areolar skin, it is uncommon compared to ductal carcinomas. D is incorrect because breast adenocarcinomas do not originate from lymphatic structures. E is incorrect because muscle-derived sarcomas are extremely rare in breast tissue.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after sustaining an injury to the arm during a motor vehicle collision. A photograph is shown. Physical examination shows inability to extend the index or long fingers, and a rent in the dorsal wrist capsule. Which of the following extensor zones is most likely involved?


A) II
B) III
C) IV
D) V
E) VI
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


The patient described sustained a dorsal wrist injury involving extensors of the wrist and fingers, with the injury at the base of the hand and over the carpus. Typically this is considered zones VI and VII. The other zones represent the following areas with some common conditions listed for each zone. Knowing and reporting zones of injury are helpful not just for descriptive purposes, but also for communicating with other doctors and therapists. Common therapy protocols are based on which zone or zones are involved in the injury.






References
1. Moore KL, Dalley AF. Clinically Oriented Anatomy. 5th ed. Philadelphia: Lippincott Williams & Wilkins; 2005:725-884.
2. Strauch RJ. Extensor Tendon Injury. In: Wolfe SW, Pederson WC, Hotchkiss RN, et al, eds. Green‚Äos Operative Hand Surgery. Vol 1. 6th ed. Philadelphia: Churchill Livingstone; 2010:159-188.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old man undergoes resection of a sarcoma involving the posterior neck. Photographs are shown. Which of the following arteries supplies the musculocutaneous flap used to reconstruct this defect?


A ) Circumflex scapular
B ) Deep temporal
C ) Internal carotid 
D ) Superficial temporal
E ) Transverse cervical
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


The transverse cervical artery is the blood supply to the trapezius flap which is used to reconstruct the defect described. 


The circumflex scapular artery is the blood supply to the scapular/parascapular flap. This artery has a length of approximately 6 to 7 cm and does not have the arc of rotation to reach a posterior neck defect. 


The deep temporal artery is the blood supply of the temporalis muscle. The arc of rotation of this muscle does not enable repair of posterior neck defects. 


The internal carotid artery does not give rise to branches that supply the muscles of the neck/back that may be useful for reconstruction of this defect. 


The superficial temporal artery is the blood supply of the superficial temporal fascia. This flap is quite thin with a limited reach and would not be appropriate for reconstruction of an extensive resection that includes skin, subcutaneous tissues, and muscle as shown.


References
1. Ugurlu K, Oz√ßelik D, H√ºth√ºt I, et al. Extended vertical trapezius myocutaneous flap in head and neck reconstruction as a salvage procedure. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2004 Aug;114(2):339-350.
2. Halvorson EG, Avram R, Disa JJ. The lower trapezius "reverse-turnover" flap. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2008 Jul;122(1):45e-46e.

questions.question:
