The lesion could represent a post-traumatic subungual hematoma, benign nevus, or subungual melanoma. Variegated color and irregular borders raise suspicion for melanoma. A shave biopsy provides adequate tissue for diagnosis without the nail bed deformity that could result from a core biopsy. Since nail bed histology and staging differ from skin, depth assessment through core biopsy is unnecessary. A) Amputation to the next joint is incorrect because definitive surgical treatment should not be performed without first establishing a diagnosis through biopsy. B) Radiation therapy is incorrect because treatment cannot be initiated without a confirmed diagnosis. D) Wide excision is incorrect because surgical treatment requires histologic confirmation before proceeding. E) Observation is incorrect because the lesion has persisted for 3 months without growing out to the sterile matrix, and without trauma history, malignancy must be ruled out rather than observed.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old male patient visits the clinic due to an infected lesion on the bottom of his left foot. His past medical history is significant for type 2 diabetes mellitus. The dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses cannot be felt by palpation but can be detected using a handheld Doppler device. An ankle brachial index measurement is not feasible due to incompressible blood vessels in the left lower leg below the knee. What is the most suitable next step for assessing the arterial blood flow to this patient's foot?
A) CT angiography
B) MR angiography
C) Invasive arteriography
D) Repeat ankle brachial index measurement
E) Toe brachial index
questions.answer:
E)
The most suitable next step for assessing arterial blood flow in this diabetic patient's foot is performing a toe-brachial index (TBI). The TBI is determined by dividing the systolic pressure in the great toe by the brachial systolic pressure. A value greater than 0.7 is regarded as normal. Diabetic patients frequently develop peripheral arterial disease, with atherosclerotic changes typically affecting below-knee arteries that often exhibit medial calcification, leading to vessel wall stiffening and unreliable ankle-brachial index readings. The small arteries in the great toes are typically unaffected by disease, making TBI a valuable diagnostic tool. A) CT angiography is incorrect because it is more invasive and would typically be reserved for cases where a normal TBI doesn't provide adequate information. B) MR angiography is incorrect because it is also more complex and would likely be unnecessary if TBI results are normal. C) Invasive arteriography is incorrect because it carries procedural risks and should be reserved for cases where surgical or endovascular interventions are being considered. D) Repeat ankle brachial index measurement is incorrect because the same technical limitations (incompressible vessels due to calcification) would persist, yielding similarly unreliable results.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male patient arrives with partial-thickness burn injuries covering 15% of his total body surface area from a residential fire. After stabilization and fluid resuscitation, topical 1% silver sulfadiazine cream is administered to the burned areas. What property best describes this antimicrobial medication?
A) Significantly improved effectiveness when combined with thiol chelating agents
B) Causes metabolic acidosis
C) Limited ability to penetrate the wound surface
D) Ineffective against Candida albicans
E) May cause transient increase in white blood cells
questions.answer:
C)
Silver sulfadiazine has limited penetration capacity into wound beds, particularly when eschar is present, because silver ions bind to surface proteins and remain primarily at the epithelial surface level. This represents a significant limitation of this otherwise commonly used topical antimicrobial agent. A) Significantly improved effectiveness when combined with thiol chelating agents is incorrect because this property is characteristic of bismuth compounds, not silver preparations. B) Causes metabolic acidosis is incorrect because this adverse effect is associated with mafenide acetate, not silver sulfadiazine. D) Ineffective against Candida albicans is incorrect because silver sulfadiazine actually provides good antifungal coverage, including against Candida species. E) May cause transient increase in white blood cells is incorrect because silver sulfadiazine typically causes reversible neutropenia (decreased white blood cells), not leukocytosis.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male patient develops a 3-cm ulcerative mass in his oropharynx that has grown progressively over 4 months. His physical examination is otherwise normal. Neck and chest CT imaging and liver function studies show no abnormalities. Besides obtaining a tissue biopsy of the lesion, what additional test would be most beneficial for this patient?
A) Head and neck CT angiography
B) p16 protein expression analysis
C) Sentinel lymph node sampling
D) Epstein-Barr virus IgA antibody levels
E) Urine cotinine measurement
questions.answer:
B)
p16 protein expression analysis is the most appropriate additional test because this lesion is suspicious for oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, and p16 serves as a marker for HPV-associated malignancy. HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers have distinct staging, prognosis, and treatment considerations compared to HPV-negative tumors, with HPV-positive cases generally having better outcomes and more indolent behavior. A) Head and neck CT angiography is incorrect because oropharyngeal cancers are not particularly vascular lesions, unlike juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibromas which occur in different anatomical locations. C) Sentinel lymph node sampling is incorrect because while it may assess for occult metastases, it would not be the immediate next diagnostic step and its role in squamous cell carcinoma remains debated. D) Epstein-Barr virus IgA antibody levels is incorrect because EBV is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not oropharyngeal malignancies. E) Urine cotinine measurement is incorrect because while tobacco exposure is a risk factor for head and neck cancers, cotinine testing doesn't aid in diagnosis or treatment planning.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with pain and swelling along the radial side of her distal forearm. The discomfort increases when she performs ulnar deviation of her wrist while grasping her thumb. Conservative treatment with immobilization and steroid injection has been unsuccessful, and surgical decompression is being considered. Which anatomical variation most likely contributed to her clinical condition?
A) Missing extensor pollicis brevis tendon
B) Fusion of first and second compartments
C) Muscle belly extending distally on extensor pollicis brevis
D) Multiple branches of abductor pollicis longus
E) Dividing septum between abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
questions.answer:
E)
A dividing septum between the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis within the first dorsal compartment is the anatomical variation most likely contributing to this patient's de Quervain's disease. The presence of such septa is significantly more common in patients with de Quervain's disease compared to the general population and often predicts failure of conservative treatments like steroid injections. During surgical release, recognition and complete division of these septa is essential for successful treatment. A) Missing extensor pollicis brevis tendon is incorrect because absence of this tendon is not associated with increased risk of de Quervain's disease. B) Fusion of first and second compartments is incorrect because this anatomical variation is not linked to de Quervain's syndrome development. C) Muscle belly extending distally on extensor pollicis brevis is incorrect because distal muscle bellies are not specifically associated with this condition. D) Multiple branches of abductor pollicis longus is incorrect because studies have shown no correlation between the number of APL slips and the development of de Quervain's disease.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old female patient has her 30-year-old round 280-cc silicone gel breast implants removed and replaced with new silicone gel implants that measure 10 cm in width, 12 cm in height, and have 5 cm of projection. Compared to her previous gel implants, the newer implants have an increased likelihood of which complication?
A) Capsular contracture
B) Infection
C) Visible rippling
D) Malposition
E) Device failure
questions.answer:
D)
The newer implants have an increased likelihood of malposition (rotation) because the described dimensions suggest shaped/anatomical implants rather than round ones. Shaped implants must be positioned precisely within an appropriately sized surgical pocket to prevent rotation, which can cause breast deformity and may require reoperation. While malrotation rates are generally low (approximately 1.5%) when proper surgical technique is used, this risk is essentially non-existent with round implants since rotation doesn't affect their appearance. A) Capsular contracture is incorrect because newer shaped implants typically have textured surfaces that actually reduce contracture rates compared to older smooth implants. B) Infection is incorrect because infection rates do not vary significantly between different implant types or generations. C) Visible rippling is incorrect because modern cohesive gel implants have lower rippling rates compared to older, less cohesive silicone or saline implants. E) Device failure is incorrect because newer generation implants have improved durability with lower rupture rates (approximately 0.7% annually) compared to older implant designs.

questions.question:
Transplant recipients receiving immunosuppressive medications are at highest risk for developing opportunistic pathogen infections during which of the following time frames following transplantation?
A) Between 1 month and 1 year post-transplant
B) Between 1 week and 1 month post-transplant
C) Beyond 1 year post-transplant
D) During days 3-7 post-transplant
E) In the first 48 hours post-transplant
questions.answer:
A)
Transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy face the greatest risk of opportunistic infections between 1 month and 1 year after transplantation. This period represents the time of maximum immunosuppression when classic opportunistic pathogens like cytomegalovirus, herpes viruses, Aspergillus, Nocardia, and Pneumocystis commonly cause infections. B is incorrect because the first month typically involves standard postoperative nosocomial infections rather than opportunistic ones. C is incorrect because after 12 months, immunosuppression is usually reduced and community-acquired infections become more common. D is incorrect because this early period involves typical surgical site infections. E is incorrect because infections within 48 hours are usually related to immediate surgical complications rather than immunosuppression-related opportunistic infections.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old man with controlled chronic hypertension undergoes facelift with neck muscle tightening and upper eyelid surgery. Six hours after surgery, he develops severe pain, firm swelling, and bruising on the left side of his face. What is the most probable cause of this swelling?
A) Excessive intraoperative fluid administration
B) Omission of blood pressure medications
C) Nausea from excessive narcotic use
D) Ketorolac use
E) Inadequate postoperative pain management
questions.answer:
B)
The most likely cause is omission of antihypertensive medications, leading to postoperative hypertension and subsequent hematoma formation. Patients with hypertension have an 8% hematoma risk after facelift compared to 3% in normotensive patients. Rebound hypertension occurs as injected epinephrine is absorbed, typically 4-10 hours postoperatively. Hypertensive patients should take their blood pressure medications on surgery day to prevent this complication. A is incorrect because while excess fluids can raise blood pressure, it's less likely than inadequate preoperative hypertension management. C is incorrect because nausea may contribute to hypertension but isn't the primary cause in a known hypertensive patient. D is incorrect because studies show ketorolac doesn't increase hematoma risk. E is incorrect because poor pain control may raise blood pressure but isn't the main factor in this hypertensive patient.

questions.question:
A 33-year-old woman seeks evaluation for facial discomfort. Examination reveals facial pain, jaw joint clicking sounds, and inability to close her front teeth together. What is the most frequent physical examination finding in jaw joint dysfunction?
A) Tooth pain
B) Jaw shifting during mouth opening
C) Bite misalignment
D) Enlarged chewing muscles
E) Tenderness when pressing on chewing muscles
questions.answer:
E)
Tenderness when palpating the muscles of mastication is the most consistent and common clinical finding in temporomandibular joint dysfunction. This condition predominantly affects women aged 20-40 years, and muscle tenderness is the hallmark physical sign. A is incorrect because localized tooth pain is not typically associated with TMJ dysfunction. B is incorrect because jaw deviation during opening, while possible, is not the most common finding. C is incorrect because bite problems like open bite are not proven to be major causes of TMJ dysfunction and don't respond well to bite correction therapy. D is incorrect because masseter muscle enlargement is specifically associated with teeth grinding (bruxism) rather than general TMJ dysfunction.

questions.question:
A 345-lb (156-kg), 5-ft 1-in (155-cm), 59-year-old woman comes to the office because of the condition of the lower extremities in the photograph shown. BMI is 65 kg/m2. She says she has tried "everything" and "nothing seems to work." She states that the left leg is worse than right. The condition first appeared over 20 years ago after she underwent surgery of the left leg. She was hospitalized 10 times for cellulitis/infection in the past 1 year. She refuses compression therapy because it has become too painful. Which of the following are the most likely diagnosis and most appropriate management?


A) Primary lymphedema; medical management
B) Primary lymphedema; surgical management
C) Secondary lymphedema; medical management
D) Secondary lymphedema; surgical management
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The morbidly obese patient described suffers from severe secondary lymphedema. Assuming she doesn‚Äot have any contraindications to an operative procedure, she has failed medical management and should be offered surgery.


Lower extremity lymphedema can be considered either primary or secondary. Primary lymphedema can be congenital, praecox, or tarda based on the age at presentation. Secondary lymphedema can be due to either lymphatic obstruction (due to cancer, infection, or radiation) or lymphatic interruption (due to groin surgery or lymph node excision).


By far, the most common approach to lymphedema (either primary or secondary) is medical management. However, the most common indication for surgery is failure of medical management.


There are a variety of surgical options. These include procedures to improve lymphatic flow and procedures to debulk the affected tissue.


References
1. Cormier JN, Rourke L, Crosby M, et al. The surgical treatment of lymphedema: a systematic review of the contemporary literature (2004-2010). Ann Surg Oncol. 2012 Feb;19(2):642-651. Epub 2011 Aug 24.
2. Murdaca G, Cagnati P, Gulli R, et al. Current views on diagnostic approach and treatment of lymphedema. Am J Med. 2012 Feb;125(2):134-140.
3. Tiwari A, Cheng KS, Button M, et al. Differential diagnosis, investigation, and current treatment of lower limb lymphedema. Arch Surg. 2003 Feb;138(2):152-161.
4. Warren AG, Brorson H, Borud LJ, et al. Lymphedema: a comprehensive review. Ann Plast Surg. 2007 Oct;59(4):464-472.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old man presents with an ear lesion. Biopsy reveals a melanoma measuring 2.01 mm in depth without surface breakdown, containing 11 cell divisions per microscopic field, and extending to the deep surgical margin. Which factor most significantly influences the surgeon's decision to perform sentinel lymph node biopsy?
A) Tumor depth measurement
B) Ear location
C) Absence of surface breakdown
D) Cell division count
E) Involvement of deep margin
questions.answer:
A)
Tumor depth (Breslow thickness) is the primary factor determining the need for sentinel lymph node biopsy. For intermediate-thickness melanomas (1-4 mm), the MSLT-1 trial demonstrated that sentinel node status is the strongest predictor of patient outcome. At 2.01 mm thickness, this melanoma falls into the intermediate category where sentinel node biopsy is indicated regardless of other factors. B is incorrect because head and neck location doesn't preclude sentinel node biopsy, as recent studies show similar accuracy to other body sites. C is incorrect because absence of ulceration doesn't influence the decision for sentinel node biopsy in tumors over 1 mm thick. D is incorrect because mitotic rate doesn't affect staging decisions for melanomas thicker than 1 mm. E is incorrect because positive deep margins may indicate sentinel node biopsy in thin melanomas but not in tumors already over 1 mm thick.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents one week after a golf-related hand injury. Examination reveals tenderness at the pinky side of her palm base and loss of sensation in her small finger. Which injury is most clearly visualized using a carpal tunnel radiographic view?
A) Hamate hook fracture
B) Lunotriquetral ligament tear
C) Scaphoid bone fracture
D) Scapholunate ligament rupture
E) Trapezium body fracture
questions.answer:
A)
A hamate hook fracture is best visualized using the carpal tunnel view, which is a hyperextended wrist radiograph that displays the carpal tunnel anatomy. This specialized view clearly shows the hook of the hamate, pisotriquetral joint, and palmar surfaces of the trapezium, pisiform, and triquetrum bones. The clinical presentation of ulnar-sided palm tenderness and small finger numbness is consistent with hamate hook injury. B is incorrect because lunotriquetral separation is better seen on standard wrist views or specialized stress views. C is incorrect because scaphoid fractures require dedicated scaphoid views for optimal visualization. D is incorrect because scapholunate dissociation is best evaluated with stress views and standard radiographs. E is incorrect because trapezium body fractures are typically visible on standard anteroposterior and lateral wrist radiographs.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 10 weeks' gestation presents with a 1.5-mm thick melanoma on her right cheek. Lymphatic mapping is being considered. What is the most suitable management approach for this patient?
A) Wide excision under general anesthesia with 0.5-cm margins plus immediate sentinel lymph node biopsy
B) Wide excision under general anesthesia with 1-cm margins plus immediate sentinel lymph node biopsy
C) Wide excision under general anesthesia with 2-cm margins plus immediate sentinel lymph node biopsy
D) Wide excision under local anesthesia with 0.5-cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy in second trimester
E) Wide excision under local anesthesia with 1-cm margins and sentinel lymph node biopsy in second trimester
questions.answer:
E)

The correct approach is wide local excision under local anesthesia with 1-cm margins and delayed sentinel lymph node biopsy during the second trimester. Current guidelines from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists recommend deferring non-urgent surgical procedures to the second trimester to reduce risks of spontaneous abortion and preterm labor. For melanomas measuring 1.01-2.0 mm in thickness, the standard excision margin is 1 cm. A) is incorrect because 0.5-cm margins are inadequate for a 1.5-mm melanoma. B) is incorrect because general anesthesia in the first trimester carries increased risks. C) is incorrect because 2-cm margins are excessive for this thickness and general anesthesia is inappropriate timing. D) is incorrect because 0.5-cm margins are insufficient for adequate oncologic resection.

questions.question:
A 39-year-old woman presents with a 6-month history of increasing firmness and upper pole enlargement of her left breast. She underwent bilateral breast augmentation with textured saline implants placed in a dual-plane submuscular position 15 years prior. Physical examination reveals the left breast is larger, firmer, and has increased upper pole fullness compared to the right. What is the most appropriate initial step?
A) Complete capsulectomy with pocket revision
B) Mammographic imaging
C) Three-month trial with montelukast therapy
D) Magnetic resonance imaging
E) Ultrasound examination
questions.answer:
E)

Ultrasound examination is the most appropriate initial step to evaluate for periprosthetic fluid or capsular masses in a patient with late-onset breast changes who may have breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL). Ultrasound has equal or superior sensitivity and specificity compared to other imaging modalities for detecting seromas and allows for immediate aspiration if fluid is present. The fluid can then be sent for cytology and flow cytometry to test for CD30-positive T-cells. A) is incorrect because surgical intervention should not be performed until a diagnosis is established. B) is incorrect because mammography has limited utility in evaluating periprosthetic fluid in implant patients. C) is incorrect because montelukast therapy is unproven and inappropriate as an initial diagnostic step. D) is incorrect because while MRI may eventually be needed, ultrasound is the preferred first-line imaging study for this presentation.

questions.question:
An 8-year-old boy is scheduled for otoplasty to address protruding ears. The surgical plan includes antihelical fold reconstruction, conchal repositioning, and earlobe correction. Mustardé sutures will be utilized to create the antihelical fold. Where should the Mustardé sutures be positioned in this patient?
A) Between conchal cartilage and conchal cartilage
B) Between conchal cartilage and mastoid fascia
C) Between scaphal cartilage and conchal cartilage
D) Between scaphal cartilage and mastoid fascia
E) Between scaphal cartilage and scaphal cartilage
questions.answer:
C)

Mustardé sutures are horizontal mattress sutures placed between the scaphal cartilage and conchal cartilage to recreate the antihelical fold, which is the standard technique for otoplasty. This suture placement draws the scapha toward the concha, creating the desired antihelical fold contour. A) is incorrect because conchal-to-conchal sutures are used only when closing defects after conchal cartilage excision, not for antihelical fold creation. B) is incorrect because conchal-to-mastoid sutures are used for conchal setback procedures, not antihelical fold formation. D) is incorrect because scaphal-to-mastoid fixation would create severe pinning deformities and is not indicated. E) is incorrect because scaphal-to-scaphal sutures serve no purpose in standard otoplasty techniques.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old man presents for evaluation of a secondary palatal fistula following palatoplasty performed 20 years ago. He has a history of three failed fistula repairs using local tissue. A tongue flap is planned to provide soft tissue coverage for the palate. The primary vascular supply of the tongue is located in which area?
A) Lower third
B) Central third
C) Upper third
D) Evenly distributed throughout
questions.answer:
A)

The primary blood supply to the tongue comes from the paired lingual arteries, which run laterally within the lower (ventral) third of the tongue. Understanding this vascular anatomy is crucial for tongue flap procedures to ensure adequate perfusion. Additional blood supply comes from the facial and ascending pharyngeal arteries, with cross-circulation occurring mainly at the tongue tip while the median septum remains relatively avascular. B) is incorrect because the middle third does not contain the main vascular channels. C) is incorrect because the upper (dorsal) third has minimal primary vascularity. D) is incorrect because the blood supply is not evenly distributed but concentrated in the ventral third.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with left facial paralysis referred by her primary care physician. Two weeks ago, she was hiking and removed a tick from her leg. Three days ago, she developed a rash and fever. This morning, she awoke unable to move the left side of her face and experiences painful spasms on the right side when attempting to smile or speak. Physical examination confirms complete left facial paralysis. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's condition?
A) Antiviral therapy with acyclovir
B) Botulinum toxin type A injections
C) Contralateral facial nerve reconstruction with free muscle transfer
D) Corticosteroid treatment
E) Antibiotic therapy with doxycycline
questions.answer:
E)

This patient has facial paralysis secondary to Lyme disease (Lyme neuroborreliosis), evidenced by the tick exposure, characteristic rash, fever, and neurologic symptoms occurring within the typical timeframe. Doxycycline is the first-line antibiotic treatment for Lyme disease unless contraindicated. Treatment should target the underlying infection rather than the symptoms. A) is incorrect because antivirals are not effective against bacterial Lyme disease. B) is incorrect because while botulinum toxin can treat contralateral hyperkinesia, the primary disease should be addressed first. C) is incorrect because surgical reconstruction is premature and contraindicated in acute Lyme disease. D) is incorrect because corticosteroids are beneficial for Bell's palsy but not recommended for Lyme neuroborreliosis.

questions.question:
In velocardiofacial syndrome, the connection between facial abnormalities and heart defects stems from disrupted development of which cellular component?
A) Cardiac mesoderm
B) Ectodermal thickenings
C) Lateral mesoderm
D) Neural crest cells
E) Segmented mesoderm
questions.answer:
D)
Neural crest cells originate from the neuroectodermal layer of the developing embryo in the fore-, mid-, and hindbrain regions. These cells play a crucial role in craniofacial development and also contribute to the conotruncal endocardial cushions that separate the heart's outflow tract into distinct pulmonary and aortic pathways. Disruption of neural crest cell development commonly causes both facial and cardiac septal abnormalities, as seen in conditions like Treacher Collins syndrome, Pierre Robin sequence, 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, and oculoauriculovertebral syndrome. A is incorrect because cardiac mesoderm forms from splanchnic mesoderm and creates endocardial and myocardial precursors but doesn't contribute to head/neck structures. B is incorrect because ectodermal thickenings are distinct from neuroectoderm and help guide neural crest cells in cranial sensory ganglia formation. C is incorrect because lateral mesoderm contributes to laryngeal cartilages and associated connective tissue but not the specific structures affected in this syndrome. E is incorrect because segmented mesoderm forms skull, meninges, voluntary facial muscles, and dorsal head dermis/connective tissue but not the conotruncal cardiac components.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents with right jaw pain, speech difficulties, and swallowing problems 5 years after successful chemoradiation treatment for tongue base cancer. CT shows no recurrence or metastases. Panoramic radiograph reveals bilateral mandibular changes with right-sided pathologic fracture. What is the optimal treatment approach?
A) Mandibular debridement
B) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment
C) Open fracture repair with hardware
D) Vascularized fibular bone reconstruction
E) Rib bone grafting
questions.answer:
D)
This patient has bilateral osteoradionecrosis with pathologic fracture requiring comprehensive reconstruction. A vascularized fibular free flap provides the optimal solution because it can be fashioned into two osseous segments from a single pedicle, allowing restoration of the entire mandibular defect while minimizing anastomotic complexity in a previously irradiated neck. This approach restores function, improves occlusion, and addresses the underlying hypoperfusion problem. Modern stereolithographic modeling enables precise reconstruction in a single procedure. A is incorrect because debridement alone would leave the patient functionally disabled with bilateral involvement. B is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen's benefit for craniofacial osteoradionecrosis is questionable and wouldn't address the pathologic fracture. C is incorrect because the irradiated bone quality is poor and simple fixation won't promote healing or restore function. E is incorrect because free bone grafts without vascularized tissue don't address the fundamental hypoperfusion issue in irradiated bone.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman sustains deep partial and full-thickness burns to her face, neck, chest, back, and both arms in a cooking accident. After intubation, resuscitation, and surgical wound care, what is the optimal splinting position for the burned areas?
A) Elbow at full extension
B) Hand in claw position
C) Neck bent forward 45 degrees
D) Shoulder raised 60 degrees
E) Wrist bent down 10 degrees
questions.answer:
A)
The correct splinting position involves neck in slight extension, shoulder abducted to 90 degrees, elbow fully extended at 180 degrees, wrist in neutral or slight extension, and hands in intrinsic plus (functional) position. This positioning prevents contractures that would pull joints into positions causing functional limitations. Full elbow extension is specifically important to prevent flexion contractures that would significantly impair arm function. B is incorrect because the claw (intrinsic minus) position would lead to functional deficits - the intrinsic plus position is preferred. C is incorrect because neck flexion would promote contractures that limit neck extension and function. D is incorrect because 60 degrees of shoulder abduction is insufficient - 90 degrees is needed to prevent adduction contractures. E is incorrect because wrist flexion promotes contractures that limit hand function - neutral or slight extension is preferred.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old man with T3 spinal cord injury develops severe headache, nausea, flushing, and diaphoresis in recovery after ischial pressure sore debridement. Vital signs show temperature 37.0°C, blood pressure 180/90 mmHg, heart rate 50 bpm. What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?
A) Give intravenous dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg
B) Apply sublingual nitroglycerin
C) Place urinary catheter
D) Apply carotid pressure
E) Position patient head-down
questions.answer:
C)
This patient exhibits autonomic dysreflexia (AD), which occurs in 50-70% of patients with spinal injuries above T6. The syndrome results from uncontrolled sympathetic response to stimuli, commonly bladder distention, bowel impaction, or musculoskeletal irritation. Initial management focuses on identifying and removing precipitating factors, with bladder distention being the most frequent cause. Inserting a Foley catheter addresses potential bladder distention as the trigger. The constellation of headache, hypertension, bradycardia, and flushing above the lesion level is classic for AD. A is incorrect because dantrolene treats malignant hyperthermia, not autonomic dysreflexia. B is incorrect because nitrates are not first-line treatment for AD - nifedipine may be used secondarily if needed. D is incorrect because carotid massage increases vagal stimulation and is contraindicated in this hypertensive patient. E is incorrect because Trendelenburg position is used for hypotension, not hypertension.

questions.question:
A 39-year-old woman seeks evaluation for abdominal appearance concerns. Her obstetric history includes five pregnancies: two full-term births and three second-trimester pregnancy losses. She doesn't use hormonal contraception. Examination reveals significant rectus separation and excess abdominal skin. BMI is 28 kg/m2. Abdominoplasty with umbilical repositioning is planned. Which complication risk is most elevated in this patient?
A) Venous thromboembolism
B) Bleeding complications
C) Surgical site infection
D) Muscle separation recurrence
E) Incision breakdown
questions.answer:
A)
The patient's history of two second-trimester pregnancy losses is a significant red flag for underlying thrombophilia (both inherited and acquired conditions), substantially increasing her risk for venous thromboembolism. This obstetric history necessitates further evaluation for clotting disorders and mandatory chemoprophylaxis if surgery proceeds. Factor V Leiden, the most common inherited thrombophilia, affects 3-7% of Caucasians, and multiple thrombophilic conditions can coexist. While BMI ≥30 kg/m2 increases abdominoplasty complications, this patient's BMI of 28 doesn't significantly elevate other complication risks. B is incorrect because her history and examination don't suggest increased bleeding risk beyond the thrombophilia concern. C is incorrect because no factors specifically increase infection risk in this case. D is incorrect because no specific risk factors for recurrent diastasis are present. E is incorrect because wound dehiscence risk isn't specifically elevated based on the provided information.

questions.question:
A healthy 14-year-old male presents with bilateral breast tissue growth developing over the last 3 months. He expresses concern about peer awareness. He denies recreational drug use and is not on any medications. Clinical examination reveals age-appropriate hair pattern, absence of testicular abnormalities, and palpable firm tissue discs beneath both areolae. What is the most suitable initial management approach?
A) Subareolar direct excision preserving a small tissue button with peripheral breast liposuction
B) Complete breast liposuction using cutting cannula beneath the areola
C) Clinical reassessment in 9 months
D) Testosterone supplementation
E) Wise pattern skin removal with nipple transplantation
questions.answer:
C)
This patient demonstrates typical pubertal gynecomastia, which frequently resolves without intervention. The appropriate management is watchful waiting with follow-up evaluation. Surgical intervention early in the course is typically reserved for cases with severe psychological distress. Testosterone therapy would be inappropriate as the patient shows normal physiological development otherwise. While the three surgical options represent valid treatments for gynecomastia, surgery is generally not recommended within the initial six months of gynecomastia onset in adolescent males. A is incorrect because early surgical intervention is not indicated for typical pubertal gynecomastia. B is incorrect as it represents premature surgical treatment. D is incorrect because testosterone replacement is not indicated in normal pubertal development. E is incorrect as this extensive procedure would only be considered for severe cases with significant skin and fat excess.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female presents with a 6-year history of bilateral lower extremity lymphedema causing persistent fatigue and leg swelling that interferes with routine activities. Conservative management including weight reduction, compression therapy, and daily pneumatic compression has failed. Left thigh examination demonstrates thick, fibrotic, non-pitting tissue with a circumference 10 cm greater than the right thigh. What is the most suitable surgical intervention?
A) Buried dermal flap procedures
B) Microsurgical lympholymphatic connections
C) Omental transfer
D) Sequential skin and subcutaneous tissue removal
E) Complete excision of all skin and subcutaneous layers
questions.answer:
D)
Sequential skin and subcutaneous tissue removal has emerged as the preferred approach for many surgeons. This technique is safe, dependable, and demonstrates the most consistent outcomes with minimal complications. Physiologic reconstructive procedures have not demonstrated favorable long-term outcomes. A is incorrect because buried dermal flaps have not shown sustained long-term benefits. B is incorrect as microvascular lympholymphatic anastomoses lack favorable long-term results. C is incorrect because omental transposition has not proven effective long-term. E is incorrect as total excision is too aggressive and associated with higher morbidity than staged procedures.

questions.question:
A healthy 17-year-old female with congenital absence of the vagina seeks consultation for vaginal reconstruction. Clinical examination demonstrates normal external genital anatomy but complete absence of the vaginal canal. She requests a single-stage procedure with minimal scarring and optimal sensation. What is the most suitable reconstructive approach?
A) Bilateral gracilis muscle-skin flaps
B) Bilateral pudendal fasciocutaneous flaps
C) Extended groin flap
D) Split-thickness skin graft with mold (McIndoe technique)
E) Vertical rectus abdominis muscle-skin flap
questions.answer:
B)
Bilateral pudendal fasciocutaneous flaps represent the optimal choice for this patient. These flaps utilize branches of the superficial perineal vessels (terminal branches of internal pudendal vessels) and can incorporate the superficial perineal nerve for sensation. They are technically straightforward, reliable, completed in one stage, thin, sensate, and ideal for vaginal reconstruction. The donor site closes primarily with well-concealed scars in the groin crease. A is incorrect because gracilis flaps lack sensation and create conspicuous donor scars. C is incorrect as extended groin flaps are insensate. D is incorrect because the McIndoe procedure creates less concealed donor site scarring and requires ongoing dilation. E is incorrect because rectus flaps are insensate and leave large, visible donor scars.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old female presents with acute extensor tendon rupture following conservative management of a non-displaced distal radius fracture 6 months prior. Which extensor compartment most likely contains the affected tendon?
A) First
B) Second
C) Third
D) Fourth
E) Fifth
questions.answer:
C)
Spontaneous extensor pollicis longus (EPL) tendon rupture occurs in approximately 0.3-5% of non-displaced or minimally displaced distal radius fractures. This results from vascular compromise and degenerative changes within the compartment. The tendon is typically too degenerated for primary repair, requiring tendon transfer using extensor indicis proprius. The EPL traverses the third extensor compartment. A is incorrect because the first compartment contains abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis, which rarely rupture spontaneously after distal radius fractures. B is incorrect as the second compartment houses the extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis, which are not typically affected. D is incorrect because the fourth compartment contains extensor digitorum communis and extensor indicis proprius, not commonly involved in post-fracture ruptures. E is incorrect as the fifth compartment contains extensor digiti minimi, which is rarely affected in this scenario.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old female with moderate neck skin looseness, minimal submental adiposity, moderate cheek sagging, and moderate jowl formation undergoes short scar facelift using the dual-suture minimal access cranial suspension method. Upon completing skin closure, a vertical skin fold appears near the earlobe in the lateral neck region. What is the optimal approach to manage this vertical skin fold?
A) Extend the facelift incision behind the ear with excess skin removal
B) Insert a third purse-string superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) plication suture
C) Re-position the cheek flap in a superior direction
D) Perform a subsideburn wedge removal
E) Monitor without intervention
questions.answer:
A)
A significant limitation of short scar facelifts involves patients with substantial skin redundancy. When postauricular incisions are omitted, as in traditional minimal access cranial suspension, vertical skin folds may develop in the lateral neck below the earlobe in patients with moderate to severe neck laxity. The optimal treatment involves extending the incision posteriorly in the conventional postauricular fashion, elevating a postauricular skin flap, and removing the excess tissue. B is incorrect because the third purse-string suture addresses midface issues, not skin excess. C is incorrect as flap re-rotation creates closure problems in the visible temporal area without addressing horizontal neck skin excess. D is incorrect because subsideburn wedge excision provides vertical cheek elevation but incorrect vector for this problem. E is incorrect as the skin fold typically persists without surgical correction.

questions.question:
An infant presents with a cystic lesion anterior to the tragus and a visible sinus opening within the external auditory canal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Epidermoid cyst
B) First branchial cleft cyst
C) Second branchial cleft cyst
D) Third branchial cleft cyst
E) Lymphatic malformation
questions.answer:
B)
The first branchial cleft gives rise to the external auditory canal. During embryologic development, the second, third, and fourth branchial clefts normally fuse to create the sinus of His, which typically involutes. Failure of proper involution results in branchial cleft cyst formation. Sometimes both the branchial pouch and cleft fail to involute, creating a complete fistulous connection between the pharynx and skin surface. First branchial cleft cysts are classified as type I and type II variants. Type I lesions occur near the external auditory canal, typically positioned inferior and posterior to the tragus, though they may also involve the parotid gland. Type II variants appear at the mandibular angle and may affect the submandibular gland. Second branchial cleft anomalies represent 95% of all branchial abnormalities, typically presenting along the anterior margin of the upper sternocleidomastoid muscle. Third branchial cleft cysts are uncommon, with fistulas extending from similar skin locations as second branchial fistulas but coursing posterior to the carotid vessels. A is incorrect because congenital epidermoid cysts typically occur at the lateral orbital region over the zygomaticofrontal suture. C is incorrect because second branchial cleft cysts present along the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not near the external auditory canal. D is incorrect because third branchial cleft cysts are rare and located deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. E is incorrect because lymphatic malformations can occur anywhere on the face but do not present with sinus tracts into the external auditory canal.

questions.question:
In normal development, which of the following cranial sutures undergoes physiologic closure earliest?
A) Sagittal
B) Metopic
C) Coronal
D) Lambdoid
E) Squamosal
questions.answer:
B)
Normal physiologic closure of the metopic suture occurs earliest among all cranial sutures. Contemporary research indicates closure begins earlier than previously documented, potentially starting as early as 6 months of age, with most children showing a fused metopic suture by 9 to 12 months. The remaining sutures close significantly later in life: the sagittal suture closes around 22 years, the coronal suture at approximately 24 years, the lambdoid suture near 26 years, and the squamosal suture at about 35 years of age. A is incorrect because the sagittal suture closes much later at around 22 years. C is incorrect because the coronal suture closes at approximately 24 years. D is incorrect because the lambdoid suture closes around 26 years. E is incorrect because the squamosal suture is the last to close at about 35 years.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old male presents with purulent discharge from the distal wound margin 2 weeks following free latissimus dorsi muscle flap reconstruction for a motorcycle-related degloving injury of the left lower leg. Initial emergency evaluation revealed a Gustilo type IIIB tibia/fibula fracture with 6 cm of tibial bone loss. Primary bone debridement and external fixation were performed immediately, with soft-tissue reconstruction completed 8 days post-injury. Current examination demonstrates purulent drainage from the inferior flap region. What is the most probable cause of this complication?
A) Patient age
B) Delayed soft-tissue reconstruction
C) Distal flap tissue death
D) Insufficient debridement
questions.answer:
D)
Lower extremity post-traumatic reconstruction involving substantial soft-tissue defects exposing bone, joints, and tendons typically requires free tissue transfer. The Gustilo-Anderson classification system describes these injuries when associated with long bone fractures. Type IIIB fractures involve periosteal stripping and bone exposure with contamination. While Godina advocated for coverage within 72 hours of injury in 1986, the complex nature of polytrauma injuries often prevents this timeline. Staged debridement and negative pressure therapy have become standard management approaches. Insufficient bone or soft-tissue debridement before reconstruction commonly causes failure, as the wound must be completely free of contaminants prior to reconstruction. A is incorrect because patient age does not contribute to this specific complication. B is incorrect because an 8-day delay is unlikely to cause breakdown given current management standards. C is incorrect because distal flap necrosis would present with superficial breakdown rather than deep space infection.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents for evaluation 6 weeks post-septorhinoplasty with clear nasal drainage. He reports the discharge increases with forward bending or straining and has a salty taste. Physical examination reveals minimal watery drainage from the right nostril, with nasal speculum examination showing no additional abnormalities. What is the most appropriate initial management step?
A) Skull base MRI
B) Beta-2 transferrin fluid analysis
C) Fluid glucose testing
D) Corticosteroid nasal spray trial
E) Oral antihistamine trial
questions.answer:
B)
This patient's presentation strongly suggests cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak following septoplasty. Characteristic features include unilateral clear nasal discharge with a salty or metallic taste that worsens with straining, Valsalva maneuvers, or forward leaning. During septoplasty, rocking or twisting forces commonly cause traumatic cribriform plate injury, resulting in CSF leak. This complication occurs more frequently on the right side (2:1 ratio) and predominantly affects males. Beta-2 transferrin testing provides high specificity for CSF leak diagnosis, as this protein exists exclusively in cerebrospinal fluid, though the test may not be available at all facilities. A is incorrect because MRI of the skull base is not particularly useful for CSF leak detection; high-resolution CT is the preferred imaging modality. C is incorrect because glucose testing lacks specificity and has high false-positive rates. D and E are incorrect because neither corticosteroid nasal sprays nor antihistamines are used in CSF rhinorrhea management.

questions.question:
According to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act's Security Rule, which of the following is the basic requirement for storing patient photographs on a personal computer?


A) De-identification of patient names in files
B) Encryption using an approved process
C) Institutional review board approval
D) Password protection of the personal computer
E) Storage of patient photographs is not permitted on personal devices
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


According to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, ‚Äuthe Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Security Rule establishes national standards to protect individuals‚Äo electronic personal health information (ePHI) that is created, received, used, or maintained by a covered entity. The Security Rule requires appropriate administrative, physical and technical safeguards to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and security of electronic protected health information.‚Äu To this end, HIPAA requires that ePHI be protected using encryption processes that have been tested by the National Institute of Standards and Technology and judged to meet this standard.


Password protection can prevent access to electronic devices but does not allow for data on a device to be deleted in the event of a breach. De-identification of file names does not change the electronic information that is stored within a file and, therefore, is inadequate in protecting ePHI. Institutional review boards are primarily responsible for reviewing and monitoring research that involves human subjects and are generally separate from HIPAA-related regulations.


References
1. U.S. Department of Health & Human Services. Summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule. Available at: http://www.hhs.gov/ocr/privacy/hipaa/understanding/summary. Accessed April 7, 2014.
2. Indiana University. HIPAA Guidance ‚Äi Safeguarding Patients‚Äo Photographs and Recordings. Available at: http://www.iub.edu/~vpgc/docs/Compliance/HIPAA-G02_HIPAA_Guidance_Safeguarding_Patients_Photographs_Recordings.pdf. Accessed April 7, 2014.
3. Williams JR, Schafer MF. HIPAA and its effect on graduate medical education: a literature review. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2014 Jan 15;96(2):e13.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with erythema at a cat bite site 24 hours post-injury. Vital signs: temperature 98.6°F (37.0°C), heart rate 77 bpm, respirations 16/min, blood pressure 125/82 mmHg. Physical examination reveals mild erythema and swelling around puncture wounds on the volar aspect of the left long finger's second phalanx. No purulent drainage is present. Digital resting position appears normal with no pain during passive extension. Given no medication allergies, what is the most appropriate antimicrobial treatment?
A) Amoxicillin-clavulanate
B) Cefazolin
C) Cephalexin
D) Erythromycin
E) Vancomycin and gentamicin
questions.answer:
A)
Cat bites typically create puncture wounds due to their long, slender, sharp teeth, with infection rates reaching 80%. Pasteurella species are the predominant pathogens, found in up to 75% of cat bite infections. Additional bacteria may include Streptococci, Staphylococci, and anaerobes. Effective antimicrobial therapy must address the typical bacteriology of these infections. Pasteurella species demonstrate sensitivity to penicillin, ampicillin, second- and third-generation cephalosporins, doxycycline, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, fluoroquinolones, clarithromycin, and azithromycin, but resist cephalexin, dicloxacillin, erythromycin, and clindamycin. Appropriate prophylaxis and treatment options include amoxicillin-clavulanate or penicillin combined with cephalexin. For penicillin-allergic patients, moxifloxacin or ciprofloxacin plus clindamycin combinations are suitable. Community-acquired MRSA coverage is unnecessary due to unlikely oral colonization in humans and animals. B is incorrect because cefazolin, an intravenous first-generation cephalosporin, is inappropriate as Pasteurella species are resistant. C is incorrect because cephalexin resistance makes it unsuitable for Pasteurella coverage. D is incorrect because erythromycin is ineffective against Pasteurella species. E is incorrect because vancomycin and gentamicin combination is unnecessarily broad and doesn't target the typical pathogens.

questions.question:
A term infant is delivered by cesarean section because of a prenatally identified mass in the posterior neck. Postnatal MRI is described as showing a well-circumscribed, multiloculated, thin-walled mass in the left posterior cervical triangle composed of several cysts measuring 2 to 4 cm, uniformly hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences, with thin septations, no solid enhancing component, and no flow voids. The lesion extends inferiorly toward the supraclavicular region but does not compress the trachea or displace the great vessels. Following delivery, the infant is feeding well and shows no signs of respiratory distress. What is the most appropriate initial management approach?
A) Propranolol therapy
B) Tissue biopsy via incision
C) Sclerotherapy treatment
D) Complete surgical removal
E) Watchful waiting
questions.answer:
C)
The described lesion is a macrocystic lymphatic malformation (previously called cystic hygroma): a multiloculated, T2-hyperintense, thin-walled cystic mass with large (greater than 2 cm) cysts, no solid enhancing component, and no arterial flow voids. Sclerotherapy (for example, doxycycline, bleomycin, or OK-432) is the preferred initial treatment for macrocystic lesions, since large cysts respond well to aspiration and instillation of a sclerosant and this approach avoids the bleeding, nerve injury, and recurrence risks of resection in a neonate, particularly when the malformation extends toward central cervical and supraclavicular structures. A) Propranolol is incorrect because it treats infantile hemangiomas, which typically are not fully formed at birth, proliferate over the first months of life, and appear as solid enhancing masses with high-flow vessels rather than as septated cysts. B) Incisional biopsy is incorrect because the imaging characteristics are diagnostic; biopsy adds infection and bleeding risk without changing management. D) Complete surgical resection is incorrect as an initial step because it carries significant morbidity in a neonate, especially with extension toward midline and supraclavicular structures; surgery is reserved for lesions that fail sclerotherapy, are predominantly microcystic, or cause airway or functional compromise. E) Observation alone is incorrect because macrocystic lymphatic malformations do not involute, may enlarge abruptly with infection or intralesional hemorrhage, and respond reliably to sclerotherapy.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to the office by her father, who noticed a lump on the back of her right wrist approximately 3 months ago. She has had no pain and uses the hand normally for writing and for gymnastics. Physical examination shows a soft, mobile, 1.2-cm mass over the dorsal wrist that transilluminates. Wrist range of motion is full and symmetric, and there is no tenderness at the scapholunate interval. Plain radiographs show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
A) Reassurance and serial observation
B) Aspiration with corticosteroid injection
C) Open excision including resection of the capsular stalk
D) Arthroscopic resection
E) Closed rupture by manual compression
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.

Pediatric ganglion cysts behave very differently from those in adults, and the natural history strongly favors nonoperative management. Longitudinal series report that the large majority of wrist ganglia in children resolve spontaneously — frequently within 1 to 2 years — without any intervention. In a child with a classic presentation (soft, mobile, transilluminating mass over the dorsal wrist, full motion, normal radiographs), the diagnosis is clinical, and advanced imaging is not required.
Open excision (Option C) commits an otherwise well child to general anesthesia, a scar, and a recurrence rate that in pediatric series has been reported as high as 30 to 40% — no better than simply waiting. Arthroscopic resection (Option D) is a technique for symptomatic or recurrent adult ganglia and is not a first-line pediatric option. Aspiration with steroid injection (Option B) is poorly tolerated by young children, does not alter the natural history, and carries high recurrence. Closed rupture (Option E) — historically "Bible therapy" — is an abandoned, traumatic maneuver with high recurrence and no role in modern practice.
Surgery should be reserved for lesions that are painful, functionally limiting, persistent into adolescence with symptoms, or clinically atypical (solid, nontransilluminating, rapidly enlarging, or associated with carpal instability or neurologic findings), where an alternative diagnosis such as giant cell tumor of tendon sheath, anomalous extensor digitorum brevis manus, or a neural tumor must be excluded.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman comes to the office because of chronic irritation and discomfort with exercise caused by protuberant labia minora. Reduction labiaplasty using a central wedge resection with a superiorly based flap is planned. Which of the following vessels provides the dominant arterial supply to the labia minora?
A) Deep external pudendal artery
B) Inferior epigastric artery
C) Internal pudendal artery
D) Obturator artery
E) Uterine artery
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.

The labia minora derive their dominant arterial supply from the internal pudendal artery, a branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery. The internal pudendal gives off the posterior labial arteries, which enter the labium from its posterior and lateral aspect, along with anterior contributions from the dorsal artery of the clitoris. Cadaveric injection studies have shown two to five dominant vessels entering posteriorly, feeding a longitudinally oriented, richly anastomotic subdermal plexus that runs the length of the labium.
This anatomy is the reason multiple labiaplasty techniques are all reliably perfused. Both the trim (edge) technique and wedge techniques — central, inferior, or superior wedge, with either a superior or inferior pedicle — leave enough of the longitudinal plexus intact to perfuse the residual labium. Flap loss is uncommon and is more often attributable to closure under tension, aggressive de-fatting or over-thinning of the pedicle, or hematoma than to true arterial insufficiency.
The superficial and deep external pudendal arteries (Option A) arise from the femoral artery and supply the mons pubis and anterior labia majora, contributing comparatively little to the labia minora. The obturator artery (Option D) supplies the medial thigh and hip joint. The uterine artery (Option E) supplies the uterus and upper vagina. The inferior epigastric artery (Option B) supplies the anterior abdominal wall.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man with a long lower face, lip incompetence, and an anterior open bite is undergoing orthognathic evaluation. As part of the lateral cephalometric analysis, the surgeon calculates the Frankfort–mandibular plane angle. Which of the following pairs of landmark sets is used to construct the two planes required for this measurement?
A) Nasion to sella, and gonion to menton
B) Porion to orbitale, and gonion to menton
C) Porion to nasion, and condylion to gonion
D) Orbitale to anterior nasal spine, and pogonion to menton
E) Sella to nasion, and point A to point B
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.

The Frankfort horizontal is drawn from porion — the most superior point of the bony external auditory canal — to orbitale, the most inferior point of the infraorbital rim. The mandibular plane is drawn from gonion to menton. Gonion is the most posteroinferior point at the mandibular angle, constructed on a cephalogram as the point where the bisector of two lines (one tangent to the posterior border of the ramus, one tangent to the inferior border of the body) intersects the angle. Menton is the most inferior point of the mandibular symphysis.
The Frankfort–mandibular plane angle averages roughly 25 degrees. A high (hyperdivergent) angle accompanies a long lower face, vertical maxillary excess, steep mandibular plane, and a tendency toward anterior open bite — the pattern described here. A low (hypodivergent) angle accompanies a short lower face and deep bite.
The other landmarks in the distractors are worth distinguishing. Gnathion is the midpoint between pogonion and menton on the chin contour and substitutes for menton in some analyses (condylion–gnathion is used to express mandibular length). Pogonion is the most anterior projecting point of the chin and is used for the facial plane and SNPg. Condylionis the most superoposterior point of the condylar head. Sella–nasion is the cranial base reference line used for SNA and SNB, not for the Frankfort–mandibular plane angle.

questions.question:
A 41-year-old woman comes to the office 17 days after undergoing bilateral vertical mastopexy. She reports that she can feel a "tight string" beneath the skin of the right breast that pulls when she raises her arm. She is afebrile. Physical examination shows a firm, linear, mildly tender subcutaneous cord extending from the inferior pole of the right breast toward the epigastrium, with visible skin dimpling along its course when the arm is elevated. There is no surrounding erythema, fluctuance, or drainage, and the incisions are intact. Leukocyte count is within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
A) Warm compresses, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and reassurance
B) A 10-day course of oral cephalexin
C) Therapeutic-dose low-molecular-weight heparin for 3 months
D) Duplex ultrasonography with hypercoagulable laboratory workup
E) Surgical excision of the cord
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.

The findings are classic for Mondor disease, a benign superficial thrombophlebitis of the thoracoepigastric, lateral thoracic, or superior epigastric venous system. It characteristically appears 2 to 4 weeks after a breast operation — most often reported after augmentation through an inframammary incision, but also after mastopexy, reduction, core needle biopsy, radiation, or trauma — and can occur spontaneously. The hallmark is a palpable, tender, linear cord with skin dimpling or retraction that becomes more apparent with arm elevation.
The condition is self-limited and typically resolves over 4 to 8 weeks. Symptomatic management with warm compresses, gentle massage, analgesics or anti-inflammatory agents, and reassurance is all that is required. Antibiotics (Option B) are not indicated, as this is not an infectious process and there are no signs of cellulitis. Systemic anticoagulation (Option C) is not warranted for superficial thrombophlebitis in this distribution and exposes a recently operated patient to unnecessary bleeding risk. Duplex ultrasonography and a hypercoagulable workup (Option D) are unnecessary for a classic postoperative presentation. Excision (Option E) is never the initial treatment and would create a new scar for a process that resolves on its own.
Two related points are worth knowing. Mondor disease arising spontaneously, without a preceding operation, biopsy, or trauma, warrants breast imaging, since a small proportion of cases are associated with an underlying carcinoma. Separately, cording in the axilla and medial arm after axillary lymph node dissection is axillary web syndrome — a related but distinct entity managed with stretching and physical therapy.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old man has a 4-month history of burning pain over the dorsoradial forearm with paresthesias radiating into the dorsum of the thumb and first web space. Symptoms began after several months of wearing a tight metal wristband and are worsened by forearm pronation. Physical examination shows a Tinel sign approximately 8 cm proximal to the radial styloid; the Finkelstein test is negative, and there is no tenderness over the first dorsal compartment. Symptoms have not improved after 7 months of splinting, activity modification, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Surgical decompression is planned. Release of the antebrachial fascia at which of the following intervals is most appropriate?
A) Between the abductor pollicis longus and the extensor pollicis brevis
B) Between the brachioradialis and the extensor carpi radialis longus
C) Between the extensor carpi radialis longus and the extensor carpi radialis brevis
D) Between the extensor digitorum communis and the extensor carpi radialis brevis
E) Between the flexor carpi radialis and the brachioradialis
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.

This is Wartenberg syndrome, compression of the superficial branch of the radial nerve in the distal forearm. Through the proximal and mid forearm the nerve travels deep to the brachioradialis. Approximately 8 to 9 cm proximal to the radial styloid it emerges between the tendons of the brachioradialis and the extensor carpi radialis longus, piercing the antebrachial fascia to become subcutaneous. With forearm pronation the brachioradialis tendon rotates over the extensor carpi radialis longus and scissors the nerve at this transition point, which explains both the symptom pattern and the site of the Tinel sign. Decompression consists of releasing the fascia at this brachioradialis–extensor carpi radialis longus interval, extended proximally and distally past the transition zone.
The same anatomy defines where to place a subfascial radial nerve block: just proximal to where the nerve becomes subcutaneous. At the wrist, the nerve has already fanned into multiple branches and is blocked instead by subcutaneous field infiltration over the radial styloid.
The other intervals are anatomically real but wrong for this nerve. The abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis (Option A) constitute the first dorsal compartment — the site of de Quervain tenosynovitis, which coexists with Wartenberg syndrome in a substantial minority of patients and is excluded here by the negative Finkelstein test. The extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis (Option C) form the second dorsal compartment; intersection syndrome occurs where the first compartment tendons cross over them 4 to 6 cm proximal to the Lister tubercle. The interval between the extensor digitorum communis and the extensor carpi radialis brevis (Option D) is the approach to the radial nerve and posterior interosseous nerve in the proximal forearm. The interval between the flexor carpi radialis and the brachioradialis (Option E) contains the radial artery.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old woman has complete flaccid facial paralysis 14 months after resection of a vestibular schwannoma with sacrifice of the facial nerve. She has 6 mm of lagophthalmos, a poor Bell phenomenon, and punctate keratopathy despite maximal lubrication. Placement of an upper eyelid platinum weight is planned. In which of the following planes should the weight be positioned?
A) Between the tarsal plate and the palpebral conjunctiva
B) Between the orbicularis oculi and the anterior surface of the tarsal plate and levator aponeurosis
C) In the subcutaneous plane superficial to the orbicularis oculi
D) Deep to the levator aponeurosis, superior to the upper border of the tarsus
E) Within the preaponeurotic fat pad
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.

The weight is placed in the pretarsal plane: deep to the orbicularis oculi and superficial to the levator aponeurosis and tarsal plate. Through a lid-crease incision the orbicularis is split, the anterior tarsal surface is exposed, and the implant is seated with its inferior edge 2 to 3 mm above the lash line, centered over the medial limbus — roughly the junction of the medial and central thirds of the lid. It is secured to tarsus with nonabsorbable suture through the implant fixation holes, and orbicularis and skin are closed over it to reduce visibility and extrusion.
Placement posterior to the tarsus (Option A) exposes the implant to the conjunctiva and cornea, risking abrasion, erosion, and extrusion. Subcutaneous placement (Option C) produces a visible, palpable bulge and has an unacceptably high extrusion rate. Positions above the upper tarsal border (Options D and E) sacrifice mechanical advantage over the lid margin, blunt the effect on closure, and produce ptosis and contour irregularity; a described modification places thin platinum chain between the septum and levator aponeurosis in very thin-skinned patients, but the pretarsal plane remains the workhorse.
Two related decisions are commonly tested. Weight is selected preoperatively by taping trial weights to the lid and choosing the lightest weight that brings the upper lid to within 2 to 4 mm of the lower lid with full corneal coverage on relaxed closure; the common error is over-weighting in pursuit of complete closure, which causes ptosis, visual field obstruction, and reoperation. Platinum is increasingly favored over gold because its higher density allows a thinner, less visible profile with lower rates of allergic reaction and capsule formation.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old woman is referred for evaluation 2 years after undergoing septoplasty elsewhere. She reports worsening nasal obstruction and progressive flattening of her nasal profile. Physical examination shows loss of dorsal height through the middle third with supratip depression, cephalic rotation of the tip, loss of tip projection, columellar retraction, and widening of the tip. Intranasal examination shows a nearly absent cartilaginous septum with a deficient caudal strut; the mucosa is intact and there is no crusting or perforation. Serologic studies are negative and she does not use intranasal drugs. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
A) Injection of hyaluronic acid filler along the dorsum
B) Dorsal onlay grafting with temporoparietal fascia alone
C) Placement of a silicone dorsal implant
D) Autologous costal cartilage reconstruction with caudal septal replacement and dorsal onlay grafting
E) Bilateral conchal cartilage onlay grafting to the dorsum
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.

This is a major saddle nose deformity, and the defining problem is loss of the structural L-strut, not simply a contour depression. The tell-tale findings are the associated derangements of tip support — cephalic rotation, columellar retraction, loss of projection, tip widening — which indicate that the caudal septum is no longer supporting the nose. Restoring dorsal height without re-establishing that support fails predictably: the tip abnormalities persist and the dorsum recollapses.
Autologous costal cartilage supplies both the volume and the rigidity required. Reconstruction typically combines a caudal septal replacement graft or extended spreader grafts fixed to the nasal spine and remaining septal remnant to rebuild the L-strut, with a dorsal onlay — solid carved cartilage or diced cartilage in fascia — to restore height and smooth the contour. Warping is mitigated with balanced carving, allowing carved grafts to sit before use, and K-wire stabilization when indicated.
Septal cartilage is unavailable in this patient. Conchal cartilage (Option E) is thin, curved, and insufficient in volume and strength for a structural strut; it is reasonable only for minor saddling or camouflage. Filler (Option A) and fascia-only onlay (Option B) camouflage a mild contour depression but restore no support and do not address obstruction. Alloplastic dorsal implants (Option C) in a scarred, previously operated nose with compromised soft-tissue cover carry high rates of infection, extrusion, and displacement, and provide no caudal support.
Etiologies of saddle nose worth recalling: overresection at septoplasty with an inadequate L-strut (at least 10 mm of dorsal and caudal strut should be preserved), unrecognized L-strut fracture, untreated septal hematoma or abscess with avascular necrosis of cartilage (a classic pediatric cause), trauma, intranasal cocaine use, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, relapsing polychondritis, and leprosy or congenital syphilis. Active vasculitis or ongoing cocaine use must be excluded and the disease quiescent before reconstruction is attempted.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old boy comes to the office because of multiple firm, painless enlargements of the fingers of both hands and several soft, bluish, compressible subcutaneous masses of the forearms that swell when the arm is held dependent. He has a history of two pathologic fractures of the phalanges. Radiographs show multiple expansile lucent lesions of the phalanges and metacarpals with cortical thinning, and several phleboliths within the soft tissues. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
A) Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome
B) Maffucci syndrome
C) Ollier disease
D) Parkes-Weber syndrome
E) Sturge-Weber syndrome
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.

The combination of multiple enchondromas and venous malformations defines Maffucci syndrome. The venous component is the discriminating finding: soft, compressible, nonpulsatile lesions that enlarge with dependency and contain phleboliths, growing proportionately with the child rather than involuting. Maffucci syndrome is nonhereditary and typically becomes clinically apparent in adolescence. The critical counseling point is malignant potential — the risk of transformation of enchondromas to chondrosarcoma approaches 30%, and there is an additional risk of intracranial and other visceral malignancies. Any enchondroma that becomes painful, enlarges rapidly, or recurs after curettage should be regarded as a possible low-grade chondrosarcoma.
Ollier disease (Option C) is multiple enchondromatosis without the vascular lesions. Klippel-Trénaunay syndrome (Option A) is the triad of capillary malformation, venous varicosities, and limb overgrowth without arteriovenous fistulae, and its principal morbidity is limb-length discrepancy. Parkes-Weber syndrome (Option D) resembles Klippel-Trénaunay but includes arteriovenous fistulae and carries a risk of high-output cardiac failure. Sturge-Weber syndrome (Option E) pairs a trigeminal-distribution capillary malformation with leptomeningeal vascular anomalies and seizures.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old woman with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis has a 3-year history of episodic pallor, cyanosis, and reperfusion hyperemia of all digits of both hands, now accompanied by constant rest pain and a nonhealing ulcer of the index fingertip. She does not smoke. Calcium channel blockade, phosphodiesterase inhibition, and topical nitrates have failed to control her symptoms. Arteriography shows patent radial and ulnar arteries with diffuse distal spasm and no discrete occlusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Catheter-directed thrombolysis
B) Injection of botulinum toxin type A perivascularly around the digital neurovascular bundles in the palm
C) Intradermal injection of botulinum toxin type A at the wrist
D) Stellate ganglion injection of botulinum toxin type A
E) Ulnar artery resection with interposition vein grafting
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.

Perivascular injection of botulinum toxin around the digital neurovascular bundles at the level of the distal palm is an effective, low-morbidity treatment for refractory secondary Raynaud phenomenon. Roughly 10 units are bathed around each bundle. Reported outcomes include substantial reduction in rest pain in the majority of patients and healing of chronic digital ulcers in up to half. The mechanism is incompletely understood but is thought to involve inhibition of sympathetic vasoconstrictor input, blockade of C-fiber sensory afferents, and effects on substance P signaling. The main adverse effect is transient intrinsic muscle weakness.
Injection intradermally or too proximally at the wrist (Option C) has not reproduced these results. Stellate ganglion blockade (Option D) is performed with local anesthetic, not botulinum toxin. Thrombolysis (Option A) requires a thrombotic occlusion, which arteriography excluded — the pathology here is vasospasm on a patent arterial tree, which is typical of autoimmune disease. Ulnar artery resection and grafting (Option E) is the operation for hypothenar hammer syndrome, a unilateral, occupation-related thrombosis of the ulnar artery. Surgical digital periarterial sympathectomy — stripping the adventitia from the radial, ulnar, and digital vessels — is the appropriate escalation if botulinum toxin fails.

questions.question:
A 4-month-old girl is brought to the office because of a flat, well-demarcated, nonblanching pink-red patch involving the right forehead, upper eyelid, and nasal sidewall that has been present since birth and has grown only in proportion to the child. She has had two episodes of focal seizure activity. Which of the following is the most appropriate combination of additional evaluations?
A) Abdominal ultrasonography and serum alpha-fetoprotein
B) Coagulation studies and platelet count
C) Echocardiography and serum brain natriuretic peptide
D) MRI of the brain and ophthalmologic examination with tonometry
E) Skeletal survey and serum calcium
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.

A capillary malformation (port-wine stain) in a V1 distribution raises concern for Sturge-Weber syndrome, particularly when it involves the forehead and upper eyelid. The two organ systems at risk are the brain and the eye. Ipsilateral leptomeningeal vascular anomalies produce seizures, developmental delay, and hemiparesis and are best evaluated with contrast-enhanced MRI. Ipsilateral glaucoma occurs in a substantial minority of affected children, may be present at birth or develop later, and is a preventable cause of blindness — hence serial ophthalmologic examination with intraocular pressure measurement. Both Sturge-Weber syndrome and isolated nonsyndromic capillary malformations are associated with somatic GNAQ mutations.
Capillary malformations do not involute; they darken, thicken, and develop nodularity over decades, and associated soft-tissue and skeletal overgrowth is common. Pulsed-dye laser (595 nm) beginning in infancy is the treatment of choice for the cutaneous lesion.
Coagulation studies (Option B) address Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon, which occurs with kaposiform hemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma, not capillary malformations. Echocardiography (Option C) is relevant to high-flow lesions with potential for cardiac overload. Options A and E do not correspond to recognized associations.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old girl comes to the office because of a 6 × 8-cm bluish, soft, compressible mass of the medial thigh that has been present since birth, enlarges when she stands, and has become increasingly painful over the past year with intermittent episodes of acute swelling and tenderness. MRI shows a T2-hyperintense, lobulated lesion with phleboliths involving subcutaneous tissue and the adductor musculature, with no flow voids. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
A) Arterial embolization
B) Oral propranolol therapy
C) Pulsed-dye laser therapy
D) Sclerotherapy
E) Surgical resection
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.

This is a symptomatic venous malformation, and sclerotherapy is first-line management.
