B and D are incorrect because even single-dose prophylaxis is not indicated for this procedure type. The timing differences (30 vs 60 minutes) are also not clinically significant for this low-risk procedure.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old child presents following closed reduction and internal fixation of a supracondylar humeral fracture and is assessed in recovery due to absent radial pulse palpation at the left wrist. Clinical examination reveals the left hand appears warm with coloration matching the right hand. No pulses can be felt at the wrist level. Without operative exploration, what is the most probable outcome for the left forearm?
A) Deep flexor compartment fibrosis
B) Radial hand ischemic necrosis
C) Median nerve dysfunction
D) Forearm bone growth plate arrest
E) No functional deficit
questions.answer:
E)
The most likely outcome is no functional impairment. Vascular compromise following pediatric supracondylar fractures affects approximately 5-10% of cases. Recent large retrospective studies show that absent wrist pulses after reduction alone do not correlate with poor outcomes when the hand remains perfused. Most patients lacking immediate post-reduction pulses but maintaining hand perfusion regain palpable radial pulses within 24-48 hours. With a well-perfused hand, observation typically yields excellent results. A) is incorrect because deep flexor compartment fibrosis (Volkmann contracture) occurs with compartment syndrome, which is uncommon in this scenario. B) is incorrect because radial hand necrosis would not be expected given adequate hand perfusion. C) is incorrect because while median nerve injury with vascular compromise may indicate surgical exploration, new median palsy as a late consequence is unlikely. D) is incorrect because growth plate arrest from ischemia would not be anticipated with maintained hand perfusion.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old male presents with right facial nerve paralysis requiring upper eyelid reanimation. A gold weight implant has been chosen. What is the most appropriate consideration for this patient?
A) Permitting upper limbus coverage when at rest
B) Positioning the upper eyelid 2-4 mm from the lower eyelid
C) Achieving complete upper eyelid closure
D) Providing the fastest upper eyelid closure
E) Establishing optimal symmetry with the opposite eye
questions.answer:
B)
The most appropriate consideration is positioning the upper eyelid within 2-4 mm of the lower eyelid. Gold weight implants are frequently utilized for upper eyelid reanimation in facial nerve dysfunction. Preoperative weight estimation involves using adhesive tape to test various weights until finding one that brings the upper lid to within 2-4 mm of the lower lid while ensuring complete corneal coverage. A) is incorrect because simply covering the limbus at rest is insufficient for proper function. C) is incorrect because using excessive weight to achieve complete closure often causes ptosis and visual field obstruction, frequently requiring revision surgery. D) is incorrect because closure speed is typically slower than the normal side and is not a selection criterion. E) is incorrect because contralateral symmetry is rarely achievable with gold weights and is not an assessment factor.

questions.question:
The ABPS Continuous Certification Program in Plastic Surgery requires annual self-evaluation and assessment of knowledge and competencies. What additional requirement must be fulfilled to maintain certification?
A) 300 continuing medical education (CME) credits over 3 years
B) Oral examination following 5 years of practice
C) Documentation of unrestricted state medical licensure
D) Written examination every decade
questions.answer:
C)
Verification of unrestricted state medical licensure is required to maintain certification. The ABPS Continuous Certification Program (formerly MOC-PS) involves ongoing annual self-assessment and learning throughout certification periods. The program encompasses four fundamental components: professionalism, lifelong learning and self-assessment, assessment of knowledge and skills, and medical practice improvement. An unrestricted state medical license is mandatory for participation. A) is incorrect because only 150 CME credits are required over a 3-year cycle, not 300. B) is incorrect because no oral board examination is required after 5 years of practice. D) is incorrect because no written examination is mandated every 10 years in the continuous certification model.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old, right-hand-dominant man comes to the office because of a 2-year history of a deformity of the ring finger of the left hand that has worsened progressively. History includes rheumatoid arthritis that is managed with multiple disease-modifying medications. A photograph and an x-ray study are shown. Which of the following anatomical abnormalities is the most likely cause of this patient's ring finger deformity?


A) Contraction of the oblique retinacular ligament
B) Flexor digitorum profundus avulsion at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint
C) Palmar subluxation of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint
D) Rupture of the central slip of the extensor mechanism
E) Volar plate laxity of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Swan-neck deformity can occur in the post-traumatic setting as well as in the rheumatoid arthritis population. The PIP joint hyperextends, and the DIP joint flexes. Unlike boutonni√®re deformity, which is always initiated by a rupture of the central slip of the extensor mechanism, the origin of a swan-neck deformity can be at the DIP, PIP, or MCP joint. Regardless of the initiating problem, a swan-neck deformity can only occur if there is laxity of the volar plate of the PIP joint to allow hyperextension.


Flexor digitorum profundus avulsion would lead to inability to flex the DIP joint and would not cause hyperextension of the PIP joint. The oblique retinacular ligament can be used to repair a swan-neck deformity but is not causative of the pathology. Palmar subluxation of the MCP joint can lead to a swan-neck deformity in rheumatoid arthritis patients, but the photograph and x-ray study show this is not present in this patient. Rupture of the central slip of the extensor mechanism would lead to a boutonni√®re deformity.


References
1. Feldon P, Terrono AL, Nalebuff EA, et al. Rheumatoid arthritis and other connective tissue diseases. In: Wolfe SW, Hotchkiss RN, Pederson WC, et al, eds. Green's Operative Hand Surgery. 6th ed. Philadelphia: Churchill Livingstone; 2011:2041-2052.
2. Sebastin SJ, Chung KC. Reconstruction of digital deformities in rheumatoid arthritis. Hand Clin. 2011 Feb;27(1):87-104.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male is evaluated as a potential organ donor following traumatic brain injury from a motorcycle accident. Which finding would most likely establish brain death?
A) Loss of deep tendon reflexes
B) Slight cough during tracheal tube manipulation
C) 1 mm pupillary constriction during pupillary reflex testing
D) Absence of lid or eye movement when cornea is touched
E) Nystagmus during caloric testing
questions.answer:
D)
Absence of lid or eye movement when the cornea is touched confirms brain death. Brain death determination requires complete absence of all brainstem reflexes for organ donation eligibility. Loss of corneal reflex indicates absent brainstem function. A) is incorrect because deep tendon reflex evaluation is not part of brain death assessment. B) is incorrect because any cough or gag response during tracheal manipulation demonstrates preserved brainstem reflexes. C) is incorrect because pupillary constriction indicates positive brainstem reflex function. E) is incorrect because nystagmus during caloric testing represents positive brainstem reflex activity.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old female has a 1-cm primary superficial basal cell carcinoma on the left volar mid-forearm. Her history includes kidney transplantation, right breast carcinoma treated with lumpectomy and radiation, and treatment for a gunshot injury to the left forearm. The basal cell carcinoma developed within the prior traumatic scar. Which clinical characteristic indicates Mohs micrographic surgery for this patient?
A) Basal cell carcinoma developing in traumatic scar tissue
B) Previous radiation exposure
C) Patient's immunocompromised condition
D) Basal cell carcinoma dimensions
E) Superficial basal cell carcinoma subtype
questions.answer:
A)
Basal cell carcinoma arising in traumatic scar tissue is the indication for Mohs micrographic surgery. Clear indications for Mohs surgery include specific size, histology, and anatomic location criteria, all recurrent lesions, and basal cell carcinomas occurring in irradiated skin, traumatic scars, areas with chronic inflammation/ulceration/osteomyelitis, or patients with genetic syndromes. This patient has a superficial basal cell carcinoma in the L zone (trunk/extremities), which typically does not require Mohs surgery regardless of pathology subtype. B) is incorrect because the radiation was remote from the basal cell carcinoma location. C) is incorrect because for a 1-cm superficial subtype lesion, immunocompromised status alone does not mandate Mohs surgery. D) is incorrect because the 1-cm size with superficial pathology in the L zone does not meet Mohs criteria. E) is incorrect because superficial subtype in the L zone is generally not an indication for Mohs surgery.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old woman is scheduled for breast reduction surgery. Preoperatively, she receives an intravenous infusion of vancomycin 1.5 g for infection prevention. Her medical history reveals allergies to penicillin and clindamycin, though she has no prior vancomycin exposure. Within 5 minutes of starting the continuous infusion, she develops a red rash across her chest, neck, and face, along with headache and widespread itching. Her vital signs remain stable with no other symptoms. Following discontinuation of the antibiotic, what is the most appropriate subsequent management?
A) Give intramuscular epinephrine
B) Give intravenous morphine
C) Record vancomycin allergy in her chart
D) Obtain emergency vancomycin blood level
E) Restart infusion at reduced rate after symptom resolution
questions.answer:
E)
This patient experienced a mild case of red man syndrome (RMS) from vancomycin. The most appropriate management after stopping the infusion is symptomatic treatment with antihistamines (such as IV or oral diphenhydramine), followed by resuming the vancomycin infusion at a slower rate once symptoms resolve. RMS is a non-allergic, infusion-rate-related reaction that can occur even on first exposure. A) is incorrect because epinephrine is reserved for true anaphylaxis, not RMS. B) is incorrect because opioids like morphine can actually worsen RMS and should be avoided. C) is incorrect because RMS is not a true allergy but an infusion-rate reaction. D) is incorrect because serum levels would not provide useful information for managing this reaction.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old man arrives at the emergency department following a facial stab wound. He is hemodynamically stable, and examination reveals a laceration extending from the right ear tragus to the right corner of the mouth. What is the most probable primary complication when saliva leaks into the wound due to parotid duct damage?
A) Parotid gland shrinkage
B) Salivary fistula
C) Sialocele
D) Wound infection
E) Dry mouth
questions.answer:
C)
When parotid duct injury is not immediately repaired, saliva extravasation into surrounding tissues most commonly leads to sialocele formation (a pseudocapsule containing saliva), followed by salivary fistula development. A) is incorrect because parotid gland atrophy is an uncommon complication of duct injury. B) is incorrect because while salivary fistula can occur, sialocele is the more common primary complication. D) is incorrect because wound infection is not the most likely primary complication from saliva extravasation. E) is incorrect because xerostomia (dry mouth) is an uncommon result of parotid duct injury.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a deep glass laceration on the back of her right forearm. She experiences pain when trying to extend her middle and ring fingers. Physical examination shows she cannot extend her fingers past the neutral position when her right hand is placed flat on a table, but she can fully extend all fingers at the interphalangeal joints in any hand position. What best explains these clinical findings?
A) Complete extrinsic extensor tendon rupture with preserved intrinsic muscles
B) Extrinsic extensor tendons maintain digit extension despite injury
C) Juncturae tendinum provide digit extension
D) An accessory extensor tendon is present
E) Only partial extensor tendon injuries occurred
questions.answer:
A)
The ability to extend interphalangeal joints and reach neutral position at metacarpophalangeal joints after forearm extensor tendon injury indicates intact intrinsic hand muscles (lumbricals and dorsal interossei) compensating for completely severed extrinsic extensors. Only extrinsic extensors can extend MCP joints beyond neutral. B) is incorrect because if extrinsic extensors were functional, extension beyond neutral would be possible. C) is incorrect because juncturae tendinum help with isolated single tendon injuries but cannot maintain extension in all affected fingers with complete tendon division. D) is incorrect because no clinically significant accessory extensor tendons exist. E) is incorrect because partial lacerations would typically allow some extension beyond neutral, though possibly painful.

questions.question:
What anesthesia method is inappropriate for a 44-year-old man undergoing open carpal tunnel surgery?
A) General anesthesia
B) Local anesthesia using lidocaine with epinephrine
C) Local anesthesia using lidocaine alone
D) Regional anesthesia via Bier block
E) Regional anesthesia with cubital tunnel nerve block
questions.answer:
E)
A cubital tunnel nerve block targets the ulnar nerve but does not anesthetize the median nerve, which travels through the carpal tunnel and is the primary nerve involved in carpal tunnel release surgery. This would provide inadequate anesthesia for the procedure. A) is incorrect because general anesthesia is perfectly acceptable for hand surgery. B) is incorrect because local anesthesia with epinephrine has been proven safe for hand surgery, contrary to outdated beliefs. C) is incorrect because local anesthesia with lidocaine alone is appropriate for carpal tunnel release. D) is incorrect because Bier block regional anesthesia is a suitable option for hand procedures.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old woman with a history of left mastectomy for breast cancer is scheduled for right breast reduction to achieve symmetry. What is the approximate likelihood of finding unexpected breast cancer in the tissue removed during her reduction mammaplasty?
A) 0.4%
B) 1%
C) 5%
D) 15%
E) 23%
questions.answer:
C)
Studies show that women undergoing reduction mammaplasty for symmetry after mastectomy have a significantly higher incidence of occult breast cancer (approximately 5.5%) compared to those having reduction for symptomatic macromastia (0.4%). This patient's cancer history places her in the higher-risk category. A) is incorrect because 0.4% represents the rate for women without cancer history undergoing reduction for symptoms. B) is incorrect because 1% underestimates the risk in this high-risk population. D) is incorrect because 15% is too high even for the post-mastectomy population. E) is incorrect because 23% greatly overestimates the actual incidence rates found in studies.

questions.question:
A 36-year-old female patient receives treatment for horizontal forehead lines. Initial assessment reveals transverse wrinkles during eyebrow elevation. Her brows sit 1 cm above the supraorbital ridge. The central forehead receives 24 units of botulinum toxin type A. After two weeks, the patient expresses dissatisfaction with her eyebrow appearance. Examination reveals the medial brow remains 1 cm above the supraorbital ridge, while the lateral brows are markedly elevated, producing an abnormal arch. Additional botulinum toxin type A injection into which muscle would be the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Corrugator supercilia
B) Lateral frontalis
C) Levator palpebrae
D) Orbicularis oculi
E) Procerus
questions.answer:
B)

This patient exhibits a "Spock eyebrow" deformity characterized by excessive lateral brow elevation compared to the medial portion. This occurs when the medial frontalis receives excessive treatment, causing paradoxical lateral brow elevation. The appropriate correction involves injecting botulinum toxin type A into the lateral frontalis muscle (2 cm above the eyebrow) to allow the lateral brow to descend to a normal position. A) Corrugator supercilia is incorrect because it's a brow depressor located in the glabellar region and wouldn't address lateral brow elevation. C) Levator palpebrae is incorrect as it controls upper eyelid elevation, not eyebrow position, and injecting it could cause eyelid ptosis. D) Orbicularis oculi is incorrect because while it can depress the brow, it's primarily used for treating lateral canthal lines, not correcting asymmetric brow elevation. E) Procerus is incorrect as it's a brow depressor in the glabellar area that creates horizontal wrinkles and wouldn't correct lateral brow asymmetry.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male patient seeks evaluation for body contouring surgery following bariatric surgery and a subsequent 100-pound weight reduction. Which characteristic would render this patient unsuitable for the procedure?
A) BMI of 30 kg/m2
B) History of deep venous thromboembolism
C) Protein intake of 25 g daily
D) Transverse abdominal scar
E) Type 2 diabetes
questions.answer:
C)

Daily protein consumption of 25 grams represents severe malnutrition and constitutes a contraindication for body contouring surgery. Post-bariatric patients require 60-100 grams of protein daily to prevent malnutrition and ensure proper wound healing. Inadequate protein intake significantly impairs healing rates in massive weight loss patients. A) BMI of 30 kg/m2 is incorrect because while higher BMI (>35) increases complication rates, a BMI of 30 is acceptable for body contouring procedures. B) History of deep venous thromboembolism is incorrect as it's not a contraindication but requires hematologic evaluation and appropriate prophylaxis. D) Transverse abdominal scar is incorrect because previous surgical scars don't preclude body contouring procedures. E) Type 2 diabetes is incorrect as it's not a contraindication for circumferential body lift procedures.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old female patient undergoes bilateral mastectomy with autologous breast reconstruction. On postoperative day four, she reports moderate abdominal pain and several episodes of loose stools. Her vital signs remain stable, and physical examination reveals mild abdominal distention. Laboratory analysis confirms Clostridium difficile toxin in the stool sample. Which medication represents the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?
A) Fidaxomicin
B) Metronidazole
C) Rifaximin
D) Teicoplanin
E) Vancomycin
questions.answer:
B)

Oral metronidazole is the recommended first-line therapy for patients with mild to moderate Clostridium difficile infection, as demonstrated by this patient's stable vital signs and moderate symptoms. Metronidazole effectively treats C. difficile colitis and is the standard initial approach for non-severe cases. A) Fidaxomicin is incorrect because while effective, it's typically reserved for recurrent infections or when standard therapy fails, not as first-line treatment. C) Rifaximin is incorrect as it's not recommended for C. difficile treatment and lacks established efficacy for this indication. D) Teicoplanin is incorrect because it's not a standard treatment for C. difficile infections and has limited supporting evidence. E) Vancomycin is incorrect for initial therapy in mild/moderate cases; it's reserved for severe disease or when metronidazole fails to achieve clinical improvement.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old female patient presents with a significant degloving injury to her dominant right thumb requiring repair. During soft tissue reconstruction, a 4-cm gap is identified in the radial proper digital nerve. Which repair technique would be most appropriate for this nerve defect?
A) Autologous nerve graft
B) Autologous vein graft
C) Collagen conduit
D) Nerve transposition
questions.answer:
A)

Autologous nerve grafting is the most reliable technique for nerve gaps of 3 cm or greater that cannot be repaired primarily without tension. This approach provides the best functional outcomes for longer nerve defects and is the gold standard when primary repair is not feasible. Despite donor site morbidity, nerve grafts offer superior regeneration potential for significant gaps. B) Autologous vein graft is incorrect because vein conduits are limited to shorter gaps (2-3 cm) and smaller diameter nerves, with poor regeneration beyond 3 cm. C) Collagen conduit is incorrect as biodegradable conduits are restricted to gaps under 3 cm and show no significant nerve regeneration beyond this distance. D) Nerve transposition is incorrect because this technique is not applicable for digital nerve repairs and wouldn't address the 4-cm defect requiring bridging.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man has the ear deformity shown in the photograph. He would like to know if there is a name for the appearance of his ear. On the basis of the image, which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?


A) Constricted ear
B) Cryptotia
C) Microtia
D) Prominent ear
E) Stahl ear
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


Constricted ear deformities have a varying degree of hypoplasia of the superior third of the auricle. This patient has a mild form of a constricted ear deformity with presentation of a lop ear. Emblematic for a lop ear is the "folding" of the helical rim. In more severe cases, the antihelical fold can efface and the patient can present with a cup ear deformity. In an infant, ear molding is the treatment of choice. If the patient presents later in life, and in instances where the vertical height is near normal, excision of the folded aspect of the helix may suffice. If there is considerable lack of vertical height, the folded cartilage can be used as a flap to increase the auricular height. A variety of cartilaginous and loco-regional flap combinations have been described for this indication. The most well-known is the Banner flap.


A Stahl ear is characterized by an additional prominent fold in the scaphoid fossa, which results in an everted helical fold and pointed appearance of the ear. Like a constricted ear, this can be addressed with ear molding or with surgical correction later in life.


Prominent ears are defined as having an increased auriculocephalic angle (>25 degrees) and distance (>2 cm). This is measured between the mastoid and the posterior concha. Contributing factors can be an increased conchoscaphal angle (usually <90 degrees) due to inadequate development of the antihelical fold or an increased conchal depth (>1.5 cm). Surgery addresses one or both of those issues by excision of conchal cartilage and/or conchoscaphal sutures (Mustard√© sutures).


Cryptotia is defined by the superior helical cartilage being buried underneath the temporal skin. On clinical examination, the ability to recreate a normal ear appearance with digital manipulation is the defining feature. In patients who did not have access to ear molding, a variety of techniques using locoregional flaps have been described to externalize the buried segment.
Microtia exists on a spectrum and involves absence of some or all structures of the ear (anotia). Molding is therefore not an option, and reconstructive procedures including use of autologous and synthetic material are indicated. This patient is suffering from a deformity and not an absence of auricular tissue.


ReferencesAli K, Meaike JD, Maricevich RS, et al. The protruding ear: cosmetic and reconstruction. Semin Plast Surg. 2017;31(3):152-160.Joukhadar N, McKee D, Caouette-Laberge L, et al. Management of congenital auricular anomalies. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2020;146(2):205e-216e.

questions.question:
A 76-year-old male patient seeks consultation for a 5-year history of upper eyelid drooping. He reports no significant medical history, trauma, or current medications. What is the most probable underlying cause of his condition?
A) Levator dehiscence
B) Muscular dystrophy
C) Myoneural dysfunction
D) Oculomotor (III) nerve palsy
E) Paralysis of the Müller muscle
questions.answer:
A)

Levator aponeurosis dehiscence is the most common cause of ptosis in elderly patients. Age-related weakening and separation of the levator aponeurosis from its insertion causes the eyelid to drop while the supratarsal crease moves upward, creating the characteristic appearance of involutional ptosis. B) Muscular dystrophy is incorrect because chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia is rare compared to levator dehiscence and typically presents with additional extraocular muscle involvement. C) Myoneural dysfunction is incorrect as myasthenia gravis primarily affects young women, causes fatigue-related worsening, and would show improvement with anticholinesterase medications. D) Oculomotor nerve palsy is incorrect because it would present with additional signs like diplopia, pupil abnormalities, or other extraocular muscle deficits. E) Müller muscle paralysis is incorrect as this occurs with sympathetic denervation in Horner syndrome, which would include miosis and anhidrosis.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman seeks consultation for breast augmentation surgery. She expresses concern about potential adverse events associated with silicone gel implants during the initial 5 years following surgery. Which of the following represents the most frequently encountered complication with cohesive silicone gel breast implants?
A) Capsular contracture
B) Granuloma
C) Hematoma
D) Infection
E) Rupture
questions.answer:
A)
Capsular contracture is the most frequently reported complication with cohesive silicone gel breast implants. Studies show capsular contracture rates (Baker III/IV) of 9.8% for aesthetic procedures and 13.7% for reconstructive procedures, making it significantly more common than other complications. B) Granuloma formation is uncommon with modern cohesive gel implants. C) Hematoma occurs in approximately 2% of cases, making it less frequent than capsular contracture. D) Infection rates are 1.6% for aesthetic and 6.1% for reconstructive procedures, lower than capsular contracture rates. E) Rupture rates are only 1.1% for aesthetic and 3.8% for reconstructive procedures, making it the least common of the listed complications.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old man develops facial redness and perspiration during meals 4 weeks following parotid gland surgery. Which of the following diagnostic tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
A) Cottle maneuver
B) Ice pack test
C) Jones test
D) Minor iodine-starch test
E) Schirmer test
questions.answer:
D)
The Minor iodine-starch test is the diagnostic test of choice for confirming Frey syndrome (auriculotemporal syndrome). This test involves painting the affected facial area with iodine, then challenging the patient with a sialogogue like lemon juice - areas of gustatory sweating will turn blue, confirming the diagnosis. A) The Cottle maneuver is used to evaluate the internal nasal valve, not gustatory sweating. B) The ice pack test is used to diagnose myasthenic ptosis, not Frey syndrome. C) The Jones test evaluates lacrimal drainage system patency, unrelated to gustatory sweating. E) The Schirmer test measures tear production and is used to assess dry eyes before blepharoplasty, not for diagnosing Frey syndrome.

questions.question:
An otherwise healthy 4-year-old boy is brought to the office for evaluation of a large scalp hemangioma. A photograph is shown. The family has requested removal of the hemangioma before he enters school. Which of the following is the most appropriate management in this patient?


A) Deferral of surgery for 2 years
B) Excision and skin grafting
C) Single-stage excision and closure
D) Staged excision and closure
E) Tissue expansion
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


Although the hemangioma shown is sizable, judicious mobilization of the scalp and galeal scoring allow the resultant defect to be easily closed without resorting to delayed rotational flaps, tissue expanders, or skin grafting. Single-staged excision and linear closure is the simplest, most predictable manner of closing small to intermediate-sized scalp defects such as the one in the patient described. The maximum defect using this technique is not well defined, but at least one series has demonstrated successful primary closure of defects in infants of up to 7 cm without using the other alternatives listed or tissue expansion. Delaying the resection for another 2 years might be productive in a younger child, but further involution is unlikely in a 4-year-old. Staged excision is possible, but unnecessary for this lesion; moreover, repair along the edge of the friable hemangioma can lead to wound problems.


References
1. Spector JA, Blei F, Zide BM. Early surgical intervention for proliferating hemangiomas of the scalp indications and outcomes. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2008 Aug;122(2):457-462.
2. Couto RA, Maclellan RA, Zurakowski D, et al. Infantile hemangioma: clinical assessment of the involuting phase and implications for management. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012 Sep;130(3):619-624.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old man presents with a 20-year history of rheumatoid arthritis. Which of the following thumb deformities is most likely to occur in this patient?
A) Boutonnière
B) Clinodactyly
C) Gamekeeper's thumb
D) Swan-neck
E) Thumb-in-palm
questions.answer:
A)
Boutonnière deformity is the most common thumb deformity in rheumatoid arthritis patients. It results from metacarpophalangeal joint synovitis that stretches dorsal structures, disrupts the extensor pollicis brevis tendon insertion, and causes volar subluxation of the extensor pollicis longus tendon. B) Clinodactyly is a congenital developmental abnormality, not associated with rheumatoid arthritis. C) Gamekeeper's thumb results from ulnar collateral ligament injury, typically traumatic rather than rheumatoid in origin. D) Swan-neck deformity is the second most common rheumatoid thumb deformity but occurs less frequently than boutonnière deformity. E) Thumb-in-palm deformity is characteristic of cerebral palsy, not rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.question:
Which of the following represents the most frequent cause of elongated head shape without suture fusion?
A) Fibromatosis colli
B) Hereditary dolichocephaly
C) Ocular torticollis
D) Prematurity
E) Ventriculoperitoneal shunt
questions.answer:
D)
Prematurity is the most common cause of scaphocephaly without craniosynostosis. Premature infants in the NICU develop this elongated head shape due to positioning and decreased muscle tone, which typically corrects with growth, improved tone, and repositioning. A) Fibromatosis colli is associated with severe muscular torticollis and plagiocephaly, not scaphocephaly without craniosynostosis. B) Hereditary dolichocephaly is not a recognized hereditary condition causing scaphocephaly without craniosynostosis. C) Ocular torticollis causes head tilt and is associated with deformational plagiocephaly, not scaphocephaly. E) Ventriculoperitoneal shunts may cause secondary craniosynostosis if over-shunting occurs, but do not typically cause scaphocephaly without craniosynostosis.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old man undergoes surgical repair of multiple facial fractures when the nasal endotracheal tube becomes disconnected from the ventilation system. During electrocautery use, the surgeon observes an unexpected flash in the surgical field. The procedure is immediately halted and the anesthesiologist is notified. Smoke and burning smell emanate from the patient's airway. Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate action?
A) Reduce airway gas flow by 50%
B) Immediately remove the endotracheal tube
C) Fill oral and nasal cavities with gauze sponges
D) Perform emergency bronchoscopy
E) Reconnect the endotracheal tube
questions.answer:
B)
Immediate removal of the endotracheal tube without delay is the most appropriate first step when managing an airway fire. This prevents further fuel supply to the fire and allows for airway assessment and management. A) Reducing gas flow by half is insufficient - all airway gases must be completely interrupted in an airway fire. C) Packing cavities with sponges would add flammable material and worsen the situation. D) Emergency bronchoscopy should be considered after the fire is extinguished and ventilation re-established, not as the immediate first step. E) Reconnecting the endotracheal tube would maintain the fuel source for the fire and is contraindicated until the fire is completely extinguished.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old female patient is having a dorsal wrist ganglion removed using a lidocaine Bier block technique. While the surgery is in progress, she complains of discomfort, becomes increasingly agitated, experiences a metallic taste, and reports ear ringing. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
A) Give intravenous diphenhydramine and proceed with the operation
B) Lower the tourniquet pressure by 50 mmHg to reduce tourniquet discomfort
C) Release the tourniquet entirely, allow several minutes for arm reperfusion, then re-exsanguinate and re-inflate
D) Apply local bupivacaine (Marcaine) injection for pain control and continue the procedure
E) Secure the airway and provide supplemental oxygen
questions.answer:
E)
This clinical presentation indicates tourniquet cuff failure resulting in lidocaine systemic toxicity. Risk factors for cuff failure during Bier block include obesity (conical arm shape) and elevated blood pressure. Early manifestations of lidocaine toxicity include restlessness, auditory disturbances, and circumoral tingling; muscle fasciculations, convulsions, and cardiorespiratory collapse may follow. Essential immediate treatment involves airway protection, oxygen supplementation, and IV fluid support. A is incorrect because diphenhydramine is not indicated as these symptoms represent drug toxicity, not allergic reaction. B and C are incorrect because releasing or reducing tourniquet pressure would increase systemic lidocaine levels and worsen toxicity. D is incorrect because the problem is not inadequate local anesthesia but rather systemic drug toxicity, and continuing surgery could lead to serious complications.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female patient comes for evaluation of a right volar radial wrist lesion. She states the lesion appeared suddenly 6 weeks prior and varies in size intermittently. Physical exam reveals the lesion is translucent to light. From which joint does this lesion most commonly arise?
A) Lunotriquetral
B) Metacarpotrapezial
C) Radioscaphoid
D) Scapholunate
E) Scaphotrapezial
questions.answer:
C)
Ganglion cysts are benign soft tissue masses commonly found at the wrist but can occur at any joint location. Approximately 60-70% of ganglion cysts occur dorsally on the wrist and connect to the joint through a stalk, typically originating from the scapholunate ligament or other dorsal capsular sites. About 13-20% of ganglion cysts appear on the volar wrist surface, arising through a stalk from the radioscaphoid joint, scapholunate interval, scaphotrapezial joint, or metacarpotrapezial joint in decreasing order of frequency. A is incorrect because lunotriquetral ligament is not a typical origin for either dorsal or volar ganglion cysts. B is incorrect because while metacarpotrapezial joint can be a source, it is less common than radioscaphoid. D is incorrect because scapholunate is more associated with dorsal ganglions. E is incorrect because scaphotrapezial joint is less frequent than radioscaphoid as an origin.

questions.question:
A healthy 34-year-old female patient contacts the clinic reporting vague left chest discomfort and slight breathing difficulty occurring 2 weeks following abdominoplasty with rectus muscle plication and flank liposuction. The surgery lasted 3 hours and 15 minutes under general anesthesia. She stayed overnight and received perioperative subcutaneous heparin including a preoperative dose. She denies any postoperative issues and feels excellent overall. She mentions she is "finally returning to normal physically" and prefers not to alarm her family. She simply wanted to confirm she hadn't "strained something or caused damage." What is the most appropriate response from the plastic surgeon?
A) Emergency department assessment
B) Patient reassurance
C) Activity restriction
D) Home incentive spirometry for pulmonary hygiene improvement
E) Over-the-counter anti-inflammatory medication use
questions.answer:
A)
This patient likely has a pulmonary embolism requiring immediate evaluation and anticoagulation treatment. Despite perioperative heparin prophylaxis, deep vein thrombosis and subsequent pulmonary embolism can still occur. Pulmonary embolism is the leading cause of death after liposuction procedures. Abdominoplasty patients have higher venous thromboembolism risk compared to other elective cosmetic procedures, with rates from 1:1000 to 1:300 for standard abdominoplasty. Any suspicious PE symptoms, even weeks postoperatively, require urgent emergency department evaluation for imaging and laboratory studies. B is incorrect because these symptoms suggest serious pathology requiring immediate attention. C is incorrect because activity modification alone is inadequate for suspected PE. D is incorrect because spirometry won't address the underlying thromboembolism. E is incorrect because anti-inflammatory drugs don't treat PE and may delay appropriate care.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old woman is planning breast augmentation with highly cohesive, anatomically contoured silicone gel implants. She asks how she should be monitored for implant rupture after surgery. According to current FDA labeling recommendations, what should she be told regarding postoperative rupture surveillance?
A) No imaging is needed; annual physical examination beginning at 1 year is sufficient
B) MRI at 1 year postoperatively, then annually thereafter
C) Ultrasound or MRI at 2 years postoperatively, then annually thereafter
D) Ultrasound or MRI at 5 to 6 years postoperatively, then every 2 to 3 years thereafter
E) Mammography at 3 years postoperatively, then every 2 years thereafter
questions.answer:
D)
Current FDA labeling recommendations for silicone gel-filled breast implants advise screening for silent (asymptomatic) rupture with ultrasound or MRI beginning 5 to 6 years after implantation, and then every 2 to 3 years thereafter. If ultrasound findings are equivocal, MRI should be obtained. This replaced the older recommendation of MRI at 3 years postoperatively and every 2 years thereafter; ultrasound is now accepted as a first-line screening modality because of comparable performance for this indication at lower cost and greater accessibility. Imaging surveillance is recommended because physical examination alone cannot reliably detect silent rupture, which accounts for the majority of implant failures. Highly cohesive ("gummy bear") form-stable devices can still rupture when the shell fails, but the gel rarely migrates extracapsularly, making clinical detection even less reliable. A is incorrect because manual examination cannot reliably detect silent rupture. B and C give intervals that are too early and too frequent. E is incorrect because mammography is a breast cancer screening tool and is not recommended for implant integrity surveillance; it can also compress and potentially damage the implant.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old male patient has a 24-hour history of diabetic foot infection. His medical background includes type 1 diabetes mellitus. Physical exam reveals palpable dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses with preserved sensation. There is tissue death and redness on the foot's dorsal surface between the first and second metatarsals. Besides prompt surgical debridement and antibiotic treatment, which additional intervention reduces the probability of below-knee amputation?
A) Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor application
B) Hyperbaric oxygen treatment
C) Topical antibiotic application
D) Topical iodophor gauze treatment
E) Topical Kalanchoe pinnata (Wonder of the World plant) treatment
questions.answer:
A)
Extensive research on diabetic foot infections has established surgical debridement and systemic antibiotics as primary treatment. Multiple adjunctive therapies have been investigated and studied. Through systematic literature review analyzing various treatment modalities including topical antibiotics, hyperbaric oxygen, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, Wonder of the World plant therapy, and iodophor gauze application, only granulocyte colony-stimulating factor application was demonstrated to decrease below-knee amputation risk. B is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen therapy did not show significant amputation reduction in systematic reviews. C is incorrect because topical antibiotic therapy alone was not proven to reduce amputation rates. D is incorrect because iodophor gauze treatment did not demonstrate amputation risk reduction. E is incorrect because Kalanchoe pinnata treatment did not show evidence of reducing amputation likelihood.

questions.question:
A 37-year-old female arrives for assessment of a mid-humeral laceration from a car accident. Physical exam reveals inability to extend her wrist, digits, or thumb. Operative exploration demonstrates complete radial nerve severance; median and ulnar nerves remain undamaged. Following debridement and nerve end mobilization, direct nerve repair is completed. Which muscle listed below will be the final one to regain innervation during neural recovery?
A) Abductor pollicis brevis
B) Abductor pollicis longus
C) Brachioradialis
D) Extensor carpi radialis brevis
E) Extensor indicis proprius
questions.answer:
E)
Extensor indicis proprius is the last muscle to be reinnervated following radial nerve repair. The typical sequence of radial nerve muscle reinnervation proceeds from proximal to distal: brachioradialis, extensor carpi radialis longus, supinator, extensor carpi radialis brevis, extensor digitorum communis, extensor carpi ulnaris, extensor digiti quinti, abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and finally extensor indicis proprius. A is incorrect because abductor pollicis brevis receives innervation from the median nerve's thenar branch, not the radial nerve. B is incorrect because abductor pollicis longus is reinnervated earlier in the sequence, before extensor indicis proprius. C is incorrect because brachioradialis is typically the first radial-innervated muscle to recover function. D is incorrect because extensor carpi radialis brevis recovers earlier than extensor indicis proprius in the reinnervation sequence.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female with rectal carcinoma will undergo abdominoperineal resection and posterior vaginectomy after neoadjuvant chemoradiation. What represents the optimal reconstructive approach for the posterior vaginal defect?
A) Free anterolateral thigh fasciocutaneous flap
B) Primary repair of the perineal and vaginal defects
C) Pudendal thigh (Singapore) flap
D) Skin grafting
E) Vertical rectus abdominis myocutaneous flap
questions.answer:
E)
The vertical rectus abdominis myocutaneous (VRAM) flap is the optimal choice for this complex, irradiated, three-dimensional defect. It offers straightforward harvest, minimal donor site complications, a large skin paddle capable of resurfacing both perineum and vagina, dependable vascular supply, and excellent rotational arc. The VRAM flap remains the gold standard despite recent descriptions of pedicled ALT flaps for vaginoperineal reconstruction. A is incorrect because while free ALT flaps can be used, they are more complex and VRAM remains superior for this indication. B is incorrect because primary closure in an irradiated field carries unacceptable wound healing complications. C is incorrect because the pudendal thigh flap has limited reach and bulk for this extensive defect. D is incorrect because skin grafting alone cannot provide adequate coverage for this complex three-dimensional defect requiring bulk and reliable healing.

questions.question:
What represents the most precise anatomical location for the elliptical skin paddle of a profunda artery perforator (PAP) flap?
A) Anteromedial thigh with the superior border within the groin crease
B) Inferior buttock with the inferior border within the gluteal fold
C) Lateral hip superior to the iliac crest
D) Middle buttock, from the posterior superior iliac spine to the apex of the greater trochanter
E) Posteromedial thigh with the superior border within the gluteal fold
questions.answer:
E)
The PAP flap skin island is correctly positioned on the posteromedial thigh with its superior border at or within the gluteal fold, extending approximately 7 cm inferiorly in an elliptical configuration that keeps the scar concealed within the gluteal fold. This positioning allows optimal access to the profunda artery perforators located in this region. A is incorrect because this describes the transverse upper gracilis (TUG) flap location. B is incorrect because this describes the inferior gluteal artery perforator (IGAP) flap positioning. C is incorrect because this describes the Rubens or lateral hip flap location. D is incorrect because this describes the superior gluteal artery perforator (SGAP) flap anatomical boundaries.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old female presents with a large distal femoral shaft osteosarcoma. A 15-cm bone resection is planned, creating a substantial intercalary segmental gap. The overlying skin and soft tissue remain uninvolved. The patient strongly desires limb salvage. What represents the optimal reconstructive approach for this defect?
A) Bone allograft
B) Contralateral vascularized fibula free flap
C) Contralateral vascularized fibula free flap with bone allograft
D) Ilizarov bone transportation
E) Ipsilateral pedicled vascularized fibula flap
questions.answer:
C)
The contralateral vascularized fibula free flap combined with bone allograft (Capanna technique) is optimal for this large intercalary defect in a young patient seeking limb preservation. This approach places the fibular flap within the allograft construct, bridging both osteotomy sites and providing the structural support needed for weight-bearing while reducing fracture risk compared to fibula alone. A is incorrect because bone allograft alone has high nonunion rates (34% versus 8-10% with vascularized bone). B is incorrect because a fibula flap alone may be insufficient for weight-bearing in such a large defect and has increased fracture risk. D is incorrect because Ilizarov bone transport is suitable for smaller defects (4-6 cm) but not feasible for 15-cm gaps. E is incorrect because an ipsilateral pedicled fibula flap would have insufficient reach for this large defect and still face weight-bearing challenges.

questions.question:
A healthy 17-year-old nulliparous female presents for evaluation of marked breast asymmetry. She reports progressive left breast enlargement over 2 months. She takes combined oral contraceptives. Mammography and biopsy are performed. Histopathologic analysis reveals a benign phyllodes tumor. What is the most appropriate management approach?
A) Enucleation
B) Mastectomy with sentinel lymph node biopsy
C) Progestin-only oral contraceptive
D) Tamoxifen followed by lumpectomy
E) Wide local excision
questions.answer:
E)
Wide local excision with 1-cm margins is the standard treatment for all phyllodes tumors, including benign variants. This approach provides adequate local control and excellent prognosis while preserving breast tissue in this young patient. The primary concern with benign phyllodes tumors is local recurrence, which is minimized with appropriate surgical margins. A is incorrect because enucleation provides inadequate margins and increases recurrence risk significantly. B is incorrect because mastectomy is unnecessarily aggressive for benign phyllodes tumors, and lymph node involvement is extremely rare. C is incorrect because hormonal manipulation has no established role in phyllodes tumor treatment. D is incorrect because tamoxifen is not indicated for phyllodes tumors, which are stromal-derived tumors that don't respond to hormonal therapy like breast carcinomas.

questions.question:
Following Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty treatment for velopharyngeal insufficiency, velar function success is most closely associated with which of the following factors?
A) Patient's age when surgery is performed
B) Adherence to postoperative speech therapy
C) Patient's sex
D) Size of preoperative velopharyngeal gap
E) Classification of cleft type
questions.answer:
D)

The size of the preoperative velopharyngeal gap is the strongest predictor of successful velar function following Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty. Research demonstrates that patients with smaller preoperative closure gaps measured by nasendoscopy achieve better postoperative velopharyngeal competence. A) Patient age at surgery is incorrect because while younger patients may have better outcomes, age is not the most significant predictor compared to gap size. B) Speech therapy compliance is incorrect as it does not influence surgical outcomes according to studies. C) Patient sex is incorrect because gender has no demonstrated impact on surgical success. E) Cleft type is incorrect because although overt clefts may have worse outcomes than submucous clefts, this factor is less predictive than the preoperative gap measurement.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male presents with a deep, palpable 6-cm mass in the mid-volar aspect of his forearm. MRI findings are inconclusive, necessitating a diagnostic biopsy. Which approach is most appropriate for this procedure?
A) Avoiding electrocautery use
B) Leaving the biopsy wound open with compression dressings
C) Performing complete excisional biopsy
D) Making a transverse skin crease incision
E) Using tourniquet without Esmarch bandage for exsanguination
questions.answer:
E)

For large forearm masses requiring biopsy, a tourniquet should be used without an Esmarch bandage - only arm elevation for exsanguination to create a bloodless field while minimizing contamination risk. This approach allows for proper hemostasis before closure. A) Avoiding cautery is incorrect because cautery can be used appropriately during the procedure. B) Leaving the wound open is incorrect as meticulous closure is required to prevent contamination. C) Excisional biopsy is incorrect for large lesions as incisional biopsy minimizes contamination risk of the surrounding surgical field. D) Transverse incisions are incorrect because they may complicate future limb-sparing surgery if malignancy is discovered.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female presents with concerns about loose, sagging neck skin following significant weight loss. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?
A) Dermabrasion
B) Fat grafting
C) Laser therapy
D) Facelift surgery
E) Liposuction
questions.answer:
D)

Facelift surgery (rhytidectomy) with SMAS and platysmal suspension along with skin tightening is the only effective treatment for the skin laxity and platysmal banding that occurs after massive weight loss. This addresses both the excess skin and underlying muscle changes. A) Dermabrasion is incorrect because it treats surface irregularities and fine wrinkles, not skin laxity, and may cause neck scarring. B) Fat grafting is incorrect as it addresses volume loss but cannot tighten loose skin or treat platysmal bands. C) Laser therapy is incorrect because while it provides some skin tightening, it cannot address the degree of laxity shown and has no role in neck rejuvenation. E) Liposuction is incorrect as it would worsen the problem by further reducing soft tissue volume without addressing skin excess.

questions.question:
A 17-year-old female with bilateral cleft lip/palate history presents after previous repairs and bone grafting. She has hypernasal speech and severe midface retrusion with 12mm negative overjet. Cephalometric measurements show SNA 73° (normal 80-82°) and SNB 79° (normal 79-81°). What is the optimal initial treatment to address her concerns?
A) Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy for mandibular setback
B) Combined Le Fort I maxillary advancement with mandibular advancement
C) Maxillary distraction osteogenesis
D) Pharyngoplasty procedure
E) Speech therapy intervention
questions.answer:
C)

Maxillary distraction osteogenesis is the best initial option because it addresses the severe maxillary hypoplasia while preserving the current velopharyngeal anatomy, avoiding worsening of her speech. This technique allows midface advancement without compromising velopharyngeal function, and pharyngoplasty can be performed later if needed. A) Mandibular setback is incorrect because her mandible is in normal position (SNB 79°) and doesn't require reduction. B) Combined advancement is incorrect because Le Fort I advancement would worsen her existing velopharyngeal dysfunction. D) Pharyngoplasty alone is incorrect as it would address speech but not her primary concern of facial appearance and would make future maxillary advancement more difficult. E) Speech therapy alone is incorrect because it cannot address the structural velopharyngeal deficiency or facial deformity.

questions.question:
A thin 40-year-old female has an 8×5-cm defect on the distal anterior leg extending to the foot dorsum, with exposed tibia lacking periosteum and visible tendons. This occurred after fracture fixation 3 days prior, with the distal posterior tibial artery having been ligated. No infection is present. What reconstruction method is most appropriate?
A) Bilaminate neodermis (Integra) application with negative pressure therapy
B) Dorsalis pedis flap coverage
C) Free anterolateral thigh (ALT) flap coverage
D) Free transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous (TRAM) flap coverage
E) Reverse sural flap coverage
questions.answer:
C)

A free anterolateral thigh flap provides adequate tissue volume for the large defect, can be thinned for better contour and shoe fitting, and allows potential primary donor site closure. This is ideal for lower extremity reconstruction in this scenario. A) Integra with negative pressure therapy is incorrect because the avascular wound bed with exposed bone and tendons makes this option suboptimal for reliable take. B) Dorsalis pedis flap is incorrect as it would sacrifice the remaining foot blood supply, risking foot viability. D) Free TRAM flap is incorrect because muscle harvest creates unnecessary donor morbidity and unpredictable final contour compared to ALT. E) Reverse sural flap is incorrect because the posterior tibial artery ligation eliminates the blood supply needed for this flap's survival.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning discomfort and rigidity in her right hand occurring 6 weeks following treatment for a distal radius fracture. She reports sleep difficulties and ongoing pain despite narcotic medication use. Physical examination reveals a glossy appearance of the right hand, limited finger mobility, and heightened sensitivity to gentle touch. Radiographic imaging demonstrates proper fracture alignment. Which of the following diagnostic tests would be most suitable for assessing this patient's condition?
A) Bone scan
B) CT scan
C) Digital subtraction angiography
D) Lymphoscintigraphy
E) Ultrasonography
questions.answer:
A)
This patient demonstrates clinical features consistent with complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), making a bone scan the most appropriate diagnostic test. CRPS is characterized by persistent pain, autonomic dysfunction, and trophic changes following injury or surgery. While no single test is pathognomonic for CRPS, triple-phase bone scans provide valuable diagnostic support by showing asymmetric flow patterns and increased periarticular uptake in multiple joints of the affected extremity. B) is incorrect because CT scans are primarily used for evaluating bony alignment and articular anatomy, not for diagnosing CRPS. C) is incorrect because digital subtraction angiography evaluates vascular circulation, which is not the primary concern in this case. D) is incorrect because lymphoscintigraphy is used to assess lymphatic drainage in lymphedema cases. E) is incorrect because ultrasonography is typically used to evaluate venous outflow and detect deep venous thrombosis.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female with constricted breast anatomy is planned for breast enhancement with lift surgery. A smooth, round, cohesive silicone implant will be utilized. Compared to enhancement/lift surgery in patients with normal breast anatomy, this patient faces increased risk for which of the following complications?
A) Capsule contracture
B) Double bubble
C) Hematoma
D) Nipple-areola depigmentation
E) Rippling
questions.answer:
B)
Patients with tuberous breast deformity have an elevated risk of double bubble deformity due to their anatomical characteristics, including a constricted base and high inframammary fold. The tight, elevated native crease must be released to accommodate the implant, but if this crease fails to expand adequately, a double bubble appearance results. This occurs when the implant creates a new, lower contour while the original high crease remains visible. A) is incorrect because capsule contracture rates are similar between tuberous and normal breast patients undergoing periareolar procedures. C) is incorrect because hematoma risk is not specifically increased in tuberous breast patients. D) is incorrect because nipple-areola depigmentation risk remains comparable to standard procedures. E) is incorrect because rippling incidence is not specifically elevated in tuberous breast cases compared to normal anatomy.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old female seeks consultation regarding cosmetic concerns about her neck appearance. Despite proper lifestyle changes and maintaining a BMI under 25 kg/m2, she exhibits a blunted neck-to-chin angle due to preplatysmal fat accumulation. The patient chooses non-operative treatment of her submental fullness using deoxycholic acid (DCA) injections. Which of the following best characterizes this agent's mechanism of action?
A) Disruption of cellular membrane
B) Injury to endoplasmic reticulum
C) Irreversible binding to cellular mitochondrion
D) Protein binding of Golgi apparatus
E) Targeted injury to cell nucleus
questions.answer:
A)
Deoxycholic acid functions as a nonspecific cytolytic agent that destroys adipocyte cellular membranes upon subcutaneous injection into fat tissue, triggering an inflammatory response that clears cellular debris and released lipids from the treatment area. This membrane disruption is the primary mechanism by which DCA eliminates unwanted submental fat deposits. B) is incorrect because DCA does not specifically target the endoplasmic reticulum, which is involved in protein folding and calcium storage. C) is incorrect because DCA does not bind irreversibly to mitochondria, the cellular organelles responsible for energy metabolism. D) is incorrect because DCA does not interact with the Golgi apparatus, which handles post-translational protein modifications. E) is incorrect because DCA does not specifically target the cell nucleus, which controls gene expression and cellular processes.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female is assessed in the emergency room following a fall onto her extended hand during a tennis match. Physical examination reveals pain on both the back and palm sides of her wrist. Which of the following bones was most probably fractured in this patient?
A) Capitate neck
B) Distal radius
C) Lunate body
D) Scaphoid wrist
E) Triquetral ridge
questions.answer:
B)
Distal radius fractures are the most common wrist injury in adults over 40 years, particularly in women due to increased osteoporosis prevalence, and typically result from falls on outstretched hands. The mechanism described and the patient's demographics make this the most likely diagnosis. A) is incorrect because capitate neck fractures are much less common than distal radius fractures in this age group and mechanism. C) is incorrect because lunate body fractures occur less frequently than distal radius fractures following falls on outstretched hands. D) is incorrect because while scaphoid fractures are the second most common wrist fracture, they are still less frequent than distal radius fractures in this demographic. E) is incorrect because triquetral ridge fractures are less common than distal radius fractures in this clinical scenario.

questions.question:
Which of the following best describes the ear anomaly seen in the photograph?


A) Cryptotia
B) Microtia
C) Pixie ear
D) Prominent ear
E) Stahl ear
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


Cryptotia is a congenital anomaly in which the upper part of the retroauricular sulcus is absent or buried under the temporal skin. Various surgical techniques have been reported for correction of cryptotia, starting with a V-Y plasty in 1933. Conventional methods using local flap, skin grafting, tissue expander, Z-plasty, and any combined approaches correct the skin deficiency of the upper auricle. However, cosmesis can still be unsatisfying because of a visible periauricular scar, color mismatch, or a contracture deformity. Cryptotia may be treated early nonsurgically with splinting of the ear or with surgical release at a later age.


Microtia is a hypoplastic condition of the ear which includes a spectrum from complete absence of the ear (anotia) to a smaller than normal ear with normal morphology. Microtia is seen in patients with the hemifacial microsomia. In fact, patients with isolated microtia are considered to have a mild form of hemifacial microsomia.


Pixie ear deformity is a complication of rhytidectomy.


Prominent ear has a widening of the conchal-scaphal angle, an increased auriculocephalic distance, and loss of the antihelical fold.


Stahl ear, also known as Spock ear, has a third crus, a flat helix, and a malformed scaphoid fossa.


References
1. Chang CC, Wu CI, Chang SC. Aesthetic and functional reconstruction of bilateral cryptotia. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2010 Feb;125(2):54e-56e.
2. Dancey A, Jeynes P, Nishikawa H. Acrylic ear splints for treatment of cryptotia. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2005 Jun;115(7):2150-2152.
3. Kajikawa A, Ueda K, Asai E, et al. A new surgical correction of cryptotia: a new flap design and switched double banner flap. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2009 Mar;123(3):897-901.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with intense pain following a crushing injury to his left lower leg from a forklift accident. Physical examination shows the lower leg is firm and swollen throughout its circumference. Foot sensation is reduced. Peripheral pulses remain detectable. Radiographic examination reveals no bone fractures. Which of the following represents the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Ace wrap compression
B) CT angiography
C) Emergent fasciotomy
D) MRI
E) Observation and leg elevation
questions.answer:
C)
This patient presents with classic signs of acute compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency requiring immediate fasciotomy to prevent irreversible tissue damage. The combination of severe pain, tense swelling, and diminished sensation following crush injury indicates elevated compartment pressures that compromise tissue perfusion. Delayed treatment can result in permanent nerve and muscle damage. A) is incorrect because compression wrapping would worsen compartment pressures and is contraindicated in suspected compartment syndrome. B) is incorrect because CT angiography is unnecessary when vascular injury suspicion is low and pulses are present, and would delay essential treatment. D) is incorrect because MRI is used for chronic exertional compartment syndrome diagnosis but has no role in acute traumatic cases. E) is incorrect because observation and elevation would be inappropriate and dangerous in acute compartment syndrome, potentially leading to tissue necrosis.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman presents to the clinic seeking consultation about breast augmentation surgery. She reports no history of breast lumps or nipple discharge, and her family history is negative for breast cancer. Following discussion, she selects saline implants. She expresses concern about breast cancer risk and asks about screening recommendations. Which of the following screening modalities is most appropriate for this patient following augmentation?
A) CT scan
B) Mammography
C) MRI
D) Positron emission tomography
E) Ultrasonography
questions.answer:
B)

Mammography with Eklund views represents the current standard for breast cancer screening in women with breast augmentation. The Eklund technique involves displacing the implant posteriorly against the chest wall while pulling breast tissue anteriorly around the prosthesis, which enhances mammographic sensitivity for cancer detection. Due to potential interference from breast implants with tissue visualization, diagnostic rather than screening mammography may be recommended even for asymptomatic patients. A) CT scanning is incorrect because while studied for breast evaluation, it is not routinely employed for breast imaging or screening. C) MRI is incorrect because although it has high sensitivity, it has lower specificity and high cost, making it unsuitable for general population screening (though it may be considered for high-risk patients). D) PET scanning is incorrect because it is not used for breast cancer screening but rather as an adjunct in diagnosed patients to assess nodal or distant spread. E) Ultrasonography is incorrect because while it may serve as a screening adjunct, it is not recommended as a primary screening tool due to its operator-dependent nature.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old man presents with a fungating mass of the right shoulder that has been enlarging for the past 12 years. A photograph is shown. Medical history is unremarkable. The patient reports that he spent his youth working outside. He has a history of smoking. Which of the following is the most significant risk factor for development of this lesion in this patient?


A) CDK4 mutation
B) Previous use of topical steroids
C) Smoking history
D) Sun exposure
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The patient presents with a nodular ulcerated basal cell carcinoma to the right shoulder. Basal cell carcinoma is the most common malignancy in the United States due to the increase in sun exposure and tanning salons. The most common risk factor for basal cell carcinomas is sun exposure. Generally, they do not metastasize and are resectable, but do lead to large oncologic resections if left to progress, as is the case in the patient described. Smoking history, although important, does not have a major impact on the risk for basal cell cancer. Marjolin ulcers are a variant of squamous cell carcinoma that results from the chronic inflammatory process that follows burns and is not a risk factor for basal cell carcinoma. Immunosuppression is a risk factor for basal cell carcinomas, but it is not as great as sun exposure and this patient has no history of immunosuppression. Other risk factors for basal cell carcinoma include being male and of older age, but these are not listed as possible choices. A mutation in the CDK4 gene is linked to familial melanoma and would have no relation to the basal cell tumor in this patient. Topical steroid use has no known impact on risk for development of basal cell carcinoma.


ReferencesConnolly KL, Nehal KS, Disa JJ. Evidence-based medicine: cutaneous facial malignancies: nonmelanoma skin cancer. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2017;139(1):181e-190e.Mendez BM, Thornton JF. Current basal and squamous cell skin cancer management. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2018;142(3):373e-387e.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old fair-complexioned man presents for evaluation of an irregular dark lesion on his back. His history includes multiple episodes of sunburn. Physical examination reveals an 8 mm dome-shaped, dark lesion resembling a blood blister, with regular borders. Biopsy demonstrates a well-demarcated proliferation of atypical melanocytes with vertical extension throughout the dermis and no lateral spread of the intraepidermal component. Which of the following represents the most likely melanoma subtype?
A) Acral lentiginous
B) Desmoplastic
C) Lentigo maligna
D) Nodular
E) Superficial spreading
questions.answer:
D)

This presentation is characteristic of nodular melanoma, which comprises 10-20% of melanomas and commonly affects the trunk, head, and neck with male predominance. These lesions exhibit rapid vertical growth upon dermal invasion, contrasting with the radial growth pattern of superficial spreading types. They typically appear as dark, dome-shaped lesions resembling blood blisters and carry increased metastatic risk. Histologically, they show sharply demarcated epidermal components with extensive dermal proliferation of atypical melanocytes. A) Acral lentiginous is incorrect because it predominantly occurs in dark-skinned individuals on palms, nail beds, and soles. B) Desmoplastic is incorrect because while locally aggressive, it rarely metastasizes and histologically resembles spindle cell tumors. C) Lentigo maligna is incorrect because it represents a rare, low-malignancy form that grows slowly in radial fashion, typically appearing as large tan lesions with convoluted patterns on sun-exposed areas in older women. E) Superficial spreading is incorrect because it features lateral epidermal spread of malignant melanocytes with prolonged radial growth before vertical development.

questions.question:
Which of the following bony abnormalities of the anterior nasal spine are most frequently observed in patients with unilateral cleft lip and palate?
A) Deviation toward the cleft side with reduced projection of the pyriform aperture and dentoalveolar arch on the cleft side
B) Deviation toward the cleft side with enhanced projection of the pyriform aperture and dentoalveolar arch on the cleft side
C) Deviation toward the noncleft side with reduced projection of the pyriform aperture and dentoalveolar arch on the cleft side
D) Deviation toward the noncleft side with enhanced projection of the pyriform aperture and dentoalveolar arch on the cleft side
questions.answer:
C)

In unilateral cleft lip and palate, the anterior nasal spine characteristically deviates toward the noncleft side, while the inferior border of the bony nasal septum deviates toward the cleft side. Additionally, there is diminished sagittal projection of both the pyriform aperture and dentoalveolar arch on the affected side. A) is incorrect because the anterior nasal spine deviates away from, not toward, the cleft side. B) is incorrect because it incorrectly describes both the direction of deviation and suggests increased rather than decreased projection. D) is incorrect because while the deviation direction is correct, the projection is decreased, not increased, on the cleft side.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old woman receives reconstruction of a defect using an anterolateral thigh flap. Which of the following branches of the lateral femoral circumflex artery most commonly serves as the dominant vascular supply for the flap perforator?
A) Ascending
B) Descending
C) Oblique
D) Transverse
questions.answer:
B)

The descending branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery serves as the dominant vascular supply for anterolateral thigh flap perforators in approximately 85% of cases. While significant perforators can originate from ascending, transverse, or descending branches, the descending branch is most frequently the primary source, followed by transverse and ascending branches in order of frequency. A variable oblique branch may occasionally serve as the primary supply in about 15% of cases when present. A) Ascending is incorrect because while it can provide perforators, it is less common than the descending branch. C) Oblique is incorrect because this variable branch, when present, only serves as primary supply in approximately 15% of cases. D) Transverse is incorrect because although it can provide perforators, it is the second most common source after the descending branch.

questions.question:
A 10-month-old female infant is examined for an enlarging bright red lesion affecting the left cheek and lower eyelid. Her parents note the lesion was absent at birth but has expanded rapidly over the past 9 months. After cardiac evaluation clearance, propranolol therapy is started and titrated to 2 mg/kg/day. Which of the following electrolyte disturbances is the most likely adverse effect in this patient?
A) Hypercalcemia
B) Hyperkalemia
C) Hypermagnesemia
D) Hypernatremia
E) Hyperphosphatemia
questions.answer:
B)

Infantile hemangiomas represent the most frequent benign tumors in infancy, characterized by rapid proliferation over 6-12 months followed by gradual involution over 1-5 years. Propranolol, a nonselective beta-adrenergic antagonist, has become first-line therapy for these lesions. However, treatment can cause adverse effects including bradycardia, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte abnormalities, particularly hyperkalemia. A) Hypercalcemia is incorrect because elevated calcium levels are not associated with propranolol administration. C) Hypermagnesemia is incorrect because increased magnesium levels are not a recognized side effect of propranolol therapy. D) Hypernatremia is incorrect because elevated sodium levels are not linked to propranolol treatment. E) Hyperphosphatemia is incorrect because increased phosphate levels are not associated with propranolol use.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old African American male presents for assessment of a 3-mm pigmented band on his left index finger nail. Complete nail matrix biopsy establishes a melanoma diagnosis. Which factor below is most critical for determining this patient's prognosis and 5-year survival?
A) Mitotic activity
B) Clear surgical margins
C) Anatomical location
D) Disease staging
E) Lesion width
questions.answer:
D)
Disease staging is the most crucial prognostic factor for this patient with acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM). This melanoma subtype occurs predominantly in darker-skinned individuals and presents as pigmented streaks on nail beds, palms, or soles. While ALM has a generally poorer prognosis than other melanoma types (80% vs 91% 5-year survival), tumor depth remains the primary staging determinant and strongest predictor of outcomes. Deeper tumors correlate with higher rates of nodal metastasis and distant spread. A is incorrect because while mitotic activity can influence staging, it's no longer part of early melanoma staging criteria and is not the primary prognostic determinant. B is incorrect because although achieving clear margins can be challenging in nail unit melanomas and may require amputation, prognosis is still primarily determined by tumor depth at diagnosis rather than margin status. C is incorrect because anatomical location doesn't directly affect prognosis - the poorer outcomes in ALM relate more to delayed diagnosis leading to advanced stage rather than the location itself. E is incorrect because lesion width, while lesions >2mm are more likely to be invasive, is not incorporated into staging systems or prognosis determination.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male patient who recently had cardiac bypass surgery develops a sternal infection requiring surgical debridement. After assessment of the resulting defect, reconstruction with an omental flap is planned. Which vascular supply below nourishes this flap?
A) Gastroepiploic vessels
B) Left gastric vessels
C) Right gastric vessels
D) Short gastric vessels
E) Superior mesenteric vessels
questions.answer:
A)
The omental flap receives its blood supply from the gastroepiploic vessels. The omentum is vascularized by both left and right gastroepiploic arteries, with the right gastroepiploic typically used as the primary pedicle when increased length is needed. This flap is excellent for sternal reconstruction due to the omentum's angiogenic and immunologic properties, making it particularly suitable for infected wounds. The right gastroepiploic artery originates from the gastroduodenal artery, while the left branches from the splenic vessels. B is incorrect because the left gastric vessels supply the lesser curvature of the stomach, not the omentum. C is incorrect because the right gastric vessels also supply the lesser curvature of the stomach rather than the omentum. D is incorrect because short gastric vessels are splenic artery branches that supply only a portion of the stomach's greater curvature, not the omentum. E is incorrect because superior mesenteric vessels supply the lower duodenum through mid-transverse colon and pancreas, not the omentum.

questions.question:
A 14-year-old female with Crouzon syndrome has severe Class III malocclusion, midface hypoplasia, and significant sleep apnea. Le Fort III advancement with distraction osteogenesis is planned. The complication rate for this procedure most closely approximates which percentage?
A) 5%
B) 20%
C) 40%
D) 60%
E) 80%
questions.answer:
B)
Le Fort III distraction osteogenesis carries approximately a 20% complication rate based on recent literature. While this technique offers advantages over traditional single-stage advancement including reduced relapse, greater advancement distances, and elimination of bone graft requirements, it is associated with significant risks. Reported complications include hardware failure, pin displacement, bone resorption, central nervous system complications like meningitis and seizures, and cerebrospinal fluid leaks. Multiple recent studies consistently demonstrate complication rates near 20% for this procedure. A is incorrect because 5% significantly underestimates the actual complication rate reported in the literature for this complex procedure. C is incorrect because 40% overestimates the complication rate - while serious, the procedure doesn't have this high a complication rate. D is incorrect because 60% greatly exceeds the documented complication rates for Le Fort III distraction. E is incorrect because 80% is far higher than any reported complication rates for this procedure.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old male with T11 paraplegia will undergo reconstruction of a Stage IV ischial pressure ulcer using an inferior gluteal artery thigh flap. He receives intravenous clindamycin every 6 hours empirically for suspected osteomyelitis. What is the most appropriate next step to confirm osteomyelitis in this patient?
A) Bone biopsy
B) CT imaging
