questions.question:
A 38-year-old woman with symptomatic breast enlargement seeks reduction mammaplasty consultation. A medical assistant takes her history, and the plastic surgeon conducts a brief history and thorough physical examination. The patient is deemed suitable for surgery, and the medical assistant obtains a standard hospital consent form without further discussion. The patient signs the document without a witness present. The surgeon faces increased legal liability due to which of the following?
A) Absence of a specialized plastic surgery consent document
B) Failure to verbally discuss reduction mammaplasty risks
C) Missing witness signature on the consent document
D) Involvement of a medical assistant in the consultation
E) No increased risk exists since the patient signed consent
questions.answer:
B)
The surgeon has increased legal risk due to the absence of verbal risk discussion for reduction mammaplasty. Informed consent requires three elements: disclosure, capacity, and voluntariness. The lack of verbal communication about procedure-specific risks represents inadequate disclosure. Written forms alone are insufficient without personal discussion of risks, benefits, and alternatives. A is incorrect because generic hospital forms are acceptable if accompanied by verbal discussion of specific procedural risks. C is incorrect because while witnesses may be hospital policy, they are not legally required for valid informed consent. D is incorrect because medical assistant involvement in consultations is standard accepted practice. E is incorrect because a signed form without proper disclosure does not constitute valid informed consent and increases liability.

questions.question:
A 44-year-old man is referred by his lung specialist for surgical evaluation of obstructive sleep apnea after failing continuous positive airway pressure therapy. His history includes nasal septum repair and soft palate surgery 2 years prior, plus orthodontic treatment 30 years ago. Current examination reveals Class I molar occlusion with normal overjet. Cephalometric measurements show SNA angle 76.7° (normal 80°), SNB angle 72.1° (normal 78°), and posterior airway space 4 mm (normal 11.0 ± 1). Orthognathic surgery is being considered. What is the most appropriate surgical approach?
A) Mandibular advancement alone
B) Maxillary advancement alone
C) Combined maxillary and mandibular advancement
D) Maxillary/palatal widening
questions.answer:
C)
Combined maxillary and mandibular advancement is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's obstructive sleep apnea. The cephalometric analysis shows both maxillary (SNA 76.7° vs normal 80°) and mandibular (SNB 72.1° vs normal 78°) retrusion, along with severely compromised posterior airway space (4 mm vs normal 11 mm). Simultaneous advancement of both jaws provides maximum airway enlargement and soft tissue advancement, achieving success rates of 75-100% in adult OSA patients. The advancement is typically greater than 10 mm regardless of cephalometric findings. A is incorrect because mandibular advancement alone would not address the maxillary retrusion component. B is incorrect because maxillary advancement alone would not correct the mandibular deficiency. D is incorrect because palatal expansion addresses transverse dimension but not the anteroposterior airway compromise evident in this case.

questions.question:
An otherwise healthy 35-year-old man arrives at the emergency department following a motorcycle collision with a stationary bus at 20 mph. After trauma clearance, he undergoes orthopedic management of an open tibia-fibula fracture with external fixation and irrigation of a 15-cm anterior wound exposing bare bone. Plastic surgery consultation is requested for soft-tissue coverage planning. Which additional finding would most likely indicate below-knee amputation rather than limb salvage?
A) 4-cm tibial nerve defect
B) Grade 2 hepatic laceration
C) Ipsilateral complete plantar skin loss with metatarsal fractures
D) Absent pedal pulses after external fixation
E) Parietal brain contusion requiring intubation and neurosurgical care
questions.answer:
A)
A 4-cm tibial nerve defect represents an absolute indication for amputation in Gustilo Type IIIB/IIIC open tibial fractures. Microsurgical nerve reconstruction in this setting has very poor outcomes, and an insensate foot leads to poor functional results with high complication rates. The tibial nerve provides critical plantar sensation essential for weight-bearing function. B is incorrect because liver laceration is a relative contraindication that may resolve, allowing future reconstruction once the patient is stable. C is incorrect because plantar skin loss and metatarsal fractures, while challenging, can be reconstructed with flaps or grafts and do not constitute absolute contraindications. D is incorrect because recent pulse loss after fixation represents acute ischemia that may be correctable and does not meet the 6-hour warm ischemia threshold for absolute amputation indication. E is incorrect because brain injury, while concerning, may improve and is not an absolute contraindication to eventual reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency room 2 hours following an avulsion trauma to the back of his left hand from a motorcycle crash. Clinical assessment reveals total loss of dorsal skin with exposed extensor tendons on the dorsal hand surface without viable peritenon. A lateral arm free flap reconstruction is being considered for the defect. Which of the following vascular pedicles provides blood supply to this flap?
A) Anterior interosseous
B) Inferior cubital cutaneous
C) Posterior radial collateral
D) Radial recurrent
E) Superior ulnar collateral
questions.answer:
C)
The posterior radial collateral artery is the correct vascular supply for the lateral arm free flap. This vessel branches from the profundus brachial artery, which originates from the brachial artery and travels with the radial nerve. The posterior radial collateral artery courses behind the lateral intramuscular septum between the deltoid tubercle and epicondyle. This flap provides flexible tissue coverage and can be harvested from the same limb, and may include muscle, bone, or cutaneous nerves for complex reconstructions. A is incorrect because the anterior interosseous artery supplies the posterior interosseous flap on the forearm dorsum. B is incorrect because the inferior cubital cutaneous artery is used for fascial cutaneous flaps in the forearm. D is incorrect because the radial recurrent artery creates a reversed pedicle flap that can only reach the mid-forearm, not the hand. E is incorrect because the superior ulnar collateral artery supplies the medial arm flap.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old child presents with a central cleft of the upper lip. This cleft develops from incomplete fusion of which of the following embryologic components?
A) Lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
B) Maxillary and mandibular prominences
C) Medial and lateral palatine processes
D) Medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence
E) Medial nasal prominences only
questions.answer:
E)
A central cleft lip occurs due to incomplete fusion of the medial nasal prominences during embryonic development. This represents a failure of the two medial nasal prominences to properly unite in the midline. A is incorrect because failure of fusion between the lateral nasal prominence and maxillary prominence causes oblique facial clefts. B is incorrect because failed fusion of maxillary and mandibular prominences results in lateral oral commissure clefts. C is incorrect because failure of medial and lateral palatine process fusion produces primary palate clefts. D is incorrect because incomplete fusion of the medial nasal prominence and maxillary prominence creates unilateral cleft lip.

questions.question:
A 62-year-old female patient has a left mastectomy with axillary node dissection and tissue expander reconstruction. Drainage tubes are positioned near the tissue expander and in the axillary region. An IV line is inserted in her left arm, and blood pressure monitoring occurs on the same extremity. Her BMI is 42 kg/m2. Which of the following risk factors has the strongest association with lymphedema development in this patient?
A) Compression from a blood pressure cuff
B) Drain placement in the axilla
C) Obesity
D) Placement of an intravenous catheter
E) Tissue expander reconstruction
questions.answer:
C)
Obesity with BMI >30 kg/m2 represents the most significant lymphedema risk factor among the options provided. Patients undergoing axillary lymphadenectomy and radiation face approximately 30% lymphedema risk, with obese patients at even higher risk. Severe obesity (BMI 50-60 kg/m2) can independently cause lymphedema, particularly bilateral lower extremity involvement, without other precipitating factors. A is incorrect because blood pressure cuff compression does not cause lymphedema and compression is actually used therapeutically for lymphedema treatment. B is incorrect because axillary drain placement does not increase lymphedema risk. D is incorrect because IV catheter placement lacks evidence for increasing lymphedema risk. E is incorrect because tissue expander reconstruction does not elevate lymphedema risk.

questions.question:
Which of the following pedicle techniques in reduction mammaplasty carries the highest risk for compromised nipple sensation?
A) Inferior
B) Inferocentral
C) Lateral
D) Superior
E) Superomedial
questions.answer:
D)
The superior pedicle technique poses the greatest risk for diminished nipple sensation because it requires resection of breast tissue at the base, potentially damaging nerve branches that supply the nipple-areolar complex. The lateral cutaneous nerve branches travel deeply within the pectoral fascia before turning anteriorly to innervate the nipple from its deep surface, making them vulnerable during superior pedicle procedures. A is incorrect because the inferior pedicle preserves tissue containing lateral cutaneous branches, reducing nerve injury risk. B is incorrect because the inferocentral pedicle also maintains the lateral cutaneous nerve supply. C is incorrect because the lateral pedicle technique preserves the nerve branches providing nipple sensation. E is incorrect because the superomedial pedicle maintains the anterior cutaneous branches that run superficially from the medial breast and provide nipple sensation.

questions.question:
A 2-month-old baby is evaluated for abnormal skull shape. Physical findings include low-positioned ears, short webbed digits, and duplicated great toes. CT imaging demonstrates sagittal and lambdoid suture fusion. A genetic mutation in which of the following genes most likely accounts for these clinical features?
A) FGFR1
B) FGFR2
C) FGFR3
D) RAB23
E) TWIST1
questions.answer:
D)
This constellation of findings represents Carpenter syndrome, which results from RAB23 gene mutations located on chromosome 6. Carpenter syndrome follows autosomal recessive inheritance but can also arise from de novo RAB23 mutations. The syndrome combines craniosynostosis with symbrachydactyly and preaxial polydactyly as seen in this patient. A is incorrect because FGFR1 mutations cause Pfeiffer syndrome, which has different clinical features. B is incorrect because FGFR2 mutations result in Apert and Crouzon syndromes with distinct presentations. C is incorrect because FGFR3 mutations lead to Muenke syndrome, not the features described. E is incorrect because TWIST1 gene mutations cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome with different characteristics.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old male presents to the clinic with a 2-cm pigmented lesion on his right lower back that has been gradually increasing in size over 3 years. No palpable lymph nodes are detected. Punch biopsy analysis reveals Clark Level IV malignant melanoma with Breslow thickness of 1.2 mm and ulceration present. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?
A) Surgical excision with 2-cm margins
B) Preoperative lymphoscintigraphy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and surgical excision with 1-cm margins
C) Preoperative lymphoscintigraphy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and surgical excision with 2-cm margins
D) Surgical excision with 1-cm margins, then lymphoscintigraphy and sentinel lymph node biopsy performed subsequently
E) Surgical excision with 3-cm margins, split-thickness skin grafting, and right axillary lymph node dissection
questions.answer:
C)
The optimal treatment is preoperative lymphoscintigraphy, sentinel lymph node biopsy, and surgical excision with 2-cm margins. For melanomas 1.2 mm thick on the lower back, 2-cm margins are preferred over 1-cm margins because punch biopsy may underestimate final tumor thickness, and adequate tissue is available in this location. Standard margin recommendations are 5 mm for in situ lesions, 1 cm for <0.8 mm thickness, and 2 cm for 0.8-4 mm thickness. Intermediate thickness melanomas (0.8-4 mm) have 20-25% risk of microscopic regional disease, making sentinel lymph node biopsy valuable for staging and identifying high-risk patients for adjuvant therapy. Preoperative lymphoscintigraphy is essential to map drainage patterns, especially on the trunk where aberrant drainage occurs in 20-35% of cases. Concurrent procedures are preferred as prior excision can alter lymphatic drainage patterns. A is incorrect because it omits sentinel lymph node biopsy needed for staging intermediate thickness lesions. B is incorrect because 1-cm margins may be inadequate given potential underestimation from punch biopsy. D is incorrect because delayed sentinel lymph node biopsy after excision may be inaccurate due to altered drainage patterns. E is incorrect because 3-cm margins are excessive and axillary dissection is not indicated without positive sentinel nodes.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male presents for post-traumatic skull reconstruction 6 months following a motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals a 5 × 4-cm full-thickness skull defect in the left parietal area. Titanium/hydroxyapatite cement cranioplasty reconstruction is being considered. Which mechanism best characterizes the healing process of hydroxyapatite?
A) Endochondral ossification
B) Osteochondrosis
C) Osteoconduction
D) Osteogenesis
E) Osteoinduction
questions.answer:
C)
Osteoconduction is the primary healing mechanism of hydroxyapatite cement. During osteoconduction (creeping substitution), the hydroxyapatite acts as a non-living scaffold that allows ingrowth of blood vessels and bone-forming cells from the surrounding recipient tissue. The material is gradually resorbed and replaced with new bone tissue. Hydroxyapatite cement consists of tetracalcium phosphate and dicalcium phosphate anhydrous that form a moldable paste in aqueous solution, setting without heat generation (isothermically). This bioactive calcium phosphate compound integrates directly with bone through osseointegration, forming chemical bonds without intervening fibrous tissue. A is incorrect because endochondral ossification involves cartilage transformation to bone during fracture healing, not the mechanism of hydroxyapatite integration. B is incorrect because osteochondrosis refers to pediatric ossification disorders, unrelated to implant healing. D is incorrect because osteogenesis involves viable bone cells producing new bone, which occurs with living bone grafts, not synthetic materials. E is incorrect because osteoinduction involves bone morphogenetic proteins stimulating stem cell differentiation into bone cells, which is associated with demineralized bone matrix, not hydroxyapatite cement.

questions.question:
A 2-year-old boy with VATER syndrome is brought to the office for evaluation because his parents are concerned that the thumb of the right hand appears small and weak. Physical examination shows weakness of intrinsic function of the right thumb. The flexor pollicis longus flexion crease is absent and the thenar eminence is flat. The left hand, including the thumb, appears normal. The patient uses a pincer-type motion between the right index and long fingers to pick up small objects. The ulnar collateral ligament at the metacarpophalangeal joint of the right thumb is lax. There is no gross dislocation at the carpometacarpal joint of the right thumb, but 6 mm of passive dorsoradial mobility is noted. An x-ray study and photograph are shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?


A) Amputation of the thumb and pollicization of the index finger
B) Flexor digitorum sublimis opponensplasty and ulnar collateral ligament stabilization
C) Huber transfer and ulnar collateral ligament stabilization
D) Tendon graft reconstruction of the flexor pollicis longus and ligament stabilization
E) Observation and occupational therapy until the child is age 4 to 5 years, followed by reassessment of function
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


The child described has a classic Blauth Type IIIB hypoplastic thumb. Although the carpometacarpal (CMC) joint does not dislocate, the subluxation described is consistent with the instability noted in Blauth Type IIIB thumbs. The photograph shows a thumb with a broad base, which is distracting to the examinee who is not familiar with this disorder. However, the thumb described has significant hypoplasia and pollex abductus. The x-ray study shows the classic finding of a narrowed and underdeveloped metacarpal base, the hallmark of CMC instability.


X-ray study is essentially diagnostic of the Blauth Type IIIB thumb. The most accepted treatment for this type of thumb is ablation/amputation of the existing thumb and replacement with the index finger in the thumb position (pollicization).


In the scenario described, the patient has no significant cortical representation or intentional control of the right thumb. The child picks up objects between the index and long finger, ignoring the thumb. No matter what maneuvers are undertaken to power and stabilize the existing thumb with tendon transfers, the child will still have little to no natural predilection to actually use the thumb. Although opponensplasty and ulnar collateral ligament stabilization are common solutions for Types II and IIIA thumbs, they would not be appropriate. These treatments are often combined with first web space deepening.


Treatment is recommended earlier than age 4 or 5 years to avoid resistance to the thumb ablation and pollicization, which can occur with time on the part of the parents and the child. The younger child will accommodate the pollicized digit better. Treatment of the hypoplastic thumb should be decisive and performed at the appropriate age, if possible.


Flexor pollicis longus reconstruction with a tendon graft will not improve thumb function in the scenario described. This type of surgery is not a standard therapy for hypoplastic thumbs in general. Ulnar collateral ligament stabilization is not recommended because the thumb requires pollicization.


References
Schecker LR, Cendales LC. Correcting congenital thumb anomalies in children: opponensplasty and pollicization. In: Gupta A, Kay SPJ, Scheker LR, eds. The Growing Hand: Diagnosis and Management of the Upper Extremity in Children. Philadelphia: Mosby; 2000:171-182.
Hostin R, James MA. Reconstruction of the hypoplastic thumb. J Hand Surg Am. 2004 Nov;4(4):275-290.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male returns for evaluation 3 years after sustaining a scaphoid fracture in his dominant right wrist that was managed with casting until radiographic union. Current examination demonstrates decreased wrist extension to 35 degrees, diminished grip strength, and dorsoradial wrist discomfort. Scaphoid malunion is suspected, and oblique sagittal CT imaging is performed. What is the minimum intrascaphoid angle threshold requiring surgical correction?
A) 10 Degrees
B) 25 Degrees
C) 45 Degrees
D) 65 Degrees
E) 80 Degrees
questions.answer:
C)
Surgical intervention for scaphoid malunion or "humpback" deformity is indicated when the lateral intrascaphoid angle exceeds 45 degrees. This angle is measured by drawing lines tangent to the dorsal cortex of the distal fragment and palmar cortex of the proximal fragment, with normal values being 30-40 degrees. Research by Amadio demonstrated that patients with intrascaphoid angles less than 35 degrees had good clinical outcomes in 83% of cases with 22% developing arthritis, while those with angles greater than 45 degrees had good outcomes in only 27% with 54% developing posttraumatic arthritis. Opening interposition wedge bone grafting is the recommended treatment for angles exceeding this threshold. A is incorrect because 10 degrees is well below the normal range and would not indicate malunion. B is incorrect because 25 degrees falls within the normal range and surgical intervention would not be warranted. D is incorrect because while 65 degrees would certainly require surgery, it is not the minimum threshold - intervention is needed at the lower 45-degree cutoff. E is incorrect because 80 degrees represents severe deformity but again is not the minimum threshold for surgical intervention.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old female seeks consultation for nasal surgery. She expresses dissatisfaction with her nasal tip, describing it as "overly large and broad." Which suture technique would be most effective for creating a more refined triangular tip configuration?
A) Columellar septal
B) Interdomal
C) Lateral crural mattress
D) Medial crural
E) Transdomal
questions.answer:
E)
The transdomal suture is the most effective initial technique for refining a broad, bulbous nasal tip. This suture technique narrows the dome area and reduces the convexity of the lateral crus while providing mild tip projection enhancement, creating the desired triangular tip refinement. It is considered the primary suture for addressing tip width and bulbosity. A is incorrect because columellar septal sutures are used to restore tip strength and integrity, particularly after transfixion incisions, rather than for tip refinement. B is incorrect because interdomal sutures primarily address asymmetry in dome height or reduce interdomal distance, not overall tip bulbosity. C is incorrect because lateral crural mattress sutures are designed to create lateral crural concavity rather than narrow the tip. D is incorrect because medial crural sutures are used to modify tip projection (increase or decrease) rather than address tip width or bulbosity.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old former landscaper with Fitzpatrick type I skin presents with a 5-year history of multiple flat, red, scaly lesions (>20) on his hairless scalp. He notes several additional similar lesions during routine follow-up. Shave biopsy of multiple specimens demonstrates cellular atypia confined above the basement membrane with overlying parakeratosis. He has no previous skin cancer history. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Cryotherapy
B) Systemic pembrolizumab
C) Topical 5-fluorouracil
D) Wide local excision
E) Observation
questions.answer:
C)
Topical 5-fluorouracil represents the most appropriate initial treatment for multiple widespread actinic keratoses. These premalignant lesions have a 0.025-16% annual risk of progression to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Field-directed therapy with topical agents like 5-fluorouracil is ideal for treating both clinically visible and subclinical lesions across areas of chronic sun damage. 5-Fluorouracil is an FDA-approved pyrimidine analog that interferes with DNA synthesis by inhibiting thymidylate synthetase, achieving 84% clearance rates with 1-2 daily applications for 2-4 weeks. A is incorrect because cryotherapy is lesion-directed therapy appropriate for fewer than 15 individual lesions, not widespread field treatment of >20 lesions. B is incorrect because pembrolizumab is a PD-1 inhibitor used for metastatic or unresectable melanoma, not for premalignant actinic keratoses. D is incorrect because wide local excision is reserved for individual malignant lesions, not appropriate for extensive benign premalignant conditions. E is incorrect because continued observation alone is inadequate given the patient's development of new lesions and the malignant potential of actinic keratoses.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old female presents to the clinic with a 1-week history of redness and clear fluid discharge from her right breast occurring 6 weeks following bilateral breast augmentation surgery. She has no fever and her vital signs are normal. Fluid from the breast is cultured. Wide-spectrum antibiotics are given, but no improvement occurs after 48 hours. Surgical cleaning and removal of the implants are performed. After 7 days, cultures reveal Mycobacterium fortuitum growth. What is the most appropriate next management step?
A) Give ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 6 weeks
B) Give ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 6 months
C) Give isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide for 6 weeks
D) Give isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide for 6 months
E) No antibiotic treatment is necessary since the infected implants have been removed
questions.answer:
B)
The most appropriate next management step is to start a 6-month treatment course with ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Mycobacterium fortuitum is an atypical, nontuberculous mycobacterium (NTM) and represents one of the most frequent causes of NTM soft-tissue infections. It typically occurs with foreign body presence, such as breast implants. These opportunistic infections have become more common over time. NTM infections can be more subtle and appear weeks or months after surgery. They typically present with redness, swelling, and clear discharge, though pus may occur. Fever may be absent. During surgical exploration, excessive granulation tissue and cloudy, odorless fluid are commonly found. Standard Gram stains and cultures are typically negative. Therefore, requesting acid-fast bacilli staining and mycobacterial cultures is crucial when NTM infection is suspected. Implant removal and complete debridement of the surrounding space, followed by extended (3 to 6 months) antibiotic treatment, is necessary to treat this infection. Culture sensitivity results should guide antibiotic selection, but ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, clarithromycin, and doxycycline are commonly used. A) is incorrect because 6 weeks of treatment is insufficient for NTM infections. C) and D) are incorrect because isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide are tuberculosis medications for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, not atypical mycobacteria. E) is incorrect because although implant removal is required, extended antibiotic therapy is essential for treatment.

questions.question:
An otherwise healthy 14-year-old female with Poland syndrome presents to the clinic due to breast asymmetry and severe right breast enlargement symptoms. She wears size E cup bras and must pad the left side for clothing symmetry. Physical examination reveals absent breast development and missing sternal portion of the left pectoralis major muscle on the left side, with enlarged right breast. What is the most appropriate reconstructive approach for this patient?
A) Left breast reconstruction using latissimus dorsi flap with right breast reduction surgery
B) Left breast reconstruction using latissimus dorsi flap alone
C) Left subcutaneous tissue expander placement with right breast reduction surgery
D) Delay surgery until puberty completion
questions.answer:
C)
The most appropriate reconstructive approach is to place a subcutaneous expander on the left side and perform right breast reduction. This patient is still undergoing puberty with several years of growth remaining. However, her breast asymmetry is severe, causing symptoms, and negatively affecting her quality of life. Additionally, she has strong family support with engaged parents. Surgery that may cause permanent anatomical changes (such as scarring) and potential negative outcomes (such as breastfeeding difficulties) requires very thorough informed consent, particularly in minors. Conversely, avoiding treatment could also result in negative social, emotional, psychological, and physical effects. Therefore, if the patient and parents comprehend the risks and benefits with complete information, surgical intervention is justified in cases like this. Simply placing an expander on the left without addressing the symptomatic right breast fails to resolve all her concerns. Right breast reduction will help with breast enlargement symptoms and enable more symmetric reconstruction. Using a prosthesis to match an E cup breast is not optimal and will not succeed. Reducing the breast to approximately C cup size gives the surgeon a realistic opportunity to reconstruct the left side to match the right breast. A) is incorrect because latissimus dorsi flap alone lacks sufficient tissue volume for larger breast reconstructions like this case. B) is incorrect for the same reason as A) and doesn't address the symptomatic right breast. D) is incorrect because the severe asymmetry and symptoms justify intervention despite ongoing puberty.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old woman is scheduled to undergo breast reduction with resection of 2.4 lb (1100 g) from each breast. Current weight is 200 lb (91 kg), and height is 5 ft 8 in (173 cm). Physical examination shows macromastia with nipple-sternal notch distance of 34 cm on the left and 35 cm on the right. A photograph is shown. Which of the following postoperative complications is most likely in this patient?


A) Bleeding
B) Fat necrosis
C) Infection
D) Seroma
E) Wound breakdown
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Breast reduction is one of the most commonly performed procedures in plastic surgery, and outcomes following breast reduction have been well studied. Common risks associated with breast reduction include infection, symptomatic scar, seroma, wound healing complications, fat necrosis, asymmetry, and need for reoperation. BMI, volume of breast tissue resection greater than 1000 g per breast, and tobacco use are the greatest risk factors for complication following surgery. Wound healing complications are more likely to occur following breast reduction in a young, healthy, but obese patient with large resection volumes. Other complications might occur but are less common. None of the other complications have been associated with risk factors.


References
Cunningham BL, Gear AJ, Kerrigan CL, et al. Analysis of breast reduction complications derived from the BRAVO study. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2005 May;115(6):1597-1604.
Eggert E, Schuss R, Edsander-Nord A. Clinical outcome, quality of life, patients' satisfaction, and aesthetic results, after reduction mammaplasty. Scand J Plast Reconstr Surg Hand Surg. 2009;43(4):201-206.
Roehl K, Craig ES, G√≥mez V, et al. Breast reduction: safe in the morbidly obese? Plast Reconstr Surg. 2008 Aug;122(2):370-378.

questions.question:
Appropriate restoration of a zygomaxillary complex (ZMC) fracture requires restoration and realignment of which of the following structures?
A) Zygomatic arch, infraorbital rim, alveolar process
B) Zygomaticofrontal suture, infraorbital rim, alveolar process
C) Zygomaticofrontal suture, zygomaticomaxillary buttress, infraorbital rim
D) Zygomaticofrontal suture, zygomaticomaxillary buttress, orbital floor
E) Zygomaticomaxillary buttress, infraorbital rim, alveolar process
questions.answer:
C)
A zygomatic fracture involves displacement of the zygoma that connects with the frontal bone, maxilla, and sphenoid. To stabilize the fracture after proper reduction, the zygomaticofrontal suture, zygomaticomaxillary buttress, and infraorbital rim must be fixed. If a large (>2 cm²) orbital floor defect exists after reduction, orbital floor reconstruction is also required to prevent enophthalmos. These three anatomical points represent the key structural connections that must be restored to achieve proper ZMC fracture reduction and stability. A) is incorrect because the zygomatic arch alone is insufficient and the alveolar process is not a primary structural component requiring fixation. B) is incorrect because while it includes two correct structures, the alveolar process is not a primary fixation point. D) is incorrect because although the orbital floor may need reconstruction in some cases, it is not one of the three primary structural points requiring fixation. E) is incorrect because it omits the zygomaticofrontal suture, which is a critical fixation point.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male cyclist presents to the clinic with numbness in the left ring and small fingers. Dorsal sensation is normal. Guyon canal decompression is planned. Which of the following structures forms a boundary of the Guyon canal?
A) Capitate
B) Dorsal distal radioulnar ligament
C) Lunate
D) Pisohamate ligament
E) Volar distal radioulnar ligament
questions.answer:
D)
Guyon canal, also called ulnar canal and ulnar tunnel, provides passage for the ulnar nerve and artery into the hand. It is a semi-rigid fibro-osseous longitudinal tunnel, approximately 4 cm long, starting at the proximal margin of the transverse carpal ligament and ending at the hypothenar aponeurotic arch. The roof consists of the volar carpal ligament. The medial wall includes the pisiform and pisohamate ligament. The lateral wall is the hook of the hamate. The floor consists of the flexor retinaculum and hypothenar muscles. The pisohamate ligament forms part of the medial wall boundary of Guyon canal. A) is incorrect because the capitate is part of the carpal tunnel floor and does not contribute to Guyon canal boundaries. B) and E) are incorrect because the volar and dorsal distal radioulnar ligaments are components of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) and do not form Guyon canal boundaries. C) is incorrect because the lunate is part of the carpal tunnel floor and does not contribute to Guyon canal.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female visits the plastic surgery clinic complaining of eye dryness and burning sensation 1 week following bilateral upper eyelid surgery with skin and muscle removal only performed by another surgeon. Her preoperative history included contact lens wear for over 20 years and laser vision correction (LASIK) 3 months before surgery. Her preoperative examination revealed upper eyelid skin excess, positive orbital vector, normal upper eyelid position, and corneal shields were used during surgery. What is the most likely cause of her postoperative symptoms?
A) Eyelid surgery technique used
B) History of contact lens wear
C) History of laser vision correction (LASIK)
D) Positive orbital vector
E) Use of intraoperative corneal shields
questions.answer:
C)
Eyelid surgery should not be performed within 6 months following LASIK surgery. This waiting period is required to allow corneal sensation to recover. The dryness results from decreased sensation and reduced blinking, leading to increased tear evaporation. Temporary dry eyes occur in up to 26% of patients after eyelid surgery. Initial dry eye treatment involves ocular lubrication. Patients with eye protrusion, exophthalmos, horizontal lid laxity, or negative orbital vector are more susceptible to dry-eye syndrome. LASIK surgery temporarily reduces corneal sensation, and performing eyelid surgery too soon after LASIK compounds this problem, leading to severe dry eye symptoms. A) is incorrect because the blepharoplasty technique (skin and muscle excision only) is standard and not the primary cause of her symptoms. B) is incorrect because patients who wear contact lenses comfortably typically have adequate tear production. D) is incorrect because positive orbital vector (posterior corneal position relative to malar eminence) does not increase dry eye risk; negative vector does. E) is incorrect because intraoperative corneal shields and lubrication are protective measures that decrease ocular exposure.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old male presents to the emergency room 6 hours after reportedly falling asleep on his right arm following consumption of significant amounts of narcotics and alcohol. Physical examination reveals a warm, edematous, and firm arm upon palpation. The patient demonstrates absence of sensation and motor function in the fingers, wrist, and forearm. Following initiation of resuscitative measures, what is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Arteriography
B) Fasciotomy for decompression
C) Home discharge with outpatient follow-up
D) Magnetic resonance imaging
E) Conservative management with limb elevation
questions.answer:
B)
This patient exhibits classic signs of upper extremity compartment syndrome requiring urgent surgical intervention. The clinical presentation of a swollen, tense, warm extremity with complete loss of sensation and movement following prolonged compression indicates compartment syndrome. Time is critical to preserve muscle viability and function, making immediate fasciotomy the priority treatment. A) Arteriography is unnecessary as this is a clinical diagnosis of compartment syndrome, not a vascular injury. C) Discharge would be inappropriate given the urgent nature of compartment syndrome. D) MRI would delay necessary treatment and imaging is not indicated for compartment syndrome diagnosis. E) Observation and elevation would result in irreversible muscle necrosis and permanent disability.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female presents to the clinic with burning pain in her left wrist that began 5 months following hospital discharge. During her hospitalization, a radial arterial catheter was placed for hemodynamic monitoring in the ICU. Physical examination demonstrates focal tenderness and a positive Tinel sign over the volar radial forearm, just medial to the radial artery and above the flexor carpi radialis tendon. What nerve is most likely the source of this suspected condition?
A) Anterior interosseous nerve
B) Median nerve
C) Musculocutaneous nerve
D) Radial nerve
E) Ulnar nerve
questions.answer:
C)
The patient has developed a neuroma of the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve, which provides sensation to the volar forearm including the area over the flexor carpi radialis tendon. This nerve represents the terminal continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve in the forearm. A) The anterior interosseous nerve is primarily motor and provides minimal sensory innervation only to the wrist joint capsule. B) The median nerve provides sensory innervation to the palm and fingers, not the forearm skin. D) The radial nerve's sensory branch (superficial radial nerve) innervates the dorsal radial hand and wrist, not the volar forearm. E) The ulnar nerve provides sensation to the ulnar palm and fingers, not the radial volar forearm.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male with a stage 4 ischial pressure ulcer on the left side undergoes surgical debridement, bone removal, and gluteal myocutaneous flap reconstruction for wound closure. Which risk factor is most strongly associated with ulcer recurrence?
A) Bowel and bladder incontinence
B) Excessive body weight
C) Spinal cord injury with paralysis
D) Advanced patient age
E) Nutritional vitamin deficiency
questions.answer:
C)
Paraplegia represents the highest risk factor for pressure ulcer recurrence, with studies showing an 82% recurrence rate in paraplegic patients compared to 0% in non-paraplegic patients. The inability to sense pressure and reposition independently leads to repeated tissue ischemia and breakdown. A) Incontinence has not been proven to correlate with pressure ulcer formation or recurrence rates. B) While malnutrition increases risk, obesity itself is not the primary predictor of recurrence. D) Age over 70 years is a risk factor, but paraplegia carries much higher recurrence rates. E) Vitamin deficiencies and nutritional supplementation have not been shown to significantly impact pressure ulcer healing or recurrence in evidence-based studies.

questions.question:
A 3-month-old girl is evaluated for abnormal head configuration. Physical examination demonstrates brachycephaly with orbital abnormalities. Genetic analysis reveals no mutations in fibroblast growth factor receptor genes. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Antley-Bixler syndrome
B) Apert syndrome
C) Crouzon syndrome
D) Pfeiffer syndrome
E) Saethre-Chotzen syndrome
questions.answer:
E)
Saethre-Chotzen syndrome is the only craniosynostosis syndrome among the options that is not caused by FGFR mutations, but rather by TWIST gene mutations. It presents with brachycephaly, maxillary underdevelopment, prominent ear crus, and digit fusion. A) Antley-Bixler syndrome variants are associated with FGFR mutations and present with craniosynostosis, choanal atresia, and radiohumeral fusion. B) Apert syndrome results from FGFR2 mutations and features brachycephaly, severe syndactyly, and developmental delays. C) Crouzon syndrome is caused by FGFR mutations and characterized by shallow eye sockets, craniosynostosis, and midface hypoplasia. D) Pfeiffer syndrome involves FGFR1 and FGFR2 mutations with brachycephaly, mild syndactyly, and enlarged thumbs and great toes.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old woman presents with a 4-week history of a rapidly growing left parotid gland mass. Physical examination shows left eyebrow drooping, incomplete left eyelid closure, and inability to depress the left corner of the mouth. These clinical findings most likely indicate tumor extension through which skull base opening?
A) Jugular foramen
B) Foramen lacerum
C) Foramen ovale
D) Foramen rotundum
E) Stylomastoid foramen
questions.answer:
E)
The combination of progressive facial weakness with a parotid mass suggests malignant tumor invasion of the facial nerve main trunk. The facial nerve exits the skull through the stylomastoid foramen, and involvement of multiple facial nerve branches (temporal, zygomatic/buccal, and marginal mandibular) indicates main trunk compromise at this location. A) The jugular foramen transmits cranial nerves IX, X, and XI, not the facial nerve. B) The foramen lacerum contains the internal carotid artery, not neural structures relevant to facial paralysis. C) The foramen ovale carries the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), which controls jaw muscles, not facial expression. D) The foramen rotundum transmits the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2), providing facial sensation but not motor control.

questions.question:
A 26-year-old male experienced a crushing trauma to his left middle fingertip with a fracture at the dorsal aspect of the distal phalanx base and nail bed damage 6 months prior. He received no medical care. Current examination reveals non-healing of the distal phalanx fracture. What secondary deformity is most likely to develop in this patient?
A) Boutonniere deformity
B) Jersey finger
C) Quadriga
D) Swan neck deformity
E) Trigger finger
questions.answer:
D)

This case describes a bony mallet injury where a distal phalanx fracture disrupts terminal extension at the DIP joint. Without treatment, the loss of DIP extension from the non-united bony mallet can lead to swan neck deformity through compensatory hyperextension of the proximal phalanx while the DIP joint remains persistently flexed due to unopposed flexor digitorum profundus pull. This secondary swan neck pattern develops from dorsal migration of the lateral bands and weakening of the volar plate and transverse retinacular ligament at the PIP level. A) Boutonniere deformity results from central slip injury, not terminal extensor disruption. B) Jersey finger occurs from flexor digitorum profundus rupture, not extensor injury. C) Quadriga happens when a shortened repaired FDP tendon limits finger flexion compared to normal-length adjacent tendons. E) Trigger finger involves tendon catching in pulleys, not DIP joint fractures.

questions.question:
Which federal legislation requires insurance companies to provide coverage for breast reconstruction following complete mastectomy and also mandates coverage for related procedures to achieve symmetry in the opposite breast?
A) Affordable Care Act
B) Breast Cancer Patient Education Act
C) SB-255 Amendment to the Knox-Keene Health Care Service Plan Act
D) Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act
questions.answer:
D)

The Women's Health and Cancer Rights Act of 1998 (WHCRA) is the federal legislation that requires insurance coverage for breast reconstruction after mastectomy and related symmetry procedures for the contralateral breast. Despite being enacted over two decades ago, significant disparities in reconstruction access and patient education persist. A) The Affordable Care Act focuses on expanding healthcare access and reducing costs but contains no specific breast reconstruction mandates. B) The Breast Cancer Patient Education Act of 2015 requires educational campaigns about reconstruction options but doesn't mandate insurance coverage. C) SB-255 is California state legislation extending coverage to include reconstruction after lumpectomy, not a federal law addressing post-mastectomy reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 53-year-old male presents to the emergency room with a degloving avulsion injury of his left non-dominant thumb that occurred 3 hours earlier. The severed portion cannot be recovered. Examination reveals skin loss from the interphalangeal joint extending distally on both palmar and dorsal aspects. The distal phalanx bone and both flexor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis longus tendons remain intact. He has no additional injuries. What is the optimal reconstructive approach for this thumb?
A) Revision amputation at the mid-proximal phalanx
B) Great toe wraparound flap
C) Radial forearm osteocutaneous flap
D) Second toe-to-thumb transfer
E) Volar neurovascular advancement flap
questions.answer:
B)

Thumb reconstruction presents significant challenges for hand surgeons. While palmar advancement flaps can address distal skin loss, they're limited to defects under 50% of the thumb's palmar surface distal to the IP joint. For more extensive proximal injuries requiring length and function preservation, regional or distant flaps are necessary. The great toe wraparound flap involves microvascular anastomosis of digital vessels and nerves, delivering superior sensation and cosmetic outcomes. The toe donor site can be skin grafted to maintain length. E) A volar neurovascular advancement flap cannot adequately cover such an extensive defect. A) Mid-proximal phalanx amputation would create an extremely short, poorly functional thumb. C) A radial forearm flap could cover the defect but would lack proper sensation, and the osteocutaneous version is unnecessary since bone is preserved. D) Second toe-to-thumb transfer is inappropriate when bone structure remains intact.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old right-handed male presents to the clinic 3 months after completely transecting both flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus tendons in Zone II of his right middle finger. He did not receive immediate medical care. Physical examination demonstrates complete inability to actively flex at both the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Passive motion remains intact. What is the most appropriate treatment approach?
A) Single-stage tendon grafting
B) Primary repair
C) Tendon transfer
D) Two-stage tendon reconstruction
E) Conservative observation
questions.answer:
D)

Optimal management of Zone II flexor injuries involves repair of both tendons within 10 days before excessive retraction prevents primary end-to-end approximation. Late flexor injuries (beyond 2 weeks) in Zones I, III, IV, and V can be addressed with single-stage grafting. However, Zone II late injuries require two-stage reconstruction because the tendon sheath has collapsed and grafts cannot be easily passed under intact pulleys. The first stage involves pulley reconstruction over a silicone rod, followed by a second stage where the rod is replaced with a tendon graft pulled proximally to distally after suturing to the rod. Two-stage reconstruction is indicated for late Zone II repairs, cases requiring critical pulley reconstruction (A2, A4), or when volar soft tissue reconstruction is needed. B) Primary repair is impossible after 3 months due to tendon retraction and scarring. A) Single-stage grafting fails in Zone II due to collapsed sheath and pulley issues. C) Available tendon transfers lack sufficient length to reach the distal phalanx. E) Observation would leave the patient with permanent functional disability.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male is assessed for inability to abduct or externally rotate his shoulder and inability to flex his elbow 4 months following a high-velocity motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals numbness over the lateral upper arm and forearm regions. Which nerve transfer would be most suitable for restoring shoulder external rotation?
A) Ipsilateral C7 root to upper trunk anterior division
B) Medial pectoral nerve to medial cord
C) Phrenic nerve to long thoracic nerve
D) Radial nerve to axillary nerve
E) Spinal accessory nerve to suprascapular nerve
questions.answer:
E)

The clinical findings suggest a C5-6 avulsion or very proximal upper trunk injury. Shoulder external rotation is accomplished by the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles, both innervated by the suprascapular nerve. Multiple described techniques for harvesting the distal spinal accessory nerve and transferring it to the suprascapular nerve can successfully restore external rotation function. D) Radial to axillary nerve transfer provides deltoid and possibly teres major innervation, improving overall shoulder function but not specifically restoring external rotation. C) While the phrenic nerve serves as a good donor, the long thoracic nerve innervates the serratus anterior, not external rotators. A) Contralateral C7 transfer can innervate the upper trunk, but ipsilateral C7 wouldn't be used since C5-6 roots are destroyed, and coaptation to the anterior division would be distal to the suprascapular nerve origin. B) The medial pectoral nerve has limited reach, and coaptation to the medial cord would innervate the uninjured ulnar nerve.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old male patient with a body mass index of 36 kg/m2 presents to the clinic seeking evaluation for gynecomastia. He is not currently taking any medications. Physical examination reveals no additional abnormalities. Which of the following represents the most probable etiology of this patient's gynecomastia?
A) Reduced circulating estrogen levels
B) Diminished estrogen receptor activity
C) Increased androgen receptor activity
D) Enhanced conversion of androgens to estrogens through aromatization
E) Elevated circulating androgen levels
questions.answer:
D)
Gynecomastia represents benign breast tissue proliferation in males, affecting 40-50% of men above age 40. While it can occur during puberty and in elderly men, the underlying causes vary and may include elevated estrogen levels, reduced androgen levels, or androgen receptor deficiency. In middle-aged and older males, it most frequently results from enhanced aromatization of androgens to estrogens. A is incorrect because decreased estrogen would not cause gynecomastia. B is incorrect because reduced estrogen receptors would decrease, not increase, breast tissue response to estrogen. C is incorrect because excessive androgen receptors would promote masculine characteristics rather than breast development. E is incorrect because increased androgens alone would not cause gynecomastia without conversion to estrogens.

questions.question:
Which of the following situations best exemplifies a medical "near miss" incident?
A) A patient scheduled for right carpal tunnel release undergoes surgical preparation for left carpal tunnel release
B) A patient reports breast stiffness and asymmetry three months following breast implant surgery
C) A patient experiences an asymptomatic pneumothorax following central line insertion
D) A patient prescribed hydroxyzine receives hydralazine instead
E) A patient with documented penicillin allergy receives cephalosporin treatment
questions.answer:
A)
This scenario represents a near miss because the incorrect surgical site preparation could have led to wrong-site surgery if proper time-out procedures had not been implemented. A near miss is defined as an unplanned occurrence that does not cause harm but has the potential to do so. B is incorrect because breast firmness and asymmetry are expected complications of implant surgery, not near misses. C is incorrect because pneumothorax is a known procedural complication, not a near miss. D is incorrect because this represents an actual medication error with potential harm, not a near miss. E is incorrect because treating penicillin-allergic patients with cephalosporins is standard practice given the low cross-reactivity rate.

questions.question:
A 70-year-old male pedestrian is transported to the emergency department following a motor vehicle collision. Assessment reveals multiple rib fractures, a conservatively managed splenic laceration, a right humeral fracture, and a Gustilo Type IIIC fracture of the left mid-tibia. Physical examination demonstrates an 8 × 7-cm anterior soft tissue defect with bone exposure. The patient cannot dorsiflex his left foot, and plantar sensation is absent. Surgical exploration reveals complete transection of the posterior tibial artery and nerve. What is the most appropriate treatment approach for the injured extremity?
A) Above-knee amputation
B) Below-knee amputation
C) Debridement, irrigation, external stabilization, free flap reconstruction, and delayed nerve repair
D) Debridement, irrigation, external stabilization, immediate vascular and nerve repair, and free flap reconstruction
E) Debridement, irrigation, internal stabilization, immediate vascular and nerve repair, and skin grafting
questions.answer:
B)
Given this patient's advanced age, multiple trauma, and insensate lower extremity with complete nerve transection, below-knee amputation represents the most appropriate management. The goal is limb preservation only when the salvaged extremity will provide superior function compared to amputation. Below-knee amputation offers better prosthetic function and requires less energy for ambulation than above-knee amputation. A is incorrect because above-knee amputation provides inferior functional outcomes compared to below-knee amputation. C is incorrect because the extensive injury pattern and patient factors make salvage unlikely to achieve better function than amputation. D is incorrect because nerve repair outcomes in the lower extremity are poor, and anticoagulation for free tissue transfer would increase bleeding risk given the splenic injury. E is incorrect because skin grafting over exposed bone is not viable.

questions.question:
A 154-lb (70-kg), 42-year-old female patient is scheduled for wide-awake flexor tendon repair under local anesthesia. The operative site receives infiltration with 20 mL of 1% lidocaine containing epinephrine. To achieve optimal hemostasis, what is the ideal time interval between anesthetic injection and surgical incision?
A) 5 minutes
B) 10 minutes
C) 15 minutes
D) 25 minutes
E) 45 minutes
questions.answer:
D)
Wide-awake hand surgery techniques enable procedures without general anesthesia or sedation, often eliminating tourniquet use. Achieving optimal hemostasis requires allowing adequate time for epinephrine's maximal vasoconstrictive effect. A prospective randomized study measuring subcutaneous hemoglobin levels demonstrated that optimal vasoconstriction occurs at 25.9 minutes post-injection, significantly longer than the commonly cited 7-10 minutes. Therefore, waiting 25 minutes after injection provides optimal visualization. A is incorrect because 5 minutes is insufficient for maximal vasoconstriction. B is incorrect because 10 minutes, while commonly cited, does not achieve optimal hemostasis. C is incorrect because 15 minutes still does not provide maximal vasoconstriction. E is incorrect because 45 minutes exceeds the optimal timing and may lead to diminishing vasoconstrictive effects.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient is scheduled for abdominoplasty surgery. The plastic surgeon intends to perform a regional nerve block targeting the anterior branches of the segmental spinal nerves. Which anatomical plane represents the most appropriate location for local anesthetic injection?
A) Between the external oblique and internal oblique muscles
B) Between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles
C) Between the skin and external oblique muscle
D) Between the transversus abdominis muscle and peritoneum
questions.answer:
B)
The transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block is optimally performed between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, commonly utilized during abdominoplasty and abdominal wall reconstruction procedures. The anterolateral abdominal wall contains three primary muscles: external oblique, internal oblique, and transversus abdominis. The thoracoabdominal nerves along with ilioinguinal and iliohypogastric nerves provide innervation to this region. The TAP block effectively targets these nerves within the fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles. A is incorrect because this plane does not contain the target nerves for effective blockade. C is incorrect because subcutaneous injection would not reach the deeper nerve structures. D is incorrect because injection near the peritoneum risks intraperitoneal complications and does not target the appropriate nerve location.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old female presents to the clinic complaining of bilateral hand discomfort. She describes increased discomfort when handling frozen items and states that during cold weather, she experiences finger pain requiring electrically heated gloves, with occasional episodes of fingers becoming white and blue. Her medical history reveals no personal or family history of joint or dermatologic conditions. On examination, her fingers are warm with palpable wrist pulses. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for her condition?
A) Botulinum toxin type A injection
B) Oral nifedipine
C) Temperature biofeedback
D) Thoracoscopic sympathectomy
E) Topical nitroglycerin
questions.answer:
B)
The correct answer is oral nifedipine because calcium channel blockers like nifedipine are the established first-line therapy for primary Raynaud syndrome, effectively managing vasospasm in patients without underlying autoimmune conditions. A is incorrect because botulinum toxin injections are reserved as second-line treatment for refractory cases due to cost and risk of temporary muscle paralysis. C is incorrect because temperature biofeedback has shown inconsistent results in studies and is not recommended as primary therapy. D is incorrect because surgical sympathectomy is the most aggressive option, reserved only for patients with non-healing wounds or chronic ischemic changes. E is incorrect because topical nitrates alone have proven ineffective for managing Raynaud syndrome and are only used as adjunct therapy.

questions.question:
A 5-year-old male child is evaluated for a throbbing mass on the palm side of his forearm. His parents report the mass initially developed 10 days prior. Examination reveals a palpable, throbbing mass located at the radial artery. CT angiography demonstrates a true aneurysm of the radial artery. What is the most probable etiology of this patient's condition?
A) Arterial catheterization
B) Crush injury
C) Infective embolism
D) Kawasaki disease
E) Regional block with administration of a local anesthetic agent
questions.answer:
D)
The correct answer is Kawasaki disease because it is a classic cause of true aneurysms in pediatric patients, involving arteriosclerotic changes that affect all three arterial layers (endothelium, media, and adventitia). A is incorrect because arterial catheterization typically causes pseudoaneurysms from acute endothelial injury rather than true aneurysms. B is incorrect because crush injuries usually result in pseudoaneurysms from acute vessel trauma and rupture. C is incorrect because infective emboli cause pseudoaneurysms through acute infectious damage to the vessel wall. E is incorrect because regional anesthetic blocks can cause pseudoaneurysms from needle trauma but do not typically produce true aneurysms.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old male presents with nasal breathing difficulties. The obstruction has persisted since his functional septorhinoplasty procedure 9 months earlier. Acoustic rhinometry demonstrates external nasal valve collapse. What is the most effective intervention for this patient's problem?
A) Alar batten grafting
B) Butterfly grafting
C) Flaring sutures
D) Splay grafting
E) Spreader grafting
questions.answer:
A)
The correct answer is alar batten grafting because it is the most effective treatment for external nasal valve collapse, strengthening and augmenting the weakened lateral crus of the lower lateral cartilage that was likely over-resected during the previous rhinoplasty. B is incorrect because butterfly grafts are used to treat internal nasal valve collapse, not external valve dysfunction. C is incorrect because flaring sutures address internal nasal valve problems rather than external valve collapse. D is incorrect because splay grafts are designed for internal nasal valve correction, not external valve issues. E is incorrect because spreader grafts and flaps are specifically used for internal nasal valve collapse repair.

questions.question:
A 2-month-old male infant presents for assessment of complete unilateral cleft lip and palate. Which tooth bud development is most likely to be compromised in this patient?
A) Central incisor
B) First molar
C) Lateral incisor
D) Premolar
E) Third molar
questions.answer:
C)
The correct answer is lateral incisor because the upper lateral incisor tooth bud is most frequently affected by cleft defects in both primary and permanent dentition due to its proximity to the cleft area. A is incorrect because central incisor tooth buds are typically located too far from the cleft region to be significantly impacted. B is incorrect because first molar tooth buds are positioned too distant from the cleft area to be commonly affected. D is incorrect because premolar tooth buds are generally too far removed from the cleft location to sustain damage. E is incorrect because third molar tooth buds are positioned too remotely from the cleft site to be typically involved.

questions.question:
Which statement best characterizes the growth pattern of skull bones in relation to a fused suture?
A) Oblique
B) Parallel
C) Perpendicular
D) No relation
questions.answer:
B)
The correct answer is parallel because Virchow's law states that bone growth occurs only parallel to a prematurely fused suture while growth perpendicular to the suture is restricted, creating characteristic cranial deformities in various synostosis patterns. A is incorrect because oblique growth does not describe the specific directional restriction imposed by suture fusion according to Virchow's law. C is incorrect because perpendicular growth is actually restricted when a suture fuses prematurely, not enhanced. D is incorrect because there is a definite relationship between suture fusion and growth direction, as clearly defined by Virchow's law governing craniosynostosis patterns.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a 4-year history of numbness and paresthesias affecting the tips of her thumb, index, and middle fingers. These symptoms have progressively worsened and currently disturb her sleep. On examination, she demonstrates weakened thumb opposition and thenar muscle wasting. Pinprick sensation is reduced in the median nerve territory. What electrodiagnostic findings are most likely present?

1. Median sensory latency, 2. Median motor latency, 3. Fibrillations

A) Decreased decreased absent
B) Decreased decreased present
C) Unchanged unchanged absent
D) Increased increased absent
E) Increased increased present
questions.answer:
E)

The correct findings on electrodiagnostic testing are prolonged median sensory latency, prolonged median motor latency, and presence of fibrillations. This patient has advanced carpal tunnel syndrome with median nerve compression causing demyelination and axonal damage. Nerve conduction studies show increased latencies because demyelination slows signal transmission across the compressed nerve segment. Electromyography reveals fibrillations and positive sharp waves in the thenar muscles, indicating ongoing denervation from chronic nerve injury. A is incorrect because latencies increase rather than decrease with nerve compression. B is incorrect because while fibrillations may be present, latencies are prolonged, not decreased. C is incorrect because both latencies would be abnormally prolonged and fibrillations would be present given the clinical severity. D is incorrect because fibrillations would be present with the degree of muscle atrophy and weakness described.

questions.question:
A 51-year-old woman with a history of right breast invasive ductal carcinoma underwent right skin-sparing mastectomy, axillary lymph node dissection, and adjuvant radiotherapy. She now seeks consultation for delayed breast reconstruction. Recent PET imaging shows no distant metastases. Pathology reveals estrogen receptor positive, progesterone receptor positive, HER2 negative invasive ductal carcinoma measuring 2.5 cm with involvement of three axillary lymph nodes. What is the appropriate TNM staging for this malignancy?
A) T1 N2 M0
B) T1 N3 M1
C) T2 N1 M0
D) T2 N3 M0
E) T3 N2 M0
questions.answer:
C)

The correct TNM classification is T2 N1 M0. The primary tumor measures 2.5 cm, which falls into the T2 category (tumors >2 cm but <5 cm). Three positive axillary lymph nodes classify as N1 (1-3 ipsilateral axillary nodes involved). The negative PET scan indicates M0 (no distant metastases). A is incorrect because a 2.5 cm tumor is T2, not T1 (which is <2 cm), and three nodes is N1, not N2. B is incorrect because the tumor is T2, not T1, three nodes is N1, not N3, and there are no distant metastases (M0, not M1). D is incorrect because while the tumor is correctly staged as T2, three positive nodes is N1, not N3 (which requires ≥10 nodes). E is incorrect because the tumor is T2 (2.5 cm), not T3 (which requires >5 cm), and three nodes is N1, not N2.

questions.question:
A healthy 65-year-old woman seeks evaluation for sagging upper eyelids. Physical examination reveals elevated eyelid creases and 3 mm of ptosis. Levator muscle excursion is measured at 10 mm. What surgical intervention would most effectively address the blepharoptosis in this patient?
A) Brow lift surgery
B) Fasanella-Servat procedure
C) Frontalis sling
D) Levator advancement
E) Upper eyelid blepharoplasty
questions.answer:
D)

Levator advancement is the most appropriate treatment for this patient's moderate acquired ptosis. The high eyelid crease and excellent levator function (10 mm excursion) indicate aponeurotic ptosis caused by levator aponeurosis disinsertion from the tarsal plate due to aging. Levator advancement reattaches the muscle to restore proper eyelid position. A is incorrect because brow lift addresses brow ptosis, not eyelid ptosis from levator dysfunction. B is incorrect because the Fasanella-Servat procedure is reserved for mild ptosis (1-2 mm) and works by shortening the posterior lamella rather than addressing aponeurotic disinsertion. C is incorrect because frontalis sling is used when levator function is poor (<4 mm), typically in congenital ptosis cases. E is incorrect because blepharoplasty removes excess skin and fat but does not correct the underlying levator aponeurosis problem causing the ptosis.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man requires reconstruction of a soft-tissue defect on the posterior right elbow using a reverse lateral arm flap. He has no significant medical history and is a nonsmoker. Vascular assessment is normal. Which artery primarily supplies arterial blood flow to this flap?
A) Artery to the biceps muscle
B) Inferior cubital
C) Musculocutaneous perforating branches from the brachioradialis muscle
D) Posterior radial collateral
E) Radial recurrent
questions.answer:
E)

The radial recurrent artery is the primary arterial supply to the reverse lateral arm flap. This vessel branches from the radial artery in the cubital fossa and connects with the posterior radial collateral artery above the lateral epicondyle. The reverse flap relies on retrograde flow through the posterior radial collateral artery via the radial recurrent artery to maintain viability when rotated for elbow coverage. A is incorrect because the artery to the biceps muscle supplies the medial arm flap, not the reverse lateral arm flap. B is incorrect because the inferior cubital artery is the main supply for the antecubital flap. C is incorrect because musculocutaneous perforating branches from the brachioradialis are minor contributors to the antecubital flap. D is incorrect because the posterior radial collateral artery is the dominant supply for the standard (non-reverse) lateral arm flap, not the reverse version.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old boy presents to the physician following a non-displaced mandibular body fracture from a fall. He was placed on a soft diet. Two days later, he returns complaining of pain in the right mandibular lateral incisor when consuming cold beverages. The fracture base has a yellow appearance and is sensitive to probing. Examination reveals a lingual crown fracture. Based on these clinical findings, what is the deepest tooth layer that has been exposed?
A) Cementum
B) Dentin
C) Enamel
D) Pulp cavity
E) Root canal
questions.answer:
B)

The deepest exposed tooth layer is dentin. The yellow coloration at the fracture base and sensitivity to cold and touch indicate that the fracture has penetrated through the enamel into the underlying dentin layer. This represents an Ellis II fracture involving both enamel and dentin. The symptoms of thermal sensitivity and tenderness are characteristic of dentin exposure, as dentin contains tubules that transmit stimuli to the pulp. A is incorrect because cementum covers the tooth root and would not be involved in a crown fracture. C is incorrect because enamel-only fractures (Ellis I) are typically non-tender and would not cause thermal sensitivity. D is incorrect because pulp cavity exposure (Ellis III) would present with a red or bloody appearance at the fracture base, not yellow. E is incorrect because the root canal is part of the pulp system within the tooth root and would not be exposed in a crown fracture.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old female patient requests cosmetic improvement of her nasolabial region to reduce prominent creases. She has previously achieved satisfactory outcomes with hyaluronic acid-based dermal fillers but now wants a more durable solution. Calcium hydroxylapatite is selected to meet this requirement. During her follow-up visit 2 weeks post-treatment, white nodular formations are observed along the nasolabial creases. Which of the following treatment approaches is LEAST effective for managing these white nodules?
A) Surgical removal of the filler material
B) Corticosteroid injection
C) Manual manipulation of the creases
D) Needle puncture and opening of the lumps
questions.answer:
B)
Corticosteroid injection is the least effective treatment for calcium hydroxylapatite-induced nodules. While intralesional steroids work well for complications from poly-L-lactic acid or polymethyl methacrylate fillers, they are not as effective for calcium hydroxylapatite nodules. A) Surgical removal is incorrect because direct excision is an effective treatment option for these nodules. C) Manual manipulation is incorrect because massage is a proven effective treatment method. D) Needle puncture is incorrect because needle disruption and unroofing is a well-established effective treatment approach.

questions.question:
A healthy 25-year-old female patient is scheduled for excision of a 3 × 5-cm atypical nevus on her right thigh. Her medical history is significant for systemic lupus erythematosus, and she has been on continuous oral corticosteroid treatment for over 5 years. She maintains good nutritional status. Which vitamin supplement given perioperatively would most likely enhance wound healing in this patient?
A) A
B) B complex
C) C
D) D
E) E
questions.answer:
A)
Vitamin A supplementation is most beneficial for wound healing in patients on chronic corticosteroid therapy. Corticosteroids impair wound healing by stabilizing lysosomal membranes, while vitamin A has the opposite effect, destabilizing these membranes and counteracting most negative effects of steroids on wound healing. B) B complex is incorrect because B vitamins do not significantly improve wound healing in well-nourished patients. C) Vitamin C is incorrect because while deficiency impairs collagen synthesis, supplementation doesn't benefit well-nourished patients. D) Vitamin D is incorrect because it has not been shown to significantly improve wound healing in well-nourished individuals. E) Vitamin E is incorrect because it does not provide significant wound healing benefits in well-nourished patients.

questions.question:
A 63-year-old male patient comes to the clinic with a 4 × 4-cm heel wound. A local foot specialist has performed debridement of the calcaneal bone, revealing healthy granulation tissue. Following thorough patient consultation, the decision is made to perform a distally based sural fasciocutaneous flap for reconstruction. Which risk factor is most strongly associated with the highest complication rate for this flap?
A) Coronary artery disease
B) Diabetes mellitus
C) Hypertension
D) Obesity
E) Venous insufficiency
questions.answer:
E)
Venous insufficiency carries the highest risk for complications with distally based sural flaps, showing a nine-fold increase in complication risk according to recent meta-analysis. This is because the flap's distal-based design requires reversed venous flow, making venous insufficiency particularly problematic. A) Coronary artery disease is incorrect because it has not been associated with increased flap complication rates. B) Diabetes mellitus is incorrect because while it increases complications, the risk is lower than venous insufficiency. C) Hypertension is incorrect because although it can increase complications, it poses less risk than venous insufficiency. D) Obesity is incorrect because while it increases complication rates, venous insufficiency poses the greatest risk.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old female patient arrives at the emergency department 2 hours following deep partial-thickness burns to her right elbow from a campfire accident. The burn area measures 8 × 20 cm. Following surgical debridement, autograft placement, and application of petrolatum gauze, which dressing type would best support graft survival?
A) Cotton balls with tie-over bolster dressing
B) Dry gauze with compression bandaging
C) Negative pressure wound therapy
D) Occlusive dressing
E) No additional dressing
questions.answer:
C)
Negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) is superior for autograft fixation in burn patients, providing optimal graft stabilization, fluid removal, and enhanced local circulation, which improves graft survival rates. A) Cotton balls with tie-over bolster is incorrect because while effective for small grafts, it's less suitable for larger surface areas and inferior to NPWT. B) Dry gauze with compression is incorrect because although it's a simple fixation method, it doesn't provide the superior outcomes seen with NPWT. D) Occlusive dressing is incorrect because while appropriate for donor sites, it doesn't effectively secure autografts. E) No additional dressing is incorrect because grafts require proper fixation for optimal survival.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old electrical worker is assessed following a high-voltage electrical trauma while servicing a transformer. Clinical examination reveals entry wounds on the palm side of his right distal forearm. He describes numbness and tingling in his little finger along with diminished grip strength in his right hand. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Forearm elevation and monitoring
B) Escharotomy with carpal tunnel decompression
C) Escharotomy with burned tissue removal
D) Forearm fasciotomy
E) Fasciotomy with Guyon canal decompression
questions.answer:
E)
Fasciotomy with Guyon canal release is necessary because this patient has compartment syndrome with ulnar nerve involvement requiring decompression of deeper structures beyond what escharotomy can provide, including the ulnar nerve pathway through Guyon's canal. A) Elevation and observation is incorrect because active compartment syndrome requires immediate surgical intervention. B) Escharotomy with carpal tunnel release is incorrect because escharotomy alone is inadequate for electrical injuries affecting deeper structures, and this doesn't address the ulnar nerve compression. C) Escharotomy with tissue excision is incorrect because escharotomy is insufficient for electrical injury compartment syndrome. D) Forearm fasciotomy alone is incorrect because it doesn't address the ulnar nerve compression at Guyon's canal.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old male presents for evaluation 15 months following a motorcycle accident that resulted in a left humeral fracture and complete avulsion of the left brachial plexus. He has experienced no recovery of motor or sensory function in the left upper extremity but wishes to regain the ability to actively flex his elbow. Which of the following surgical interventions is most likely to restore active elbow flexion in this patient?
A) Free functioning gracilis muscle transfer
B) Pedicled bipolar latissimus dorsi muscle transfer
C) Proximal transfer of the flexor-pronator mass onto the humerus
D) Triceps-to-biceps transfer
E) Ulnar nerve to musculocutaneous nerve transfer
questions.answer:
A)
Free functioning muscle transfer (FFMT) is the optimal choice for restoring elbow flexion in patients with complete brachial plexus injuries presenting more than 12 months after injury. The gracilis muscle is the preferred donor due to its reliable neurovascular anatomy and adequate tendon length. Since this patient presents 15 months post-injury, nerve reconstruction options have exceeded the viable timeframe for motor endplate survival. B) is incorrect because pedicled latissimus dorsi transfer requires intact brachial plexus function. C) is incorrect because Steindler flexorplasty requires residual forearm muscle function. D) is incorrect because triceps-to-biceps transfer needs functioning triceps muscle, which is absent in complete plexus injury. E) is incorrect because nerve transfers are only effective within 6 months of injury and require intact proximal nerve segments.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old female presents to the clinic with a 1-day history of infection involving the right index finger. Physical examination reveals tenderness and swelling of the fingertip pulp. No history of trauma is reported. Which of the following pathogens is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
