A) The cavernous artery is incorrect because it lies deep within the corpus cavernosum making microsurgical repair technically challenging. B) The circumflex artery is incorrect because it provides collateral circulation and is not routinely repaired during replantation. D) The pudendal artery is incorrect because it is located proximally in the pelvis and gives rise to other arteries including the deep dorsal artery. E) The subtunical venous plexus is incorrect because these vessels are too small for reliable microsurgical repair.

questions.question:
A 7-month-old male infant presents with complete syndactyly requiring surgical separation. Which of the following represents the optimal method for web space reconstruction?
A) Coverage with a distally based zigzag flap
B) Coverage with a dorsal rectangular flap
C) Coverage with a volar triangular flap
D) Full-thickness skin grafting
E) Split-thickness skin grafting
questions.answer:
B)

A dorsal rectangular flap based proximally is the standard technique for web space reconstruction in complete syndactyly cases. This approach provides reliable coverage of the newly created web space while allowing for proper digit separation. The flap is designed as part of the overall interdigitating flap pattern used to maximize available skin coverage. A) A distally based zigzag flap is incorrect because it does not provide adequate web space coverage and the distal base may compromise blood supply. C) A volar triangular flap is incorrect because it does not provide sufficient tissue for proper web space reconstruction. D) Full-thickness skin grafting is incorrect because while preferred over split-thickness grafts for digit coverage, grafts are not typically used for web space reconstruction. E) Split-thickness skin grafting is incorrect because it has higher contracture rates and is not the primary choice for web space coverage.

questions.question:
A critically ill 65-year-old female patient in the ICU experiences respiratory failure. Her vital signs show temperature 101.3°F (38.5°C), pulse 105 bpm, and blood pressure 85/60 mmHg with hematocrit 35%. Following intubation, pulse oximetry monitoring is started. Which of the following factors is most likely to compromise pulse oximetry accuracy in this patient?
A) Anemia
B) Fever
C) Hypotension
D) Tachycardia
E) Tachypnea
questions.answer:
C)

Hypotension is most likely to compromise pulse oximetry accuracy by decreasing peripheral arterial blood flow. Pulse oximetry requires adequate pulsatile blood flow to differentiate between arterial and tissue/venous oxygen saturation levels. Low blood pressure reduces the amplitude of arterial pulsations, making it difficult for the device to detect the fluctuations needed for accurate readings. A) Anemia is incorrect because pulse oximetry measures the percentage of hemoglobin that is oxygenated, not the absolute amount, so normal hematocrit levels don't significantly affect readings. B) Fever is incorrect because elevated temperature alone does not directly interfere with the optical detection of pulsatile flow. D) Tachycardia is incorrect because increased heart rate does not impair the device's ability to detect arterial pulsations. E) Tachypnea is incorrect because respiratory rate changes do not directly affect pulse oximetry measurements.

questions.question:
A 29-year-old male presents with pain and inability to bend his dominant right little finger at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint, occurring 6 weeks after a football injury in which he "jammed" the finger. He wants to maintain an active lifestyle with maximum finger mobility. Examination reveals a swollen, tender PIP joint held in slight flexion with inability to actively flex or fully extend at the PIP joint. X-rays and CT of the finger show a chronic dorsal fracture-dislocation of the PIP joint with impaction and comminution of the volar base of the middle phalanx involving approximately 60% of the articular surface, with persistent dorsal subluxation of the middle phalanx and preserved condylar surface of the proximal phalanx. What is the most appropriate treatment?
A) Arthrodesis
B) Dynamic external fixation
C) Hemi-hamate arthroplasty
D) Open reduction and internal fixation
E) Silicone implant reconstruction
questions.answer:
C)

This is a chronic (6-week-old) dorsal PIP fracture-dislocation with impaction and comminution of the volar base of the middle phalanx involving roughly 60% of the articular surface — well beyond the ~30-40% threshold at which the collateral ligament and volar plate attachments are lost and the joint becomes unstable. Because the volar buttress is destroyed and the fragments are impacted and comminuted, the articular surface must be reconstructed rather than reduced. Hemi-hamate arthroplasty uses an osteochondral autograft from the dorsal distal hamate (the ridge between the fourth and fifth metacarpal facets) to recreate the volar articular surface and buttress of the middle phalangeal base, restoring stability while preserving motion. This makes it the preferred option for a young, active patient with a high-demand hand and an intact proximal phalanx condylar surface.

A) Arthrodesis is incorrect because, although it reliably provides stability and pain relief, it eliminates all PIP motion and is reserved as a salvage procedure — particularly poorly suited to the little finger of a young patient wanting maximal mobility, and inappropriate when the proximal phalanx condyles are preserved.

B) Dynamic external fixation (traction/distraction with ligamentotaxis) is incorrect because it depends on mobile, reducible fragments and an intact enough volar rim to remodel; at 6 weeks the fragments are impacted, malunited, and no longer amenable to ligamentotaxis, and with >50% articular loss there is no volar buttress to hold the reduction.

D) Open reduction and internal fixation is incorrect because the comminuted, impacted volar fragments cannot be adequately mobilized, reconstructed, or stably fixed this long after injury; ORIF is best suited to acute injuries with a single large, non-comminuted volar fragment.

E) Silicone implant reconstruction is incorrect because silicone arthroplasty lacks the durability and lateral stability required in a young, active patient (especially in the border digit exposed to lateral stress) and yields inferior motion and higher failure/implant fracture rates compared with hemi-hamate reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old man presents for reconstruction of a 6 √o 11-mm defect involving the nasal alar margin after excision of basal cell carcinoma utilizing Mohs micrographic surgery. The defect involves the skin, cartilage, and nasal lining just lateral to the nasal soft triangle. Photographs are shown. Which of the following reconstructive options is most appropriate?


A) Composite auricular graft
B) Dorsal nasal flap
C) Full-thickness skin graft
D) Nasolabial flap
E) Primary closure
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


Alar rim defects present a challenging reconstructive problem. The primary reconstructive goals are to reestablish structural support, provide nasal lining if necessary, and provide external skin of similar color and texture. Complications of alar rim reconstruction include poor scars, alar notching, nasal obstruction, and narrowing of the nostril. Several choices are available, but a composite graft from the ear will often obtain an excellent cosmetic result. Skin along the alar rim, soft triangle, and columella is quite thin and firmly attached to the lower lateral cartilages. Likewise, skin along the helical rim is firmly attached to the underlying cartilage and useful for replicating the delicate topography of the columella, soft triangle, and nostril margin. Composite grafts are typically harvested from the helical root, but can be harvested from throughout the ear.


Composite cartilage grafts only interface with the recipient bed around the graft‚Äos perimeter. As a result, their size should be limited to defects less than 1.0 to 1.5 cm in maximal diameter. It is recommended that no portion of the graft be greater than 1.0 cm from the wound edge. Additionally, the wound bed should be well vascularized, and the patient should be a non-smoker. Composite cartilage grafts follow a predictable healing pattern: white, blue, and then progressively pink/red as revascularization improves. Perioperative strategies recommended by some authors to increase graft take include steroids, hyperbaric oxygen, and cooling of the graft with iced compresses.


Primary closure would lead to a poor result and distortion of the alar rim. Dorsal nasal flap, nasolabial flap, and a full-thickness skin graft do not provide cartilage support, which would result in likely alar notching and potential collapse. Additionally, the skin from these donor sites would be too thick to replace the thin skin that normally inhabits this location.


ReferencesBurget GC. Aesthetic reconstruction of the nose. In: Mathes SJ, ed. Plastic Surgery. 2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders Elsevier; 2006:586-590.Constantine FC, Lee MR, Sinno S, Thornton JF. Reconstruction of the nasal soft triangle subunit. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2013 May;131(5):1045-1050.Jewett BS. Skin and composite grafts. In: Baker SR, ed. Local Flaps in Facial Reconstruction. 2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA: Mosby Elsevier; 2007:359-364.Menick FJ. Nasal reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2010 Apr;125(4):138e-150e.Menick FJ. Restoring nasal lining ‚Äi the composite skin graft for small full-thickness marginal defects. In: Menick FJ, ed. Nasal Reconstruction Art and Practice. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders Elsevier; 2009:313-323.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for a right-sided grade III microtia (a small, vertically oriented soft-tissue lobular remnant with no recognizable helix or concha) and an absent external auditory canal. Temporal bone CT of the affected ear demonstrates absence of both the stapes and the incus. Reconstruction using autologous rib cartilage is being planned. The child's parents ask about possibilities for enhancing hearing in the affected ear. Which of the following represents the most suitable recommendation?
A) Canal atresia correction should occur following ear reconstruction
B) Canal atresia correction should occur prior to ear reconstruction
C) A bone-conduction hearing device should be implanted following ear reconstruction
D) A bone-conduction hearing device should be implanted prior to ear reconstruction
E) Auditory improvement is not possible for this patient
questions.answer:
C)

The most appropriate response is option C. Staged reconstruction with autologous costal cartilage remains a preferred method for correcting microtia. The timing and approach for addressing associated conductive hearing loss depend on whether the deformity is unilateral or bilateral, whether external ear construction is planned, and the status of middle ear anatomy.

Candidacy for atresia repair is assessed with the Jahrsdoerfer grading system (10 points: stapes present = 2 points; and 1 point each for oval window, middle ear space, facial nerve course, malleus-incus complex, mastoid pneumatization, incus-stapes connection, round window, and appearance of the external ear). This patient loses 2 points for the absent stapes, 1 point for the absent incus (malleus-incus complex), 1 point for the incus-stapes connection, and 1 point for the abnormal external ear, yielding a score of 5 or less. A score of 6 or below predicts poor hearing outcomes, so canal atresia repair is not indicated.

A bone-conduction (bone-anchored) hearing device provides superior and more reliable hearing restoration than atresia repair in this setting. It should be placed after completion of the autologous cartilage ear reconstruction so that the implant, its incision, and any soft-tissue reaction do not compromise the skin envelope, mastoid soft tissue, and vascular supply required for framework coverage.

Options A and B are incorrect because atresia repair is unlikely to succeed with this middle ear anatomy, regardless of timing. Option D is incorrect because device placement should follow, not precede, autologous ear reconstruction. Option E is incorrect because a bone-conduction device can effectively improve hearing in this scenario.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of swelling and pain in the finger. He says that he first started noticing symptoms 4 days ago. Physical examination shows warmth of the fingertip and fluctuance of the nail fold. A photograph is shown. Which of the following bacteria is the most likely cause of this infection?


A ) Enterococcus faecalis
B ) Mycobacterium marinum
C ) Pasteurella multocida
D ) Pseudomonas aeruginosa
E ) Staphylococcus aureus
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


A paronychia is an infection occurring in the space between the nail plate and the paronychial or eponychial fold. Common causes include nail biting and aggressive manicuring. In an otherwise healthy individual, Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus species are the most common pathogens causing a paronychia.


The remaining bacteria listed would only be expected to cause a paronychia in special circumstances. Enterococcus is an enteric bacterium. Mycobacterium marinum can be present in aquatic environments including fish tanks and has also been reported in the Chesapeake Bay. Pasteurella multocida is a common flora of cat mouths. Pseudomonas occurs in areas with moist environments and can be problematic in a burn unit.


References
1. Rigopoulos D, Larios G, Gregoriou S, et al. Acute and chronic paronychia. Am Fam Physician. 2008 Feb 1;77(3):339-346.
2. Lifchez SD, Harriman DA. Impact of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus on treatment of hand infections. Eplasty. 2009 Nov 20;9:e56.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient seeks consultation for nasal surgery. She expresses concern about the downward displacement of her nasal tip during smiling. Which of the following muscles causes this movement?
A) Alar portion of nasalis
B) Depressor septi nasi
C) Levator labii superioris alaeque nasi
D) Procerus
E) Transverse portion of nasalis
questions.answer:
B)

The depressor septi nasi muscle is responsible for this downward nasal tip movement during animation. This muscle originates from the maxillary incisive fossa and inserts into the nasal septum and posterior alar nasalis, causing septal depression and downward tip motion while narrowing the columellar-labial angle. Surgical release of this muscle during rhinoplasty can reduce tip depression during facial expression. Option A is incorrect because the alar nasalis primarily functions to open the external nasal valve and dilate the nostrils. Option C is incorrect because the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi elevates the upper lip and dilates nostrils rather than depressing the tip. Option D is incorrect because the procerus muscle depresses the glabella and assists with nostril flaring, not tip depression. Option E is incorrect because the transverse nasalis elongates the nose and constricts nostrils but doesn't cause tip depression during smiling.

questions.question:
A 6-month-old male child is being evaluated for facial asymmetry observed since birth. Clinical examination reveals symmetrical upper facial third, but decreased prominence of the right cheek compared to the left. The bite plane tilts upward on the right side, and the chin deviates rightward. Additionally, the right ear appears small and constricted with an adjacent preauricular skin tag. Right marginal mandibular nerve weakness is present. The child is otherwise well. The parents should be told that this asymmetry most likely resulted from which of the following?
A) Autosomal dominant genetic mutation
B) Disruption of normal developmental sequence
C) Maternal tobacco use
D) Omega fatty acid consumption during pregnancy
E) Intrauterine deformation
questions.answer:
B)

This patient exhibits hemifacial microsomia (also called craniofacial microsomia or Goldenhar syndrome), which results from disruption of normal developmental sequence, specifically impaired neural crest cell migration during embryogenesis. This condition affects structures derived from the first and second branchial arches, explaining the mandibular hypoplasia, auricular malformation, and cranial nerve involvement. While both genetic and environmental factors can influence neural crest cell activity, the majority of cases occur sporadically without family history. Option A is incorrect because less than 2% of cases involve autosomal dominant inheritance. Option C is incorrect because while maternal smoking may weakly increase risk, it is not causative in most patients and doesn't explain the specific pattern of anomalies. Option D is incorrect because omega oil ingestion has no established association with hemifacial microsomia. Option E is incorrect because uterine deformation typically causes temporary facial asymmetry that improves with growth and doesn't produce the ear and jaw structural anomalies seen in this patient.

questions.question:
Which of the following represents the axon fiber type (neuron) that is predominantly responsible for the autonomic manifestations observed in complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) type 1?
A) A delta sensory
B) Alpha motor
C) C sensory
D) Gamma motor
E) Ia sensory
questions.answer:
C)

C sensory fibers are primarily responsible for the autonomic changes in CRPS type 1. These unmyelinated fibers have both afferent pain transmission functions and efferent neurosecretory functions, releasing neuropeptides like substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). These neuropeptides explain the neurogenic inflammatory symptoms including swelling, erythema, hyperhidrosis, and trophic changes characteristic of CRPS. Elevated CGRP levels correlate with autonomic disturbances, particularly hyperhidrosis, while substance P influences osteoclastic activity and bone changes. Option A is incorrect because A delta fibers conduct faster, more localized acute pain signals but don't mediate the autonomic features of CRPS. Option B is incorrect because alpha motor neurons control skeletal muscle contraction, not autonomic functions. Option D is incorrect because gamma motor neurons regulate muscle spindle sensitivity for proprioception. Option E is incorrect because Ia sensory fibers are proprioceptors that monitor muscle length and don't contribute to CRPS autonomic symptoms.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old female patient is scheduled for anterior and posterior trunk liposuction under general anesthesia. Using super-wet infiltration technique, 4 L of fat and fluid will be removed. The surgeon intends to give tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg intravenously as off-label therapy to further minimize operative blood loss. Which of the following represents a contraindication for tranexamic acid use?
A) Active heavy menstrual bleeding
B) Color vision deficiency
C) Increased liver enzymes
D) Known dairy product allergy
E) von Willebrand disease
questions.answer:
B)

Color vision deficiency (color blindness) is a contraindication to tranexamic acid use. Tranexamic acid can cause transient color vision changes, and patients receiving the medication for extended periods require ophthalmologic monitoring including color vision assessment as part of toxicity surveillance. Since patients with pre-existing color blindness cannot be monitored for these visual changes, the manufacturer lists color blindness as a contraindication. Other contraindications include known tranexamic acid allergy, intracranial hemorrhage, and history of thromboembolic disease. Option A is incorrect because tranexamic acid is actually FDA-approved for treating heavy menstrual bleeding. Option C is incorrect because elevated liver enzymes are not a contraindication to tranexamic acid use. Option D is incorrect because milk allergies do not contraindicate tranexamic acid use. Option E is incorrect because tranexamic acid can actually be used therapeutically in certain bleeding disorders including von Willebrand disease.

questions.question:
A healthy, non-smoking 30-year-old auto mechanic sustains sharp amputation of the long, ring, and little fingers through Zone II of his right hand. The severed digits are properly preserved, and he arrives for surgery within 2 hours of injury. Which of the following represents the optimal replantation sequence?
A) Individual digit approach: bone, tendons, arteries, nerves, veins
B) Individual digit approach: bone, tendons, arteries, veins, nerves
C) Anatomical structure approach: bone, nerves, tendons, arteries, veins
D) Anatomical structure approach: bone, tendons, arteries, nerves, veins
E) Anatomical structure approach: tendons, bones, veins, arteries, nerves
questions.answer:
D)

The optimal replantation sequence follows an anatomical structure approach: bone, tendons, arteries, nerves, then veins. This method has been demonstrated to significantly reduce operative time compared to completing all repairs on one digit before moving to the next. The procedure begins with bone shortening and fixation to establish skeletal stability before proceeding with delicate microscopic repairs. While individual surgeon preferences may vary for subsequent steps, the structure-by-structure approach is most efficient. A is incorrect because it uses the less efficient digit-by-digit method. B is incorrect for the same reason and places veins before nerves. C is incorrect because nerves should not be repaired before tendons in the standard sequence. E is incorrect because tendons should not be repaired before bone fixation, which must come first for stability.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old woman receives breast reconstruction using a free transverse rectus abdominis musculocutaneous (TRAM) flap. Zones I and II are utilized while portions of Zone III and the entirety of Zone IV are removed. The cartilaginous segment of the third rib is excised to access the internal mammary vessels. Microscope-assisted microvascular anastomosis is performed between the flap vessels and internal mammary vessels. Which Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code is most appropriate?
A) Breast reconstruction with free flap (19364) and partial rib excision (21600)
B) Breast reconstruction with free flap (19364) and microsurgical techniques requiring operating microscope (69990)
C) Breast reconstruction with free flap (19364); partial rib excision (21600); and skin/subcutaneous tissue debridement (11042)
D) Breast reconstruction with free flap (19364) only
E) Breast reconstruction with TRAM flap, single pedicle, including donor site closure; with microvascular anastomosis (supercharging) (19368)
questions.answer:
D)

The appropriate code is 19364 (breast reconstruction with free flap) only. This comprehensive code includes flap harvest, breast reconstruction and shaping, microvascular anastomosis, operating microscope use, and donor site closure. All components described in the scenario are bundled within this single code. A is incorrect because partial rib resection (21600) is bundled within 19364 and should not be coded separately. B is incorrect because the microscope code (69990) is also bundled within 19364, and separate coding would constitute inappropriate unbundling. C is incorrect because it includes multiple bundled codes, and debridement (11042) is not appropriate for routine flap trimming during reconstruction. E is incorrect because 19368 describes a pedicled TRAM with supercharging, not the free flap procedure described.

questions.question:
A 9-month-old male infant presents with a midline glabellar mass. His parents note gradual enlargement over the past 6 months, with no size variation during crying episodes. Examination reveals a fixed, firm, non-tender mass. The nasal root appears normal width, and intercanthal distance is within normal range. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Dermoid cyst
B) Encephalocele
C) Glioma
D) Hemangioma
E) Pilomatricoma
questions.answer:
A)

A dermoid cyst is the most likely diagnosis. These represent the most frequent congenital nasal masses, typically occurring in the lateral brow or midline glabellar area in children. They characteristically demonstrate slow growth and present as fixed, firm masses. The normal nasal root width and intercanthal distance make intracranial connection less likely. B is incorrect because encephaloceles are present at birth, feel soft and mobile, and often change size with crying. C is incorrect because gliomas commonly cause nasal root broadening and increased intercanthal distance, which are absent here. D is incorrect because hemangiomas show variable growth patterns in the first year, are neither fixed nor firm, typically have color changes, and may fluctuate with crying. E is incorrect because pilomatricomas are usually superficial, not fixed, and represent a different type of benign epithelial tumor.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male patient presents with an exposed knee prosthesis. Reconstruction using a complete gastrocnemius muscle flap is planned to cover the anterior knee defect and hardware. Which movement will most likely demonstrate the biomechanical impact of this flap harvest?
A) Dorsiflexion
B) Foot eversion
C) Foot inversion
D) Leg extension
E) Plantar flexion
questions.answer:
E)

Plantar flexion will show the primary biomechanical consequence. The gastrocnemius muscle, with medial and lateral heads originating from the femoral condyles, inserts on the posterior calcaneus via the Achilles tendon (shared with soleus). While both heads can be harvested, patients retain approximately 75% of plantar flexion strength due to the remaining soleus muscle. The gastrocnemius functions in plantar flexion and knee flexion, making plantar flexion the relevant movement affected. A is incorrect because dorsiflexion is primarily controlled by the anterior compartment muscles, not the gastrocnemius. B and C are incorrect because foot eversion and inversion are controlled by peroneal and tibialis muscles respectively, not the gastrocnemius. D is incorrect because leg extension is performed by the quadriceps muscles, while the gastrocnemius assists with knee flexion, not extension.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old woman is scheduled for abdominoplasty. She has a 10-year history of smoking one pack daily. During her preoperative consultation, she reports using nicotine patches and abstaining from cigarettes for 3 weeks. Which mechanism is most likely responsible for wound healing complications in this patient?
A) Decreased availability of hemoglobin
B) Decreased red blood cell deformability
C) Impairment of leukocyte function
D) Increased fibrinogen production
E) Increased microvascular vasoconstriction
questions.answer:
E)

Increased microvascular vasoconstriction is the primary mechanism causing wound healing complications. Nicotine directly causes cutaneous blood vessel constriction, resulting in decreased tissue oxygenation. This vasoconstriction persists for up to 90 minutes after smoking a single cigarette, meaning daily smokers remain tissue hypoxic most of the time. Nicotine mediates vasoconstriction both directly and indirectly through thromboxane A2 enhancement and catecholamine release. A is incorrect because while carbon monoxide reduces oxygen-carrying capacity by forming carboxyhemoglobin, this represents decreased oxygen availability rather than decreased hemoglobin availability. B is incorrect because although decreased red blood cell deformability occurs in smokers, it's not the primary mechanism affecting wound healing. C is incorrect because while smoking does impair leukocyte function through hydrogen cyanide and acrolein, this is secondary to the primary vascular effects. D is incorrect because increased fibrinogen production contributes to thrombogenesis but is not the main wound healing impediment.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman is evaluated 6 hours after undergoing delayed breast reconstruction with deep inferior epigastric artery perforator flaps. On Doppler examination, arterial signals are present. Capillary refill time is 3 seconds on the right and 1 second on the left. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the left breast?


A) Administration of systemic heparin
B) Administration of systemic tissue plasminogen activator
C) Application of leeches
D) Return to the operating room
E) Observation
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


The most appropriate management is exploration of the left flap to assess anastomotic patency and pedicle orientation. This flap is hyperemic with brisk capillary refill and present arterial signals. These are all signs of venous insufficiency, and emergent exploration is indicated to assess the vascular pedicle for kinking or thrombosis. Application of leeches will drain excess blood from the flap but will not address the underlying problem. Observation is unacceptable because there are signs of venous insufficiency, and this requires urgent intervention. Systemic heparin will prevent further clot formation but will not dissolve an acute clot or resolve pedicle kinking. Systemic tissue plasminogen activator would greatly increase this patient‚Äos risk of bleeding. This agent should only be used within a flap.


References
1. Sbitany H, Mirzabeigi MN, Kovach SJ, et al. Strategies for recognizing and managing intraoperative venous congestion in abdominally based autologous breast reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012 Apr;129(4):809-15.
2. Blondeel PN, Arnstein M, Verstraete K, et al. Venous congestion and blood flow in free transverse rectus abdominis myocutaneous and deep inferior epigastric perforator flaps. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2000 Nov;106(6):1295-9.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old male patient with mucoepidermoid carcinoma affecting the left parotid gland undergoes surgical removal of the parotid gland. What complication is most likely to occur in this patient?
A) Gustatory sweating
B) Hyperacusis
C) Loss of taste
D) Tardive dyskinesia
E) Tearing while eating
questions.answer:
A)
Gustatory sweating (Frey syndrome) is the most probable complication following parotidectomy. This condition develops when cutaneous sweat glands in the cheek overlying the parotid surgical site receive aberrant innervation, leading to sweating and flushing during meals. B) is incorrect because hyperacusis occurs with intracranial facial nerve injury before the stylomastoid foramen, not during parotidectomy. C) is incorrect because taste loss to the anterior tongue results from chorda tympani injury in the middle ear, not facial nerve damage within the parotid gland. D) is incorrect because tardive dyskinesia is an antipsychotic medication side effect unrelated to facial nerve dysfunction. E) is incorrect because crocodile tear syndrome occurs after Bell's palsy with nerve regeneration, not parotidectomy.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman is scheduled to undergo correction of the defect shown in the photographs. Physical examination shows an elevated inframammary fold and herniation of breast tissue through the areolar complex. Which of the following is the most appropriate operative plan?


A) Latissimus dorsi musculocutaneous flaps and placement of silicone gel prostheses
B) Subfascial placement of silicone gel prostheses with mastopexy
C) Subglandular placement of silicone gel prostheses
D) Submuscular placement of silicone gel prostheses
E) Submuscular placement of silicone gel prostheses with mastopexy and scoring of the gland
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Tuberous breast deformity is a rare congenital condition that results in aberrant breast shape due to a constricting ring at the breast base. Abnormal development results in breast tissue deficiency, herniation of breast tissue into the nipple-areola complex, areolar enlargement, and breast asymmetry.


Although latissimus flaps could be used for severe primary cases or reoperative secondary cases, such an aggressive intervention would not be warranted in the patient described. Surgical correction is challenging, but it can be achieved in a single-stage operation. This procedure should include submuscular placement of silicone or saline prostheses, mastopexy with areolar reduction, and scoring of the gland to relieve the constricting tissue. Postoperative results are depicted in the photograph shown.






References
Bach AD, Kneser U, Beier JP, et al. Aesthetic correction of tuberous breast deformity: lessons learned with a single-stage procedure. Breast J. 2009 May-Jun;15(3):279-286.
Panchapakesan V, Brown MH. Management of tuberous breast deformity with anatomic cohesive silicone gel breast implants. Aesthetic Plast Surg. 2009 Jan;33(1):49-53. Epub 2008 Aug 28.
Elwood E, Hultman CS. Reconstruction of congenital and traumatic breast defects. Breast Dis. 2002;16:129-139.

questions.question:
A 54-year-old man comes to the office for reconstruction of an 8 √o 10-mm defect involving the right nasal margin after excision of basal cell carcinoma. A photograph is shown. The defect involves the skin and cartilage of the alar border. Which of the following one-stage reconstructive options is most appropriate?


A) Composite auricular graft
B) Dorsal nasal flap
C) Forehead full-thickness skin graft
D) Nasolabial flap
E) Primary closure
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option A.


Alar rim defects present a challenging reconstructive problem. The primary reconstructive goals are to reestablish structural support, provide nasal lining if necessary, and provide external skin of similar color and texture. Complications of alar rim reconstruction include poor scars, alar notching, nasal obstruction, and narrowing of the nostril. Several choices are available, but a composite graft from the ear will often obtain an excellent cosmetic result.






Skin along the alar rim, soft triangle, and columella is quite thin and firmly attached to the lower lateral cartilages. Likewise, skin along the helical rim is firmly attached to the underlying cartilage and useful for replicating the delicate topography of the columella, soft triangle, and nostril margin. Composite grafts are typically harvested from the helical root, but can be harvested from throughout the ear.


Composite cartilage grafts only interface with the recipient bed around the graft‚Äos perimeter. As a result, their size should be limited to defects less than 1.0 to 1.5 cm in maximal diameter. It is recommended that no portion of the graft be greater than 1.0 cm from the wound edge. Additionally, the wound bed should be well vascularized and the patient should be a nonsmoker. Composite cartilage grafts follow a predictable healing pattern: white, then blue, and then progressively pink/red as revascularization improves. Perioperative strategies recommended by some authors to increase graft take include corticosteroids, hyperbaric oxygen, and cooling of the graft with iced compresses.


Primary closure would yield a poor result and distortion of the alar rim. The other options do not provide a cartilage support, which would result in likely alar notching and potential collapse. Additionally, the skin from these donor sites would be too thick to replace the thin skin that normally inhabits this location.


References
1. Burget, GC. Aesthetic reconstruction of the nose. In: Mathes SJ, Hentz VR, eds. Plastic Surgery. 2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders; 2006:586-590.
2. Jewett, BS. Skin and composite grafts. In: Baker SR, ed. Local Flaps in Facial Reconstruction. 2nd ed. Philadelphia, PA: Mosby; 2007:359-364.
3. Menick, FJ. Restoring nasal lining ‚Äi the composite skin graft for small full-thickness marginal defects. In: Menick FJ, ed. Nasal Reconstruction Art and Practice. 1st ed. Philadelphia, PA: Saunders; 2009:313-323.

questions.question:
A 64-year-old female patient presents with a non-healing irradiated scalp defect. Her history includes removal of invasive basal cell carcinoma from the scalp, reconstruction using a scalp rotation flap, and high-dose postoperative radiotherapy (60 Gy) administered 10 years previously. Physical examination reveals a full-thickness defect with erythematous, ulcerated, and necrotic tissue, plus exposed, malodorous skull visible at the wound base. What is the most appropriate initial management step for this patient?
A) Biopsy of the wound
B) Craniectomy with free flap reconstruction
C) MRI
D) Resection of involved scalp with split-thickness skin grafting
E) Vacuum-assisted closure (VAC)
questions.answer:
A)
Wound biopsy is the essential first step to exclude cancer recurrence before proceeding with further treatment. While osteoradionecrosis of the skull is the most probable diagnosis, ruling out malignant recurrence is mandatory before implementing additional therapeutic measures. B) is incorrect because craniectomy would be premature without first confirming the diagnosis through biopsy. C) is incorrect because MRI cannot adequately assess bony involvement and would delay necessary tissue sampling. D) is incorrect because split-thickness skin grafting cannot address the underlying bone necrosis and would be inadequate for this complex defect. E) is incorrect because VAC therapy is not suitable for wounds with exposed necrotic bone and foul-smelling discharge.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old female patient visits the clinic for facial skin assessment and discussion of non-surgical rejuvenation options. Compared to skin from a younger individual, her skin will most likely demonstrate which of the following characteristics?
A) Dermal thickening
B) Epidermal thickening
C) Flattening of dermal-epidermal junctions
D) Increased capillary density
E) Increased cellular turnover
questions.answer:
C)
Flattening of dermal-epidermal junctions is a characteristic feature of aged skin, which reduces nutrient exchange between skin layers and increases fragility. This structural change occurs as part of the normal aging process. A) is incorrect because aged dermis actually undergoes thinning and atrophy, not thickening. B) is incorrect because the epidermis becomes thinner with age, not thicker. D) is incorrect because aged skin shows decreased vascularity and reduced capillary density. E) is incorrect because cellular turnover and keratinocyte proliferation decline with aging, not increase.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old female patient receives 0.5 mL hyaluronic acid filler injection in each nasolabial fold. She returns 30 minutes later complaining of pain and mottled skin discoloration affecting the nasal tip and right ala nasi. What is the most appropriate immediate management step?
A) Doppler ultrasonography
B) Hyaluronidase injection
C) Lidocaine injection
D) Massage
E) Prostaglandin E1 injection
questions.answer:
B)
Hyaluronidase injection is the emergency treatment of choice for suspected intra-arterial hyaluronic acid injection causing vascular compromise. This enzyme breaks down hyaluronic acid and can restore circulation when administered promptly into the injection site and affected tissue areas. A) is incorrect because Doppler ultrasonography would delay critical treatment and is not the primary intervention needed. C) is incorrect because lidocaine injection is a secondary treatment option that should only be considered after hyaluronidase administration. D) is incorrect because massage alone cannot resolve arterial occlusion from filler material, though it may help distribute hyaluronidase after injection. E) is incorrect because prostaglandin E1 is a secondary treatment that should follow hyaluronidase as the primary intervention.

questions.question:
A 4-month-old infant is evaluated because of a lesion near the lateral aspect of the left eyebrow. A photograph is shown. The mass is firm, well-circumscribed, and does not move with overlying skin movement. Which of the following preoperative imaging studies is most appropriate?


A) CT scan
B) MRI
C) Ultrasonography
D) X-ray studies
E) Imaging studies are not necessary
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Dermoid cysts of the craniofacial region represent about 7% of all dermoid cysts and have an incidence of around 1 in 1000 live births. These masses can arise in multiple anatomic locations on the head, including the lateral eyebrow (sometimes referred to as an angular dermoid), midline nose, glabella, medial canthus, temporal or occipital scalp, frontal/anterior fontanel, and postauricular sulcus. Intracranial extension occurs in midline nasal dermoid cysts (13% below and 0% above the nasofrontal suture), frontal/fontanel (36.8%), temporal (16.2%), and occiput (16.3%), while this almost never occurs in the remaining locations (lateral brow, parietal, medial canthus, auricular). Cysts of the lateral brow represent almost two-thirds of all craniofacial dermoid cysts, and intracranially, extension or contact with the dura does not occur. Thus, the diagnosis is clinical, and further imaging in a child this young is not warranted. Overland et al. advocate imaging (CT or MRI) in older patients (>2 years of age) due to an increased risk for orbital extension with growth.


ReferencesBartlett SP, Lin KY, Grossman R, et al. The surgical management of orbitofacial dermoids in the pediatric patient. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1993;91(7):1208-1215.Overland J, Hall C, Holmes A, et al. Risk of intracranial extension of craniofacial dermoid cysts. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2020;145(4):779e-787e.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old male patient presents with severe malocclusion 8 weeks following injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident. Physical examination reveals healed lacerations, infraorbital nerve sensory loss on the affected side, and absence of orbital rim step-off deformity. CT imaging demonstrates a unilateral orbital blowout fracture with midface fracture involvement. No mandibular fracture is present. What is the most appropriate initial management approach?
A) Le Fort I osteotomy with fixation
B) Maxillomandibular fixation
C) Open reduction and internal fixation of the fracture
D) Open reduction and reconstruction of the orbital floor fracture
questions.answer:
A)
Le Fort I osteotomy with fixation is required because 8 weeks post-injury, the fracture lines have consolidated and become immobile, necessitating controlled osteotomy to reestablish proper occlusion. B) is incorrect because maxillomandibular fixation alone cannot achieve normal occlusion when fractures have already healed in malposition. C) is incorrect because open reduction and internal fixation is not indicated for consolidated, minimally displaced fractures at this late stage. D) is incorrect because orbital floor reconstruction would not address the primary problem of malocclusion, though it might be considered later if orbital volume or entrapment issues persist.

questions.question:
An otherwise healthy 50-year-old right-hand-dominant rodeo cowboy is brought to the emergency department immediately after he sustained a roping injury to the nondominant thumb. On examination, the digit is completely separated from the remaining hand, and is cool and pale. The flexor pollicis longus (FPL) tendon is attached to the amputated part, which has been avulsed from its musculotendinous junction. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate operative management?


A) Completion amputation and wound closure
B) Immediate toe-to-thumb transfer
C) Nonvascularized bone grafting and a reverse radial forearm flap
D) Tendon repair into the FPL muscle belly
E) Replantation with vein grafting
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.



The most appropriate option for this patient is to perform a replantation with the use of vein grafts to the snuffbox for arterial inflow. Roping injuries are a combination of both an amputation as well as an avulsion, resulting in a significant zone of injury to all structures, but especially to the vessels, which sometimes have up to 4 cm of involvement with bruising of the intima and adventitia and separation of the media from the vessel walls. This zone of injury can result in anastomotic failure and digital demise if not recognized both by the mechanism of injury as well as careful examination of the structures under the operating microscope during attempted repair. Primary anastomosis in these particular injuries is most often not possible; therefore, the use of vein grafts after resection of the involved segment is an optimal strategy. The use of an end-to-side anastomosis into the radial artery at the snuffbox has been described with good success, and would be the preferred choice in this situation.


A completion amputation of the thumb at this level (just distal to the metacarpophalangeal joint) would sacrifice needed thumb length and compromise ultimate function. As the thumb is reported to be responsible for up to 40% of hand function, this would represent a significant impact to the patient.


It is difficult to repair the FPL tendon once avulsed from the musculotendinous junction, and many authors advocate for FPL resection rather than attempted repair. As the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is intact, it will afford good range of motion of the thumb in all directions, even if the thumb serves merely as a ‚Äupost‚Äu without ability to flex at the interphalangeal joint.


Nonvascularized iliac crest bone grafting with a reverse radial forearm coverage is a surgical option but would not be the primary option in this acute amputation with an intact amputated part eligible for replantation, nor would it be preferred over staged toe-to-thumb transfer for better restoration of function and appearance.


A toe-to-thumb transfer would be a good option in this patient if the thumb could not be replanted due to extensive distal injury, distal contamination, or loss of the digit during injury. In this particular case, none of those criteria are met.


References
1. Bieber EJ, Wood MB, Cooney WP, et al. Thumb avulsion: results of replantation/revascularization. J Hand Surg Am. 1987 Sep;12(5 Pt 1):786-790.
2. Isenberg JS. Rodeo thumb: an unusual etiology of avulsion amputation of the thumb. Ann Plast Surg. 1996 Aug;37(2):187-190.
3. Kirwan LA, Scott FA. Roping injuries in the hand: mechanism of injury and functional results. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1988 Jan;81(1):54-61.
4. Moneim MS, Firoozbakhsh K, Gross D, et al. Thumb amputations from team roping. Am J Sports Med. 2003 Sep-Oct;31(5):728-735.

questions.question:
A 22-year-old male presents for evaluation of multiple facial fractures following an assault. Which of the following fracture patterns carries the highest risk for developing temporomandibular joint dysfunction?
A) Bilateral parasymphyseal mandibular fractures
B) Comminuted unilateral mandibular condylar fracture
C) Complete Le Fort I maxillary fracture
D) Displaced unilateral subcondylar mandibular fracture
E) Unilateral zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture
questions.answer:
B)
Comminuted unilateral mandibular condylar fractures have the highest association with temporomandibular joint dysfunction. TMJ complications including clicking, pain, locking, malocclusion, and trismus are serious sequelae that can develop after facial trauma. Fractures causing significant disruption to the condylar-glenoid apparatus are most prone to causing TMJ dysfunction, with comminuted condylar head fractures being particularly susceptible. A) Bilateral parasymphyseal fractures are anatomically distant from the TMJ and less likely to cause dysfunction. C) Le Fort I fractures involve the maxilla and rarely affect TMJ function. D) While subcondylar fractures can cause TMJ issues, comminuted condylar fractures pose greater risk. E) Zygomaticomaxillary complex fractures are unlikely to result in TMJ symptoms.

questions.question:
A 60-year-old female presents with a 15-year history of rheumatoid arthritis involving both hands. She experiences severe pain, wrist collapse with carpal supination, marked ulnar deviation with volar subluxation of the metacarpophalangeal joints, and flexion contractures of the distal interphalangeal joints. These deformities significantly impair her grip strength. Which of the following represents a contraindication to performing immediate MCP joint arthroplasty?
A) Flexion contractures of the DIP joints
B) Impaired grip strength
C) Subluxation of the MCP joints
D) Intractable pain
E) Collapse of the wrist
questions.answer:
E)
Wrist collapse is a contraindication to immediate MCP joint arthroplasty because reconstruction of the rheumatoid hand must proceed from proximal to distal joints. Untreated wrist deformity can lead to recurrent ulnar deviation after MCP arthroplasty, and persistent wrist pain may continue to limit hand function despite successful MCP joint treatment. The wrist must be addressed before proceeding with MCP joint reconstruction. A) DIP joint flexion deformities do not preclude MCP arthroplasty. B) Grasp weakness is actually an indication for MCP arthroplasty to improve function. C) MCP joint subluxation is a primary indication for arthroplasty in rheumatoid patients. D) Severe pain is a key indication for MCP joint arthroplasty.

questions.question:
A 25-year-old male suffers a high-voltage electrical burn to his right upper extremity with an entry point on the volar wrist. If elevated compartment pressures are not promptly addressed, which muscle is most susceptible to developing ischemic contracture?
A) Brachioradialis
B) Extensor carpi radialis brevis
C) Flexor carpi radialis
D) Flexor digitorum profundus
E) Palmaris longus
questions.answer:
D)
The flexor digitorum profundus is most likely to develop ischemic contracture following untreated compartment syndrome. In Volkmann ischemic contracture, the deeper muscles experience higher pressures earlier and for longer durations, making them most susceptible to ischemic damage. The FDP, particularly the segments to the middle and ring fingers, lies deepest against the ulnar bone and interosseous membrane in the deep forearm compartment. Along with the flexor pollicis longus, these deep muscles are most prone to contracture formation. A) Brachioradialis is more superficial and less likely to develop contracture. B) Extensor carpi radialis brevis is superficial and rarely affected. C) Flexor carpi radialis is in the superficial compartment and less susceptible. E) Palmaris longus is superficial and uncommonly develops contracture.

questions.question:
A 51-year-old female seeks breast reconstruction after being diagnosed with left breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma. She has bilateral textured submuscular implants placed 8 years prior. She requests removal of the contralateral implant during her left-sided procedure. What is the probability of discovering BIA-ALCL pathology in her opposite breast?
A) 1.6%
B) 4.6%
C) 7.6%
D) 10.6%
E) 13.6%
questions.answer:
B)
The likelihood of finding BIA-ALCL pathology in the contralateral breast is 4.6% according to reported cases. This risk supports the consideration of prophylactic contralateral implant removal as recommended by National Comprehensive Cancer Network guidelines. Treatment of BIA-ALCL involves implant removal, complete capsulectomy, and excision of suspicious lymph nodes, with contralateral implant removal being a reasonable option given this bilateral risk. A) 1.6% underestimates the actual reported bilateral occurrence rate. C) 7.6% overestimates the bilateral risk. D) 10.6% is higher than documented bilateral occurrence rates. E) 13.6% significantly exceeds the established bilateral risk percentage.

questions.question:
A 28-year-old male seeks consultation for excess chest tissue. His medical history reveals no weight fluctuations and no medical conditions. His BMI is 26 kg/m2. Examination reveals normal nipple positioning in the vertical plane and firm tissue beneath the central breast area bilaterally. What is the optimal surgical treatment approach?
A) Horizontal scar reduction with nipple-areolar grafting
B) Inverted-T reduction with inferior pedicle technique
C) Liposuction only
D) Periareolar incision for direct glandular excision combined with liposuction
E) Skin-sparing mastectomy with nipple-areolar tattooing
questions.answer:
D)
Periareolar incision for direct glandular excision combined with liposuction is most appropriate for this patient with minimal skin excess and firm central glandular tissue. This approach minimizes scarring while effectively addressing both the fibrous glandular component through direct excision and providing peripheral contouring through liposuction. The patient's stable weight, normal BMI, and preserved nipple position indicate minimal skin redundancy, making him ideal for this limited-scar technique. A) Horizontal scar reduction creates unnecessary extensive scarring for this presentation. B) Inverted-T reduction involves excessive scarring without indication for such extensive surgery. C) Liposuction alone cannot adequately remove the firm central glandular tissue described. E) Skin-sparing mastectomy with tattooing is overly aggressive and creates unnecessary scarring.

questions.question:
A 59-year-old man with hypertension, peripheral vascular disease, and coronary artery disease has sternal osteomyelitis after coronary artery bypass grafting with saphenous vein and left internal mammary artery grafts. Reconstruction with bilateral pectoralis advancement flaps is performed, but the flaps do not survive. Debridement is performed, and a defect remains. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate reconstruction?


A ) Adjacent tissue transfer and coverage with bilateral skin advancement flaps
B ) Coverage with left rectus abdominis turnover flap and skin grafting
C ) Coverage with left superior epigastric artery perforator fasciocutaneous flap
D ) Coverage with omental flap and skin grafting
E ) Coverage with right latissimus myocutaneous flap
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.






The most appropriate option in the patient described is an omental flap with skin grafting. The defect encompasses the entirety of the sternum, from the sternal notch to the xiphoid. The first-line muscle flaps for this defect would usually be bilateral pectoralis muscle flaps (that do not include a left pectoralis turnover flap option due to the lack of a left internal mammary artery (IMA) used for the coronary graft). However, this option has already been used.


An omental flap has an axial blood supply that is not compromised (the gastroepiploic) and the ability to completely span the defect and obliterate the dead space; the skin graft provides the skin coverage needed to complete the reconstruction. Hence, it is the optimal choice in this patient.


An adjacent tissue transfer of random skin flaps bilaterally would not obliterate the dead space and would not provide robust axial blood supply to the necessary area, with the tenuous coverage existing along the sternal midline, exactly where the most vital blood supply would be necessary.


A left rectus abdominis turnover flap would not be an appropriate option for two reasons: 1) the left IMA has been harvested, thereby compromising the superior epigastric vessel on which this flap would be based; and 2) it would not reach the upper portion of the defect.


A left superior epigastric artery perforator fasciocutaneous flap would not be an appropriate option for two reasons: 1) the pedicle is compromised from the left IMA harvest; and 2) muscle flaps have been proven to be optimal for sternal defects more than fasciocutaneous flaps.


A right latissimus muscle flap may be a viable choice to get full coverage of the defect with dead space obliteration. However, the option indicates this is a myocutaneous flap, which would not allow for sufficient skin to be harvested to reconstruct the size of this defect.


References
1. Jones G, Jurkiewicz MJ, Bostwick J, et al. Management of the infected median sternotomy wound with muscle flaps. The Emory 20-year experience. Ann Surg. 1997 Jun;225(6):766-776.
2. Nahai F, Rand RP, Hester TR, et al. Primary treatment of the infected sternotomy wound with muscle flaps: a review of 211 consecutive cases. Plast Reconstr Surg. 1989 Sep;84(3):434-441.
3. Stump A, Bedri M, Goldberg NH, et al. Omental transposition flap for sternal wound reconstruction in diabetic patients. Ann Plast Surg. 2010 Aug;65(2):206-210.
4. Schroeyers P, Wellens F, Degrieck I, et al. Aggressive primary treatment for poststernotomy acute mediastinitis: our experience with omental- and muscle flaps surgery. Eur J Cardiothorac Surg. 2001 Oct;20(4):743-746.
5. Hultman CS, Culbertson JH, Jones GE, et al. Thoracic reconstruction with the omentum: indications, complications, and results. Ann Plast Surg. 2001 Mar;46(3):242-249.
6. Milano CA, Georgiade G, Muhlbaier LH, et al. Comparison of omental and pectoralis flaps for poststernotomy mediastinitis. Ann Thorac Surg. 1999 Feb;67(2):377-380.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old female patient arrives at the emergency room one day following outpatient liposuction due to breathing difficulties and mental confusion. The procedure utilized a tumescent approach with lidocaine, involving infiltration of 4000 mL tumescent solution and extraction of 4000 mL lipoaspirate. Clinical assessment reveals respiratory compromise and a petechial rash. What is the most probable etiology of this patient's presentation?
A) Allergic drug reaction
B) Fat embolism
C) Lidocaine toxicity
D) Pulmonary edema
E) Pulmonary embolism
questions.answer:
B)
Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a recognized complication of liposuction procedures. The patient presents with the classic triad of FES: respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash, typically occurring within 48 hours post-procedure. During liposuction, mechanical disruption of adipose tissue and blood vessels releases fat microparticles that embolize to the lungs, brain, kidneys, and skin, causing mechanical obstruction and inflammatory responses. A) is incorrect because drug allergies typically cause laryngeal edema without petechial rash. C) is incorrect because lidocaine toxicity presents with neurological symptoms like tinnitus and seizures but not petechial rash. D) is incorrect because pulmonary edema causes respiratory distress that doesn't respond to oxygen therapy but lacks the rash component. E) is incorrect because pulmonary embolism causes respiratory symptoms but is not associated with petechial rash and can occur at any postoperative time.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old male presents with an intercanthal measurement of 37 mm (normal = 30 mm) and an interorbital measurement of 35 mm (normal = 28 mm). What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Esotropia
B) Exophthalmos
C) Exotropia
D) Hypertelorism
E) Pseudohypertelorism
questions.answer:
D)
Hypertelorism is characterized by increased interorbital distance (measured from dacryon to dacryon), which is elevated in this patient at 35 mm compared to the normal 28 mm for males. This condition occurs in various craniofacial malformations and syndromic disorders. A) is incorrect because esotropia refers to inward eye deviation, which may coexist with hypertelorism but requires additional clinical data for diagnosis. B) is incorrect because exophthalmos involves globe protrusion due to increased orbital contents, not increased orbital spacing. C) is incorrect because exotropia refers to outward eye deviation, which may accompany hypertelorism but needs additional examination findings. E) is incorrect because pseudohypertelorism (telecanthus) involves increased intercanthal distance with normal interorbital distance, but this patient has both measurements elevated.

questions.question:
A 42-lb (19-kg), 5-year-old female presents to the emergency department with multiple facial dog bite lacerations. Following IV sedation by the emergency physician, the plastic surgeon begins repair by infiltrating 60 mL of 0.5% lidocaine with 1:200,000 epinephrine. Ten minutes later, the patient develops seizures while pulse oximetry and vital signs remain normal. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
A) Administer epinephrine
B) Administer propofol
C) Initiate lipid emulsion therapy
D) Secure the airway and ventilate with oxygen
E) Transfer the patient to the PICU
questions.answer:
D)
This patient received 300 mg of lidocaine (60 mL × 5 mg/mL), exceeding the safe dose of 133 mg (19 kg × 7 mg/kg with epinephrine). Lidocaine toxicity typically progresses from tinnitus to seizures and cardiac arrhythmias. The immediate priority is airway management and oxygenation to prevent hypoxia and cardiac complications. A) is incorrect because epinephrine is indicated for anaphylaxis, which would present with hypotension and tachycardia, not seizures with normal vital signs. B) is incorrect because propofol can worsen cardiac arrhythmias associated with lidocaine toxicity and should be avoided. C) is incorrect because while lipid emulsion therapy helps eliminate lidocaine, airway security takes precedence. E) is incorrect because immediate stabilization is required before any transfer considerations.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old female with no surgical history undergoes breast augmentation under nitrous oxide, isoflurane, and propofol anesthesia. One hour into surgery, the anesthetist reports rising end-tidal CO2 levels, tachycardia, and severe masseter rigidity. What is the most appropriate immediate action?
A) Administer intravenous saline
B) Administer a muscle relaxant
C) Stop isoflurane
D) Stop nitrous oxide
E) Stop propofol
questions.answer:
C)
The patient exhibits classic early signs of malignant hyperthermia: elevated end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, and masseter rigidity. This life-threatening condition is triggered by volatile inhalational anesthetics like isoflurane, which must be discontinued immediately to prevent progression to hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and multi-organ failure. A) is incorrect because while cold saline may be used as adjunctive therapy, stopping the triggering agent takes priority. B) is incorrect because muscle relaxants don't address the underlying hypermetabolic crisis and may complicate management. D) is incorrect because nitrous oxide is not a triggering agent for malignant hyperthermia. E) is incorrect because propofol is not associated with malignant hyperthermia and may actually be beneficial in management.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old African-American male presents with an elevated, thickened chest scar that is itchy and cosmetically concerning. Another physician excised it 4 years ago, and it has gradually returned over the past year. Examination reveals a firm, hyperpigmented lesion extending beyond the original scar boundaries. Based on his previous pathology report, which histologic feature is most characteristic?
A) Higher type III to type I collagen ratio
B) Abundant myofibroblasts and smooth muscle actin
C) Parallel collagen bundles
D) Thick, wavy, and randomly oriented collagen fibers
questions.answer:
D)
This clinical presentation is consistent with a keloid: recurrence after excision, growth beyond original boundaries, late recurrence after years, and continued expansion. Keloids are histologically characterized by thick, randomly oriented collagen fibrils that lack organized bundle formation. A) is incorrect because keloids actually contain more type I collagen than type III, similar to normal skin, while hypertrophic scars show increased type III collagen. B) is incorrect because abundant myofibroblasts with smooth muscle actin are characteristic of hypertrophic scars, not keloids. C) is incorrect because parallel collagen bundles are found in hypertrophic scars, whereas keloids display disorganized collagen architecture.

questions.question:
A 15-year-old male patient experienced a traumatic severing of his left index finger at the level of the proximal interphalangeal joint due to a sharp trauma. Digital replantation was performed with vein grafting to repair the radial digital artery and vein. The fingertip shows signs of venous congestion, prompting the use of medicinal leeches. What antibiotic provides the most suitable prophylactic coverage for this patient?
A) Amoxicillin-clavulanate
B) Ampicillin
C) Cephalexin
D) Ciprofloxacin
E) Vancomycin
questions.answer:
D)
Ciprofloxacin is the optimal prophylactic antibiotic for patients receiving leech therapy. Medical leeches (Hirudo medicinalis) harbor gut bacteria including Morganella, Rikenella, and Aeromonas species, all of which demonstrate sensitivity to ciprofloxacin. This fluoroquinolone has been approved for pediatric use since 2004 for patients aged 1-17 years. A) Amoxicillin-clavulanate is incorrect because most Aeromonas and Morganella strains show complete or partial resistance to this combination. B) Ampicillin is incorrect as most Aeromonas strains are resistant to penicillins including ampicillin. C) Cephalexin is incorrect because this first-generation cephalosporin lacks adequate coverage against the leech-associated bacterial flora. E) Vancomycin is incorrect as this glycopeptide antibiotic has limited efficacy against Aeromonas strains with high resistance levels.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old healthy female patient seeks consultation regarding the aging appearance of her forehead region. She is a non-smoker. Clinical examination reveals horizontal forehead lines with prominent glabellar furrows. The forehead measures 11 cm in height. What surgical technique would be most suitable for brow elevation in this case?
A) Endoscopic technique
B) Open coronal approach
C) Open pretrichial approach
D) Transpalpebral method
questions.answer:
C)
The open pretrichial approach is most appropriate for this patient with an elongated forehead (11 cm). This technique reduces forehead height while effectively addressing deep rhytides, making it ideal for patients with foreheads exceeding the normal 6-10 cm range. A) The endoscopic technique is incorrect because it works best for patients with normal forehead dimensions due to technical challenges when working across extended, curved surfaces. B) The open coronal approach is incorrect as it actually increases forehead height, making it suitable only for patients with short foreheads. D) The transpalpebral method is incorrect because it is primarily used for corrugator muscle resection in patients without significant brow ptosis.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old female patient has a Gustilo Type IIIB open tibia fracture with extensive soft tissue defects. Free rectus abdominis flap reconstruction is being considered. CT angiography demonstrates a functional posterior tibial artery, but the peroneal and anterior tibial arteries are damaged and unusable beyond the fracture site. What is the primary benefit of performing an end-to-side arterial anastomosis rather than an end-to-end connection in this situation?
A) Permits anastomosis within the injury zone
B) Reduces ischemic time
C) Improves surgical visualization
D) Prevents vessel kinking
E) Maintains distal circulation
questions.answer:
E)
Maintaining distal circulation is the key advantage of end-to-side arterial anastomosis in this case with single-vessel runoff. Preserving blood flow to the distal extremity is crucial when only one patent vessel remains. A) Allowing anastomosis in the injury zone is incorrect as this technique does not specifically facilitate working within damaged tissue areas. B) Reducing ischemic time is incorrect because end-to-side anastomosis actually requires longer operative time and increases ischemia duration. C) Improving surgical visualization is incorrect as this technique typically makes vessel visualization more challenging compared to end-to-end anastomosis. D) Preventing vessel kinking is incorrect since end-to-side anastomosis can still result in vessel kinking and offers no particular advantage in this regard.

questions.question:
A 56-year-old male patient presents for evaluation of gynecomastia. Clinical assessment reveals mild, generalized breast tissue enlargement without visible inframammary crease or sagging. What surgical intervention would be most suitable for treating this patient's condition?
A) Complete resection of skin and breast tissue with free nipple transplantation
B) Direct breast tissue excision combined with mastopexy
C) Subcutaneous mastectomy while preserving the nipple
D) Suction-assisted lipectomy
E) Superior periareolar excision with skin removal
questions.answer:
D)
Suction-assisted lipectomy is the appropriate treatment for mild to moderate gynecomastia without ptosis, which corresponds to Grade I or II gynecomastia. This minimally invasive approach effectively addresses breast enlargement when no sagging is present. A) Complete resection with free nipple grafting is incorrect as this extensive procedure is reserved for severe gynecomastia with significant ptosis (Grade IV). B) Direct excision with mastopexy is incorrect because mastopexy techniques are only indicated when ptosis is present. C) Subcutaneous mastectomy is incorrect as this more invasive approach is not necessary for mild enlargement without ptosis. E) Superior periareolar excision with skin removal is incorrect because skin excision is not indicated when there is no ptosis or excess skin.

questions.question:
A 21-year-old male patient presents to the emergency department 10 days following septorhinoplasty with recent onset of fever, general malaise, sore throat, and painful skin eruption. He recently finished a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate. Vital signs show temperature 39.1°C (102.4°F), blood pressure 75/40 mmHg, and pulse 140 bpm. Physical examination demonstrates widespread cutaneous blistering affecting the face and entire torso (45% TBSA). Oral examination reveals mucosal redness and ulcerations. Nasal examination shows surgical splints in place. Skin biopsy demonstrates complete epidermal necrosis with dermal swelling and minimal dermal inflammatory infiltrate. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis
B) Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms
C) Stevens-Johnson syndrome
D) Toxic epidermal necrolysis
E) Toxic shock syndrome
questions.answer:
D)
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) is the correct diagnosis based on the extensive skin involvement (45% TBSA), characteristic histology showing full-thickness epidermal necrosis, mucosal involvement, and recent antibiotic exposure. TEN is diagnosed when skin detachment exceeds 30% TBSA and carries high mortality. A) Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis is incorrect because it presents with sterile pustules rather than blistering and typically has minimal mucosal involvement. B) Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is incorrect as it presents with morbilliform rash and eosinophilia rather than extensive blistering. C) Stevens-Johnson syndrome is incorrect because it involves less than 10% TBSA, whereas this patient has 45% involvement. E) Toxic shock syndrome is incorrect as it typically occurs within 48 hours of surgery and causes desquamation weeks later, not immediate blistering.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with a posterior thigh sarcoma. He undergoes resection of the tumor as well as some of the surrounding muscle. Partial sacrifice of the sciatic nerve is required, leaving a 40% circumferential defect and an 11-cm gap between proximal and distal ends. A photograph is shown. Which of the following is the most appropriate method of nerve reconstruction?A) Mobilization and primary coaptationB) Polyglycolic acid nerve tubeC) Processed human allograft conduitD) Saphenous vein graftE) Sural nerve cable graft
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Fundamentals of nerve repair include coaptation in a tension-free manner. If there is any tension, nerve grafts or conduits are indicated. In this clinical scenario, there is a large nerve gap that precludes tension-free primary coaptation, even with extensive proximal and distal mobilization. Therefore, a nerve graft is indicated. Common choices include sural, lateral, or medial antebrachial cutaneous. For the size and length of the defect and the fact that multiple cable grafts would be needed, the sural is the most appropriate choice.Nerve conduits such as PGA tubes and processed human allograft conduits serve as scaffolds to promote nerve regeneration, although these are typically used for gaps less than 3 cm. Given the distance involved, a sural nerve graft using a grouped fascicular or epineurial repair is the most appropriate choice, although a gap this large is almost certain to leave permanent deficits. Appropriate levels of expectation must be set with the patient.ReferencesPanagopoulos GN, Megaloikonomos PD, Mavrogenis AF. The Present and Future for Peripheral Nerve Regeneration. Orthopedics. 2017 Jan 1;40(1):e141-e156.Strauch B, Goldberg N, Herman CK. Sural nerve harvest: anatomy and technique. J Reconstr Microsurg. 2005 Feb;21(2):133-6.Millesi H. Bridging defects: autologous nerve grafts. Acta Neurochir Suppl. 2007;100:37-8.

questions.question:
When performing coverage of a defect using a reverse cross-finger flap, where should a full-thickness skin graft be optimally placed?
A) Back surface of the middle phalanx of the donor finger
B) Back surface of the middle phalanx of the recipient finger
C) Palm surface of the distal phalanx of the donor finger
D) Palm surface of the distal phalanx of the recipient finger
E) Palm surface of the middle phalanx of the donor finger
questions.answer:
B)
The correct choice is B. A reverse cross-finger flap involves elevating skin from the donor finger's side nearest the recipient, then raising the dorsal subcutaneous tissue as a flap. This flap is transferred to the recipient finger and serves as the foundation for a full-thickness skin graft. The original skin is then repositioned over the dorsal middle phalanx of the donor finger. A is incorrect because the graft goes on the recipient, not donor finger. C is incorrect because volar distal phalanx coverage would use a standard cross-finger flap, not reverse. D is incorrect because the volar surface isn't the target for reverse cross-finger flaps. E is incorrect because volar middle phalanx isn't the appropriate location for this technique.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old man with worsening carpal tunnel syndrome despite conservative treatment is scheduled for surgical release using an open, limited scar approach. What is the most accurate comparison between this technique and endoscopic release?
A) Both approaches provide equivalent long-term symptom resolution and recovery
B) Endoscopic release is significantly superior due to better long-term symptom resolution
C) Endoscopic release is reserved exclusively for bilateral cases
D) Open, limited scar technique requires regional anesthesia, while endoscopic release does not
E) Open technique has a greater association with recurrent median nerve injury
questions.answer:
A)
The correct response is A. Research demonstrates that open limited scar and endoscopic carpal tunnel release achieve equivalent long-term symptom resolution and recovery outcomes. Both techniques show similar results for strength recovery, return to work, symptom relief, and reoperation rates when measured up to one year post-operatively. B is incorrect because studies show no significant difference in long-term outcomes between techniques. C is incorrect because bilateral involvement doesn't dictate technique choice. D is incorrect because both techniques can be performed under local or regional anesthesia. E is incorrect because open technique is actually associated with lower rates of recurrent median nerve injury.

questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman has bilateral breast reduction surgery. Histopathological examination of the removed breast tissue reveals atypical ductal hyperplasia in the left breast. What is the most appropriate next management step?
A) Gail model risk evaluation
B) Hormonal treatment with aromatase inhibitors
C) Hormonal treatment with selective estrogen receptor modulators
D) Left-sided mastectomy
E) Post-surgical radiation therapy
questions.answer:
A)
The correct response is A. Atypical ductal hyperplasia increases breast cancer risk 3-5 fold in both breasts, with higher risk ipsilaterally. When found in excisional biopsy, no additional surgery is required. The appropriate next step is comprehensive risk assessment using the Gail model, which, despite limitations in atypical hyperplasia cases, remains the most suitable option listed. If overall risk is sufficiently elevated, preventive hormonal therapy may then be considered. B and C are incorrect because hormonal therapy should only follow comprehensive risk assessment. D is incorrect because mastectomy is not indicated for atypical hyperplasia found on excisional biopsy. E is incorrect because radiation therapy is indicated for positive margins, large tumors, or advanced disease, not atypical hyperplasia.

questions.question:
A 20-year-old man presents 2 months after injuring his right long finger during rugby. Examination reveals a boutonnière deformity. The distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint shows 20 degrees of hyperextension with active flexion to 85 degrees. Radiographs show no fracture. What is the most appropriate initial management?
A) Surgical central slip repair
B) Excision of the lateral bands and oblique retinacular ligament
C) Excision of the lateral bands alone
D) Immobilization of both the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and DIP joints in extension
E) Immobilization of the PIP in extension with active DIP flexion exercises
questions.answer:
E)
The correct response is E. This passively correctable boutonnière deformity should be managed conservatively by splinting the PIP joint in extension while encouraging active DIP flexion. PIP extension splinting promotes central slip healing, while active DIP flexion with the PIP extended helps relocate the displaced lateral bands dorsally and reduces DIP hyperextension. A is incorrect because surgical repair is only indicated for open wounds, not closed injuries. B is incorrect because resecting both structures has no role in this condition's management. C is incorrect because lateral band resection is reserved for chronic, fixed deformities. D is incorrect because immobilizing both joints in extension will not address the deformity correction.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old construction worker experiences amputation of his dominant right long finger through the middle portion of the nail plate. Which anatomical structure is most likely damaged?
A) Dorsal roof
B) Germinal matrix
C) Hyponychium
D) Lunula
E) Sterile matrix
questions.answer:
E)
The correct response is E. An amputation through the mid-portion of the nail plate would most likely involve the sterile matrix, which lies distal to the lunula and comprises the nail bed beneath the visible nail plate. According to Allen's classification, this would be a Zone 2 injury involving the sterile matrix. A is incorrect because the dorsal roof refers to the eponychium, which is proximal to this injury level. B is incorrect because the germinal matrix is located proximally and ends at the lunula, not in the mid-nail plate region. C is incorrect because the hyponychium is the skin distal and volar to the nail, not within the nail plate itself.
