D is incorrect because the lunula is the proximal, visible portion of the nail bed, not the mid-nail plate area.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male patient arrives at the emergency room with a complete thermal burn affecting the left ear cartilage. Which of the following treatment options provides the best protection for the affected cartilage?
A) Acetic acid solution
B) Medical-grade honey
C) Mafenide acetate cream
D) Silver nanocrystalline wound dressings
E) Silver sulfadiazine ointment
questions.answer:
C)

Mafenide acetate cream is the correct choice because it uniquely penetrates through burn eschar and cartilage tissue, significantly reducing the risk of suppurative chondritis in ear burns. Applied twice daily, it provides superior cartilage protection compared to other topical agents. However, monitoring for metabolic acidosis is essential since mafenide acetate metabolizes to sulfamoylbenzoic acid, which inhibits carbonic anhydrase. A) Acetic acid solution is incorrect because it lacks the deep penetration and anti-chondritis properties needed for cartilage protection. B) Medical-grade honey is incorrect as it has not demonstrated equivalent efficacy in preventing burn-related cartilage infection. D) Silver nanocrystalline dressings are incorrect because they do not provide the same level of cartilage penetration and chondritis prevention. E) Silver sulfadiazine ointment is incorrect as it has not shown comparable effectiveness in preventing auricular chondritis.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old healthy woman weighing 154 pounds (70 kg) is having liposuction performed at several body areas. Five minutes following local anesthetic injection, she experiences cardiac arrest. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity is suspected. Once cardiopulmonary resuscitation begins, which of the following should be administered as the most appropriate immediate intervention?
A) Adenosine
B) Intralipid emulsion
C) Propranolol
D) Vasopressin
E) Verapamil
questions.answer:
B)

Intralipid emulsion is the correct treatment for local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) causing cardiovascular collapse. The Lipid Rescue protocol calls for an immediate 20% intralipid bolus of 1.5 mL/kg administered over one minute, followed by continuous infusion at 0.25 mL/kg/min. This lipid therapy helps sequester the local anesthetic and restore cardiac function. A) Adenosine is incorrect because it is used for supraventricular tachycardia, not LAST-induced cardiac arrest. C) Propranolol is incorrect as beta-blockers reduce contractility and should be avoided during cardiovascular instability from LAST. D) Vasopressin is incorrect because increasing peripheral vascular resistance can impair cardiac output and hinder resuscitation in LAST patients. E) Verapamil is incorrect since calcium channel blockers decrease contractility and are contraindicated when cardiovascular instability is present.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old male patient with a previous squamous cell carcinoma diagnosis has a glossectomy with free radial forearm flap reconstruction. During surgery, he develops hypotension requiring norepinephrine administration. What is the most probable impact of this vasopressor therapy on the free flap outcome?
A) Impaired wound healing
B) Clotting in small vessels
C) Incomplete flap survival
D) Complete flap failure
E) No adverse impact
questions.answer:
E)

No adverse impact is the correct answer because multiple research studies have demonstrated that intraoperative vasopressor use does not significantly increase complications in free flap reconstruction. While vasopressors are generally avoided when possible due to theoretical concerns about vasoconstriction affecting anastomoses, clinical evidence shows they do not substantially harm flap outcomes when medically necessary. A) Impaired wound healing is incorrect as studies have not shown vasopressors to cause significant wound healing problems in free flaps. B) Clotting in small vessels is incorrect because despite theoretical concerns about vasoconstriction, research has not demonstrated increased thrombosis rates. C) Incomplete flap survival is incorrect as clinical studies have not found increased rates of partial flap loss with vasopressor use. D) Complete flap failure is incorrect since research has not shown increased total flap loss rates when vasopressors are used intraoperatively.

questions.question:
A 58-year-old female patient presents one week following facelift surgery with SMAS flap elevation and platysma muscle tightening. She complains of complete numbness in the right lower ear area. Examination reveals bruising over the right sternocleidomastoid muscle without a palpable fluid collection. What is the most appropriate management approach?
A) Steroid injection into the bruised area
B) Nerve conduction testing of the great auricular nerve
C) Surgical exploration with nerve reconstruction
D) Removal of SMAS sutures in the neck region
E) Conservative monitoring
questions.answer:
E)

Conservative monitoring is the correct approach because early postoperative numbness of the lower ear following facelift surgery is a common occurrence that typically resolves spontaneously within 6 months. This numbness usually results from great auricular nerve injury during surgery, and the majority of cases improve without intervention through natural nerve recovery processes. A) Steroid injection is incorrect because corticosteroid injections are not indicated for early postoperative numbness and do not improve nerve recovery. B) Nerve conduction testing is incorrect as electrodiagnostic studies are not warranted in the early postoperative period when spontaneous recovery is expected. C) Surgical exploration is incorrect because operative intervention is only considered for persistent numbness lasting longer than 6 months, particularly when accompanied by chronic pain. D) Removal of SMAS sutures is incorrect since suture release is not indicated when most cases resolve naturally without surgical intervention.

questions.question:
A 12-hour-old male infant is being assessed in the neonatal intensive care unit with suspected CHARGE syndrome. Medical records and physical findings reveal cardiac malformation, eye colobomas, small ears, underdeveloped genitalia, and poor growth. Which additional feature is most commonly associated with this condition?
A) Premature skull suture fusion
B) Liver blood vessel malformations
C) Small pits in the lower lip
D) Cleft lip and/or palate
E) Fused fingers or toes
questions.answer:
D)

Cleft lip and/or palate is the correct answer because it occurs in approximately 20% of CHARGE syndrome patients, making it the second most frequent syndrome associated with orofacial clefts after van der Woude syndrome. CHARGE syndrome results from CHD7 gene mutations or microdeletions and includes various associated anomalies beyond the classic features. A) Premature skull suture fusion is incorrect as craniosynostosis is not typically part of CHARGE syndrome's clinical spectrum. B) Liver blood vessel malformations are incorrect because intrahepatic hemangiomas are not characteristic features of CHARGE syndrome. C) Small pits in the lower lip are incorrect as lip pits are specifically associated with van der Woude syndrome, not CHARGE syndrome. E) Fused fingers or toes is incorrect because syndactyly is not a recognized component of CHARGE syndrome.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old male presents to the emergency room following an open complex fracture of his left tibia from a car accident. Clinical examination reveals a laceration exceeding 10 cm with extensive periosteal damage at the mid-diaphysis. What is the correct Gustilo classification for this patient's fracture?
A) I
B) II
C) IIIA
D) IIIB
E) IIIC
questions.answer:
D)

This patient has a Gustilo type IIIB open fracture. The Gustilo classification system categorizes open fractures based on soft tissue damage severity and vascular compromise. This case demonstrates a wound larger than 10 cm with severe comminution and no vascular injury mentioned, which defines a IIIB injury. Option A is incorrect because Type I fractures have clean wounds less than 1 cm with minimal bone fragmentation. Option B is incorrect because Type II fractures have contaminated wounds greater than 1 cm but with only moderate comminution. Option C is incorrect because Type IIIA fractures have wounds between 1-10 cm, whereas this patient's wound exceeds 10 cm. Option E is incorrect because Type IIIC fractures require major vascular injury necessitating repair for limb preservation, which is not present in this case.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old healthy female patient has bilateral breast reduction surgery for symptomatic macromastia. Histological examination of one specimen reveals ductal carcinoma in situ. What percentage most accurately reflects the frequency of this discovery in reduction mammoplasty specimens?
A) 1%
B) 7%
C) 10%
D) 12%
E) 25%
questions.answer:
A)

The incidence of occult breast malignancy in reduction mammoplasty specimens is approximately 1%. This finding represents ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS), with invasive ductal carcinoma being the most frequently identified malignant lesion overall. All breast tissue from women over 40 should undergo pathological examination. Option B is incorrect because 7% significantly overestimates the actual incidence rate. Option C is incorrect because 10% represents a tenfold overestimation of the true frequency. Option D is incorrect because 12% greatly exceeds the documented incidence in the literature. Option E is incorrect because 25% represents a massive overestimation that would suggest one in four reduction specimens contain malignancy, which is not supported by clinical data.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old male experiences traumatic loss of the weight-bearing medial heel region. Reconstruction using an instep flap is being considered. Which nerve provides sensory innervation to this flap?
A) Lateral plantar nerve from the deep peroneal nerve
B) Lateral plantar nerve from the superficial peroneal nerve
C) Lateral plantar nerve from the sural nerve
D) Medial plantar nerve from the deep peroneal nerve
E) Medial plantar nerve from the tibial nerve
questions.answer:
E)

The instep flap (medial plantar artery flap) receives sensory innervation from the medial plantar nerve, which is a terminal branch of the tibial nerve. This flap provides sensate, glabrous skin ideal for weight-bearing reconstruction and can be used as either a pedicled or free flap. Option A is incorrect because the lateral plantar nerve does not arise from the deep peroneal nerve, and it does not innervate the instep region. Option B is incorrect because the lateral plantar nerve originates from the tibial nerve, not the superficial peroneal nerve. Option C is incorrect because the lateral plantar nerve does not derive from the sural nerve. Option D is incorrect because while it correctly identifies the medial plantar nerve, this nerve branches from the tibial nerve, not the deep peroneal nerve.

questions.question:
A 27-year-old male arrives at the burn unit 4 hours after becoming lost in a blizzard during a hiking trip. Clinical assessment reveals severe frostbite of both feet with purple discoloration of digits, extensive blistering, and significant swelling. Doppler studies show bilateral absence of pedal pulses. He has no additional trauma and is otherwise well. Besides rewarming and analgesia, what is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
A) Angiography
B) Fasciotomy
C) Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
D) Intravenous administration of heparin
E) Technetium-99 triple-phase scanning
questions.answer:
A)

Emergent angiography with tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) infusion is the most appropriate next step for severe frostbite with absent pulses when performed within 24 hours of injury onset. This intervention has been demonstrated to significantly reduce amputation rates in severe frostbite cases. Option B is incorrect because fasciotomy may be needed after reperfusion but is not the primary initial intervention for frostbite. Option C is incorrect because hyperbaric oxygen therapy has not been proven to improve outcomes in frostbite injuries. Option D is incorrect because intravenous heparin administration has not been shown to enhance frostbite treatment outcomes. Option E is incorrect because while technetium-99 scanning can help predict amputation levels, it is diagnostic rather than therapeutic and would delay the critical angiography and tPA treatment.

questions.question:
A 10-year-old female is evaluated for a large full-thickness skull defect following trauma. Reconstruction is performed using a split cranial bone graft. What is the primary mechanism through which this bone graft achieves healing?
A) Dural ossification
B) Osteoconduction
C) Osteogenesis
D) Osteoinduction
E) Vasculogenesis
questions.answer:
B)

Osteoconduction is the primary healing mechanism for split cranial bone grafts. The predominantly cortical graft becomes devascularized and functions as a scaffold for blood vessel ingrowth and osteoprogenitor cell migration from the recipient site through "creeping substitution," ultimately leading to graft resorption and replacement with new bone. Option A is incorrect because spontaneous dural ossification only occurs in infants under 12-18 months of age and would not apply to this 10-year-old patient. Option C is incorrect because osteogenesis is the primary mechanism for cancellous or vascularized grafts where osteoblasts survive transplantation, not for avascular cortical grafts. Option D is incorrect because osteoinduction involves stimulating mesenchymal cells to differentiate into bone-producing cells, which is characteristic of demineralized bone matrix or bone morphogenetic proteins. Option E is incorrect because vasculogenesis refers to de novo blood vessel formation during embryogenesis, while graft revascularization occurs through angiogenesis from existing vessels.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old female patient visits the clinic presenting with newly developed left upper eyelid drooping that began 1 week following botulinum toxin type A injections for treating frown lines between her eyebrows. The physician prescribes apraclonidine eye drops for the affected left eye. Complete recovery is observed within 2 days. Which of the following best describes the primary mechanism through which apraclonidine led to the improvement of this patient's eyelid drooping?
A) Removal of botulinum toxin type A from its presynaptic binding sites
B) Blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors in the levator palpebrae superioris muscle
C) Blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors in the superior tarsal (Müller) muscle
D) Activating alpha-adrenergic receptors in the levator palpebrae superioris muscle
E) Activating alpha-adrenergic receptors in the superior tarsal (Müller) muscle
questions.answer:
E)
The primary mechanism by which apraclonidine improved this patient's eyelid drooping is through activating alpha-adrenergic receptors in the superior tarsal (Müller) muscle. Botulinum toxin type A works by preventing acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions, which can affect the levator palpebrae superioris muscle when the toxin migrates through the orbital septum. The superior tarsal (Müller) muscle is smooth muscle innervated by sympathetic fibers with alpha-adrenergic receptors. Apraclonidine, being an alpha-2 receptor agonist with some alpha-1 activity, stimulates these receptors causing muscle contraction that can compensate for 1-3 mm of ptosis from levator dysfunction. A is incorrect because apraclonidine does not significantly displace botulinum toxin from receptors. B and C are incorrect because blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors would cause muscle relaxation and worsen ptosis. D is incorrect because the levator palpebrae superioris is skeletal muscle controlled by cholinergic, not adrenergic, receptors.

questions.question:
A 45-year-old female patient seeks consultation regarding breast enhancement surgery. She expresses worry about the elevated risk of capsular contracture and requests prophylactic antibiotic treatment following surgery. Her medical history reveals no known medication allergies. Which of the following represents the most suitable postoperative antibiotic regimen for this patient?
A) Cephalexin; 500 mg, four times daily for 7 days
B) Ciprofloxacin; 500 mg, twice daily for 7 days
C) Clindamycin; 300 mg, every 6 hours for 7 days
D) Sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim; one double-strength tablet, twice daily for 7 days
E) Postoperative antibiotics are not indicated
questions.answer:
E)
Postoperative prophylactic antibiotics are not indicated for this patient. While capsular contracture remains the most frequent long-term complication following breast augmentation, routine postoperative antibiotic therapy has not been proven to reduce this complication's occurrence. Although capsular contracture may result from subacute bacterial infection leading to biofilm formation (commonly involving Staphylococcus epidermidis), preventive strategies focus on surgical techniques such as betadine irrigation, antibiotic irrigation, and no-touch techniques rather than systemic antibiotics. Research has not demonstrated effectiveness of postoperative antibiotic therapy in preventing capsular contracture. A, B, C, and D are all incorrect because they represent unnecessary antibiotic prophylaxis that lacks evidence-based support for preventing capsular contracture in breast augmentation patients.

questions.question:
A 3-year-old female child is brought to the clinic because her second and third toes on both feet are joined together. The child's mother requests surgical correction of this condition. Physical examination reveals simple complete syndactyly. Which of the following represents the most suitable surgical approach following syndactyly release?
A) Local flaps
B) Local flaps and full-thickness skin grafts
C) Local flaps and split-thickness skin grafts from the lateral thigh
D) Primary closure
questions.answer:
B)
The most appropriate surgical treatment for complete syndactyly of the toes involves local flaps combined with full-thickness skin grafts. Complete syndactyly requires skin grafting because there is insufficient local tissue to achieve closure with flaps alone after separation. Full-thickness grafts are preferred and should be harvested from the lateral groin area to avoid unwanted hair growth that may occur with medial groin grafts as the child matures. The procedure also requires careful thinning of fat around neurovascular bundles to facilitate closure with local flaps. A is incorrect because local flaps alone are insufficient for complete syndactyly, though they may work for incomplete cases. C is incorrect because split-thickness grafts are not the preferred choice for toe syndactyly repair. D is incorrect because primary closure is not possible in complete syndactyly due to tissue deficiency after separation.

questions.question:
A 34-year-old female patient undergoes laser-assisted liposuction of the abdomen, hips, and inner and outer thighs using tumescent technique. A total of 2500 mL of fat is aspirated. Initial postoperative recovery proceeds normally, and she is discharged home the same day. She presents to the emergency department 4 days later complaining of severe pain over the lower abdomen and flanks. Her temperature is 101°F (38.3°C). Physical examination reveals well-defined areas of skin redness, firmness, and blister formation at multiple locations. Her surgical incisions are draining clear, grayish fluid. Which of the following represents the most appropriate treatment approach?
A) Exploratory laparotomy for presumed bowel perforation
B) Intravenous administration of antibiotics and local burn care
C) Intravenous administration of antibiotics only
D) Oral administration of antibiotics
E) Surgical debridement of the involved tissue
questions.answer:
E)
Surgical debridement of the involved tissue is the most appropriate management for this patient who has developed necrotizing fasciitis following liposuction. The clinical presentation of severe pain, fever, well-demarcated erythema, induration, bullae formation, and drainage of "dishwater" fluid is pathognomonic for necrotizing fasciitis. This rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection involves necrosis of fascia and subcutaneous fat with subsequent skin necrosis. Early diagnosis and immediate aggressive surgical debridement combined with antibiotic therapy are essential, as mortality rates can reach 70% but decrease to 4.2% with prompt surgical intervention. Delay in debridement significantly increases mortality. The wound is typically left open for planned second-look operations and additional debridement if necessary. A is incorrect because there are no signs of bowel perforation. B and C are incorrect because antibiotics alone are insufficient without surgical debridement. D is incorrect because oral antibiotics are inadequate for this severe, life-threatening infection.

questions.question:
Which of the following represents the primary blood supply source to the mandibular condylar head?
A) Articular disk
B) Capsule of the temporomandibular joint
C) Deep branch of the superficial temporal artery
D) Facial artery
E) Medullary branch of the inferior alveolar artery
questions.answer:
E)
The medullary branch of the inferior alveolar artery provides the most significant blood supply to the mandibular condylar head. The condyle receives blood from three main sources: a branch of the inferior alveolar artery that travels upward through the condylar neck and anastomoses with muscular vessels, the temporomandibular joint capsule with its rich vascular network, and branches from the lateral pterygoid muscle through its attachment at the pterygoid fovea. Research in primates has demonstrated that the medullary blood supply from the inferior alveolar artery branch is the most important source. This explains why subcondylar or neck fractures can severely compromise condylar viability by disrupting this primary vascular supply. A is incorrect because the articular disk does not provide significant blood supply to the condyle. B is incorrect because while the TMJ capsule contributes to condylar blood supply, it is not the primary source. C and D are incorrect because neither the superficial temporal artery's deep branch nor the facial artery are major contributors to condylar head vascularity.

questions.question:
A newborn female presents with a lesion on the occipital scalp/posterior neck. A photograph and x-ray are shown. MRI has been performed. It is most appropriate to order which of the following studies before formulating a treatment plan?


A) Brain MRI to rule out structural anomalies
B) Doppler ultrasonography to assess flow of the lesion
C) Echocardiography to assess cardiac function
D) Incisional biopsy for genetic analysis
E) Lymphatic mapping with isosulfan blue to identify the sentinel lymph node
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


This patient has a rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma (RICH). These are often large and fast-flow and can cause high-output cardiac failure. Therefore, it is important to assess cardiac function to ascertain whether this patient needs cardiac support (eg, digoxin). While Doppler ultrasonography may have been indicated as a first-line imaging study, the MRI and magnetic resonance angiography demonstrated the extent of the lesion and flow; Doppler ultrasonography will not give additional information at this time. Incisional biopsy may be indicated if there are concerns about the diagnosis. However, performing a biopsy to obtain tissues for genetic analysis is not indicated, as the genetic information will not give information to direct treatment. Brain MRI to rule out structural anomalies is indicated when a patient is suspected of having posterior fossa brain malformations, hemangioma, arterial lesions, cardiac abnormalities, and eye abnormalities (PHACE) syndrome, a large segmental infantile hemangioma in the face. Lymphatic mapping for sentinel node is used for head and neck malignancies and has no role here.

In this case, the patient did develop mild cardiac failure. This lesion was embolized one day before she underwent resection of this lesion.
ReferencesAyturk UM, Couto JA, Hann S, et al. Somatic activating mutations in GNAQ and GNA11 are associated with congenital hemangioma. Am J Hum Genet. 2016;98(4):789-795.Haggstrom AN, Garzon MC, Baselga E, et al. Risk for PHACE syndrome in infants with large facial hemangiomas. Pediatrics. 2010;126(2):e418-e426.Nakano TA, Zeinati C. Venous thromboembolism in pediatric vascular anomalies. Front Pediatr. 2017;5:158.Sur A, Manraj H, Lavoie PM. Multiple successful angioembolizations for refractory cardiac failure in a preterm with rapidly involuting congenital hemangioma. AJP Rep. 2016;6(1):e99-e103.

questions.question:
A healthy 35-year-old woman presents for evaluation of a 3-cm mass in her left parotid gland. Clinical examination reveals facial muscle weakness on the affected side. Imaging demonstrates multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Following parotidectomy, histological analysis reveals a heterogeneous collection of undifferentiated epithelial cells and intermediate cells with scattered secretory cells and nerve infiltration. What is the most probable diagnosis?
A) Hemangioma
B) Mucoepidermoid carcinoma
C) Pleomorphic adenoma
D) Squamous cell carcinoma
E) Warthin tumor
questions.answer:
B)
Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the correct diagnosis. This malignancy represents the most frequent malignant tumor of the parotid gland and contains both mucus-producing cells and epidermoid-type epithelial cells. The presence of facial nerve weakness indicates neural invasion, which is characteristic of malignant salivary gland tumors. High-grade mucoepidermoid carcinomas show predominantly poorly differentiated epidermoid cells with few mucus-secreting cells, matching this patient's histology. The enlarged cervical lymph nodes suggest regional metastasis, supporting the malignant nature.

A) Hemangioma is incorrect because these are benign vascular tumors primarily seen in children, composed of proliferative endothelial cells lining capillaries, not the mixed epithelial cell population described.

C) Pleomorphic adenoma is incorrect because this is the most common benign parotid tumor, characterized by epithelial and connective tissue elements in a myxoid background, and would not cause facial nerve paralysis or lymph node enlargement.

D) Squamous cell carcinoma is incorrect because primary squamous cell carcinoma rarely occurs in the parotid gland and would show sheets of keratinizing epithelial cells with keratin pearls, not the mixed cell population described.

E) Warthin tumor is incorrect because this benign tumor consists of papillary cysts with lymphoid tissue and predominantly affects males, without causing facial nerve dysfunction or the described histological features.

questions.question:
Which artery is most likely to provide vascular supply to a free vascularized bone graft harvested from the femoral medial condyle?
A) Descending genicular
B) Medial femoral circumflex
C) Posterior radial collateral
D) Posterior tibial
E) Sural artery
questions.answer:
A)
The descending genicular artery is the primary vascular supply for medial femoral condyle bone flaps. This artery provides reliable and consistent perfusion to the medial condyle region, being present in approximately 89% of specimens. It courses at an average distance of 13.7 cm proximal to the articular surface, making it an excellent pedicle for vascularized bone transfer from this donor site.

B) Medial femoral circumflex artery is incorrect because it supplies the upper thigh region and femoral neck, not the medial condyle area used for bone grafting.

C) Posterior radial collateral artery is incorrect because this vessel serves as the pedicle for lateral arm flaps, not femoral condyle bone flaps.

D) Posterior tibial artery is incorrect because it provides circulation to the plantar foot region, not the femoral condyle.

E) Sural artery is incorrect because it supplies the posterior calf skin, not the medial femoral condyle bone.

questions.question:
A 55-year-old, right-hand‚Äidominant man who is a machinist comes to the office because of inability to fully extend the right ring finger. Photographs are shown. The patient reports that his symptom began 5 years ago and has worsened progressively. Examination shows a 45-degree flexion contracture of the right ring finger (PIP) joint during attempts at full extension. All other joints demonstrate full extension, and the patient can create a complete fist during flexion. Regarding treatment options for this patient, which of the following interventions is most likely to provide the longest relief of his symptom prior to recurrence?


A) Collagenase injection and manipulation
B) Limited fasciectomy
C) Percutaneous aponeurotomy with lipografting
D) Percutaneous needle fasciotomy
E) Radiation therapy and splinting
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


Radiotherapy has been proposed as a potential treatment to slow or stop progression of Dupuytren contractures (palmar fibromatosis). A prospective study of radiotherapy revealed no greater efficacy than observation as an intervention for slowing the disease process. There is no evidence to suggest radiotherapy for correction of an established contracture.


Rijssen and colleagues established quantitative criteria for recurrence, using an increase of total passive flexion contracture of 30 or greater, compared to the 6-week follow-up values in previously treated joints. After 5 years, their recurrence rate following percutaneous needle fasciotomy was 85%; 21% for limited fasciectomy; and 32% of joints successfully treated with Clostridial collagenase. Percutaneous aponeurotomy with lipografting is an experimental technique which has shown some promise with correction of contractures and prevention of recurrence, but the evidence is level 4, with no controlled studies looking at this technique, in comparison to other established techniques.


Although limited fasciectomy provides the greatest degree of initial correction for Dupuytren contractures, as well as the longest period prior to recurrence, the costs associated with the procedure are by far the highest. When comparing the QALY costs of three interventions (limited fasciectomy, percutaneous needle fasciotomy, and collagenase injection), limited fasciectomy yielded the highest cost per QALY. The authors emphasize that this does not indicate limited fasciectomy is an inappropriate intervention‚Äionly that it is relatively the most expensive.


References
Eaton, C. Evidence-based medicine: Dupuytren contracture. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2014 May;133(5):1241-51.
Peimer CA, Blazar P, Coleman S, et al. Dupuytren Contracture Recurrence Following Treatment With Collagenase Clostridium histolyticum (CORDLESS [Collagenase Option for Reduction of Dupuytren Long-Term Evaluation of Safety Study]): 5-Year Data. J Hand Surg Am. 2015 Aug;40(8):1597-605.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male arrives at the emergency department with a wrist laceration from punching through a glass window one hour prior. Examination reveals a 2-cm horizontal cut across the volar ulnar wrist fold. Surgical exploration confirms complete transection of the ulnar nerve. Which motor function is most likely to be impaired in this patient?
A) Adduction of the thumb carpometacarpal joint
B) Extension of the metacarpophalangeal joint of the ring and small fingers
C) Extension of the thumb interphalangeal joint
D) Flexion of the interphalangeal joint of the index and middle fingers
E) Flexion of the interphalangeal joint of the ring and small fingers
questions.answer:
A)
Thumb adduction at the carpometacarpal joint will be lost due to denervation of the adductor pollicis muscle. The ulnar nerve's deep motor branch, which arises after the nerve passes through Guyon's canal at the wrist, specifically innervates the adductor pollicis muscle. Complete ulnar nerve transection at the wrist level will interrupt this innervation, resulting in inability to adduct the thumb toward the palm.

B) Extension of the ring and small finger metacarpophalangeal joints is incorrect because this function is controlled by the radial nerve through the extensor digitorum communis and extensor digiti minimi muscles, which remain intact.

C) Extension of the thumb interphalangeal joint is incorrect because this is performed by the radial nerve-innervated extensor pollicis longus muscle, which is unaffected by ulnar nerve injury.

D) Flexion of the index and middle finger interphalangeal joints is incorrect because this function is mediated by the median nerve through the flexor digitorum superficialis, which is not damaged in this ulnar nerve injury.

E) Flexion of the ring and small finger interphalangeal joints is incorrect because while the flexor digitorum profundus to these fingers is ulnar-innervated, the nerve branches to this muscle arise proximal to the wrist injury site and would remain functional.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old woman seeks consultation for treatment of deep facial wrinkles and pigmentation irregularities. Her medical history reveals Fitzpatrick skin type II. A chemical peel procedure is being considered. Which chemical peeling agent requires cardiac rhythm monitoring during treatment?
A) Glycolic acid
B) Phenol
C) Resorcinol
D) Salicylic acid
E) Trichloroacetic acid
questions.answer:
B)
Phenol requires cardiac monitoring because it is systemically absorbed through the skin and can cause potentially dangerous cardiac arrhythmias. These rhythm disturbances can include supraventricular tachycardia, premature ventricular contractions, atrial fibrillation, and ventricular fibrillation. The risk is higher with greater phenol concentrations and full-face treatments. Standard protocol requires electrocardiographic monitoring, intravenous access, and staged treatment with 15-minute intervals between aesthetic units to minimize systemic absorption.

A) Glycolic acid is incorrect because this alpha-hydroxy acid used in superficial peels does not cause cardiac complications or require rhythm monitoring.

C) Resorcinol is incorrect because this component of Jessner's solution does not produce cardiac arrhythmias requiring monitoring.

D) Salicylic acid is incorrect because this beta-hydroxy acid, also found in Jessner's solution, does not necessitate cardiac surveillance.

E) Trichloroacetic acid is incorrect because this medium-depth peeling agent does not cause cardiac rhythm abnormalities requiring electrocardiographic monitoring.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old woman presents for consultation regarding upper eyelid skin excess and lower eyelid puffiness. Her medical history includes hypothyroidism and type 2 diabetes mellitus. She had LASIK eye surgery one year ago. Current medications include hormone replacement therapy, thyroid supplementation, and metformin. Combined upper and lower blepharoplasty is being planned. Which postoperative complication poses the highest risk for this patient?
A) Bleeding
B) Blindness
C) Chemosis
D) Dry eye syndrome
E) Eyelid malposition
questions.answer:
D)
Dry eye syndrome represents the greatest risk for this patient due to multiple predisposing factors. Simultaneous upper and lower blepharoplasty increases dry eye risk compared to staged procedures due to orbicularis oculi muscle dysfunction. Her hormone replacement therapy further elevates this risk, as estrogen supplementation is associated with increased dry eye development after blepharoplasty. Although her LASIK procedure was performed one year ago (beyond the recommended 6-month waiting period), previous laser vision correction can still contribute to corneal sensation changes and altered tear production.

A) Bleeding is incorrect because while possible, it is primarily associated with uncontrolled hypertension rather than her specific risk factors, and major bleeding complications are rare.

B) Blindness is incorrect because vision loss after blepharoplasty is an extremely rare complication and is not specifically increased by her medical history or medications.

C) Chemosis is incorrect because conjunctival swelling, while possible, is not specifically increased by her risk factors and is generally a manageable complication.

E) Eyelid malposition is incorrect because this complication is more common in patients with negative vector anatomy or poor eyelid tone, which are not mentioned in her presentation.

questions.question:
Which of the following patients has a skin lesion with clinical characteristics most concerning for malignancy?
A) A 14-year-old boy with a 5-mm, circular, brown spot that has been present since birth on the lower thigh
B) A 22-year-old woman with a 6-mm bleeding, stalk-like bump that appeared 6 weeks ago on her cheek
C) A 55-year-old man with a 5-mm pink, shiny bump that has been present for 6 months on the side of his nose
D) A 70-year-old man with a 1.5-cm waxy, yellow-brown, rough patch that has been present for several years on his left temple
questions.answer:
C)
The 55-year-old man's pink, shiny papule on the lateral nasal sidewall is most concerning for basal cell carcinoma, which commonly presents as pearly, translucent nodules with telangiectasias in sun-exposed areas of older adults. A is incorrect because congenital nevi in young patients that remain stable are typically benign. B is incorrect because the friable, pedunculated nature suggests a pyogenic granuloma, which is benign despite its bleeding tendency. D is incorrect because the waxy, scaly, "stuck-on" appearance is characteristic of seborrheic keratosis, a common benign lesion in elderly patients.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old woman seeks consultation for management of excessive subcutaneous tissue in her lower abdomen that developed following cryolipolysis procedures performed 6 months earlier. The affected area is painless, soft, movable, and not well-defined. What is the most suitable treatment recommendation for this patient?
A) Liposuction
B) Massage therapy
C) Additional cryolipolysis treatment
D) Corticosteroid injection
questions.answer:
A)
This patient has developed paradoxical adipose hyperplasia (PAH), a rare complication of cryolipolysis that typically manifests months after treatment. The standard treatment involves waiting 6-9 months for tissue softening, then performing liposuction or abdominoplasty to remove the affected tissue. B is incorrect because while massage may be used after cryolipolysis for general improvement, there is no evidence supporting its effectiveness for PAH. C is incorrect because repeat cryolipolysis is not indicated for PAH and could worsen the condition. D is incorrect because steroid injections have no proven benefit for treating PAH.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man arrives at the emergency department following a degloving injury to his long, ring, and little fingers on the back of his non-dominant left hand from a high-speed rollover car accident. After surgical cleaning, he has exposed proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints on all three affected fingers. What is the optimal management approach for these defects?
A) Cross-finger flap reconstruction
B) Full-thickness skin graft from the groin
C) Pedicled lateral arm flap reconstruction
D) Reverse radial forearm flap reconstruction
E) Split-thickness skin graft from the thigh
questions.answer:
D)
The reverse radial forearm flap provides optimal coverage for this extensive defect with exposed joints, offering thin, well-vascularized tissue with excellent gliding properties for joint function. A is incorrect because cross-finger flaps are suitable for single digit injuries but inadequate for this large zone of injury involving multiple fingers. B is incorrect because groin flaps are bulky, require attachment of the arm to the trunk, and need staged procedures. C is incorrect because the lateral arm flap cannot reach the fingers due to insufficient length. E is incorrect because skin grafts, whether split or full-thickness, cannot provide adequate coverage for exposed joint surfaces and lack the necessary durability.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman presents for assessment 6 days following a jamming injury to her left long finger that resulted in central slip rupture and acute boutonnière deformity. Radiographs show no fracture or joint displacement. Splint immobilization treatment is planned. What is the optimal finger positioning for splint application?
A) Distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint straight, proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint straight
B) DIP straight, PIP unrestricted
C) DIP bent, PIP bent
D) DIP bent, PIP unrestricted
E) DIP unrestricted, PIP straight
questions.answer:
E)
The correct splinting position for boutonnière deformity is PIP joint extension with DIP joint free to move. This positioning allows the central slip to heal while permitting DIP flexion exercises that encourage dorsal migration of the lateral bands, restoring their extensor function and correcting the deformity. A is incorrect because immobilizing both joints in extension prevents the beneficial dorsal migration of lateral bands. B is incorrect because this positioning is used for mallet finger injuries, not boutonnière deformities. C is incorrect because flexing both joints would worsen the boutonnière deformity. D is incorrect because PIP flexion perpetuates the deformity rather than correcting it.

questions.question:
A 46-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of severe physical decline, nausea, and vomiting. She had breast reconstruction 3 weeks prior. Her medical history includes delayed right latissimus dorsi tissue expander breast reconstruction performed 1 year after completing radiation therapy. She has no other medical conditions. Physical examination reveals an erythematous rash extending beyond the surgical sites. No fluid collections are present and surgical wounds are not draining. Her temperature is 103.5°F (39.7°C) and blood pressure is 90/50 mmHg. Intraoperative cultures from the explored surgical sites will most likely yield which organism?
A) Bacteroides
B) Clostridium
C) Enterobacter
D) Pseudomonas
E) Streptococcus
questions.answer:
E)
This clinical presentation is consistent with toxic shock syndrome, which is most commonly caused by exotoxin-producing Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus. The combination of high fever, hypotension, rash, and systemic symptoms following surgery supports this diagnosis. A is incorrect because Bacteroides is associated with polymicrobial necrotizing fasciitis, which typically presents with skin discoloration and crepitus not seen here. B is incorrect because Clostridium causes necrotizing fasciitis with different clinical features including skin blistering and crepitus. C is incorrect because Enterobacter is also associated with necrotizing fasciitis rather than toxic shock syndrome. D is incorrect because Pseudomonas is another necrotizing fasciitis pathogen that doesn't match this clinical presentation.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man is evaluated for a wound over the lateral aspect of his right lower leg, located 5 cm distal to the knee, sustained during a bicycle accident 2 months earlier. Electromyography and nerve conduction studies reveal findings consistent with a complete isolated injury of the common peroneal nerve. Which of the following impairments is most expected on physical examination?
A) Ankle dorsiflexion
B) Great toe plantarflexion
C) Lateral foot sensation
D) Medial foot sensation
E) Plantar foot sensation
questions.answer:
A)
The common peroneal nerve arises from the bifurcation of the sciatic nerve at the apex of the popliteal fossa. It courses along the medial border of the biceps femoris muscle and tendon, passes posterior to the fibular head, and winds around the fibular neck, where its superficial position makes it the most frequently injured nerve of the lower extremity. It then divides into deep and superficial peroneal branches. The deep peroneal nerve innervates the anterior compartment muscles of the leg and supplies sensation to the first web space; the superficial peroneal nerve innervates the peroneus longus and brevis and supplies sensation over the distal third of the anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot.

Complete transection paralyzes all anterior and lateral compartment muscles (ankle and toe dorsiflexors and foot evertors), producing loss of ankle dorsiflexion and the characteristic foot drop with a steppage gait. Sensory loss involves the anterolateral leg and the dorsum of the foot.

B is incorrect because great toe plantarflexion is mediated by the tibial nerve via the flexor hallucis longus. C is incorrect because sensation over the lateral foot is supplied by the sural nerve. D is incorrect because sensation over the medial foot is supplied by the saphenous nerve and the medial plantar nerve. E is incorrect because plantar sensation is supplied by the terminal branches of the tibial nerve (medial and lateral plantar nerves).

questions.question:
What is the earliest timeframe one could anticipate finding electromyographic abnormalities following suspected median nerve injury during carpal tunnel decompression?
A) 1 Week
B) 3 Weeks
C) 5 Weeks
D) 7 Weeks
questions.answer:
B)
Electromyographic muscle changes typically appear 2 to 3 weeks following nerve injury and include fibrillation potentials and reduced motor unit potential recruitment. While nerve conduction velocity abnormalities (decreased amplitude, reduced velocity, increased latency) may occur earlier, the specific muscle changes detected by EMG require this 2-3 week period to develop. Sensory nerve latency exceeding 3.5 ms and motor nerve latency above 4.5 ms are considered pathological. These studies have approximately 66% sensitivity but maintain 95% specificity. A is incorrect because one week is too early for EMG changes to manifest in muscle tissue. C is incorrect because 5 weeks exceeds the typical 2-3 week onset period for detectable EMG abnormalities. D is incorrect because 7 weeks is well beyond the expected timeframe for initial EMG changes to appear.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old boy sustains a deep laceration over the right side of the face. A photograph is shown. Injury to the parotid (Stensen) duct is suspected. At the anterior edge of the parotid gland, the duct should lie immediately superficial to which of the following structures?


A) Deep subcutaneous fat
B) Masseteric fascia
C) Submuscular aponeurotic system (SMAS)
D) Superficial parotid fascia
E) Temporoparietal fascia
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


The parotid gland is the largest of the three paired salivary glands (parotid, submandibular, and sublingual). It has two lobes, the deep and superficial, each of which is enveloped in a fascial sheath (parotid sheath) and between which passes the facial vein and nerve. The superficial lobe lies lateral (superficial) to the masseter muscle, and the deep lobe lies between the mastoid process and the mandibular ramus. The parotid, or Stensen, duct arises from the deep lobe of the parotid gland and receives contributions from the superficial lobe as it travels anteriorly. After exiting the anterior edge of the superficial lobe, the duct passes directly over the masseter muscle, crosses over the anterior edge of the masseter, extends medially and anteriorly over and through the buccinator muscle, and enters into the mouth via the parotid papilla, typically located opposite the second maxillary molar. The course of the duct has classically been described as following a line connecting the tragus and the midportion of the upper lip, but there is significant variation, and some studies report that this line should end in the lower half of the upper lip. The laceration shown in the photograph is just at the anterior border of the parotid and, at this level, the duct should be passing over the masseter muscle and its fascia. The course of the duct is below the superficial lobe of the parotid and, therefore, well below the subcutaneous tissue and the submuscular aponeurotic system (SMAS), which is confluent with the platysma inferiorly and the temporoparietal fascial superiorly. Superficial parotid fascia defines the layer of fascia that invests the superficial lobe of the parotid gland.


ReferencesCotofana S, Schenck TL, Trevidic P, et al. Midface: clinical anatomy and regional approaches with injectable fillers. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2015;136(5 suppl):219S-234S.Mendelson BC, Wong CH. Surgical anatomy of the middle premasseter space and its application in sub-SMAS face lift surgery. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2013;132(1):57-64.Stringer MD, Mirjalili SA, Meredith SJ, et al. Redefining the surface anatomy of the parotid duct: an in vivo ultrasound study. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012;130(5):1032-1037.

questions.question:
The postoperative CT scan displayed is obtained to assess wound separation in a patient who had left unilateral breast reduction for asymmetry six weeks previously. Which of the following upper limb abnormalities is most likely present in this patient?
A) Contralateral radial club hand
B) Contralateral "pouce flottant" thumb
C) Ipsilateral brachysyndactyly
D) Ipsilateral radial head subluxation
E) Ipsilateral type IV Wassel preaxial polydactyly
questions.answer:
C)
The chest CT demonstrates right-sided absence of pectoralis major and minor muscles with breast hypoplasia, indicating Poland syndrome. This congenital condition of unclear cause is theorized to result from subclavian artery or branch hypoplasia during the sixth embryonic week. Common manifestations include absent anterior axillary fold and pectoralis major sternal head, breast tissue thinning, rib and cartilage underdevelopment, and ipsilateral brachysyndactyly (short, webbed fingers on the same side). A is incorrect because radial club hand, while a congenital deformity, has no association with Poland syndrome. B is incorrect because "pouce flottant" thumbs (rudimentary thumbs attached by skin bridges) are not linked to Poland syndrome. D is incorrect because radial head subluxation ("nursemaid's elbow") is an acquired childhood injury unrelated to Poland syndrome. E is incorrect because type IV Wassel preaxial polydactyly (thumb duplication) is not associated with Poland syndrome.

questions.question:
A 40-year-old female with a history of severe postoperative nausea and vomiting is scheduled for bilateral breast tissue expander replacement with permanent silicone implants. Which of the following medications is most likely to reduce the risk of postoperative nausea?
A) Bupivacaine
B) Fentanyl
C) Isoflurane
D) Midazolam
E) Nitrous oxide
questions.answer:
A)
Local anesthetics like bupivacaine, when used during general anesthesia through subcutaneous, tumescent, or regional block techniques, can reduce the required doses of sedatives and analgesics that commonly cause nausea and vomiting. This reduction in nauseogenic medications helps prevent postoperative emesis. Effective local anesthesia allows for decreased reliance on opioids and inhalational agents that promote nausea. B is incorrect because fentanyl is an opioid that commonly causes nausea and vomiting. C is incorrect because isoflurane is an inhalational anesthetic agent known to promote nausea and emesis. D is incorrect because midazolam, while less commonly associated with nausea than opioids and inhalational agents, can still cause nausea and does not actively reduce nausea risk. E is incorrect because nitrous oxide is an inhalational agent that promotes nausea and vomiting.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old female undergoes removal of a 3-cm recurring keloid from the presternal chest area. Immediate reconstruction uses a collagen-glycosaminoglycan scaffold dermal regeneration template, with thin (0.008-in) epidermal autografting performed 21 days later. After complete healing, punch biopsy is conducted. The lack of which histologic feature would most likely indicate regenerated skin in this patient?
A) Capillary loops at the dermal-epidermal junction
B) Elastic fibers
C) Hair follicles
D) Neovascularization
E) Rete ridges
questions.answer:
C)
Regenerated skin demonstrates many characteristics similar to normal physiologic skin, including mechanical strength, vascularization, temperature sensitivity, rete ridge formation, capillary loops at the dermal-epidermal junction, elastic fibers, increased reticular dermis collagen density, and often nerve fiber regeneration. However, regenerated skin lacks dermal appendages such as hair follicles and sweat glands that are normally present throughout physiologic skin, even when resurfaced with split-thickness skin grafts. A is incorrect because capillary loops at the dermal-epidermal junction are present in regenerated skin. B is incorrect because elastic fibers are found in regenerated skin. D is incorrect because neovascularization occurs in regenerated skin and contributes to its functionality. E is incorrect because rete ridges form at the dermal-epidermal junction in regenerated skin.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old male patient underwent femoral-popliteal bypass surgery 2 weeks prior and now presents with a proximal groin infection. A muscle flap is being considered to obliterate the dead space. Which muscle flap choice demonstrates type IV Mathes-Nahai classification (multiple segmental vascular pedicles) blood supply pattern?
A) Gracilis
B) Rectus abdominis
C) Rectus femoris
D) Sartorius
E) Vastus medialis
questions.answer:
D)
The sartorius muscle exhibits type IV Mathes-Nahai vascular pattern, characterized by multiple segmental blood supply, which may restrict its rotational arc. Recent research indicates that despite having numerous segmental pedicles, the sartorius typically possesses codominant superior and inferior vessels that potentially allow most of the muscle to survive on either the upper or lower dominant pedicle. The Mathes-Nahai classification includes: Type I (single dominant pedicle), Type II (dominant pedicle with minor secondary vessels), Type III (two codominant major pedicles), Type IV (multiple segmental pedicles), and Type V (dominant pedicle with segmental secondaries that can sustain muscle if primary is severed). A, C, and E are incorrect because gracilis, rectus femoris, and vastus medialis all demonstrate type II anatomy. B is incorrect because rectus abdominis shows type III vascular pattern.

questions.question:
What dental landmark provides the optimal timing reference for secondary alveolar bone grafting in a patient with unilateral complete cleft lip and palate?
A) Full eruption of the central incisor adjacent to the cleft
B) Complete eruption of the permanent canine through the cleft
C) Crown formation of the permanent canine
D) Exfoliation of the primary canine next to the cleft
E) Loss of the primary ipsilateral central incisor
questions.answer:
C)
Secondary alveolar bone grafting should be performed when the permanent canine is crowning, during the mixed dentition phase. This timing ensures adequate bone support for the erupting canine while avoiding root exposure that occurs with delayed grafting. The procedure aims to stabilize the alveolar segment and provide sufficient bone volume for permanent tooth health. Grafting should occur after primary tooth loss but before complete eruption to optimize outcomes. A is incorrect because waiting for complete central incisor eruption may be too early for optimal canine support. B is incorrect because grafting after complete canine eruption risks root exposure and poor bone coverage. D and E are incorrect because primary tooth loss alone doesn't indicate optimal canine development timing for grafting.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old man comes to the office because he says the ring and little fingers of his right hand ‚Äucatch‚Äu when he puts his hand in his pocket and that he ‚Äupokes‚Äu himself in the eye when washing his face. History includes repair of a complete transection of the right ulnar nerve at the wrist 1 year ago. On physical examination, he is unable to extend the interphalangeal joints of the ring and little fingers when the metacarpophalangeal joints are flexed. Photographs are shown. Which of the following tendon transfers is the most appropriate management?


A) Extensor indicis proprius (EIP) to adductor
B) EIP to extensor digiti minimi
C) EIP to first dorsal interosseous
D) Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) of the little finger to A2 pulley
E) FDS of the little finger to lateral band
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Of the tendon transfer choices offered, only the FDS transfer to the lateral band (of both the ring and little fingers) will correct the loss of interphalangeal joint extension described, thereby diminishing the tendency for the flexed/abducted finger to catch on pocket edges.


The clinical scenario and photographs demonstrate failure of the intrinsic muscle function to return following a low ulnar nerve repair. The deformities demonstrated include ulnar clawing of the little finger primarily, abduction of the little finger (Wartenberg sign), hyperflexion of the interphalangeal joint of the thumb, and atrophy of the intrinsics (especially notable in the hypothenar eminence on the lateral view). Of these deformities, the patient is bothered primarily by the little finger deformity.


Correction of clawing can be achieved actively or passively. Patients who can extend the interphalangeal joints while hyperextension of the metacarpophalangeal joints is blocked (Bouvier test) can achieve correction of clawing with active or passive transfers. Active transfers attempt to re-create the normal function of the intrinsics by directing pull through the lateral bands. Passive transfers re-create the intrinsic function of metacarpophalangeal joint flexion (similar to externally blocking hyperextension) but do not extend the interphalangeal joints.


EIP transfers are useful for correction of the lateral pinch functions of the intrinsic minus hand. An EIP transfer to the adductor tendon re-creates the thumb component of lateral pinch, while the EIP transfer to the first dorsal interosseous tendon would improve the index function in pinch.


EIP transfer to the extensor digiti minimi is one method used to reduce hyperabduction of the little finger. This would not correct the flexion deformity at the level of the proximal interphalangeal joint.


FDS transfer to the A2 pulley provides a passive transfer, which, based on the patient‚Äos inability to extend the interphalangeal joints during the Bouvier test, would not correct the deformity.


References
Sammer DM, Chung KC. Tendon transfers: Part II. Transfers for ulnar nerve palsy and median nerve palsy. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2009 Sep;124(3):212e-221e.
Chung MS, Baek GH, Oh JH, et al. Extensor indicis proprius transfer for the abducted small finger. J Hand Surg Am. 2008 Mar;33(3):392-397.

questions.question:
A 75-year-old man comes to the office because of a 5-year history of a pruritic lesion on the right groin that has been enlarging gradually in size. A photograph is shown. Examination of a specimen obtained on biopsy shows Paget disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?


A) Oral miltefosine
B) Topical hydrocortisone
C) Topical miconazole
D) Wide excision
E) Observation
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option D.


This patient described has extramammary Paget disease and the treatment is wide excision. Paget disease of the breast also presents with eczematous skin changes and is associated with breast cancer. Extramammary Paget disease, however, is an intraepithelial carcinoma that commonly involves the vulvar, perianal, perineal, scrotal, and penile regions. It presents as well-defined, moist, erythematous plaques associated with pruritis. Histopathologic examination shows epidermal acanthosis and elongated rete ridges. Paget cells are large intraepidermal cells with a large nucleus and abundant pale cytoplasm. There is a 7 to 40% rate of associated malignancy. Wide excision is the standard of care, and recent reports have shown that Mohs micrographic surgery can improve evaluation of resection margins.


Observation is not appropriate for extramammary Paget disease given the potential risk for malignancy. Topical treatment with steroids or antifungals is also not appropriate. Oral miltefosine is a treatment for leishmaniasis, an infectious disease that can involve the skin, mucous membranes, and internal organs. Although cutaneous leishmaniasis can present with ulcerating lesions or a dense dermal infiltrate, the histology is predominantly histiocytes, lymphocytes, and plasma cells.


References
1. O'Connor EA, Hettinger PC, Neuburg M, et al. Extramammary Paget's disease: a novel approach to treatment using a modification of peripheral Mohs micrographic surgery. Ann Plast Surg. 2012 Jun;68(6):616-620.
2. Reveiz L, Maia-Elkhoury AN, Nicholls RS, et al. Interventions for American cutaneous and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis: a systematic review update. PLoS One. 2013 Apr 29;8(4):e61843. Print 2013.
3. Douglas SR, Narayan D. Extramammary Paget's Disease in Males: A Caveat for the Plastic Surgeon. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2013 Apr;131(4):652e-653e.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old male presents with a "mallet" finger deformity of the long finger's distal joint from a baseball injury 12 years ago, having never received treatment. What secondary deformity is most likely present on examination?
A) Boutonnière
B) Camptodactyly
C) Clinodactyly
D) Hook-nail
E) Swan-neck
questions.answer:
E)
Chronic mallet finger deformity leads to swan-neck deformity due to force imbalance. The flexion contracture at the distal joint causes compensatory hyperextension at the proximal joint in a zigzag pattern. When the terminal tendon is displaced proximally, the lateral bands migrate proximally and become extensors to the proximal joint, creating the characteristic swan-neck appearance. A is incorrect because boutonnière deformity results from central slip disruption causing proximal joint flexion and distal joint hyperextension. B is incorrect because camptodactyly is a congenital fixed flexion deformity of the little finger's proximal joint. C is incorrect because clinodactyly is a genetic condition causing fifth finger curvature toward the fourth finger. D is incorrect because hook-nail typically results from nail bed support loss after amputation.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old female with micromastia and bilateral tuberous breasts seeks breast augmentation and aesthetic improvement. Examination reveals bilateral mild ptosis with glandular herniation through the nipple-areolar complex, lower pole deficiency in medial and lateral quadrants, and nipple-to-inframammary fold distance of 5.5 cm on stretch. What surgical approach is most suitable?
A) Implant insertion with circumareolar mastopexy
B) Implant insertion alone
C) Implant insertion with vertical mastopexy
D) Implant insertion with Wise-pattern mastopexy
E) Two-stage reconstruction using tissue expander followed by permanent implant
questions.answer:
A)
This mild tuberous breast deformity requires implant placement with circumareolar mastopexy, typically combined with dual-plane implant positioning, inframammary fold adjustment, and radial parenchymal scoring. The periareolar approach addresses the nipple-areolar complex deformity while the implant provides volume enhancement. This represents the standard treatment for 96% of tuberous breast cases according to recent literature. B is incorrect because implant alone cannot correct the nipple-areolar complex deformity even with parenchymal scoring. C is incorrect because vertical mastopexy would be excessive for mild ptosis. D is incorrect because Wise-pattern mastopexy is unnecessary and overly aggressive for this mild deformity. E is incorrect because two-stage expansion is reserved for severely deficient cases and would constitute over-treatment here.

questions.question:
Following open rhinoplasty performed through a transverse columellar incision, which artery provides the primary vascular supply to the nasal tip?
A) Columellar
B) Lateral nasal
C) Posterior ethmoid
D) Sphenopalatine
E) Superior labial
questions.answer:
B)
After columellar skin division, the lateral nasal artery becomes the primary blood supply to the nasal tip. This vessel branches from the anterior ethmoid artery, which is part of the internal carotid circulation. During external rhinoplasty with stepped columellar incision, the columellar artery (from superior labial artery/external carotid system) may be compromised through division or cauterization, making the lateral nasal artery the dominant supply. A is incorrect because the columellar artery may be disrupted during the transcolumellar approach. C is incorrect because the posterior ethmoid artery supplies the upper central nasal septum. D is incorrect because the sphenopalatine artery provides blood to the posterior nasal septum. E is incorrect because the superior labial artery primarily supplies the upper lip region.

questions.question:
In surgical coding for orbital fracture repair, which of the following represents a distinct Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code?
A) Fracture elevation
B) Infraorbital nerve exploration
C) Malar fracture fixation
D) Orbital floor exploration
E) Entrapped orbital content release
questions.answer:
C)

Malar fracture fixation requires a separate CPT code when performed alongside orbital fracture repair. Orbital fracture codes are comprehensive and include fracture elevation, infraorbital nerve exploration, orbital floor exploration, and release of entrapped orbital contents (such as inferior rectus muscle and orbital fat). When both a malar fracture and orbital fracture require surgical treatment, each procedure is coded separately. A is incorrect because fracture elevation is included in the global orbital fracture codes. B is incorrect because infraorbital nerve exploration is bundled within orbital fracture repair codes. D is incorrect because orbital floor exploration is part of the comprehensive orbital fracture procedure. E is incorrect because release of entrapped contents is included in the global orbital fracture codes.

questions.question:
An 84-year-old male patient presents with his son-in-law for assessment of an ischial ulcer. Examination reveals a Stage IV right ischial ulcer and multiple extremity bruises, including circumferential upper arm ecchymoses. The son-in-law attributes injuries to a fall, but the patient remains quiet and avoids eye contact during questioning. Given the concerning physical findings and inconsistent history suggesting possible elder abuse, what is the most appropriate action?
A) Continue with ulcer excision and flap reconstruction since elder abuse is not definitively proven
B) Speak privately with the son-in-law regarding suspected elder abuse
C) Make a referral to a wound care specialist
D) Report suspected elder abuse to adult protective services
E) Report elder abuse suspicions only if the patient consents
questions.answer:
D)

Healthcare providers have a legal and ethical obligation to report suspected elder abuse to adult protective services, similar to mandatory reporting requirements for child abuse. This duty exists even when the patient denies abuse or refuses to cooperate, as elderly patients may be vulnerable and reluctant to report due to fear of retaliation or loss of care. A is incorrect because suspected abuse must be reported regardless of definitive proof. B is incorrect because confronting the suspected abuser privately is inappropriate and potentially dangerous. C is incorrect because wound care referral does not address the suspected abuse situation. E is incorrect because reporting suspected elder abuse does not require patient permission and should not be delayed.

questions.question:
To achieve credentialing and approval from the American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association, what provider must be included as part of the minimum core team alongside a surgeon and speech-language pathologist?
A) Audiologist
B) Geneticist
C) Orthodontist
D) Psychologist
E) Social worker
questions.answer:
C)

The American Cleft Palate-Craniofacial Association (ACPA) mandates that accredited teams must include three core specialties: surgery, speech-language pathology, and orthodontics. These core providers must actively participate in team meetings and their involvement must be documented in patient records. A is incorrect because audiologists are considered accessible specialists but not core team members. B is incorrect because geneticists are part of the accessible professional network but not required core providers. D is incorrect because psychologists are among the accessible disciplines but not mandatory core team members. E is incorrect because social workers are included in the accessible professional group but are not core requirements.

questions.question:
A newborn girl presents with severe Treacher Collins syndrome and bilateral Pruzansky III mandibular deformity (absent condyles). A tracheostomy was performed due to airway compromise. Which surgical intervention is most likely to enable tracheostomy decannulation?
A) Alloplastic condylar reconstruction
B) Bilateral sagittal split osteotomy
C) Costochondral rib grafts
D) Mandibular distraction
E) Tongue-lip adhesion
questions.answer:
C)

Costochondral rib grafts provide the best option for airway improvement in patients with absent temporomandibular joints and condyles. These grafts can reconstruct the missing anatomical structures and provide adequate airway support, with the additional benefit of potential future distraction. A is incorrect because alloplastic reconstruction may not provide sufficient airway improvement and has higher complication rates. B is incorrect because sagittal split osteotomy requires existing condyles and temporomandibular joints, which are absent in this case. D is incorrect because mandibular distraction requires intact condyles and joints for proper function. E is incorrect because tongue-lip adhesion is primarily used for Pierre Robin sequence and would not address the fundamental structural deficiency.

questions.question:
Which condition is most likely to respond favorably to botulinum toxin type A treatment?
A) Bruxism
B) Cervical paroxysmal dyskinesia
C) Hemifacial dyskinesia
D) Tardive dyskinesia
E) Vertical maxillary excess
questions.answer:
C)

Botulinum toxin type A has well-established efficacy for treating hemifacial dyskinesia, along with other conditions like blepharospasm and cervical dystonia. Strong evidence supports its use for these movement disorders involving facial muscle spasticity. A is incorrect because while botulinum toxin may reduce muscle contraction amplitude in bruxism, it does not decrease the frequency or rhythm of episodes, making it ineffective. B is incorrect because paroxysmal dyskinesia is an immune-mediated disorder requiring treatment with antibiotics, corticosteroids, or immunotherapy rather than botulinum toxin. D is incorrect because tardive dyskinesia results from antipsychotic medication side effects and requires VMAT2 inhibitors, not botulinum toxin. E is incorrect because vertical maxillary excess is a skeletal deformity requiring surgical correction, not botulinum toxin treatment.

questions.question:
What surgical approach is most frequently employed for reconstructing Blauth IIIB thumb hypoplasia in the United States?
A) Transfer of the great toe to thumb
B) Pollicization of the index finger
C) Stabilization of the metacarpophalangeal joint with opponensplasty
D) Transfer of the second toe to thumb
E) Toe wrap-around transfer procedure
questions.answer:
B)
Pollicization of the index finger is the standard treatment for severe thumb hypoplasia. The Blauth classification system categorizes thumb hypoplasia severity, with the most severe forms (types IIIB, IV, and V) requiring removal of the rudimentary thumb and reconstruction, typically achieved through index finger pollicization. A is incorrect because great toe transfer is less commonly used and more complex. C is incorrect because MCP stabilization with opponensplasty is used for less severe cases where the thumb can be preserved. D is incorrect because second toe transfer is rarely performed due to donor site morbidity and complexity. E is incorrect because toe wrap-around transfers are technically demanding and less frequently utilized.

questions.question:
During a job interview, which of the following questions is most legally appropriate to ask a candidate?
A) Whether the candidate has any physical impairments
B) The candidate's current age
C) How many hours per week the candidate can work
D) If the candidate has a history of arrests
E) Whether the candidate is a parent
questions.answer:
C)
Inquiring about work availability and hours per week is legally permissible and relevant to job requirements. Employment law requires compliance with federal and state regulations regarding hiring practices. A is incorrect because asking about physical disabilities violates the Americans with Disabilities Act unless directly related to essential job functions. B is incorrect because age-related questions violate age discrimination laws. D is incorrect because asking about arrest history (as opposed to convictions) is generally prohibited and may violate fair hiring practices. E is incorrect because questions about family status, including having children, violate equal employment opportunity laws.

questions.question:
A 6-month-old child presents with a growing vascular skin lesion that partially blocks vision. Which histologic marker would most definitively establish the diagnosis of infantile hemangioma?
A) Fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR-3)
B) Glucose transporter 1 (GLUT-1)
C) Transforming growth factor beta (TGF-B)
D) Tumor necrosis factor 1 (TNF-1)
E) Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)
questions.answer:
B)
GLUT-1 serves as the most specific and reliable histologic marker for diagnosing infantile hemangioma, making it the gold standard for pathological confirmation. A is incorrect because FGFR-3 is associated with various genetic syndromes like achondroplasia and Muenke syndrome, not hemangiomas. C is incorrect because while TGF-B may be present in hemangiomas, it lacks the specificity of GLUT-1 for definitive diagnosis. D is incorrect because TNF-1 staining is not a standard diagnostic tool for hemangioma identification. E is incorrect because although VEGF may be found in hemangiomas, it is not as diagnostically specific as GLUT-1.

questions.question:
A 6-year-old child with surgically corrected unilateral complete cleft lip and palate attends a routine cleft team evaluation. The parents are counseled about beginning palatal expansion. What factor should primarily determine when to start palatal expansion?
A) Width of the alveolar cleft
B) Eruption of the canine teeth
C) Current bite relationship
D) Child's chronological age
E) Degree of alveolar bone collapse
questions.answer:
B)
The optimal timing for alveolar bone grafting occurs during mixed dentition, specifically after incisor eruption but before canine emergence, as this maximizes surgical success. Dental development varies among children, making tooth eruption more reliable than chronological age for timing. A is incorrect because cleft width determines the volume of bone graft needed, not the surgical timing. C is incorrect because occlusal relationships will be addressed later through orthodontics or orthognathic surgery after skeletal maturity. D is incorrect because chronological age is less reliable than dental development stages for determining optimal surgical timing. E is incorrect because the severity of collapse affects the duration of expansion treatment, not the timing of initiation.

questions.question:
Which peripheral nerve tumor type shows the strongest association with von Recklinghausen disease?
A) Astrocytoma
B) Glioblastoma
C) Neurilemoma
D) Neurofibroma
E) Schwannoma
questions.answer:
D)
Neurofibromas are the characteristic peripheral nerve tumors of von Recklinghausen disease (neurofibromatosis type 1), arising from Schwann cells, perineural cells, and fibroblasts. They present as either plexiform (deep, potentially malignant) or dermal (superficial, benign) variants. A is incorrect because astrocytomas are central nervous system tumors, though optic gliomas can occur in NF1. B is incorrect because glioblastomas are central nervous system malignancies not typically associated with NF1. C is incorrect because neurilemoma is another term for schwannoma, which is more associated with NF2 than NF1. E is incorrect because schwannomas, while possible in NF1, are more characteristically associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

questions.question:
A 12-month-old boy presents for evaluation of a soft, fixed lateral brow mass that has been enlarging since it was first noted at 2 months of age. The parents report that the mass does not change in size during crying or activity, nor did it change in size during recurrent pink eye infections. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?


A) Branchial cleft cyst
B) Dermoid cyst
C) Hemangioma
D) Lacrimal gland
E) Lymphatic malformation
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option B.


Dermoid cyst is the correct answer and the most common cause of a lateral brow mass in an infant. If it were a hemangioma, its size would change during crying or any activity that increases blood flow. Lacrimal gland ptosis is unlikely in a child but can be seen in the adult population, and is inconsistent with a mass at the lateral brow above the orbital rim. The mass is not in the distribution of any of the different types of branchial cleft cysts. Lymphatic malformations typically change in size during infections.


ReferencesAl-Muhaylib A, Alkatan HM, Al-Faky YH, Alsuhaibani AH. Periorbital lesions misdiagnosed as dermoid cysts. J AAPOS. 2017;21(6):509-511.Rezaei E, Shams Hojjati Y. Misdiagnosed extranasal mass: report of a 2-year old child with maltreated rare nasal neuroglial heterotopia. World J Plast Surg. 2019;8(1):122-124.Van Wyhe RD, Chamata ES, Hollier LH. Midline craniofacial masses in children. Semin Plast Surg. 2016;30(4):176-180.Vincent J, Baker P, Grischkan J, Fernandez Faith E. Subcutaneous midline nasal mass in an infant due to an intramuscular lipoma. Pediatr Dermatol. 2017;34(3):e135-e136.

questions.question:
A 48-year-old male presents with discomfort 4 days following elective right hand surgery. The operation involved administering 1% lidocaine with 1:100,000 epinephrine into the palmar region. Clinical examination reveals cool, blanched fingers with delayed capillary refill time. What is the most suitable treatment approach?
A) Hospital admission with hourly wound monitoring for necrotic changes
B) Local phentolamine injection
C) Topical nitroglycerin application with warm water soaking
D) Topical terbutaline injection
E) No additional treatment required
questions.answer:
B)
Phentolamine injection is the most appropriate treatment because it is an alpha-adrenergic antagonist that effectively reverses epinephrine-induced vasoconstriction by blocking alpha-adrenergic receptors.
