This patient shows signs of digital ischemia from epinephrine's vasoconstrictive effects, and phentolamine (1-2 mg in 1-5 mL saline) injected into the epinephrine site typically reverses vasoconstriction within one hour. A is incorrect because observation alone risks tissue necrosis when active treatment is available. C is incorrect because topical nitroglycerin with warm water has not proven effective for reversing alpha-adrenergic vasoconstriction. D is incorrect because terbutaline is less reliable than phentolamine and should only be considered when phentolamine is unavailable. E is incorrect because untreated prolonged ischemia can lead to digital necrosis and amputation.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old male seeks consultation regarding a prior amputation of his dominant thumb. His medical history includes factor V Leiden mutation. He explicitly refuses any microsurgical flap reconstruction. Radiographic imaging demonstrates amputation at the metacarpal base. Which reconstruction technique would provide the optimal aesthetic and functional result for this patient?
A) Metacarpal lengthening
B) Osteoplastic reconstruction using iliac bone graft with radial forearm flap coverage
C) Index finger pollicization
D) Silicone prosthetic device
E) Web space deepening using Z-plasty technique
questions.answer:
C)
Index finger pollicization is the most appropriate reconstruction because it provides the best combination of function and aesthetics for thumb loss at the metacarpal base level. The thumb contributes approximately 40% of hand function, requiring mobility, opposition, sensation, stability, strength, and appropriate appearance. Pollicization creates a functional thumb with these essential characteristics. A is incorrect because metacarpal distraction produces an oversized, aesthetically poor thumb without a nail. B is incorrect because osteoplastic reconstruction creates a stable but immobile post with poor sensation and cosmetic appearance. D is incorrect because silicone prostheses offer good cosmetics but no functional capability. E is incorrect because web space deepening alone cannot provide adequate length for reconstruction at the metacarpal base level.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old patient undergoes a total rhinectomy and partial septectomy for squamous cell carcinoma followed by postoperative radiation therapy. A photograph is shown. He has tried a nasal prosthesis, but he is unhappy with it and wishes to undergo autologous surgical reconstruction. A paramedian forehead flap with rib cartilage grafts are planned for the external nasal skin reconstruction and support, respectively. Which of the following is best suited to replace the nasal lining?


A) Folded forehead flap
B) Nasolabial flap
C) Radial forearm fasciocutaneous free flap
D) Septal hinge flap
E) Split-thickness skin graft
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option C.


For restoration following total rhinectomy, all three layers of the external nose must be addressed: lining, support, and cover. Of these options, the radial forearm fasciocutaneous free flap is the preferred method because it provides an ample amount of thin, pliable skin that resists contracture that could lead to nasal obstruction, particularly around the nostrils. The septal hinge flap, based on the anterior ethmoid artery, is not an option because of the loss of the septum. The nasolabial flap tends to be too thick and adds facial scars. A folded forehead flap involves using the forehead flap for both external and internal coverage; this is reasonable for full-thickness reconstruction along the nostril rim, but the flap is stiff and usually not large enough (without removal of a very large quantity of forehead and scalp) to line a defect of this size. Split- and full-thickness skin grafts can be applied as nasal lining to the underside of the forehead flap and then cartilage grafts can be inserted secondarily between the frontalis and external skin; however, they are subject to contracture, which can diminish the ultimate result of nasal reconstruction.


ReferencesMenick FJ. Nasal reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2010;125(4):138e-150e.Menick FJ. Principles and planning in nasal and facial reconstruction: making a normal face. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2016(6);137:1033e-1047e.Salibian AH, Menick FJ, Talley J. Microvascular reconstruction of the nose with the radial forearm flap: a 17-year experience in 47 patients. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2019;144(1):199-210.

questions.question:
Which bone substitute material possesses both osteoconductive and osseointegrative properties?
A) Hydroxyapatite
B) Polymethylmethacrylate
C) Porous polyethylene
D) Silicone
E) Titanium
questions.answer:
A)
Hydroxyapatite is correct because it demonstrates both osteoconduction (ability to guide bone growth along its surface) and osseointegration (direct chemical bonding to bone without fibrous tissue interface). As the primary mineral component comprising 60% of human bone, hydroxyapatite is biocompatible and forms the foundation for many bone substitutes used clinically for over 25 years. B is incorrect because polymethylmethacrylate generates harmful exothermic reactions that damage surrounding tissues and lacks these biological properties. C is incorrect because porous polyethylene aids tissue ingrowth but does not truly osseointegrate or osteoconduct without special coatings. D is incorrect because silicone materials neither osseointegrate nor osteoconduct. E is incorrect because titanium osseointegrates well but lacks osteoconductive properties.

questions.question:
A patient who has undergone bariatric surgery with excessive medial arm skin is planned for posteromedial scar-approach brachioplasty. What represents the primary benefit of this brachioplasty technique compared to alternative approaches?
A) Concealed placement of the surgical scar
B) Increased mechanical tension on the surgical incision and resulting scar
C) Elevated risk for surgical scar expansion and hypertrophic formation
D) Extended surgical scar dimension
questions.answer:
A)
Concealed scar placement is the primary advantage because the posteromedial approach positions the incision in a less visible location on the arm, improving cosmetic outcomes. This technique also reduces tension on the surgical closure, leading to superior scar quality and decreased visibility compared to other brachioplasty approaches. The procedure involves longitudinal excision of excess skin and fat from axilla to elbow in post-bariatric patients with arm laxity. B is incorrect because this approach actually minimizes rather than increases mechanical stress on the incision. C is incorrect because reduced tension leads to better scarring with lower risk of widening and hypertrophy. D is incorrect because scar length is not an advantage but rather a necessary aspect of the procedure to address the tissue excess.

questions.question:
A 65-year-old male is evaluated for a 3 x 4-cm wound exposing tendon over the distal anterior tibia following a lateral malleolar fracture that was successfully managed with cast treatment. The wound has received local care for several weeks. Physical examination demonstrates a clean wound with minimal fibrinous material. Periosteum and peritenon remain intact. Pulses are not palpable, but pencil Doppler detects signals in both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibialis arteries. What diagnostic study should be performed next?
A) Ankle brachial index
B) CT angiography
C) MRA
D) MRI
E) Percutaneous angiography
questions.answer:
A)
Ankle brachial index is the most appropriate initial study because it provides essential quantitative assessment of lower extremity perfusion necessary for wound healing. This patient shows signs of asymptomatic peripheral vascular disease, and ABI measurement effectively stratifies disease severity: ABI ≤0.9 indicates peripheral artery disease, 0.5-0.79 suggests wound healing complications, and <0.5 indicates arterial insufficiency with rest pain. This information directly guides treatment decisions for the pressure ulcer from cast immobilization. B is incorrect because CT angiography provides anatomical detail but not functional perfusion assessment. C is incorrect because MRA shows vascular anatomy but doesn't quantify perfusion adequacy for healing. D is incorrect because MRI evaluates soft tissue but not vascular sufficiency. E is incorrect because percutaneous angiography is invasive and provides anatomical rather than functional perfusion data needed for wound healing assessment.

questions.question:
What represents the optimal tooth visibility when the lips are at rest?
A) 2 mm of mandibular incisor visibility
B) 4 mm of mandibular incisor visibility
C) 2 mm of maxillary incisor visibility
D) 4 mm of maxillary incisor visibility
E) Complete absence of tooth visibility
questions.answer:
C)

The optimal tooth visibility with lips at rest is 2 mm of maxillary incisor display. For women, up to 4 mm may be considered acceptable. Excessive upper tooth display creates an unaesthetic gummy smile appearance, which may result from maxillary vertical excess and typically requires orthognathic surgery with maxillary impaction for correction. With aging, upper lip lengthening reduces maxillary tooth display while gravitational effects on the lower lip may increase mandibular tooth visibility. A) is incorrect because mandibular incisors should not be visible at rest. B) is incorrect because 4 mm of lower tooth show is excessive and abnormal. D) is incorrect because 4 mm of upper tooth show, while acceptable in some women, exceeds the ideal amount. E) is incorrect because some upper tooth show (2 mm) is desirable for optimal aesthetics.

questions.question:
A healthy 35-year-old male presents to the emergency department 5 hours following traumatic amputation of his thumb and index finger. Both digits are non-salvageable. Examination reveals thumb amputation occurring 1 cm proximal to the metacarpophalangeal joint, with replantation not feasible. Which reconstructive approach would best maintain grip strength?
A) Thumb metacarpal distraction osteogenesis
B) Index finger pollicization
C) Microvascular toe-to-hand transfer
D) Digital advancement (Moberg) flap application
E) Ring finger neurovascular island flap transfer
questions.answer:
C)

Microvascular toe-to-hand transfer provides optimal strength and function following thumb amputation when replantation is impossible. Either the great toe or second toe can be used, with great toe transfer offering better aesthetics but greater foot morbidity, while second toe transfer results in a smaller thumb with minimal foot deficit. This technique provides the best functional outcome for grip strength preservation. A) is incorrect because distraction osteogenesis is only useful for more distal amputations at the proximal phalanx level or beyond, and cannot provide sufficient length for power grip at this proximal level. B) is incorrect because index finger pollicization would result in weaker grip strength compared to toe transfer. D) is incorrect because Moberg flaps are only suitable for distal phalanx coverage and cannot provide bony reconstruction needed at this proximal amputation level. E) is incorrect because neurovascular island flaps provide sensation restoration but no bony reconstruction.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old male presents with nasal breathing difficulties. Examination reveals a C-shaped septal deformity without dorsal deviation, negative Cottle maneuver, and intact external nasal valves. What surgical approach is most appropriate?
A) Alar batten graft placement
B) Columellar strut graft insertion
C) Septoplasty procedure
D) Spreader graft placement
E) Submucous septal resection
questions.answer:
E)

Submucous septal resection is most appropriate for this patient's caudal septal deviation with C-shaped deformity causing nasal obstruction. Since internal nasal valve function is normal (negative Cottle maneuver) and external nasal valves are competent, the septal deviation is the primary cause of obstruction. Resection of the deviated septum while preserving a 9-10 mm L-strut will improve airflow and relieve symptoms. A) is incorrect because alar batten grafts address external nasal valve incompetence, which this patient does not have. B) is incorrect because columellar struts provide nasal tip support and projection but do not address septal deviation causing obstruction. C) is incorrect because septoplasty (scoring cartilage) alone is insufficient to correct a significant C-shaped deformity. D) is incorrect because spreader grafts address internal nasal valve collapse and dorsal septal deviation, neither of which are present in this patient.

questions.question:
A 72-year-old right-handed male presents with clicking, locking, and pain at the distal palmar crease of his right ring finger. He received a 40 mg triamcinolone injection 4 weeks ago with partial symptom improvement. What is the minimum waiting period after corticosteroid injection before A1 pulley release to reduce surgical site complication risk?
A) 1 week post-injection
B) 4 weeks post-injection
C) 8 weeks post-injection
D) 12 weeks post-injection
E) No increased complication risk exists
questions.answer:
D)

The risk of surgical site complications is minimized at approximately 80 days (~12 weeks) following corticosteroid injection. Research analyzing 999 patients who received corticosteroid injections for trigger finger and subsequently underwent surgery demonstrated that patients without infections had significantly longer intervals between injection and surgery (mean 260 days vs 79 days). Given this patient's demographics (elderly male with single digit involvement), corticosteroid injection success rates are low (35%), making early surgical intervention reasonable after the appropriate waiting period. A) is incorrect because 1 week is insufficient time for complication risk reduction. B) is incorrect because 4 weeks, while the current timeframe, does not provide adequate risk mitigation. C) is incorrect because 8 weeks is still shorter than the evidence-based 12-week recommendation. E) is incorrect because multiple studies demonstrate increased surgical site occurrence risk following recent corticosteroid injection.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old female seeks consultation for bilateral ear keloids that formed following ear piercing 5 years prior. She has no history of previous surgical treatment. What is the expected recurrence rate following surgical excision combined with corticosteroid injection?
A) 5%
B) 15%
C) 35%
D) 50%
E) 75%
questions.answer:
B)

The recurrence rate after surgical excision combined with intralesional corticosteroids is 15.4% based on meta-analysis data. Earlobe keloids affect approximately 2.5% of the population following piercing. Various adjuvant therapies including corticosteroids, radiation, interferon, 5-fluorouracil, silicone, and pressure devices help reduce recurrence after excision. While radiation therapy shows slightly lower recurrence (14%), it carries higher costs and significant complications including reported carcinogenesis cases. The primary disadvantage of corticosteroid therapy is injection pain, with injections performed preoperatively, intraoperatively, or postoperatively depending on the protocol. A) is incorrect because 5% significantly underestimates the actual recurrence rate. C) is incorrect because 35% overestimates the recurrence rate with proper adjuvant steroid therapy. D) is incorrect because 50% represents recurrence rates without adequate adjuvant treatment. E) is incorrect because 75% vastly overestimates recurrence rates and would represent treatment failure.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old male presents to the emergency room with pain and swelling in his left lower leg after being trapped under a heavy granite boulder for 2 hours. Physical examination reveals a swollen, tight, and red left leg with a detectable pulse. Radiographic imaging shows no fractures. The patient experiences severe pain that remains unresponsive to escalating narcotic medications. Passive movement of the ankle and toes causes significant pain. What is the most appropriate next management step?
A) Arteriography
B) Elastic bandage wrapping
C) Computed tomography
D) Duplex ultrasound examination
E) Surgical fasciotomy
questions.answer:
E)
Surgical fasciotomy is the most appropriate next step. This patient demonstrates classic signs of compartment syndrome following a significant crush injury to the lower leg. Key indicators of compartment syndrome include pain with passive stretching, elevated compartment pressure on examination, sensory changes, motor weakness, pallor, and absence of pulses. Prompt recognition and intervention are crucial to prevent irreversible damage. Increased pressure within muscle compartments impairs blood circulation and nutrient exchange at the cellular level. Fasciotomy is warranted when compartment pressure surpasses 30 mm Hg, or when the gradient between compartment pressure and diastolic blood pressure falls below 30 mm Hg. Without treatment, muscle ischemia and necrosis occur, leading to permanent impairment. A) Arteriography is incorrect because it evaluates vascular patency and blood flow, but passive stretch pain is not characteristic of arterial insufficiency. B) Elastic bandage wrapping is incorrect because compression therapy is used for venous stasis and lymphedema, not acute traumatic compartment syndrome. C) Computed tomography is incorrect because it would provide detailed imaging but is unnecessary in this clinical scenario and would delay critical treatment. D) Duplex ultrasound examination is incorrect because it is used to detect deep vein thrombosis, which typically occurs postoperatively or after prolonged immobilization, not in acute crush injuries.

questions.question:
An 18-year-old football athlete presents to the clinic reporting inability to bend his ring finger following a tackle 3 hours earlier. Physical examination demonstrates the distal joint held in neutral position with loss of active flexion capability. What is the most probable injury mechanism?
A) Axial loading compression force
B) Forced extension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint during maximum flexion attempt
C) Forced extension of the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint with maximum abduction effort
D) Forced crush-type pilon injury
E) Forced extension of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint during maximum extension attempt
questions.answer:
B)
Forced extension of the DIP joint during maximum flexion attempt is the correct mechanism. This describes a jersey finger injury, which occurs when an athlete grasps an opponent's jersey. The DIP joint is flexed when the tackle is broken, causing forced extension. Flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) avulsion happens in 75% of cases involving the ring finger. Type I involves tendon retraction into the palm requiring urgent repair within 7-10 days. Type II shows retraction to the PIP joint level, held by the long vinculum, allowing delayed repair for 6-12 weeks. Type III involves a large bone fragment preventing tendon entry through the A4 pulley and can be repaired at any time. The FDP insertion tears away from the distal phalanx with or without bone fragments. A) Axial loading compression is incorrect because it does not create the specific mechanism needed for FDP avulsion. C) MCP joint extension with abduction is incorrect because this mechanism affects different structures and does not cause FDP injury. D) Crush-type pilon injury is incorrect because it involves different force vectors that do not result in FDP avulsion. E) PIP joint extension during extension attempt is incorrect because this mechanism does not produce the necessary forces for FDP tendon rupture.

questions.question:
What effect is linked to the application of compression garments in treating burn scars?
A) Diminished scar tensile strength
B) Enhanced production of tissue-degrading enzymes
C) Formation of larger, less compact collagen bundles
D) Decreased transformation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts
questions.answer:
D)
Decreased transformation of fibroblasts into myofibroblasts is correct. Significant differences in scar contracture were observed between scars treated with compression garments versus untreated control burns. Compression garments apply forces both perpendicular and parallel to the scar surface, opposing contracture direction. The proposed mechanism involves wound tension acting on integrins through stretching, leading to focal adhesion kinase phosphorylation and increased smooth muscle actin and collagen production. When compression is applied perpendicular to wound tension, scarring is minimized. This suggests mechanical forces help reduce fibroblast differentiation to myofibroblasts, decreasing scar contracture and collagen deposition. A) Diminished scar tensile strength is incorrect because pressure garment therapy actually improved scar strength with a 34% increase in ultimate tensile strength compared to controls. B) Enhanced production of tissue-degrading enzymes is incorrect because this describes the mechanism of corticosteroids, not pressure garments. C) Formation of larger, less compact collagen bundles is incorrect because pressure garment therapy actually produces smaller, more densely packed collagen fibers.

questions.question:
A 68-year-old woman presents with recurring looseness of the neck and lower face 10 years after an uneventful facelift procedure. She is a non-smoker. What is most probable?
A) Concurrent medical conditions are now more frequently encountered
B) Greater skin removal will usually occur in the revision facelift compared to the initial procedure
C) Superficial musculoaponeurotic system (SMAS) layer scarring now prevents re-elevation of a SMAS flap
D) The skin and SMAS layer thickness would be similar to those observed during the initial facelift
E) Skin flap blood supply compromise is now more probable
questions.answer:
A)
Concurrent medical conditions are now more frequently encountered is correct. Secondary facelift patients are typically older than primary facelift patients and have been shown to have more coexisting medical diseases. Therefore, a more comprehensive preoperative medical assessment is advisable for these patients. One study found that depression requiring selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor treatment was the most common coexisting condition in one-quarter of secondary facelift patients studied. Hypertension was the second most frequent medical condition. B) Greater skin removal is incorrect because in secondary facelifts, less skin is typically removed, though more careful tailoring and positioning of the skin is often required. C) SMAS layer scarring preventing re-elevation is incorrect because sub-SMAS scarring does not preclude careful and safe re-elevation of a SMAS flap. D) Similar skin and SMAS thickness is incorrect because these layers are typically thinner than in a primary procedure, making surgical elevation of SMAS flaps more challenging. E) Increased skin flap blood supply compromise is incorrect because vascular compromise is actually less likely in secondary cases due to the delay phenomenon from the primary procedure.

questions.question:
A 16-year-old female needs skin grafting to her dorsal forearm following injuries from a motorcycle crash. Which wound coverage method will result in the MINIMAL secondary contracture?
A) Full-thickness skin graft, 1:4 mesh pattern
B) Full-thickness skin graft, unmeshed
C) Natural wound healing without grafting
D) Split-thickness skin graft, unmeshed, 0.010-inch thickness
E) Split-thickness skin graft, unmeshed, 0.014-inch thickness
questions.answer:
B)
Full-thickness skin graft, unmeshed is correct. Secondary wound contracture depends on multiple factors. Research demonstrates that thicker grafts produce less scar depth and secondary contracture, while thinner grafts contract more significantly. Quantitatively, thick split-thickness skin grafts (0.03 inch, 760 mm) achieve similar final wound dimensions as full-thickness skin grafts. Greater mesh ratios cause increased secondary contracture. Myofibroblast differentiation is considered a primary driver of contracture. Full-thickness skin graft application appears to accelerate their lifecycle compared to wounds treated with split-thickness grafts. In contrast, thin grafts demonstrate greater alpha-smooth muscle actin expression that persists longer after grafting. Additional mechanisms include reduced expression of pro-inflammatory genes one week after full-thickness grafting, such as insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) and transforming growth factor beta-1 (TGFB1), compared to wounds treated with thin split-thickness grafts. A) Meshed full-thickness graft is incorrect because meshing increases secondary contracture compared to unmeshed grafts. C) Natural wound healing is incorrect because healing by secondary intention produces greater contracture than graft coverage. D) and E) Split-thickness grafts are incorrect because thinner grafts, regardless of exact thickness, contract more than full-thickness grafts.

questions.question:
A 67-year-old male presents to the clinic with histologically confirmed Merkel cell carcinoma located on his forehead. Beyond performing a wide local excision, what represents the most appropriate additional treatment?
A) Interferon therapy
B) Local 5-fluorouracil injections
C) Preoperative chemotherapy
D) Radiotherapy
questions.answer:
D)
Radiotherapy is the optimal adjuvant treatment for Merkel cell carcinoma due to its radiosensitive nature and should be considered for all patients with this diagnosis. A is incorrect because interferon has not demonstrated efficacy in treating Merkel cell carcinoma. B is incorrect because 5-fluorouracil injections have never been proven effective for this malignancy. C is incorrect because neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not the standard approach for localized Merkel cell carcinoma, where surgery followed by radiation is preferred.

questions.question:
A 43-year-old female seeks consultation for tummy tuck surgery. She expresses worry about potential numbness of her abdominal skin following the procedure. Following a standard abdominoplasty, which anatomical region is most prone to experiencing the most significant sensory loss?
A) Upper abdomen
B) Lower abdomen below the umbilicus
C) Side abdominal areas
D) Pubic mound
E) Area below the breastbone
questions.answer:
B)
The infraumbilical (lower abdominal) region experiences the greatest sensory loss because the anterior cutaneous nerves are severed during flap elevation, making this the most distant area from remaining intact lateral nerve branches. A is incorrect because the epigastric region maintains better innervation from upper intercostal nerves. C is incorrect because lateral abdominal areas retain sensation from lateral cutaneous nerve branches. D is incorrect because the mons pubis lies below the surgical incision and maintains its innervation. E is incorrect because the subxiphoid area is typically not affected by the undermining performed in abdominoplasty.

questions.question:
A 19-year-old woman with a medical history significant for Poland syndrome and a BMI of 19 kg/m² undergoes first-stage breast reconstruction with a tissue expander. Forty days after implantation, she presents with expander extrusion through a periareolar wound dehiscence, accompanied by surrounding erythema and purulent drainage. Attempts at implant salvage are made. The presence of which of the following factors is most likely to lead to decreased salvage rates?
A) BMI of 19 kg/m²
B) Culture-positive Staphylococcus sp.
C) Hemoglobin A1c of 6.5%
D) Prepectoral placement of the device
E) Use of acellular dermal matrix
questions.answer:
B)
The correct answer is B. This patient has a threatened expander with both exposure (periareolar extrusion) and clinical infection. Device salvage can succeed if treated promptly with surgery and antimicrobials, but culture-positive Staphylococcus (S. aureus or S. epidermidis) is consistently associated with lower salvage rates. Other factors linked to salvage failure include obesity, poorly controlled diabetes, smoking, prior radiation, postoperative seroma, and early biofilm contamination. A BMI of 19 kg/m² and an HbA1c of 6.5% do not represent those high-risk metabolic conditions. A is incorrect because a BMI of 19 kg/m² is low-normal, not obese; obesity, not a low BMI, decreases salvage rates. C is incorrect because an HbA1c of 6.5% does not indicate poorly controlled diabetes. D is incorrect because prepectoral and subpectoral expander placement have comparable complication profiles and prepectoral position is not associated with lower salvage. E is incorrect because acellular dermal matrix has not been shown to increase failure of attempted device salvage.

References:
Prince MD, Suber JS, Aya-Ay ML, et al. Prosthesis salvage in breast reconstruction patients with periprosthetic infection and exposure. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2012;129(1):42-48.
Spear SL, Howard MA, Boehmler JH, et al. The infected or exposed breast implant: management and treatment strategies. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2004;113(6):1634-1644.
Washer LL, Gutowski K. Breast implant infections. Infect Dis Clin North Am. 2012;26(1):111-125.
Sinha I, Pusic AL, Wilkins EG, et al. Late surgical-site infection in immediate implant-based breast reconstruction. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2017;139(1):20-28.
Bettinger LN, Waters LM, Reese SW, et al. Comparative study of prepectoral and subpectoral expander-based breast reconstruction and Clavien IIIb score outcomes. Plast Reconstr Surg Glob Open. 2017;5(7):e1433.

questions.question:
Which skin replacement product is composed of cultured human keratinocytes and fibroblasts derived from neonatal foreskin tissue?
A) AlloDerm
B) Apligraf
C) Biobrane
D) Integra
E) Surgisis
questions.answer:
B)
Apligraf is the correct answer as it is a living, bilayered skin substitute made from cultured neonatal foreskin-derived human keratinocytes and fibroblasts grown on a bovine collagen matrix. A is incorrect because AlloDerm is acellular cadaveric dermis without living cells. C is incorrect because Biobrane contains porcine collagen in a synthetic membrane, not human cells. D is incorrect because Integra is a temporary scaffold made of bovine collagen and shark glycosaminoglycans without living cells. E is incorrect because Surgisis is derived from porcine intestinal tissue, not human cells.

questions.question:
Which cranial nerve supplies parasympathetic control to the parotid salivary gland?
A) V
B) VII
C) VIII
D) IX
E) X
questions.answer:
D)
Cranial nerve IX (glossopharyngeal) provides parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland and also carries taste sensation from the posterior third of the tongue. A is incorrect because cranial nerve V is purely sensory and provides facial sensation, not parasympathetic control. B is incorrect because cranial nerve VII provides parasympathetic innervation to the submandibular and sublingual glands, not the parotid. C is incorrect because cranial nerve VIII is responsible for hearing and balance, not salivary gland function. E is incorrect because cranial nerve X primarily innervates the external ear canal and does not control parotid gland secretion.

questions.question:
A 71-year-old male with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is brought to the emergency department with facial injuries and fractures from a fall. He appears increasingly disoriented upon arrival, and his spouse reports substantial bleeding occurred after the incident. Based on the laboratory findings, what is this patient's underlying metabolic disturbance?
A) Metabolic acidosis secondary to COPD worsening
B) Metabolic acidosis secondary to blood loss dilution
C) Metabolic alkalosis secondary to COPD worsening
D) Metabolic alkalosis secondary to blood loss dilution
questions.answer:
A)
The patient has a respiratory acidosis (low pH with elevated CO2) due to acute exacerbation of his underlying COPD, which causes CO2 retention and respiratory failure. The elevated bicarbonate represents metabolic compensation for the chronic respiratory acidosis. B is incorrect because hemodilution from bleeding does not cause metabolic acidosis with this pattern of elevated CO2. C is incorrect because the pH is acidic, not alkalotic, ruling out metabolic alkalosis. D is incorrect because both the pH is acidic rather than alkalotic, and hemodilution would not cause this specific acid-base pattern with markedly elevated CO2.

questions.question:
A 42-year-old male arrives with an open tibial fracture from a car accident that occurred 4 hours prior. Clinical examination reveals a 3-cm laceration at the fracture location, absence of foreign material or contamination in the wound, and no visible bone exposure. Radiographic imaging demonstrates a simple transverse fracture of both tibia and fibula without fragmentation. What is the most appropriate initial antibiotic prophylaxis?
A) First generation cephalosporin
B) First generation cephalosporin, aminoglycoside, and penicillin
C) First generation cephalosporin and aminoglycoside
D) Third generation cephalosporin
E) Third generation cephalosporin, aminoglycoside, and penicillin
questions.answer:
A)
The correct choice is A. Based on the Gustillo-Anderson classification, this represents a Grade II open fracture, which requires only first-generation cephalosporin coverage for adequate prophylaxis against typical wound pathogens. B is incorrect because the combination of three antibiotics is excessive for a Grade II fracture and is reserved for heavily contaminated Grade III injuries. C is incorrect because aminoglycoside addition is not necessary for Grade II fractures without significant contamination. D is incorrect because third-generation cephalosporins alone do not provide optimal gram-positive coverage needed for open fractures. E is incorrect because this triple antibiotic regimen is overly aggressive for a Grade II fracture and typically reserved for Grade III injuries with severe contamination or vascular compromise.

questions.question:
A 23-year-old male arrives at the emergency room comatose following a frontal collision motor vehicle accident. Clinical assessment reveals left-sided periorbital ecchymosis. Upon illuminating the left eye with a penlight, no pupillary response occurs, but when the light is directed to the right eye, both pupils contract. When the light is moved back to the left eye, the right pupil contracts while the left pupil enlarges. What best accounts for this clinical presentation?
A) Extraocular muscle entrapment
B) Hyphema
C) Inadequate brain perfusion
D) Optic nerve injury
E) Tentorial herniation
questions.answer:
D)
The correct answer is D. This describes a Marcus Gunn pupil (relative afferent pupillary defect), which occurs when there is damage to the optic nerve or retina, disrupting the normal afferent pathway for the pupillary light reflex. The paradoxical dilation when light swings back to the affected eye is pathognomonic for this condition. A is incorrect because extraocular muscle entrapment affects eye movement but does not interfere with pupillary light reflexes, as the muscles controlling pupil size are separate from those controlling eye movement. B is incorrect because blood in the anterior chamber (hyphema) does not cause abnormal pupillary reflexes or create a Marcus Gunn pupil. C is incorrect because inadequate cerebral perfusion typically causes bilateral, symmetrical pupillary abnormalities (dilated and fixed or sluggish), not the asymmetric response seen here. E is incorrect because tentorial herniation with oculomotor nerve compression causes a fixed, dilated pupil on the affected side with associated eye movement abnormalities, not the swinging flashlight test findings described.

questions.question:
A 30-year-old man sustains a laceration to the radial nerve at the mid-humerus level. Physical examination shows wristdrop. A photograph is shown. Which of the following transfers is most appropriate to restore wrist extension in this patient?


A ) Axillary to radial nerve transfer
B ) Biceps to triceps muscle transfer
C ) Brachioradialis to extensor carpi ulnaris tendon transfer
D ) Phrenic nerve to posterior cord transfer
E ) Pronator teres to extensor carpi radialis tendon transfer
questions.answer:
The correct response is Option E.


Pronator teres to extensor carpi radialis brevis (ECRB) transfer is well described for restoration of wrist extension in isolated radial nerve injury or palsy. The pronator teres is harvested from its insertion on the radius along with an extension of radius periosteum (necessary to have sufficient length for the transfer) and is woven either end-to-end into the ECRB or end-to-side into the ECRB if the surgeon feels the ECRB may recover some function. Some authors also advocate weaving a portion of tendon graft harvested from the extensor carpi radialis longus (ECRL) to increase the strength of the repair. The image shown demonstrates the transfer. The pronator teres is raised with an extension of radius periosteum and woven into the ECRB tendon. Tendon grafting from ECRL reinforces the repair.






Axillary-radial nerve coaptation is performed in the proximal upper arm and uses the radial nerve as a donor to provide axons to the axillary nerve and deltoid muscle. Transfer of median nerve axons to the nerve to the ECRB may be used to provide wrist extension. Biceps to triceps transfer has been described to restore a component of radial nerve dysfunction in tetraplegia, but this transfer would provide elbow extension, not wrist extension. The brachioradialis muscle is innervated by the radial nerve. If the nerve were lacerated at the mid-humerus level, the brachioradialis would not be functional. The phrenic nerve could provide donor axons to the posterior cord, which would eventually become the radial nerve; however, axons transferred at this level would face the problem of interruption at the mid-humerus level within the radial nerve.


References
1. Colbert SH, Mackinnon SE. Nerve transfers for brachial plexus reconstruction. Hand Clin. 2008 Nov;24(4):341-361, v.
2. Brown JM, Mackinnon SE. Nerve transfers in the forearm and hand. Hand Clin. 2008 Nov;24(4):319-340, v. 
3. Leclercq C, Hentz VR, Kozin SH, et al. Reconstruction of elbow extension. Hand Clin. 2008 May;24(2):185-201, vi. 
4. Ropars M, Dreano T, Siret P, et al. Long-term results of tendon transfers in radial and posterior interosseous nerve paralysis. J Hand Surg [Br]. 2006 Oct;31(5):502-506. Epub 2006 Aug 22.
